I usually structure my reviews properly, with a solid introduction and laid out in a pretty well written fashion. Today, I'm not going to bother with that, since honestly there's not much to say about BMC Studio other than they're comprised of a few grade school age French Canadian guys. Kimulator: Fight For Your Destiny is undoubtedly their end-of-year school project, or perhaps I'm misjudging their ages and it's their entry level Year One college project. Either way, even having gone in to this "game" with an open mind ready for comedy, laughs, and overall silliness, this is a terrible title.
What sold me on this game primarily was the thought of supporting some French Canadians. I live in Canada myself, and I enjoy regular trips to Montreal for metal concerts. I have friends in Montreal, it's a beautiful city. And, tabarnak, I love to curse in Canadian French because it's all blasphemies against the church. For $1.33 CAD I figured I could help an indie team from my country buy a good ol' Tim Horton's coffee, at least. To be honest, these reasons are the only ones that I'm not hitting the refund button.
Kimulator: Fight For Your Destiny has a simple plot; kill the leader of North Korea. You're accompanied by Jesus, câlisse baptême, who helps guide you on your quest. Of the main game, 98% of it is all live action cutscenes while there are only two small first-person shooter sections where you don't have to kill anyone at all. The enemy AI is terrible, and unless you get close to them, they don't bother to fire at you. The live action sequences primarily consist of one lanky guy in a red Canada sweater. To be very honest, I didn't laugh once at any of this even though I was really hoping for a game that would make me at least chuckle. It's akin to watching a very embarrassing grade school project, which in all probability is what this is; just a bunch of guys screwing around, not even caring if what they're doing turns out well or not.
Surprisingly, the optimization of this title is decent enough. However, in my experience most of the textures loaded as pure black; trees, the building, enemies, guns. The game for me looked nothing like it did in the screenshots on the store page, at least when it came to actual game play. You do have a HUD, which features how many health points and ammo that you have left. After going a while without getting hit, your health will also replenish. Aside from the story mode, there's also a practice mode, and some bonus missions to tackle... which I didn't. I also didn't bother with Dreamblaster which is the "bonus game".
I think the thing that ticked me off the most about Kimulator: Fight For Your Destiny was the end game plea for "positive ratings". This came up not once, but twice. Sacrament viarge maudit... don't beg for positive reviews mauzus. Anyway... just avoid this obvious no-cost school project that was probably funded on to Steam by these guys' parents. It's not funny, and the story barely even makes any sense. Good luck in the future dudes, maybe one of you will make it to Ubisoft Montreal sometime.

I used to play the original Carrier Command every day after school (the version without warp). While I can see how some folks would find Gaea Mission confusing, I was able to pick it up immediately because of my familiarity. As a former Carrier Command player, I find this incarnation a worthy homage to the original and fun beyond belief.
The graphics are on-par for the release-date and, even without any familiarity with the original title, I think a new player would find the game fun. The concept is unique; think of it as a real-time strategy game where you can take over units and even control them. Doesn't that sound fantastic? It is.
I will say this, though: The story mode is absolute garbage. First person shooter? No, that is not what Carrier Command was. Ignore the story mode altogether and focus on the strategy mode. Even with the elimination of an entire mode, this game is still worth it*. Strategy mode is basically what the original was, and it's all that's needed.
*When I say "worth it," I really mean worth about, oh, $20. I picked it up for $6.49 during a sale, but $29.99 for this title is a bit ridiculous. It has long-term playability but, I have to admit, I would feel a little ripped off if I had paid $30.

Let me start off this review by saying that I'm not too well-versed in hidden object games (yet). I played a free-to-play hidden object game years ago and remembered liking it well enough. I love finding things in games. Anything. Collectibles, secret areas, shinies, etc. Heck, I love searching for and finding things in real life, too. I'm a married woman and I still insist on my mother hiding my Easter basket every year. I'm not sure what's sadder; that my mother actually listens to me and hides my basket every year, or that she still gives me one at all.
Nonetheless, thanks to the Steam queue, I have been introduced to the genre yet again. I purchased a few on a whim one day, and Abyss: The Wraiths of Eden was the first I played. I was in a casual game type of mood after putting much thought and effort into a lengthy RPG, and this game was really enjoyable in that respect.
The game opens up with your character's voice laying out the prologue to the story, and it made me giggle a bit because she sounded like a generic Microsoft computer voice at first. While the environments in this are beautiful and colorful, the entire game has a type of B-movie feel, with iffy voice actors, a "meh" story, and no sense of danger at all. The game definitely tries to throw some creepy moments at you, but never did I feel like my character was in danger or that a save would need to be reloaded. The game isn't scary at all for adults, but for young kids, it might be sufficiently creepy on rare occasions (and this game is definitely E-rated).
Abyss surprised me in that the game, while in the Hidden Object genre, was not overflowing with hidden object puzzles. I saw one review mention there were too many of them, but I wished for more. The game relies on an exceptionally well done and intelligently designed point and click adventure model for most of the gameplay, and the hidden object screens are mostly a distraction that include an object or two that you'll need to take from the hidden object puzzle and insert into the story gameplay. Sprinkled throughout the game there are also various mini-puzzles that go from sliding puzzles to jigsaw types to wire connecting puzzles. Not once did I feel like a puzzle was out of place or overly complicated. Even if (say, for kids) a puzzle is too confusing or hard, you can skip it. The game encourages you not to via some unlockable achievements, but it is an option. Unlike many point and click games, I never felt like combining objects to meet a goal was unnecessarily complicated. All of them made sense, so this game never frustrates.
Overall, while I did wish for more hidden object puzzles, I felt like Abyss: The Wraiths of Eden surprised me in its quality. It's relaxing and takes you on a nice little journey over about a four hour playthrough (I played on Expert despite being fairly new to the genre and never once was frustrated, so it's definitely casual!). While I would personally advise you to wait for a sale because I go by the $1.00 per hour of gameplay rule, I definitely recommend this game to anyone looking for a casual romp through some pretty environments. I'm giving this a 7/10. This is a great game for kids or for adults looking for a shorter game with little commitment. I was pleasantly surprised with this game, and I now consider myself a fan of the Hidden Object genre.

This game is very under rated... It is a mixture of tactical gameplay and action gameplay and works really well. It falls short of being a masterpiece because of a few issues, but it wasn't too far in my opinion. I mostly play the Campaign so haven't done many Skirmishes. The story and voice acting is quite low budget, but the focus is on the gameplay anyway. The music is great and the graphics are nice. The controls and physics are good in this game, vehicles feel solid, weight affects their speed so what you equip them with has an impact, they slip on mud, they struggle up steep hills and whizz down the other side etc. It is realistic and handles well.
The gameplay overall is good but not great. You have to capture a series of islands, so you travel there in your uber Aircraft Carrier, and then you launch some flying pew pew pew craft to scout the island and work out where all the resources are etc. The flying craft are weak though so you have to use them to scout carefully and then get them back to safety. Later in the game you get to use them more to shoot or bomb key targets, but early in the game they are only really used as scouts. Then you launch your tanks which will do all the capturing. You can have 4 tanks and each one can have a few gear upgrades of your choice, heavier armour that makes them slower but tankier, a variety of weapons, a hacking device, etc. The campaign is slow to get going, the first dozen or so islands you have to do with basic gear, but it gets more interesting later on when you get to start using your carrier's big guns, and your units get more interesting weapons like the gattling gun and your can drop bombs from the flying units etc.
Capturing the islands is done by driving around and capturing mini bases all over the island, and killing anything that gets in your way - preferably by waiting for your squad to keep up with you so you can get the benefit of all their firepower at once. Sometimes there are fixed turrets shooting at you, sometimes a bunch of robots come at you, and sometimes some vehicles or aircraft come at you. Occasionally you have to deal with all of those at once, but you can tend to pick stuff off bit by bit if you go slow and steady, especially earlier in the game. Also you can park your flying craft nearby and you can use those to help you finish off stuff once the main defences are dead. This capturing of the islands is the bulk of the game and it is fun, but this is the part of the game I think should have been a bit better. It isn't bad by any means, but it could have been better, and there other bits of gameplay I think they should have ignored and instead just focused on this part of the game.
You also have to manage your carrier in the meantime, building gear to replace whatever you lose in battle, and generating more fuel, etc. There is a little bit of strategy with the island capturing too, because you can choose if the island should produce stuff, mine stuff, or be a defensive island, so depending where on the map it is, you can use this to your advantage. Although the game doesn't seem to focus on this enough in the Campaign at least.
Overall it is fun and actiony, but it does fall short from greatness in several ways and I'll try to explain. First off, as you can see from a lot of the negative reviews, some people try to play the game as a tactical RTS type game. Technically the game should have let people do that, but the AI just isn't up to it. The way I play is to take direct control over the main tank, and set the other 3 tanks to follow me, and the game plays fine like that. You somtimes need to wait a moment for them to catch up, but mostly the pathing is fine and the AI does ok at following you and shooting whatever you shoot. The problem is if you want to sit back at the carrier or fly around command the ground units from afar, like a real strategy game, bad things will happen due to pathing and AI failures. They AI and pathing is not terrible, but it isn't good enough to just send things off on their own and expect them to make it. Often they will get whooped by the enemy or stuck on a tree, tumble down a cliff etc.. It is a shame because it could have been a bit more RTS. Personally I don't really care about this though, because if you lead the troops into battle (surely this is the most fun thing to do anyway?), they will follow you just fine.
Also the actual capturing of the islands (which is the bulk of what you do) is quite repetitive and shallow and could have been better. Each island might have a different shape, but they all work the exact same way. There are several bases on the island and you have to hack a building or clear out the enemies in each base, and on to the next one, and then you can capture the command center in the final base. Do that then it is on to the next island to repeat, in exactly the same way. It is a bit more interesting in that you unlock better gear as you make progress, and in the campaign especially, this can make the game quite addictive. You start with very basic basics, and gradually you unlock many little upgrades. Also the enemy bases start getting tougher and more interesting as you progress through the islands. At first it is just a handful of guys who die with 1 shot. Then you start getting occasional tanks, but later you get fortress style bases with many turrents, ambushes of several enemy tanks, and flying craft all over the place. The game is repetitive, but at least you are repeating fun things, so not a major problem, but to me this is the bulk of the game and it could have used something to jazz up this basic combat.
Lastly, there are some wasted opportunities. Clearly they just didn't have the time or budget to do everything they wanted, but it is a shame because there are things that could have fleshed the game out more. Like I said you can customise the islands to do what you want, but there should have been more to this. Also you can actually shoot things from your carrier, but you very rarely get to enjoy this because most of the stuff on each island is inland so it is out of your range. Also you can choose priorities of repairs on your ship, but this hardly ever gets used so it is like a wasted feature. Also you can put different weapons on your tanks but the game doesn't really require you to play smart. The sensible option would be to have 1 of each weapon, so the lazer can blow up stuff, while the anti air cannon guy can you protect you from flying stuff, etc.. etc.. But really, just the lazer alone is enough to deal with everything. Also there are a few FPS on foot sections in the game but they seem a bit weak and gimpy compared to a real FPS. They are not terrible, but a far cry from Halflife 2 or System Shock or something. So there are a lot of under developed features, and I think the game would have benefitted hugely from the devs scaling back all this stuff, and focusing on the key gameplay and making that great instead of ok.
Overall it is good game though, and quite a unique experience. If you want deep strategy, or visceral action, look elsewhere. But a blend of both those things is not often seen so this game is worth thinking about. I wish it had better sales because a bigger budget sequel to this game would be a big deal in gaming, especially nowadays. I think the game really suffered from limited marketing, I never even heard about this game until years after release.

The map is divided into a lot of areas which you need to indiviually "colonize". Each area can support 2-5 buildings, but each type of building may be only placed once per area. Assign your workers to the approriate buildings in the appropriate situation and you might make it through winter.
High replayability, due to procedually generated maps. As of the time of this review there are still minor bugs and exploits in the game, but it is already a really good experience.

Northgard is very fun and is highly recomended to be played with friends. I have not played any single player although that should be given a go. This game has many pros and cons.
PROS
- Simple Mechanics
- Minimalist graphics
- Variety of play styles
- Easy multiplayer game setup
CONS
- 'Broken mechanics'. This can be seen in the power of the villagers. Raiding a base with maybe 10 troops and a bezerker would be quickly broken down with nothing but just the shear power of 20 - 30 villagers in the village. I would be able to kill a few, retreat and fully heal the troops but once I return, more villagers return, essentially making no difference.
- Games can't be saved (on multiplayer)). When games take about 3 - 4 hours (with three friends on a small map) the option to save the game should be avaliable instead of needing to finish the game all in one sitting. This would allow the player to plan out larger attacks and spend more time developing their economy instead of rushing the game.
- Some options of winning are unrealistic. Winning through domination is simply unrealistic and would be much simpler to defend, controlling your economy and obtaining the blessings/gold/fame. It's just too hard and takes too long to accuire the soldiers whilst keeping you're food, wood and happiness positive.
OVERALL
Northgard should have some of its mechanics tweaked to have the game be more 'balanced' in order to give all players no matter the clan, an equal chance of winning. For example Wolves should have more attacking power so they DON'T just die from villagers so easily. Non the less, everyone should atleast attempt to play the game and simply refund it if you don't like it (although that would be unlikely).

Wickland is a fast paced, old school, online multi player first person shooter with a medieval fantasy theme. Most medieval games have slow movement, melee combat and shields, but not in Wickland. In this game, you have a machine gun like crossbows, rapid fire magic spells and quick thrown bombs. Every player moves super fast, has a lot of mobility and a decent jump. The big twist here is the fact that you don't collect weapons, you collect monsters that have their own abilities. So another weapon is one of seven monsters each with their own ammunition and health. Monster health is like armor. If the monster loses all its health, you lose that monster and need to get it again. When you're taking damage as a monster, you're also losing your overall health. If you lose all your overall health, you're dead even if you're a monster. It keeps things interesting and the monster skins are a good way to tell who is using what weapon. Although the action is so fast it turns into shoot whatever is moving. As a human crusader, you can pick up armor for extra resilience against attacks. If you are a monster when you pick up armor, that monster gets extra health, but your overall player health stays the same. Its all a nice system.
The monsters feel like they're from black and white cinema classics. You've got a werewolf with quick bombs that will bounce around before it explodes. Players caught in the explosion will fly through the air a bit. A gorilla (mini king kong?) with an arm cannon and the alternate fire is a double blast. A blue creature from the black lagoon with a long electric laser blast and a blue floating orb alternate fire. A yellow kracken that slowly fires a beam from its claw and spits acid that ricochets off the walls. A green lizard that has invisibility when you hold down the primary weapon and a strong claw melee for an alternate. Even when invisible, I could never catch up to anyone because everyone moves so fast. A goat beast that throws flaming red skulls that I can only think of the barons from Doom. Finally there is a bat that quick fires green glowing orbs and the alternate fire is a spread shot of the orbs. They all have the same movement speed, so there's nothing special about them other than their weapon.
Currently, the game has six maps, each has its own unique theme and some good action. Each passageway on every map is nice and wide. You'll always be able to run by other players or joust with them. Most maps have an upper and lower floor with most of the action happening on the lower one. There are plenty of balconies to fire down from and staircases to get up there. The maps aren't too big, so you'll always find action. There are bottlenecks, and wide open spaces to jump over gaps and have good fire fights. The game also makes use of jump plates that shoot you from the floor to the ceiling pretty easy. You'll even find paintings that act like portals for you to pass through. Each portal shows what's on the other side even if its a distorted ripple. There is slight fall damage, but only from the highest possible peaks I could find.
You'll discover armor, power ups and health of every shape and size. These items are everywhere. Health adds to your overall player health. The monster heads are on pedestals and the ammunition for the monsters is strewn about. You're never truly out of ammunition, if you run out of one type, just switch off, but keep in mind your monster's health. Would you rather use a healthy monster with no ammo or one that's about to die with plenty of ammo? Some power ups give you health or armor which exceeds your maximum and then it slowly drains down. Its a good way to keep players aggressive and hungry. These items are all commonplace in a first person shooter and it all feels familiar.
The game looks great all for a small file size under 1 GB. Closer scrutiny might find low quality textures, but for the most part the aesthetic is beautiful. Everything has a wonderful glow to it that adds to things. All the projectiles look different. Blue electricity, flaming red skulls, yellow acid spit and so on. Its another deeper way to let you know who has what weapon. It turns into a subtle rainbow of chaos on the battle field. Since killing something is so difficult, there is a satisfying giant red explosion of blood to let you know you've finally done it.
So why don't I recommend it? First of all, the game feels like I've played it before. It feels like other UDK (Unreal) engine shooters. So it feels familiar, just with a beautiful new theme. The biggest glaring issue is that its a multi player game with no players. At the peak I've found nine players at the most, but this is a few months after the game's release. Sure there could be a cheap sale and the game can find itself packed to the gills with players, but for how long? There are maybe ten dedicated servers across the globe. A few in Europe, one in Asia, another in Australia, South America and a few in the United States. From what I've seen, it seems like the European servers are the busiest. My ping was over one hundred, so while it was manageable, its not as good as the few servers in the US with even fewer people playing.
Since the lack of bodies is an issue, Wickland does include a practice mode. Its essentially a single player offline mode where you compete against bots. When you start practice, you need to then pause the game and push the "add bot" button to dump them into the game. So you can have one on one or all out mayhem with as many bots as you can add. Maybe even a gold collecting to see who has the most at the end of the round. Any extra modes would only fragment what little player base there is.
What about the modes? These games need to have a robust amount of modes right? Its all just a timed death match. At the end of the time limit you see the score. You can also see the score board before then with the press of a key. There just isn't a good amount of modes to keep me interested. I'd like team death match, king of the hill, even capture the flag, but I guess for a medieval spin it would be capture the torch. After playing fast twitchy first person shooters for twenty years, this one felt like a change in theme, but nothing else. I'd love to be able to make my own server instead of using the dedicated ones. Its still great that the game has dedicated servers.
For those that care, there is a wide array of settings. Rebindable keys, different resolutions and advanced graphical settings. There is even mouse sensitivity up to 100 and field of view up to 150 if you like. The game performs excellently, and I think it could perform well even on older systems. One thing I would prefer is being able to visit the settings menu while in game. If not in multi player then in practice mode.
There is a lot of potential here, but I'm just not sure the world is ready for a new old school online multi player FPS. There's nothing wrong with it, I just didn't feel like there was enough to keep me invested. It needs more modes, more players and more fun. Even if the game says its in beta (but not Early Access), I'm not sure it will ever get in the modes or player base to keep it going or even get it started.

Wickland is a fast paced and brutal 1v1 arena shooter set in a world of magic, sorcery, and in my case especially, much death. Your weapons are not merely handheld devices of destruction but transform yourself into beasts of various kinds, and picking one up denies your enemy of it as well. This leads to some very suspenseful fights over resources, and it's really quite deep and unique.
But as great as the dueling is, it's a bit of a shame there aren't any other game modes, other than a FFA-like warmup mode. It feels like even just some simple TDM could do well and be very interesting with the game mechanics. Duelling can be mentally exhausting and sometimes you want to play something more relaxing where you can blame your team mates for your shortcomings.
Brilliant sound and visuals. Shame about the menus and options being perhaps a little too simplistic.
I highly recommend this game, but it might not be everyone's cup of tea. But if all else fails, you can just marvel at the fact you can play as a gorilla with shotgun arms.

Short Version:
Did you love Sanctum? Don't dive this one expecting more of the same. First timer? Buy if you want to play a co-op FPS with TD elements.
Long Version:
Gameplay - As the SV says, Sct2 takes the hybrid TD/FPS of it's predecessor and pumps the FPS part of it while streamlining the TD parts so it feels more conducive to the experience. Everything is more limited, you can have towers, but not that many, you can have tower bases but mazing is limited, you get weapons, but don't choose when to upgrade them, getting a perk system that greatly affects how you are able to tackle the invading forces. The shooting part feels much better and is often more efective, especially when alined with the right perks, so you might find yourself clearing 100% of the wave by yourself, or having to because the towers are ill-equipped to do so. On a bright note, co-op'ing the game is pretty great and gives you a few more TD'ing/perk options, I had a blast clearing the campaign with friends.
Story - You are now given a choice of character with different looks, motivations, fighting perks, etc. Alongside that, we are given a context to all the missions in the form of comic book style narrative before them. Playing Sct2 feels much more personal, we know what's at stake and the very decent voice acting cries out to fallen friends and critical hits alike, a big plus for the campaign mode.
Sound - As a huge fan of Sct1 soundtrack I was slightly disapointed by Sct2's. It's not bad, it's just not as good, the tunes feel more repetitive and there's less gems in the rough. Still a decent fit for the game's theme.
Graphics - Just like Sct1, they fit the futuristic theme the game and I have little of note to complain about, everything is, of course, more detailed.
Extra note - Having invaders that destroy structures is not impossible to do in TD's, but they are not very well done here, your whole round can go to hell because your maze was destroyed and that's not fun when there's no save or checkpoint.

The boss fights are very difficult, (Yes there are boss fights in an abstract platformer.) but rewarding to complete. This is a short game, but well excuted. Challenging, but a low penalty for failure keeps you going.  No mid-level saving, which is annoying, but otherwise an enjoyable little experience.

I first played kingdom rush back in the early days on a website called Kongregate and thought it was extremely fun. I never imagined that they would be able to improve it so much as to be able to sell the game on Steam!
This is a Tower Defense game, meaning that you have to strategically place buildings (There are four buildings to choose from) in locations so the waves of oncoming enemies don't overrun you (get to the other side of the map). The game offers three modes for each map, each giving you currency to upgrade your abilities, buildings and your heroes.
Probably the best part about Tower Defense games in general is that there is always more than one way to successfully beat a level, so if you want to beat down your enemies with only arrows, you go girl! (or guy ;p). Unfortunately sometimes a single type of building, despite how many times you upgrade it using the money the monsters you kill drop (which you don't need to worry about picking up thank goodness), won't be sufficient in beating said level. You'll need to adapt sometimes.
What sets this game apart from the other Tower Defense games for me is the beautiful art style. I am not a huge fan of pixelated games, though I will try them if I hear good things about it. Another thing are the heroes and their unique abilities to help you in battle, as well as your own abilities.
Reviews for this game are generally overwhelmingly positive, and rightfully so. This game is perfect for that coffee break during work hours, or for sitting at home when you want something casual yet challenging and stimulating at the same time. I highly recommend this game, and if you don't feel like paying for the full version before you get a taste, go try it out on
and get a taste of the game for yourself!

Over 800 hours in to Fallout New Vegas, and still counting. Barely over 300 hours in to Fallout 4, and already deleted it from my computer.
Fallout 4 does a better job with graphics and gunplay then any prior Fallout game, but fails in basically every other way possible.
You'll see dozens upon dozens of other reviews all stating similar things to this simple statement: "It doesn't feel like a Fallout game." As a shooter with RPG elements, sure, it's a good game on it's own, but as a part of the Fallout Universe? No, absolutely not.
The RPG element of the game is broken by things like repetitive quests that are advertised as voluntary, but suddenly become quite mandatory. The abandonment of the "Karma" system definitely hurt the feel of the game as well. The game is bright, and vibrant, which would be fine for most games, but for a world that was plunged in to nuclear winter, it's just far too bright of a game to make it a true part of the Fallout realm. That analogy even applies to the NPC's as well. Perhaps they are just moving too far forward timeline wise from the day the bombs fell, but virtually every NPC in the game doesn't seem to feel the same urgency of survival that you get from them in other Fallout games. On one hand the "Settlement" system is a welcome touch, but on the other it's broken on it's own and very much responsible for hurting Immersion in the game. 5 minutes in, and all of the Settlers feel the same. There are mods to help that, but, even so the generic shallowness of their overall personalities makes them all just feel the same. Impact of choice itself is heavily lacking in Fallout 4 compared to all prior Fallout games. You essentially feel pidgeonholed in to either "Good guy" or "Bad Guy" roles, but even then the "Bad Guy" options feel lackluster at best. You are constantly bombarded by dialogue choices that do not matter at all. Literally, no matter what button you press, the same outcome will occur. (learn from that, stop inundating players with hordes of meaningless choices! Meaningless choices should be few and far between if at all!). In a shallow way player impact on the world would seem greater because you can directly control the shape of several parts of the world, but that ultimately contributes to the lack of immersion more then helping it because most of the quests all feel far too linear in nature to truly call it a reactive world. Putting up a town seems to, and feels, like it has virtually no impact on the other settlements or cities in the game. You can build a virtually impervious fort with enough firepower and walls to hold off an army, but a dozen raiders still wind up attacking and getting inside of it? Even that, on it's own, doesn't hinder immersion as badly as a world that does not react. In Fallout 3, a great example of world reactions, is the radio itself. 3 Dog is constantly touting things you have done, or have not done, and while that partially remains true in Fallout 4, the radio broadcaster is mostly ignorant or simply does not care about the vast majority of things you do in the "Wasteland". On one hand this is more realistic because how could they know everything you do? On the other hand, you feel less impactful on the world in general. Now on to the music, the music is literally copy and pasted from Fallout 3. Lets just, no, don't do that. Seriously, 200 years later, in a world that has fertile ground capable of harvesting plants, it just falls flat. In fallout 3 that made more sense, because food, and clean water, were MUCH harder to get, and without those basic essentials to life, it made sense that no one really had time for leisurely activities like music. But in Fallout 4, food and water are hardly issues anymore. If you're going to continue taking the timeline further ahead, then NEW MUSIC NEEDS TO HAPPEN TOO!!!
Even with all of these problems, Bethesda is taking far too much example from companies like EA and Activision. Paid mods? After a person has spent almost $100 on the base game, and all DLC, any sponsored mods should be free after that. Pick a model, F2P, or pay up front for a full product. If you get Fallout 4 for under $15, including all DLC, then fine, put in a F2P type of model. Don't charge full price for the base game and all DLC and then behave like a F2P game.
Honestly, I won't be preordering the next Fallout game if it is made by Bethesda, and I may be boycotting the company in general if they decide to go the EA route.

This game shows A TON of potential.
First of all, I want to congratulate the delevopers for not giving up on this game like most companies do with their Early Access titles.
Anyways, here we go.
Graphics: Not bad, really has the 90's arena vibe and best of all, you don't need a good computer to run this game!
Sound: Eh, it's okay - it gets a bit annoying after a while with the constant "ooh" and "ugh". It seems like there is only one sound for each time your character is hit. "ooh", "ugh", it never changes.
Characters: Each character has their own set of little moves and powers but it didn't give me any satisfaction (see gameplay). It seems like the character "Neymar" doesn't really have any useful attacks - choking himself, or clawing (which only works if your opponent is 3 cm away).
Gameplay: Very, VERY fast-paced - essentially a modern "Quake". When I said the attacks didn't give me any satisfaction I meant that to kill someone you have to hit them MANY, MANY times, and you will probably run out of ammo before you actually have a chance to kill them. It feels like there isn't any...POWER...behind the powers. It is extremely hard to aim and hit where you want, especially on the insanely-hard AI. Either Neymar or the Archer guy you start out with are probably the most underpowered.
Multiplayer: Good luck on finding ANY players. I've opened the game about 8 times and have played a total of 49 minutes because I've only seen a total amount of THREE players online - at SEPRATE times. 3 times it would just be me and some other guy in the server, and we just end up leaving because there's nobody else to join and we're sick of the AI.
Overall this game does show a lot of potential and it really could be something if the devs stick with it. I know I bashed Wickland pretty hard in this review, but it really isn't a bad game. (Plus, it's still in Early Access) They just need to slow it down a tad, slow the AI down a bit, work on the mechanics slightly and it would be a much more enjoyable experience.

Honestly this game is a work of art. From the textures, to the effects down to even the sounds of the city itself. This game makes it's world feel alive in ways that a lot of games simply don't. Add to that having to balance two lives, complete with their own skill trees and you've got a game worth playing.
A few gripe, though. First, combat. While the melee is smooth and responsive, feeling much like Arkham's combat, both normal and heavy attacks are bound to a single key/button. You press for normal and hold for heavy. This makes timing far more important since one slip and the move you were going for becomes something else. Also the guinplay is a bit sluggish and seems out of place given the polish of the melee system.
Second, that the 'dating' aspect of this game is so severely limited; one date, you get lucky, get a bonus and never see the girl again (save for one under the right conditions). It would have been nice (IMO) if they'd made that a larger part of the game play, giving you a 3rd thing to manage along with your Triad and Police work. showing the effects undercover work can have on relationships and the stress of it all.
Those minor gripes aside, this still a great game.

Where this game fails is in the multiplayer. Multiplayer is legit broken. Imbalanced maps and species' makes playing this game barely fun at all, and more of a rage quit simulator than anything else. The game is full of camping marines who sit in hard to reach areas/corners with shotguns and sniper rifles. Predators also use instant kill, auto-aim plasma casters. And hard to see, instant kill plasma mines to rack up most of their kills. These types of people are cancerous, because they use the OP weapons and methods, and yet they actually think they're good.
Alien is severly underpowered. With no means of a ranged attack, they have to use melee only. The problem is, they can't without dying. Marine shotguns will almost always instant kill you, and sniper rifles will kill you in just 1 or 2 hits. And Predator heavy attacks are literally a second faster than Alien heavy attacks, making melee combat against Predators almost undoable unless the Predator player is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
Some people have told me "Well, if Predators and Marines are OP, why not just play them?" Two reasons, 1. I'm a Alien fan, and want to play as Alien. 2. I have way to much self respect to lower myself to the standards of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ who don't know how to actually play. I refuse to use OP weapons like the Plasma caster, shotgun, sniper rifle, etc.
And this problem has plagued the game since its release, and probably is one of the leading causes of the games low amount of online players. The other cause is the developers at Rebellion abandoning the game months after release back in 2010. The game can be fun at times, It has the 3 diverse species and the mechanics to do so, but Multiplayer is far to broken to take seriously.

Bastion is a truly fantastic game. This one had been on my radar for a while, and I was lucky enough to grab it at a discount. I have to say, though, that after playing it, it's worth every penny at full price.
There's truly something for everyone here. It's got RPG elements, beautiful world design, post-apocalyptic storyline, hack and slash "everything dies" free-for-alls, weapon mechanics, challenging achievements, and an intriguing story with heavy moral choices along the way.
The full controller support couldn't function any more perfectly, and the graphics are astounding. The soundtrack is also excellent and seems to enhance the experience even more. Characters are multi-dimensional, and combat is dynamic. There's definite replayability here, as well as many challanging, yet fun, achievements.
The Stranger is beyond a doubt my favorite character, and it seems that a lot of thought went into character development and world-building. It's a fantastical combination of old West and ethereal  fantasy realm.
This looks like a game that was designed by gamers who just happen to know how to create video games. It's got so many wonderful elements strung together that it's very likely that the developers sat down to design and code a game that they themselves would enjoy playing. I have to say, they hit the ball way out of the park with Bastion.
Without spoiling anything, I'll just add that a cerebral gamer will find other hidden gems in the storyline. I found myself speculating about time paradoxes, time travel, self-fulfilling prophecies, and the identity of The Stranger. I'm so fascinated with this game that I'm beginning my second playthrough now. I highly recommend it.

If you liked Rez, you'll probably love this game. It's a platformer where the environment moves in sync with the music (moving platforms follow the bassline, blocks appear and disappear on snare hits, etc.) The music is similar in style to Rez: minimalist techno.
The main downsides to this game are that it's short (only 3 distinct levels that you can play in a "normal" mode or a "challenge" mode), and that there's not much creativity in secrets, exploration or achievements (there are 6 achievements, which are to beat the previously mentioned 3 levels both in normal and in challenge mode).
Because it's so short, I feel that at $5, it's right at the edge of a good value proposition. Definitely get it if it goes on sale, and consider getting it at full price if you're a fan of Rez.

After 1.0 came out I got really excited to start playing this game again. To add some context I've been playing since maybe a month or two after the game came out as a beta. And in this time I've had a love/hate relationship with Starbound. When I first bought the game it had several bugs/glitches which were eventually fixed only to be replaced by more of them. Thats fine. Thats what beta testing is all about. So I would go on streaks of playing with or without friends (its fun either way but having a party is a whole new experience).
But really at this point I should be reviewing what I thought of 1.0 which is why i gave it a positive review for the game. There are a lot of bad reviews coming up complaining about how the game used to have so many bugs and such. note "used to" in my experience I encountered maybe 2 bugs. The story was well done and of decent length (It took me about 20 hours to complete). It also included several sidequests for the player to participate in if they chose to do so which helps with replayability a lot. There are some very good and enjoyable things that you can experience in this game so I'll put a pro/con list here for anyone still reading.
-Story is a good length
-Story is well told
-Several races to choose from with their own unique cultures/appearances
-Character customization
-Outfits
-Pets
-Near infinite number of planets to explore
-Lots of biomes to explore
-Boss fights were difficult but not impossible
-Lots of replayabilty value from side quests, colonies, upgrading, etc
-Nice graphics
-GREAT music
-Spooky moon ghosts
-Seems like there are plans to keep adding new content
-Lots of item variety
-Balance is off in the early stages of the game (enemies very hard to kill/deal a lot of dmg)
-Bug where you can get stuck in a block while building (Easily fixed by breaking it)
-Has some FPS issues in certain areas (On a well built PC)
-Upgrades are not very well explained
-Wiki can be unreliable from all of the previous builds (Not the dev's fault though)
-Combat is very boring early on in the game and stays mediocre into the end game
-EPP augments dont transfer with upgrades and are destroyed when a new one is applied
I hope this helps people who may be considering buying the game. In my opinion it is very worth your money. If you liked Terraria then you will like this game as well. As a preface, I had been following Starbound since it's first announcement, purchased it the day it came onto Steam (a copy for me and a friend) and have been following development on and off for a few years. Recorded playtime wise, I don't seem reliable, but I have been watching this game flourish- or moderately expand in this case.
If you don't know what Starbound is, it is a 2 dimensional procedurally generated sandbox RPG, bearing many similarities to Terraria if you've ever seen/played that. I'm sure other reviews go into depth on exactly what Starbound is, so I won't waste your time and will instead explain why I do not recommend this game.
I can't seem to find the right words to make this super lengthy and in detail (third time trying to write this section), so I'm going to simply touch on the issues that stuck out to me in the cons section above.
- So Starbound has crafting, looting, and buying and selling. These ideas tend to clash with each other more often than not which makes the progression system speedy for some parts and slow for others. For instance, crafting weaponry for the first few hours is seemingly useless as almost all the loot you find will be better. Then as you take on harder monsters, loot you find will become useless in favor of crafting. It's the opposite for armor in the beginning. You'll find almost no armor requiring you to craft it. If you do find any in loot, it'll almost be guarenteed to be worse than your current stuff due to how all armor is defined in
. It's inconsistent.
- This is heartbreaking because it's the soul of Starbound. The pool for parts that the planet generator picks from feels really small, as almost all your planets will look and feel exactly the same. For a game that has you jumping across the universe, it's really jarring when you warp lightyears away to a distant planet only to see that the major difference is the
. The same goes for the creatures you find. Creatures are either unique, procedurally generated, or bosses. Unique are specifically created by the developers as are bosses. You'll end up running into the exact same unique creatures more often than not and it really makes the planets feel even more uniform. Once in a while you'll find a generated one, but they seem so uninspired and not-fleshed-out that you'll probably wonder what the point is anyway.
- The game has a story. This is a good thing as it will provide a decent amount of base content for you. Unfortunately once you're done with that, there really doesn't feel like there's a point to continue playing. Yes, you can create a colony which is an interesting feature. Yes, you can go around collecting various creatures from different planets to make a zoo of sorts (which would be much more interesting if the creatures were more diverse). But the problem is this: there is no point other than personal satisfaction. This is a good thing for some and if it is, more power to you. However, some people like myself need a good incentive to use these features. Why make a colony when you can have a crew and can visit the Outpost for buying and selling? It's a decently fleshed out feature but ultimately pointless. I'm sorry to make the comparison, but in Terraria having a colony was essential because
. Why make a zoo or catch a companion if you already fare well by yourself in combat, and the creatures aren't interesting in their own right?
- So when Starbound was first released here, it had a hunger system, a dynamic temperature system, an enemy leveling system, a destruction system, and a few others I can't recall. Hunger recently came back which was received happily, but most of the other systems have been watered down and spread out across the game to the point where they're barely recognizable. Temperature is just now extremely cold planets or extremely hot planets all the time which are circumvented by wearing a magical backpack. Enemy leveling is now simple overall planet threat level (which is far less interesting and dynamic). The destruction system was almost completely removed (you could shoot out walls and break things with projectiles, which some people disliked but I found it to be an interesting mechanic).
- The game has no pause function. Some people will argue to the death saying that the game does not need one. Here's the thing- this isn't Dark Souls. You're not often in super-intense situations where pausing the game would cheapen the effect. This isn't so much a problem on casual difficulty, but if you have the hunger system enabled, hit esc to go tend to something, you may be surprised to find yourself back on the ship with 30% lost money and most of your items gone since you starved to death in your absence. This is something that really irks me. Being able to pause in
game is absolutely essential. If somebody knocks at my door, I shouldn't need to be in a situation where I either need to save and quit (losing any progress if on a planet since you're warped back to the ship on load) or risk losing all my stuff and some money because my character starves while I'm away. The excuses that have been given to this issue are even more outlandish, being along the likes of, "This would break multiplayer" and "Single player is basically local client side multiplayer" in which case I would point to Minecraft which also has a perfectly functional pause menu while having everything done on a local server. The game also doesn't have any sort of auto-saving of any capacity- or even conventional saving. In order to save, you must save and quit to the menu. No mid-game saving and if your game crashes or power goes out, then you've lost all progress from your previous save which could easily be hour wasted. I never judged the game too harshly about this and figured it would surely be added when the game was released. Unfortunately, this is not the case and is mind boggling that the game managed to go through almost 3 years of QA in the form of Early Access and still not have this.
- This game also has questing- which is also a good thing as it adds variety. Unfortunately it's similar to most of the other features in that it is ultimately pointless. Rewards that are given to you are laughable compared to the effort that you need to put in for some of them. Travelling half-way across the entire planet to find somebody, travelling all the way back while protecting them for a bag that will most likely randomly give me a few torches or some throwing daggers? No thank you.

A surpringly well done, fun title with touch support and actual challenge on normal mode.
I searched for touch-screen capable games so I could have small games to play on my tablet.  I didn't think much of Kingdom Rush at first, because the graphics and first 5 missions made it look like a generic mobile tower defense albeit with some interesting mechanics.  However, when I got to around mission 10, I couldn't just hobble together some defenses based on my favorite tower.  I had to actually think, "Okay, based on the mission description, what is the best combination of defenses?"
Despite having most of the research points earned from previous missions, it took me almost 8 attempts to beat that mission.  It wasn't due to unfair difficulty, or personal ham-handedness.  Every attempt was me throwing together all sorts of combinations of research, towers, heroes, and progression in one strategy after another until I found a strategy that worked, and it worked WELL.  It was extremely satisfying too, because even though the strategy was refined through practice, the level was STILL challenging.  A perfect clear requires a perfect strategy, and perfect management of the map, and despite getting a 2/3 star rating it was...hectic.  There were few moments where I could simply watch the battle unfold, because there were constantly things I could be doing, whether it was reevaluating my hero/soldier placement, using abilities based on enemy type and movements, or examining my defenses to allocate funds.
All in all, this game is easy to learn, hard to master.  On the surface, the mechanics are fun and simple, but if you dig deeper, you'll find that the developers have balanced every defense you have with an enemy type.  No one tower is a "go-to", and situations can change in the blink of an eye if you aren't careful.  I may not be much for TD games, but I highly recommend this if you like macro-managing strategy games but don't feel like playing a huge one like Sins of a Solar empire for example.

Fallout 4 does however have some reedeming aspects that make it worth your while, the modding scene on this game is very alive (at the time of writing this.). Overall, I give this game a 6/10, I have this on console and it's just ok, I got a 2 day trial of the steam version and there wasn't much to be had, but if it's the only thing you have to play you certainly won't be dissatisfied

It’s always hard for me to give thumbs down to a game I had so much expectations for and really wanted to like, I think reviews should be honest, open and must examine most of the aspects, quality and details of a game, it is normal to see funny and one liner reviews on steam that do not even bother to analyze a game in depth, which is downright sad.
But again, I had such expectations for this title… it happened it is just really not my cup of tea.
We play as “The Kid”, according to the narrator lines, a silent protagonist that takes over a mission. He is one of the few survivors of a disaster called the Calamity, an event that ended up wiping out the whole population of Caelondia. It is said when something bad happens people should go to the Bastion, it is here that The Kid finds out about his mission and must find some weird crystal shards which powered up the former city of Caelondia, a mission that will send him to different locations filled with many enemies and beautiful and colorful landscapes.

The game is quite simple, there I not much complicated mechanics or weird and uncomfortable controls, it plays well with an Xbox controller I must say. Bastion works in an isometrically point of view, the areas we discover build up as we approach while the surrounding environment is filled with all sort of details, walls and colors, beautiful scenarios deep in detail. We have many weapons that will help us defeat many type of enemies, from the littlest of the enemies to the big scumbags, as well as towers that fire different projectiles depending on the type of tower. Melee weapons and long ranged ones can be upgraded so you can more chances to deal even more damage, we also have special abilities that will consume black oil, this one works as fuel for that ability. The simplicity of the gameplay is nice, just follow the path, fight enemies, look for secret artifacts and finally, look for the shards, level clear.
Our task is based on the construction of the Bastion, the shards will power it up giving us the chance to build different structures such as the arsenal, the forge, the distillery, etc. all of these structures will help us gain more abilities, improve our weapons or buy new tools and skills for them, for this we must gather fragments, which will work as currency.
As we advanced throughout the many levels, we have a voice over narrator who explains in detail the things we do, part of The Kid’s personal story and views, the stories of the levels and some monsters as well as past events that took place on said scenarios, every one of these places hides secrets, anecdotes and are filled with a rich storytelling. Depending on the situation, the narrator will change his voice tone fitting the situation, sometimes kidding on what is happening at some points of the journey.
I must say the game is extremely beautiful, every level is detailed in depth, and every color is vivid and stands out on its own, animations are great and plenty. Also the variety of material, walls, crates, barrels, pillars, abandoned shops fill the settings, some green areas are also part of the view, flowers, trees and the little grass we get to see are pretty. Overall, Bastion is a game that is highlighted by the many little things that make it look great. Definitely, the developers show the passion and dedication which the game was created with. Gorgeous.
I believe most people find the soundtrack one of a kind, just take a look on the reviews and you will see it for yourself. Yes, the soundtrack is good, sometimes it evokes a Wild West feeling and atmosphere, sometimes you feel like the game couldn’t have made it without the soundtrack, the electro-acoustic work is awesome, truthfully praised. Every tune fills the gameplay with different sensations.
On the other hand, the sound effects do a decent job, there is nothing superb or anything, but they stick to what they were created for, fantasy-theme games can have a lot of liberties when it comes to this subject, let’s say they are not the worst I have ever heard nor the best, but the music will always be the main protagonist here.
While the game has many things worth mentioning and I should say they are, because let’s be honest, in my opinion the game has potential, but I believe this potential was not well exploited. Bastion tends to be extremely monotonous and at times slow-paced, the narration helps a bit to keep you aware of the elements of the main plot, but the gameplay ends up being boring most of the time and unsatisfying, this is what kept me from continuing playing the game, the slow, tedious and dull gameplay, in my book, graphics are not everything, sure the game looks awesome, but it falls short when it comes to the mechanics, for some reason I felt that not even leveling up was challenging, I never felt the need to continue exploring due to the fact that many levels look the same.
The storyline never caught my attention, since the beginning I did not feel interested on it, not even with the great narration. Maybe the lack of dialogue is part of this or maybe the feeling that the main plot is just not fascinating nor attractive, many times the narrator talks about the people that died during the catastrophe and the few survivors, I never cared about them, there was nothing that could possibly made feel the slightest of the emotions for them. Alive or dead, it did not matter. Also, another thing that might be part of my negative view on this game is the absence of more enemies, repetitive foes, just small variations in size, and that’s it, a pity.
I must say that I was really excited about this game, maybe it was my fault not investigating more about it, perhaps youtube videos, more reviews detailing the dull gameplay and mechanics, the good and the bad, or simply this is not my kind of game. I love atmospheric games, I love the feeling of being part of the world, caring for the characters and the plot, but Bastion does not offer that to me. I will try and finish the game, though with low expectations for sure if the gameplay doesn’t change a bit more.
I do think that the game deserves all the praise because of its soundtrack and beautiful and colorful environments. My expectations were high, now I feel I made a mistake, unfortunately I must give my thumb down to Bastion, I wish there was another option for games that do not fully deliver what was expected but at the same time you see the passion and work that was put in their creation.

(super-long and spoiler-free review as far as I can)
Decided to play it to the end on easy mode before writting a review. Please forgive any writting mess as I'm not English-speaking/writting native.
Usually I'm not a plataformer game player (I usually mess when jumping and end dying a lot - and sure thing, I died a lot here)
Bastion is an interesting game where all the game talking is done by Rucks, an old man (who acts as the game narrative, he also makes some funny remarks) you (as the Kid, a silent protagonist) find in the Bastion, a place somehow safe from the Cataclysm, an event that broke (most of) the world.
Said Bastion is the central base for Kid and need the Cores to be useful (they open shops and other useful structures), and after it is heavily damaged after an event, you need Shards to repair it.
Some items also add interesting features, and open maps you can redo - these give some indeep info about Zulf and Zia, the two other characters you will find: Zulf and Zia. Zulf was an ambassador from Ura (a neighbour subterranean country which was in war with Kid's Caelondia years ago), Zia is a girl of Ura origin but born in Caelondia.
Equippables: You can use two weapons and a skill (linked with a wepon or having another useful feature). For weapons I chose to use both melee and ranged weapons (some mobs can and will munch you from distance). The weapons can be upgraded or switched in Bastion (you also find some Arsenals to change weapons on the maps, but thet are rare).
Two interesting features is the Spirits, drinks you can equip on slots you get one per level - they give some good bonuses (some also give disadvantages too); the other are the Gods; those give bonuses on XP and Scraps, but they also cam make the game much harder if you select more than one.
The game is quite linear, except for two situations near the game end where you decide what to do (I chose both right-side choices, won't spoil it here). Ending the game open the NewGame+ mode, where you start with all levels, gear, items and scraps (the $ here) from the 1st play, and you get new features on the new gameplay.
The music is incredible, when I heard Zia's song I was delighted to see that the singer on Transistor game is also here - I don't have Bastion soundtrack yet, will get it on a future sales.
Bastion is not a new game, and have a TON of positive reviews - if you never played it, get the demo (it's free) and try a bit - you won't be disappointed.

TBH I got this game from a key giveaway, but I feel like I should have payed for it. It's not one of those cheap 99 cent games you usually get from key giveaways. It's a great game, well worth the money if you enjoy the genre(and if you can actually find people to play with). It's one of those fast paced arena shooters where you run around really fast and try to get the highest score before the time runs out. It reminds me of playing Quake 3 on the school network but with a lot better graphics and a cool class-like system. Basically, there are different items around that you pickup. In Quake there were potions, armor, guns, ammo, all of these are self explanitory. The unique thing about Wickland is that rather than guns to pickup, you have monster souls. There are multiple different souls available, each with it's own unique abilities. You can carry multiple different monster souls at once, and can easily switch between them with the scroll wheel. The soul transforms you into a monster that has both a weak left click ability, and a strong right click ability. When you get hit enough, you will lose the soul of your current monster, and once you lose all your souls, you're dead. Respawn time is very short though because this is a fast paced game. I want to play this game more, but the bad thing about it is that there's never a single player online. Lot's of people giving Wickland bad reviews because of the nearly nonexistant amount of players has probably kept people away from buying it.

Rebellion were the brains behind 2000's "Aliens vs Predator" ,  which was known for two things :  Brutal difficulty, and intense atmosphere.  Both aspects make their way into this 2010 re-imaging ,  but some unfortunate design choices ruin what could have otherwise been an incredible game.
Let's talk about the good:
Atmosphere:
This game absolutely drips with it.   The lighting,  the audio,  it all comes together to create one of the most atmospheric and authentic AVP experiences you will ever find.  In fact, I'd be hard pressed to think of a better audio visual representation of the AVP universe in video games.  With the possible exception of Alien : Isolation, this is as good as it gets.
Gore:
It has lots of it, and it's gratuitous.   You can dismember enemies limb by limb, punch holes through their head, tear off their faces,  punch your tail through their♥♥♥♥♥and out their mouth ( yeah, literally that's a thing you can do).  It's great to see such attention to detail,  and it really sells the idea of a brutal world where it's kill or be killed.
Controls:
Generally speaking,  each of the 3 species controls in a way that feels appropriate and fluid.   The marine moves at a suitable plodding pace, the predator can gracefully jump from place to place, and the alien can stick to the ceiling and transition to any other surface it desires.  With the exception of  some minor hiccups (it's possible to get caught on the edges of geometry when trying to transition between surfaces) The controls feel responsive and true to the species.
Well that all sounds encouraging?  Why isn't this a 90% GOTY must-buy experience?
Pretty much one reason:
UNSKIPPABLE KILL ANIMATIONS.
This game forces you into lengthy "Kill Animations" whenever you are in a contextual position to do a "take down" on an enemy.  Many games do this, and it's usually a quick punch or a throat slit, or something that might take a second or two.  Here, it's about 5 ♥♥♥♥ING SECONDS  (no this is not an exaggeration, I've timed it).   For example,  If I'm playing as an Alien and I sneak up behind someone and catch them unaware,  I have now screwed myself over if I choose to perform a takedown on them.  My character releases a loud hissing sound when performing the takedown as well, which draws any nearby enemies to my position,  so they can just pump me full of lead as I am forced to watch this 5 second, unskippable animation of the kill.   Oh, and this isn't just in single player, it's in multiplayer as well, which completely ♥♥♥♥s up the balance and makes playing non-human species a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥
"Press E to die"  Basically sums it up.
While you don't *have* to do takedowns ( The Alien does have basic claw and tail attacks that don't lock you into an animation) the entire game has been balanced assuming that you don't use these unless you *really* have to.  Their damage is pitiful, and somehow your basic melee attacks can actually be blocked by basic human enemies.  I can't recall the last time I saw a marine who was able to parry claw attacks from a massive Alien drone with his bare hands, but there you go.  In this game,  it happens.
So yeah, in summary it's a flawed game.  But it still manages to deliver some of the best atmosphere you will find in the AVP universe.  So if you can cope with the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ kill animations you'll find something to like here,  just don't expect a perfectly balanced masterpiece.   And don't bother with the multiplayer, it's imbalanced garbage.

'It Came From Space and Ate Our Brains', is an arcade, top-down shooter, of the 'twin-stick' variety, developed by Triangle Studios and released on Steam in 2015.
The game has an overall Steam rating of 'very positive', with reviewers often praising it's fluid gameplay, tight controls, variety of weapons, and the co-op mode (both local split-screen, and online).
You play as Jerry, a regular guy who somehow managed to survive an alien invasion, while the rest of the human race have apparently had their brains eaten. With little chance of survival, and nothing left to live for anyway, Jerry decides he will go out in a blaze of bullets and explosions, taking as many of the invading alien scum with him as he can. If he can't defeat the aliens, he may at least set a new high-score!
The game begins with Jerry dumped in an ominously dark level, with just a flashlight to guide him, and a puny pistol to fend off the pending hordes of glowing aliens, all eager to feast on his pulsing, fleshy brain. Once the timer has counted down, the first wave begin their attack.
Killing aliens increases both your score and your coin tally, the latter of which can be used to buy new weapons, power-ups, and upgrades. Once you aquire enough coins, a message will flash on the screen to indicate that a new weapon or power-up is available to purchase from the shop, which can be accessed with the press of a button at any time. The purchasable weapons and upgrades become available gradually, to match the growing difficulty of the incoming enemies. This presents the player with tactical options to suit their play style - do they spend their coin on upgrading their pistol to maximum, or hold out to purchase more powerful base weapons, such as the shotgun? Or perhaps even hold out for something a little more explosive - maybe a rocket-launcher? Power-ups may be dropped randomly around the level, as time passes, and these can be collected to be used when the player feels appropriate, to increase defenses, replenish health, or provide a temporary boost to fire-power.
As the game progresses, and each wave of ever more powerful aliens are destroyed, the player will eventually face the final wave & the final boss, whose defeat signals the end of that level. With the level completed, you are presented with a summary of your performance, such as kills, deaths, and favourite weapon, along with your score and the option to proceed to the next level, where the action starts over again in a new setting.
Graphically, the game is of the '3D-block' style, so common amongst modern indie games, but the colour pallet used, and the fluid animations, provide for a fairly unique and pleasing aesthetic. I did at times, however, find that during particularly frantic moments of action, the screen has a tendancey to blur into an indistinct lightshow of fluro colours and flashes, causing the player character to be difficult to spot in amongst the mayhem. I must also admit, it took me a while to learn what each power-up was, as the only differentiating feature of them, in the game world, is their color, as they are all represented by identical floating cubes. The sound effects, although fairly rudimentery, are sufficient for this style of game, while the music is very much suited to the atmosphere, with a rocking techno track, just dark enough to fit in with the eerie environment.
Control is simple and effective, as should be expected by now for this kind of 'top-down' shooting genre, using the tried and true 'twin-stick' method, with player movement being controlled with the left controller stick (or the keyboard) and aiming being accomplished with the right stick (or the mouse). I had no issues with this control method, though it took me some time to realise that I had to press a button to use the power-up I was apparently carrying, as this wasn't made clear in the game. With all the action happening on screen, I was initially under the impression that walking over the power-up was enough to activate it.
Gameplay is fun and addictive, as is so common with these kinds of games. I found the weapon upgrades were made available at just the right intervals to relieve the onset of boredom, which, for all but the most hard-core fan of the genre, becomes inevitable in these repetitious 'score-chasing' games. The boredom, however, does eventually set in - for me it was after around an hour's play, which is probably more time than I would give most games of it's ilk. After playing for a while I discovered, on medium difficulty at least, that I could just pick a strategically adventageous spot, which is pretty much any location where the enemies are 'funneled' into a group in order to reach you, and camp there, picking-off the oncoming aliens one by one as they got within range. This quickly results in a tedious gaming experience. Of course, there is nothing making you play this way - if you want to gain the most enjoyment from the game, simply avoid doing this.
Overall, I found the game to be above average for this genre. Being able to instantly compare your score on a leaderboard of your friends, or against the whole world, adds some incentive for 'one more go'. Unless you are a score-chasing fanatic, however, the eventual onset of boredom is inevitable - especially with the lack of variety in scenery and enemies. But the multiplayer aspect, particularly local co-op, make the game a good choice to break out every now and then for a quick round with some friends. I should mention at this point, that others have spoken of unusual lag in multiplayer, though I personally didn't experience this during my short time playing online. This is one of those games you may just pick up every couple months for a little play, maybe while you're waiting for a video to render, or a file to download - but just keep an eye on the time, as you may find yourself ever so slightly addicted... for a while, at least.

Edit: July 26, 2016

Lag reliability has inproved signigicantly, almost to the point it was when I first started the beta. Much still to be worked on, but the game is playable.
On to a more reliable (and usable) review, now that lag isn't killing the game outright; Starbound is in the same catagory as Minecraft and Terraria. The spacific differences of note would be 2D style side scrolling play, a trans server hub (your ship), multiple world to play across, and a lively number of options within the games compatable mods. Like Minecraft, this game may never actually finish developing, providing players reason enough to keep coming back for more.

This is a fun game if you don't mind holding left click with your crosshair centered at bad guys. You build towers and have them shoot aliens (lumes), and you proceed to shoot them as well, all while creating the most complicated maze to stall them as long as possible while you mow them down.
That being said, I enjoyed this game for the strategy that goes into defending your base. At first glance, most towers will seem to do the same thing, and the differences between them seem to be minimal. However, in my opinion, figuring out the best towers for each level is an accomplishment on its own, especially when it comes to setting the level to the highest difficulty with all five "feats of strength" enabled. Protecting your core when it can only take a single hit and finally completing the level is a great feeling, emphasized by the fact that since this is a first-person shooter, as you are part of the playing field and have the most impact in defending the core.
One thing about this game is that you should defnitely get friends to play with you. I have only played one level in multiplayer, but with a non-unified team, compensated increased health of the enemy lumes, and shared resources, it's not nearly as enjoyable. I happened to really enjoy single-player, but different people have different tastes.
Last bit: get the DLC! It adds a lot more new towers, weapons, levels, enemies, and of course, more fun.

Pros
-Extremely beautiful pixel art with cute characters and breathtaking environments.
-Extremely beautiful music.
-Good building mechanics.
Cons
-Huge lack of content.
-Uninteresting and unoriginal Plot.
-Shallow.
-Empty.
-Boring and extremely repetitive randomly generated fetch quests (take this A item to this B dude and return to me)
-Not sure why people say it's a sandbox, if you consider gta v or elite dangerous a sandbox, then yes, it may be a sandbox for you.
-Few survival elements that end up just being a annoyance. (cold and heat management have been cut off from the game.
-Souless characters without personality.
-Every race feels the same. No racial weapons, no racial food, same story. Only tiered racial gear without any special bonuses, just cosmetic.
-Few uninteresting weapons and abilities, all randomly generated. Don't expect a Terraria here.
-There are few biomes for each planet, which end up looking the same.
-Eventually you'll find some kind of shockingly easy and BORING ''labyrinth puzzle platformer'' dungeons that add nothing to the game.
-Slippery movement that doesn't make platformer mechanics better.
-You can see all that the game has to offer after an hour of playtime.
-Everything in this game seems like a placeholder. It doesn't feel ''finished''.
-Boring boss fight mechanics, some are incredibly easy, other ones just annoying.
-Novakid race, at the moment, has zero background lore.
-Too many items that are just cosmetic or/and funny.
-Every village you find looks exactly the same. (villages have different themes for each of the seven races.
-Not very smart AI behaviour
-Grind, grind, grind, die, grind.
-Vendor npc and shops can be quite useless.
-Shallow colony system.
In general terms, it's great on the artistic side, but it's not a good game in my opinion, still amazed at all those positive reviews.

TL;DR A good game, but a bad Fallout game.
Honest opinion, the story sucks. It doesn't really make any sense when looking at the core of it. My mine gripe is it feels the plot twist that you were frozen for another 60 years not 10 seemed to have been added at the last second to make Shuan Father because between Coursers showing up in Kellog's memories (who needed Shuan's DNA to exist in the first place) and Kellog not aging at all, there are a lot of holes in the plot. All this aside, choices you make and do outside of the main story missions have no real impact to the outcome of the story. Your character is fixed on trying to find his son, becoming a drug filled cannibal or living saint really mean nothing.
It's certainly a step up from what I remember, obviously mods add more flavour but without mods its still great. However this all kinda goes down the drain because your character has a voice of their own. On top of that, they have their own background, family,
personality. It indirectly really limits how far you can mold your character since they already have a background.
The Dialogue is lacking at the best of times. Any given choices usually boil down to Yes, Sarcastic Yes/Ask for more money which means Yes, Repeat/Yes, and No. Compared to previous games, skill checks have been reduced to being chance based so no need for certain levels of Speech/Barter/etc (not like those skills were in the game) but I'll get into that later. There's also the case that what you say doesn't really matter. You could choose the rude dialogue, the NPC will be upset but then be fine and dandy like nothing happened when you return to turn in (unless you've come back to kill them, obviously). There's also the case that you have no idea what you're going to say, just a one to two word summary of what you will say. Not a big issue, just personal preference.
The game as a whole feels a lot smoother than previous games, that's undeniable, but it's so streamlined that it feels like a generic shooter with minor RPG elements. Gunplay is amazing, no doubt. The Good Karma/Bad Karma system has been removed for the most part (it's kind of there with Companion Reputation) so your actions don't really have consequences unless you're caught. Perk Builds also don't really matter. At any point you can decide to branch out and generalize where as in previous games you had to more or less commit. Sure it goes both ways as a good and bad thing, but on my second playthrough of the game my character plays no different from the first by the end since certain skills (particuarly combar ones) become mandatory in order to keep up. Settlements are whatever, I kinda liked them.
