Fallout 4 is awful. For a game where you can build your character and chose how you play, Fallout 4 gives us too much backstory. We get a whole life of the Sole-Survivor laid out for us, as we know their career, their name, where they lived, and they even have a voice. The voice ruins everything, as the male character's voice is obnoxious. It gives no no ability to role-play and build a character. There is also an area of the map (The Glowing Sea) which was made to save time. The landscape is barren and there is almost nothing there save a few cool locations.
The main story of Fallout 4 is incredibly shallow. The characters are not interesting, the quests are all "go and get something" no matter who you pick. Speaking of choices, there are only 2 game endings. The after-game content is minimal. Automatron is a DLC you can beat in one sitting, its a bigger side quest. Far Harbor is the only good DLC, and actually has a decent main quest and has as different endings, 7 I can think of. Nuka World just has you going and killing things as you try to navigate Kiddy Kingdom while getting nailed by a coaster cart. Don't get the workshop DLC either. They should have come with the base game and thier are better mods that add these things in for free.

The Hellfire armor has no story, nor does the Chinese Stealth Armor. The worst thing on Creation Club is the Doom gear. It has no reason to exist, as it is from another game and frankly looks awful.
The weapons, other than Far Harbor, this is the only redeeming quality of the game. The weapons, armor, and power armor modding is amazing. The gunplay is very smooth. But that is not the focus of an RPG. Fallout New Vegas has smooth gunplay and amazing RPG elements.
Fallout 4 is really just a FPS, after all Bethesda worked with Doom Devs as well.

I haven't played very far into this game (see below for why), but man. I was a huge fan of the original Carrier Command back on my Mac Classic computer, and I was excited to see someone remade it. Until I actually tried to play this mess of a game.
The game starts with a literally 45-minute-long inexplicable Halo-ripoff first-person shooter section that has absolutely nothing to do with Carrier Command and serves only to confuse the bejeezus out of players. It's also, frankly, not very good at all.
If you get past that obstacle, you do finally get into the carrier's captain's seat, you know, that thing that should have happened in the first 30 seconds of the game. However, here the game somehow gets even worse.
Your first mission is to take over an enemy island. Ok, fine, that's like 75% of the original Carrier Command's gameplay, so I should feel right at home here. To do so you move the carrier to the island. (Which, BTW, takes ages-- the game supposedly accelerates time, but even despite that it takes a solid few minutes to arrive.) Once there, you equip a Walrus amphibous vehicle with your only command center hacking took and get onto the island.
Once there, you have to squint to find the white-on-light-blue waypoint markers the game uses to tell you where to go, assuming you notice them at all which I didn't for the longest time because they're so goddamned invisible. The Walrus you get lands with almost no fuel, so you first have to find a fuel station. It took me a long time to get past this because the tutorial never tells you:
1) What the fuel station looks like (hint: lightning bolt icon)
2) That you have to use F to "activate" it and actually refuel. I assumed I was doing it wrong because I was sitting there for ages and nothing happened.
Once you've finished that obstacle, your next task is to enter the command center. If you take the direct path, you end up falling down a cliff, destroying the only hacking unit thing, and getting a Game Over. Seriously. This game could not have been playtested even one bit.
During your next play through, you telepathically realize you’re supposed to continue down a road that looks on the map like it goes in the entirely opposite direction you want to go. When you do arrive at the command center, a force field seals it off, and here’s where the tutorial really goes off the rails.
You have two Walruses and two buttons you have to hit at the same time. The solution is obviously to position one Walrus at each button, then press the buttons quickly to open the force field. The problem is: the second Walrus always follows the first one on autopilot when you switch! So it’s virtually impossible to get them positioned correctly! There are also a lot of quirks the game never tells you about—for example when you get into a Walrus you can’t actually steer it until you tap the throttle with W or S on the keyboard. Until you accidentally discover that, you’ll probably just assume the game is broken like I did. Again: no playtesting whatsoever.
I did manage to finish this challenge mostly by accident. Then the tutorial voiceover lady tells you to drive into the command center, quickly get close to the building, and hit the F key to begin hacking. If you do that, you of course get another Game Over, because it’s the entirely wrong thing to do. What you need to do is go slowly, extremely slowly, past the base defenses because it turns out that while you’re hacking, if you get hit by even a single bullet, your progress is reset to zero. There's no point to even starting the hacking until you've taken out all of the robots and turrets defending the base. Of course the game doesn’t tell you this, and of course you assume the tutorial text is correct, so of course you get another Game Over. Then you come here to Steam and write a review of this worthless garbage game.
I spent 40 minutes on the first damned mission and wasn’t able to complete it. Partly because the tutorial text doesn’t tell you important things you need to know. Partly because what the tutorial text *does* tell you is a lie. And partly because the AI actively fights against you when you’re trying to complete the level.
Unbelievable garbage.

This game is exactly what I've been looking for since growing out of Warcraft III more times than I'm comfortable to admit. I personally feel it has more in common with WC than AOE, but maybe it's just a good blend and so it's needless to say that I'm one happy customer!
The reasons I'm happy about my purchase are;
- The atmosphere is next level immersive, from the sounds to the visuals of, serene forest landscapes, snow and blizzards etc.. so beautifully done.
- The AI unlike in games from yesteryear aren't nearly as stupid (unit single handedly following an army back to their base etc)
- It appears the game designers have taken out the hard work of over micro-managing to mix things up with their own parameters which also create a sense of deceptive simplification whilst paving way for more actual strategic play.
- The size of this game is under 1gb meaning no one who isn't as privillaged as to have giant download limits misses out.
- The graphics look fantastic and run quite fine on lower spec machines which again means nobody misses out. I'm personally running a R7 250x and only occasionally experience a bit of lag (namely when the seasons change from snow to greenery)
- Emphasis on village/base creation always makes me feel more attached to the play
- Overall I'm happy about the uniqueness of the play experience and surprising difficulty!
What I believe could be improved;
- The WC fanboy in me would like to see some leveling up of heroes and potentially even allowing multiple heroes per player. Levelling up generally occurs by taking out foes and acquiring experience points.
- Villagers who've been doing a task like farming or chopping wood shouldn't have to walk all the way back to a house or town centre before being allowed to repair something that was right next to where they where.. usually you're taken away from watching them do this and they end up foraging until you come back to them, in the mean time your defence tower is nearly burned to the ground..
- I'm only new to the game, but in the 4+ hours in which I played multiple games yesterday, I found few indicators to whom's 'winning' which left for a rather anti-climatic finish to an otherwise immersive and involved game.
Despite these few shortfalls, I'm still inclined to give this game 4/5 stars. I can't wait to play it with some friends. Enjoy!

Bastion is a charming little game that easily captures your heart as you battle your way through the ravaged world of Caelondia in order to rebuild the Bastion.  As you find shards that restore pieces of the Bastion you will be able to build various buildings that assist you in customizing your character and the way you play the game.  And it's this customization that makes Bastion a novelty to play, offering a unique experience many other isometric action RPG's fail to deliver.
The first thing you'll notice about Bastion is it's stylized hand drawn environments which piece themselves together as you move through the level giving it a personality uniquely its own.  This is further reinforced by the marvellous voice acting of the 'Stranger' as he narrates your progress through the game world making it feel as if you were sitting by a warm camp fire as your Grandpa tells a story of dreams and fantasy.
Without much delay though you’re smashing your way through environments and enemies alike.  The combat in Bastion is smooth and intuitive enabling you to smash, block and shoot your way around waves of diverse enemies achieving some pretty giddy feats of accomplishment narrowly avoiding that gasbags sliding strike.  The only annoying instance I occasionally had was with blocking the wrong targets even though I was aiming elsewhere, but this generally only happened in 'Dream' dungeons.
After clearing an area a shard can be placed in the Bastion enabling a building or upgrade to be built.  These building's really make Bastion a great experience as they provide weapon upgrades to suit different playstyles, shrines which allow the player to tailor their own difficulty curve and in-game achievements to earn more creds to upgrade those weapons faster.  There are other buildings but they provide bonuses we're typically used to seeing in games like a 'buffs' building for example.
Depending on what shrines you use and how far you delve into the 'Dream' and 'Proving Ground' areas will generate approximately 5-7 hours’ worth of game time on a single run.  But with various other weapon combo's to try and new shrines unlocked this game can easily retain you for a further 2-3 run throughs especially with the fantastic narration this game has.
So in summary, Bastion is a wonderful story set in a beautifully unique world that offers immersive gameplay that can be tailored to suit your desired skill level as you play.  With a minimum 5 hours of content you won't be disappointed by buying this game.

I dedicate this review to the German media censorship program. If you are German, and you've seen some of their work such as the first Terminator movie or the Fallout games, then you will know what to expect from a low-violence edition. In places, the games assets feel out of place and just plain random, when you have a plate of swordfish-heads facing upward, begging to have a bad guy thrown into them. When you realize that you wont be performing these brutal yet entertaining finishers, you will notice the absence of combat variety due to this absence aswell, and all I can say is that this is a bloody shame for German videogamers, as they are missing out.
With no more restraints, let's continue with the review.
In this chinese Grand Theft Auto with less smooth controls and the typical wrong-side-of-the-road nonsense, you play as the bland badass-cop-gangster from the latest attempt of a crime thriller by a freelance fiction author. You get to experience such fun things as physics-defying pedestrians that decide to do backflips when so much as scratched by the player; visuals from the current generation of video game consoles (that means somewhat two generations behind current PC standards); wonderfully absolutely not balanced gun combat, including a variety of six weapons in total; and last but not least, warping space and time as you hover 20 meters vertically to roundhouse-kick some goon in the face, spraying him with low-rez blood in the process.
This is a very fun set of activities, and although the game does lack some variety, it quite definitely is a good take on the genre in a different and new setting - including decent challenge, writing, graphics and a fantastic overworld.
You will most likely have a good time if you go into the game with medium expectations and fancy a mix between driving, freerunning, melee- and gun combat and some gore.

Sleeping Dogs has never been a game at the top of my must play list, to me it was just another GTA clone. But with the latest Humble Bumble package that it was included with, I thought why not give it a go.I’m glad I did too, as its not at all what I expected. Yes its an open world sandbox game, but that’s pretty much where the similarity’s end. In Sleeping Dogs you wont find yourself taking on hundreds of police witha machine gun and RPG, you wont be stealing cars constantly ether. Sleeping Dogs is very much a re-imagining of the genre.
Sleeping Dogs puts you in the role of an undercover cop trying to rather successfully infiltrate the triads, the twist being your never completely sure that he hasn’t turned. The character grew up inthe neighborhood and many of your missions involve people he grew up with. It adds an interesting layer to the story, your not just finding out about other characters but also yourself.
The Hong Kong that Sleeping Dogs puts you in is not the biggest map out there but its densely populated and really gives the impression of a living breathing city. A lot of work has gone into it and itreally shows, the best example being the night market that you spend much of the start of the game in. People browse the stalls, have conversations, interact with each other and you. At times its easy to forget your missionand get drawn into it all.
The missions are good, they make you feel like your watching a gangster film. That’s probably because you’ll spot many elements taken from such films. But I’m not complaining about that, there well
put together and flow. The side missions tend to vary from the average too, instead of for instance taxi missions or pimp missions like the other big titles you will be doing favors for people. These favors could
be doing free running or stopping a thief and even singing karaoke. But there are racing missions and fight clubs like most sandbox’s.
Sleeping Dogs offers the player an upgrade system that’s quite unique too, there are three areas to upgrade. The first is Triad, the experience for this skill are earned through doing triad missions
and criminal acts. The second is Police where the reverse is true, this makes the player walk a tightrope of sorts trying to stay clean while being a criminal. The last skill is Face, this is increased by improving peoples
view of you through favors and such. Its also worth noting though not a skill per-say you can also improve your fighting skills through finding lost Jade statues for the local gym owner.
And talking of the fighting, Sleeping Dogs does a great job with this, I’ve hear some compare it to the Arkham games but I disagree. The combat is far more methodical and slower paced. If you go in throwing punches willy nilly the game will punish you, you’ll find yourself waiting for counters and then throwing a few attacks in and back to waiting again. This might sound boring, but when playing its very inviting and seems to fit the whole style of the game well.
This game try’s hard to be different from the rest, it succeeds well too. You can steal a car, but you can’t keep it. Your garage is for purchased cars only. You can use guns, but only carry hand
gun concealed and most of the time you will be using hand to hand combat. The game feels fresh and new, but its not perfect by any means.
My one biggest gripe with this title is the driving, now its not terrible by any means but feels stiff and not natural. Its certainly better than some games I’ve played, but its not really fun its functional.
The controls could be laid out better and the ability to jump from car to car seems out of place. But its not a huge issue and shouldn’t put you off playing it. The other issue is the camera, the camera seems to go crazy when reversing a car. It puts it self in some of the least helpfull possisions. But thankfully you probably wont be reversing too much so it shouldn’t give you too much trouble.

For the cantonese speakers out there, this is an excellent game as more often than not you don't really hear that many convincing cantonese sounding accents like anywhere other than in HK opera itself. I also IMDB'd this game and there are surprisingly a lot of high profile actors that voice in this game, for instance Emma Stone! and Lucy Liu!
This game reminds me of a lot of triad deep cover cop movies like Infernal Affairs movies made in HK, in which this game actually nods its head to. The story is pretty standard in the way the Triad fueds and internal fighting pan out, but the novelty for me is that i've never seen it done in a game before and it reminds me a lot of blood opera type films which i grew up with.
The gameplay is pretty fluid in mostly melee combat and it's very Batman Akrham like, which is only a good thing as the combat system in that is pretty awesome. I love breaking bones and countering in this and i love it when the enemies flinch because you've just broken someone's bones. Of course there's a slowmo jumping over counters stuff which is the stuff of any blood opera included too.
As far as EXP and levelling, the face system which is a term used a lot in anything chinese, nets you additional perks and unlocks new clothes that have attributed boneses. You can also level as a cop or triad, which give you different skills to perform in combat.
You can also drive of course being on the GTA engine, and why wouldn't you be able to perform drive bys and things like that? These come as standard you'll be glad to know.
Overall i'm not sure if it's brings anything new to the table that GTA does, but i find the story extremely gratifying, fun and enjoyable with all the sides! Even though the story itself isn't fresh for anyone who watches triad type films coming out of HK, it's amazing to see it actually play on a game, so this game really stands out for me and i would love to see a sequel.

I was really, really patient with this one. I honestly was.
I even played it right up to what turned out to be - upon quick consultation of a walkthrough - a room mere MINUTES away from the final boss battle. A room full of platforms one has to jump across, with fiery death awaiting just below. A room which was not the first but the SECOND of such rooms, in quick succession to each other; in a game which had precisely NO tricky jumping bits PRIOR to these moments. But most importantly...a room which was SEVERAL MINUTES away from the last save or checkpoint.
And what did I do? I misjudged one of the jumps, and died. And frankly, found myself lacking the will to try again. EVER. AGAIN.
Up until that point, I was going to sum this game up in one word: "fine". No great shakes, certainly lacking in ambition...but y'know..."fine". "Okay". "Passable". And I'm still going to use those words, if only because when a game is this simplistic and repetitious, does it really matter that I didn't actually SUFFER through the final boss battle - which looked awfully like, y'know, a pretty standard final boss battle - and merely WATCHED it in a video walkthrough? I don't think it would have enriched my life greatly to actually finish the game; though I do believe that passing on such an honour has left me short at least one whole Achievement.
Oh well. Sometimes life is tough, but we must all endure. Sometimes we must look our failures unerringly in the face, and say: "I am still a worthwhile human being. Even though I lacked the patience to REPLAY THAT STUPID ♥♥♥♥ING FIVE TO TEN MINUTES OF DEMENTIUM II HD, just to fight SOME ♥♥♥♥ING STUPID WORM CREATURE WHICH SOMEHOW, BAFFLINGLY CONSTITUTES THE FINAL NEMESIS OF A "PSYCHOLOGICALLY"-THEMED HORROR GAME SET IN AN ASYLUM...does not mean that I am not a worthwhile entity in the scope of the universe. I still have a valid contribution to make, even if it won't be GETTING THAT STUPID ♥♥♥♥ING ACHIEVEMENT. But hey...I still have all the hair on my head. And that's more important, to have a full head of hair than to TEAR IT ALL OUT BECAUSE SOME STUPID ♥♥♥♥ING THRIFT-SHOP GAME DESIGNERS COULDN'T BE BOTHERED STICKING ANY ♥♥♥♥ING SAVE POINTS ANYWHERE NEAR THE CLIMAX. I am...still valid...worthwhile...deep breaths...deep breaths..."
Funny thing is, up to that point, one of my main "complaints" about the game was going to be that it was a tiny bit too easy. I mean, I had 4 medkits and 14 bottles of pills on me when I died. But did all this healing I'd saved up during the rest of the game save me from dying when I fell into the flames? Noooooooo. And what about that ridiculous amount of ammo I'd conserved...could I maybe use that to...FIGHT the flames as they devoured my body? Noooooooooooooooooo. Am I ever liable to play this rather shoddy (and not exactly "HD"-looking) Nintendo DS port again? ♥♥♥♥ nooooooooooooooooooooooooooooo. And I wouldn't recommend anyone else doing so for the princely sum of fifteen dollars, either.
But if you're a glutton for punishment, and don't mind wasting a bunch of hours on a game haunted by the ghosts of the countless similar yet superior games which have trodden these well-worn floors so many times before, it MIGHT be worth picking up in a sale for a fiver. MIGHT. The funeral is yours (or cremation, should you happen to die in the exact same spot that I did).

After 5 years of development, Starbound is damningly mediocre. A promising but flawed early access and tremendously successful kickstarter campaign lead many of us to believe there was a great foundation in place for a fantastic game to emerge from, but very little has improved for the better--in fact, if anything, Starbound has gotten
Starbound's basic gamplay is supposedly that of Terraria. Beam down to a procedurally generated planet and dig for resources to upgrade yourself with, fending off the assaults of strange enemies and possibly stumbling upon cool equipment in chests that augment your abilities in some way. You soon unlock the ability to fly to other planets, where you can find new materials--provided you have the equipment to survive there.
This all seems promising, of course; "Terraria in space" sounds awesome and was indeed the premise that was sold to many of us during the kickstarter/early acces... but Starbound fails to make these basic mechanics feel particularly entertaining or rewarding.
The experience of mining is where the first flaws become apparent. Starbound makes the promise to the player that their main mining tool, the Matter Manipulator, is able to extract any ore in the game provided you can reach it. Like many things in Starbound, this sounds awesome until you discover that Chucklefish decided this should mean you ought to be unable to actually find rarer ores on planets you can survive on for more than a few seconds without the appropriate gear.
Thus becomes apparent a strict, calculated, linear "tier" system of progression. You can't mine Titanium because the only resources on the planets in your starting planet are Coal, Copper, Silver, Iron and Gold, so you need to leave your starting system... but you can't leave your starting system because you need fuel for your ship. You can't mine fuel for your ship because there's no atmosphere on the moons it appears on, so you need to build an oxygen tank... but you can't build an oxygen tank because it requires tungsten, which only appears on desert planets, which are distinct from the lush starting planet you spent the last 2 hours digging around looking for Titanium on. This basic cycle of ~tier progression~ iterates multiple times until you can at last land on frozen and volcanic planets. You'll never find the next metal you need on the planets currently accessible to you, or by any other means. You'll always need to get some environmental augment to survive for more than a handful of seconds on the new type of planet. There's no reason to map out a cave you've dug or build rapid transport around a planet because you'll only be there until you've extracted X amount of ore Y and will then be moving on to the next planet.
Mining itself is boring. The worldgen leaves much to be desired; you'll be spending most of your time boring through solid rock, and the rest of it eyeballing the inky darkness below trying to find out whether or not that fall will instantly kill you. Monsters are pretty rare underground and are little more than annoyances. Also, you don't get a map, which is extremely lame in a mining game.
In addition, Chucklefish has implemented a new Survival character type, and new characters default to it! This ruleset causes you do lose 30% of all your money AND drop all your ores (and possibly upgrade materials) on death, and forbids you from warping back to your ship from underground (you'll always need to climb back out of whatever you dig). The death penalty in particular means you can potentially lose hours work with an accidentally missed jump!
To Starbound's credit, there are a lot of cool and fun things that exist as peripheral to the game's core mechanics. There are hundreds of goofy costumes, janky hover bikes that amusingly bump and crash their way over planets, loads of charmingly animated props and furniture, a pokemon-like system where you can capture monsters and use them as minions, recruitable crew members, instruments that can play user-provided MIDI files, and a lot more. The implementation of this cool stuff appears to be where the majority of Starbound's development time has gone, and that would have been fine if the basic systems in the game were entertaining enough to hold water.
In summary, Starbound does achieve the goal of being Terraria in space.... except it's Terraria circa 2011, a very crude and basic game produced in a short amount of time on a shoestring budget whose true potential would later be realized by dozens of fantastic, free updates post release. Starbound's millions upon millions of kickstarter dollars and 5 years' development time might lead you to believe it would be at the very least competitive with the Terraria of 2016 (which still manages to be 2/3rds the price), but you would be wrong.

It's Fallout 4. Like most Bethesda games, it not a shining example of what the state of the industry should be. There are bugs, glitches, poor AI, poorly writen stories, less than stellar voice acting, etc. Dispite all of this I have sinked 293 hours into the game and plan to sink another 100+ in the coming weeks.
The game gives you an interesting open world to play around in with fun senanarios and some interesting characters to interact with. You can play the game multiple different ways, non of which are flawlessly implemented but do the job well enough to get some enjoyment out of.
Currently many players are mad about mod support, which I support them, Bethesda should support the community that has supported them for so long. I for one don't use mods (I know right? I'm crazy...) and find the base game completely enjoyable, but of course, its not without flaws.
All that said, Fallout 4 is probably the best implemented(it has very few game breaking bugs) of all the games released by Bethesda, and from that, I can have faith that they are at least trying to tighten up there games for the future. I love Fallout 4 dispite the some times glaring issues and hope that the quality gets better in later releases from Bethesda.

Abyss: The Wraiths of Eden offers everything one can want in a hidden object puzzle game: a good story, fluent game flow, interesting puzzles, nice graphic design. A definite grab if you like this genre.
There are hidden object games that try to ascend the limits of their genre to stand out. Abyss: The Wraiths of Eden chose to be good in the known game elements instead.
Although the story is just a mishmash of Bioshock and Cthulhu, it is an almost perfect mixture. It is engaging, features genuinely good twists, and has a realistic, interesting main character. The only real downside is the voice acting, it is spectacularly bad even by hidden object standards.
The puzzles themselves are spread out evenly and offer a steady progression. They require a fair amount of backtracking, but the map design doesn’t make you feel like you are walking around endlessly. The hidden object scenes are drawn well, although they have a few problems, especially if the required item is in the water.
I also have to mention the bonus chapter: not only it gives you great insight of the main story, but it even puts one of the side characters in the limelight, adding even more depth to the game.

I want to like this game. I really want to.
When I saw the concept of a strategy games with highly customizable units that you can control by yourself, I was amazed. The graphics are nice - nothing awe-inspiring, but they more than suffice. The scenery on multiple occasions looks like you'd want to go on a holiday there. I lost quite a few units just staring into a magnificent sunset over an idyllic archipelago, not noticing how a hostile attack chopper moved in to engage. The guys designing the islands really put a lot of effort into making the islands beautiful and fun to drive over in first person.
Engaging the enemy requires moving with care, you need to manage the ammunition and fuel of your units and be on guard for counterattacks, which makes for a nice challenge - so far, Carrier Command: Gaea Mission seemed like a great revival of an old classic to me.
Where the game lost me was the tank/APC AI. That's not an artificial intelligence, it's an artificial stupidity. Your ground units are apparently incapable of doing proper pathfinding while not on the dirt roads on the island. they fail to engage clearly visible enemies and often cause more damage to allied units than to the enemy.
The aiming when controlling a vehicle feels like the most sloppy console port I have ever played, sucking the fun out of controlling units yourself after less than 30 minutes - which is just made worse by the fact that you *have* to do that since there is no AI that could do it.
To make matters worse, the endgame is incredibly bothersome and dragged out to the point where you just stop playing after a certain point, because there is no real motivation to keep going. What you do will always be the same, you can outplay the enemy with ease and take an entire Island with a single fighter when fully equipped, but still cave to land and refuel a dozen times. At that point, the game stops being fun and slows down to a painfully slow grind.
I really like the concept. I really like the scenery. I like the way the units were designed. I like how it feels if you mount a massive howitzer on every single of your vehicles and simultaneously open fire on a docked enemy carrier and watching it burst into flames trying to escape. I like how it feels to finally defeat the heaviest type of island defence grid there is.
But Everything else about this game is just so much off.
If this game would allow your friends to join your game, take control of a unit and seize an island together, this game would be much more fun. If the AI could actually put up a fight, making it unnecessary to just spam units at you, it would be so much more fun. If the controls were responsive and not so prone to oversteering, fighting inside a controlled unit would be so much less exhausting.
But it sadly isn't like that.
If some dev reads this, please see if you can somehow try to do something about it. Everything I see in this game screams of the passion, enthusiasm and heart you poured into this game, and I think I can see what you hoped it could become - and I'm to this day still dreamy about it. If you think you can fix some of the issues with this game, please give it a try - I am certain this game is worth it.
But until then, I sadly can't in good faith recommend this game to anyone just stepping by looking through the steam store.
Maybe you don't mind the grind, maybe you are okay with an AI that needs a guiding hand 75% of the time, and maybe you're not bothered that much by the things that bothered me so much, and you love games with good scenery that make you want to take a screenshot to print on a postcard - in that case, this game might be something for you.
But before you really choose to spend money on it, be aware that this game has some big flaws.

This is a fantastic arena shooter that is a very strong throwback to the Quake III/Unreal Tournament days. The twist is that instead of being able to select from different weapon varieties, you get to select from (so far) eight different monster characters, each one specializing in their own weapon varieties and style of play. The player selects and changes between them using the scroll up and down mouse wheel just like you would with weapon selection. As it stands right now, you start each match as a Crusader knight with a rapid fire machine gun-like cross bow, and quickly collect icons that allow you to transform into a King Kong ape looking monster, Creature from the black lagoon fish monster, Nosferatu vampire character, some crab looking creature, a wolf man, ect. ect. It's great and so much fun. The big problem for me is that there isn't a large player community right now. It's a shame because it's such a hidden gem. This game definitely needs more publicity. Hopefully the addition of bots and more maps when it happens will stimulate and grow the player community. Great job developers and programmers. This game is fantastic!

Slightly worse than the original's Binding of Isaac-soundtrack though I wouldn't say it's bad. It's just...there's nothing good to say about it either .
Graphics: 7/10
The design looks all in all pretty clean, all in all better than the original. Nothing ground breaking though.
Presentation: 7.5/10
In the end "The Binding of Isaac - Rebirth" made something quite good out of the weak story. We have different characters with some lore behind every one of them, the different dungeons dish out an uneasy vibe design-wise and there are lots of endings to unlock. The deeper the player goes down the basement, the better it gets.
Gameplay: 10/10
Okay,no question about that. The gameplay IS the absolute main selling point of "The Binding of Isaac - Rebirth".
- The character's movement is like butter.
- The game is challenging but at all times fair. It seems unfair at first but after a while, when you've learned the pattern of monsters and which item does what, you'll get easily used to each run.
- You WILL NOT finish it below the 100 hour mark. Dpending on your skill it can take up 150 hours, maybe 300.
- There are daily challenges to compete with other players in highscore and finish time.
- Mods. A lot of them. Good ones. You don't even need the Afterbirth+ expansion as long as you're looking through the Modding of Isaac-website.
- If you're not satisfied with the content then add a bunch more with the two expansions.
Though I've to add two things I don't like: For once there's way too much RNG to get to Mega Satan. If you need to get to him you most likely won't most of the time.
The second thing is the newest and final superboss Delirium. The way it moves and teleports there's some sort of luck you need not to get hit. It really feels like a bugged boss.
Replayability: HIGH
The whole game centers around replaying the game and in hindsight unlocking new stuff to play the game anew. With the sheer amount of content, in that regard it might be one of the best games

McPixel is pretty short but quite funny if you enjoy raunchy nonsense.
Definitely not everyone's sense of humour but I can't imagine anyone being that upset about the price tag. That is, if it were on sale. I believe the regular price on this game is $5 at the moment  and if you want to support the developer that's your prerogative. My advice would be to spend less than that on it though.
Each level is a different scenario that puts the responsibility of preventing an explosive from detonating (or equivalent disaster). A mouse only game, you click on one of the various items in the scenario, McPixel interacts with it, and you hope for the best. The humour usually lies in what happens if McPixel DOESN'T prevent the disaster.
There are several levels to play through and in each one two endings to aim for, either a win or specifically funny outcome. The whole game can be completed in a relatively short sitting, maybe 3 hours of straight play. I wouldn't recommend this though since the quickly moving and sometimes flashing backgrounds can be hard on the eyes. The music can also become grating since it repeats mostly the same one track. A saving grace may be that the first time you hear that track you will probably like it.
In summation it is a fun experience and I would recommend this to a friend who isn't offended by the idea of a man pleasuring a giraffe to completion. Still, the $5 price tag may cause buyers remorse especially if you don't smile at the idea of manual giraffe gratification. Buy it for less.

Bastion is a short but meaningful game. Bastion follows the story of a nameless protagonist who survives "the calamity" which was a huge world shattering event that put whats left of the world as floating islands in the sky. In order to restore whats left of the world you look for pieces to a new home called the Bastion. The combat in the system is quite fun with dodging rolls that function similar to in Kingdom Hearts. There are a plethora of weapons and special abilities to choose from in order to suit your playstyle. Due to how short the game is the story is somewhat lacking, the main protagonist is somewhat of a blank slate with little to no backstory or development other than the narrator explaining what happens. The side characters feel hardly invested in by the end of the story as they were only put into it about a few hours back (with one exception being the narrator/stranger). Overall though, the fun combat style and interesting customization helps make Bastion a short but enjoyable experience.

I bought and played the original Dementium games years ago when they came out on the Nintendo DS. I loved these games because unlike many indie survival horror games that use cheap jump-scares, these games heavily utilized the environment to unsettle the player, similar to Silent HIll (the player is even taken to another world while he searches for his wife). So I was excited when I heard they were going to make and HD port, unfortunately, this port was not made by the original dev team, and it shows.
This port has "cleaned up" all the visuals, the environments are not as dirty and rusty as they were. At points it even has a cartoony look to it, taking away any unsettling feeling the original gave off. The indoor areas are suppose to be the scariest part due to them being dark and the player would rely on the flashlight, yet here they're bright enough to not even need the flashlight, worse still, most of them give off sunlight through the windows or cracks. The weapons feel weaker, they don't have the same kick. During some cutscenes, only one side of the speakers gave off any audio. If you wanna know how much the visuals were "cleaned up", simply look at the box arts between the original and this HD port.
The original is a great indie survival horror game, this port undoes most of the visuals the original did so beautifully. I recommend buying the original on the Nintendo DS or getting an emulator.

I rate the game Sanctum 2 3.5/5. Pretty good.
Essentially, this is a tower defense game with a twist; The whole game takes place from a first person perspective and once the towers are built you get in on the action and play it like a cooperative multiplayer FPS game. You can go it alone and try to play through the whole game by yourself if you want to but that's a lot less fun and oftentimes, is a whole lot harder. I always began public matches which anyone could join if they wanted to, playing through the game pretty much systematically from beginning to end. With the help of other players, I played through all the DLC/add-on content also. I had an extremely fun time but if it hadn't been for running into some nice people and a few lucky breaks it could have easily been pretty frustrating.
The Good:
+This game has a good community. The other players are generally friendly and helpful, particularly if you do what I did and let higher-level players do what they want (they usually know what they are doing too) and defer to them to give you advice and help, at least until you rank up also. If you try to be cooperative and friendly and relaxed this game can often help foster some great feelings of camaraderie and mutual accomplishment and led to me adding two people to my steam friends list who I met through this game.
+The graphics are pretty good especially if you like comic-book styled clean graphics. Think Borderlands 2 except less messy looking, wherein everything is clean and new. The tropical-futuristic settings are at least nifty but more often are awe-inspiring (though the environments are not destructible and are generally lacking a great deal of interactivity. The nice environs are mostly just backdrops for what are essentially tower-defense arenas. The lighting is usually so bright that this game could be easily played in a very well-lit room.
+This game has a wonderful variety of unlockable weapons, gun turrets and special abilities. Generally I dislike unlockables in games but this game did a good job, automatically unlocking more stuff as my experience rank increased. The game has 50 levels of experience and I only achieved level 33 (or something like that) by the time I finished it. You can go back and play through each level with harder settings at any time if you wish to level up even further (and so unlock more abilities and stuff) causing this game to have some good replayability (though I wish the game had more levels/arenas to fight in than it does and hence more story to encourage me to play even further. Indeed I feel that, as good and as varied as this game is, it could have had even more levels and even more variety.
+Although push-to-talk is a feature I've seen in other games it seemed very well suited for this game (if you dont mind sounding like stephen-hawking whenever you chat with someone).
+Very, very few bugs and the game never froze up for me.
The Mediocre:
+/- As this game is not an extremely new game there are not a great many people still playing it. It's not uncommon to still run into 2 or 3 people at a time though and since the maximum number of players per map is just 4, you will get to play fairly closely with whoever does happen to show up.
+/-As this game is getting old most of the other players you will find are already hardened, die-hard, veteran fans ranked at level 50 (the maximum level) and as a new person you will often feel like you are contributing relatively little to the battles. However, this game is made to be played cooperatively with others and can become frustrating in places if you try certain missions by yourself as the difficulty is sometimes simply too high for individual play. More players means the game throws more enemies at you but generally having more players still makes the game much easier.
+/- The music is mostly mediocre (but it is good in a few places) and the sound is consistently mediocre and the stuff characters automatically say can get fairly repetitive after 30 hours of playing this game.
+/-There is great enemy variety and they exhibit a good range of behaviors but they also look sort of like a 50/50 combination of cuteness and ugliness. The enemies have a very weird style to them and I personally didn't care for the style much.
+/- The story is told through sleek anime-styled pages which allow you to read them quickly without keeping anyone else in the match waiting for too long. However, the background for this game's story is, for the most part, pretty unclear and you are left to your own devices if you want to figure out what is going on or what the meaning of anything is. There definitely feels like a very fleshed-out backstory should exist but it isn't overtly told to you at any time.
+/- The action is fun, frenetic, frantic and gets highly repetitious. I found that this game was best to play for 1 or 2 matches at a time only.
The Bad:
-Some levels can be so difficult (particularly some of the DLC levels) that you really need some high level players with you to complete them and yet you will probably be a fairly low rank by the time you unlock those levels. This leads to a sense of terrible stagnation and frustration which almost caused me to move on to a different game at one point.
-The ending of the main game is a bald-faced cliff-hanger and the final DLC has a bittersweet ending.

What is Starbound? Well it's that time of year again where I revisit some old games and I revisited Starbound! What can I say?
I've followed Starbound a long time. A real long time. Since before the alpha I was enthralled by the game's personality, and wanted to see if just maybe it could deliver on translating that personality into a big, sandboxy romp of a good time. Well, the verdict is: no.
There are why's and reasons I'm sure Chucklefish could give, but as far as I'm concerned, the game isn't much more engaging than day one of the beta. Less so, probably, because in this 'complete' state, my naive optimism is quashed.
Starbound is an amalgemation of decent ideas with no follow-through. The most interesting aspects of the game, the alien races, exploration, building... they all feel somehow lackluster. Starbound is a big puddle with no depth. Now puddles can be fine to splash in, but Starbound promised more than a puddle. The game disposed of all its interesting concepts, all of its unique characterization of alien races, all of its everything in favor of a bland storyline and less-than-stellar (heh) gameplay.
Combat isn't particularly interesting, the races have all blended together thanks to the soul-crushingly generic Protectorate, their lore and settlements are no deeper than they were on day 1 of the beta, and worse, many of them have lost a lot of what made them unique and interesting.
Beneath Starbound, there is Starbound -1. All the promise and interesting concepts, a game of wasted art and writing assets buried by rushed development and an inability to commit to a project. Like a highschooler throwing together a collection of short writings when they realize that writing a full novella is difficult and their motivations and inspirations are fluid. All buried underneath what we got.
And that's a shame. Chucklefish mismanaged their time, their money, and their priorities. And the product they provided was a tragedy of overpromising and underachieving.

One of the most appreciated aspects of the game though, is how well it handles multiplayer. Most games desync all the time because I live in a apartment complex with 12 suites, each with their own wireless router, on top of my tower being opposite of the breaker panel in the wall. This game refuses to cause rage-inducing problems and made playing with friends actually fun instead of frustrating (Looking at YOU Risk of Rain.)
In short: This game may not have the sheer amount of stuff that Terraria does, but it easily makes up for it in many other areas.

Abyss: The Wraiths of Eden is a Hidden Object Game.
The adventure backdrop is fine, the areas are rendered with great details and the hidden object scenes are even in Expertmodus quite simple. Instead of Hidden-Object Riddles you might also opt to play a kind of Domino to solve the HOG. The riddles in the game are also quite simple and none of the riddles required a deeper explanation than a simple sentence.
The story of the game is mysterious, and sinister. I like mysteries, and I love lovecraftian horror - but even with some hints in this direction the game has overdone it in a way that in the end all is only ridiculous.
This is no "Nancy Drew" game, that is for sure, and the riddles are much less challenging than any of the Nancy Drew game series. Still it is a decent HOG-Game, and sure something that fans of that genre can't wait to dig their teeth into.
Even though I am sceptical about this genre, it was a pleasing - even if at times insultingly ridiculous - game. Of course they are short casual games, but that is - what they were made for.
Graphics: 7/10 (Adventure style graphics with some artistic sights)
Sound: 8/10 (A fitting soundtrack to the game, that is fitting to the game)
Playability: 7/10 (It is fun to play it through once, and try out the two other modes of game - but once played through, they soon loose their ... color?)
Story: 6/10 (Ok Story, a bit far-fetched. But hey it's all a fantasy, isn't it?)
Value: 6/10 (The value of the game might lie between 4 and 8 bucks, so 6,49 isn't bad at all, if you can try to get it cheaper)
Overall: 6,8 (A mediocre game, which might please friends of the genre or people who love underwater adventures)

This game is one of my all-time favorite games. I really can't say when the last time I enjoyed a game this much was. The sanctum series really took the tower defense genre is a great direction, and the feel, look, and sound of the game is stellar. The soundtrack alone is enough for me to recommend you checking it out, but thankfully this game is much more than just a beautiful package.
You've got a variety of towers, characters, passives, and weapons to select from, and each of them matters. The character you pick determines what primary you bring, but you get to choose a secondary along with it, and that secondary can be the primary of another character. Synergy is the name of the game, so there's a lot of fun to be had experimenting with different strategies for different maps and enemies. Each character plays differently and brings their own unique passive, and most every weapon, tower, and passive plays a vital role in how you effectively play the game. Stronger weakpoint hits? Looks like you'll want to bring a strong accurate weapon to abuse weakpoints while you bring another tower to make up for your lack of heavy AoE. Or maybe you'd like to bring a strong single target primary, AoE secondary, and bring only utility towers to supplement your weaponry.
The amount of experimentation that you can do in this game, along with the wide map variety and consistently fantastic soundtrack really kept me enjoying this game for dozens and dozens of hours. I've bought it every time it's been on sale just so I have copies to give to friends. I love this game that much.

Those familiar with other Bethesda 'RPGs' will be glad to learn that the clunky controls have been improved dramatically and that this game can be played fairly comfortable as an FPS. The art design, environments and animation are mostly an improvement from Fallout 3. I enjoyed the changes made to power armor. Despite some gripes I think that handling power armor like a vehicle of sorts was an overall plus. Weapon and armor customization is also a big plus.
Pretty much everything else. The story is terrible. The removal of branching dialog trees and lack of any real choice is almost painful. This game would honestly be better without a story if they just focused on making an open world sandbox. Ridiculous OP weapon drops in the guise of 'fun' are a horrible design choice for a Fallout game, especially when weapon customization is already present. The constant UI noises and animations are annoying and immersion breaking. The restructuring of the damage and radiation systems to move further from a RPG are unwelcome. The introduction to the game (tutorial) is poorly done despite being a novel idea that had merit. Building your own settlements is a complete waste of time in a single player game and simply drained resources that could have been focused (and were needed) elsewhere during development. Radiant quests are a good idea but were implemented so poorly that they should have been cut. Also the bugs.
Bethesda has a complete disregard for the lore and mechanics of the original series. Fallout 1 and 2 were far better in terms of role play, world building, implementing their mechanics and creating cohesive experiences. There was a satisfying focus on character builds in those games that significantly changed the way you played them and experienced their worlds. Bethesda completely abandons that design philosophy and the complete restructuring of the skills system is abhorrent. Unlike the original Fallouts the solution to every problem seems to be through force. No playing as a sleazy con artist or diplomatic pacifist. Everything in this game feels like it's catered toward instant gratification and has no regard to buildup or pacing, making everything ultimately unsatisfying. So many of the features feel like afterthoughts or feature creep. This game, like Fallout 3 is an amateurish piece of fan-fiction and is why I've abandoned Bethesda as a developer.
After 80+ hours and restarting the game in an attempt to find any meaningful enjoyment (which was not found) I can only recommend this game if it's on sale for $5 or less. Fallout 1, a twenty year old game is a more rewarding, varied, immersive, deeper and well thought out experience. In a landscape filled with so many great indie games that offer so much more there is no reason to bother with Fallout 4. Play the original Fallouts, pick up Underrail or Wasteland 2 or get ATOM RPG, which even in early access is still more of a true Fallout game than Bethesda could ever dream of making in it's current state. There are elements of a good game here but this is certainly not a good game.

Some games dont look like much at first, but keep you coming back for more and more without realizing why. This is one of them.
With so many top down shooters and alien themed games on Steam, why is this so good? Because the aliens are pink and glow in the dark? Thats actually cool too , but here is why you should get this game:
Game play / Game mechanics: the controls are very smooth , so is the scrolling / gameflow and motion in general, creating a very pleasing game experience. For top down shooters with "twin stick" controls ( move with one stick , aim freely with the other ) this is critical.  Not many people realize but this is usually what decides whether the game is great or terrible in this genre.
Graphics: A lot of game uses Pixelated or "retro" graphics as an excuse to do a lousy job - not this one.  The graphics look beautiful especially in the details ( lightning , character outlines and movement ... ) retaining the purpose of the type of graphics employed.
Easy to learn and simple to play: not only you can start playing a few seconds after launching the game , you will need another few to get a grip of the basic controls and maybe a couple of minutes to understand all of them.
Leaderboards: So its easy to learn and simple to play. But what about reaching the top of the leaderboards? Clever way to please competitive players and add replay value.
All these would already make this game good for anyone; Now if you are a fan of local coop or an old time gamer who enjoys playing ( physically ) together with other people or having games running when you throw in a party THIS GAME IS SIMPLY AWESOME!

Carrier Command: Gaea mission is a Real-Time Strategy game that also allows you to jump into either your air or amphibious land vehicles to capture islands with the goal being either to capture every island on the map and/or destroy your enemy's carrier, or at least that's how I understand it 6 hours in.
Like the start of a rollercoaster, you'll start to anticipate how much fun you're going to have with this game: a tech tree (albeit randomized), logistics management, the cameras that show you what your unit sees.  Then the cart flies off the tracks when the Tropic Thunder A.I. that manages your pathfinding clashes with the enemy's Skynet's A.I..  Units equipped with grenade launchers will stand still point their guns in the air upon receiving a command to attack a structure, or straight up murder your own carrier if you deploy them to chase a nearby enemy unit.  Thankfully, the air unit's A.I. is on point, and probably better than your own flight skills.
I would be amazed if you could lose an island at all to the A.I., as conquering an enemy island requires you to do a side mission, including fuse-boxing scramblers so that your units can reach the command center, or fuse-boxing firewalls so that capturing a center doesn't take five years.  It's 50/50 that your unit will reach the area and activate the point without getting stuck on a rock or tree.  Units even get tripped up on things as nebulous as water on the main map screen.  By the time you've spent half an hour taking an island the size of five minutes, the game crashes on the very next move you make.  If you won't save your money, at least save your game after every conquest you make here.
The game makes other bizzare decisions: You aren't told how long an area you've captured will be ready for production.  You can't speed up time outside of running out of gas and trying to gun it to an island anyway.  An invisible tech tree that you make random progress in when you capture an island or click a factory.
The other reviews here are accurate.  I'm not deterred by a few glitches here and there, but this game made me throw in the towel.

I'm not a big fan of fighting games, but there's always been something about Mortal Kombat that just made it more accessible than other fighting games. And it's the same with this installement, which is probably the best one I've played yet.
I played through the story mode and enjoyed myself. There's quite a lot of story going on here, with each fight having some sort of set up. However I would necessearily call it good, but it does keep up the pace even if it sometimes does feel rushed. Despite that I felt quite engaged with the story, and I'm excited for it to continue.
Having to fight the same enemies at different stages of the game just becomes repetitive. It makes you feel like your actions don't matter, so it would be nice if beating someone, actually had some effect instead of them getting up the next second your character turns their head. Whereas when the game decides that someone has to die, well then they die in pretty much one hit. It does help that there's quite a large roster of characters present, perhaps too large for the story mode since you only get glimpses into the motivations of each character. I wish that the sections where you control a single character would be expanded with even more story, then the game would feel truly epic.
It would be nice if the game offered some more help to beginners like myself. It's true that you can always pause the game and look at the move list, however the game doesn't let you practice them outside of the practice matches which are completely dull. Carrier Command: Gaea Mission is four years old, but good luck finding a game anything like it. You command a carrier, with 4 amphibious vehicles and 4 airborne helicopter-thingy's, all of which are commandable by you. You can even control them directly, taking the wheel.
Since launch, the AI was a biiig problem, but thankfully, commanding your 8 units now makes much more sense and they mostly do what you want them to do. You'll still want to jump in against some enemies to ensure they don't get chopped up but they can handle themselves for the most part.
Your job is to island hop onboard the carrier and capture the islands. The island variety is fantastic, and while enemies don't change that much, finding yourself on peculiar and different islands is a solid point in the books. It's also worth noting, the weapon and gadget variety for your vehicles is pretty good too. Nothing ground-shattering, but useful and fun.
The voice-acting is pretty bad and the storyline is paper thin, but that's really not the point. I have not been able to find a game like this and it deserves its due respect, even four years later when there's still nothing like it on the market.

I've played this game since early access. I enjoyed it then, but less so now.
My experience has been that the same mechanics and features have remained under-developed through most of its development. A trap I notice with games similar is part of how the game is deisgned. Games like this require you to progress through tiers, for example in Starbound you progress through iron to tungsten to titanium and so on, Instead of adding more to do in the iron tier it's often easier to just add another tier. While this creates more hours played, it quickly devolves into a collect-a-thon instead of an exploration game. I would have liked to see more focus on exploration and less on adding these tiers.
With the completion of the game, I notice that the largest changes have been to the story, much less with the actual features of the game. For a game like this, I would consider the story a means to access the actual meat of the game which is the exploration, base-building, and crafting. Some might like the story and that's fine, but I don't find it that important. While I have my own issues with the story, in part because it's a little uninspiring, but mostly because you can't skip the story to get at the actual gameplay. All of that can be overlooked if you have a good group of friends which leads me to my reccomendation.
I would not reccomend this game in general. There are interesting mechanics and some might be interested in the collect-a-thon aspect which I will admit is fun the first time.
I would only suggest buying this if you have a group of friends to play with, but no more than four (4) because you cannot form parties larger than that for some reason.

[Note: At the time of this writing, Starbound is at v1.0.]
I have been told once or twice in my life not to let perfect be the enemy of good. If you allow yourself to get too bogged down with what could be better, you blind yourself to the things you should appreciate. With Starbound, Chucklefish have taken this a step further and not allowed good to be the enemy of passable.
While managing to do competently everything a game in the sandbox builder genre needs to do, Starbound still lacks the organic progression from goal to goal that makes such a game stand out. The game does little to draw a player into the crafting system or compel exploration. There are plenty of hints of an entertaining fiction, though they are inconsistently delivered. Starbound frequently feels like a game where development of various aspects ceased when they reached a certain baseline of quality so as to avoid having any one thing stand out enough to contrast the weaker elements. The game has modding support through Steam Workshop, though at this point it would be pure speculation to say whether mods can complete the game experience.
To their credit, Chucklefish walked back more than a few questionable design choices that were met with player antipathy, but at the end of the day the bottom line is that there is little to capture and engross an audience. If you are a fan of the genre and want to play a new game that does more of the same, Starbound is certainly that. If you are new to the genre and want to play the best it has to offer, other options exist, most notably Terraria.

Where do I start with this game....?
I will probably be just another person telling you to buy this game but seriously you should and I will tell you why.
Lets start with the graphics....the aesthetic of Bastion is beautiful, colorful, and full of taste. Not only will Bastion's graphics hold up over time for years to come, not only should the gamer enjoy the aesthetic but the team at Supergiant Games should be proud of them. Some Gamers may disagree about the games graphics but what they can't do is ignore the amount of time, expression, and hard work that has gone into creating the world of Bastion.
Gameplay remains to be the very core of all video games made. In this department Bastion shines with wonderful action and tones of a role playing game. Bastion will control a lot like a normal game using the WASD for movement and left/right clicking for attacks. Bastion also introduces other key strokes for abilities that make the gameplay not only fun but strategic on how to tackle your enemy. By introducing new weapons with different play styles Bastion remains fresh in changing it up not too often but just enough to give the player a taste of what a new weapon is and how to use it.
Story....Where do I begin with this.....I have been playing games for a little over 20 years and can't recall off the top of my head a game that tells an amazing story in 3rd person in such a successful way as Bastion. I was not expecting this going into the game nor did I find it odd that the main character never has a voice out loud. The decisions you make will reflect the outcome of the game with a story powerful and demanding of me to finish my first playthrough within 2 days of starting! The game length is just long enough to enjoy and sink yourself into the world but not long enough to exclude the casual gamer or multiple playthroughs.
Overall I had a great time with Bastion, if anyone asks me for a recommendation or directly asks me about Bastion I would not hesitate to offer my opinion. Supergiant Games you really outdid yourself on Bastion and have gained a loyal fan to the games you create. I hope to see more from this developer in the future of gaming.
If you want my review in audio/video form check out my YouTube channel for the Bastion Review.

This is DEFINITELY a "rated M for mature" game, so don't let kids near it. That being said, it is as scary as advertised, bug-free for the most part (not entirely) except for xenomorph bugs (hee hee), & is very much a sci-fi experience, as is the intended effect. If you are in the mood for & are looking for sort of a newer-ish DOOM3 but with a team context and a somewhat realistic non-cheesy sci-fi feeling, you've come to the right game. Chris Miller of Rebellion Developments, the software developing firm that makes the game, must be extremely proud of how it turned out.
The graphics are "realistic enough" to where you feel somewhat immersed in the gameplay but the game can also even be played on older machines, as the new DOOM (Doom 4) can NOT. It is better than Red Faction: Armageddon, which seems cheesy & kidsy in my opinion. If you think the whole Aliens thing is super cool & scary you will be in to this sort of thing. A sadistic short character is featured in the game, just a heads up. This game goes well with Taco Bell & a Full Throttle energy drink, as I just discovered for myself today.
Negatives: No crouching is allowed, for some reason, & I don't know why, that is a tiny bit irritating. Especially the Alien's controls are optimized for use with a controller and so the keyboard & mouse use isn't as good. No biggie though. I think that things are maybe a little TOO dark for the Marines, in terms of plot, & that is a bit of a downer. is only my second encounter with a so-called "Hidden Object Game". It's a prime example of the quality that Artifex Mundi delivers in this particular genre of games, which can best be defined as a point-and-click adventure light with as an extra ingredient the Hidden Object-screens. Artifex Mundi delivered a really interesting game with this one, which is like an overtly hommage to
. The setting shows a lot of parallels to that of the famous and revolutionary shooter: just as in
, I found myself exploring an underwater city where an utopian society had crumbled into tyranny and civil war. Even the art déceau-style of the city is very similar in Abyss to that of Bioshock. It may be a bit too obvious for some, but it's so well done and the screens are so well-drawn and full of details, that for me it felt more a parallel reality, an alternative, to the world of Bioshock than like any sort of plagiate.
In all possible departments,
truly shines. Artifex Mundi invests a lot in putting a convincing story into their Hidden Object-games, and they certainly managed to do so in this game. They also managed to integrate the several hidden object-screens and the mostly cleverly designed puzzles very convincingly into the story. The adventuring-part of the game plays very smoothly and intuitively, helped by the minimal inventory. As far as the musical score and sound-effects are concerned: they do their job in conveying the sometimes scary atmosphere in the game. It would be too much to call this a horror-game, but there are some very rare scaring moments.
Being a collector's edition, there are quite some neat additions included, such as an extra chapter to the story and some downloadable screens. All in all, this is a very recommendable game. Hidden Object Games-lovers will certainly know that they safely can expect a high level of excellence from this company, but I'd surely recommend it as well to those gamers who haven't yet played this genre before. They may not be difficult or competitve, but certainly entertaining and addictive!

Starbound is infamous for staying docile for a long, long time, but with the 1.0 update bringing promising content, I think it's a solid time to renew our reviews, and cover Starbound at its current state. Keep in mind this is covering content up to major content update 1.0.
Gameplay has you moving across the galaxy in your little ship, exploring new planets with a variety of strange creatures and flora to discover. Starbound's impressive and large starmap allows players to find all kinds of randomly-generated planets which they can explore to the fullest extent. Jumping on to the planets, players find themselves in a side scrolling game, mixing in the qualities of adventure as you find NPCs and ancient dungeons, and throwing in the aspects of mining and resource gathering from the undergrounds. The amount of content is fairly massive, with NPCs giving you side quests, to much more large scale platformer-esque dungeons that you navigate through for loot. You feel rewarded for exploring, and you find yourself getting lost in the vast expanses of the galaxy, something that I personally, absolutely love. New weapons, gear, and ores are given at a steady pace and you never feel like you're underequipped unless you deliberately rush the game, something you really shouldn't do. This is what Starbound excels at doing. Giving the player a great experience with exploration.
Unfortunately, Starbound suffers from floaty, almost slippery controls that make you wanna jam your keyboard into your ear. It's very difficult to manuever on particularly precise platforms and you'll find yourself taking fall damage a lot. There are upgrades for your character that are somewhat early-game that allow you to double jump and nulify the awfulness of the controls but even then, it hurts to do anything with accuracy.
Building and combat are both very hit-or-miss things. Combat is interesting, I suppose, with the multitude of weaponry that you'll be able to find, but can get boring unless you're fighting one of few bosses that are strewn out your quest line. Similarly, building can be a lot of fun with how many blocks and furniture items you can find, but do require you to find those items first, something that requires a lot of searching since certain planets with certain conditions house certain dungeons with certain items.
Overall, the gameplay is more then palpable, but does require a lot of getting used to and are finicky.
I should probably cover progression in this game since, for a sandbox game, a quest line of any kind seems like some kind of disgusting heresy. The progression in this game comes in the form of quests that you can do at any time. You're not really forced to do any of the story line quests, since they don't really lock out anything in particular, but they are encouraged. The quests themselves are fairly linear (no block breaking, almost purely combat and NPC chatting), which might displease some of the more open-minded players. It's certainly not bad, but a bit strangely designed.
Most definitely a beautiful game. From the stellar treetops of a jungle planet to the vast beauty of the ocean seafloor, Starbound is able to deliver you an excellently sprited game experience that features color and variety. It's honestly what makes the Starbound experience so wonderful.
...Unfortunately those beautiful graphics also lead into the performance issues that seem to plague players. I can, personally, run this game at a solid 60 FPS at all times, but many of the less fortunate players find themselves getting lag spikes and painful framerate drops. This isn't helped by the less then stellar options menu which doesn't really help you much on keeping the performance issues down. Be wary of this, it can be unplayable due to the lack of optimization.
This is something that is almost necessary to speak out on for an Early Access game, especially one like Starbound. I love Starbound's atmosphere and concept, and the developers are certainly working with that to make a wonderful game. However, the gameplay mechanics themselves are less then stellar. With that being said, the game is still a lot of fun. I see a lot of potential in it, not from just the developers, but from the game's heart itself. If the devs continue working on it as they've been doing, it might just have a chance of really becoming something special.
At it's current state and price, Starbound is worth it. It's a fun adventure game that combines the magic of discovering something new, with the enjoyment of progressing through a variety of worlds with unique weapons and items. Build, kill, do whatever. The galaxy is yours in Starbound. Buy it, preferably with friends (It even has the four pack option!).
Hope to see more players bound for the stars.

Another terrific casual adventure from Artifex Mundi!  This one mashes up a bit of the Mythos with a whole lotta Bioshock, for a story in which you head out to rescue your undersea-explorer husband who has gone missing.  You dive at his last known location and find first a broken-down lab, and then a stark, sprawling, deserted city on the sea bottom.
The city is called Eden, not Rapture, but the principles are the same, and the explorations and puzzles that follow are tricky enough to be interesting and pliant enough to cave under pressure.  NOTE that the "Hint" button becomes a "Skip" button during puzzles, so if you are paying the wrong kind of attention, trying to figure out what the puzzle rules are can turn into a whoops-skip (this happened to me twice).

== Starbound 1.0 Review ==
FINAL SCORE: 7.5 / 10  -  So many stars, so many things to wish for
DISCLAIMER: I have finished this game already when it was in beta like a year or so ago, withh the same 2 people i finished it now.
+ Pros +
+ A whole galaxy to explore
+ Many different races, biomes and places to discover
+ Plenty of items, weapons and accessories to craft and loot
+ Build your own colony
+ Upgradeable ship, survival pack and digging tool
+ Immense crafting to do
+ Procedural side-quests
+ Many books to read to discover lore of races
- Cons -
- Short, for having been 3+ years in development. With a group of 3 people we played around 25 hours (yeah, in 2 days), and that took to get all the top-tier stuff, finish main quest and all main secondary quests, not to mention finding all biomes and dungeons.
- Lategame / endgame gear is way overpowered comapred to enemies you face, making fights really easy
- Boring and uninspired main quest, also with useless rewards compared to what you find by simply going around
- Too few secondary quests, and most are too easy with Pixel Converter to create items you already scanned an infinite number of times
- Procedural (infinite) quests given by random NPCs round the galaxy are always the same 2-3 types and give out useless rewards
- Boss fights are way too easy, apart from final boss which is decent but not the challenge level it should be for an entity of that power
- Colony building is really accessory and has no depth, you simply build a small cell, put the colony deed inside it, and you will have a colonist to pay you a periodical rent. Repeat as desired. No defending it against waves, no special quests, no upgrading.
===
I had my fun these (sadly) few days with Starbound. I personally found the universe and general gameplay enjoyable, especially at the start with lots to discover.
25 hours of content for aa game that has been in development for so long is not nearly enough. Make a comparison with Terraria, a game with a single world, older, but very similar to Starbound in many aspects, and undoubtably the game that inspired it in great part.
Well, Terraria has roughly 3 to 4 times the amount of content of Starbound, i played it, with the very same people i mentioned earlier in this review, and it took us 2 weeks to get all the stuff, playing 6/8 hours a day. Also, it has better pricing, and less crashes, bugs and launch problems.
I'm not saying Starbound is bad, in fact it IS great fun and a very good game, but it simply lacks the depth and the core content, in terms of gameplay lenght not all the fancy decorations, hats and whatsoever, to truly be a great game.
Think about this before deciding whether to buy or not.
