I've played this game since early access. I enjoyed it then, but less so now.
My experience has been that the same mechanics and features have remained under-developed through most of its development. A trap I notice with games similar is part of how the game is deisgned. Games like this require you to progress through tiers, for example in Starbound you progress through iron to tungsten to titanium and so on, Instead of adding more to do in the iron tier it's often easier to just add another tier. While this creates more hours played, it quickly devolves into a collect-a-thon instead of an exploration game. I would have liked to see more focus on exploration and less on adding these tiers.
With the completion of the game, I notice that the largest changes have been to the story, much less with the actual features of the game. For a game like this, I would consider the story a means to access the actual meat of the game which is the exploration, base-building, and crafting. Some might like the story and that's fine, but I don't find it that important. While I have my own issues with the story, in part because it's a little uninspiring, but mostly because you can't skip the story to get at the actual gameplay. All of that can be overlooked if you have a good group of friends which leads me to my reccomendation.
I would not reccomend this game in general. There are interesting mechanics and some might be interested in the collect-a-thon aspect which I will admit is fun the first time.
I would only suggest buying this if you have a group of friends to play with, but no more than four (4) because you cannot form parties larger than that for some reason.

Sorry, but no. There are some significant caveats, but on the whole, it's still a bit more "no" than "yes".
The game is standard fare HOG/adventure, which, true, aren't that much represented on Steam (currently), but the simple truth is - I've seen some much better.
Everything just smells of laziness. Lazy graphic, lazy animations, lazy story, which, without even batting an eyelash is heavily ripping of Bioshock, lazy puzzle design, lazy minigames. It's not that it is bad, it's just not good enough. It's not that it's full of glitches, or has technical problems, it's just - lazy.
Story is Bioshock with a cthulhu twist (and without *that one* twist). As said, many of 'shock's tropes are present. I'd say uncomfortably many - underwater grand city, but which has gone wrong, but whose magnificent glass domes still function, are full of air and warmth and haven't somehow collapsed, even though there are explosions, earthquakes, etc. in the game; then we have jump scare shocks; ominous monsters; dirtiness superimposed with splendor of buildings and blue ocean "skies"; there are even small girls with pigtails in skirts.
Though voice acting is competent enough for an indie game, again it's nothing special and there are HOG games with better ones (though at least here we are spared cheesy live action acting of such games as Mystery Case Files franchise).
The game makes it's worst crimes with the inconsequential puzzles. E.g. you have a sturdy stick, rope and thread and needle in inventory and you need to get something out of a grate. There are several possible logical ways of going around doing it, but the game doesn't acknowledge any of them except the default one (say in my non spoilery example - bend needle on some pipe, combine with thread, but not rope, and fish the thing out of grate. Stick could have been used as a lever, or rope could have been tied to grate, but this gets ignored). Other thing - badly implemented HOG scenes. In one location you need something to cut the rope, and in the HOG scene you find two knives and one hack saw. But in the end you get from it something completely unrelated, some specific key, and you have to go and search for default knife in some other location. Objects in HOG scenes get ignored.
Maybe few (well... more than 5, I'm old) years ago this kind of sloppy design would be awesome, or tolerated, but I think the genre has gone a ways and there are already many better games. Drawn series as well as various bigfishgames or ERS games have done it far more coherent. So no. I'd recommend to wait for them on Steam, not to get bad-ish first impressions of perfectly viable genre of games.
As for the good things - scenes are painted nicely and even if heavily "borrowed", the atmosphere is very nice and can be properly chilly. Though constant jump scares quickly wear thin. This is no Amnesia - the jump scares come by the book and on the clock without much inspiration. Some mini games are fun and interesting and interaction in HOG scenes can be varied and satisfying. There are 3 levels of difficulty, though for me, playing it on normal, the game was much too easy.
So there. I can't end this review without repeating myself over and over again. Not all components are bad, but there are many bland ones which make the Abyss not seasoned enough. If you want to try HOG games, you could, and you could be perfectly satisfied if you don't expect the next Monkey island, but bare in mind there are even better entries in the genre.

On the plus side, the story is excellent, the scenery is lovely (I'm tempted to say I now understand why Vancouver looks the way it does ;) and the driving is pretty confident. On the uneven to negative side, the missions, while imaginatively framed, aren't very hard, and there's too much of the rather routine melee fighting. By the back third of the game I was feeling a bit bored, although I saw it through. A shame: a missed opportunity to really go to town in an excellent environment. But it's a little too polite.

Let's start this off by actually reviewing Fallout 4, and not Bethesda's controversial business decisions. Fallout 4 is a good game. You can see for yourself that the graphics are the best that Bethesda's ever put out in their Elder Scrolls/Fallout style RPGs. The music offers you a choice between classical and Fallout 3's late jazz/dawn of rock crooner music. I've grown to like it quite a bit.
Regarding gameplay, one aspect I think is an improvement over past Fallouts (since 3, anyway) is removing equipment durability. It was never a challenge in past games, only an annoyance, and it's no longer. Thumbs up for that. I like Fallout 4's combat mechanics. VATS is much less in 4, only really working with guns. One gameplay aspect I didn't like was Fallout 4's omnipresent scavenging and crafting. It all ties into a town building aspect that comprises a lot of the content. I wasn't really into it. In every other Bethesda-style RPG of either universe, I travel light. The whole raw materials scavenging and junk collecting wasn't for me.
If you want to max out your character in Fallout 4, you're looking at 285 levels to gain, and there's effectively no level cap, aside from some absurd 65,000ish level point where the game apparently crashes, but you'll only see that in this lifetime if you use the console. Getting to level 286 in Fallout 4 is about as time intensive as getting every perk in Skyrim.
Your main character has a voice in Fallout 4, and I've been happy with the voice acting - there are only two voice possiblilties: male or female, which you'll cover in the prologue when you make your character, and, optionally, design your character's spouse -- the combination of the two doing a great job of determining your baby's appearance. Bethesda seems to have done a bit of research here, as dominant genes seem to play out as in real life.
Now to the elephant in the room: the Creator's Club. Right now, it's not a bad thing. It really isn't. Mods are also still free, and they work. The offerings in the Creator's Club are currently pretty meager, and aren't much of a threat to the status quo. If they remain such, there's no problem. The biggest worry is that Bethesda's begun a slippery slope towards incomplete games riddled with inconsequential microtransactions, like less scrupulous companies have. This would be bad, but it isn't so just yet, so a lot of the negative reviews are unfair at this point in time. We will see how things unfold from here. Every turn for the worse begins innocently enough, but Bethesda makes good games, and I don't see that changing too quickly. I can't imagine a timeline where Elder Scrolls 6 and Fallout 5 are terrible because of the Creator's Club. If the accountants get too much sway in the game development, maybe 8 and 7 will start getting overbearingly money-grubbing, but let's give Bethesda the benefit of the doubt that they won't screw us over. Fallout 4 isn't the game that's screwing us over. It's worth your time.

I have been told once or twice in my life not to let perfect be the enemy of good. If you allow yourself to get too bogged down with what could be better, you blind yourself to the things you should appreciate. With Starbound, Chucklefish have taken this a step further and not allowed good to be the enemy of passable.
While managing to do competently everything a game in the sandbox builder genre needs to do, Starbound still lacks the organic progression from goal to goal that makes such a game stand out. The game does little to draw a player into the crafting system or compel exploration. There are plenty of hints of an entertaining fiction, though they are inconsistently delivered. Starbound frequently feels like a game where development of various aspects ceased when they reached a certain baseline of quality so as to avoid having any one thing stand out enough to contrast the weaker elements. The game has modding support through Steam Workshop, though at this point it would be pure speculation to say whether mods can complete the game experience.
To their credit, Chucklefish walked back more than a few questionable design choices that were met with player antipathy, but at the end of the day the bottom line is that there is little to capture and engross an audience. If you are a fan of the genre and want to play a new game that does more of the same, Starbound is certainly that. If you are new to the genre and want to play the best it has to offer, other options exist, most notably Terraria.

I would highly recommend this game to fans of both hidden object games and traditional point-and-click adventures.
The story is engaging, the plot is coherent, and the horror atmosphere is fully immersive.
The hidden object puzzles are straightforward and clearly labeled, with absolutely none of the "entire object is hidden except for a pixel" or "all of the objects blur together" problems that plague other HOGs.  There is a hint system, although you most likely won't need it, and you can always choose to substitute a game of dominos if you get stuck.  They also use common English/British synonyms for all of the item names (which may sound like a minor point, but is a big deal for those of us who have played other HOGs where a "fishnet" could be labeled as a "landing," or where items are randomly in a foreign language for no reason).
As for the mini-games, they are intuitive and fairly easy, and never feel tedious or like filler.  Instead, you feel a sense of accomplishment, as each mini-game serves to advance the plot in some way.
Additionally, the point-and-click puzzles are logical.  It was always pretty obvious what an item was going to be used for, so there was never any sense of frustration.  If for some reason you aren't sure of where to go next, though, your map (on the easier difficulties) will show you where you can perform actions.  Experienced gamers will not find this game challenging, even on the highest difficulty rating, but it is worth playing through anyway just to experience the setting and the craftsmanship of the gameplay.  I played through multiple times in one day so I could get all of the achievements, and it never got old.
The voice acting is top-notch, the music provides just the right amount of creepiness or action, the backgrounds are beautiful, and even the CG people aren't horrible to look at.
The game is fairly short, less than 3 hours, but there is an optional bonus mission that adds depth and backstory to the characters.  Also, while there is a fair amount of backtracking, they make it feel fresh by having many areas change visually upon revisiting them.
All in all, I would give this game a 9.5/10, and feel it is worth the full $7.99.  It is far superior to any other HOG I have played.

I played the first two games when they came out. The second was pretty much identical to the first except for the "loyalty" system and has been largely forgotten but never mind. They were fun games, and whilst they weren't the first to let you be the bad guy, it was somewhat satisfying the way the city seemed to work around you to clear up your mess and try to restore the status quo. Unfortunately however I never actually finished either of them because there didn't seem to be much progression. Yes, you'd get a new map to play on every now and then, and some of the missions could be done in different orders, but there wasn't much personality. The missions were just a means to an end - namely collecting enough cash to move on to the next level.
Ultimately I think they could have been largely forgotten in years to come, save for the "controversy" aspect.
Then this gem came along. Rather than just moving the same games into a 3D environment, the game has been designed entirely from scratch. It might as well have been called something different for all the similarity it has to it's predecessors. Not only do we have full voice acting by many household names which flesh out the characters and add that much needed personality, but the city itself feels far more alive and real than ever before.
Corners are no longer all at 90 degrees, there are literally hundreds of bonuses, secrets and extra missions you can do on the side whenever you want, you can backtrack at any point to visit previous areas of the game and see what's changed (although be careful of straying into the wrong neighbourhood if you've been upsetting people), full radio stations with a good selection of licensed music (and the ability to play your own MP3s on the PC version - nice touch), fully working public transit systems and a fascinating storyline of betrayal, loyalty and trust make this something that has to be played by everybody, no matter what your view on the violence aspect. Come on. Even if you don't want to complete the missions themselves you can spend hours just riding a taxi around town. Yes, this game even managed to make "Crazy Taxi" almost entirely redundant.
Whilst many people could argue (and with good cause) that the later games in the series such as Vice City and 4 are better in nearly every way, for me this will always be my favourite simply because it was such a welcome surprise - were it not for 3 then GTA wouldn't be the multi-million dollar franchise it is today.

I gave this a positive early access review and I'm afraid that I'm going to have to change my mind about that. The positive points are still here: Wickland is beautiful, has great optimization, and brings some interesting gimmicks to the arena shooter genre, but it desperately needed for more modes to be added during early access, which never happened. Map selection is sparse too, and the maps are generally too large for the game's 1v1 focus. Perhaps the biggest condemnation is that no one is playing it, and unless you're challenging a friend you're not going to get into a duel immediately. Bots were added as promised, which helps take away from the sting of low player numbers, but there's only so much fun to be had playing what is intended as a multiplayer game with only AI opponents.
Wickland still has some interesting ideas, but unfortunately this is a game that emerged from early access only half-baked, and that is its downfall. There's a nice coat of polish on what content is there, but it's not enough to justify picking up a limited multiplayer game that is bordering on dead. It's a shame this wasn't created as a primarily single player title instead, I think that it's mechanics would be interesting in that context and the game's visual flair could be put to better use. Unfortunately making a multiplayer focused indie game is an inherently difficult proposition because of how difficult it is to keep a player base, and Wickland hasn't managed to break free of that rendering it basically dead in the water. Proper deathmatch options and a CTF mode would help this one a lot, but most post-launch patches seem to be minor fixes, and even with that it's hard to bring back a player base once they've departed. Unfortunately my tentative recommendation for this title must be rescinded.
My original review:
Polished, beautiful, fun, and well optimized arena shooter let down by a non-existent playerbase and lack of bot support (which is planned) or any sort of single player campaign (which is not, and understandably so since it would basically mean making an entirely new game). It's good if you're willing to wait for more people to be playing it, or buy copies for your friends to get them playing it. Hopefully the lack of players will change over time, since the game is only a few days old as of the time of this review. Tentatively recommended, just be warned that for the moment you're going to be looking at a lot of empty servers.

Think Tom Clancy's Endgame combined with Advance Wars, except you can hop into one of your units for direct control--and you will because the AI is seriously awful.
Accolades:
+ Cool premise--If Bohemia put more work into this concept it could really shine.  Island-hopping with your newly upgraded units is pretty fun.  Enemies attacking your islands add a sense of urgency to a normally slower-paced game type.
+ Easy and intuitive multitasking controls--The controls range from basic to advanced to accommodate all play styles.
+ Aircraft carrier is badass
Criticisms:
- Painfully awful forced 1st person missions in campaign mode--I don't know how any of the devs could defend these missions and say that they were fun or well-designed.  Why?  To name a few reasons:  You can't jump, you only have one gun, the autoaim is crazy, and you kill the one enemy type (in 1st person mode) 3 bullets a piece.  90% of the missions you literally just need to W+M1 to the next objective marker and you'll win--which reminds me that you can't pick a difficulty mode.  I would recommend playing the 'strategy game' mode.
- Story--You crash land on a planet and you hijack an aircraft carrier to take it over.  Good blue guys shoot red bad guys and vice versa.  They should have left it at that but the game crowbars in cut scenes of the unrelatable Lt. Australia and his inconsequential friends.
- Aforementioned AI--Unless your units severely outclass the enemies on an island, trust the AI to only take out buildings.  There seems to be no way to suit your walruses up nicely and send them into an area without taking very heavy losses.
There really could (and should!) be a lot more to this game but if you like games like Endwar, check it out.

I've held off on writing a review until I've experienced Duel (1v1) firsthand, but now that I have, here are my impressions.
Wickland is a fast-paced arena FPS centered around the Duel game mode. While you're free to participate in Free-For-All/Deathmatch games in warm-up, Duel is the real meat of the game. For an Early Access title, the game plays and feels complete based on the features it advertises, both graphically and mechanically.
If you're on the fence because gameplay looks fast, don't be afraid - mechanical movement complexity is kept to a minimum compared to games like Quake and Unreal Tournament (you get WASD, jump, and a simple wall-jump that's easy to perform; that's it). This is so that you can focus on item control and timing straight away, which are two of the foundations of Duel; grab and hold onto as much of the map's pick-ups and beasts as possible, while denying your opponent the same.
Speaking of beasts, they replace the role of weapons. Upon first glance, they seem to be simply re-skins of weapons that have functional equivalents in other arena shooters, but you'll soon notice that each beast has its own armor value, and these beasts can soak up a major portion of incoming damage. In Duel, beasts do not respawn until they die, which makes armor pick-ups an important element to control, since your weaponry also have a lifeline of their own. It's this tug-of-war of attempting to relinquish your opponent's control of their beasts while keeping up your own item timings that makes Duel exciting and tense. Map sizes are also just right; many veteran arena shooter fans may find the maps a bit claustrophobic, but they are kept small enough so that it's easy to remember where most pick-ups and beasts are located after running through them a few times.
If you've ever entertained the idea of playing Duel in an arena shooter, give Wickland a chance. It's unique take on Duel makes for some very fun experiences, and I like it for being an accessible arena shooter that also doesn't hesitate to punish you for your mistakes. Highly recommended.

Speaking of creatures, in the game you pick up a 'creature' head where you gain the ability to transform into it and use it's unique abilities, and you can stack those creatures and always have them with you, and to translate those abilities, you got your sniper creature, melee, full auto 'human' shooter, SMG-er..etc.

I'll have to speak honest on this game, and in general for games like it, and since it's still in development might as well use this opportunity to give my feedback. The game doesn't have many players in it, and if it's in the state that it is now when it launches, it won't have any players after a week to a months time after release, same thing happened with another game called Rise Of The Triad, where the game's MP died in about a months to two's time, only a group of people keeping it alive only one day a week. So what I'm going to say, in the game's current state, is that if you have a friend or more to play with, and if you like old school twitch shooters, then go get it and have fun, if not, going in this solo, even with the tempting low price, don't get it.
Here's my one feedback i can provide that will make me recommend this game to both types of people i.e anyone, and this one solution is for all these types of fun games that go down, and that solution is.. add bots. That's it, and i don't know how hard it is to add bots/AI in the game, but that's the solution i find that's needed.
Other feedback i can provide is, add LAN matches, music in matches, numbering the characters/weapons you collect on the keyboard instead of just scrolling, explain and have a tutorial for the confusing score system, and what each character does (which adding a dummy to shoot at helps). That's all i can think of add the moment, and I'm probably nailing the game now, but i do honestly like it and that's why I'm saying all this, and i hope these notes are taken into considerations for, in my opinion, improving the game dramatically.

This is a FANTASTIC game. However, before you read this review I have one thing to say: Do NOT buy this game unless you want The Coven DLC. That said, you won't always have a good time. As with any game, there are trolls, griefers and general asshats who just like to ruin things by gamethrowing; however, if you can look past the occasional negative experience, you'll have an amazing amount of fun.
Incredibly easy to pick up, fantastic fun for a solo player or someone looking for a game to play with friend and constantly supported by devs who obviously care about their work, Town of Salem is a great time for the whole witch-hunting town.

This game pretty much tries to copy the quake 3 arena experience. It offers very fast movement, jumppads, a somewhat crappy walljump (you have to completely face the wall to jump off it), a variety of ~7 guns/armors including rocket and grenade launcher, machinegun, plasma gun, shotgun, sniper, a cloakable melee creature, diverse health, ammo, armor pickups and only 3 maps so far.
It feels pretty good to play BUT the combined weapon/armor gimmick comes with a lot of downsides... Elaboration: Guns in this game are creatures, but those guns are also your armor, but you can also pick up armor, that will increase the gun given armor. If you get shot enough to get down to 0 creature gun armor, the enemy will earn a point and you will lose that gun. Given that, you can just switch guns to prevent dropping to 0. You can also just run over already picked up guns to reset the gun/armor back to 100.
Your player, lets say the shell of collected creature gun armors, also has a certain amount of health points, wich will result in a bloody mess, a point for the enemy and the loss of all contained guns if lowered to 0.
Clearly the developer tried to bring fresh air into the old but gold arena shooter formula, but this doesn't feel right for now. I do not recommend this game for casual players at the moment, hardcore arena lovers looking for something new and interesting should pick this up tho.

- Load game, setup video and other settings

- Get through intro cut scenes and begin game
- Looks good, feels good, I like what I see
- Walking around for a little while , pistol at the ready - Eerily empty, quiet
- Bagged my first Alien, he never stood a chance
- Note to self - stop looking for items, nothing is here, or there, or anywhere (only the odd stimpak or magazine)
- Very linear story and travel route, heavily scripted - feels mechanical - not instinctive or natural - wandering or veering off path results in verbal reminders of where you should be headed
- First firefight, multiple aliens. Was impressed.  Those buggers crawl everywhere, walls, ceiling etc... and are hard to hit.  Maybe I'm just a crap shot
- About half an hour into the game and I'm beginning to like it.  Guns handle well, ammo is in short supply for the Pulse Rifle and I keep running out and have to swith to pistol (infinite ammo for pistol)
- Make sure I'm saving after each check point, just in case
- Hit a tight spot and keep getting killed whilst trying to escape, waiting for a lift to open.  Again, scripted scene, hold off the Aliens until the door opens.  Try a few different strategies - I'm smarter than these Aliens
- Each time I died I noticed that I was presented with an option to change difficulty setting - ignore it, I'm tougher than that, and there's no need I can do this
- After my seventh death, at the same location and without much progress, I decide to change the difficulty setting from "NORMAL" to "EASY" - Don't judge me! LOL
- Get a warning that this will "overwrite" the previous save.  What the hell, what's the worst thing that can happen?
- Game restarts from the very beginning - Not good.  It never said "WILL RESTART GAME", only that my previous save would be "Overwritten".  Besides I still had a few saved games.

Dementium II was originally a game for the Nintendo DS. It is a FPS-Horror game and the sequel to Dementium: The Ward.
Dementium II HD does a poor job explaining the details of what is going on. It drops the player inside a sanitarium that is haunted, or something and your job is it to fight through hordes of ghastly monsters and stop the mad doctor behind it all.
The combat is simple, but fun. The ability to chose from over eight different weapons in a roughly five hour experience is a solid addition. Enemies are usually slow and repetitious and it is very possible to engage all creatures with the same technique.
Dementium II HD comes with a handful of puzzles. Sadly they are there just for the sake of having puzzles and do not bring any real meat into the game.
The graphics, are far from optimal for the platform. This game was originally designed for the Nintendo DS and while there have been some improvements made to match PC gaming standards, it still plays like a game built in the early 2000s.
Dementium II was probably an amazing DS game but on PC it is a waste of money and time.

Overview:
In Sleeping Dogs, you play as Wei Shen, an undercover cop tasked to infiltrate the Sun On Yee triad in Hong Kong. The city feels authentic, the atmosphere in the city really does feel like Hong Kong. On the other hand, the outdoor areas are heavily butchered and shrunk (particularly the Victoria Peak). There's also nothing much to do once you finish the game. Nevertheless, the game is still worth to play just to experience the story alone.
Gameplay:
Sleeping Dogs really loves free-running. It's certainly feels great doing parkour, but the excitement dies out as you progress far in the game. Gun fights are a rarity, there are few types of guns but the cover system makes up for this. There's also the famous Max Payne-styled bullet time in here, too. The melee fighting is where this game shines though. It really does feel like the Batman Arkham series' combat system.
In terms of content, the game doesn't truly feel open when compared to other sandbox games. What you're able to explore is actually limited. The game's map itself is modeled after the Hong Kong Island, which is only a small part of Hong Kong itself. The map is shrunk even more, butchering several areas of the Hong Kong Island. Although it does feel like Hong Kong, several landmarks are missing from the game. On top of that, there's nothing much to do once you finish the game except completing all the sidequests and races.
Sound Tracks:
Like the GTA series, Sleeping Dogs has radio stations which will play once you ride a vehicle. The radio stations feel authentic, loaded with many kinds of music genre and even advertisements. What's truly unique about this game is the voice acting. Combining the usage of English and Cantonese really contribute towards its authenticity.
Pros:
+ Enjoyable storyline
+ Great fighting system
+ Authentic atmosphere of Hong Kong
+ Great Soundtrack
+ Great graphics
Cons:
- Doesn't seem to be properly optimized. Even on lowest graphic settings, the game still lags, especially while driving.
- Occasionally crashes
- Nothing much to do once the game is finished
- Not much to explore
- Stale 'hacking' system
- Low amount of pedestrians (Still not surprising as this game was made with 2012 engine in mind)
Score: 9/10

This game by Artifex Mundi is one of the most astounding Point-and-click games I have ever played.
Firstly, the graphics. The amount of detail and color gives the underwater environment, as well as the ruined city, a mixture of wonder, destitution and haunting, telling the tale of a once wonderful city reduced to ruins. While it may remind you of Bioshock, the game's enviroment is still totally unique in my opinion.
As for the gameplay, the Hidden Object gameplay never gets boring. It has two kinds of objects: one where you click on the correct one, and poof! Item found, while the second one has you find an item to open/reveal another before it is considered found, and done. This added a little bit of challenge and variety to the otherwise simple Hidden Object Scene.
Tired of Hidden Objects? Switch it to Dominoes, where you will have to place the tile to reach the seashells to complete the game. Pretty simple, except that you must align the tiles correctly to move forward.
Also other than those two above are the puzzles. While most are actually a piece of cake, some are really challenging. The puzzle design, as all I can say, well made.
The story, although it overall looked simple, doesn't mean it can't hook you up to this game. Though low-quality cutscenes sucked some beauty away from the story, it can still be interesting due to the mystery surrounding the sunken city. Voice acting is also top notch, as you can feel whatever they said, they really mean it. That is a redemption for the low-quality cutscenes at least.
Overall, I love this game. Though the characters aren't really memorable, the game's environment and gameplay makes this game unqiue compared to other Point-and-click games. The Collector's Edition also added other goodies (such as musics, and wallpapers) as well as an extra mission to understand how the city came to be.
For the price tag of $7.99, it was totally worth it.

The biomes are vast, yet they feel samey with how they can be boiled down to "forest, lava place, or ocean", I recall tentacle planets and eye biomes being EVERYWHERE in the alpha, yet I saw less and less eye biomes as the EA went on, and just flat out stopped seeing tentacles anywhere as the game hit the beta stage.
The soundtrack and graphics are absolutely great, but that's mostly because literally everyone at chucklefish is an artist or musician, not a programmer. Explains a lot about the game.
The story to this game..who cares? It's a terraria clone, caring about the story is like watching bad animes "for the plot", we know what you're watching that for, and we know that this game is played for running around and exploring things.
Crafting is a bore, not because of gathering the materials, but because there's a timer on crafting, and that's a big problem in a ton of games. I suspect the reason of crafting timers being a thing is because usually games with crafting have multiplayer modes, but it's not like they couldn't just disable it for single player.
Races are just pick your color, they'd really be more diverse if they had bonuses or special traits tied to them, but..nope! They even changed how the different races ship AI would look, it used to be they all got a special AI design related to the race, but now it's all just a recolor of the human ship AI, and that just feels like taking out some of what is supposed to make the game unique, what's supposed to make it look alive.
Techs are just stupid, why lock double jumping and dashing behind RNG? I can understand hiding things like cool mechs and cars in random dungeons, but double jumping/dashing is kind of a must when you're slower than being overencumbered in Fallout. I've heard that some techs like butterfly wings or the bubble tech were removed without an explanation, but I think the explanation is that it was too "silly" for their serious game about fishmen and star people fighting gigantic tentacles
Movement, like I said, is slow. Which is very bad, especially when your enemies are faster than a buttered-up Sonic the Hedgehog, and backwalking is just horrendously awful. Why do you have such slow back walking? No other game does this. Heck, even in Castlevania: Symphony of the Night, backwalking was favorable to just walking, because it was faster. I'm stating that as an example if only because SotN has been said to have inspired a lot of aspects of Starbound
The RNG is just, awful. Oh, look, a rusty, slow, two-handed hammer with deplorable damage..Oh, there's a rusty knife next to it that has higher DPS on top of slightly more damage. the randomized weapon abilities don't help much, either, because they feel like flashy energy drainers as opposed to actual ways of saving your applebottom in a battle.
Healing is absolute garbage, because food does not stack in your inventory any more, it will ROT now, and above all of that, there's now potion sickness! So you'll just heal a bit of your health bar, and then you have to wait for the crossed out ham icon to fade away before you can heal another bit!
I know that a lot of the reasons I've stated this game is more mediocre than Mighty Number 9 can be solved with mods and the workshop, but that's a terrible reason for a game not being a waste of fifteen dollars! If mods are the only thing saving a mediocre game from being awful, they must need to fix a lot of things!
The game has gigantic memory leaks, bugs galore, unrefined EVERYTHING, but it looks and sounds pretty. 3/10.

After the atrocity that was Empress of the Deep, I wasn't particularly excited to take on another Bioshock "inspired" hidden object game (or HOG for short). Nevertheless I descended into Abyss and its city of Eden, cautious but hopeful that it wouldn't be the stodgy adventure I half expected it to be. Color me surprised then when I became completely swept up in the remarkably high production values, enjoyably casual puzzles, and varied mini-games peppered throughout (heck, there's even some squirrel love). Abyss: The Wraiths of Eden isn't only exceptional for its genre, but a polished and entertaining game in its own right. It's elements may be something less than inspired, but Artifex Mundi mixes them together into far more than the sum of its parts, and certainly one of the best HOGs I've yet to find.
The obvious influence of Bioshock on Abyss can be seen everywhere, from the narrative of a lone traveler entering an underwater city intended as a bastion of all of humanity's greatest minds and creations, to the neon art deco environments, and the persistent theme of a city that failed under its own ambition. Abyss doesn't pretend to be more than it is though, and actually uses its limited resources to rework the plot of the game it so heavily borrows from into something more manageable, forgoing the heavy questions of morality for a more simplistic ghost story that while nothing remarkable is enough to hold the game together. The iffy voice acting and horrendous facial animation is another matter, but thankfully you are subjugated to these often enough to make you turn the game off in horror.
I call Abyss a HOG, but often it falls far more along the lines of a basic point and click adventure game. You explore locations, picking up objects along the way to help you solve puzzles, with just the occasional mini-game popping up often enough to remind you that you are still playing a HOG (if only in some respects). Personally I enjoy this combination quite a bit more than straight up Highlights, and found the simplicity of the puzzles oddly satisfying. It doesn't require much thought and there's always a hint button if you should get stuck, but it also doesn't treat you like a complete imbecile, requiring just enough from the player to keep from feeling like an interactive slideshow.
If you have been turned off from HOGs in the past from their lackluster presentations, mind numbing stories, or over reliance on the sole act of finding hidden objects, I'd suggest you take a look at Abyss before writing the genre off entirely. Its visuals are top notch, the gameplay at just the right level of casual friendliness without becoming tediously easy, and the whole experience feels like its operating a far higher budget with a better development team than I've come to expect from this sort of game. Let's just say I'm impressed, Artifex Mundi; here's hoping this is a sign of the quality we can expect going forward from one of my favorite gaming guilty pleasures.

For a children's game; it's okay. The graphics are on the lower end and it's definately a lower-budget game. I definately do not suggest getting this game at full price. I do however think that if you have a daughter or son who loves the Disney Princesses, that this game is something they will enjoy.
The game tends to be a bit repetitive in it's game play, however there's an actual, well-thought out story and many references to your child's favorite movies. A lot of places they'll explore are straight from scenes on the big screen. The customization is also well done and gems are easy to find so it's not taxing on the player to try to stay frugal: I found that I could buy almost all of the dresses right away in just collecting gems in the first area (use the magic twirl "n" near bushes at least 3 times to get all of the gems- you can do this again once you leave the area and come back to keep farming for more gems to shop to your heart's content). The voice acting isn't grating although I did experience some issues on the playback.
Keyboard controls can be changed in the options menu, however for a small child, the arrow keys to move, spacebar to jump, and "n" and "m" to cast spells are easy enough to grasp, as well as easy enough for their smaller hands to reach all keys. Only issue with this default setting is that this is awkward to use this and then toggle the mouse from time to time. However the camera and controls work smoothly, and even the platforming sections were easy enough.
The game's length can actually give a bang for your buck- even outside of taking time to explore and unlocking each item, each princess has a good handful of quests to do. Unfortunately, the only princess left out of the attention is Princess Tiana, who only has three missions, and can't be unlocked until the very end- doesn't look too well compared to the other princesses.
At the end of it all however, this games has what feels like an equal amount of up's and down's about it. At first I was going to not recommend this game until I saw the other screenshots posted. Sure, there are a few joke postings there from adults (like myself), but the young players who took pictures seemed to genuinely enjoy the game and interacting with their beloved fairy tale characters. If you can find this game for a good discount for your kid- go for it.

Wickland is a breath of musty putrid air for those who think modern arena shooters are too bright and glossy. If you long for the dark labyrinths of Hexen you'll feel at home here. Wickland is strictly oriented around competitive multiplayer dueling in the spirit of Quake; no single player campaign to be found here, although there may be bots eventually. The weapons are a crazy mix of unreal and quake, with an alternate fire mode for some interesting combos, but retaining the fundamental balance and simplicity of the quake arsenal. The game runs very nicely in the unreal engine, and they've incorporated a wall-jump movement mechanic that feels simple and unique compared to the manic bunnyhopping of some other games. The result is there's less tricks to learn and you can jump right into the dueling metagame, which is where Wickland really shines.
They've put a twist on the classic duel ruleset, where players fight for control of armor and health; in Wickland each weapon is its own monster with armor and doesn't respawn on the map until it is "killed" off your opponent. The winner is not the person with the most kills, but simply who manages to frag the base human character first. It's amazing how fresh this mechanic feels, and also how much more accesible it makes AFPS dueling which is notorious for its difficulty. Perhaps the best part about it is if you are hopelessly outmatched by your opponent, the game will simply end and you wont have to sit through the 10-15 minutes of humiliation that turn so many off to dueling.
Although they have borrowed elements from other shooters, Mad Ram cite real life duelling sports like Kendo as their inspiration. Players expecting over the top free for all combat may be dissapointed. Also, there are only three maps right now, which is a good thing since you'll need to know them inside out. Wickland is as close as you can get to a pure distilation of duel culture--where reflexes are only a means of executing a sophisticated mental game, and the ethos is relentless self-improvement. Whether it's chess or martial arts or Quake, if you enjoy the intensity of competitive one-on-one sports, Wickland is for you.

McPixel is a point and click adventure game in a WarioWare-like situation where your character is attempting to prevent a bomb (or other device) from blowing up. This is played out by interacting with various objects in the game which usually have completely unpredictable results.
This is not a terribly fun game. Ultimately, while you "control" the outcome, there's no real way to determine "right" or "wrong" - it's all trial and error until you find the idea which the designer thought would be the funny actual solution. Half the time they're not all that funny in the first place. Additionally, the game is quite short - it takes longer to run the game to drop all the steam trading cards than it does to beat the game itself, literally.
If I'm not mistaken, this game was originally a phone game and is far better suited to that format - clicking the screen, seeing stuff happen, and consuming in very, very bite sized increments. As a PC game where you're generally sitting down for somewhat longer play sessions, the novelty wears thin very rapidly and it becomes more tedious then entertaining.

I have over 500 games in my Steam account, and the vast majority of them are still unplayed. So now I'm dedicating an hour to each of these games and writing a series of One Hour Reviews. An hour isn't very long to judge a game on, so think of this as more of a first impression, and take this review in the spirit in which it's given. One Hour Reviews #32 - Command Carrier: Gaea Mission
This is another example of a very mediocre game from Bohemia Interactive.  The production values are not that great.  The graphics aren't bad, and the sound effects were alright, but honestly I could have just played this with the sound off and been just as happy not to listen to anymore of the voice acting or music.
The opening of the campaign just plays like a straight up sci-fi based shooter with some dull characters and story.  But eventually you get command of a carrier, and the game morphs into a real time strategy.  I did not get very far into the strategy part of the game, so I may be missing some of the better parts of the game.   But even in the short time I did play, I could already get a sense of how bad the AI was.  I admit I am not the biggest fan of RTS games to begin with, so if I have to fight my own units AI on top of that, it makes it even more difficult to look forward to.
Perhaps fans of the original game will be more forgiving. I actually didn't realize ahead of time this was a remake of a classic game.  Somehow I missed this the first time around.  Now I wish I had missed it the second time as well.

Abyss:Wraiths of Eden was the first Artifex Mundi game I have played, and it stands out in a genre that can be swamped in games that feel nearly indistinguishable from one another.
The casual puzzle genre has always fallen into three categories for me.
A) Pure hidden object, nearly each scene is just finding objects in a jumbled mess, very little straying from the base.
B) Puzzle point-and-click, where you have a lovely balance of varying types of puzzles, story, and hidden objects (generally 1st person)
C) Adventure point-and-click where you have a character who physically moves around scenes, like "The Longest Journey" (generally 3rd person)
Abyss would fall into the "B" Category on this one, and it was an absolute delight. It was pretty well voice acted, the difficulty wasn't too great, even on expert, but not a walk in the park either. The Dominos minigame was a neat and fun addition in lieu of doing the hidden object puzzles, the story was interesting although unfortunately left us wanting more, and the game itself flowed well and was very nice to look at.
I only have two complaints really about Abyss. First, the lack of backstory on the cool Rapture-like place called Eden that is used as the backdrop for the game. Second, that I tried to start the game on expert so I'd only have to play through once. Why complain? Well, I managed to get myself stuck a couple times, and after exhausting all possible options, I went to the internet.
Every single time it was because I missed clicking on something I had already interacted with that was now useable a second time. Now that it was able to be interact with them again, they would give me an item I could then use to progress. Mostly my own fault, but I felt this was counterintuitive, as I had already eliminated these objects from use.
I enjoyed it enough that I played the bonus (check it out from the extras menu for a little more story) AND I'm going back through again on easy so I can get the Dominos achievement :) Highly recommend if you are a fan of class-B point-and-click games. From this experience, I will definitely buy all Artifex Mundi games going forward. They have a different feel from any other point-and-clicks. They stand out as higher quality, and more fun to play. A+

Well, this was an unexpected little slice of awesome.
The first time I actually encountered this particular game was via a review of it courtesy of Yahtzee Croshaw (AKA Zero Punctuation). And I have to say, I'm very glad I decided to satisfy my burning interest in this game.
Aliens VS Predator is a game set in (You guessed it) the universe of Ridley Scott's Alien, with the Predators also being featured heavily in this universe. The campaign in the game is divided into three; One for the Marines (which is essentially just Generic Dudebro Filler for all the CoD lovers out there), one for the Aliens/Xenomorphs (which has much more stealth and facebiting), and one for the Predator(s) (which is a combination of the two, minus the facebiting). Each of these campaigns is linked chronologically, with the Alien campaign becoming the starting point, and the reason for the marines turning up in the first place. However, the predators have also turned up since the ever idiotic Weyland Yutani Corporation has unearthed a Predator Pyramid, and open it, unleashing an energy nullifying wave. This not only allows the Aliens to escape, but alerts the predators. The rest I'll let you figure out yourself.
As mentioned, the Marine campaign is essentially just a standard sci-fi military shooter with horror elements, and the gameplay is so generic you've likely already seen it before in most shooters; you have your infinite ammo pistol, your shotgun, your machine gun, and to make it seem like you are infact in the Alien world, you have an Alien tracking smartgun.
As for the Aliens however, their gameplay is completely different. Success in Alien levels relies on two things: Your mobility and your Stealth abilities. Since you're a Xenomorph, you can crawl through vents, across walls, ceilings etc at a lightning speed, making you incredibly difficult to hit when escaping enemies. Your speed is a double-edged sword however, since if you're not mentally prepared first, you may get a tad queasy; the speed at which you go at and the sometimes automatic wall crawling can be very disorientating. You will likely not notice after a little while however, as in comes the second element of the Aliens; stealth. Now unfortunately, rather than hunting Sigourney Weaver, you're hunting an organised Marine Corp. Or at least that's what they call themselves. More often than not you'll be presented with a room/area full of Dudebro marines, all spouting out repeating (and VERY irritating) lines. You'll then have to pick them off one by one, and if you try and take on multiple marines at once, you will likely get filled with bullet holes for you trouble. Because of this, I do feel that the stealth is rather like the Batman Arkham series of games; you have to take out your enemies slowly and with patience, or you'll be punished severely. However, to make up for this, the killing animations you have access to are incredibly satisfying, if not very f**king brutal; you can stab people in the back with your tail, rip people heads off, expose people to the wonders of facehuggers, or just go all Vlad the Impaler on them with your tail instead. Just remember to clean the s**tstains afterwards.
And for the final slice of gameplay: The Predator. In my humble opinion, I feel this is the best of the three campaigns, since it manages to successfully balance Combat and Stealth and ensure the two aren't intertwined when they don't need to be. Not only this, but the gadgets the predator has access to are the most interesting in the game by far; you can mess about with the typical claw gadgets, a combi stick/spear, the plasma projector, a Captain America shield esque saw blade boomerang, and some old-but-gold mines. When you play as a predator, (similarly to the Alien) there will be two main aspects of gameplay you will need: Strategy and (again) Stealth. The strategy comes into play because you'll have to ensure you have some form of battle plan before you go charging in headfirst and get killed by some smarmy chucklef**k with a shotgun. You remember how I mentioned the stealth in this game is similar to the stealth used in Batman Arkham? The similarities are much more prevalent with the predator, who has heat vision, and even a jumping and vantage point system similar to the grappling used in Batman Arkham. However, unlike Batman, you don't leave your prey alive. You collect their heads. You blow them into cartilage with a plasma projector, or just sneak up on them and stick claw gadgets in their back and lift them at least one metre in the air whilst yelling like a caveman who just beat a sabre cat in a fist fight. However, whilst most of the Predator campaign (and gameplay) is very fun and pleasantly challenging in areas, the final boss for this particular campaign is complete and utter horses**t, and nothing else. This particular enemy is not only incredibly aggressive towards you, deals a s**t ton of damage that you cannot block or avoid (unlike with other enemies and bosses the predator encounters), and is also very VERY agile. Agile to the point of you being completely unable to hit it without using mines, which slow you down whilst you arm them and leave you open to an attack. Did I mention the high aggression and high damage? To top it all off, the area where you fight contains destructible platforms, lava that kills you instantly and sticks you back at the start, and also a checkpoint that will stick this c**t right back at full health once you die. There's no checkpoint once he'd down at half health, just anger and foaming mouths. The only upside of this fight is that your energy (which you rely on to help you charge your mines and plasma projector) recharges quickly, a quality that isn't shared with the rest of the campaign. However, this is essentially p***ing in the wind with regards to this bossfight, and doesn't help bury the other s**tty aspects.
All in all, a slightly flawed but very enjoyable game that is well worth your time, regardless of whether or not you've actually watched the films this game was based on.

It's mindblowing how much was the game improved since it has first launched, it's an entirely different experience now! Plus, it runs butter smooth, when it used to tank the framerate on a computer that should have zero problems with it. Every area the game was good at got improved and is now great or near perfect. Even I used to say it's just a poor man's Terraria, but saying that now would be straight up lying. It's so much more than it was, and so much more than other games from this genre are right now. Whereas other survival sandboxes feel like a game, Starbound feels like an experience. Note: While my play time on this account is very low, I've played the game for hours and hours on my brother's account, which I initially bought the game on, I did NOT receive it for free.
This game has only gotten worse from Alpha to full release
The combat is as shallow as a puddle in the hot summer sun - melee combat requires you to run up to your enemy and smack them, however, there is damage on contact with enemies, meaning that you're constantly having to space yourself from enemies that are attacking, on top of DoC. Guns are garbage because of the energy system, because rather than having bullets like any GOOD game would, they use energy, but this wouldn't even be a problem if the good guns didn't use all your energy in two shots, and even then some of them just dont do anything to enemies. The biggest problem with combat is HEALING, and I'll get to that later
Exploration is the main draw to this game, randomly generated worlds, villages, and loot..This would be fine if a lot of quests didn't involve "Find the holy grail in this certain type of house! Where's the house? Eh..I'm sure you'll pass by it." The biomes are vast, yet they feel samey with how they can be boiled down to "forest, lava place, or ocean", I recall tentacle planets and eye biomes being EVERYWHERE in the alpha, yet I saw less and less eye biomes as the EA went on, and just flat out stopped seeing tentacles anywhere as the game hit the beta stage.
The soundtrack and graphics are absolutely great, but that's mostly because literally everyone at chucklefish is an artist or musician, not a programmer. Explains a lot about the game.
The story to this game..who cares? It's a terraria clone, caring about the story is like watching bad animes "for the plot", we know what you're watching that for, and we know that this game is played for running around and exploring things.
Crafting is a bore, not because of gathering the materials, but because there's a timer on crafting, and that's a big problem in a ton of games. I suspect the reason of crafting timers being a thing is because usually games with crafting have multiplayer modes, but it's not like they couldn't just disable it for single player.
Races are just pick your color, they'd really be more diverse if they had bonuses or special traits tied to them, but..nope! They even changed how the different races ship AI would look, it used to be they all got a special AI design related to the race, but now it's all just a recolor of the human ship AI, and that just feels like taking out some of what is supposed to make the game unique, what's supposed to make it look alive.
Techs are just stupid, why lock double jumping and dashing behind RNG? I can understand hiding things like cool mechs and cars in random dungeons, but double jumping/dashing is kind of a must when you're slower than being overencumbered in Fallout. I've heard that some techs like butterfly wings or the bubble tech were removed without an explanation, but I think the explanation is that it was too "silly" for their serious game about fishmen and star people fighting gigantic tentacles
Movement, like I said, is slow. Which is very bad, especially when your enemies are faster than a buttered-up Sonic the Hedgehog, and backwalking is just horrendously awful. Why do you have such slow back walking? No other game does this. Heck, even in Castlevania: Symphony of the Night, backwalking was favorable to just walking, because it was faster. I'm stating that as an example if only because SotN has been said to have inspired a lot of aspects of Starbound
The RNG is just, awful. Oh, look, a rusty, slow, two-handed hammer with deplorable damage..Oh, there's a rusty knife next to it that has higher DPS on top of slightly more damage. the randomized weapon abilities don't help much, either, because they feel like flashy energy drainers as opposed to actual ways of saving your applebottom in a battle.
Healing is absolute garbage, because food does not stack in your inventory any more, it will ROT now, and above all of that, there's now potion sickness! So you'll just heal a bit of your health bar, and then you have to wait for the crossed out ham icon to fade away before you can heal another bit!
I know that a lot of the reasons I've stated this game is more mediocre than Mighty Number 9 can be solved with mods and the workshop, but that's a terrible reason for a game not being a waste of fifteen dollars! If mods are the only thing saving a mediocre game from being awful, they must need to fix a lot of things!
The game has gigantic memory leaks, bugs galore, unrefined EVERYTHING, but it looks and sounds pretty. 3/10.

Okay, I've got a little over 700 hours into the game, if you count the unstable branch (check my profile if you dont believe me)
I dont quite understand most of the reviews on here, they complain that the old one was better, however thats completely irrelevant.
The reviews system isnt if you like the game or not, its wether or not its something you could suggest people to play, something youd "recommend" or not.
Yet the reviews talk about how its a dissapointment, that it isnt what it was supposed to be. When the real question should be "Is the game good?" Because a new player, shouldnt give a single flying f**k about what it was or might have been, its about what it is right now.
And what is it right now? Its a brilliant game, I admit that I am a little dissapointed too, its not what they promised, I have this over-arching feel that im not quite playing the right game, its strange, and hard to explain.
That, however, is still irellevant, the game is good, its fricking amazing, I love playing it, and I can play it for ages, theres so much to do, and you can do whatever you want. Dont want to do the story? You dont have to, you
want to kill things? perhaps just get the new gear, perhaps only build stuff? You can do that, all of that is entirely possible, you dont need to do all things, every part of the progression is tied off from eachother so you can play the game however you please.
That, was an idea the devs were clear on from the beginning, they wanted the game to be sandbox, in the sense that you play it, your way.
and it does exactly that.
There is so much to do, theres the story, with AMAZING boss fights, the kind that most sandbox games could only dream of doing. Theres the exploration, with some truly great things to do and find, I remember the first time I found a mini village undeground, it had tons of houses, breaking them sometimes gave you "balls of gnomes" which you could toss, and theyd make little horrible screams.
Absolutely brilliant.
I also found a gnome I could use on my head, too.
Theres the building, which is great fun, its a little tough with the new UI, but its simple enough to just grab the blocks from your inventory, and just use that instead, and you can make some truly awesome things with it.
You can make entire cities of interesting people with all kinds of cool stuff. and you can find some crasy places, you can farm too, both with crops, and animals.
Theres the pets, the techs, the cool weapons you can get, the guns, the staffs (yay! techno magic!) and soooooo much more.
I cant recommend the game enough, its brilliant, its fun, its light, its got serious elements too.
Dont get me wrong, it has its problems, the hotbar is quite annoying, I much preferred the old one. there are some lag issues here and there.
I'd say what so many others say, that the Novakid needs a part in the story, because they do seem oddly lacking.
However, pay CLOSE attention, to the end of the game, and youll notice
Doesnt mean they cant get a bigger role, perhaps they should get that, but ohh well. Its not that huge of a deal.

You need scouts to expand and wood to build building, but you need food to grow your population and colonize, but you need warriors to defend everyone and you need a healer to heal up your warriors, but you need more space for all those people, which means you need houses, which you need to upgrade, but you need stone for that, but the stone is in a heavily defended area, so you need better warriors, but they need money, for which you need a merchant, but you were out of very limited space, etc. etc.
Good RTS allow you to win by making smart choices, make you lose if you didn't make the best ones and can even end the game prematurely if you make choices so poorly that the other players take you out. In this game, it feels like the only goal is to figure out the one and only build order for each map.
But you need scouts to have a look at it first...

Do you like luck? Do you like randomness? Do you like feeling almighty and powerful? Well then you have found the right game for you!
The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth, and Afterbirth, are a fantastic concoction of fun. You got a wide variety of enemies, bosses, playable characters, rooms as well as the most important part of the games: Items, some good and some absolutely terrible. Luck is a very important factor in this game, you might get the worst items with the easiest bosses, or you might get to fight the Haunt on your first floor ffs Edmund please nerf the Haunt PLEASE FOR THE LOVE OF GOD ALMIGHTY (while you are at it, nerf Ragman's spiders too, they have too much health).
You play as Isaac, who is forced down a trapdoor in his room when his Christian mother hears a voice from above telling her to kill her son because he is corrupted by sin. And in the basement he finds all kinds of spooky scary things such as flies... or spiders... or maybe a headless body walking around spraying blood everywhere. Your goal? Kill your mother, before she, or everything else in the basement, kills you. You start out with nothing, but as you progress you will unlock more and more items, bosses, floors and challenges that expand the game greatly to make it worth playing for more than just a couple of hours. You can also co-op with your friends, test your skill against the leaderboard or try out Afterbirths' Greed Mode, which throws you into the same scenario except you must now kill a huge money spewing Jew with a noose around his neck.  The game is extremely fun, and I recommend you get it sooner than later, you won't regret it.
The soundtrack is fantastic as well, throw that in with your purchase, and cross your fingers and hope that Afterbirth+ comes out this Christmas...

I listened to Bastion's soundtrack way before I sat down and played through the game itself. I'm glad that the game is just as enchanting as its music. Bastion is one big errand mission as you travel through the skies to find the essential pieces needed to rebuild the Bastion--the hub world you escaped to when the world was nearly destroyed by a 'calamity.' I don't mean to tear down Bastion, as it's a fun game that I thoroughly enjoyed. The only unfortunate thing about such a straightforward task is that it can't go on too long before it gets old, which the developers must have realized as they kept the game at a perfect length.
Bastion offers several weapons that you can hold in any combination. You can also upgrade them with abilities that strengthen their unique attributes--meaning most people are going to have different setups by the time they reach the climax of the game. I had a lot of fun messing around with different combinations to see which weapons best fit my playstyle. To top it off, you can also use different 'tonics' to give yourself a boost via an assortment of perks. Once you're finished with your customization the gameplay is solid. Blocking, attacking and rolling all feel great and you feel like a pro after a few minutes messing with the controls.
The story is intriguing, but I'm going to leave it at that since I could easily give something of the plt away. If you're hoping for a deep, fulfilling story, you'll certainly find it here. I can say that the narration of 'the stranger' is one of my favorite parts of the game. I thought I would grow tired of his constant talking as I fought through and explored the world, but it's well done and never overbearing. Overall, you should definitely pick this one up if you want a fun adventure with a great story and stellar soundtrack.

This is the ninth in the Mortal Kombat series if you start all the way from the very first Mortal Kombat. That makes this game Mortal Kombat 9. This game has some pretty good features compared to previous Mortal Kombat games because it has lots of modes to choose from! You got your arcade ladder classic gameplay where you fight one fighter after another until you finally reach the final boss at the top of the ladder. The opponents are randomize except for the final boss Shao Khan. There is the story mode which added some more depth besides the usual fighting gameplay. It gives the characters more personality because of that! There's also the Practice and Training modes for combos, specials, fatalities, and other stuff! You also got your Challenge Tower which basically gives you different kinds of mini games as well as the usual kombat but with some challenges added like unblockable attacks, being only able to use some abilities and not others, test your luck, test your might, and many more! There's 300 challenges in the tower so good luck! You can skip some of the challenges if you have enough Koins but you get an achievement for beating every single one! There's the options menu where you can adjust the game's resolution, anti-aliasing, and other stuff to make it work on your computer. Choose the best setting that works for you so just play around with it! Mine has no problem running at a smooth 60 fps at 1080p so that's nice! I haven't tried the online matches yet so I'll do that later. So far I'm liking the game a lot and it gets quite addictive trying to master combos and juggling your opponents in the air! I also love the usual fatalities! They're pretty easy to execute in this game. The controls are fluid and the game is challenging. I'm still working on medium difficulty so I'm no pro yet. I'd definitely recommend this game if you're a fan or not of the Mortal Kombat games or just fighting games in general! One thing that hasn't changed over all the Mortal Kombat games since the first one is the usual gore and blood so you just gotta love this series for that! Mortal Kombat X is out so I'll probably try out that one later. Meanwhile, I'll enjoy this one for now!

One of the first PC/Console cross platform games that I can remember and I'll be honest... it was great to finally getting around to actually playing it.
I never had a PS2 as a child, or an amazing PC to play and experience GTA III when it was first released over 10 years ago. Instead like the pauper child I was, I had to go around a friend's house and 'play' the game. You might be surprised to find out that when I say 'Play' I actually mean mess about, such as the innocence of youth.
So visiting the game 10 years later, as an older, wiser, sillier man with the hindsight of GTA IV's version of Liberty City has been a great experience. There's actually a really good story within GTA III, something that I never appreciated or cared for back when playing at a friend's house (all I wanted to do was steal cars and shoot people). The story that is complimented well by some pretty fun missions and voice acting with one voice stealing the show - there aren't many games out there with Japanese American Accents with a strong double lisp.
In general GTA III has aged well, which I don't always find from those first wave of 3D games ~2000ish. The soundtrack has held up well, and it's nice to visit the early days of Lazlow on Chatterbox, and I'm sure some of the stations have even been remastered .
Graphically the game looks pretty solid even if I did have a few issues, but I think that was more my fault than the games (I had installed the Xbox Mod). There is a generally known 'issue' with the Steam gtaIII.exe file which can be resolved with an easy to install TXD file on the official forums and Steam forums (it'll fix the dark coloured cars).
The one criticism I might have would be an improvement to the camera controls, but I can forgive the lack of control (and the frustration that can sometimes be caused). This issue really comes to head during the gun battles, which at times can be awkward to aim due to a general lack of free aim mode.
GTA III might not be as vast or as epic as GTA V, but it captures the reality and craziness that I suspect GTA IV was attempting to offer. The blend of comedy within the serious tones and themes works well, most of which coming across in the now trademark radio stations, but also within Liberty City.
There are a ton of easy to miss signs and shops that hold double meaning and spoof popular icons and culture (most of which still relevant today). So while there aren't any real random encounters in GTA III, it's still worthwhile exploring Liberty City as the Sandbox Nature can still reward you with a few laughs due to ad-lib citizen remarks, billboards, shops, and funky AI.
In short...
GTA III is a blast from the past that's still well worth checking out, especially if it's cheap during on the Steam Sales. As long as you realise this game is over 10 years old, and can appreciate the early attempts of a sandbox game I think you'll enjoy it. If nothing else it's nice to see the genesis of what we know as modern GTA.
Check the Steam Forums/Rockstar Forums for the fix for the Steam version before you play, and enjoy.

Essentially, this is best described as point-and-click adventure WarioWare on crack/acid/meth/whatever drugs it is you kids take these days. Or perhaps there's a better way to describe it other than that, but doing so involves runes and scripts and languages not spoken or written by any human society on this planet. Well you get the idea. It's weird.
While the puzzles take either an insane person or complete moon logic to solve, they still are a humorous and overall enjoyable experience, and you're not overly penalized for making what would rightfully sound like the right decision (which sometimes is actually the right one just to mess with you), you just sort of keep going through the set of 20-second stages in each level until you get them all "correct". And even if it takes you only about an hour or two to complete the 4 chapters (which is highly probable), there's other challenges that involve performing the wrong (but funny) solutions to all the puzzles, and some bonus content and level editors and whatnot.
The humour involves quite a lot of pop culture references but it pulls them off quite well unlike every single other thing that makes excessive pop culture references (though I guess in this one they aren't quite as excessive). It also has some so-called adult themes like♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥or whatever, so if you're a kid or easily offended, you should probably go to bed or something.
The soundtrack (yes I will talk about this in every game I review) is mostly okay, maybe above average or so, it's free on the game's website so you might as well check it out (it's done in an 8-bit style like the rest of the game though with noticeable 16-bit instruments included). Why not?
It's not the game for people who are expecting anything resembling a serious experience, but for those of us who aren't, it's a good way to blow off some steam or whatever.

While I do love this game, it took me a long time to realize it isn't -  and really can't be - what I want it to be.  My playtime consists of probably 200 beta hours from the earliest of releases, with a good chunk of release hours in there.  Each new build, each update, I usually played through it again, and it was always missing something halfway through the progression and at endgame.
Because everything is so cheap, accessible, and sometimes entirely random, it takes away the weight of achievement.  After having lost my end game progress at least 5 times, 3 post-release, the new character always felt like a chore rather than a new adventure.  I know all there was to discover, it wasn't much of a challenge, and I just needed to drip-feed my resources back to the top.
What that means in the end is that if progression is simple and nigh-guaranteed, the depth has to come from somewhere else.  Except there's nowhere else to draw from.
Rather than being a builder / fighter / delver akin to Terraria, the game is actually more of a lightweight adventure / roleplaying game, with all the codex entries, lore, dialogue, racial backgrounds, customization, pixel art, decorations, and more.  Since beta, I suppose I had always looked forward to it as the new and improved Space-Terraria, but I think it stands next to it as a different equal, not above it.
The bottom line is that Starbound is still a great and fun game, but be sure to know what you're looking for and want out of it or you may end up feeling it's lacking something.

★★★☆☆ (3/5 - Ok)
(WARNING: This review contains mild spoilers)
140 is a minimalistic puzzle-platforming game featuring unique, rhythm-based obstacles and a vast array of vibrant colours. 140 explores interesting concepts by combining platforming and rhythm features. Generally these features come in the form of timed jumps and moving to specific beats given by the background tracks.
I personally found these concepts unique and enjoyable but what let the game down for me was its lack of content. There are only three 10-20 minute levels (six, if you include the inverted levels) and there is a disturbing lack of instructions or information about anything going on when you begin the game (to be fair though the goal is easy to pick up once you get started).
In terms of story, well... there is none... but the gameplay and audio are the two aspects in which this game shines. You can tell that the musician that produced the upbeat soundtracks and catchy sound effects spent a lot of time perfecting it for the game.
The controls are quite smooth and handle well, this makes the difficult parts of levels somewhat more tolerable (especially the bosses).
In terms of replay value, you have the opportunity to play the three original levels again without checkpoints for a real challenge but apart from that there isn't really anything else to do in the game.
I would suggest getting this game if you feel like something different from your average platform game and have a decent hour or two to spare but apart from that I would give it a miss. I feel bad about rating this game negatively but I felt it didn't live up to the expectations I got from reading about the game before I installed it.

I really enjoyed Sleeping Dogs, I spent a good hundred hours or so on it on my xbox before purchasing it on steam.
Sleeping Dogs is an open world, third person sandbox game, set in Hong Kong. I really liked the setting of the game, as it's something different than the ususal, small things like, driving on the left side of the road made the game a bit more interesting than it would've been, should they have left details like this out. The story revolves around Wei, an undercover cop sent to take down the mafia that operates in Hong Kong.
Sleeping Dogs has amazing fighting mechanics, it mostly revolves around melee combat, and guns are only used when absolutely neccesary. Because of this, Sleeping Dogs stands out from it's rivals, the melee combat is fluent, fun and never gets old. The gun mechanics are good, but nothing special or exceptional, just plain old shooting. The Melle however has a LOT of combos, and that makes for good variation, you can also execute enemies using the enviroment, giving you bonus points while finishing off an enemy in style. Driving mechanics is the only thing I dislike about this game and while you get used to them after an hour or so, they still bug me. The cars handle extremely unrealistic and I would consider that this games major flaw.
I do really like how well-optimised the game is for PC, it's an exceptional port with settings like 'world densitiy', which will determine how many pedestrians, cars etc there will be in the world.
Sleeping Dogs looks good, and the world feels alive and immersive, especially at night. The game's true beauty comes out when you're driving through the city at night, with all the neon lighting and advertising creating a beautiful lit up picture. So yes, this game looks good and I'm sure it'll age well.
+Great fighting mechanics, very refreshing melee combat.
