140 is a cataclysmically colorful platformer where you play as a black shape advancing through a set of three pulsating, undulatingly cheerful yet frustrating levels. The game requires you to jump and roll your way through a series of timing-based challenges, all of which are set to the throbbing, toe-tap-worthy beat of the game's Electronic Super Joy-esque soundtrack.
Your goal throughout each level is to collect dual-colored orbs and then return them to various checkpoints. Each returned orb causes the level to fluctuate, activating moving panels and changing the game's color scheme. To collect each orb, you'll be faced with moving blocks, grey-matter platforms that kill you on contact, and tricky tests of your ability to time impressively challenging jumps. However, the levels provide plenty of checkpoints, saving your progress before each threat you face.
The end of each level features, like most games, a boss. The boss levels of 140 are the only times when your otherwise peaceful shape is armed with a weapon: a beam that shoots out of your shape automatically in time to the music's beat. Boss levels are long, creatively designed levels that require you to avoid projectiles while also correctly timing your attacks, making them often frustrating (but, in the end, rewarding) moments of the game.
The only noticeable downside to 140 is its astonishing lack of true save points. While there are several checkpoints within each level that you can return to when you die, exiting out of the game entirely will cause your progress in each level to be lost. Therefore, each level must be beat in one sitting, otherwise you'll simply have to start completely over next time you come back to the game.
Despite this, the game is both fun and challenging and, if you manage to make it through all three levels, the end will unlock three extra bonus levels that allow you to play the first three levels backwards without checkpoints. This added challenge adds a few extra hours of gameplay—I have to assume, since I've never been skilled enough to play the bonus levels!

Bastion is labelled as an action role-playing game but feels more like “hack and slash” dungeon crawler due to its gameplay presentation and isometric view.  Bastion is set in a steampunk-like, post-apocalyptic fantasy world.  Quite a mouthful.
A moving painting of watercolour, ink and chalk comes to mind when travelling the different areas.  The world builds as you walk along, summoned from the bottom of nothingness up right to your feet creating the area.  It fills it with which seems to be the destruction of a civilisation as well as nature moving back in or claiming it with either lushes green, invading and threatening red and sometimes the dull marshiness colour pallets.  It is definitely a visually crisp and stunning game.
The story is simple enough to follow but details of the world may be lost due to how the story is presented.  You play as “The Kid”, pretty much a nameless character that not even the narrator cares enough to ask for his name.  You go through the City of Caelondia and other areas in the world collecting these crystal-like objects called Cores that will help rebuild the world.
As you play, there is a dynamic voiceover by a narrator that presents the story as well as comments your unique actions in gameplay.  There is a sense of a tragic storybook feeling and the use of third-person narration (and sometimes second-person), there is disjoint between “you” as the player and “you” as “The Kid”.   You may be able to make choices in the game but “The Kid” is not you but you play as “The Kid”.  Bastion feels like a viewing of an active story instead of “playing” it.
Bastion feels like a cross between a twin-stick shooter game and dungeon crawler.  Waves upon waves of enemies attack you and with a large variety of weapons and able to carry two of them and a unique skill, the combat is definitely fun and experimental.  Would you like to be up close and personal and later attack from a far?  You can equip a melee weapon of differing methods of damage, such as the hard hitting but slow “Cael Hammer” or the quick and range weapon able “War Machete”.  Range weapons also vary from the machine-like crossbow “Fang Repeater”, to cowboy-like “Dueling Pistols” or one-shot, long range accurate “Army Carbine”.
Enemies have attack patterns that can be learned but I still found them challenging in terms of timing that hacking and slashing is the way to go most of the time.  One example of an enemy is the “Gasfella”.  Varies in a different sizes, where their damage differs as well as their pattern timing.  Then there are “Gasfellas” that spin attack, dash attack or destroys part of the world beneath your feet.
Bastion has high replay value even with the new game plus feature, giving you the ability to experiment with all the weapons from the beginning as well as toggling “idols” that modifies enemies and increases the difficulty and challenge.
I found the world immersive and wanting to learn more from it.  I hope it would be expanded with the mention of different tribes skilled with each weapon and how they contribute to the world.  I want to learn more about the different cultures, clashes and history of this world and replaying it again will allow me to be more attentive to it because I found the details easy to be missed because of the dynamic narration, either being distracted by fighting or roaming around.  However, its presentation of the story feels intentional.  Where the calamity has destroyed the past and is now told through the elder and experiences of the other characters becoming folk tales.
Definitely a recommend.

I wanted to like this thing! I did! And I gave it a reasonable shot, I suspect. But honestly, it's just not that great.
Conceptually, the game's fine. Action horror first-person, focus on melee, dealing with both real-world and gross-horror type monsters. All that should've been fine.
The big problems are three-fold. First, combat is never particularly tense or challenging-with the exception of one or two points in chapter three (where you find some guys with guns), I was never in any real danger. Part of this is what I assume is a carryover from DS hardware: Only a few enemies appear on-screen at once. This results in combat-heavy rooms becoming a slog through groups of one or two enemies, who die to be immediately replaced by one or two identical enemies. Weapon damage seems seriously unbalanced, too-the knife and pistol seemed to offer considerably bigger damage then later, slower or more ammo-scarce items. If an enemy doesn't have a projectile, there's no reason not to just rush it and slice it up.
Second, there's not much of any plot to speak of. The game hints around at a few things: Eldritch terrors set loose upon an asylum and village, the main character having some sort of tie to it, dark experiments happening, cults, presumed dead people still being alive somewhere-and then there's a ridiculous non-ending. It would have, in all seriousness, been better served with a "congratulations!" screen and the credits being the only thing following the final boss.
Third, it's sorta buggy. I personally experienced: One cutscene crash-to-desktop, one bottomless void that cost me twenty minutes of backtracking from the last save when I accidentally brushed against a doorway, two achievements that did not unlock for killing the end boss (and several kill-X-monsters-with-this-weapon one that unlocked several kills later, or early in two cases), my gamepad vibrating after I turned that option off, the game not saving resolution or window/fullscreen preferences, and my first attempt at playing requiring a restart because the game decided against recognizing input from anything except basic movement.
From what I've read, your mileage will vary in that third category (and at the time of this writing it still seems to be in the middle of getting cleaned up). Getting rid of that, though, it remains a game with tedious encounters and just enough minor plot references that it's honestly a bit infuriating when nothing comes of them. I found just enough to like that I didn't give up on it, but sad to say your time is just spent better elsewhere.

So full disclosure most of my hours of play are from early access.  That being said the game I played (and loved) is no longer the game being sold here....it's better.
This is a classic 2d crafting game with some serious depth.  You have the option to play a classic crafting game, a survival crafting game (food becomes a nessessity) and a hardcore delete your character mode for the punishment enthusiasts among us.
One of the major flaws of crafting games is they tend to become bland, many of them are adding randomly generted environments to limit that but still they feel very repetitive.  Starbound gives you access to a (upgradeable) spacecraft that takes you to other planets with some very alien biodiversity that helps with  that bland feel.  If anything can be said for Starbound its that out of all the crafting games I've played this one really tries to stop the game from becoming stale.
With quests, city development (you can get people to move into buildings), planetary travel, and a robust crafting system this is one of the best 'crafting/survival' games I've ever played.  The only downside is character development is identical between playthroughs.  Your character doesnt have stats that level up as you do leaving playthroughs feeling somewhat similar, with every other aspect of the game trying to stave off that feeling I think the lack fo character diversity is a minor issue.

It just looks like a beautiful union with the stellar soundscape, that play a huge role in the game, and the damn awesome level design.

Also, I have not had any issues with latency as mentioned in some of the other reviews, but I have a pretty powerful computer with a couple 280x video cards in it, an AMD FX 8350 processor, and 36GB of DDR3 RAM (If you don't know what I just said, my computer is probably 100x more powerful than yours.  If you do, you're probably laughing at me ;) ).  Basically what I am saying is I don't have any issues, but if I did, the developer would have some pretty serious problems on their hands.
Anyway, I can see myself putting an insane amount of time into this game and am hoping it will continue to be as enjoyable as it has been since I got it.  I've been playing for 8 hours straight.  For most gamers, this probably doesn't seem like much, but it is a monumental achievement for a game to grasp my attention like that these days.

Dementium: The Ward provided a great survival-horror experience for the Nintendo DS, disempowering the player and forcing them to figure out how to move in the claustrophobic setting while trying to conserve ammo until absolutely necessary. Renegade Kid followed it up with a fantasic sequel that may not have been purely survival-horror, but found a great mix between action and horror elements with ambient spaces, creepy enemies, and a story which didn't come out and answer everything, letting the player be immeresed in the both the confusion and dreadful mystery of it all. It was by no means a spectacular game, but I was a fan of it despite the flaws. The HD port takes everything I loved about the DS version and throws it out the window. Where the gritty graphics complemented the DS's capabilities, the graphics for this game can hardly be considered HD. They look plasticy and the models can hardly look creepy when they look so clean and polished. The ambient music is gone to, some new tracks do add feeling to empty areas, but some area's music was swapped out for something that doesn't fit the mood. The combat has been scaled way back to the point of a boring chore. Where the DS weapons felt like they had weight and stopping power on the endless horde, the weapons in the PC version feel like you're shooting NERF darts at the enemies, and that's if you can hit them at all because the camera is so dang choppy when more than one enemiy come on screen. It's not my computer, I have a great computer. But looking around feels like the character has a mental problem. Also, there is a half second delay between clicking and using a weapon, which makes timing shots or swings at a fast enemy nearly impossible. The game also introduces a new enemy, an invincible snow ghost which rushes you out of an area, but they put them in the more atmospheric of areas and take away from exploration into just what is going on in the story. DO YOURSELF A FAVOR AND GET THE DS VERSION OF THIS GAME. it may not be perfect, but it is a masterpiece compared to this sorry excuse of a port.

140 puts substance far over style and therefore has a strange, charming style to it.
You've gotta get from point A to point B without getting thrown around by squares and static.  Not including the three after-levels, there are three levels in total (which I'll admit is too little) and they all have a little end boss which is very much not little at all. They are all challenging and will test your rythem and twitch skills to a very full capacity. The game never uses text or dialouge, everything is explained in game and the game trusts your intellect and instinct enough to figure it out yourself.
And it does a damn good job at it.
Nothing in this game is based on luck. You'll never feel frustrated at "The game" (and if you do, you're wrong) because every time you die, it's on you.
Gameplay: The game is really tight (However there is less than a split second difference between when you push the jump key and you jump, which never ruins anything but cannot be truly called "tight" for this reason) and the quirks and mechanics of the game are all explained by playing it. Your own experience with this game will depend on your paitence, rythem skills, and ability to perceive and predict your enviornment. If you're used to games that hold your hands and tell you where to go and how to do what you need to do, and you don't want to play any other kind of game, then you will not like this. If you don't have a high pain tolerance, you will not like this game. If you aren't paitent, you really won't like this game.
And that's okay, just don't bash this game for being "Luck dependant"
Also, this game has the hardest final boss I have ever played ever.
Audio: Being a guy who makes music himself, I can appreciate this game's music well. It isn't at all complicated (I don't think I've heard a level with more than 6 tracks) but it all flows together perfectly, and the feeling of putting an orb in it's place and hearing the song get more complicated is perfect. The levels are heavily (but not totally) influenced by the music, and in some cases, you are too. I just wish this game came with the OST, but that is not something I can fault the game for.
Graphics: No screenshot you will see of this game will do it justice. Almost every screenshot of this game will make it look like a bloody Atari game, and I agree, still, this game is very, very ugly.
But, you put it in motion and everything changes.
EVERYTHING.
The way the (completley geometric) shapes change, to the beat of the music is wonderful, and the fludity of the world makes it feel alive, even if there are no human constructs in the world.
If you don't want to buy the game for the graphics, at least watch a video, perhaps that will do it more justice.
All in all, I would give this game a very high, (As in the only reason this game didn't get a 10 is for a few very miniscule gripes) 9/10. Would eat again.

Oh, and if you don't want to play the hidden object part there's an alternate mah-jong game which is also fun and a nice change. Overall I give this game an 8/10. Hidden object games are somewhat of a guilty pleasure for me.  I am quite fascinated with them, but generally balk at the idea of ever spending money on them (and there's admittedly no logic to this stance - it's just how it is).  So it was that Abyss (and its predecessor, Nightmares from the Deep) were picked up in bundles along with other games I actually wanted.  But hey, here was my first chance to play a commercial HOG as opposed to all the free ones I've tried on the web and they're actually pretty good.  I played Nightmares first and you can read my review of it here:
So we come to Abyss: the Wraiths of Eden, a casual hidden-object/adventure game unashamedly inspired by and liberally borrowed from Bioshock.  At first, I dismissed the comparisons and thought they were simply tongue-in-cheek comments, but the truth is there is no denying Bioshock's influence on this game.  The story is this: your husband (you play a lady once again) has gone missing on a diving expedition and you're trying to track him down.  You end up in a strange submerged city called Eden (-not- Rapture), solving puzzles to defeat the forces of evil.  Pretty standard stuff.
Compared with Nightmares from the Deep, you now have high-res (720) cutscenes so no more fuzzies when they come up, but character models continue to be creepy and not purposely so.  Like Bioshock, there are little girls running around although they're not zombie creatures being followed by big dudes in diving suits, so at least the comparisons can end there, but I bring them up because they are REALLY weird looking.  I know it's not easy to model faces, but man....
Anyways, the format of the game is pretty much exactly like Nightmares from the Deep, but with a few minor differences.  Like its predecessor, Abyss is filled not just with HOG scenes (I think there's 16 of them to do in total), but also various find-object, use-object puzzles and a few brain teasers, but nothing really difficult.  On expert mode, nothing is pointed out to you and some areas will become pixel hunts; however, if you are playing with children, you might want to lower the difficulty where the game will be a little more forgiving with keeping the pace going.  Where Nightmares had the alternative of mahjong tile matching instead of playing the HOG, Abyss offers as its alternative a weird, but enjoyable domino-style game where you need to lay down dominoes in order to cover icons on a grid.  You're not REALLY playing dominoes, so it's more of a picture-matching exercise than anything else... just like "mahjong".
Other than that, the puzzles here are a little more clever than in Nightmares, and the only word of warning is there are some 'frightening' images that may not be appropriate for younger children.  Although I preferred the theme and story of Nightmares, Abyss is a fine casual game and can be enjoyed by anyone.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

The game is okay. You are basically playing a guy in third person and you have to defend yourself from an invasion of aliens. By killings aliens you earn money that you can use to buy or improve weapons or items. And that is all. No complicated plot or objectives.
Lets start with the positive points. Firstly you have a total of 6 different weapons to chose fromeach game. You start with the gun and with the money earned you can buy or upgrade the gun you want. You have the choice between the gun(starting weapon), shotgun, plasma, laser, machinegun and rocketlauncher. In addition you can also purchase items like turrents, shield, health. So depending how things are going or how you want to play you hav a decent amount of choice.
In addition to an obvious single player mode, you also have a multiplayer mode. You can play with friends or join a game with other people. I personnaly consider that the multiplayer mode is much more fun than the single play mode. Firstly because you can resurrect if there are still other players and also you have more strategies at your disposal.
There is a certain wariety in the type of aliens you encounter. I have seen around 8 different types i think. Depending on the type some guns are more effective than others. For example there is an alien that dodges your shots by teleporting sideways. This alien is difficult to kill with the normal pistol. Its however very easy to kill with a shotgun. Its interesting to see that different guns are effective against different ennemies and you can switch between guns depending on the situation.
Now lets continue with the negative/bad points. About the gameplay itself theoretically you have a varied choice of weapons to chose from (6 in total). However i consider that some are nearly always better choices than others. The rocket launcher for example is especially bad. You absolutely need a wall to explode the missiles. No wall no explosions or at least not where you want them. So depending on the map you can forget that weapon. I am always afraid to get upgrades lying on the floor because i am afraid to get a rocketlauncher which often ♥♥♥♥s me up.
Another problem is the environnement which sometime really ♥♥♥♥s you up. You can get stuck on small debris that has the same color as the ground so its hard to see. This happens a lot to me killing me very often. This is enhanced by the fact that the whole game is very dark. The only light you have is you torchlight. So debris that are hard to see become even harder to see. in addition to that environnement can influence the trajectory of your bullets. Ramps are one of the most annoying things. if you are on a ramp you can only shoot monsters on the ramp because youre shots go in the same direction as the ramp. If you are off the ramp the ramps absorb/block your shots. So when you are fighting you always have to watch out for the ramps otherwise you will be unable to hit certain ennemies.
The last problem is that there are not a lot of players in multiplayer mode. So you really need a friend that owns the game if you want to play in multiplayer mode.

Floating Point Review - Raymond KT
Summary: Floating Point is a peaceful, free game about using a grappling hook to swing yourself gracefully through randomly generated spaces. The only objective is to collect points, and the only thing that increases your points is swinging swiftly, smoothly and elegantly without hitting anything.
Floating Point is a free, peaceful game about using a grappling hook to swing yourself gracefully through randomly generated spaces. In the air, you're fighting gravity. When you splash down beneath the water, you're fighting your own buoyancy to swing yourself further into the depths.
The only objective is to collect points, and the only thing that increases your points is swinging swiftly, smoothly and elegantly without hitting anything. As you pick up momentum, you start to glow, the bars you're collecting rise up, the music kicks in, and your trajectory burns a bright red line in the air, drawing huge, beautiful mathematical curves of your arcing flight.
Honestly, this looks like a simple proof-of-concept prototype that could have been made in Unity in an afternoon. There's hardly any content and the gameplay gets boring after a few minutes. A point in the game's favour is that it's free, so I can't really complain about the price. If you're curious, you might as well download it and try it out for yourself. But I wouldn't personally recommend it.

McPixel may seem stupid and pointless from a distance, but the game game is a BLAST to play (get it? hah!). With plenty of in-game levels and tons of free extra "DLC" to play, you can spend hours with this game. Many of the levels contain a lot of jokes and references to other games or movies, and most of the bonus levels (which you unlock by not only saving the day by defusing the bombs in every level of that chapter, but also going through and discovering all the gags that involve not saving the day) are straight up homages to those things. The video game one was my personal favorite, where you have to save Cloud and Sephiroth by becoming Jenova, and saving Chell from Portal by opening a portal into her body and tossing the bomb in it, etc. I found myself laughing audibly with some of the ridiculous scenes, such as McPixel choosing to dry hump various objects instead of defusing the bomb.
The game menu itself was a delight, each option you pick containing a humorous outcome. The music, though simple was actually quite addicting, and can easily get stuck in your head as it plays in the background of every level that you're trying desperately to defuse a random bomb in less than 20 seconds. Some of the levels were pretty easy, but I don't think the game itself was actually going for a difficulty factor as much as it was a gag factor, and sometimes when the outcome was easy, I actually found myself looking for the funny alternatives instead of defusing the bomb right away. The 8-bit artstylem though simple, actually was very good at depicting the various emotions of the characters, such as McPixel screaming at a soldier to remove the bomb after putting said soldier's own hat on.
I'd definitely recommend this game if you could find it on a sale. As great and amusing as it was, it still only contains about 2 hours of actual gameplay, the rest stemming from DLC both made by the actual developers, and by the community itself via the in-game World Creator. Though than again the game only markets itself as $5, so if you've got a fiver to spend, and have a twisted sense of humor, I think you'd enjoy this game.

As a player who remembers the original Carrier Command, this game seems like a surprising step back in terms of scope, but it is, fundamentally, quite good fun.
Some bugs exist, but can mostly be worked around.  The walrus pathfinding is still unreliable, although nowhere near as bad as it was at launch.  You'll also spend most of your time flying Mantas, rather than driving Walruses as the Mantas have much greater tactical flexibility; if you're wanting to play a drive-and-shoot game, this may not be a great choice.
On the other hand, the Mantas handle well, the islands are fun to crack and the unit loadout and upgrade paths are enjoyable to work with.  There's a certain satisfaction to driving a Walrus around armed with flak cannons simply obliterating anything you can get into your crosshairs.  Choosing whether to arm your mantas with missiles to make your life easier, or rockets for greater firepower, but necessitating greater handling skills (which isn't easy when you're dodging missiles yourself) is a choice worth making and if you make a poor choice, you'll find out quickly (and possibly painfully) enough.
To do well, you'll have to work out approach and escape routes as often enough you'll find yourself sneaking around a building corner to come face to face with a flak-armed Walrus, having to flee, dropping down to wave-skimming height with Hell's fury erupting around and behind you as you limp back to the carrier to repair and try again.  There's a frisson to these moments that is well worth experiencing.
Is it worth the full asking price of £20?  Maybe not, but it's definitely worth playing, and one run through of the Campaign (linear story) and the Strategy Game (non-linear island hopping campaign) will keep you entertained for a fair few hours.  If you're willing to add mods, that might make the Strategy Game worth playing through a second time, but basically all they'll do is increase the difficulty (and remove some possible exploits) as opposed to introducing anything really new.
There's a free demo available, so try the game out and work out what price you think the game is worth.  There are plenty of newer games with more bugs and less polish being given far better reviews than this received upon its release.

While I do love this game, it took me a long time to realize it isn't -  and really can't be - what I want it to be.  My playtime consists of probably 200 beta hours from the earliest of releases, with a good chunk of release hours in there.  Each new build, each update, I usually played through it again, and it was always missing something halfway through the progression and at endgame.
Because everything is so cheap, accessible, and sometimes entirely random, it takes away the weight of achievement.  After having lost my end game progress at least 5 times, 3 post-release, the new character always felt like a chore rather than a new adventure.  I know all there was to discover, it wasn't much of a challenge, and I just needed to drip-feed my resources back to the top.
What that means in the end is that if progression is simple and nigh-guaranteed, the depth has to come from somewhere else.  Except there's nowhere else to draw from.
Rather than being a builder / fighter / delver akin to Terraria, the game is actually more of a lightweight adventure / roleplaying game, with all the codex entries, lore, dialogue, racial backgrounds, customization, pixel art, decorations, and more.  Since beta, I suppose I had always looked forward to it as the new and improved Space-Terraria, but I think it stands next to it as a different equal, not above it.
The bottom line is that Starbound is still a great and fun game, but be sure to know what you're looking for and want out of it or you may end up feeling it's lacking something.

I prefer older-school FPS horror games myself. Dementium II feels like aged FPS horror games like the Suffering, although I wouldn't compare the two. Virtually no jump-scares here. Rather, the game plays like a haunted house, with spooky ambience and a handful of creepy enemies. Lots of blood on the floor and dead bodies.
I liked the atmosphere of the game. The environments were very old-school in design. The sound design was what creeped me out the most. All of the monsters / enemies are very disturbing, mostly due to their sfx. The first two bosses had very unsettling sound effects which made the fights pretty intense. Heavy, spooky ambient noises permeate the game and provide some sense of dread. The background music is also very old-school, like Resident Evil 2.
The developers threw in a slight potential for backtracking / exploring to find better weapons, secret areas etc. so there is that.
However, there were a lot of things about this game that really disappointed me. The weapons system is weird; apparently an early-game enemy can take 4 shotgun blasts without going down but a mere prison shank can dispatch it in a couple of seconds. There is not enough ammo in the game to truly enjoy shooting higher-level weapons like the machine gun. Most of the boss fights I ended up just using the shank to beat them. Also, there is a major weapon that the main character assembles over the course of the game, and when it's complete, it doesn't do anything special (from what I could tell). However, whomping monsters with your sledgehammer is quite satisfying.
The enemy AI is wonky and you shouldn't expect to fight more than 3 enemies at a time. When you kill them, a new wave of baddies will spawn. Rinse, repeat. Not very challenging there.
But I guess my biggest complaint is that there is a complete lack of coherent story, the ending sucked and the game was too short (I took my time and beat it in 6 hours). I know nothing about the main character or what's going on.
So in conclusion, yes I do recommend this game, but really only if you're a young gamer with little experience playing horror games. Try it out if you're looking for a quick classic horror game fix.

- A well done Hong Kong, the world generally feels nice to be in.
- If you are a fan of the whole gangland scene you will enjoy the story.
- The fighting is great and something we don't usually see in this type of game.
- Driving physics can be frustrating and really are not very good.
- Guns are nothing special when introduced to you apart from one gun you get to use once the entire game.
Before I begin I completed the main game 100%. (All story missions, side cases, side missions, races and gathered all collectibles).
Now to the meaty section of the review and my experience in this game. I will try not to put any spoilers in here.
The story to this game is great, however I feel that as you progress further and especially when you get to the last few missions the main characters begins to feel less like a Triad Gangster and more like a God. The amount of punishment he can take without the slighest feeling of being in danger really broke my immersion near the end.
Now how does the game play? Well it's good and bad. All the general movement isn't a perfect reflection of reality and feels more like Saints Row than it does Grand Theft Auto. However I feel like Square Enix really dropped the ball on this. Walking around and fighting is fine, I have no real problems with it other than Wei occassionally getting stuck. But the driving is horrid. Cars feel like they have no real weight to them and the slighest bump sets them off into the walls around you. Imagine throwing a bowling ball down the alley with bumpers on. That's how it feels to drive these cars. So bad that it gets to a point where you don't want to drive cars anymore and just opt out to bikes.
As I have said the guns are nothing special but you will need to use them in certain missions. Generally it takes 1-3 headshots to kill an enemy unless you are using the Golden Pistol. This golden pistol is a real gun, this is the gun you want when you are shooting. Unfortunately I was only able to use it in one mission and then never saw it again until the last, and even then I could not take it further.
I have no real complaints about the look of the game. It looked great to me and ran at a consistent framerate. Nothing amazing but nothing to complain about either. A good bet for 2012.
Generally the audio is great. Once again nothing amazing. The only gripe I had with the audio was the radio whenever you got into a vehicle. Firstly the amount of songs on each station are very limited. You will quickly begin to hear the same songs. Secondly there is a strange bug that occurs when you get in and out of cars too quickly (found this out during collectible hunting). This bug would make the current song you were listening to repeat itself or start again from the beginning. It got to the point where I had one song playing for about an hour of game time.
Good game, nothing to blow out of the water but an enjoyable experience. Worth a pick up if on sale. If you like the whole gangland scene you will get a nice experience from the story.

I've played maybe 20-30 hidden object games to date (probably more), and I'd have to say Abyss is indeed one of the better ones out there, but has some flaws that really stuck with me as I played.
First of all, the game is beautiful.  Although the detailed artwork is clearly inspired by the Bioshock series (and a lot of story elements), it looks great with a colorful palette and some imaginative locations.  There are a lot of areas to explore, as well. The music is very nice and does a good job of setting the mood, but can get a bit repetitive after awhile.
For the game play, this is your standard IHOG/HOPA, basically adventure game lite with Hidden Object Scenes sprinkled in.  As an adventure gamer myself, I always play on Expert to give me a bit of challenge and lengthen my game experience, but I found the game to be on the easy side overall.  Not a horrible thing if you're looking for a relaxing evening, but I prefer my IHOGs to last longer than 4 hours on the hardest difficulty. Even the puzzles were fairly easy taking me only a few minutes to figure most out, and many needing only a few moves to complete.  The most challenging part for me was going back and finding older Hidden Object Scenes that have reactivated; they don't sparkle in Expert, so it's basically a game of "let's click on everything" in the hopes the scene is indeed active again.  I know this is pretty standard for Expert mode in most HOGs, but honestly, it's just an exercise in frustration, not added challenge.  If the devs are reading this, putting in an option for sparkles on reactivated HOS's would be a much welcome addition in future games.
The Hidden Object Scenes themselves are well done, nicely drawn items without too much clutter, and have a nice range of difficulty, but none of the items were what I would consider unfairly hidden.  And although I really enjoy HOS's, I know not everyone is a fan, so the option to play Dominos instead is a nice touch.   The Dominos mini-game itself is fun, relaxing and mildly stimulating,
While the story took a lot of elements from Bioshock, it didn't resonate with me as much as some of Artifex Mundi's other games.  I know HOG's aren't exactly a great source of deep, thought-provoking storytelling, but I felt like Abyss was flirting with some really interesting concepts, but those ideas kept getting derailed and neutered.
I think my biggest issue came down to the voice acting, though.  Maybe I'm being a little more critical than I should be having come off of a couple of games that had absolutely amazing voice actors, but here...it's just awful.  I wanted so badly to turn off the voices as every time any of the characters uttered something I couldn't help but cringe. If there is anything I would like to see in future HOGs it would be a toggle for the voices.  Sometimes just reading and letting my mind fill in the blanks is better than being stuck with voices that are pulling me out of the experience.
That said, I did enjoy the game quite a bit and can see myself playing it again in the future.  I certainly look forward to some of Artifex Mundi's other games making their way to Steam.

There's a lot of classic adventure elements in them, you find items, figure out how to combine said items to achieve the result you're after and thusly advance the storyline. Every now and then you're confronted with a hidden object scene, a fact that makes my eyes water and kills my inner child bit by bit. In a stroke of pure brilliance they've added an option to play an alternative game and that way bypass the hidden object scene entirely. What you're left with is an adventure game and occasional boardgame challenges, fantastic.
Rather uniquely they also tend to feature strong female protagonists that aren't constantly trying to assert the fact that they're female and strong, they just are. This is something that you'd be hard pressed to find in any other genre.
Finally, it works flawlessly in linux. As have all Artifex Mundi games I've tried so far.

140 is a tough game to review. On one hand, the various challenges and gorgeous visuals all tied into the beat of each level is implemented perfectly, offering a blissful yet difficult platforming experience that will leave a nice impression. On the other, even with the 5 dollar price tag, paying that much is a stretch for the little content provided. Consisting of only 3 levels, each about 5-10 minutes in length, 140 is stretched out through its increasing difficulty and bosses, which can last multiple times longer than the levels themselves, even with generous checkpoints.
The game shines brightest in the platforming sections, implementing the mechanics I've mentioned before and having a smooth difficulty curve that is never unfair, as you always know when it's your mistake. The first two bosses as well are decently balanced and don't take long to adapt and beat, even after a few tries, but it is the third and final boss that felt more of an excercise of frustration than any sort of challenge.
There is a method to the third boss' madness, but you have to adapt to a lot of variables to beat this one, even after you finally wrap your head around the constantly changing mechanics after every checkpoint.
Beating this boss provides no payoff either, as there is no new content following, nor a nod to your accomplishment outside of the standard steam achievement. You do unlock mirrored versions of all three levels, which could be fun if they didn't turn off checkpoints. Getting all the way to a boss only to die and lose all your progress and gain elevated blood pressure is not my idea of fun. If you're excessively masochistic and want to have an awful day, go for those challenge levels, but otherwise 140 is a nice surprise that has some nice shining moments, even if it never lives up to its potential.

While the first Sanctum focused more on the Tower defense part the first person shooter aspect suffered/ was barely there. enemies didnt react to the play, Sanctum 2 focuses this time around on the first person shooter aspect which shines not only compared to the first Sanctum but is great itself, because of the variety when it comes to enemies and their ablities and your weaponry to actually counter these.
Enemies are going to have Shields, heavy armor, long range, long range aoe, stun towers around them, revive themselves and many more.
Ofcourse there are many towers to counter these specific enemy types aswell, for example:
-Drones are able to pierce through any armor but the deploy rate is pretty low,
-The gatling tower has an incredible fire rate and is actually devastating to enemies that take more damage over time and smaller foes but doesnt even scratch enemies with armor,
-The cannon starts of as a tower with decent damage and range and by upgrading it the firerate decreases for a huge attack and range boost which allows the tower to pierce through specific armor.
Your abilities are also quite game changing, these vary from skills that allow you to either pick from passive abilities like core heal to abilities which increase your fire rate up to 200% (you can choose up to three perks which change the way you play drastically, either changing the role you play completely or further supporting it).
You are also able to choose between four characters which all come with their own unique abilities, strenghts and weaknesses:
-Setting enemies on fire and dealing damage over time depending on the damage you dealt while also gaining the ability to make moves such as strafing easier to perform (crowd controle-much harder to do critical hits/to take down enemies with specific armor)
-Increased health and increased damage in close quarters (kiting/heavy foe killer-not as useful against enemies with specific armor),
-The ability to double jump and deal more damage with each shot (allround character-depending on your weaponry and skills)
-Besides gaining more critical hit damage you also do more damage if you hit critical hits in a row while the spray pattern´s accuracy for all weapons is increased greatly  (heavy foe killer, best at taking down enemies with specific types of armor-gets overun quite easily)
Combine that with absolutely beautiful looking maps which let you play the way you want to (in terms of deploying your maze which enemies have to go through and also depending on enemy type and the tower themselves) and you have this game.
but seriously if i could choose one game which i would play for the rest of my life, it would be this one (or arguably the first).

I had been eyeing this game for a while and finally decided to buy it, and I'm glad I did. I didn't know what to expect from the gameplay as I didn't research it very much beforehand, I just found the general idea of the game intriguing coming from playing games like Civ, Age of Empires, and Impressions Games' city builders.
Right away one of the first things that stood out to me about the game was that it feels intuitive. I was able to get the gist of what I was doing in my first game with fairly little hand-holding, but I didn't last long because I hadn't learned the finer points of managing my clan and was barely able to survive the winters. By my third game, I had quickly picked up on what to do and when I should be doing it, which leads me to my next point - decision making.
As others have said in their own reviews, one of the best aspects of this game is that there are many different choices to be made at any moment to grow your clan, and how you go about them is up to you. This is supplemented by the different clans you can choose to play as which will encourage certain playstyles over others, adding an element of depth and replayability to the game.
I also really enjoy the ambience and aesthetic of the game. Despite being a game about survival, there's a certain peaceful and inviting atmosphere to it that reminds me of playing Civ, Zeus, and Pharaoh.
Overall there is hardly anything negative I can say about this game. I look forward to future updates and I highly recommend checking it out if you enjoy playing games like the ones I have mentioned here.

I absolutely love this game!
The best way I can describe it is an RTS that feels like a boardgame. You start with a small zone/plot of land and have to explore and colonize new areas. Each area can only have a set number of buildings, so you need to plan out each one strategically, ensuring you have a well balanced zone.
There's no campaign mode yet (due to early access) but the single player is a lot of fun and well worth the money to purchase this game. **I haven't played multiplayer yet--so I have no feedback on that**
However; if you enjoy the viking theme, they do it very well, and it's a lot of fun if your clan completely dominates the map, and you can choose multiple victory conditions from Domination, Fame, Trade and others. You can select one, a few or all of them. It also has a nice Runic Knowledge tree that lets you spend your Rune Points to select new perks that benefit your clan.
I highly recommend this game!

This game is strong in almost any category that matters to me. It has immersion for a 3rd person rpg and has combat styles
similar to dark souls and orcarina of time. There are lots of character customization (exept what the main character looks like). No weapon is terrible but some are better than others. The level's are all Awesome in their own way and the world will remind you of super mario galaxy. The story is great and told by an awesome narrator. It constantly makes you ask questions and some of them aren't answered. And sometimes the story may give you a slight sample of the feels. And the music OH THE MUSIC! seriosly, I need to buy the soundtrack. But sadly, this game has some flaws that holds it back from my top 10 games ever.
1. Only two difficulties at the start. The first is "No sweat" where you have infinite lives in a level. I hated that soo much because there were no satisifaction for beating something. And then there is normal mode which is No sweat mode with limitied lives. Sure you could use idols to make it harder but even with every idol activated, no sweat mode will still be easy.
2. Not enough enemies. 45% of the game you are fighting these wraiths called windbags. They are also acompanied by squirts and scumbags. In the nest 45% of the game, you are fighting plants and birds. There are 3 different variations of plants and birds but they basically do the same thing. 9% you are fighting
and 1% are other things. That was pretty underwhelming as it kinda got stale for a bit.
2.5. No multiplayer. This is only a nitpick btw. Not every game needs to be multiplayer but it would just be so cool and fun and add more depth.
3. Story Mode (which is the only mode) Is WAY too short. This is my biggest complaint because I finnished this in 1 night and 1 afternoon. WHYYY THIS WAS SUCH A GOOD GAME.
Overall, everyone needs to play this despite the downsides because of the story. Although this has little replay value even with the bonuses after 1st completion, the first playthrough is all you need to make your life better.

Bastion is developed by Supergiant Games and published by WB Games. Bastion is a wonderul top down action adventure with challenging difficulty
Bastion's graphics and environments are stunning and beautiful. Each floating abandoned city you visit and the Bastion itself is incredibly well detailed
The story is very well written and the narrator's voice actor is entertaining and comments on each action you do. The majority of the voice acting is done by the narrator, sometimes I couldn't really quite grasp the story as the narrator narrates the story while you play which can be distracting when there are a lot of enemies you have to fight. The little other voice acting done is well done too
The gameplay is simple, attack and defend whilst finding cores and shards to improve your Bastion. The Bastion itself serves as a hub between each floating city you visit. The level of difficulty can be challenging but thankfully the game offers a casual difficulty for players. I played Bastion on this difficulty not because I didn't want the challenge but I wanted to finish the game in the little amount of time I had in my spare time...
The game does offer a New Game+ mode after you finish the main storyline. The length for the game is okay as for me I found that the game did get a bit repetitive after a while and I felt like it was repeating the same things over and over again and to a certain extent this is true, the first bit of the game you have to find cores, then after a certain event you have to find shards. Same objectives and same gameplay...
The music was stunning and varied in its types of genres
Overall, Bastion is a brilliant little indie game and fun to play but it can get a bit repetitive after an hour or so playing the game, but still highly recommend buying!

This is a pre completion review so I focus on game mechanics and overall playability intead of the campaign.
Overall the game is made by the people who worked on open world simulators before and it shows similarities with ARMA and so on. Load times are pleasingly short (only good thing), graphics look decent by yesterdays standards and lighting and weather effects are not too demanding so one can say the game wont get any uglier when you turn down high graphics.
The settings are alright graphics wise, key remapping is standard simulator stuff with reminders of what key functions will be overwritten so it is best to keep the standard controls on. MOUSE settings are atrocious but at least you can fiddle with horizontal and vertical sensitivity which is good to compensate for the forever accelerated mouse view.
Biggest thing against this simulator is the fact that it is far from a simulator. It just dumbs down anything you know from ARMA and makes it controllable with a gamepad (hurr durr thats why theres an extra gamepad settings menu). The squad selection is a ♥♥♥♥♥ and requires you to HOLD Ctrl + 2 trough 9 to select specifically those units which will get orders. Otherwise EVERY unit will receive the quick command orders from the circle selector which you activate with the Space key... oh yeah NO JUMPING, NEVER! This also means, no loopings, dodging or any other stuff you can perform in ANY real simulator be it on foot, in a vehicle or aircraft... HOORAY for Bohemia stooping to these caveman standards of gameplay.
To go about your business you equip your units with gear that gets unlocked during campaign or randomly after taking an island ... that's right. You do not control the building process on any of your islands except what special purpose it should focus on (ressources, manufacturing, defence and one single central stockpile island or the island which will  spawn anything you put into production queue)
Defence function is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥T since it gives you only a few more hours before a well equipped enemy carrier cleans house.
BTT: You set waypoints and wait for the brainded AI to steer your units on automatically chosen paths in a single formation which is always a line / convoy... another dumbed down feature but it is probably better because pathfinding is  a real ♥♥♥♥♥! Sometimes you forget to put the command into execute mode and suddenly realize that your spearhead attack unit is alone against a whole base. Autoaim is strong in this game (because its the future ... oh no because it is Bohemia and they cannot ♥♥♥♥ing program merciful AI if their life depended on it... EVERYTHING has AUTOAIM except the player controlled unit.
You have to LOOK at the target, check if the reticle is YELLOW (wtf y u no red?) and select the ATTACK order from the cricle menu AND press E for execute... then you watch how awkwardly misplaced gunfire does magical one hit kills or the laser beams get bent in a weird way around your cockpit and magically do damage.
The biggest GRIPE I have with the weapons is that they are pretty useless even if you have the superior guns. The AI is too dumb to attack from afar (no comparison to ARMA Tank crews) and the early AA weapons suck♥♥♥♥♥♥because the swarm of bullets you keep spewing is 1 pixel OFF so the target just laughs and keeps dodging and attacking you.
The balancing is overall♥♥♥♥♥♥
While on foot in the campaign you can take a lot of shots from enemy droids and infantry but piloting a vehicle or aircraft those droids become a real pain unless you manage to take em out from afar or slam into them. A small group can easily bring down half if not more armor depending on their weapons.
HEAT turrets... oh god why!? There is a fire and forget weapon for almost anything. HEAT slugs can oneshot any light armored tank and the AUTOAIM can lead to your whole platoon to be wiped by a SINGLE UNIT! This means most of the time you will have to reload a save (if you saved at all or restart the island since you wont get reinforcements in time to continue where you left off.
Your carrier is equipped with a front turret that is made out of the weakest armor in the game. One hit from another plasma turret will wipe it out and the reconstruction takes a LOT of time.
The enemy carrier can OUTRUN your aircrafts... thats right. The goddamn naval units in this game are as fast as a VTOL and once they are out of radar range THEY MAGICALLY DISAPPEAR -.-
Bringing down the enemy carrier is ridiculous. You'll go trough most of your turret ammunition, your idiotic bots can't replenish ammo while the carrier is moving since the pathfinding is TOO DUMB TO LAND on a moving ship (but manually you can do it one by one while flying just above the carrier bay doors)
Basically what you do is switch from map to first person or third person camera behind a turret all thetime.
To take out turrets you switch to manual control, to kill anything up close you switch back to map and do the trategy game thing (select units then click target) ALL the while the CURSOR moves like it has parkinson disease making you feel like the game runs on 10 FPS ... it is the pinacle of awkward having to manually select everything with mouse acceleration and ♥♥♥♥♥♥ cursor design that (3 times bigger than the unit you want to select (TO APPEAL TO the console RTS crowd ... WTF BOHEMIA?)
TL;DR
GAME IS PLAYABLE but at the same time a HUGE UNFULLFILING TIME WASTING EXPERIENCE thanks to the ♥♥♥♥♥iest simulator controls ever from the bunch who specialized in making military and squad sims ...
They should be ashamed of themselves for wasting this games potential. It could be much less frustrating.

Bite Size - AvP Review
The Good:
- 3 Separate Single Player Campaigns (one for marines, aliens, and predators)
- Each story covers the same events but from the 3 different perspectives, which is kind of cool
- Sound and art style really brings back memories of the movies
- Multiple weapons and abilities for each race to use and experiment with
The Bad:
- The Campaigns are only 2 hours long each (longer if you play on higher difficulties or spend time hunting for collectables)
- The weapons and abilities of each race do sometimes feel clunky (don't expect Call of Duty feeling smooth shooting etc. and jumping from surface to surface as the aliens can be confusing)
- The grab and kill animations for the aliens and predators look cool, BUT take so long to do that you are actually better off just stabbing people (also if you are caught executing someone, you are not invunerable, so you can easily loose 3/4 of your health by doing it at the wrong time)
- Most of the levels from each single player campaign are reused for each story line, so it can be repetative
- Multiplayer as of January 2017 seems to be dead
The Verdict:
I was itching for some alien shooting fun, and for $4 I got a good 6 hours of entertainment so I really can't complain. The controls can feel a little bit clunky but you do get used to them. The campaign is relatively short, but honestly, I found it kind of nice that I could sit down one weekend and finish a game, rather than spend 20 more hours with it. For the price I acutally enjoyed my time with this game. My only knock against it is this - MULTIPLAYER IS DEAD. If you buying this for the multiplayer, skip it, no one is playing this anymore. If you just want to hear and see the iconic sounds and images of AvP this game is a cheap way to bring you back into that world.

To the untrained eye, the sheer minimalism and bold colours in 140 communicate an idea of simplicity and frugalism. A simple indie game for simple indie people.
This couldn't be further from the truth...
I've just spent an hour getting passed what I thought to be the "last" level. Turns out, I'm only half way there. But my first playthrough was an enriching experience. The feedback loop the player recieves in the form of a changing soundtrack serves as an indicator of progression, and encourages you to keep going. This background mechanism combined with levels that layer on their complexity with each checkpoint the player completes, demonstrates a subtle mastery of game design and player psycology. 140 could have gone down the route of asking the player to hunt down the next check point, hiding them in places that require a good quarter of an hour to forage for - or a couple of minutes looking at youtube videos - but teh developer's focus on "here and now" gameplay, where reflexes matter more than cunning, make the game instantly accessible and addictive.
140 is neither music game nor platformer: it surfs a gorgeous in-between. It doesn't require an instantanious on-tap supply of rythmic ability like titles such as Bit Trip: Beat or guitar hero. Essentially: you can play 140, and everyone will find it wonderfully challenging and fulfilling.

It might seem like just another third-person open-world action game, but Sleeping Dogs is quite enjoyable. The narrative follows Wei Shen, an undercover cop attempting to expose gang warfare, and occasionally, questioning his allegience. The Hong Kong setting is well-developed, and while the city isn't as large as Steelport or Liberty City, there's still a ton of stuff to do. The collectibles actually provide benefits for your character, giving you more motivation than most games to hunt them down. There's also clothing and vehicles to buy, people to extort, a variety of favor/date missions to complete, cameras to hack, skills to learn, races to win, drug-dealers to bust, cockfights to gamble on, and kareoke mimigames to complete outside of the critical path. The story missions give you cop experience, which you get less of if you injure civilians or damage property, and triad experience for bruatlizing your enemies. While there is gunplay complete with bullet time, much of the combat is melee focused. The game uses a free-flow system similar to the Batman: Arkham games, but Wei can use objects in the environment to kill his foes in some interesting ways. Everything controls fluidly enough. Each individual object and character looks servicible, but the amount of clutter that can fit on your screen with no slowdown is astounding. Cars, civilians, neon lights, and buildings flood the environment. The voice acting is also top-tier (How Square Enix and United Front were able to recruit the likes of Tom Wilkinson and Emma Stone is beyond me.). If any of this works for you, this game is worth buying.
Expectations Defied/69

Pixel Sand is a classic 2D platformer, that however introduces new interesting mechanics to the usual formula. In this game, you will control a character able to weild different Elements he will be able to find around levels; these elements will interact both with each other and with the environment, creating unique combinations required to solve the proposed puzzles.
===
In Pixel Sand, you will have to solve various puzzles and overcome obstacles in order to find the Exit Door and get to the next level. To do so, you will be able to gather and use various Elements, such as Fire, Steam, Air and many others, and then use them to cause unique interactions between them or with the environment. This fresh mechanic opens the possibility to some good puzzles, even if with this potential, much more could have been done as far as level complexity and puzzle challenge are concerned. There are no enemies in this game, which is quite unusual for a platformer, also you have unlimited lives and checkpoints in each levels, so dying is not a real issue, you just respawn and try again immediately, which quite takes away the challenge. Level design is pretty straightforward and a bit claoustrophobic, but sufficent. There are some coins scattered through levels that will require some extra thinking to collect, and are just there for the sake of being collected.

While I do love this game, it took me a long time to realize it isn't -  and really can't be - what I want it to be.  My playtime consists of probably 200 beta hours from the earliest of releases, with a good chunk of release hours in there.  Each new build, each update, I usually played through it again, and it was always missing something halfway through the progression and at endgame.
Because everything is so cheap, accessible, and sometimes entirely random, it takes away the weight of achievement.  After having lost my end game progress at least 5 times, 3 post-release, the new character always felt like a chore rather than a new adventure.  I know all there was to discover, it wasn't much of a challenge, and I just needed to drip-feed my resources back to the top.
What that means in the end is that if progression is simple and nigh-guaranteed, the depth has to come from somewhere else.  Except there's nowhere else to draw from.
Rather than being a builder / fighter / delver akin to Terraria, the game is actually more of a lightweight adventure / roleplaying game, with all the codex entries, lore, dialogue, racial backgrounds, customization, pixel art, decorations, and more.  Since beta, I suppose I had always looked forward to it as the new and improved Space-Terraria, but I think it stands next to it as a different equal, not above it.
The bottom line is that Starbound is still a great and fun game, but be sure to know what you're looking for and want out of it or you may end up feeling it's lacking something.

The Binding Of Isaac: Rebirth is the best dungeon game out there. The lore is simple yet deep once you get to explore it, the gameplay is straightforward but fun to play, and the main key to this game is to keep playing it to get better.
When you start this game you have the feeling of "Oh, that's one of these game...". But the more you play the more you fall in love with this game. There are a lot of this type of games out there, but this game really captures the best that the genre can offer.
You start with a "blank" character, but throughout the game. you get upgrades and power-ups that change your character stats and the way it interacts with the surroundings.
This game has a wide variety of Monsters and Bosses, each with their own ways to attack and move. When you encounter a certain monster for the first time you will probably have a very hard time fighting it, but very soon you will learn its behavior and will come up with the proper way to fight it (That said, *your* proper way to fight it. You may come up with a strategy that other players did not).
The item pool is vast in size and features interesting and unique different items. In my opinion, this is the game's best aspect: The variety of items, what they do, how they behave, and the way they synergize. You will have a great time mixing weird combinations from different items to create derpy, yet powerful combos.
The game starts with basic 3 chapters, each one lasts for two "floors". But the more you play, the more you unlock new levels. It's not just the levels, this is the main way that this game works: You start with a small collection of things, only to have it expanded as you play and progress in the game. The levels are randomly generated, with different kinds of rooms, monsters, bosses, and NPC's. They have a lot of attractions, and you won't get the chance to use them all in every run (Sometimes you don't have the right pickups, or enough health to fight a certain monster.).
The game has a dark atmosphere based on the game developer's childhood growing up with religious parents. If you look close enough, you will find dark aspects in almost every feature in the game. So take this as a warning.
Another plus in this game is its epic metal soundtrack, I'm listening to it right now as I'm writing this review. It is well made, and definitely sets you in the right mood for a satan fight or something. The soundtrack is an absolute masterpiece.
Before you get into the game, I must warn you: It is not easy. This game is very hard, and it will probably take you some time until you can even beat the first boss. So once you get into this game, just know that it will be challenging (especially if you're new to the genre).
So.... What are you waiting for? Just go and buy the game!

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

A solid start to an amazing franchise. However, this game does not hold up too well in 2014. Easily the shortest GTA game clocking in at 14 hrs with full mission completion. While it may have been revolutionary in 2001, it pales it comparison to later titles in the series. The characters can be best described as one note and underwritten. Claude is easily the least compelling protagonist not just in the GTA franchise, but in gaming in general. Having him silently take orders and essentially betraying anyone and everyone, the story leaves off with most gangs in Liberty City hating you. Rather than rise to the top of the criminal pyramid, Claude elects instead to kill and betray anyone at the slightest suggestion.
The controls for driving and shooting are solid, especially on PC. However, any mission involving AI can become frustrating very quickly. Some missions feel completely unrealistic and contrived, with fail states that can only be described as nonsensical. Most of this game's length can be accounted for by repeatedly failing some of the tougher missions. In almost all the firefights, the enemies simply camp around a corner and wait for their cheap shot. Death can come from myriad unfair game mechanics and can lead to some genuine frustration that is not to be found in later titles.
If you are interested in the GTA franchise, this is not the place to start. I would recommend Vice City, San Andreas, or GTA IV. These games boast far better AI as well as much MUCH better stories and characters.

This game is GREAT, but I did have a few problems.
The singleplayer campaign reuses a lot of levels for each side of the story, but it's understandable as all three take place in the same place. The many ways you can get through each level makes it feel open-ended despite each mission forcing you to do a checklist of tasks. It truly felt like I was exploring instead of going along a path, and the game had just enough hinting to allow players to find their way through levels.
As for the gameplay and controls, I have to say they're pretty good. The default control scheme is easily learned and very instinctual when you get used to them, whilst the delays used for doing anything make you feel just enough pressure to force you to make decisions. The many animations for finishing moves, however, can range from satisfyingly short to painstakingly long, especially painstaking if you're the one killing.
The multiplayer is fluid, and anyone can beat anyone else with enough practice and skill. The aforementioned action delays make reaction times justifiable and trainable. Death will be common within Multiplayer, whether you are the victim or the assailant. I only truly had a problem with Combi Sticks, which had a rather short loading time for a powerful weapon.
Despite any flaws I can find though, I think this was a really great game.

This was a very disappointing game. I expected the graphics to be dated, I mean it's  a DS port, so know that this thumbs down has nothing to do with the graphics... It's the game play.  It feels like I'm playing a tablet game with a mouse and keyboard.  The old, move forward slash, back up, to dodge, move forward slash, back up, rinse and repeat until the enemy falls down is literally how 90% of the combat plays out.  The remaining 10% is using firearms that are not nearly as effective as the melee attacks and run out of ammo quickly.  It's one of those games that just re-spawns enemies over and over again to fill time.  Oh the door is magically closed until you kill the same two enemies 5 times that spawn on opposite ends of the room and move very slowly.  The floating black clouds with 6 glowing eyes are the worst part of this game.  They teleport you to an arena where you fight... You guessed it 2 guys on opposite ends of the room that re-spawn 2 times apiece and then re-spawn on the opposite two walls 2 times.  And you don't just go through this once, OH NO, that would be too easy.  They force you to go through this every time you touch the black cloud and the black cloud doesn't go away after the arena, oh no he re-spawns and there are at times 3 of these guys in a room and each one will send you to the same arena, again and again and again.  The levels are very small, so in some ways you should feel comfortable like you couldn't get lost, but there is a lot of back tracking and little areas where you have to do something in area A before you can open a door in area C, but there is no reason area C would be unlocked no other than "magic".  I hate that kind of thing..  At least they had a good reason with the whole sledge hammer weapon (you can knock down wooden barricades) but the entire nature of these game feels like it's trying to stretch out it's game play as long as possible and it gets down right boring. It's a pretty good puzzle-y rogue-like where you pick strategic bonuses to build your character defensively and offensively and need to carefully plan your next step around the placement and damage capabilities of each type of enemy on the field. I think it's fun and makes you think, and is great for shorter sittings. I would recommend it at the asking price!
That said, I've played like a billion rounds of Hoplite, the Android game this is inspired by, and I do prefer that over this. Hoplite is really hard, and often frustrating, which this is not. I think that's not a bad thing, but neither do I feel like it's really an improvement over the original.
This game adds some more offensive skills (more ranged options, most significantly) and you can pick from the full list of special bonuses at the successful completion of every level instead of a random, limited list of choices like in Hoplite. That's nice because your build isn't as subject to RNG, but it makes the game feel less difficult (so the "puzzle"/"strategy" aspect is a little less satisfying), and some of the bonuses are clearly overpowered and more useful than others.
I think the graphics here don't look very polished; I greatly prefer Hoplite's pixel graphics. I would also like to be able to turn off the persistent blood spatter. It's a super tiny game (only 67 MB!), but feels ever so slightly sluggish on my 5-year-old laptop. That actually turned me off the game a bit, but I tried it on my desktop before writing this review and the movement feels acceptably crisp and smooth.
There are a few things I actually don't like about this game. One is the inability to make the window a) smaller and b) portrait instead of landscape. As a game inspired by a mobile game and that uses simple graphics, it doesn't need to be such a big window. I'd love to play this while watching a movie on the other half of the screen.
The second is that 23 levels is too long for one "round". There are too many same-y early levels with the first two types of monster before a third one starts appearing. You get good at killing them/avoiding damage after you survive a few levels and pick up a couple bonuses.
The third is that you're punished for not killing everything on the level, which doesn't make sense since your end goal is just to get to the bottom and kill the boss. You shouldn't lose XP for finding a way to escape without wasting time killing everything.

It wouldn't of been a bad game if it weren't for the fact that It's extremely hard to learn how to play. It's just not worth the time. Unless you get someone who knows how to play the game, it's unlikely you'll actually be playing the game instead of trying to learn how.

Before the level you pick your character, weapon and the perks and towers you want to equip. You also unlock more as you rank up and can gain more xp with applying buffs (feats of strength) to give you bonus XP. Before the waves start you run around building the blocks/foundations and then spend money to build the towers you've equipped in the loadout or upgrade them. Then you start the wave and while the towers you built are doing their job you just run around blowing up alien-like creatures and gunning them down.
I love TD games/maps and this is really fun! Even better I got this for $3 USD on the Lunar sale instead of $15.  Still worth it either way, though. It's a must-buy, especially at sale price.

140 is a very short platformer game for the PC with a simple but distinctive aesthetic.
Story
The game has no story.
Gameplay
The gameplay is mostly fairly simple, but really has two modes; there is the gameplay during the levels, and the gameplay during the “bosses”.
The levels are all full of fairly standard platforming elements; moving platforms, “spikes/lava” which takes the form of static, and various other simplistic elements. The game does mix these up somewhat, with blocks which trigger other blocks to appear or disappear, expanding and contracting blocks which hover in place but can crush the player, blocks which temporarily turn themselves into ground which will kill the player if they touch it, and, in one level, brief, periodic periods of anti-gravity, where the player will fall up (but cannot jump off the ceiling).
The game is quite brief, consisting of only three levels of increasing difficulty, and checkpoints are frequent – a very necessary feature in the third, quite difficult level of the game. The player must periodically retrieve floating orbs and bring them to platforms to transform the level in order to continue on their way through it, and each time the level grows deadlier and more complicated, until they have reached the end of it.
At the end of every level there is a boss of sorts, though in reality they are merely segments of very different gameplay. The first one is a fairly traditional boss which shoots at the player from above and splits in half every time the player shoots it with a little hovering shooter which fires automatically every few seconds, requiring the player to time their presence underneath the boss to harm them. The second one has the player navigating through an environment which feels like they are racing down a narrowing track as an enemy whose touch means death zooms back and forth past the player. The third and final one has the player trying to defend themselves from enemies, pointing their blaster at them before they attack; as the player only has one shot per group of enemies, they have to make it count. This last one is quite frustrating as it plays heavily with interface screw, first by making it so that the blaster rotates either 90 or 180 degrees before firing (in a predictable pattern), and secondly, by shifting around the entire screen and thus giving the player only a very tiny amount of time to react. This was the most frustrating part of the game, and was a poor design choice as it felt very awkward rather than like a fun puzzle.
Graphics
The game has a very simple aesthetic to it; everything in the game is a geometric shape of some sort, and the player themselves turns from a triangle to a circle to a square depending on their movement and actions. Even the music is very simple, the game being silent at first, then gradually building up a more and more complicated soundtrack which beats in time with movements of objects in the environment.
Final Summary
The game is decent overall, but it is very short, and the third “boss” is quite obnoxious as the game experimented with interface screw in the place of interesting gameplay. On the whole the game was not terrible, but given its very short length, with the entire game likely taking no more than an hour to beat, and the frustrating final “boss”, there’s not a whole lot to recommend beyond its aesthetic.
