Another day in Hong Kong...
From the creator's of the 'True Crime' series comes 'Sleeping Dogs' a third person, open-world game.
Plot is quite engaging. You play as a undercover cop Wei Shen, who is tasked with infiltrating a ruthless Hong Kong crime syndicate. You will meet a wide range of memorable characters as you try to balance your loyalties between the triads and the police.
Gameplay is quite good. Similar to GTA, you have an open world to explore with a vast range of activities. The city of Hong Kong is split into three areas, which are basically smaller cities. There are main quests that are available and accessable at your free will, as well as side quests scattered around the city. Besides combat, there are other activities to partcipate in such as♥♥♥♥♥♥fight betting, street racing, brawling, buying food, clothing etc. Unlike GTA and Saints Row, weapons can't be purchased and need to be obtained from certain areas or fallen enemies. Although you are an undercover cop, you are free to shoot/ram civilians to your pleasure, but be prepared to face the Hong Kong law enforcement (which gets stronger and more persistsant as your crime spree increases, like GTA). There is also an upgrade system in place which allows you to gain new moves, more health etc through gaining experience from playing the game. You also have a health bar (that regenerates when in cover), which when depleted, will make you spawn at a hospital. Beside the usual guns such as pistols, shotguns etc melee combat plays a major role in the game. You can grab and throw enemies, smash enemies against walls, counter melee attacks and use elements of the environment (e.g. saw) to dispose of foes.  Gun play does play a role in this game with cover, slow time mechanics, although they aren't that spectacular. The main enemies you will be facing are gun guys, while others will be going at you melee style with fists, knives, bats etc. There are also a variety of vehicles available including cars, bikes, vans and boats (no flying vehicles though).
Audio is great. Voice actors sound excellent and believeable. Background music does a great job at setting the asian atmosphere.
Grapahics are quite decent as well. Thanks to the free 'High Resolution Texture' DLC, buildings and the overall environment looks beautiful. Although the main characters  also look good, regular NPC's don't look that great.
If you're tired of playing open world games set in America (ie. GTA and Saints Row), Sleeping Dogs is a breath of fresh air.

Unremarkable.
The game is a basic arena twin stick shooter where you fight hordes of aliens with a "limited" variety of weapons.
The game is not strictly "bad", as it doesn't have any blatantly broken features. Everything feels mediocre, unremarkable. It's just hard to stay interested after a couple arenas.
Graphically the game is hit and miss; I mostly enjoy the setting and the alien style; the character model is pretty badly designed and animated, and the weapons range from interesting (rocket launcher blasts, lasers) to very bland (the projectile weapons). Some people complained about the darkness being overdone, but I'm mostly okay with it.
So, cute enjoyable purple neon aliens: charming, until you find out after fifteen minutes the enemy variety is very, very limited (as in, 5-6 enemies which in the end look quite similar).
Mechanically, the game again is not bad but is unremarkable. You are dropped in an arena and you fight waves of aliens until the end of the level. There are 6 weapons available but there is no reason to switch between them, since there is no ammo management and the most viable strategy is maxing out your favorite weapon and sticking with it: every maxed weapon is strong enough to clear basic enemies and the "big guys" are easily kited. You'll probably end up sticking with lasers or plasma for the whole game with little reason to spend on anything else.
Level design is good, and probably the best aspect of the game. They got the "city in ruins" style reasonably well and let you use corners and obstacles to control the aliens' movements. Some levels have a "height" element in the form of stairs, but they basically are obstacles you can walk over since you can shoot up or down.
SWAT helicopters will drop powerups around the arena, encouraging movement and exploration, which combined with the overwhelming darkness makes the levels a bit more interesting. The powerup themselves are serviceable.
I wasn't able to play multiplayer because no matches were on for the entire time I've played and nobody joined my games when I was hosting.
Overall, the game does nothing remarkably poorly, but also nothing remarkably well. Not enough enemy variety to keep it fresh, not enough "wow" factor to hook you in, not enough creativity to set it apart from the mass.
If you like the base game, you will love this. Plus, you can play with your friends and wreck havok in Panau.

Recommended - with caveats.
Controls: A major hurdle.  For a while I was prepared to give in and call the system broken.  After working through it, I eventually began to find a work around.  I spent most of the game using a 360 controller because, as the title implies, much of the game is spent inside vehicles and the mouse/keyboard vehicle control is dire.  However the combat controls are much easier with mouse/keyboard, where you have the option to point directly at a target and move the camera at will.  When using a controller, one has to rely on the faulty targetting system which will rarely aim at who you wanted it to and is in general quite clunky.  I could also find no option to turn off inverted y-axis aiming for the controller.  The upshot of all this was that if I was using a first-person weapon, I would have to grab the mouse to aim, and if a particularly challenging foot-based mission cropped up, I would have to change the control scheme entirely.  Workable, but flawed.
Gameplay:  I thought this game was exceptionally well structured but first I should add that this is not a good sandbox by modern standards.  It was probably the archetype for the modern sandbox 'genre' but things have moved on a lot since then.  GTA III is just not able to compete with more recent games in terms of scale, scope or variety.  This does not mean however that the game cannot be enjoyed on its own terms.  One specific example from my experience was my initial frustration with the lack of any kind of overworld map - something that would be unthinkable in any modern-day open world game - but this merely led to me developing a more thorough knowledge of the city streets than possibly any other game I've played.  The areas are large enough to become immersed in, but never so large that you feel lost or overwhelmed and each street almost feels like it has its own unique personality of sorts, which aids navigability and adds to the charm of the experience.  If it had not been for the quality of the gameplay, I would not have had the patience to stick with the controls that I described in the previous paragraph.
Story:  Behind a minimalistic mission-based story progression, there is actually quite an intriguing plot going on in the background.  Nothing particularly special, but more than I was expecting.  On a side note, I'm not sure if our protagonist is a soulless mercenary or just a bit dim, but either way he seems more than happy to go along with whatever maniacal schemes his employers hatch for him.
Graphics:  This is not a pretty game.  I don't believe this to be particularly pertinent, but it's worth pointing out.  The best that can be said for them is that they are functional and I was able to tell what everything was.
Sound:  Very good.  There is no background music in the game besides the intro and credits sequences, but the soundtrack to the game is provided by radio stations which can be accessed while in a vehicle.  These cater to a diverse selection of musical tastes, and most players will find at least two favourites which they will keep coming back to.  The scripts for the DJs has also been artfully written and it's clear a lot of effort went into creating a cohesive aural environment that acts as a reflection of the city you drive in.  This applies tenfold to the talk radio station, Chatterbox, which bears several repeat listenings.  The sound effects are also of top quality and you can get a feel of the car you have just entered merely by the sound of its engine revving.
Overall, I do recommend this game to anyone with the patience to work around a poor control scheme and somewhat archaic design to see the unpolished gem that lies beneath them.  I do not think it still deserves the piles of praise that were heaped upon it on its initial release, but equally it is impossible to deny its merits, and the irrepressible charisma with which it flaunts them.

The Good
The original Carrier Command, while primitive by modern standards, was a really good game for it's time. A good combination of strategy and action. BIS has rebooted this game and fixed many shortcomings of the original's design...well, almost.
First thing I will say is that the graphics are very nice. There is a "film grain" effect you cannot turn off, but that aside, I have no complaints whatsoever. The models of the carrier look awesome and the animations are pretty solid. Good job BIS!
The interface has also had a huge overhaul since the original. Commanding units is very easy to do (once you get the hang of it). I get a feeling this was designed with consoles in mind, however it works fine on PC, so again no complaints from me.
I'd also like to praise the unit customisation added to gameplay. You can now outfit your Mantas and Walruses with different armour and weaponry to engage threats more effectively...but sadly, this is where the praise ends.
The Bad
The story mode is just a glorified tutorial with bad voice acting. Some parts of it are good for learning the game - the sole reason I played all the way through it was to prepare me for the REAL game; Strategy Mode.
The lack of multiplayer is also quite disappointing. Why this was not implemented is not clear - some forum posts suggest it was axed due to development costs, other say it was to be added in a later patch. I personally suspect the former was more likely the case. Either way, it's a pity as multiplayer could have probably boosted the sales of the game.
The Ugly
The Walrus pathfinding is so bad it's not even funny. Mantas are OK, but Walruses have trouble driving in a straight line. I've tried every patch released since day one and some third party mods, but nothing works. I'm not exaggerating here, feel free to look it up on YouTube.
Final Thoughts
Been on the edge for so long about this game, finally decided to buy it and can absolutely say it was worth it! What made me step back at the Summer sale was all the complain about the AI, but now when I'm playing it I see no particular problem with it. Yes sometimes its kinda dumb, but this is not really a strategic game like Starcraft, the AI is just a "helper", the point is that you are supposed to remote control the vehicles. You can't just assign all your units to advanced task and believe you can lean back and stay cool. No, in this game you have to take the lead. I haven't spend much time in the campaign, mostly in the strategic game mode, where I have found the most fun.

Graphically, it's not likely to win any awards. However, given that it was originally a Nintendo DS title, I'd say the developers did a pretty good job with it.
The combat, at times, can be a bit repetitive. In many cases, you simply grab your shank and hack to your heart's content while circle strafing. There seems to be a decent enough enemy variety, though, to keep things flowing nicely. The bosses are gruesome looking. Absolutely disgusting. I've made my way through 3 of them and all 3 were a blast to hack, shoot, and smash to bloody bits.
All in all, I'd say it's a pretty decent game for what it is. Certainly worth the $10 I paid for it. If a Doom/Silent Hill mix up seems like you're kind of thing, definitely give it a look.

This game promises a lot, and it delivers all of it. Problem is, it's not all delivered in equally good shape. The game has great graphics, lots of unit customization, and most important of all, the ability to choose if you want to control your units manually, or just tell them where to go and what to do. If you're like me, it gets incredibly annoying when one of your units in a strategy game is right next to an enemy, and misses the shot. You'll probably be going "HOW DID THAT BUFFOON MISS THAT SHOT! MY GRANDMA COULD'VE HIT THAT!". In this game though, you can get rid of that moment by instead being the one that misses that shot, and blaming yourself instead of the AI.
Other things that are great about this game, is the fact that the controls feel great. The walruses all handle rather well as long as you manage to not spin out in the mud. When flying in the mantas, you'll first have to get used to the controls, but when that's out of the way, you'll easily do amazing aerobatics, and destroy all that oppose you. Except for the missile turrets. ♥♥♥♥ the missile turrets...
Not to say that it doesn't have problems of course. The AI is frustrating to say the least. If you tell one of your units to go somewhere, the waypoint system that the game uses to set your units's destination will♥♥♥♥♥♥up, and send them 50 meters in the wrong direction before finally going on the right course. When they are on the right course though, they will sometimes get stuck going forwards and backwards, because the AI can't figure out how to escape a corner.
If you like RTS games, you'll probably love Carrier Command: Gaea Mission, and while lots of people here have been saying that the game isn't worth the money unless bought on sale, I couldn't disagree more. The campaign alone has taken me over 35 hours to complete, and considering the game is 24,99€ it's a pretty good bang for the buck. Even after you've finished the campaign, you can play strategy game, where everything is unlocked, and you just have to destroy the enemy carrier to win.
I would all in all give this game a 7/10. The game is great, and has tons of replay value. While the AI drags it down a bit, it's still something an RTS lover like me is glad to not have missed. Besides, with a cost of less than a euro per hour, it's cheaper than drugs, and that means it's worth it.

Post-apocalyptic settings are in no means a stranger in the world of video games.
What sets Bastion apart from a majority of other post-apocalyptic games is how it forgoes the typical dull, grey and ashen city atmosphere and trades it for a surprisingly vibrant and vivid, if not tangled and menacing, sprawl of mother nature at her wildest.
For all its deceptively bright colors, the ideology behind Bastion's compelling storyline borders heavily on grey and gray morality.
The story is simple but complex at the same time, with heavy tones of survival, rebuilding, indecision, limits, and both the inner and outer struggles people face during times of calamity, which all unfold brilliantly through the words of the Narrator whose raspy, ragged voice ala Sam Elliot will keep you hanging and eager to listen for more as the game presses on.
The design blends a good amount of Arabic and Egyptian aesthetic with the gruff, steampunk-y feel of a cowboy-western further strengthened and exemplified in its melancholic soundtrack.
Gameplay wise, it's a typical hack-and-slash RPG though with a unique penchant for having the player limit his/her time spent on grinding for experience and currency by closing off areas of the game upon completion. While this may sound bothersome, it actually forces the player into a position where he/she has to plan the correct strategies and decisions in choosing which weapons are the most important to upgrade, as well as how much stronger the player character is allowed to grow, creating a limit that gives more of a challenge than an annoyance. This, as well as the added New Game Plus upon completion of the first playthrough, allows for great replayability as you revisit previous locations with small yet noticeable changes as you keep growing and growing.
Even items are limited to a degree in this game, as you're forced to keep conserving your restorative items only to be used when the time is right while maneuvering through bullet hell-esque obstacles, which can be really daunting if you're not quick on your fingers.
This lines up rather solidly with the game's core message of rebuilding and limitations as well as the ambiguous multiple endings which, without giving much spoilers away, preaches a very hard yet inevitable reality that we all will face at the mystery that is the epilogue to the end of the world.
With very few, nitpicked flaws ranging from a tedious grinding mechanic and rather short overall playthrough, this is one game you best not build a wall against.

Dementium II HD is definitely among the worst pieces of software which I have ever bought on steam. There are only a few games which made me wish there was refund system. You wake up in a mental hospital after a brain surgery. While you are trying to find out what has happened to you, you also attempt to remember why the heck you have bought the game. In the hospital you discover a lot of mustaches. Wait, what? Yes, right. Unfortunately Dementium II HD looks like a mediocre pre-2000 shooter (in HD!) and features horribly bad non-surround sound effects. This brilliant combination chokes off every piece of athmosphere. Enemies look like sketches from a psychopathic first-former and sound like someone emptying his bowels after 20 extra hot tacos. Sometimes I felt pity for them and ran away instead of killing them with one of the neat toy guns. The only class of enemies which made me feel a bit of discomfort is the warden. Imagine a hospital crawling with guards wearing all identical tremendous creepy mustaches, approaching you wagging their electric sticks on sight. Horrific.
If you feel masochistic today and might consider buying this, let me quote the following meme: "But wait, there's more!" The gameply of DIIHD is awefully slow. Movement and weapon handling feel terribly sluggish. Additionally, the save point system is simply an impudence in a 2013 release. It even occured to me that on resuming a game I was put to the wrong save point, having to play through old parts again. Also, the developers take the "HD" pretty serious. They did not only put pre-2000 graphics in 1920x1080, they also made sure you do not use higher resolutions. If you dare to enable higher resolutions nonetheless, the HUD is rendered completely useless and several "puzzles" do not work anymore.
My advice: If you feel the urge to try the game, at least play it on your DS. Maybe it's not as bad on thea small handheld device for which is was originally made.

Was fun for a while, but yes, the combination of bad AI and even worse pathing, and some other issues, I ended up having to baby-sit and/or micromanage each unit (including the carrier's weapons) to keep things alive and get things done. And since things in this game happens fast (well, not in the CS-like fast) and simultaneously, it is a nightmare at times.
Of the other issues, I could mention how weirdly the interaction between map-level unit commands and in-vehicle control works: I typically did the final approach or attack setup manually to get the much needed sanity to it.. Alas, the previous map-level command often was left lingering (without clear sign of that fact), and after I left the vehicle controls, it started to go for its previous commands. The method of adjusting those commands wasn't really that helpful, even if it is one of things sort of advertised as easy.
Sometimes the map/radar/whatnot was showing ground defense point, when it actually was doing air defense, and vice versa. And the air defense points can drop a flier very quickly. I.e. in AI control, its a suicide. One has to approach in manual control and be ready to back away if it reveals to be air defense. The ground vehicles are better in scouting in this sense, they can take the beating, but they suffer badly from the pathing, so it is still manual control. (Note, the fliers are affected by the pathing issues, too, even if they seemingly should be able to ignore ground obstacles. That shows how bad the AI and pathing is.)
As a hint for others who still want to try this game (buy it only while it is super-cheap): I mostly drove the ground vehicles as "backups" to various strategic points, left them there, then took one flying vehicle for manual control, cleared some defenses, and then ordered the rest of the fliers to assist. That worked for the best effect/time ratio for most cases, and the least frustration about the AI/pathing issues.
Also, I could never figure out how to affect, or even if it is possible to affect, the defense levels of islands (after been conquered). They apparently have some level, but since showing that level was also bugged in the map, no idea which island was semi-ready to welcome the enemy and which one was not. Though what I have read elsewhere, seem no island will ever be a significant threat, or even significant slow down for the enemy... So, no "strategy" from there.
The game had a lot of potential, but all those pretty simple to fix bugs and design flaws makes it flop. Well, AI can be difficult to get good, but even fixing the pathing to a working, even if not optimized, level would help a lot.

If you dropped this game because of the previous owner company, Kabam, and their shoddy treatment of the game, consider picking it up again.
Kabam sold it off to a new dev, Deca, and they've been doing a great job at trying to repair the relationship between consumer and developer that was pretty bad for a long while.
Lots of stuff that was behind paywalls can now be earned in game without paying money, and earning these things like extra vault space, character slots, etc feels really satisfying when you finally get them.
Deca's done a great job with ROTMG so far, and I can't wait to see what they do next.

Tower Defense is one of my favorite genres, and in my mind, nothing will ever beat Gemcraft, but Kingdom Rush is a very, very close second. There really isn't much to complain about here other than difficulty, but if you're asking me, it's a total plus. The main campaign maps are great and challenging and most people should be able to get through them, but the true test comes after you've completed them. The bonus content is phenomenal. There's more to winning than just sticking towers on the map. You must strategize, realize what types of enemies are coming from where and place your defenses accordingly - and sometimes, that isn't even enough. I can't praise the devs enough for their effort in this department. I've only got a few achievements left to grab, but I've enjoyed this game the entire way. Looking forward to more from these guys!

I don't get the "overwhelmingly positive" reviews for this game. It's not a terrible game, but it's not great either. The gameplay consists of using a grappling hook (really just a red line) to swing around in arcing trajectories in order to collide with some red bars. The levels consist of some randomly-placed grey boxes to which are attached red bars. The more bars you collide with (while avoiding collisions with the grey boxes), the higher your score. That's. . . basically the whole game. Pressing "enter" allows you to skip to the next level, but as far as I can tell all of the levels are pretty much exactly the same. Just randomly-placed boxes. There doesn't seem to be a clear objective to the game either, aside from simply getting a high score. There is no endgame as far as I can tell.
Honestly, this looks like a simple proof-of-concept prototype that could have been made in Unity in an afternoon. There's hardly any content and the gameplay gets boring after a few minutes. A point in the game's favour is that it's free, so I can't really complain about the price. If you're curious, you might as well download it and try it out for yourself. But I wouldn't personally recommend it.
You should check out the developer's other game,
. It's a much better game in my opinion.

I wish to write a good, constructive review of Fallout 4. Without bringing up Creation Club, as that has been done to death at this point.
Pros:
The gunplay and combat has been greatly improved. That time is slowed down during VATS instead of paused adds a certain tension to it, the need to select the parts you want to take a shot at before the enemy can attack. Plus that the enemy can take cover does make them look less stupid.
Companion Perks: I like them, they are good. Has you motivated to gain their approval and the perks are there to stay once earned, even when you dismiss the companion. Good call there.
Power Armor: I Freaking LOVE the redesign of the Power Armor. No longer something you keep in your inventory, it is instead a massive suit you have to climb into. The HUD could have been done better, but overal it really made me feel like a walking tank. Could definately believe the Power Armors turned the tide against the Chinese in Alaska.
Cons:
Before going into the cons, I want to say that I am a long time fan of the Fallout games. Fallout 2 was my first RPG I ever played when I was a kid, so the series has a special place in my heard. Fallout 3 was rather disappointing overal but all right, while New Vegas was damn awesome compared to it. Not perfect, but a lot more Fallout than F3 was, and their DLCs held interesting new environments, stories and items that added more to the game.
Dialoge tree: Yeah, I hate it. Its overly simplified, does not really tell you what the character will say most of the game and it does not tell you when the dialogue will advance, what questions you can ask to the side before moving onwards. Even Todd Howard has fully admitted that the system was a bad idea, but it does not change the fact that its there.
The Protaganists: That the two protaganists can talk? Honestly, I have nothing against that. The voice actors did a damn fine job. Its what Bethesda did with the material, and didn´t do, that infuriates me. Case in point; when exploring Vault 111 and see a radroach, the character reacts to that, saying "What the hell was that?" I loved that, thinking that there would be more instances like that. It wasn´t.
That you played someone that was around before the bombs? Freaking Love it, so many possibilities to do with it. That Bethesda didn´t do. A few dialogue options you could pick when commenting how the world is now are damn few. I know, because I picked them at every chance I got.
The Husband is a former Soldier and the Wife was a Lawyer. But nothing is done about that. The wife can´t find her old office, where she used to work, stuff like that. The only thing that pops up is then the Husband stumbles on that crashed flying ship and the Robot IDs him as a former infantry, that's it. Both of them should have unique perks or abilities, like the Husband maybe knew instantly how to use Power Armor or was better at combat, while the Wife was better at persuasions or bartering, that sort of thing.
Lot of potential, but Bethesda just made two voiced protaganists with a lame dialoge tree. Was pretty disappointed when I realized that. On several occasions I have wondered what Obsidian would have done with this idea, playing someone from before the War, is frozen and wakes up after X amount of time. I would freaking love to see what they would have thought up with that alone.
Settlements: Another feature that had a lot of promise that got half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥done by Bethesda, or so it feels. Some have argued that this has nothing to do with Fallout at all and I can see that arguement, but I am not wholly against something like this. However, Bethesda really dropped the ball on this one. There are close to 30 spots to create settlements. Freaking 30. And they all are just...settlements. That's it. Just places to build houses, have people work in the fields, act as traders and....that's it.
Creating Settlements does nothing to change the Commonwealth, at all. No decrease of Raiders, no talkings about the rising settlements, no signs of the settlements really helping the Minutemen. Nothing.
Have thought about this a lot, and I feel they first should have seriously downsized the number of settlements. Next, there should have been unique ones, or in uniqie places that served a certain purpose. Remember that quarry near Sanctuary Hills? Clear it out, set up a settlement and build up machineries so that the people there can work there, creating materials that opens up more things to build. Rebuild a factory, like the Corvette one, where the cars there are stripped down for metal parts, again opening up for more items to build. Work on creating couple of farms that are vital for those locations to survive, invest in Caravan guards or upgrade their gears to protect them. Set up Checkpoints to keep the roads safe. Again I wonder what Obsidian would have done with this, if they considered having it in a Fallout game.
The Minutemen: Only one serious complaint about them; you can´t customize their appearances, they don´t LOOK like the Minutemen but simple townfolks where maybe one or two has a Laser musket and a Minuteman hat, so I got a mod that did the job. Investing in the Minutemen, spending caps to upgrade gears and get trainers to toughen them up, that would have been a good thing to have.
DLCs: "The settlemen system is completely optional, you can ignore it completely if you want." Pretty much a direct quote from Todd Howard during the E3 of the game. And yet, over half their DLCs are focused on the settlements. What the hell?
Far Harbor was lot of fun to play in, I really liked the island, the fog and such. Pretty good storyline there, too. At the time, I honestly thought they were going to go somewhere with you possibly being a Synth, that there would be more DLCs that left hints and clues that lead to a confrontation or a conclusion, like with Ulysses and the Courier. But no. Just a question on not really knowing if one is a Synth and that's it.
Nuka World was fun to explore, but I am a goody goody two shoes, so I refused to become a Raider Chief and thus was unable to play 90% of the storyline. I had heard about that before playing it, and yet during the first part and talking to some people it honestly felt like there was a possibility to pit the Raider groups against each other. That you could sabotage something, pin it somone else and stand back as they fought each other. But no, had to kill all of them by yourself. Fun, fun.
Weapon Moddings: Overal, I am fine with the weapon moddings you can do.Its just that it does make the weapons lose their indentities, or sure feels like that to me. And there are only a handful of core weapons, at least when compared to New Vegas. Also, how the hell is it that I can take a Laser Pistol and turn it into a freaking Sniper weapon???
Storyline: Father and son plot. Wait, wasn´t that in F3 as well?
Factions killing Factions: Can´t work uniting them together against the Institute. The Railroad has a tunnel vision when it comes to Synths and then some.
RPG Elements: What RPG Elements? Seriously, there are practicly none, even Skyrim is more of an RPG than this game. The Perk charts could have worked if set up differently, given players the choise of focusing on specializing in something, like revolvers or automatic pistols. Or to wield a weapon using its full potential, your perk level had to be certain level etc.
Majority of the perks are just about boosting damage, that's it. Bit of improving lockpicking and hacking. And modifying gears. That's it, really. Removing skills and going with this set up was a big, big mistake.
They went with overly simplifying things and to try and appease to general players as much as possible (more so than Skyrim) and the game suffers because of it.
That's about all I Can think of, though it wouldn´t surprise me if I remember something soon after I post this. Hope you found my review to be helpful or illuminating.

140 is a minimalist style platformer where the music is the key to completing levels. In the platforming you have to go from point A to point B to dodging and using objects in the map. The game has in total 3 levels with each of them having 1 endboss. The endbosses are pretty challenging and really let you know you have to focus on what is happening on screen but also to the music that you hear.  What I like about the game is that it explains itself with no text, using only music and the world itself. This really helps the minimalist style. As you progress through the game, you can really hear and see that the levels are getting harder and have to think about what you are doing. The game is well designed, so when you die you know it is your fault. The music is also fun to listen to.  I first played the game on okay-speakers and later on a good-headset. The difference in enjoyment was huge. So I would recommend good audio equipment while you play the game.  Steam says the game took me in total 104 minutes.( I have to say that I left level 2 partway through once, so I had to start from the beginning of level 2. So the games doesn't save your checkpoints in a level. ) After you complete the main game you also unlock all the levels in mirror mode where you don't have any checkpoints. This can be fun for people who are searching for a challenge but I am not interested in playing it. All in all, the game was fun but felt too short for me. I had hoped the game had more harder levels.
In short: A nice, but short, minimalist style platformer where music is the key.

TL;DR Verdict: 9/10 - Finally an sandbox game based in Hong Kong, and hopefully not the last. While it doesn't have the polish of a GTA, it's just as fun and immersive. I recommend picking up the Definitive Edition as it contains all the DLCs. I also recommend playing with a controller for the best experience.
+ Great story & characters
+ Fun martial arts combat system (similar to Arkham / Mordor but with environmental kills and weapons)
+ Does not overdo the use of guns unlike GTA / Saints Row
+ Lots of different costumes (which show in the cut scenes)
+ Good variety of cars & motorbikes which handle well (Class A vehicles do give a sense of speed)
+ Above average parkour
+ Vibrant environment / atmosphere (Plenty of Cantonese NPC profanity)
+ Good voice acting (but kinda weak in the Cantonese parts)
+ Side quests / events were mostly decent, but karaoke mechanics needs work (Yakuza style Karaoke would be better)
+ Roughly a 30-35 hour game if you do all the side quests / collectables / achievements
+ Nice graphics, runs well at 3440x1440 on a ATi XFX Radeon HD7970 (Medium-high settings)
+ Free HD Texture Pack which makes it look even better
+ Good controller support (I wouldn't recommend playing on a keyboard)
- The dating side "game" feels rushed, seems like there should be more to it
- The Mahjong gambling game is actually poker, not real Mahjong
- Some weird physics glitches from time to time
- Lacks the final bit of polish and finish seen in GTA games
- Expensive DLCs (pick up the Definitive Edition to avoid this issue)
- Only 1 difficulty and it's kind of on the easy side
- No multi-player (which added to the Saints Row experience)
- Needs better radio stations
- Massive imbalance of the cash rewards (Tran's car fetch missions payout 10 times more)
- No sequel in the works, only a spin-off MMO: Triad Wars :(
- Decent size sandbox but missing a lot of HK (Where's Kowloon?)
- In-game radio needs the song "Everybody Was Kung Fu Fighting"

We did it! We left Early Access!
Starbound is an open-world sandbox survival game developed by Chucklefish Studios, and has been in development for a very, very long time. Five years, in fact. It has humble origins from the Humble Bundle website, which launched a Kickstarter-style campaign to fund the development of the game. The game launched on Steam in 2013, and soon joined the “early-access” program where it reached commercial success and was already being hailed as a brilliant game, despite the fact that it was early on in development.
Personally? I bought the game around that time and initially couldn’t stand it. I’d recently been playing Terraria and couldn’t shake the feeling that Starbound was just cashing in on Terraria’s success. I was, however, proven wrong. Very wrong.
Starbound, as I said, is an open-world sandbox survival game a la Terraria or Minecraft, but with a Sci-Fi/Fantasy twist. The game features dungeoneering, survival elements, questing, and much much more.
After the player starts a new game, you’re prompted to make a character. You’re given a choice of different races to choose from, which are all cosmetic (aside from the “Novakid” race; they’re allowed to craft guns as their weapon rather than the swords other races are allowed to craft). The character creation is nice, but rather limited due to the pixel-style graphics. A nice touch is that you can choose a default pose for your character – something not often seen in character creation which gives a little more of a personal touch and identity to your avatar.
After character creation, Starbound’s story (added with the 1.0 update) with the player’s graduation from the academy for the Terran Protectorate, an alliance of all of the universe’s races to provide safety across the stars. The introduction mission acts as a tutorial, and after an entertaining Lovecraftian-inspired disaster, the player is flung into the stars with their very own ship and encouraged to explore and craft their way across the universe.
Due to the nature of the game, there is no “goal”, you simply do what you want. Crafting, exploring, building colonies to fill with rent-paying tenants (I may or may not have received an achievement berating me for the poor living conditions in my colony), or doing the all-new and all-awesome randomly-generated quests that NPCs give to you. There is, however, a story.
With 1.0, Chucklefish added a story to the world of Starbound, giving a new lease on the lore and feel of the universe. The story is told through a series of instanced missions, and details the player’s investigation into the Eldritch horrors that interrupted your graduation ceremony. Between instances, the player must gather “clues” by using a told to scan various objects belonging to the different races. Each instance ends in a boss battle, and the few that I’ve played so far have been satisfying, blending both platforming and the game’s intuitive combat system.
As for building, the game is as good as it gets in the genre. The building is very similar to Terraria’s system, but additional tools such as paint mode, interactable furniture and a wiring mode adds a new depth, and the variety of building blocks allows for some awesome builds. I’m currently working on a shrine dedicated to the saviour of the universe, Big Ape.
Starbound has a great aesthetic to it, the futuristic ambience surrounding the planets and colonies really pack a punch, and the pixel art is a cracking way to emulate the sci-fi feel. Despite the somewhat simplistic approach to the graphics, the game still looks and feels great. The character design is also brilliant, and the multitude of different monsters sprawled across the universe never fail to surprise or impress. The penguins, too. Oh lord, the penguins.
The music for the game is also beautiful, with an airy and out-of-this world feel to the soundtrack. The music has been designed excellently and really adds to the atmosphere (or lack thereof!) of the planets, coming together with the graphics to form an awesome experience.
The game runs excellently, which one would expect after five years of optimization! I’ve only run into a few bugs, but since the 1.0 launch I’ve not managed to emulate any of them. Multiplayer can be a little touch-and-go at times and I’ve heard reports of memory leaks when using a server, but simply joining a friend’s game through the Steam servers is an easy fix. My game runs at a smooth 60fps, and friends with lower-specced rigs are reporting similar frame rates.
To wrap things up, I’d say Starbound should be the model that all Early Access games base themselves on. The journey has been long, but the condition the game is in right now is a masterpiece, and I can’t wait for what Chucklefish have in store for the future. The game plays like a more-polished Terraria, with as many gameplay options as any triple-A title. Simply exploring the galaxy can keep you occupied for hours. At £12, this game is an absolute steal and I couldn’t recommend it more. It’s worth it simply to wear a gnome as a hat.
There is, however, one criticism…. Needs more Big Ape.

You'll note that a large amount of the negative reviews are based, in part, by experience in the alpha/beta stages, when the game was, in fact, in development. I think the largest flaw with early access games is people tend to think that when developers say something will be in or they add something in with the intent to keep it, that thing will be kept, but that's not the case-- for an unfinished game or a finished game.
In this day and age, a 'finished' game is a formality. 1.0 means nothing. Those numbers mean nothing besides how updated the game is. In the olden days, it was extremely hard to make a game and then update it afterwards to fix bugs or add features, which is why it didn't happen. Now, with things like Steam and Minecraft practically creating the "Early Access" fad, games are constantly being added to and updated in a way that makes it hard to "review" a game in it's finished state. This has been covered, recently, by TotalBiscuit and NerdCubed, and potentially other critics/YouTubers I'm not aware of.
Beyond that, I still think this is a good game. I still think that, although Chucklefish has made some mistakes, this is a game worth buying and playing. Things will be fixed, things will be added, because that's how games work nowadays. I suppose that's just my optimistic side speaking, but I have owned this game before it was available to even install, and followed the development track a long time before and after that, and I'm not at all surprised to see them go back on things they promised because this is a game that was, and still is, in development.
If you want a decently good space exploration game, with sandbox and RPG features, then this is the game for you. If you want the pinnacle of all your hopes and dreams wrapped up in one $15 package, then I'm afraid no game is ever going to be to your liking.

Realm of the Mad God (or RotMG) is a Mass-Multiplayer Online Role-Play Game (MMORPG). If you are deadly opposed to pay to win... Stay anyway because I have something to say. This game uses a Pay to Win (or P2W. Man, I love acronyms!) system that can be cumbersome but I'll get into that later when I compare it to Team Fortress 2... Like every time I see a FTP system that I don't like.
Where to start with this beast... Oh I know! The play time! I have a friend who is really into this game! He showed me it and I spent a fair bit of time watching him! So that four hours is more like 6-8 hours of pure enjoyment.
With that out of the way, let me lay down how this sexy beast plays: pretty good. It's like a bullet hell with RPG elements. (Which I've always wanted to see) and the gameplay is pretty fluid. Sure, It looks like crap but that's okay! That means that My first computer, a Compaq Pressario X1000 laptop, actually ran it pretty well.
The level cap is set at level 20 and you gain them pretty quickly. Normally this would be an issue were it not for the death mechanics. When you die, your character gets completely wiped. DEAD. All the items you had on you are also gone and you have to start from scratch. This isn't an issue as teleporting to the hub world is bound to the "F" key and health potions drop like cash during a Hylian lawn mowing job. You'll die only if you aren't fast enough or stop paying attention.
"So what's the catch?" I hear you ponder, "Is this the free game we've been seeking? The one foretold in legend?"
In a word: No.
The problem is the RotMG's use of P2W features. You technically don't have to spend money, but the grind to unlock new classes for your character's is borderline psycopathic. You see, once you surpass level 20 you start gaining fame, pretty much just higher levels that you can spend. You gain these much slower, however and if you die... well back to level one, and you have to grind all the way back up 20 levels to get more fame.
However, you can pay to unlock these new classes. You can pay to get pets with special buffs. You can pay to get more storage space so you don't lose everything when you die. You don't need to, and part of the fun is trying not to, but if you want to play the game, you'll part with your money. Especially for chest space. you can only hold 8 (don't quote me) Items with the storage. And you can find some pretty sick loot.
If you can ignore this, as I have. You'll find a solid game, that's a blast to play with friends in discord! 5/ 10 It's not perfect, but it's definately worth a try!

I had actually been going back and forth for a few months to purchase the original Dementium: The Ward and Dementium II for the DS before noticing that there was going to be a PC port. I still have yet to play them, but now that I've completed the game, I'm certainly interested in buying/completing the originals, and for additional ports/sequels in the future.
3.5/5 Controls: Iffy at times, but certainly not terrible by any means. The run would cut out (had it happened a handful of times, I would blame it on either my keyboard or my fingers; not the case) and walk was a bit too slow for my liking so I constantly ran. Part of this could be because I've been playing Damned too much and am used to the faster pace. A few of the doors/items wouldn't trigger with the right click unless done several times. These are easy fixes done through future patches, so I would take this worth a grain of salt once there's patches out in the future.
4/5 Graphics: Very well done for a port, yet to keep the aesthetics of the original game it was decently well done. I did check out 1-2 hours of gameplay from Youtube, so I'm decently qualified to speak on it. I'm a horror fan (Doom, Alone in the Dark, Fatal Frame), but not so much of modern games. By no means am I a graphics snob, so obviously this isn't a turn-off by any means, especially since I play through all my old favorites all the time. If you do prefer high-tier graphics to use your fancy video card, go right on ahead to Outlast or other similar games. If you don't mind middle to middle-low range, you'll be comfortable with Dementium II. A minor thing I noticed from time to time was that some textures would either be misplaced (ie. above the surface it was supposed to lay on) or be removed. When gone completely, the game would lag, as if it was still trying to load them (ie. wood grain from stilted houses on ice when you were walking on the ice). It never happened anywhere where you'd be fighting, or where anything would spawn, so it's not too large of an issue. It may even be addressed in a future patch.
3.5/5 Story: Decent, a bit repetitive at times, but with enough twists and puzzles to keep you going for the 4-6 hours to finish it out. Major gripe: I wish they would have did something a bit more special with the final cut scene. I understand what was going on, but it felt rushed and flat.
3.5/5 Gameplay: The revolver was...strange at times, crosshairs laggy, recoil weird and clunky. Reloading was terribly annoying when guns were required (tab, click on held gun, wait for reload). I won't even talk about how annoyed I was with the shotgun. For the most part I stuck to my shank since I dislike shooters anyways. A few other glitches, but with a major patch coming either today or tomorrow, I'm going to withhold those since they'll most likely be address anyways. HINT: In doubt, just restart the game. It seems to fix itself a lot if you run into any issues.
4/5 Music: From the quality I heard from the DS version to the reboot, I'm very happy with the changes. It's been said that all of the audio has been redone with this release, and it's all been for the better. I never had any issues with the audio up until the final boss fight, where it wobbled and shrieked a bit; I felt like I was in Lavender Town again. Again, most likely will be fixed with future patches, so I'm not worried about it either.
3.7 Overall now, rounded to 4/5 when patches correct the most glaring issues. Most things are going to be updated with future patches, anyways, so don't let those critiques bother or drive you away from a solid overall horror experience if you like the old feel with some solid updates. Not to mention the dev's have been completely helpful, understanding, and rushing to get the game patched up as soon as possible, so no qualms whatsoever for me. Have fun and immerse yourself into the mind of the insane.

140 is a short rhythm-based platformer. The obstacles in the game are essentially variants of moving and jumping to the beat while attempting to dodge "noise" blocks; this can get quite tricky as the game goes on. Each of the three stages ends with a pseudo-boss battle that switches the action from platforming to something entirely different. Finishing the game unlocks the ability to play mirrored versions of each stage with no checkpoints, which is a bit too much for me to handle but it is nice that the option is there.
The aesthetics, on the other hand, are hard to care about. On one hand, the use of color is vibrant, the way everything syncs to the music is cool, and there are some neat visual effects to see throughout the game. On the other hand, simplistic shapes are basically the only objects in the game and the tunes themselves are rather bland as well. The game is minimalist to the point of feeling uninspiring, and I can't say it will stick around in my memory for long.
Overall, while it's not the most interesting game out there, I had fun with 140 and it certainly didn't overstay its welcome. I wouldn't say it's worth its standard price of $5, but on sale it wouldn't be the worst game to pick up for a quick experience.

Dementium II was a Nintendo DS FPS-Horror game, sequel to Dementium: The Ward. I never played either of them, so I can't say how this compares to the original, but I can say a general opinion on the title, and how it stands on the Steam market.
Firstly, you'll have to acknowledge its DS origins to understand some of the design decisions in the game. The combat is somewhat simplistic for a FPS. Enemies do react to being hit in certain spots more than others, but it feels somewhat simplified. The beginning enemies especially are noticeable as you start the game with just a knife, and the first few are pretty simplistic (enemies that just try to approach you and hit you with a melee attack). How you attack, how the enemies react... It all has a very handheld feel to it, combined that most objects in the environment have simple geometry and some of the textures are kind of low. Not a terrible looking game, but it does look a bit dated. The graphics have been completely reworked for the HD version, but it mainly tries to update them rather than fully modernize them.
The audio also is notciable just upgraded DS tunes as well. The music is not bad, there's actually some very nice songs in the collection, but it sounds like Silent Hill 1-level quality. Also, the game has a bad habit of making a certain battle theme playing when enemies are near. It isn't TOO repetitive, but you will hear the song a number of times before the game is up. But the sounds can be pretty competent to fit the mood.
But the game does a good job at slowly but surely introducing new elements and enemies to keep things interesting. The enemies are surprisingly varied, and new ones keep on getting added until the last fourth of the game. I hear the original game had respawning enemies, but that's thankfully not the case here. Enemies don't respawn when backtracking or re-entering a room, which is nice and makes defeating enemies with supplies feel worthwhile. You can run in most instances though if you feel so inclined. Bosses, while not amazing, are pretty good. Definitely not bad, more than serviceable, so yeah, pretty good. And like the normal enemies, they're pretty varied. There's a few puzzles tossed into the mix, no real brain teasers, but they can be fun little distractions, and like other elements, they switch-up the puzzles so you aren't doing too much of the same thing. In fact, I have to applaud the developers on trying to switch things up enough to avoid the game from becoming too repetitive. The locations even are pretty varied and feel different, and even backtracking doesn't really overdo itself. The locations main 'themes' switch between asylum-type levels, nightmare-type levels, and outdoor snowy-type levels, but they each have a different sub-theme and different environments and design. The developers seemed to have found a sweet middleground for making elements familiar, but not treading too much of the same ground to be repetitive.
The game isn't scary. Tense sometimes, but the game never really tries to scare you. No scripted scares, no jump scares... Which could be a good thing. The game simply uses audio, and its environment and monsters. The atmosphere can be tense sometimes, and even creepy, but the game possibly relies too much on its combat for itself to really settle in.
And that's one thing you'll need to know about Dementium. It is a very action-focused title. While you can run from most encounters, you will be fighting a lot of enemies, with limited supplies, and the monsters are the main focus of the game. There's a total of 10 weapons in the game, and each feels very different, though noticeably you gain five of the game's ten weapons in the last third of the game, and three weapons right in the final chapter, making how they're spread maybe a bit uneven.
I'd say it's a good game, not an AMAZING game, but if something that's like a mixture between Doom and Silent Hill interests you, this may be right up your alley. Not a bad game, or a bad remake, I'd give it a solid 6-8 our of 10, but keep in mind its handheld origins definitely show and I did find a few of the game's enemies a bit frustrating, and the combat was pretty simple. Can be a very nostalgic feeling game, if that's what you're looking for.

Nothing was heard from it until Square Enix found the game concept at the bottom of a trash bin that I happened to be eating from, thank you very much for interrupting my dinner, Mr. Yasuhiro Fukushima. We did it! We left Early Access!
Starbound is an open-world sandbox survival game developed by Chucklefish Studios, and has been in development for a very, very long time. Five years, in fact. It has humble origins from the Humble Bundle website, which launched a Kickstarter-style campaign to fund the development of the game. The game launched on Steam in 2013, and soon joined the “early-access” program where it reached commercial success and was already being hailed as a brilliant game, despite the fact that it was early on in development.
Personally? I bought the game around that time and initially couldn’t stand it. I’d recently been playing Terraria and couldn’t shake the feeling that Starbound was just cashing in on Terraria’s success. I was, however, proven wrong. Very wrong.
Starbound, as I said, is an open-world sandbox survival game a la Terraria or Minecraft, but with a Sci-Fi/Fantasy twist. The game features dungeoneering, survival elements, questing, and much much more.
After the player starts a new game, you’re prompted to make a character. You’re given a choice of different races to choose from, which are all cosmetic (aside from the “Novakid” race; they’re allowed to craft guns as their weapon rather than the swords other races are allowed to craft). The character creation is nice, but rather limited due to the pixel-style graphics. A nice touch is that you can choose a default pose for your character – something not often seen in character creation which gives a little more of a personal touch and identity to your avatar.
After character creation, Starbound’s story (added with the 1.0 update) with the player’s graduation from the academy for the Terran Protectorate, an alliance of all of the universe’s races to provide safety across the stars. The introduction mission acts as a tutorial, and after an entertaining Lovecraftian-inspired disaster, the player is flung into the stars with their very own ship and encouraged to explore and craft their way across the universe.
Due to the nature of the game, there is no “goal”, you simply do what you want. Crafting, exploring, building colonies to fill with rent-paying tenants (I may or may not have received an achievement berating me for the poor living conditions in my colony), or doing the all-new and all-awesome randomly-generated quests that NPCs give to you. There is, however, a story.
With 1.0, Chucklefish added a story to the world of Starbound, giving a new lease on the lore and feel of the universe. The story is told through a series of instanced missions, and details the player’s investigation into the Eldritch horrors that interrupted your graduation ceremony. Between instances, the player must gather “clues” by using a told to scan various objects belonging to the different races. Each instance ends in a boss battle, and the few that I’ve played so far have been satisfying, blending both platforming and the game’s intuitive combat system.
As for building, the game is as good as it gets in the genre. The building is very similar to Terraria’s system, but additional tools such as paint mode, interactable furniture and a wiring mode adds a new depth, and the variety of building blocks allows for some awesome builds. I’m currently working on a shrine dedicated to the saviour of the universe, Big Ape.
Starbound has a great aesthetic to it, the futuristic ambience surrounding the planets and colonies really pack a punch, and the pixel art is a cracking way to emulate the sci-fi feel. Despite the somewhat simplistic approach to the graphics, the game still looks and feels great. The character design is also brilliant, and the multitude of different monsters sprawled across the universe never fail to surprise or impress. The penguins, too. Oh lord, the penguins.
The music for the game is also beautiful, with an airy and out-of-this world feel to the soundtrack. The music has been designed excellently and really adds to the atmosphere (or lack thereof!) of the planets, coming together with the graphics to form an awesome experience.
The game runs excellently, which one would expect after five years of optimization! I’ve only run into a few bugs, but since the 1.0 launch I’ve not managed to emulate any of them. Multiplayer can be a little touch-and-go at times and I’ve heard reports of memory leaks when using a server, but simply joining a friend’s game through the Steam servers is an easy fix. My game runs at a smooth 60fps, and friends with lower-specced rigs are reporting similar frame rates.
To wrap things up, I’d say Starbound should be the model that all Early Access games base themselves on. The journey has been long, but the condition the game is in right now is a masterpiece, and I can’t wait for what Chucklefish have in store for the future. The game plays like a more-polished Terraria, with as many gameplay options as any triple-A title. Simply exploring the galaxy can keep you occupied for hours. At £12, this game is an absolute steal and I couldn’t recommend it more. It’s worth it simply to wear a gnome as a hat.
There is, however, one criticism…. Needs more Big Ape.

As many people say, the game has a good presentation. But under its covers lies a very cheap gameplay design.
There is no real progress in playing the campaign. Every level is just a different map with no variates but visual ones. Upgrading weapons doesn't feel rewarding, and there is no strategy involved (except for kiting enemies). The "campaign" is just a bunch of unlockable survival maps.
I can imagine it being a great game with a *real campaign*. The levels could have different "Left For Dead-style" objectives: Reach a specific destination (like a draw bridge), prepare defenses (mines, turrets, ...), then set off the horde and survive until you can finally escape.
For more strategy and deeper gameplay experience, especially in coop, weapons would need to be more different. Right now, all weapons are more or less bullet sprayers (except the rocket launcher). E.g. pistols could make players more agile while a sniper rifle could be used by a player to stay on a higher position and take of the big guys from far away. Having limited ammunition could engage players to use different weapons.
But I doubt that any of these changes will ever make it into the game (since what I'm suggesting is almost a complete redesign). And since I had very little and short fun playing it with my friend, I cannot recommend this.

It came from space, and ate our brains is off to a strong start due to its charming art style and frantic gunplay but sadly soon stutters and grinds to an halt due to its repetitiveness and lack of features.
As an unnamed hero you'll face alien invaders in twelve different levels using six different and upgreadable weapons while a swat drone hovers over the levels and sometimes drops random bonuses to help you.
-lovely art syle
-all weapons feel suitably powerful and are equally useful
-good level design
-nice soundtrack
-overall quite difficult and pretty unforgiving
-no story whatsoever
-no tutorial/hint system, you'll have to find out by yourself how to beat a level (get through 6 waves), what your max health is (4) and what the dropped bonuses do
-UI is a bit barebones lacking useful info such as wave number and remaining enemies
-repetitive gameplay, while the levels change the few alien classes are always the same and there's no variety whatsoever, not even a boss fight
-no permanent upgrades, you always start with the basic pistol on each level
-multiplayer is almost dead
I enjoyed my first hour with the game despite having been taken by surprise by how unforgiving it was even on Normal difficulty: blasting aliens, trying the various weapons and seeing what each upgrade would do was fun.
Sadly after a bit I realized I was doing the same things over and over: blast aliens, choose a weapon to stick with and upgrade it, try to survive the final wave, go to the next level. The fact there was no story to tell me why I was visiting the various locations and fighting back made it hard to push through the whole game: the ending was also sorely disappointing with no cutscene or text to explain if I won or anything, just a meager "back to main menu" prompt.
It came from space, and ate our brains is honestly too barebones to be enjoyable enough to recommend, on sale price (I got it for 3$) it'd possibly be decent for hardcore fans of the genre looking for something straightforward and challenging to play in short bursts but everyone else can safely pass this up.

You'll note that a large amount of the negative reviews are based, in part, by experience in the alpha/beta stages, when the game was, in fact, in development. I think the largest flaw with early access games is people tend to think that when developers say something will be in or they add something in with the intent to keep it, that thing will be kept, but that's not the case-- for an unfinished game or a finished game.
In this day and age, a 'finished' game is a formality. 1.0 means nothing. Those numbers mean nothing besides how updated the game is. In the olden days, it was extremely hard to make a game and then update it afterwards to fix bugs or add features, which is why it didn't happen. Now, with things like Steam and Minecraft practically creating the "Early Access" fad, games are constantly being added to and updated in a way that makes it hard to "review" a game in it's finished state. This has been covered, recently, by TotalBiscuit and NerdCubed, and potentially other critics/YouTubers I'm not aware of.
Beyond that, I still think this is a good game. I still think that, although Chucklefish has made some mistakes, this is a game worth buying and playing. Things will be fixed, things will be added, because that's how games work nowadays. I suppose that's just my optimistic side speaking, but I have owned this game before it was available to even install, and followed the development track a long time before and after that, and I'm not at all surprised to see them go back on things they promised because this is a game that was, and still is, in development.
If you want a decently good space exploration game, with sandbox and RPG features, then this is the game for you. If you want the pinnacle of all your hopes and dreams wrapped up in one $15 package, then I'm afraid no game is ever going to be to your liking.

I can't say anything good about this game. I remember playing the older AVP FPS, where you had roughly 10 seconds of battery power for your flashlight before being again in the dark, hunting for ammo, alone in a bitter wasteland, while piecing together pieces of an epic horror storyline centuries in the telling. It was scary, it was blood-pumping. You might spend 20 minutes without seeing an alien, just to s*** your pants when one finally popped out. It was nightmarish.
This isn't that. Your pistol has infinite ammo, and your flashlight an infinite battery. You seem to have an enormous amount of flares (i never ran out, i don't know if you can), and health stims seem to be everywhere. The audio logs you pick up seem basically irrelevent, and the voice acting on them seems totally phoned-in. Lance Henricksen does an alright job of it, but you can almost hear the, "I can't believe I'm doing another one of these" in his voice. On top of that, the aliens seem to dance around to be sure you can see them before attacking, which they are also terrible at.
The alien wall-crawling has been vastly improved; that's one good thing. I remember throwing my keyboard several times back in the day. The alien health regenerates far too quickly.
Basically, the game is so forgiving that it ceases to be scary. You can just run through it with little difficulty, knowing that another stim pack is just down the hall. It's not a bad game, but its so obvious that they could have done far better.

Dementium II HD is a PC port of the surprisingly good DS game of the same name. If you've been playing Shadow Warrior, Rise of the Triad, or remakes of other first-person shooters, this game is certainly not on par in terms of graphical presentation. This is, however, forgivable for a low-budget remake of a DS game. It's only $15 so I wasn't surprised by it's low-budget nature and short length.
The visual concepts of D II might be a little confusing at first. The humans in this game are portrayed in a realistic manner, while the monsters, being 3D reimaginings of the monsters from the DS version, are very designed very much like cartoons. They don't feel out of place, though; the humans in the actual gameplay look pretty cartoony themselves, as well as everything else in the game. This doesn't hurt the experience, nor does the rather simple combat. I do wish they made the character faster; his run speed feels more like the walking speed in most other first-person shooters.
D II is a pretty average FPS and it doesn't try to hide that fact. For that reason, the game envokes a sense of nostalgia. It's not a very difficult game; I suggest playing on hard if you're confident in your abilities. The puzzles are actually fairly well thought out and the combat, while not the most engaging or fast-paced, is decent for being so slow and goofy. The fact that it works well lends to the playability of the game, even though the combat isn't as satisfying as most well-known first-person shooters. I do question some of the encounters, such as enemy gauntlets in areas where you could be out of ammo and inconsistent difficulty here and there. Sometimes you'll be having no trouble taking out enemies, carrying plenty of amunnition, and feeling confident with all the painkillers you've pocketed. Other times you might find yourself running out of ammo in somewhat dicy situations, and there are a few instances where death - even instant death - will just surprise you. Thankfully, there are plenty of save points which heal you completely, and when you die while fighting a boss, you can continue from the start of the fight as opposed to the last savepoint.
I have a few other minor complaints with the game, including the lack of advanced video options and the uneven sound effect levels. The volume of the sounds that guards, monsters, and paranormal phenomena are all a bit varied, while the gunfire is about three times quieter, which can kind of emasculate the gunplay. The grunts and groans the protagonist makes are often quite humorous, especially when jumping and landing, which can cause his vocalizations to overlap.
Ultimately, Dementium II HD is a relatively enjoyable game that feels neither pretentious nor incompetent. It's not the most impressive game out there, but it's fun. I'd never heard of this series before, and I'm sure this is the best way to be introduced to it. I hope to see more from this company in the future.

Personally I found the narrator the best part of the game in that he delivers all of the wisdom and tales of his world. This is what made the soul of the game which is then supplemented fantastically by the music and art style and as I played I was constantly awaiting his next words. It is truly compelling and is what you should look forward to in Bastion.
But don't get me wrong, the gameplay is also fast, punchy and smooth. As you play there are dozens of combinations of weapons that are unlocked and have unique playstyles to them as well as nice challenges for each which I enjoyed completing. The only issues I had were that I would sometimes get stuck and heavily damaged on enemies (though I suppose that is partly my own fault) and one weapon near the end is forced upon you at, what I felt, was quite an inconvenient time. Some of the gameplay takes some time to work out which I also found (eventually) enjoyable as it is satisfying to put certain weapon combinations to better use through experience.
As almost a sidenote (partly to myself), the achievements that I tried to get on the first playthrough seemed incredibly difficult to get (maybe I just suck). These achievements involve purposefully enhancing the enemies and retrying arena-style levels to acquire and after completing the game without getting them, it seems that these are supposed to be gotten through playing the "new game plus" mode. This was because attempting them seemed insane and made me rage more than Dark Souls ever did, as it wasn't as fun an experience. But the game is worth playing again anyway in terms of how the story concludes, so this is less of an issue of the game and more an issue of whether I'll be doing it soon.
To conclude, if you are considering getting this game at all and enjoy a platforming action game that has many challenges throughout it should certainly come top of any list of competitors it may have and it is unlikely that you will regret it. Great game.

I've played and beaten this on the Nintendo DS, so i'm qualified to review this after playing it for a short while. Dementium 2 "HD" and i use that term very loosely because while the lighting and textures were clearly updated other important things were not. Animation quality, while smoothed out from it's DS counterpart, is still unchanged and looks very much like it came from a DS game. Fans of Playstation 1 horror games such as Resident Evil will get good nostalgic enjoyment out of this game, because for better AND for worse it is very much a callback to classic survival horror genre games such as Alone in the Dark, Dino Crisis, and such; bad voice acting, damage sponge enemies, safe rooms where you save, cheesiness and all.
Newcomers that know nothing of this franchise will trash it hard for it's extremely primitive graphics and gameplay. And it's totally understandable if you know nothing about this game before buying it. It's because of this that I'm unsure on whether or not to leave this as a "Yes" recommendation or a "No" recommendation. I mean, this game is fantastic for a DS title, it's just not up to par with other PC releases. As I said, newcomers to this franchise will be VERY put off by the low budget looking graphics and gameplay. They should have implemented ragdoll physics and an FOV slider into the updated engine and given us more graphical settings for this to be a true "HD" rerelease.

Very beautiful game, pleasantly surprised with how much I liked it. Everything from the style to the game, to the music, to the actual gameplay made it easy to get absorbed within the world of Bastion.
Okay, let's break it down.
PROS:
-Super Interesting Setting, it definetly sets itself apart as far as the style of the world goes. I have not seen anything quite like it.
-Nice story to follow along to.
-Beautiful Music (Yes, the kind that is worthy of destroying the replay button on youtube for).
-Different outcomes for the ending, that's always a plus. Adds to the replayabilty.
-My GAWD, the Narrator's voice. A deep western voice that is very rich in telling the story . Sometimes, in-game narration bugs me, it can feel like a distraction. However, Bastion's naration was far different. His voice input made made my accomplishments feel like complete bad♥♥♥♥♥moments.
-Not difficult at all to get into the game. It is easy to follow along to.
-Levels are in that perfect not-too-difficult-yet-not-too-easy range. Also, difficulty can be adjusted too. Game too easy? Add some "idols" which add more diffculty to the game by giving you different handicaps.
-A choice of some other different game modes after you complete the story, furthing replayability.
CONS: (more nitpicky if anything)
-More alternatives for the possible ending outcomes would have been nice. To play the story mode more than a couple of times and get different outcomes would have been the icing on the cake.
-A run feature for the game would have been nice. The character is instead at a somewhat slow trot.
-Had a few instances where it was difficult to tell where would be a safe place to walk.
Overall, very impressed what the developers have done with this game; it is artistic and very fun to play. Because of this, I will keep an eye out for any other future games by them.

Dementium 2 is (in my opinion) an oustanding AAA horror title for Nintendo DS users.  Bringing this game to PC and trying to uphold that reputation is no easy feat.  However, Dementium II HD does fairly good job at its redention of the DS horror classic.
4/5 Controls: With average customizability and controller support, the game offers industry standard customizations (i.e. sensitivity, key mapping, etc.)
4.5 /5 Graphics: Trying to hold true to the DS roots, the game presents very minimalisitic graphics (you won't need a GTX 680 anytime soon to play this at 60 fps) which do add to the quality of the game (In my opinion lower quality graphics tend to lean towards a more scary experience).  What they've done was revamped the qualtity acceptable enough for current PC users.
4/5 Story: If you've played the DS version there's nothing new for you here.  Crazy doctor, his wierd experiments, main character is in a mental hospital, its pretty self explanatory but it creates a good basis for a horror game.
4/5 Gameplay: Controls in horror games differ tremeandously, with each game trying to seperate itself from the others; Dementium II HD is no exception to this trend.  You're provided a standard PC FPS experience however the combat does vary slightly from other FPS genres (i.e. The guns' crosshair has some lag to it when turning making aiming a little more challenging)
4/5 Music: The remastered and newly scored music for the HD release is quite a nostalgic experience to that of the DS version.  The music could be cut out here and there to give the atmosphere of the game a darker and lonelier feeling.
At the moment there are some glitches here and there but nothing you wouldn't expect in a game's first release.
In all, there's no reason you shouldn't be happy with spending $15 on this game considering its current status.
There's much to be ammended in the game before its a perfect port of the DS version (I would have been happy with a port of the DS version with just the addition of PC controls).
In all this game deserves a 4/5 (not averaged).
It's shy of amazing, but you won't be slamming your head on the desk wondering why you bought it in the first place.
