140 is a very simple minimalistic platformer. What sets it apart from hundreds of other minimalistic platformers is that music is playing a vital role in it, helping you surpass the obstacles by giving rhytmical cues, such as when to jump or move. Although this idea is not novel, the game executes it well and there is pretty strong sense of music being an organic part of the gameplay.
That said, the game consists of only three levels that can be beaten in less than one hour. You do get harder mirrored versions of the main levels without checkpoints when you beat the game, but it's still not enough content to justify the price tag, in my opinion.
In conclusion, I'd recommend trying it as an interesting experiment in video game design, but do buy it during a sale or in a bundle if you're concerned about the length/price ratio.
P.S. The Linux save/preferences file is ~/.config/unity3d/JeppeCarlsen/140/prefs. Be sure to back it up if you don't want to lose progress in an hour-long game!

It's games like this that make me wish Steam used a 1-5 star rating system instead of a binary recommend/not system; there's a lot in this game that I liked.  The story, while predictable, was solid.  The combat, although problematic in ways I will discuss further below, was entertaining, with an interesting skill-tree mechanic.  The storyworld was intriguing.  And, as with all games from this dev, it had a certain, indefinable charm.
Yet, I don't think I would recommend it.  The combat challenge level was kind of all over the board...there were times when I would be acing the combat and then suddenly get wiped out by same-level grunts.  And, worst of all, the big-bads (ESPECIALLY the final boss) were just so, frustratingly, keyboard-smashingly, difficult.  I almost quit about halfway through because I got terribly stuck on one of the bosses, but decided to stick with it...only to be in the same position (after a butt-load of final-level grinding, I might add) with the end boss, and chose to just swear off finishing this particular game.   Further, there were still some frustrating bugs in the game, such as the character sprites not recognising damage/death during combat, or, on two occasions, the game just freezing up during combat.  Because of this, I don't think I could recommend it, it's just too inconsistent, and the plot and storyworld aren't original or interesting enough to carry the game despite that.
I hate having to give this a negative review, because I really appreciate this dev's work, but I would generally say: give this one a pass and go spend your money on Skyborn instead.

I have decided to write this review, because all the negative ones it got.
They almost dissuaded me from playing it.
It's not about them not recommending the game, but the reasons they give as to why they don't. I finished the game and I don't even understand what some of them are even talking about.
The game is either the, or one of the first tries of the developers and it kind of shows.
It's unrefined at times, but in my experience, not enough to be a bother.
Starting from the beginning.
The characters are mediocre at best, but the dialog is generally nicely written and entertaining, so it balances out.
The story is nothing special, but still solid. You essentially play a woman you discovers she is the rightful heir to a throne that was stolen from her when she was a child. So you set out with your new companions to reclaim it from an empress who, let's say proves to be a bit of a menace to humanity. That's pretty much it, but with more dragons and prime evil demons from hell trying to kill you than I let to believe. Yeah, there is a lot of♥♥♥♥♥♥going on and are casually swimming in it.
Gameplay wise now.
The game has no difficulty settings, which seems to be the reason it drives people away.
Having said that, I found the game to be of easy to medium difficulty with the only hard area being optional. But if you are anything like me, in an rpg there are no "optional" areas, I refuse to acknowledge that term. I will come back to the game's difficulty later. Let's just say this game shouldn't have the "casual" tag it currently holds on Steam. Not much in common with Eurotruck Simulator here.
Now, if you do not have a bit of experience with rpgs of this kind, you could end up having a hard time.
There is a threat mechanic which is presented in the form of a % and in most cases corresponds directly to the chance of each character being targeted. You will want your tankiest character to have the highest one, especially in boss fights, so threat management is a core element of combat.
The combat is turned based and each character has a large collection of skills (around 20 each) which you unlock progressively. These skills include damaging (daah) healing/curing and buffing / debuffing ones, to use in various cases. Admittedly you will end up usually using only a select few of them, but for almost all of them there came a time when I was glad I had it. 
Except "slow poison" and  "protection from holy". Seriously, the first one is just LIES and the second one is as useful as "protection from good alignment" in dnd games.
You will end up unlocking all of them, so there is no real choice to be made. On the other hand you also can't go wrong, which might be a concern as one of Deadly Sin's biggest problems, is the lack of precise information.
For example there are skills that state in the description "increases party's intelligence" or "decreases enemies' strength". How much? Well, I guess that much.
Lack of info is always annoying, especially in these kind of games.
I understand why some people found the combat repetitive, but personally I only got tired of an area twice. And one them was optional 
Each of the areas of the game you enter is divided in smaller ones. Each on of those is like walking in the grass in pokemon games. Microsoft word just underlined the word pokemon. Shame on you Microsoft word. Anyway you will be getting random encounters every few steps (more than a few actually), which you can end by finding a crystal in each of the smaller areas and deactivating it.
Coming back to the difficulty. I found it to be consistent throughout the game and I never had to grind for either gold or exp.
If you use your skills efficiently no random encounter will pose a problem and after you fight a particular group once or twice, you will have learned how to quickly dispose of them.
There where a few people who found the last boss either very hard or unbeatable.
One flat out claimed that it is impossible to beat some of the bosses without cheating, like what ¿
Small spoiler here.
Not only did I find it pretty manageable, but in most of the above mentioned cases, it's not even the final boss they are talking about. After that there is one more large area with the "true" last boss this time, and a huge optional one which is a lot harder than anything else in the game. To be fair the area before the "true" last boss is way longer than it should be at that point, but come on it's like one area.
I was actually surprised by how much extra content there was in the end.
Last but not least, the music is great. Not only in this, but in all of their games.
Overall I enjoyed the game a lot and I believe that at least fans of turned based rpgs and especially people who like mastering a game's mechanics like me, would certainly enjoy it too.

A tense action game where the objective is to herd and shoot down hundreds of aliens.
Crowd control and spatial awareness is important, so in sense it plays a bit like a top-down Serious Sam game as you often find yourself running backwards and shooting at a big flock of monsters that all want you dead.
In co-op mode, teamwork and positioning is important as to not let the aliens get spread out across the whole map, which results in chaos and tight situations. Caches with gold (spent on guns and upgrades), health and temporary power-ups drop at various places on the map, which adds another layer of risk and strategy.
Most of the maps are fairly dark, apart from a few lamps, the only light sources are your torch and the aliens' glowing faces, so getting to know the maps is an important step in mastering the game. I like this art-style, however the lack of a brightness setting can be disappointing for some players with old or worn out monitors.
All in short, quite enjoyable and would certainly recommend it to anyone looking for an action packed, yet tactical game with lots of enemies to shoot.

I know nothing about the original Carrier Command, so take this review with a grain of salt. Carrier Command: Gaea Mission is primarily a strategy game with first-person elements. What seems to have been an opportunity to harness a very gorgeous and expansive universe is squandered by clunky, non-functioning, or restrictive controls, a narrow and unchangeable field of view and, most egregiously, terrible AI. The fact that the voice acting and the sound effects are poor are nearly forgivable but the fact that the AI - an absolutely essential component of the game - doesn't work is this game's undoing.
The AI, through commands that the player gives to units that operate independently due to this game's first-person perspective, should work well enough to perform the tasks delegated to them. They don't. Telling a unit to dock on the carrier does not guarantee that the unit will dock on the carrier. This is important when a unit that is low on health, the death of which means a game over in many cases, because the unit will not take anything resembling an "intelligent route" to the carrier. It will wantonly engage enemy units that it should try to avoid, making the AI entirely unreliable. This is not a good system, because micromanaging the units to the scale needed for them to do their jobs is unreasonable. Even worse, this game requires automated tasks like moving units back to the carrier, to continue the game, which may mean spending a long time just leading units back to the carrier after a mission. Once, I drove one unit manually while allowing the other to navigate itself. I got the controlled unit to the carrier, only to find that the AI controlled unit was repeatedly hitting the side of a bridge, wasting quite some time. These mindless tasks are piled on random tasks that do not serve the "story line" and are clear attempts to prolong the game, and the system that moves the carrier from map to map also takes a long time of doing nothing for absolutely no reason at all. Speaking of the story, the "Story-Driven Campaign" with its "immersive storyline" is more a very long tutorial. The story itself is initially very unclear and does not begin in any manner that could be described as “compelling”.
I was excited when I first got Gaea Mission because it looked great and the environments look stunning. Unfortunately, that's the only part of the game that I can bring myself to like.

Back in the late 1980's, there was a game called Carrier Command available on the Atari system in 3.5inch floppy disk format. I was only 4 or 5 years old at the time, so I wasn't able to fully grasp the concept of the game at that time. But I do remember enjoying many hours of Atari gaming with the original Carrier Command. So when I came across Gaea Mission on Steam, I just had to check it out.
The playable demo did not disappoint. As the commander of a large carrier (hence the name, Carrier Command), it is the player's job to colonise numerous islands scattered within a vast archipelago. These islands can then be used to perform research and production of superior weapons and technologies that can be used to enhance the combat effectiveness of the carrier and support vehicles. Meanwhile, the opponent is doing exactly the same thing. War is inevitable, it's just a matter of how well prepared and equipped you are vs your opponent, when the time comes.
Support vehicles consist of four aircraft (Manta) and four amphibious vehicles (Walrus). Each can be kitted out with various upgrades such as armour, weapons, sensors etc, some of which are only available for either Manta or Walrus. For example, Capsules enable the player to comandeer islands and can only be fitted to the Walrus. Similarly, the Hook allows the Manta to pick up and transport Walrus vehicles, therefore it can only be fitted to the Manta.
Most computers may be out of their depth trying to run Gaea Mission on maximum settings, but a high-end gaming machine will have no problem. Having tried all the settings however, I can say that the graphics are still very attractive on the lowest setting. Either way, there is so much more depth to this game than I am able to portray with a brief review. So if you're a fan of the RTS genre and/or you've played the original Carrier Command and/or you fancy exploring uninhabited islands and/or you like my review, I highly recommend Gaea Mission.

Welp, the game has declared itself released now; so I suppose its as good a time as any to review it.
I've been with this little project since its conception; and I have to say, I'm pretty disappointed. Don't get me wrong, it is most certianly a good investment for 15 dollars; and I have no doubt in my mind that plenty of people will get plenty of enjoyment out of it. Heck, I got a pretty decent amount of fun from it too. Why am I disappointed then? I mean, I certianly got my moneys worth right? Well, I am disappointed becuase this isn't the game I backed.
Originally: Ore and metal were procedurally generated, not just positions but the actual properties of the resources, every planet was to have a variety of unique ores to discover, no two sets alike.
Now: There's a set tiering system similar to terraria.
Originally: Your crew was supposed to be an invalueble asset to your space travel; you would have an engineering, science, and military portion. Your engineers would assemble things like drop ships, mechs, guns. Your Scientists would research the stuff you brought back from different worlds.
Now: Build a house, place a colony deed, and do some quests; now you can report an NPC that might give you a passive buff on your ship or act as a companion on quests.
Originally: Space ship upgrades were modular and had variety; you could also build space stations and other interesting structures.
Now: Upgrades are linear, you go from one to the other with no interesting changes added besides more space to your ship.
Originally: Every race had a unique back story that described why exactly it was you were in your destroyed space ship above an underexplored planet. Whether it was a search for the meaning of life; or an attempt at a rebellion against oppression; this games plots were supposed to be branching and interesting.
Now: Everyones the member of some group called the "Protectorate" which is your super basic group of do-gooders that just want to make the universe a better place. Also there's a giant tenticle monster. Neat.
There's probably a bunch of stuff I'm forgetting; the point here is, this game is a very different beast than the one I backed way back in the day. I guess that's just the gamble you take when you back a game early on.
All that being said though; its a fun enough experience with friends that should offer you a neat space sandbox exploration game. With mods who knows? Maybe someone can deliver what the devs promised.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

This game has managed to devour many a sleepless night. Town of Salem is essentially an online version of werewolf/Mafia - except for the fact that there is a heap of different roles to be played in your quaint town of 15 people.
In essence, 15 players enter the town, and have to spend the day time trying to figure out each others roles, and voting to potentially hang 1 person a day in the hopes of eliminating an enemy from a different faction 'Evil' generally being targeted. Then the secondary night phase begins where everyone can use their abilities anonymously, to try and influence the game via investigating players directly, killing them, healing them, and other twists and turns defined by their role. And on this goes day by day, as the players die and dwindle until only one side remains.
Whilst the classic mode of the game is fairly standard in its allotment of town and evil roles (Which is stacked towards the success of 'town') - the game really shines in it's ranked and chaos mode. Ranked is, for a game filled with randomness, surprisingly balanced, especially for veteran players who have a definite understanding of the various roles of other people - but can still have enough pandemonium to ruin peoples days. Chaos, however- is just that, as essentially any combination of roles can appear (Albeit with the limitations of 5 mafia tops, and unique roles being 1 each). That doesn't, however, prevent there from being multiple serial killers or arsonists ruining peoples days.
And for those who want more structure in their Town Of Salem, they can also choose to make their own custom match setups.
Ultimately, it's a great game- whether people want to get actively immersed in the guesswork involved, to just ride out the chaos, or to get into cheeky shenanigans with their friends (like lynching them).

I got all the way to the end of this game. I'd done a ton of grinding, and my characters had literally the best equipment in the game. I had the expensive Iridium bow and arrows for Lorelei (the main character), the Irididium daggers for Glade, the super expensive dreadnought armour and gauntlets for Dori (the tank) and a whole bunch of other stuff besides. The game considered me overlevelled, and I was hardly getting any skill points from battles (more on that later).
Despite all this, no matter what I did, I could not defeat the final boss. She is literally impossible, even with extensive grinding, to the point I don't think the devs even playtested this game. If she defeats one of your party members, she gets a ton of extra health, and you can't revive them for the rest of the fight. Basically, you have to beat her without anyone going down even once for the entire fight.
This would be fine, except SHE CAN KILL ANY OF YOUR CHARACTERS IN A SINGLE HIT, EVEN IF THEY HAVE FULL HEALTH AND YOU HAVE THE BEST ARMOUR IN THE GAME. Nothing you can do prevents this. The two tank-y characters, Dori (the armoured knight) and Glade (the evasive theif) both have moves that draw the enemy's attention, making it more likely they will be attacked instead of the other characters. However, even Dori can't stand up to this monster's attacks, and even with his evasion up move, Glade will be hit and instakilled. Have I mentioned she can inflict every status ailment, act several times in a single turn, and, best of all, the heroine's ultimate attack, supposedly designed for killing beings like the final boss does almost nothing to her?
I gave up on this game because I couldn't beat the stupidly unfair final boss. Now I can't see the ending and feel like I've wasted all the time and effort I put into this game, not to mention my money. I have a few other issues with the game as well, however.
The game is very linear, which isn't a problem in and off itself for a game like this, but there is a noticeable spike in difficulty as you enter each new area. Pretty soon, you'll be struggling even with mook enemies if you haven't yet got the strongest equipment available at that point in the game.
Levelling up does almost nothing- the stat gains are meagre at best. 50% of your characters' growth comes from equipment (weapons, armour, accessories) 45% comes from upgrading your charcters' skills (which is separate from levelling up and requires skill points that have nothing to do with experience points) and only 5%, if that, comes from gaining levels.
This makes obtaining gold of utmost importance, which brings me to my next gripe. In every area of the game there are enemies with an ability called 'mug'. Basically they hit you, and in addition to dealing damage, they take some of your coins. The amount stolen is a set percentage of your total gold carried, and you don't get it back when you beat the enemies, meaning if you're carrying more than a paltry sum of gold, you will start making a net loss in gold from enemies. This is very annoying because the dungeons are very long and convoluted, and most of the enemy encounters you will face will be in the middle of these dungeons where there is no opportunity to go back and spend your gold that you've been accumulating or convert it into gems (which can't be stolen). With the importance of up-to-date gear, this practically necessitates grinding.
There are several instances of typos throughout the story. I lost count of the number of times I had to read 'diety' instead of deity, and there are lots of other examples. Not a huge deal I admit, but that final boss has put me in a really bad mood.
Also there are a couple of stealth minigames shoehorned into the story and the second one is impossible to complete as intended. Your 'alert meter' (fail state when it fills up completely) rises rapidluy to full WHILE THE CHARACTER YOU'RE PLAYING AS IS STILL TELLING YOU WHAT TO DO AND YOU CAN'T EVEN MOVE. Like I said before, clearly not properly playtested. Fortunately, you don't have to succeed to move on with the story (not that this makes the game possible).
In summary, if you like seeing the end of games you buy, do NOT get this game. I thought I could be hardcore and power grind my way to victory against the final boss after my initial failures, but no, I am convinced it is literally impossible. Doing more than your max hp to your strongest characters even when you're a high level and have the best armour, and being unable to revive downed characters? What absolute garbage. Out of curiosity, I tried to youtube the ending, but I couldn't find any footage of anyone beating this game. Maybe that's because it's obscure, but I still find it very telling. As someone who has played this game up to its ludicrous final boss, my advice is: stay away.

As a person who played and enjoyed Deadly Sin II and Skyborn, I saw that this had come out and decided to give it the benefit of the doubt. The dearth of reviews here also made me figure I would contribute.
Yes, this is an RPG maker game; but like DSII and SB, it has alot of custom content, probably moreso than most of the Aldorlea games (though those are fine too). I can say this with some confidence since I used to make a RMXP game myself but which never got finished due to my other projects.
Anyway; I will say that DS1 is considerably more rough around the edges than its successor, though I guess this is to be expected.
After 5 hours of play (just done the desert) my slight issues include:
>> There is somewhat less freedom to build the party; for example, I built Teresa in DS2 as my prime DPS rather than my tank (which was Carrion), because I could; but here, for example, Dory is the only real tank. Its also rather hard to pull aggro off Winchester when Dory's biggest aggro pulling move requires 50 OD. Again though, this the hazard of playing the second game after the first.
>> The plot just kinda happens to our good princess. I'm rather confused about her in general. On one hand, Lorelei seemingly has some clarity of the coup de tat that deposed her (?) since she talks about it early on. However, she later asks Winchester why he didn't tell her about the fact she was a princess. Perhaps I just missed or got confused over something there? Perhaps this will all be cleared up later on in the plot though.
However, whats good:
+ Though I moaned about customisation; thats only because I'm spoilt, its still pretty decent and way more involved than most RPG maker games. Only the other Dancing Dragon games and Doom & Destiny are comparable in the same category.
+ The character battle animations are good. They're nicely hand drawn and well implemented, and I know that can be a serious pain in RPGmaker. Most of these games don't animate their actual characters at all (they just show the weapon/attack animation; and actually, that was my one big 'meh' point on Skyborn) so I give this a massive plus.
+ Progression feels about right; I tend to be the sort to wander round and get all the treasure, but rarely did I feel like it was taking too long (except maybe a little towards the end of the desert).
+ Its dangerous carrying a massive treasury. A little thing, but all those mugging thief enemies actually became the bane of your existence. The game tells you to carry your wealth in gems at one point, and you should listen! That said; WTF happens to the gold they steal; you never get it back!?
+ Some other reviews comment on bugged maps and unbeatable bosses. Not seen any myself, though will update if I do.
Anyway; its worth it enough, at least for me. I would also check out the other games by this group and I hope that they release an excellent DS3 or something eventually!

The good: This is one of my favorite games, so I could probably fill a page with "the good." I find the story line extremely enjoyable. Being an undercover cop gives you a chance to cause mayhem while not feeling like a total dirtbag. The interactions between the player & NPCs are fun, and the voice acting is good. The setting and story really make you pull for a lot of different sides and think about life and family. The atmosphere is excellent. Hong Kong feels very vibrant and alive. The fighting system is one of my favorites. There are few guns available in this game; instead, the game mostly relies on martial arts. There's a gym where you can practice your moves before you take on street thugs and rival triads.
The bad: The driving is kind of awful. I've tried it with a controller and liked it slightly better, but it still wasn't great. However, once you get used to it, it's playable, if a little frustrating. I thought the main campaign was rather short. It's an open world game with lots of side quests, but the way each of the main quests comes up sort of gives you an urgency that can push you thourgh the game at a faster pace. I raced through a lot of the main quest and suddenly went, oh, that's the end? Getting the DLC can potentially be game-breaking, especially if you have the Top Dog packs. With all the XP and items loaded on you at the beginning, you can pretty well breeze through the game, which takes a lot of the challenge out of it.
General info: The open world provides ample opportunity for exploration and side quests. The story is great and the world is very atmospheric. The art style is fairly good (better with the HD textures).
Overall: I would definitely recommend this game! If you haven't played it yet, you need to!

There are a lot of mediocre tower defense games in general.  Most of them are just flash player games, some eventually make it to other platforms in strange ways.  Kingdom Rush is actually a flash game turned cell phone game.  Brought to steam, Iron Fist Games managed to pack two cell phone games into one and bring it to the PC.  What I love most about Kingdom Rush is that it's fun and simple, which is good in a tower defense game.  There's plenty of strategy, but it reinforces those two tenets through it's art style and how it plays.
I was initially turned off by how few tower types there were, but the game becomes somewhat deep as you progress through the campaign.  Eventually you realize there are certain towers that are more powerful than others, but very few levels can be completed with a single tower.  Likewise, the addition of Heroic and Iron versions of each level give an added level of difficulty and strategy that games like Defense Grid have tried so hard to achieve.
I highly recommend Kingdom Rush to scratch that tower defense itch.  Not only did I play the game for over 70 hours (and counting,) I managed to get all of the achievements.  It's within reach, and it's very fun.

While I have never played the original Carrier Command, I have played games of similar genre, specifically "Hostile Waters", Carrier Command: Gaea Mission (CCGM), a remake of the original Carrier Command, tried to add some new elements, but ended up a confusing mess.
At its heart, CCGM is a real-time strategy game where you conquer islands with your land and air units, taking direct control if you have to, or leave AI to accomplish your orders. An enemy carrier is doing the same. However, CCGM added a few segments where you have to play first person shooter. You sometimes have to control a vehicle directly as well... which makes you wonder "why am I risking my own neck? I'm the captain!"
The developers, Bohemia, added some backstory where the UEC is fighting against the APA (apparently mostly Chinese), and UEC is losing, due to lack of water, so they decided to colonize this "Taurus" planet, take its water back to Earth, but obviously APA is there to stop them, and apparently they got there first. You, Lt Myrik, is ordered to land and hopefully make your way to an old carrier, reactivate it, and use it to help you reconquer the islands in the "Dead Zone".
The problem with the game is while the starting islands (first 4 or so) do introduce the game to the RTS player, the really important part of the game, such as setting up defenses of the island, so it can survive assaults while you're out island hopping, is left virtually unexplained. You're simply told that you can convert the islands to 'defensive' by building a "defensive module" and rebuilding the command center, but that was too vague. And it doesn't explain how to actually IMPROVE the island's defense rating, which ranges from weak all the way up to "deadly".
The ship itself also needs fuel which is also used for damage control / repairs. And the only way you can get fuel to carrier is through fuel packs sent via the cargo barge (submarine) which can also bring you various other goodies from your "stockpile" island where all the stuff your manufacturing went. Transport capacity is limited, and it takes time moving from stockpile to you (and back). The more islands you conquer, the faster your resources accumulate or the faster your manufacturing goes depending on what type of island you got.
Pathfinding is a major problem in this game. The AI units have a tough time pathfinding in groups, which makes the game at times, comical. Often you have to assume direct control to push the unit beyond the chokepoint, then the AI does a decent job of pathfinding, but it can't manuever around other friendly ground units. The atrocious pathfinding means you have to micromanage each vehicle for fuel, ammo, and repair, rather than give simple orders like "group fuel" or "group ammo" and see the units take turns by themselves.
The vehicles can often even get lost by themselves, often with hilarious results, not to mention some odd physics. Send a vehicle to go from one end of island to another, and it may end up falling off a bridge, or making a 360 turn when a simple left or right turn would do, or get stuck on some rocks. Once, one of my Walrus managed to turn turtle (upside down) in the middle of the ocean on the way to the island. Somehow that makes it move BACKWARDS instead of forwards. (Huh?)  Yet another funny is with the hook. Tried to retrieve a Walrus that ran out of fuel with the hook. Had to be flown manually, and I got too low and the Walrus is dragging in the waves... but I was flying with nose straight into the water, and my VTOL engines were pointing 45 degrees down into the water, yet I'm still moving across the water... dragging the Walrus along. Somehow the hook is still attached. Hahaha.
The game tries to mix up the bits by giving you many First-person shooter segments. You need to actually jump out of the vehicle and use your personal weapons, such as assault rifle, laser, and later plasma rifle. Usually, you go into the enemy base and do your various bits of sabotage, raid computer terminals, and so on and so forth. There are a few segments where you have to jog across the whole island. You mainly face battledroids and a few soldiers, but occasionally, turrets and vehicle (but you usually bypass them. The bases are pretty easy as you do have a personal shield and as long as you don't take too many hits at once your shield powers up again much like HALO. However, some bases have regenerating enemies (until you shut that down) and you have to watch out for exploding barrels (which can kill you).  Those segments are just... weird, out of place, even.
The end of the game, well, that gets ridiculous really fast. Spoiler ahead.
The game is also quite happy to crash here and there. I'm on a pretty standard setup and the game crashed many times, losing a hour or two of progress each time. Most of the time autosave works, but sometimes, the game just crashed when it tries to load a cutscene.
All in all, I should be playing Hostile Waters (which is now available)

Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

Don't get me wrong, this game is of high quality and brilliant ideas. It has stunning graphic, the islands maps are so detailed and well made in order to suit vehicle gameplay that I almost feel like it would be a waste to manage all your units in the RTS map mode.
　But I wouldn't recommend it to others. It's just that I found the gameplay somewhat unrewarding and repetitive. Although you got lots of weapon and modification types, the basic structure of every battle is pretty much the same. You drive your carrier to capture an island, deploy 4 Mantas (hoverplane) and 4 Walruses (armour car) with various weapon and tools and head to the command centre. You don't have any other type of units except those two.
　Although the campaign start with a FPS experience, you don't get to play as foot soldiers anymore after the first level. I was expecting the player to be at least able to walk around the commanding bridge of the carrier, staring outside the window as you wait and watch your units coming home, and I was disappointed. Even though you did walk around inside the carrier in the first level.
　You can't move your carrier in anyway besides the preset waypoints of warp positions. You can't direct control anything other than those 4 Mantas, 4 Walruses and a main gun on your carrier, dispite how many droids and turrets defences you own on an island and that even though you did play as a droid in the first level.
　There are just too many little disappointments such as these, and too few variations or distractions to keep you entertained besides the main objective, which can be frustrating at times. The game really appeared to be an nice and huge open-world playground, but far too often I feel myself restrained in actual gameplay.
　It's a well-made game coming from one of my favourite developers but IMO got loads of wasted potential. I got this game from humble bundle for a few dollars, along with ARMA series I believe, and it's well-worth it. But the full price of $32.99, I don't think so.

It seems like arena style shoot-em-ups are a dime a dozen. My earliest memories of arcades aren’t filled with Donkey Kong or Pacman. Instead, my weekly allowance was pumped into an arena-shooter called Smash TV. It’s a genre that started me on my path to video gaming glory long before my first Game Boy, and while my tastes now desire something more complex, there is a lot to be said for sitting back and shooting a mob of aliens in the face. ICFSAAOB offers a few new ideas, and the active nature of the dev team bodes extremely well for the future of the game. Weapons are a pleasure to use, and you always thirst for the next upgrade. The constant shadows do make the levels feel a bit too similar, but the dependence on your flashlight to spot the aliens is extremely engaging. Does it win out in the end? Let’s shed some light on It Came From Space And Ate Our Brains.
Whether you play with a friend or all alone, you are sure to encounter more aliens than you can handle. The difficulty of the game will determine the HP and speed of the alien horde. Combos are built by killing large strings of aliens in a row, if you want to maximize your weapon as fast as possible you need to let the aliens converge into a giant horde before splattering them to bits. It seems like a great plan on paper, but in execution this methodical method of maximizing wealth becomes quickly monotonous. The art style is extremely nice, and is determined to shine through the inky shadows that coat every stage. The terror of a mob of pink mouths marching through the dark is visceral. I’ve been telling people for years that pink is terrifying, now they will truly see.
The replayability of ICFSAAOB is largely thanks to the variety of weapons and upgrades. Lower cost weapons can be maxed out quicker, but will have less power in the long term. The weapon you end up picking should always compliment your style of play. Do you prefer to thin the horde with a rocket launcher? Or pick off the strays with a laser rifle? The choice is yours, and any pick you make will be the right one. There is a great sound to every weapon that can be noticed from the first “pop” of the default pistol. The music is a decent drum and bass track, but I feel like it is a bit too slow to really capture the frantic action that is happening on the screen especially when playing on Insane.
Overall, It Came From Space And Ate Our Brains is an extremely likeable game with an amazing aesthetic and decent gameplay. Skills are being added to the game slowly, and there is a wishlist thread over on the forums which informs me that Triangle Studios really are dedicated to making the best game possible. The game is extremely affordable at only $10. If you think you might enjoy kiting a horde while mowing them down with a chaingun, and having a friend with a plasma cannon watch your back, there is no excuse not to give this game a try. Big thanks to Triangle Studios for letting us put this game through its paces, and for the fantastic giveaway last week. This one certainly doesn’t disappoint.

Sanctum 2 is a tower defense game with an element of first-person shooting - where you yourself contribute alongside your towers to the defense of cores from the waves of aliens seeking to destroy them.
The game itself simply chronicles Skye Autumn and her crew guarding cores across multiple maps. In each map, you select a character, each with their own unique attributes (e.g. Skye herself does more damage by stacking attacks, and can double jump), and then choose your weapons, towers, and various perks to use.
It's quite fun, if a bit on the frustrating side at times (particularly when solo). Play with friends for best results.

Nowadays it seems most top-down shooters really suck. And it's hard to find ones that doen't seem rushed or use basic recycled ideas. This game is different. This game gives a new meaning to top-down arcade shooters. "The brain slurping aliens are only vulnerable to bullets. Using your flashlight, environment and special powers you have a better chance to take care of the unwanted pink guests." You are faced against waves upon waves of aliens and trust me this experience is more than fun with your friends. As your progress you get new guns you can upgrade, upgrades themselves, and more. Even though you can play by yourself, the ability to play with friends is a HUGE pro. Mess around with friends, or use real strategies to survive through the waves... There are many options on how you can tackle every scenario given the increase in difficulty. Let's not forget to mention how hilariously fun this can get. But the game lacks a content. The developers are really listening in on the players and the communication is there, but there needs to be more variety. Lastly, the price is beyond fair for the replay value alone.
In my final note, the dev team is awesome with how they respond to the community. They so-far have delivered on their promises.
I'd rate this an 8.5/10

I got my hands on ICFSAAOB (Damn that long name!) shortly after the release, we've also done a multiplayer review in form of a video with the best bits of our gameplay that you can watch below and have a TLDR version.
ICFSAAOB is an arcade topdown shooter, thus all I expect really is fun. Replayability. Some decent variety of content, guns, gamemodes maybe. I'll talk about all the aspects of the game though. Let me start with one of the best things.
Graphics, stylization. The way this game is made on the visual side of things is great. The colors are well balanced, there's perfect contrast, weapons have diverse designs and the projectiles vibrant awesome different colours. If anything, this game is a pretty thing to look at! It's like looking at slot machines, you just can't turn your head off of it.
Hand in hand with graphics comes sound design. The sound effects are really good as well, everything sounds awesome (nope, not a LEGO reference) and even the gnarling horde of aliens is believable. Both your eyes and ears will get stimuled by these things and by the end of the playthrough you will surelly have problems realizing if what you see and what you hear is the real world. I had pink goo coming out of my ears.
Fun factor is definitely high and we had a lot of laughs playing this in two, and I can bet it would be even more fun playing in four people. The increasing difficulty of the game with changing levels is keeping everyone awake and a bunch of funny achievements only make it better.
Where the game falls short right now is content-wise. The weapon store and upgrade system is very bland, predictable and it's missing that “MOM I NEED THAT” factor. Same goes for replayability, it just doesn't get anywhere else after a while and I'd much welcome an addition of different gamemodes, or even the possibility of new strategies. There's been a mention of turrets on the forums, oh hell yeah! Give me turrets and a base I have to defend against these pink f*ckers and I'll fire this game any time! That applies to level design which is bland after a while, it just need that spark, maybe a little interactivity, but definitely a change.
Dont let that fool you, this game is great and has great potential. It just need that little kick in the back to make it awesome. And given the nature of the developer we can surely expect this kick. Promised weekly updates, feature-wishlist on the forums, etc. seems like he cares and to me that's one of the things that matter the most in a game. If a developer releases a game and shortly after abandons it, then why should I care as well?
On the technical side of things, it was very easy to set up a multiplayer game so I have to give a thumbs up for that, as it's still (even in the 21st century) not easy in every game. There were acceptable lag issues (US - EU multiplayer), so yeah nothing wrong.
And that's about it for the textual review, as I feel I covered the main points and I don't want to makle this too huge. For a price of 10$ (which is absolutely fair pricing) you get a pretty good looking indie game, with some cool content and adrenaline gameplay, get it, go spam that wishlist thread and be a part of this game becoming AWESOME, you won't regret.

and a graphic designer) definitely watch this video:
Otherwise, thanks for reading this review, I hope it helped you out with your decisioning.

As much as I love the fallout series, and have enjoyed components of this game immensely (having played my fair share) I can't help but feel immense grief that the one thing I wanted added to Fallout: New Vegas that Fallout 4 has (being able to build your own base) came at the cost of almost everything that made New Vegas great.
Your Dialog options are obscured between moronic "Yes, Yes (sarcastic), Threaten With Gun, and No" type displays completely destroying the precedent of having multiple (OFTEN WELL WRITTEN) options you got to see nearly in full before selecting them, allowing you to actually feel like you have some control over the characterization. I suppose that's a fairly faint hope when Fallout 4 takes one of the mainstays of the series, the ability to play whoever you want, and makes you choose between lawyer mom and grizzled army dad. The only way to avoid it is to never interact with the plot ever and live as a king in your own private junk heap far from the idiotic and soulless radiant quests. I am so, so tired of settlements needing my help.
When I saw the demos with the weapon customization, I was extremely excited. Having become very familiar with Fallout: New Vegas's weapon mods I assumed they'd share similar levels of power, and probably similar levels of rarity. Instead you get lego guns that while engaging for the first few hours, lack the depth or oomph to let you take that gun you've grown attached to and make it viable in high levels. (at least for energy weapons. RIP in Peace, sniper lasers)
Power Armor is very, very good. Probably too good, and the ease with which it's both acquired and maintained trivializes encounters in much of the game. It's also exceptional for "Pack Muling" so you never have to leave much behind. I'm a big power armor fan, so I can't bring myself to dislike it, but I feel like it needs tuning. Rarer components making serious damage actually a concern, power cores draining faster, I dunno.
The AI and pathfinding is as stupid and broken as you'd expect from a bethesda game. You can't get companions to walk through an open door without them noclipping into the 8th dimension or angrily berating you for having the gall to suggest they walk through the clearly impassible open doorway.
I had really high hopes for fallout 4, I really wanted to like it and for awhile I convinced myself I did. But it's just... It's just so disappointing you guys. It feels hollow and rushed. It feels like the art team spent a lot of time and effort to make this beautiful game that the writing and coding teams forgot to get around to until a few months before release. Fallout games live and die by their writing, and the writing in Fallout 4 Is very, VERY bad. Painfully transparent, predictable, boring. When it's even there at all and not "I noticed (ENEMY GROUP) hanging out at the (LOCATION) Nearby, we won't be safe until you murder them" or "Preston Garvey Jumping out from behind a rock screaming that 16 different settlements all need your help at this VERY INSTANT" of course.
God, Bethesda. Just let Obsidian do it from now on, you clearly are outmatched here.

I'm conflicted over this game. On the one hand, it has a very charming presentation. On the other, there are so many design choices (flaws) that I cannot agree with for this type of game.
You play as a survivor of an alien attack that's instantly thrown into waves of attacks in a dark, minimalistic backdrop. The enemies are wonderfully designed (kind of like grues) while the character model and animations for him are noticeably subpar. In the screenshots you can see that multiplayer doesn't even give you different colored costumes. There is some clipping in the game for your hands/guns and the hitbox for guns/solid objects is buggy. You can shoot any car/wall/house and your bullets stop, but if you have a shotgun they may as well not be there. Same damage radius blocked or unblocked which reduces an element of skill for it. It's not the biggest thing but it's there and feels like something they should have fixed by full release.
The game's scoring system is entirely based around how many aliens you can chain kill. To do this you have to wait for them all to converge on your location from all over the map per wave and kite them as one big group. The money you get is always the same per kill, but you get multiplier bonuses for the alien kill scoreboard. This system is very unrewarding though and there's really only one way to do it - slow, systematic chore working. There is no variance and each time you play a level it's exactly the same as the previous time.
On the difficulty levels, you have easy all the way up to insane. Easy slows enemies down and gives them less HP, while insane adds more aliens with higher HP and speeds them up. But this turns out to be more artificial than anything. The way they scale them is that the most versatile/mobile enemies will have more HP to take down while the should-be-tankier fodder actually has less. So you spend more time trying to kill the hard to hit ones even though their evasion scales enough on its own. This type of balancing system makes no sense. The biggest and baddest enemies are also the slowest, which means you'll never get hit by them.
. Anything fully upgraded is efficient to use. This means that the ones that cost more are useless since they take too long to get when you actually need them. You only have 1 weapon slot anyway and you'll always take a one weapon upgrade path.
I would have seen this game as great potential for a co-op horde horror arcade game. Especially if it had procedurally generated levels and they fixed the balance issues. Something like using the lights and darkness to make them slower/faster would have been an amazing dynamic. As it is now though, I'm surprised it's still not in early access. The design choices make no sense for this type of game.
It's very cute, but has completely unrewarding gameplay. This surprises me because this genre isn't complicated at all. Even games like Titan Attacks are just clones with added charm and that would have been enough here. I don't recommend this game. It seems like it should be in early access still and could use a thoughtful overhaul.

This game has managed to devour many a sleepless night. Town of Salem is essentially an online version of werewolf/Mafia - except for the fact that there is a heap of different roles to be played in your quaint town of 15 people.
In essence, 15 players enter the town, and have to spend the day time trying to figure out each others roles, and voting to potentially hang 1 person a day in the hopes of eliminating an enemy from a different faction 'Evil' generally being targeted. Then the secondary night phase begins where everyone can use their abilities anonymously, to try and influence the game via investigating players directly, killing them, healing them, and other twists and turns defined by their role. And on this goes day by day, as the players die and dwindle until only one side remains.
Whilst the classic mode of the game is fairly standard in its allotment of town and evil roles (Which is stacked towards the success of 'town') - the game really shines in it's ranked and chaos mode. Ranked is, for a game filled with randomness, surprisingly balanced, especially for veteran players who have a definite understanding of the various roles of other people - but can still have enough pandemonium to ruin peoples days. Chaos, however- is just that, as essentially any combination of roles can appear (Albeit with the limitations of 5 mafia tops, and unique roles being 1 each). That doesn't, however, prevent there from being multiple serial killers or arsonists ruining peoples days.
And for those who want more structure in their Town Of Salem, they can also choose to make their own custom match setups.
Ultimately, it's a great game- whether people want to get actively immersed in the guesswork involved, to just ride out the chaos, or to get into cheeky shenanigans with their friends (like lynching them).

For those that don't know, Starbound is a 2D open world sandbox game with a lot of crafting and some platforming. Terraria is a pretty good comparison. It was in early access for a few years, and it was pretty bare bones. I wouldn't have recommended it back then, but I do now as it is a very good game in my opinion. A lot of the issues players had have been addressed, and some mechanics have been completely redone. It almost feels like a different game. So lets move on to the Good and the Bad.
GOOD
+ Extensive crafting. You can make a lot of decorations, gear, and building material. Finding what you can build and what you need to do so is easy, so long as you have the right workbench/station.
+ Fun combat. Weapon types handle differently (guns use energy, spears poke where your cursor is, shields block, all that jazz), and many come with a special ability you can use (dashing, teleporting explosions, yeah!). Equipment comes in craftable tiers, or as loot with randomized characteristics. Techs can be added to your character that give you double jumps and the ability to morph into a ball, just to list a few.
+Cool monsters. Previously this was an issue, but they've added unique creatures with their own behaviours and animations in the full release, along with randomized creatures that come with a wide assortment of monster parts to define them. You can even capture some of them and use them in combat, sort of like a Pokemon system. Some of the bosses in particular I enjoy, because beating them requires pattern recognition, platforming, and strategies that are often missing in a genre where baddies mostly just run into you until someone dies.
+Wide variety of biomes and dungeons. Exploration takes place above and below ground, across many planets. Planets have unique biomes and weather (meteor showers!), and randomized dungeons/suprises scattered through out. People like to make comparisons with Terraria here (several planets vs one world that has everything). It's a moot point. They achieve the same thing.
+Colonies. Not like SimCity deep, but suprisingly interesting. Build a house, furnish it, buy a deed, then bam- colonist moves in and pays you rent. What you use to build and decorate help determine who moves in, and some tenants have unique shops. They also have quests. I believe there's colony defense events too, but I have gotten that far yet so I can't say for sure. I'd also like to add, that building is very intuitive and easy. Good block placement range, and you don't need a damn hammer to remove background walls. You don't even have to craft background walls, any material can alt as a wall.
+Farming. Again, not a deep system, but one of many fun things you can do. Grow alien vegetables, cook a lot of food, raise a robot chicken and collect the batteries it lays. Crops need water, obviously, and you can sell produce as one of the ways to progress in the game.
+ Upgradeable ship. Your space ship can be upgraded to gain more compartments, and you can hire on a crew to give various perks, or just follow you around and shoot things. You can build inside it too. Want your ship to look like a flying dojo? Knock yourself out, freak.
+ Better multiplayer. Hosting a game used to be a nightmare. Now it's all through Steam, and playing with friends is much better. And it's online, so you don't have to actually be around them.
+Mech.
+Story and progression. Another thing that was pretty bad in the early access. The story is now implemented, and is pretty unobtrusive. Mostly serves as backdrop to get you doing something. Progression is much better now as well and doesn't feel as restrictive as it used too. Almost every item in the game has a description, and some of them are specific to whatever race you're playing as. There are also little stories/notes/lore books throughout for lore nerds.
BAD
- The UI. It's useable, but annoying. The hot bar in particular takes some getting used to. It only holds 6 items but looks cluttered despite that. I understand the reason for it (since weapons now have alt fire or duel wielding), but that doesn't change the fact that sometimes I want to punch a wall because of it. Thankfully, mods will probably create a fix for this, if you end up wanting one. The menu windows are also obtrusive, but you can move them.
- Inventory. I can't think of many games that do this right, so no suprises here. Your inventory is divided up into several tabs that auto sort your items. You mine something and it ends up in the material tab of your backpack, food in another, and so on. This can be annoying when you pick something up and want to find it for the first time, or any time for that matter. You will probably be swapping your hotbar items around a bit, and be forced to navigate the horror that lies within your backpack. A little tip: shift + right click will split stacked items.
- Lack of depth. I hesitate to call this a negative. Starbound is a pretty chill and casual game for the most part. But if you're the kind of player who desires extensive survival mechanics, or in depth systems, you might want to look for something else. The wiring options can get deep, but that's about it. Starbound offers players a lot to do, but each of those activities isn't a game in of itself, unless you have one hell of an imagination. If you want a game to revolve around a concept, like farming, to get you motivated to do it, you're out of luck here. This is more like, "Hey, growing potatoes sound like a fun distraction, I'll do that on the side." Not like, "I have to grow these carrots NOW, so i can give them to this character on their birthday and get laid."
- Tutorial. You can skip it, but that isn't the problem. Anyone new to this genre will probably just end up frozen in a perpetual scream as they tried and failed to figure out how to eat raw corn to avoid starvation, let alone find core fragments to get past the first planet (they're near the planet's core or in a mining camp). A lot of basics aren't very well explained, so if you're new to this type of game, I'd recommend playing on the Casual setting to start. The first few missions are also kind of boring, and can feel like they're just holding you back from the better parts of the game.
TLDR: Killed a space penguin with a metal folding chair 11/10 IGN (sigh...)

while i personally liked this game, its a little hard to recommend buying or not buying this game. so...
you should buy this game if:
- you like the gameplay styles of the newer fps fallouts and borderlands, specifically if you felt fallout 3 and new vegas needed better gunplay to reach its peak.
-you have fallout 3 or new vegas and felt it could've used an enhanced crafting system, settlement system, etc.
-if you like adding mods to your games in general.
-if for some reason you felt fallout needed to be streamlined and simplified. this is as straightforward as it gets short of becoming full on borderlands or cod.
on the other hand, you should think twice about this game if:
-youre a hardcore fan of the older fallouts. especially the sheer amount of choices and the depth and complexity of the stories they offered.  new vegas and even fallout 3 have a better blend of story and action. of course, the classic fallouts are dirt cheap now on steam and GOG.
-you dislike voiced protagonists. yeah, it hurts the role-playing aspect of the game, but you can always add mods to make your character more how you want it to be (kinda have to if you want decent looking non 50's esque characters.)
- the creation club scares you. the idea of making people pay for community made content is obviously terrible, but right now i dont see that happening. as far as i know, community mods are still available on bethesda's website, in game, and on several websites like nexus, and you can even make content yourself with the fallout 4 geck and f04 edit. only content from bethesda's other franchises (wanna use the official doom bfg in fallout?) is being charged for.
-BUGS! yeah, this game at one point was basically unplayable, ironically from a patch that got released. it affected the way graphics cards would render the game. beside that, the fps fallouts were notorious for being glitchy and unstable on newer OS's without unofficial patch mods, and even with such mods its not as smooth as it could be. fallout 4 is pretty much the same case.
tl;dr, good fps action game, good base for modding, lots of new features, simplified, poor role playing game, and fairly glitchy.

I've only recently found out about the game and didn't get to play much, but what I've seen actually surprized me.
For an early access title the game already has quite a lot of content, Seven resources/currencies to manage, tech trees and passive boni that vary, depending on the clan you play, a hand full of military units with individual strengths and weaknesses, randomly generated maps and events like rat plague and earthquakes. The winters are harsh and lack of food or wood can quickly take out your whole clan.
The limitation in number of buildings per captured region is probably one of the most important aspects in terms of mechanics. And since taking over those regions costs food, it is one of the most important resources to work with.
Despite it being a bit more slow paced, compared to other RTS games, there is always something to take care of. Building a new Silo, grabbing that piece of land, before your neighbor does, preparing to attack a cave of wolves, defending against some Draugr or stocking wood to be able to fix a future earthquake.
I can't wait for the campaign to release.

This is a fantastic little indie gem, and here's why.
The game is just a simple platformer which is based around the music playing in the background. The music helps drive the player into moving and jumping at the right times, to over come obstacles. The music is quite smooth and soothing electronic tunes. Nothing too extreme.
In each of the levels, you're main objective is to go along and acquire a small floating ball, which starts to follow you after you've bumped into it. You then take it to a 'point' which then changes the music playing, and how the level looks / flows. New areas are accessible, static objects start to move and even the gravity can change.
The best part of this game, in my opinion, are the boss fights at the end of each level. Each one is well thought out, and brings a challenge to the player fighting them.
It's quite a short game, around 45 minutes to an hour, if you just want to play the base 3 levels.
You'll get a lot more time out of the game if you choose to do the 'advance' levels, which are mirror worlds of the first three, without any check points. So it's a die once, start the level again situation.
Well worth the full price, which isn't asking for much in my opinion.
In conclusion:
8 / 10, still playing.

Grabbed this title when it was on sale. I played it plenty more on console back when it first came out so ignore the small time it shows me on it
Summary (WAT YOU NEED TO KNOW)
This game covers another entry into the popular AVP series. Though there really isn't any consistancy between the games its worth noting that this is the 3rd entry. with the last two entries being outstanding and very popular. You get to play thourhg a campaign as either the Alien, a Predator or a Colonial Marine each with its own distinctive gameplay, plot and levels. Usually the campaigns criss cross at some point.
Presentation:
The game looks great first off, even when it shows its age it still looks damn impressive at times. Much of the tech and level design is faithful to the lore of the setting (Though not as much as say Isolation) The Aliens look sharp and well detailed, the predator looks just as big and mean as when Arnie fought him and the marines look every bit the bad♥♥♥♥♥muthas that you expect them too.
Gameplay: I'll break this up into 3 parts to represent each campaign as they vary drastically depending on which you go with each campaign starts with a through (almost annoyingly so) Tutorial so you can figure out how each character works easily enough
Alien: The Xeno campiagn is mostly based around you being a sneaky ♥♥♥♥ and getting the drop on your enemies either through suprise, hit and run or simple bait and lure tactics. You are often at a disadvantage against your foes as you have no range alternative and your HTH options are suprisingly limited. (Basically do whatever you can to stagger your enemy than eat his face) failing that just get behind him an well...eat his face
Predator: As the galaxy's best hunter you have a decent array of options at your disposal including bombs, a laser cannon, wrist blades, razor disc etc etc...all of them draw from a energy pool that you never quite seem to have enough of so you'll spend much of your time using the same bait and lure ambush tactics as the Xeno except your HTH options are bit more fleshed out. A personal favorite of mine
Marine: The Colonial marine campaign is a pretty standard FPS fare, being more of a "OH NOES SPOOKY ALIUMS!" throughout most of it. Still its got it's charm, many of the classic weapons make a appearence including every ones favorite pulse rifle. Sadly this feels like the weakest campaign in the game and probably the weakest one of the entire series (AVP2 had a amazing marine campaign) You'll also notice some almost cringe worthy dialogue in this campaign
Multiplayer: Absolutely dead. It was fairly entertaining on console but it just never quite took off.
Summary: get the game when its on sale.

140 integrates music with mechanics better than any other game I know of. In most 'rhythm' games  music marches forward at a pre-determined speed, dictating what you must do and when in order to keep up. 140 is different. 140's background music consists of loops, each loop a single instrument, and each instrument synchronised with a particular mechanic. Platforms materialise and disappear in time with the snare drum, for example. Once you have learnt each mechanic and understood its rhythms, only then does the level advance, adding new layers to the music and therefore new mechanics to the game.
In 140 you are driving the music, rather than vice versa, and that's something new, something more enveloping, something brilliant.
I can only fault the game for its short length. It could be two or three times as large without exhausting the potential of its core concept, and I wish it would have been explored further. Nevertheless, I'll return to this one, because the finished tracks sound wonderful, perhaps thanks in no small part to your being their co-performer. Soundtrack please!

For the people who are having trouble starting up the Mortal Kombat game, it's because of the Texture configuration. For some reason the game CANNOT open with LOW quality so it has to be set to MEDIUM to run the game.
If you are stuck and cannot open the game, go to your Local Disk (C) folder and search for "MKKE" it should be a folder in (C:\User\Owner\AppData\Roaming). Open the "Options" and change the "max_texture" number to "1024" and save it. The game should start up again.

A really good example of an indie game with a really fun core mechanic, and nothing that really distracts from it.  You literally go into a game, pick 3 tanks you want to use, then jump into a match  and jump around using your assorted weapons and attachments to kill your opponent.
Pros:
1)  I haven't encountered any crashes or gameplay detracting bugs, which is really impressive for an early release title, especially having played it on a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ Mac laptop as well as my gaming PC.
2) I managed to get into a game with the devs, and they were really transparent and appreciative of feedback.
3) The combat FEELS impactful (with a caveat I'll mention below).   When you launch mega rockets, or spark rockets, or spam the lightning bolt gun, the sounds and visuals are really satisfying when you hit.
4) The turrets - There's things besides the enemies that are hazardous to your health in an active way.  It kinda makes it feel like the level itself is a 3rd side in the fight.
5) The level size is great for the sizes of the team you'd expect.  They don't feel oppressively large, even if you're fighting 1v1 in the heaviest, slowest tank you can make.
Cons:
1) This is the caveat to the impactful combat pro above: The photon shotgun doesn't feel like a shotgun at all.  It feels and sounds like I'm flinging pink confetti at my opponent with gravel mixed in.  Also the fact that the damage falloff goes from 100% to 0% after a very short distance instead of a gradual falloff (100% at the first range increment, 50% in the second, 20% in the third, for example)  makes the weapon nigh unusable, given the energy limitations of the game.  If this were any less severe I'd attribute it to 'balancing issues', and 'early release'.
2) Early release means weapon balance is still being tweaked, but this is something that could be best solved by having more players.
Verdict:
Play this game, and get your friends to play it too!

I wish steam had a star or point system. I am going to recommend Bastion, but with a few reservations. I actually found this game after playing Transistor, which I really enjoyed. This game was good too, but where Transistor embraced it's enigmatic and surreal nature, this game struggled against it. It gave me a good experience for most of the 11.4 hours played however (9.5 fun, 1.5 bored, .4 frustrated), all in all a good game.
Graphics- 8/10 - First of all this is a beautiful game. It's scenery is fun and charming, the world building itself as you go. The characters are detailed and lovely. On the down side the creatures are a little cartoonish and simple against the beautiful backdrops. Even the scenery tends to get repetative after a while.
Gameplay- 7/10 - There are a lot of ways to play Bastion. You can customize you equipment to your playstyle and increase and decrease the difficulty with the shrines. With that said I think this game was designed to be played in "No Sweat" mode. Increasing the difficulty simply makes the game feel more grindy and throws off the pace of the narration (which is one of the best parts of the game).
Music/Vocals- 10/10 - Easily the best feature of the game. The music is well blended into the gameplay and the narration is excellent and engrossing. I never buy the soundtrack to a game but this one might tempt me... Well I would buy Transistors first.
Controls- 8/10 - I think that Bastion suffers from the same troubles that plague all isometric games, funky aiming and movement. The controls are well laid out and easy to use. They also give us some help with an auto aim button (otherwise it would be unplayable). Worthy efforts were made to make movement as managable as possible, and there is only light punishment for falling off an edge.
Story- 5/10 - I know this will get me a lot of flak, because it seems like everyone raves about the story. Here's my beef, and I'll try to avoid spoilers, the ending. I know most people thought the ending was deep and enigamatic, but I found it to be lacking. This game was like reading a good book. I enjoyed the characters, the world, the conflict and the drama. And then at the end you have a choice..... and it really kinda ends there, you can make the choice of course but it doesn't really add anything to the story either way, like a choose your own adventure with the last two pages ripped out.
Overall this game is enjoyable and beautiful, if you find it interesting by all means buy it. It's worth full price.

Excellent game in it's own right. Most will compare it to previous Fallout games and judge it based on those, and while they are perfectly justified in doing so, I feel many fall flat when they fail to also give some space to it as it's own game. As such, let me start by saying that it is likely not what you are looking for if you want the same experience as Fallout New Vegas (FNV) and Fallout 3 (FO3). Just as FO3 was a distant departure from Fallout 1 and Fallout 2, Fallout 4 has had some major changes. Some are good, some not so much. The biggest change is the voiced protagonist. This has it's advantages and it's disadvantages. Mostly, it limits the possible responses because voice acting is costly. It also limits the mod community as they either have to work with what is given, make their own lines whlie trying to match the protagonist, or simply leave them un-voiced like earlier Fallout games. The other big changes are the settlement functions and the equipment modding functions. We have seen a simple version of the modding function in the weapon mods of FNV, but it is now greatly expanded and encompases armor and clothing as well. I believe that FO4 is focused more on the gameplay and various aspects of combat, while letting the RPG half the game feel a bit thin. This angers many fans of the series, but you shuold not let this rule out the game as fun by itself. It is my hope that they used FO4 as more of a testing environment for these new features and will return to the quality RPG elements fans know and love in the next installment with the improved gameplay and lessons learned from FO4's particular shortcomings. In the mean time though, I thoroughly recommend you give FO4 a try and form your own opinion on the matter before discounting it entirely.

Hello all,
After over 1000 hours of trove I came here to write a review...
Firstly, All the people saying Trove is either P2W or super boring, Throw your PC out of the window and never buy one again...
Trove is indeed realy grindy, and if u don't like to grind all day long for something, This game isn't for you.
If u love to grind and be exited for something u get even if it is a small goal, heck even getting a dragon doesn't get boring.
The grind for a dragon is long, I agree to that and yes there is a way to get Dragon coins faster.
But u either Buy them with Cubits (Ingame currency u get every day for completing dungeons or badges)
Or buy credits (Real money currency)  with flux (Ingame currency).
Or grind your♥♥♥♥♥off to get a bit of flux for a lesser dragon cache or even a greater dragon cache.
Let me tell you, I've played Trove for over 1k hours and i'm still not at the end of the game.
The way you level up your character is by doing dungeons.
Doing dungeons rewards you with Gem boxes, wich gives u either Gem dust or Gems itself.
After u level to certain levels u unlock these gem slots, U can have 9 in total, 3 Empowered gems and 6 Lesser gems.
U can earn those Empowered gems by either doing Shadow tower every week, complete weekly challenges like: Complete Dungeons, Class Power rank etc.
And u can get lesser gems out of those gem boxes u get from completing dungeons.
U can then level these gems up to a certain level wich gives u Power rank (PR),
The higher your power rank the better you get obviously.
As I have seen many people do, U can get above 10k PR in no time.
after that the real grind begins,
getting to lvl 30 will take you some time, unless you wait till saturday since u get a 50% EXP boost, and if u have Patron (Member version wich almost every F2P game hes nowadays) U get double the amouth of boost (100% EXP boost in this case)
So is it P2W ?, No since u can get credits or buy Patron with in game money.
Then getting the gems, is a grind aswell since it takes a while to get perfect gems.
Getting flux isn't that hard either.
Killing Dragons, Run Shadow towers, Farm Dungeons (Wich is a win win situation since u get Gem Boxes and alot of flux)
and flux is used for EVERYTHING...
So its mandatory to focus on something and not 10 things at once.
Then we have the Mastery rank.
This can be increased by almost everything u get.
Finding loot and deconstructing it in the loot collector, every skin gives you 2 Mastery Points
Finding mounts in chaos chests.
Getting skins for your classes,
Doing badges like complete X amouth of Dungeons, Fish X amouth of fish.
Collect Dragons.
Etc...
This Increases your Mastery rank,
Mastery rank gives you extra stuff like: Mounts, Dragons, Tomes, Chaos/battle coins, Etc...
If you have a lot of mastery points, u can get a golden name (Previously is was rank 300, now u need to be on the leaderboards under rank 2k) Wich is, Believe me a real struggle to get there...
If I didn't spend my flux for mastery i would have millions by now.
So as I said, Trove is a realy grindy game and believe me, I have been bored aswell but this game keeps sucking me right back into it if I take a break from it.
I do have to say, Trove servers are not that great and have never been.
Yes they do make a lot of money from Trove, but upgrading their servers is not their priority as they said theirselves.
This game is not Pay to win like most of people claim it to be.
It's sure helps you progress a bit faster but some people who played without paying are as high as people who payed money in the same time span.
I hope this helped you guys deciding on playing this game or not.
