It was late in the last century when I stood over a friend’s shoulder and peered into a world of terror. Pre-fab corridors drifted off into the darkest of shadows, with red emergency lighting pricking at the black. He carried a pulse rifle, with an over/under grenade launcher and some flares. The environment throbbed with ambient noise but his motion tracker was a metronome of peace.
As he picked his way through the empty halls, tossing flares to light the way ahead, the tracker would blip, until, with a not-far-enough-away familiar shriek, movement would explode towards him. They came, black serpentine creatures with razor claws and faces of teeth. The pulse rifle spat at them, the grenades tossed them back but they kept coming, until he had no choice but to run.
The first time I watched Aliens VS Predator (1999) played on a PC I was so immediately riveted and overwhelmed with tension I actually asked him to pause the game.
AVP (2010) recaptured that magic up until the point where I, as a marine, punched an alien.
In what I must assume was a concession to cross-platform developing, melee combat is introduced and robs the game of all tension. Once you punch an Alien in the face, fear is no longer an option.
Less egregious but still annoying is a similar cross-platform concession requiring separate button prompts to transition as an Alien from vertical to horizontal surfaces. Unlike the original, where the Alien moved freely with lightening speed across any surface, AVP (2010) ‘s Alien mission has neither the speed or freedom of movement afforded by the precision of a mouse and keyboard.
Unbreakable animations also prevent the only joy of playing as an Alien, that of a meaty head bite shown in all incarnations from within the mouth of the Alien. The graphic violence of popping a hole in a Marines skull is thrilling the first few times, but after suffering perforated deaths while waiting for the animation to finish, the bloom is off.
The Predator missions suffer the least in the newest version, though the plentiful vision types offered previously are reduced to 3, Normal, Infrared, and Alien. Unfortunately plagued by an overly complex control scheme, furious hack and slash moments are replaced with hop and block and once again, unbreakable animations.
AVP (2010) is a stunning game on PC, where muddy console textures have clarity and DX11 effects create weighty atmosphere. Unfortunately, the gameplay concedes too much in moving to console and retains too little on PC.

First of all, play with a controller. No, seriously. It's a kind of top-down perspective but you're not viewing your character directly from the top, instead, you're viewing him at a significant angle. Which means that, from the perspective of the player, the character moves more or less diagonally through the level... which messees up with the WSAD configuration. Also the "aiming recticle" is completely off. It constantly felt like I was shooting around my target.
Aside from that... I can't quite recommend this game. It's an one-to-one port of the Android game. Other than prettier graphics, lackluster mouse controls and the removal of the in-game Pay-to-Win store thing.
It's every bit as repetitive as the Android version. There's only eight weapons, four of which are unlocked just by leveling up and four more that are available after each of the aforementioned four are upgraded to the maximum. The problem here is that, the maximum upgrade level gets raised each time you go up a Prestige level, to a total of 13 upgrade levels. This only really increases the grind to get to the unlockable weapons (more upgrade levels means more Upgrade Chips and coins). The good thing is that, by the time you'll get to Prestige Level 3 you'll know exactly what works so possibly less resources will go to waste... Possibly.
The only really different thing per Prestige Level is the armor pieces. And that doesn't really affect gameplay as much as, say, new weapons would. Now, I've only reached Prestige Level 2 on the Android version so I don't know, maybe on the last Prestige level some new weapons will magically pop up (although locked items appear kind of black as opposed to not at all).
As I said, I can't really recommend this game. But I'll elaborate a bit more. The game is equally as repetitive and gets dull as the Android version, the grind is exactly the same, and this version costs 7€ - as opposed to something like 3€ on Android (you get a trial until you reach level 10 and then you're asked to pay to unlock the rest of the game). The only reason I'll probably keep playing this version is because I can't be bothered to connect a Dualshock 4 controller to my phone.
Lot more hours on pirate version. Admire the developer, that's why it in my library. Go buy it

Its a decent game. You more or less get what you watched on the trailers and whatnot.
The only 3 things that, not saying bother me, but are not exactly what i expected. 1 is the covering system, 2 the mission rewards and 3 a little detail about the combat system.
About the covering system. Sure, you can cover, and i was expecting more like cover, fire, reposition, rinse and repeat. It actually is more action oriented. Most enemies are too agressive, which is not bad, but makes cover virtually useless because some of them fly and bypass the cover, so you have to run and kite instead. there are very few chances to use the cover system as intended, but more likely you wont be using it much.
The mission rewards (stars) appear to be linked to the damage you take in the mission. Guess i cant do much when enemies spawn in the tile next to me and fire their shotguns in my face at point blank, or a stun bot that cc me for 2 seconds while other bots drain my health and i couldnt even react to it. I mean, its not important in the gameplay itself, just makes getting 3 stars harder, in a low way, more based in luck rather than skill.
About the combat system. Its a wave defense basically. You kill stuff, more appears, and there are some instances when they will keep spawning until you kill certain enemies, which are though (not hard, just take too many hits to kill). It gets a little bit annoying than most of the enemies take almost 1 complete clip to kill, even if you hit all of your shots, before you reload, 2 more already spawned. Its not that bad, you get some powerups and stuff to help you kill more enemies faster, but i guess ill be a better system if the enemies (some) are easier to kill, even if the spawn rate is a bit higher. Feels more rewarding.
Well, yeah, the last part is that you have to grind a bit to get more gold and upgrade credits to level your weapons, skills, and buy more weapons/armor.
Those are details, took a bit to explain, but they are not game breaking, you can live with them. Other than that, the game is quite fun, soundtrack is not epic, but it does the job, decent graphics. The controls are responsive. Technically you can get combo multipliers, but since the enemies can take a punch, you wont be getting too many of those.
The game is not unique, but there arent that many decent isometric shooters that are worth it. This one is.

After completing a good deal of the Sanctum 1 content on my first playthrough, I felt frustrated. Drawn in immediately by the premise of a FPS turret defense game, I fell in love with the freedom to play how I wanted and the amazing aesthetics. This made it harder when Sanctum 1's glaring flaws creeped up on me (difficulty by simply ramping up numbers, scatter lazer spam and the inevitability of a stale and repetitive single or multiplater experience).
When I saw Sanctum 2 announced, my hopes were high. Hoping for these issues adressed, I purchased immediatealy.
It did not dissapoint in the slightest.
Sanctum 2 fixed nearly every problem with sanctum 1. Substituting disorienting teleporters and tall towers for an easy to see and traverse envrioment on foot aided both combat, navigation, and tower planning. More unique and interesting towers, a selection of weapons to fit every playstyle, amazing graphics, complicated and entertaining enemies and a crazy fun perk system to keep everything fresh, Sanctum 2 is easily one of my favourite games of all time.
Even those poor at FPS like me can still have fun using nearly every weapon. Combat is complicated, useful and necessary to survival. Planning mazes and tower setups is both easier and more effective, and honestly makes a lot more sense. Sanctum 2 is a perfect sequel: everything you loved, nothing you didnt. It demands more from the player, and in return removes the barriers that frustated you in meeting these demands previously.
It's hard to cram all my praise for this game into words. Grab a buddy or two and get playing. There's so much replay value.

The graphics are beautiful, certainly, but I felt a little betrayed by the trailers which appeared to promise a trifecta of gameplay, as if it was Battlefront meets the rts/resource management of games like Savage!
I mean, why even put in those segments of "hacking" into computer systems to control androids, if you don't have any real control over them in the multiplayer or singleplayer aspects? You don't even produce androids- they either stick around for posterity (to show that you now control the island you spent fifteen minutes breaking into) or die with, no joke, two or three hits from your assault rifle. Why not just advertise the game as it really is, where the only units you can directly control, modify, and upgrade, are some amphibious tanks, VTOLS, and the titular Carrier itself?
Why, Bohemia? Why have you forsaken us? (In comparison to the Arma series)

Northgard is, for lack of better terms, very enjoyable. You can easily sit down for maybe an hour to an hour and a half and get through a medium size game pretty easily. Timewise it doesn't have to be a huge investment, you can sit down for a session, play through a whole game or multiple if you really have the time.
Gameplay is more or less streamlined, variable, and enjoyable, there is enough variation in how the clans work and what you can manage with starting resources in your area to decide which path towards victory you want to take, be it Lore, Conquest, reaching The World Tree. Etc. Etc.. Sometimes winter seems managable, but if you let your guard down it will KICK YOU TO YOUR KNEES AND WON'T LET YOU GET UP. True to what you might expect of a game using Norse culture, winters can be incredibly brutal even if you have what seems to be a massive stock of resources. It strikes a nice balance of being not too challenging at times, yet not letting you run ahead of everything by preventing you from amassing exponential amounts of resources.
The one critique I would make to the game is that in some ways the economy of the game is a little lacking, what I mean by that is most thing boil down to three things. 1: Out of wood? Build more Logging Sheds! 2: Not producing enough food? Build food buildings! "If you don't starve beforehand" 3: People are unhappy? Build a Tavern! Now on one hand, you could say: "Well how else should they handle it?" and to that I would say: You're very right. The problem lies with that it can rather easily boil down to just building up a stockpile. The games depth in ways of managing your nation, clan, colony, whatever you want to call it, become somewhat limited when you really nitpick at it, and thats what I call this, nitpicking. For me, there is plenty to see and do, on top of regular updates. This game is already great in my eyes and has a lot of potential to become even better. I truly like this game and want to see it flourish, it already has a very solid basis, good gameplay, and a fascinating world. I mean by Odin's Beard! You get to lead a clan of proud Vikings, become the King of all of Nortgard, fight the Valkyries themselves!
For the time I have had the game, it gets updated pretty regularly and always adds interesting content. For the price this game is at, this game is a good buy for fans of RTS games and certainly for those fascinated with Norse Mythology.

This game is still very early in development, I feel like it is held back by a few simple things.
It NEEDS a CLICK TO DRAG option, as well as a LOCKED WINDOW option. I can't stress this enough. If it is there somewhere in the options menu then I am sorry I could not find it, but the locked window especially should be default as I have two monitors and that cursor flying out of my window every second is really annoying.
For my preference, the population limits on the buildings are more of a hindrance, than anything else, particularly with the military buildings. Food is so crucial, you will spend a lot of time trying to make as many villagers as you can, but this is dependant on happiness. Your villager production rate will hit zero if the state is neutral or unhappy. I'm not sure why they have included happiness. Even in Sid Meirs Civilisation, they have done away with the happiness mechanic (its effects are more subtle now) because it doesn't really add to the game, and I feel the same applies here; again it feels more like it is holding you back. The 'building healers' element, together with the fact that they heal units so slowly, makes them seem pointless. I know it sounds cruel but if I could just kill my units with low health, that would save a lot of time, or for wishful thinking, if they just healed passively instead. This is especially jarring given that my healer wasn't really doing anything, even when I had injured units.
I enjoyed purchasing plots of land to expand my territory, and I enjoyed the art style, the way my various units interact with the world, and my autonomous workers.
If I didn't have to worry so much about how many units I could build, and having enough resources to upgrade every single building in the game, which is acquired far too slowly... Then I would enjoy it.
Hopefully the devs looks at what the negative reviews have to offer, to make the game a better experience. It was NEARLY a really good game.

140 is an indie minimalistic 2D platformer based on music. It starts out simple, but becomes very challenging as the levels progress. You play as simple shapes which change as your movements differ (i.e. run = circle, jump = triangle, stop = square). Essentially, you have to use the music as your guide to the end, as it changes with each stage, which creates more complex beats for the obstacles you are faced with to follow.
All-in-all, I'd say this game is very impressive. I was surprised that I enjoyed playing it so much, and actually wanted more after I had beat it. For something so simple and minimal, I never thought that I'd be so in love with it. I spent $5, and I don't regret a penny of that price, regardless of the length of the game.
TL;DR:
Pros:
-Simple
-Challenging
-Good progression of complexity
-Great soundtrack
Cons:
-Too short, not enough levels (~40 minutes playtime)

Northgard is a game based around Norse mythology or Norse Lore. This game has a very in depth Lore system that can determine the outcome of the game.
There are currently 4/5 ways to win the game Lore, Trade, Fame, Conquest and of course forfeit. Conquest being the most difficult for myself, but Ill talk about these more later.
Jumping into the game you have a town hall and a set number of villagers that you will utilize for food, wood, krowns, iron, stone, happiness, fame, lore and exploration. Ultimately how you utilize these villagers and assign them their tasks will determine if you can even survive winter. Now it is very important that you listen to this tip before playing, build a house, then a scout, then woodcutters. If you fail to utilize your resources properly not only will you cut yourself off from moving forward you will look like a noob and probably hate the game.
Winter in this game is very hard all production values are decreased and your units move slower outside of their terrain. If you're able to survive the winter then you might want to prepare for the next winter while colonizing and upgrading as much as you can. If you find yourself with an abundance of food you can have a feast for your people and your team which boosts happiness and production values.
If your find yourself with an abundance of wood or krowns invest in one of the trade buildings, shipyard and the special building for your clan. You will need iron and stone for any upgrades you wish you make, and thus plan your colonization accordingly. Moving on.
There are a variety of buildings in this game that are recommended to be built after enduring your first winter. Building too many troops early destroys food production leading to an early loss. Healers are by far the most efficient defenders of territory as well as any other villagers in the area that you can micro manage from and into combat. There is a lore perk in the top tree that makes healers gather food while idle, this plus a food silo can increase food production ten fold.
However no matter what path you take in this game you will ultimately meet war and you will need to build a war and to defend and attack to neutralize threats from the terrain or other clans.
There are currently 5 types of clans in this game each one of them designed for a different style of play and player. I personally enjoy the wolf and the stag they give good bonuses early.
Ill quickly go over the 5 clans and their starting bonuses.
If you're like me and not that great with micromanging armies then I recommend a trade and lore victory as you will boost yourself and your teammates economy while potentially giving yourself a sneaky win. Lore is acquired through shipyards, lorestones, and various other methods you can discover.
But however you choose to play this game with the promised campaign, active multiplayer, and single player you will find value in the 19.99 early access price tag. Act fast for this price may be gone. But if you're skeptical be sure to pick it up on sale.

Town of Salem is a game of lying, murder and deception which resembles the party game Mafia/Werewolf. Each game can consist of up to 15 players.
Players are randomly placed into one of three categories: Town, Mafia, Neutral.
Town members are uninformed of who is Town and who isn't. It is their goal to figure out who the bad people are and eliminate them before they are outnumbered.
Mafia members are informed of who the mafia are. It is their goal to eliminate every Town member along with anyone else standing in their way.
Neutral members have certain objectives that they must accomplish. Neutrals are not affiliated with Town or Mafia but may potentially use the help of any player in the game to help them win.
There is a lot more to know about ToS, but I'd recommend learning it through playing the game as it's more fun that way.

The Sanctum series really set the standards of FPS-Tower Defense hybrid. However, Sanctum 2 is very much different than the first Sanctum. While Sanctum is 90% tower defense and 10% hero defense, Sanctum 2 is 50% tower defense and 50% hero defense. This means you can't just build-and-forget like the first Sanctum, where you just have to have enough decent towers and a well-made maze and you'll make it through the waves.
In Sanctum 2, you'll have to fire your guns just as often as your towers or you'll lose the wave. This makes for a more immersive game which requires more input and interaction from players, and proper strategies will determine the border between victory or annihilation. Not to mention you can get killed if the wave mobs get close to you.
Add a little RPG element to the mix where you get to select a character, equip his/her weapons, select your towers and skills obtained by leveling up, and you have yourself a semi-complex game that will keep you occupied for many hours and offers high replayability value.
Pick up a bunch of friends and buy the pack for this game, and you can't go wrong. Most definitely recommended, better than a lot of games currently in the market, and it is very affordable and worth the money.

Introduction:
Mortal Kombat 9 is a re-imagining of the history of Mortal Kombat. It takes us back to the original game and starts afresh from there. Things will seem familiar but not quiet the same and this applies to the story, controls and style in general.
With the dawn of Mortal Kombat X in a few days, I thought it would be a good idea to take a look at 9 as X is meant to continue directly from the end of this. But with X out in just days, is 9 still relevant? Lets find out.
Story:
Mortal Kombat 9 starts by pretty much killing the whole cast of characters, but Raiden manages to send a message back in time to his former self. This means you start the game at the time of Mortal Kombat 1, this is a great idea as it means you can revisit all those old areas from Mortal Kombat history. I really enjoyed the story line and how subtle changes to the time line changed bigger things farther down the line, it means even though your covering old ground its still fresh and new.
But unfortunatly even with this reinvention it still remains a needlessly complicated and over the top story. Mortal Kombat has always sported a overly cheesy and over blown story line, 9 doesn’t change this or even try to. But if you enjoy the Mortal Kombat plots of old you’ll be right at home here, and thankfully they have left out much of the later history where things became really strained.
Gameplay:
This is perhaps the most well put together Mortal Kombat to date, the combo system is far more advanced and natural than any of its predecessors. The fights flow nicely and there is a real element of skill here, you can’t button bash and hope for the best. The game though rendered in 3D is played on a 2D plain, much like Street Fighter 4 but this works well adding beautiful detail to characters but retaining the traditional style of previous Mortal Kombat games. We are also give a super move meter like other fighters, this lets you perform more powerful versions of your special moves and when fully charged X-ray moves. These are a brutal sequence of moves that not only greatly damage your opponent but also offer some bone breaking visuals to go with it.
One other mode that’s also been introduced is the new tag battles, this allows you to pick two fighters and change between them at any time. Even in the middle of combos you can tag in your second character, or if you wish they can jump in for a second to assist then return off screen. It’s a nice addition, but hardly an original one.
Presentation:
The graphics are really nice, they walk a fine line between realistic and cartoon like, this is a good thing as some of the fatality’s might become difficult to watch if they became too realistic. The 3D models are fantastically detailed and the animation is smooth, they really have worked hard on these characters.
The stages are interesting and though old settings, are kept fresh by the 3D re-imagining. One of the really enjoyable parts of Mortal Kombat 9 is travelling the old setting that feel so familiar, but at the same time completely new as well. This really deserves credit as to achieve this without losing the original feeling is no mean feat and though the graphic of X maybe far superior, 9 is still a good looking title in its own right.

I'll start off by saying that Starbound isn't a terrible game. It certainly has some positive qualities. It looks fairly nice; it's a very colorful game with some very well-designed sprites. The mechanics are pretty solid, it feels good to play the game for the most part. It also has the potential to provide hours upon hours of entertainment.
But, despite some of these positive aspects to the game, there are huge problems with the game, and with the developer. I'll list some of these below.
1. The first of these issues is that Starbound has been released as 1.0. This is a problem because Starbound is not a complete game, there are still changes to the game's features that the developers plan to make in the future, and in fact, some features have been removed from the game so that the 1.0 release wouldn't be delayed, with uncertain statements by the devs that they
consider re-adding them in the future, post-1.0.
This is unacceptable in my opinion, because they're marketing this game as complete, and yet they may still end up making huge modifications that some players will be unhappy with, players who spent money on what they assumed was a final product.
2. As I mentioned above, Chucklefish have removed content from their game, and this has happened on multiple occasions. I would not normally condemn a developer for something like this, but much of the stuff they've removed have been things they've shown off in multiple dev blogs, content they've spent many hours working on, content that had no realistic reason to be removed. Dozens of racial weapons, racial SAIL AI, local chat, a number of vanity item sets, and much more. No reason has been given for this removal of content, content that was interesting and, in many people's opinions, contributed to a game that was originally very complex in design.
This further leads me to believe that this game is an unfinished product, and one that I fear may be subject to additional content removal in the future.
3. The third issue I have with Starbound is not so much directed at the game as it is directed at the developers, but it's an issue that affects all consumers of their product; Chucklefish's unreliability. Throughout the development of Starbound, its five year development of which half was early access, Chucklefish have made promises that they've failed to deliver on and yet have made no attempts to apologize for or acknowledge. Several release dates have been given in the past over the course of these five years, and Chucklefish failed to meet all of them. On several occasions, Chucklefish promised there would be no more universe or player wipes, and yet time and time again they forcibly wiped universe and player files thanks to seemingly arbitrary changes to file structure which have never been explained.
These would not be such concerning issues if Chucklefish had actually taken the time to explain to their players why these things were happening. Not once did we receive a blog post explaining why a release date had been missed, or why another universe/player wipe was forced.
4. And then the storyline. Admittedly, this is more of a personal feeling of disappointment than a glaring, objective issue, but the storyline is so incredibly generic. It follows the most basic formula possible; I'll do my best not to spoil anything, but you, the main character and thus the center of the universe, are one of the few survivors of a catastophe. You escape on your own and have to find your way to the hub world, where you meet the plot device meant to drive the story further. You're buried in exposition and sent off on your quest to defeat the ultimate evil, which had been sealed away ages ago and is finally breaking free. Eventually you face off against it after working with a crew of unique individuals and destroy the evil once and for all.
There was once a pretty interesting concept behind Starbound; you were a nobody trying to survive on your own after escaping certain doom, making do with what you could forage and build from the wild. They ended up trashing that idea and focusing time and effort on a boring story mission when their efforts should have been focused on the sandbox elements for their sandbox game.
I could likely rant on about this, but I've rambled long enough. Starbound isn't a terrible game, but because of the issues it's had in development, I cannot in my right mind rate it positively. It wouldn't be fair to the people who are expecting to buy a complete title. As far as I'm concerned, until Chucklefish is satisfied with Starbound's features and has no intentions to change them further, it's still an early access game.

The granddaddy of them all. I played this game back on the PS2, and repurchased the game for Steam so I could have it in perpetuity. All modern sandbox games owe everything to this series, and this game in particular.
In case you've never been exposed to a sandbox game before, you effectively are dropped into a city which "lives" - you can go around to various contacts looking for missions to accomplish (usually involving driving and shooting), explore the city looking for sights and items to collect, or even accomplish random missions like running a taxi or putting out fires with a fire engine. This game marks what was effectively the first time this sort of freedom was in a 3D game.
The game's story puts a low-down person fresh out of going to jail into a criminal underworld where he slowly climbs his way to the top to get revenge. I've played through this game multiple times and while it's ultimately the least of the trilogy, it is the giant whose shoulders the other two stands upon.
I have not yet dabbled in the mod scene for this game, but searching around seems to imply there's a fairly healthy number of them to pick from, so if that's your thing, it's worth a look. At any rate, this is a classic which should be a part of anyone's collection. Very, very highly recommended.

Northgard is a game based around Norse mythology or Norse Lore. This game has a very in depth Lore system that can determine the outcome of the game.
There are currently 4/5 ways to win the game Lore, Trade, Fame, Conquest and of course forfeit. Conquest being the most difficult for myself, but Ill talk about these more later.
Jumping into the game you have a town hall and a set number of villagers that you will utilize for food, wood, krowns, iron, stone, happiness, fame, lore and exploration. Ultimately how you utilize these villagers and assign them their tasks will determine if you can even survive winter. Now it is very important that you listen to this tip before playing, build a house, then a scout, then woodcutters. If you fail to utilize your resources properly not only will you cut yourself off from moving forward you will look like a noob and probably hate the game.
Winter in this game is very hard all production values are decreased and your units move slower outside of their terrain. If you're able to survive the winter then you might want to prepare for the next winter while colonizing and upgrading as much as you can. If you find yourself with an abundance of food you can have a feast for your people and your team which boosts happiness and production values.
If your find yourself with an abundance of wood or krowns invest in one of the trade buildings, shipyard and the special building for your clan. You will need iron and stone for any upgrades you wish you make, and thus plan your colonization accordingly. Moving on.
There are a variety of buildings in this game that are recommended to be built after enduring your first winter. Building too many troops early destroys food production leading to an early loss. Healers are by far the most efficient defenders of territory as well as any other villagers in the area that you can micro manage from and into combat. There is a lore perk in the top tree that makes healers gather food while idle, this plus a food silo can increase food production ten fold.
However no matter what path you take in this game you will ultimately meet war and you will need to build a war and to defend and attack to neutralize threats from the terrain or other clans.
There are currently 5 types of clans in this game each one of them designed for a different style of play and player. I personally enjoy the wolf and the stag they give good bonuses early.
Ill quickly go over the 5 clans and their starting bonuses.
If you're like me and not that great with micromanging armies then I recommend a trade and lore victory as you will boost yourself and your teammates economy while potentially giving yourself a sneaky win. Lore is acquired through shipyards, lorestones, and various other methods you can discover.
But however you choose to play this game with the promised campaign, active multiplayer, and single player you will find value in the 19.99 early access price tag. Act fast for this price may be gone. But if you're skeptical be sure to pick it up on sale.

Okay, first off, I do really like this game. But that doesn't mean it has no faults or flaws. So now I'll run over the Pros vs Cons.
Pros:
A good variety of tank turrets/hulls.
A huge collection of unique and cool looking paints.
A balanced, fully functioning upgrade system.
A nice variety of cool and sometimes complex maps.
A good ranking system.
Balanced weapons making everything useable.
Great, working, balacned and fully realised pick ups.
Simple graphics making it easy to run on almost everything.
Visually pleasing colour palette.
Cons:
Not very good controls.
Kind of hard to use camera controls making it hard to be accurate.
Bad connection, I get disconnected from games more often then I'd like to.
Very small maps.
Only a few gamemodes.
Takes way too long to earn a good amount of money.
Imbalanced prices, you can buy a very good turret or hull for 300, and a useless but cool looking paint for 50,000.
Accidentaly flipping your tank over happens way to often, and most times you die because of it.
Conclusion:
Overall I think it's a very fun and enjoyable game - if you have nothing else to play. The connection needs to be improved, paints need to be made cheaper and the maps bigger. But apart from that it's a good game with a lot of potential to become something more.

This game is fantastic. I got it for $18 and it's already worth every penny. Even if there were no changes implemented from now on, I'd still say it's worth $25-30 just as is, and I haven't even played MP. Considering it's still under development and there will be more things added to it, right now this game is an absolute bargain. I say this as someone with a long background in RTS. I made it to 350th place on the Battlenet East ladder in WC3, and played tons of Starcraft as well.
Is this game simple in comparison to SC/WC? Well, the combat is simpler, yes, but the economy is more complex. The thing is, complexity does not make a good game. Chess is actually extremely simple, if you think about it. You can teach someone the rules of chess in 4 minutes, but it's been one of the most popular games on the planet for centuries. What makes a good game is replayability and enough complexity to offer a variety of different, viable strategies. Northgard is simple enough to learn the basics in a few hours and learn everything in a few days, but complex enough to offer a lot of different gameplay options.
If I might make one suggestion - giving the hero units the ability to level up and earn some abilities would put this game in godlike territory for me.
I'd say it's just as good as the big strategy titles and I really hope that a big MP scene develops for this game. I can see getting just as addicted to it as I was to WC3 back in the day.

Fantastic game, was looking for something for my fiancée and me to play as couch co-op. A rare gem that has full controller support, shared-screen co-op, as well as online co-op that's balanced on its own, and is different enough from the regular game mode to make it worth the play through, not just "oh here's the same game but with two people now." Good fast-paced arcade-y action that's a lot of fun to play.
The game mechanics are pretty easy to pick up, it's challenging enough to keep you frustrated at times but with strategy and upgrades you work out the best strategy to beat every type of enemy. That's probably the game's strongest part, that almost every enemy (or combination of enemies) no matter how weak it might seem, has the ability to ♥♥♥♥ up your day. What might seem like a nuisance at the start of the game becomes a swarm of holy♥♥♥♥♥♥by level 30. The game devs have definitely done their jobs doing playthroughs and testing to make sure it's got a good balance between easy-enough-to-not♥♥♥♥♥♥you-off and hard-enough-to-make-beating-a-boss-feel-rewarding.
Levels are great, there are random props and mood that sets the backdrop and gives a decent immersion. Randomly-generated keeps it pretty new every time, and each third of the game has a slightly different style which is nice and keeps things fresh. The music is also fantastic, plenty of dubs and wubs that match the sci-fi action feel of the game, and was an awesome way to pump you up while playing. Cycles through different sets of tracks for different levels, great addition to play.
The only thing keeping this game from being "THE BEST EVER" is a larger story that kind of ties the game together...there's a bit of lip-service to the robots on a space station malfunctioning and you having to clear them out, blah blah blah...it's all the game *needs* but to make it a best-of contender it would be cool to know more about Zed. He seems like a cool guy.

Introduction:
Mortal Kombat 9 is a re-imagining of the history of Mortal Kombat. It takes us back to the original game and starts afresh from there. Things will seem familiar but not quiet the same and this applies to the story, controls and style in general.
With the dawn of Mortal Kombat X in a few days, I thought it would be a good idea to take a look at 9 as X is meant to continue directly from the end of this. But with X out in just days, is 9 still relevant? Lets find out.
Story:
Mortal Kombat 9 starts by pretty much killing the whole cast of characters, but Raiden manages to send a message back in time to his former self. This means you start the game at the time of Mortal Kombat 1, this is a great idea as it means you can revisit all those old areas from Mortal Kombat history. I really enjoyed the story line and how subtle changes to the time line changed bigger things farther down the line, it means even though your covering old ground its still fresh and new.
But unfortunatly even with this reinvention it still remains a needlessly complicated and over the top story. Mortal Kombat has always sported a overly cheesy and over blown story line, 9 doesn’t change this or even try to. But if you enjoy the Mortal Kombat plots of old you’ll be right at home here, and thankfully they have left out much of the later history where things became really strained.
Gameplay:
This is perhaps the most well put together Mortal Kombat to date, the combo system is far more advanced and natural than any of its predecessors. The fights flow nicely and there is a real element of skill here, you can’t button bash and hope for the best. The game though rendered in 3D is played on a 2D plain, much like Street Fighter 4 but this works well adding beautiful detail to characters but retaining the traditional style of previous Mortal Kombat games. We are also give a super move meter like other fighters, this lets you perform more powerful versions of your special moves and when fully charged X-ray moves. These are a brutal sequence of moves that not only greatly damage your opponent but also offer some bone breaking visuals to go with it.
One other mode that’s also been introduced is the new tag battles, this allows you to pick two fighters and change between them at any time. Even in the middle of combos you can tag in your second character, or if you wish they can jump in for a second to assist then return off screen. It’s a nice addition, but hardly an original one.
Presentation:
The graphics are really nice, they walk a fine line between realistic and cartoon like, this is a good thing as some of the fatality’s might become difficult to watch if they became too realistic. The 3D models are fantastically detailed and the animation is smooth, they really have worked hard on these characters.
The stages are interesting and though old settings, are kept fresh by the 3D re-imagining. One of the really enjoyable parts of Mortal Kombat 9 is travelling the old setting that feel so familiar, but at the same time completely new as well. This really deserves credit as to achieve this without losing the original feeling is no mean feat and though the graphic of X maybe far superior, 9 is still a good looking title in its own right.

It really is shocking how little you get for your purchase price, and how much Capcom is willing to gouge you for things that come with competing fighting games.  If you buy Tekken 7, you get 38 characters, a large cosmetic customization mode, a significant story mode, an arcade mode . . . you get the idea.  As a value propositon, Street Fighter V is insulting garbage.  It takes far, far too long to earn enough fight money to unlock the characters, and there is no real way for you to earn costumes or cosmetic items without earning Actual Money from your Actual Job.
Taken purely as a game, though, it's pretty ♥♥♥♥ing great. Fantastic animation and character art, combined with well-thought-out sound design, turn each match into a gorgeous spectacle of goofy/sexy/rad folk pummeling one another's brains out.  It controls tightly, and the single-frame precision required in SF4 is thankfully (for this scrub, at least), gone.
If you are interested in getting it, just make sure to buy it on sale, and don't give Capcom a dime for costumes or superfluous DLC.  The more we support these business practices, the more they will do them, regardless of how much we bemoan their greed on Reddit or the SpaceBooks.  Capcom is a♥♥♥♥♥♥business with some amazing artists and programmers in their development studios.  It's hard to recommend the game when you get so little for what you spend, especially when there are so many blanced, robust, and affordable fighters available on Steam nowadays.

An outstanding update to the original. Carrier Command is a game where you control an advanced carrier which has advanced amphibious tanks and VTOLs with which to slowly capture a series of islands with which to increase your resources and manufacturing capabilities, replenishing supplies and keeping you in the fight.
Island management is deeply strategic in not only your choice of base on the island (defence, mining or factory) but in always ensuring multiple supply lines. Islands are now unique, with differing terrain, base layout and so requiring much more strategy to take and hold, often requiring hitting key strategic objectives in order to claim them for your own.
The story line is a let down, but a great tutorial to walk you through the mechanics once you get past the opening FPS section. Once you're learned what you need, stick with the free mode and set about conquering the islands on your own terms.
The AI pathing can be frustrating at times for the Walruses, but once you 'learn the game' you'll begin plotting multiple point paths to avoid most of the trouble.
All in all, a deep and satisfying mix of real time strategy and fast paced vehicle assault action that provides just as many hours of enjoyment as the beloved original.

Sleeping Dogs is one of my favorite games! It's a decent open-world game that takes place in Hong Kong and this is the part that got my attention... It's something different! You take the role of Wei Shen, an undercover police officer, who infiltrates the Sun On Yee Triad organization and tries to take it down from the inside.
The story is very good! The voice acting is also incredible! All this makes you feel the game and not just play it. It's like a movie!
The game's world is big enough! You can do stuff like driving cars, motorcycles and boats... You can buy clothes at the market... or at the central and many other places when you will be able to afford it! Outfits often give you bonuses, such as increased experience (Face, Cop and Triad) or Melee damage. You can also get discounts on your in-game purchases while wearing specific outfits. You can buy different kinds of food and drinks to get yourself some temporary buffs if you intend to get on some trouble...! But don't worry... Wei Shen is an excellent martial artist and he gets better while advancing through the game by unlocking new combat moves! You can also have plenty of weapons... melee ones and firearms. But even if you don't have any weapons, your surroundings can be very useful to take down your enemies.
Driving is mostly arcade and is fun... drifting and jumping while you can also take out your enemies' vehicles by popping out their tires or shoot some bullets through their engine to get a lot of cinematic-like explosions! Fighting is nice! It has many combat moves, combos and counters that you can combine them all together to get some kung fu action and kick some butts...! Shooting is also good, but simple. All the magic is at the martial arts part!
In general it has very beautiful visuals and graphics with awesome soundtracks! The city feels so alive day and night! I like the reflections of the city's neon lights at night when it's raining...! Those nights I prefer going to K-Bar for a karaoke night! It is a game worth playing and I'm sure that you will spend a lot of hours walking and driving the streets of gorgeous Hong Kong!

If you're looking for something reminiscent of Grand Theft Auto but unique in its own right, look no further than Sleeping Dogs.  I was extremely pleased with this game.  I had expected a good time but what I ended up getting was far more bang for my buck than I had initially expected.
Sleeping Dogs has gameplay similar to Grand Theft Auto in that it takes place in an open world city where you acquire missions from contacts to progress the story but you can generally do whatever your heart desires.  However, whereas Grand Theft Auto is very gunplay oriented, the majority of Sleeping Dogs' combat is melee in a way that reminds me of a kung fu action movie.  The combat is much deeper and more complex than I had anticipated (similar in a sense to the Arkham games) and the parkour movement was a nice surprise as well.
The story, I must say, is absolutely incredible.  It has its twists and turns as you play the role of an undercover police officer navigating both the criminal underworld and the police hierarchy of Hong Kong.  If I had to choose one of the aspects of that game that was the absolute best and most standout, I would go with the story.  I highly recommend this game to all fans of modern open world games, action games, and especially to anyone who's looking to scratch that Bruce Lee itch.

Pretty much the first AVP game since the PSP-exclusive tie-in to the critically panned AVP:R, AVP(2010) is the third game in the current AVP FPS series and the second game (third AVP game developed overall) developed by Rebellion after AVP2 was developed by Monolith (a game which currently is unavailable digitally due to presumed legal issues with while Sega owns the license for Aliens/Predator/AVP games, 20th Century Fox rival Warner Bros owns the technology and assets used to create the game) and continues the trend of the AVP games by giving the player a Marine, Alien, and Predator campaign. A system in place since the release of Rebellion's own 1994 game of the same name for the Atari Jaguar.
Now the Marine campaign like its' predessors, serves as more a survival horror FPS unlike the more action and stealth oriented gameplay of the Alien and Predator campaigns. The campaign's story has you play as an unamed rookie that's part of the Colonial Marine forces sent down to the planet after all contact is lost with the colony (funded by the ever reluctant to give up Weyland-Yutani Corporation). Of course things go horribly wrong and you basically have to survive long enough to get off the planet in one piece. Now this campaign does play like most FPS games at the time (except without stuff like iron sights and quick-time events) and while at first plays like a survival horror game, it ultimately becomes slightly generic when the Weyland-Yutani androids come into play. Though thankfully they don't appear until later in the campaign's six missions. Oh and there's a Predator that shows up as a boss fight.
The Predator campaign on the other hand plays more akin to a stealth-action game. Again the story with this campaign is that while the Marine campaign is going on, you play as a Predator that recently passed the Predator's equivalent to a rite of passage that was sent down to the planet due to a trio of Youngbloods being killed while hunting on the planet. And well basically you gotta keep the humans from getting the Predator's technology as well kill a Predalien that's recking havoc.
Now the Alien's campaign is unique in the fact that whereas the Marine/Predator campaign happen around the same time, the Alien campaign takes place before each and even sets up the events seen in the two campaigns (the massacre in the garage, the birth of the Predalien, etc.). Though unfortunately the campaign is also the shortest (this campaign only has five missions whereas the Marine/Predator have six). The Alien campaign also while being a stealth-action game akin to the Predator campaign, focuses more on stealth as unlike the Predator, you'll be fighting only Marines up until you deal with a small pack of Predators in the campaign's climax. Basically here the story for this campaign is that you play as a Xenomorph taken and raised in captivity by the Weyland-Yutani members involved with the usual Weyland-Yutani tricks known as Specimen 6, which escapes and causes the Xenomoprh outbreak you see in the other two campaigns.
Basically AVP(2010) is a fun game to check out. Plus if you're part of GameStop's reward program, you can get the collection version as a reward.

This Aliens vs. Predator game is the third one made, so therefore for further reference I'm going to be referring to it as AvP3.
AvP3 was my first date with the Alien and Predator franchises, and for what it's worth it did get me hooked and really interested in the lore of both series. The thing that makes the Aliens vs. Predator games unique from any other series in its genre is that there are three playable races, each with their pros and cons and benefits.
You have the Alien; a very fast killing machine that can climb on walls, leap considerable distances, murder people from behind in spectacularly gruesome ways, and can pounce on unsuspecting prey.
The Colonial Marines are more or less standard shooter controls; the Marines carry two primary weapons (only one if using the Smartgun, which is an autolocking machine gun that tracks its targets and follows them as they move) and a handgun with infinite ammo; their most valuable asset is a motion tracker that works as radar for any movement, which can help the Marines track any moving Aliens or Predators.
The Predator is, to me, a blend of the Alien and the Marine - the Predator uses powerful weaponry: a laser cannon, plasma mines, a giant spear, wrist blades, and a spinning battle disc, and is able to engage a cloaking device that makes him very difficult to spot, though with enough observation they'll eventually become a bit easier to notice. The Predator, like the Alien, moves like the wind and is capable of leaping tremendous distances, more so than the Alien.
These three species have their own singleplayer stories that all link together; the chronological order of each story's events being Alien > Marine > Predator, though certain moments interlap. These three campaigns play out in the same way as their respective species do - the Alien's campaign is just a lengthy killing spree; the Marine's is a struggle to escape the planet, and the Predator is on a hunt for his missing clan mates, as well as to kill Aliens and Marines for sport. The Marine and Predator campaigns are pretty good; the Alien campaign is brutally short and repetitive as hell, unfortunately.
Then we have the multiplayer... and that's where the waters get rough and the boat begins to shake. The multiplayer is intense and fast-paced; you have access to your standard modes; free-for-all, team deathmatch, control point(s) on the map, horde mode, etc., and you're free to play as whichever species you'd like. The problem is that the species are horrendously unbalanced. Aliens, in particular, are underpowered since they have no ranged attacks, and unlike the Marine, who uses morphine shots to heal bars of health, and the Predator, who uses magical heroin needles to revive himself, the Aliens have no method of quickly regaining health.
Predator players are gigantic ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s in that the plasma caster (that cool thing over the Predator's shoulder) does one-shot kills when fully charged up, and can track targets from ludicrously long ranges. So as a result you get Predators spamming plasma caster bolts and getting loads of one-shot kills.
Marines generally don't have much a need to pick up different weapons, since they spawn with a pulse rifle with 99 rounds loaded, and almost 300 in reserve; not to mention the pulse rifle is highly accurate, fires quickly, and can shoot grenades if picked up on the battlefield.
This game is pretty good, I would say; the multiplayer is good in short, controlled bursts; the campaigns tell an interesting, interconnected story; the graphics are great; the gameplay of all three races is unique and not a copy-and-paste of each other, and is ultimately worth checking out. But in terms of an actual recommendation, this is by no means the BEST AvP game. AvP2 - Aliens versus Predator 2, a 2001 game, has that honor. That game isn't on Steam right now, unfortunately, but I can't begin to explain how cool and unique that game is.

This a a fantastic title, unique but familiar, simple yet difficult and it has depth but is also intuitive.
Where can I place this game for comparison....somwhere between Age of Empires and the original WOW.
It's one of those games that isn't going to wow you but will entice you to just keep going, keep expanding and keep battling.
The more you play the more you learn and the more you will achieve.  It's not a carrot on a stick type game it's more of an effort reward system.
Everything is modelled nicely, in that it is pleasant to look at and the content available in-game is certainly suitable for an EA release.
There are no bugs that I can find, performance is faultless and there is more content to come.  What's not to like???
Well to be critical, it's very simplistic:
The battle ergonomics consist of a very basic numbers game.
Send 2 of your troops in against a single enemy and the enemy will focus on just one of them....so battle on until one unit has low energy; then retreat that unit.
Your opponent will then focus on your other troop and you can send the first one back in knowing that they wont be attacked at least until your second unit has been killed....pretty basic stuff.
But then this is also a positive for this game, it's not hardcore, it is not a simulation.  It's a relaxed and chilled out game; but with elements of intensity thrown in (to achieve certain thngs before your oponents do).
There are some gameplay mechanics which could benefit from some improvements, grouping for military units for example.
It is also quite frustrating when you slect a unit to come and assist you and it drags you halfway across the map to where they are instead of just selcting the unit so you can direct them to where you want.
FIRST IMPRESSIONS
****************************

I'm giving Street Fighter V a positive review because, at least from my point of view as a fighting game amateur, the gameplay is well-done, and that's the most important thing you can ask for in a fighting game.
However, this game is riddled with baffling or at least player-unfriendly design decisions. I can see the argument for making stuff like alt colors and new stages obtainable from microtransactions, but it's still not a good look and is as undesirable in here as it is in any full-priced game. That the game requires online play for making any sort of progress is just awful, though, and while your unlockables and online records are saved on Capcom's servers, single-player progress is stored locally only.
And speaking as a mostly single-player gamer here, the single-player content right now, before the release of Arcade Edition, is quite poor. There are some good ideas here, like the character stories providing individual character contexts for the main story and the main story having battles with NPCs. However, each battle is only a single-round. Additionally, in the main story mode, you find yourself jumping from character to character without ever really getting a chance to get  a good feel for them. And on top of that, the last few battles are a major difficulty spike. The climactic battle is naturally Ryu vs. Bison, but you get three unevenly distributed matches as Ryu before this one, and Bison just never lets up. And on top of that, the story itself is riddled with bad writing and lip-synching.
The single player is a missed opportunity to ease new players into the fighting game genre, but the in-depth mechanic and characters tutorials are even worse. They're in-engine cutscenes with no player input. I get the value of demonstrating how the mechanics work, but one really learns by doing it, not by watching.
Yeah, I'm pretty harsh on this game, but I do think there is a solid foundation here. It's just that Capcom seems to be making every other decision so as to turn off potential players. Consider this a very cautious recommendation.

Sanctum 2 is the sequel to Coffee Stain Studios's world's first FPS Tower Defense game.
Gameplay:
- Players are able to select maps, each map is an area in which the players have to build a maze and construct towers to defend the Core from getting hammered by the Lumes. If the Core's health reaches zero, you lose.
- Sanctum 2 features EXP and Levels. When you level up, you get new weapons, towers and additional tower slots. Each new item will provide new arrays of tactics for the players.
- Maps' layouts are varied. Some will leave the creativity for the players, some will make them build in pre-defined locations, some will MAKE THEIR LIFE HELL.
.
- In multiplayer, players will be given equal amount of resources, but not the Tower Bases. If you receive 400 resources for each wave in Singleplayer, you will still receive 400 in Multiplayer.
- Weapons and Towers are pretty nice to look at. Recoil seems about right. Nothing to complain here.
- Sanctum 2 also features various gamemodes. Campaign, Surival and Sandbox. In Sandbox, you can adjust the amount of resources and tower bases you gain at the start of each wave. Useful for testing new stuff. In Suvival, the waves will reset after you complete the map, which means enemies' variations will stay the same no matter how far you go. But more Feats of Strength will be activated the longer you survive.
- Feats of Strength are additional options for players to challenge themselves. Each FoS will improve one aspect of the Lumes.
Characters:
- Sanctum 2 will give you 4 characters in vanilla, 5 if you purchase the 1st DLC. Each character has their own traits, which gives the game another layer of strategy.
- Skye: more bullets means better.
- Autumn: bullets set enemies on fire. Can rocket jump to great heights.
- SiMo: basically a sniper.
- Haigen: more health and wields a shotgun. The closer the better.
- TSYGAN: last shot basically kills everything. OP.
Story:
- The story of Sanctum 1 and 2 are much deeper than it seems. I find my self interested in the story, but to be honest, if you are looking at this game, all you looking for are probably bullets, towers and gibs.
- Visit
to read more about the characters and their backstory. Codes can be found
.
The only thing that irks me is that some perks sound really nice when reading their effects, but they do not scale up with enemies' health at all. This means that only perks that synergize with the Towers are the only good options.
But that does not detract me from liking this game. If what you've read so far seems fun to you, then I recommend it. Ask your friends if they like this game as well, if they do, buy it for them, too! The more the merrier, right?
Have fun!

The game description does a perfectly adequate job in summing up this experience. The 2D fighting aspect of the game is pretty enjoyable, as your character has access to a large moveset that can be upgraded. You can get a bit more mileage out of this by scouring off of the beaten path, looking for cash crates that provide currency. However, there isn't a tremendous amount of enemy diversity, and some of the environments are actually repeated multiple times during the game. There are a number of boss battles, some requiring different strategy and one in particular (at least, that I found) that allows you to take a pacifist route.
The "meta" aspect of the game was totally lost on me, to be honest. There is a dynamic narrator in the game, and he is adamant that you "follow the arrows" that direct you towards objectives. Whenever you choose a different direction or route instead, he can get testy and throw little tantrums. He could certainly be amusing, and his lines (at least, in English) are delivered with conviction. However, this aspect of the game never really added up to anything for me. I wasn't able to glean much of a takeaway, in comparison with games like The Stanley Parable that also feature dynamic narration.
It's possible that I just didn't "get" ICEY, but it's possible that others may have a similar experience. Without the "meta" aspects of the game adding up to anything, it's just a somewhat unfocused 2D action game with a bunch of repeating environments, and there are many better and more focused 2D action games out there.

I really didn't like this game when it was in the very early stages of Early Access when I last played it, but since so many people seemed to be picking it up now it's finally hit version 1.0, I thought I'd give it another shot.
I still don't like it.
Atrocious combat, tiny icons that are near-indecipherable and very difficult to distinguish from one another, vague objectives with little to no guidance on how to actually accomplish them and the mind-numbing tedium of digging out a thousand blocks of dirt painfully slowly just so you can get back on top of the hill you fell off... not a fun gaming experience for me, I'm afraid.
The pixel art is lovely (albeit tiny at high resolution) and the music is gorgeous, though, so that's something, at least.
I can't recommend this in good conscience to anyone but the biggest fans of Terraria, which is a pity, because the concept is compelling and there's a serious dearth of old-school Starflight-style "explore the galaxy and find stuff" games in the modern arena. Unfortunately Starbound just doesn't deliver in this regard, placing too much emphasis on the "mine and craft" aspect and not enough on trekking across the galaxy -- at least in the early hours. But I feel most people will probably lose interest around their seven thousandth dirt block well before they get their ship to a respectable state and start doing more interesting spacefaring things; I certainly did.

This game blew me away back when it was new, only because it was 3D. It was cool seeing the world in a new 3D perspective rather than a top-down 2D view. But my recent playthrough of this game made me realize that this game suffers from quite a few problems that makes the game almost unplayable past the 2nd half. The first thing you will notice is that you do not have a map. You actually have to look up a map on the internet if you need it. All you have to help you navigate is your minimap. Which would be fine, but nothing useful is marked on it (Like the gunstore and pay n spray). So with no overhead map, or markers on your minimap (Your safehouse and missions are marked). Navigating the city can be difficult, especially to new players. There is no GPS or anything else to help you here. All you can do is memorize your way around the old fashioned way.
Another issue is the AI. The enemy AI in this game is very unfair, especially on the later missions. You can be driving around minding your own business or on a mission. Then enemy gangs instantly open fire on you regardless of what car you're driving or if you're on a mission. How do they know where I am at all times and what car I'm in? I just stole a new car and they instantly know its me. They don't even have to be facing you, you just see their arms lock onto you and start shooting. That means your car will always take damage even if you don't crash into things. (They start to carry more heavy weaponary later game, so expect some cheap deaths while driving)
Let's talk about the vehicles. They don't feel like metal cars, they feel like some paper mache creation my little brother made in 3rd grade. The cars are not durable. The cars in GTA and GTAII felt more solid than this. If you can't keep yourself on the road and not hit traffic (And not get shot at all the time) then you are going to have a huge problem keeping your vehicle, especially if it's a sports car. They handle okay for the most part, although some of the vehicles feel like you're driving on ice.
The weapons in this game are cool, but there's 1 gun in particular that made me almost throw my controller through my wall. It's the Carbine Rifle (M16) While this gun is probably the best in the game, it will be your death on the 2nd half of the game. Remember the unfair AI? Well, imagine several of them gunning down your little paper mache car with M16's while you're trying to beat a mission. It's a nightmare. The M16 shoots very fast. I was able to blow up a fully repaired sports car with only 16 bullets from the 60 round magazine. You can also be killed by about half a clip of ammo from it with full armor and health. Sometimes you can't even react fast enough. You just drop dead and have to reload your save. There's a reason why they changed this gun in the later games, because it's unbalanced and broken.
The missions can be very difficult at times. Especially the later ones. Most of the missions have either a time limit or a waypoint you have to travel to. SInce you have no map, it's hard to plot the best route to save time. Often times, you'll turn down a wrong turn or a alley with no exit costing you precious time. This really breaks my heart but I simply cannot recommend this game, if you want a 2d exploration world please, just play terraria, if you own terraria then replay terraria, if you wish terraria had space exploration then I still cannot reccoment this game and that is due to this fundamental point:
Space exploration in a 2d exploration/survival game simply does not work.
Let me explain: in terraria you set up a base of operations which starts small and grows and grows as you grind, explore and mine. You get a real bearing with the world and form this really weird relationship with it subconsciously "oh yeah this place is past that hill on the left, theres that snowy place on the right" etc etc as you slowly expand in either direction (including under and above ground) you really learn your world and by the end you know every nook and cranny. It sounds boring and rubbish and the idea of having multiple/infinite worlds would surely be better for exploration? Well no, not at all because now theres no journey or "homliness" to each world, you don't learn that land as you trek around the planet because in the back of your mind this is simply a pit stop before the next one. You simply wandered from planet to planet taking the barebones best parts from it every time and then beaming back up and onto the next one. The slog and journey in terraria is what allowed you to form this sense of adventure and eventual overcoming of this new world to explore, adding infinite simply takes the charm away from it.
The second key point as to why the game feels soulless links to my previous. The ship. If reworked I genuinely believe it would save the game and allow it to feel like a true deep survival and exploration experience filled with wonder and interaction, however I can't ever see this happening. To link back to Terraria, the base of operations (which tended to be your spawn) started as a mud hut then shack and then grew and grew in facilities, housemates and decorations (if so desired) In starbound the ship simply grows and grows and adds NPCs, this is fine and works well and for a little while you do feel like a commander of a ship. However, the ship completely destroys any sense of exploration or feeling of being part of the universe due to the fact you beamed everywhere. Your ship never interacts with any worlds and sits in this isolated bubble causing this horrible disconnect between the worlds and the ship itself. Seeing as your ship stays with you between worlds this will be your base of operations (where you put crafting bench anvil etc) so this is where you are when you sleep, eat and make things. If you could physically fly and land and sort of see your base of operations be tangible and part of the world then it would be so interesting each planet although would be a pitstop would feel like a journey and you would feel as if you really travelled there as opposed to beaming up watching an animation of a background change behind your ship and then beaming to a planet that instead of being a forest is now a desert. You don't feel like you are travelling across a galaxy you are simply beaming to different biomes which would work better condensed into one world which you actually inhabited instead of living in this soulless safety bubbble, if only there were another 2d exploration game which did so .....

This is NOT a good tower defense game. Just compare a few pieces to any other decent TD game:
Does it have pathing? No
Can you win later levels (or even early ones) on the basis of your tower (defence) alone? No
Does it require intense micromanaging on most (and especially later) levels? Absolutely
Are there levels where there is essentially only one way to win? Yep
Are there very obvious holdover elements from its mobile roots? TAP TO UNFREEEEZE TAP! TAP! TAP!
It puts on a good front, it looks cutesy, the barrier to entry (during a sale) is pretty low, and there's lots of easy to get achievements. What you will miss out on if you play this versus another, more polished tower defence game, like Defence Grid or Anomaly, is FUN. Also, a lot of the core mechanics that have made TD games less of a chore and more of a puzzle. Go buy one of those instead.

I have played a nice handful of Tower Defense games over the years, most of which have been on the iPad.
I purchased Kingdom Rush for an insanely low price during the Steam Summer 2014 sale and it is by far my most played game that I purchased during the sale.
If you have ever played a tower defense game, you will instantly be familiar with the mechanics of the Kingdom Rush.  If you have not and you are looking at Kingdom Rush as your first foray in to the tower defense genre, you should buy this game and I will give a short, very basic run down of tower defense games for newcomers. Essentially, TD games boil down to this; build towers (your defenses) to stop the increasingly difficult waves of enemies reaching your base. You will start each level with a set amount of lives and 1 live is equal to 1 enemy making it through all of your defenses and reaching your base.  In Kingdom Rush you are able to build a variety of different towers from archer towers, wizard towers, cannon's and a barracks.  All of these towers can be upgraded, for example a Wizard Tower can be upgraded to have spells which teleport enemies further back down the path to give you some more time to deal damage.
The art style is great and it compliments the game very well, In my opinion.
The audio is nice and at times it can be pretty funny.  Hearing your soldiers from the Barracks yelling "Freedom!" or your Wizard Tower shouting "Might and Magic!" adds something to the game.
All of the content is unlocked within this one purchase and there is no microtransactions to be seen here.  All heroes are unlocked by simply playing through the campaign.
On the main game screen, a new area with new levels will be added in eventually.  However, this has apparently been there for months and no update has appeared as of yet.
This game is easy to learn but it can be extremely difficult to master.  The difficulty can ramp up fairly quickly, so make sure to pay attention to what the earlier levels teach you about your towers.
I highly recommend this game, one of the best TD games there is.

140 is a very "primitive" platformer, if not for the seemless implementation of the music into its level design.
It's great to see such a concept used this well and while simple, and very short, it's almost perfect it what it does.
Beware, I beat the game in about 1 hour. After that, you'll have an added challenge which I'll try later, but it does not seem to add much to the game, except for the challenge. (More on that later)
The game has 3 level, each with a Boss Fight in the end. 3 levels may seem waay too few content, but it's not quite like that. Basically, you'll unlock parts of the levels as you progress. You can see it as 3 chapters, but every level is integrated in the same space, which is essential in this game!
As usual,
!
140 has a very minimalist art style, with psychadelic color schemes, and even some glitchy-ness to it. It's not your typical "2D retro pixelated graphics" that lots of game are using. Not at all. This game stands on its own, even regarding the art style.
It never gets too intrusive, presenting all the information you need very clearly.
I really liked it! Besides, the background also pulses in sync with the music, so it adds to the whole "atmosphere".
It's hard to talk about its
without talking about the
at once! All I can say for now is that I enjoyed the music for this game. It's pretty much electronic dance music, but there's more to it than that.
As I said before, it's a primitive platformer. Well, kind of.
All your character does is move to left and right, and jump. The jump time it also always the same, no wall jumping, no double jumping, no gliding, nothing of the sort. It's as simple as it gets.
Well, how can you still make an unique game with that?
Music!
Similarly to Beatbuddy, this game uses music to its full potential. Every obstacle in the game is coordinated with the beat of the music, which makes this game all about timing.
Another game you can take in mind is BitTrip Runner (and the BitTrip franchise in general) regarding how it does its music. You're given layers of the songs as you progress through the game. It starts off with a very simple beat. And it builds on it, introducing new layers with the new obstacles. And it works perfectly!
I've been interested in how music can be integrated into gameplay for a while, and this game is a really, really good example!
Another noteworthy aspect about 140, is the way it
you about every obstacle. It never throws something very complicated at you, before explaining what it does, exclusively through gameplay. And music, ofcourse!
Sometimes, you'll hear a new melody in the background, and you'll immediately know that you have to look for something around you. And you'll usually be presented with a very simple obstacle, to give you a general idea of how it works. Only then, come the bigger challenges.
I never found it frustrating at all. It was a bit too easy, maybe, due to the very forgiving checkpoints (which I don't exactly mind). But if you're fond of challenge due to the lack of those, do not fret!
After you beat the game, you'll unlock 3 new levels. These are the previous 3 levels, but mirrored, and without checkpoints.
Every big level, is made up of smaller levels. Each time you complete a smaller "level", something else will start moving, and with it comes a new layer of music. And that's pretty much how the game works. You just keep going to new areas until you reach the Boss fight.
It is indeed very simple, but also very effective! The way you need to pay attention to the rhythm of the music to overcome challenges, the way even the background contributes to that, it all comes together and gets you very in tune with the game. It's surprisingly immersive, and has a very good flow!
Another thing I've found great, was the Boss fights! There are only 3, but they play really differently to one another. They're almost minigames, and reminded my of something like SuperHexagon. The surreal visuals, coupled with the music, and twitch gameplay... yeah.
But it's good! And it's not actually like SuperHexagon, only those elements. They're also timing based, and they do a great job of teaching you on the fly, with each phase getting progressively more complicated.
It really does follow the design of the rest of the game. They start out simple, presenting you how it works, and then they'll challenge you, all through the game, without any words.
One nice addition is also how they end the Boss Fights. After the crazy colors spinning around, and the hectic music from the bosses, it suddenly stops. You're back into the Hub world, where everything is silent and grey. It's a very well timed break to the flow of the game. Well done!
I could see it being frustrating if the Boss fights are also a necessity to beat the Mirrored levels, without checkpoints, but I can't hold the game responsible. Its main content is accessible to everyone, and the rest is there to people fond of the old-school approach, I'm totally OK with that!
All in all, despite its length (again, 1hour, maybe even less, if you rush through it), this work is very, very well done. From its presentation, to its level design, and how it merges music and gameplay... I can't see much to complain about.
I'm really surprised about it, great little game!
If you're a bit skeptical of the 5€ it costs... Well, maybe wait for a sale. But seriously, get this game and try it out, if you're into rhythm games, or platformers. It's definitely worth your time.
