140 is essentially a minimalistic musical platformer developed by Jeppe Carlsen, known for his gameplay direction in Limbo. Players however, will fondly remember this game as both a visual and musical marvel. Despite being relatively short, the game remains challenging and enjoyable with oodles of replay value to boot. I can confess to having completed three playthroughs myself - one of them probably under the influence of something.
Players will be in awe of the minimalistic and colourful visuals, as this is a game that is indeed rife with aesthetic beauty. One stage of a level will be coated in an abundance of pastel colours, while the next will feel as warm as a summer's day in Dubai.
The music is dynamic to the extent that it feels like a living, breathing, entity. Fortunately, for fans of electronic music like myself, the progressive techno soundtrack will melt your ears and have you floating away like you were having the best heroin trip of your life.
The gameplay is wholly unique in that it utilizes the ancient greek theory of Synesthesia in it's gameplay design. Platforms will move and enemies will shoot in time with the music like a well rehearsed play. In fact - this feature is the key to completing the game, as paying close attention to the music for cues, will signal when to traverse a platform or blast a ball of oppressive static into nothingness.
There are slight issues with the lack of a pause feature, framerate issues on lower end systems, and not being able to change the settings in the game client itself and only from the launch window. Fortunately, none of these are even anywhere close to ruining the game's integral experience.
140 is a relatively cheaply priced game, suited for stoners, contemplative thinkers, and sensory junkies looking for a quick and potent fix.

It was way too easy to move things like the workbench, building is instantaneous - which was not what I was expecting, textures on wood and other things was basically non-existent - made my pine wood house look like a mud shack, and other things.
As others have pointed out, it really does seem like an amalgamation of existing games, which is good.  The more features you can cram into games like this, the better I say.  Also, as someone else pointed out, the AI seems to be a bit more stable than most games in this genre - so far...
I haven't played long, but I'll be playing again shortly and will update this review again - shortly...
--Shortly After--
1)  Options didn't save from the first playthrough - saved them again only to find that the draw distance still reset while the other options saved this time
2)  When clicking the option for audio, it goes from quiet to loud for no reason
3)  While the AI appears to work, there does seem to be delays - they'll pause for long periods before resuming work in the same area - scripting checking priorities?
4)  The tutorial isn't really a tutorial - it isn't necessary, but is useless in its current state - basically just help tiles that appear at set intervals, regardless of where your actual progression is
5)  The UI is pretty bad, as in very unintuitive - you can easily move things when you meant to use them and in general can't accomplish tasks the way you think you should
I'm not posting these here for the devs, as I'm sure they've already been posted to the forums - this is more a compilation of things I've found that others reading the reviews may want to be aware of.  Again, if you like this sort of game - like I do - then support the devs.  Otherwise, "Move along, this is not the game you are looking for."

I really didn't like this game when it was in the very early stages of Early Access when I last played it, but since so many people seemed to be picking it up now it's finally hit version 1.0, I thought I'd give it another shot.
I still don't like it.
Atrocious combat, tiny icons that are near-indecipherable and very difficult to distinguish from one another, vague objectives with little to no guidance on how to actually accomplish them and the mind-numbing tedium of digging out a thousand blocks of dirt painfully slowly just so you can get back on top of the hill you fell off... not a fun gaming experience for me, I'm afraid.
The pixel art is lovely (albeit tiny at high resolution) and the music is gorgeous, though, so that's something, at least.
I can't recommend this in good conscience to anyone but the biggest fans of Terraria, which is a pity, because the concept is compelling and there's a serious dearth of old-school Starflight-style "explore the galaxy and find stuff" games in the modern arena. Unfortunately Starbound just doesn't deliver in this regard, placing too much emphasis on the "mine and craft" aspect and not enough on trekking across the galaxy -- at least in the early hours. But I feel most people will probably lose interest around their seven thousandth dirt block well before they get their ship to a respectable state and start doing more interesting spacefaring things; I certainly did.

Since Steam requires a yes/no, I'll give it a thumbs up, but I definitely wouldn't recommend it for everyone.
This is a decent start to a base building game (ala Gnomoria, RimWorld, etc) but currently it's missing any reason to keep playing once you get food production set up. If you're a fan of the genre and willing to take a risk on Early Access, I'd say it's worth a shot, especially if you prefer to play pacifist mode and focus on building structures. However if you like challenge or conflict, or prefer to buy Early Access games that feel mostly complete, you should wait on this one.
I really like the base mechanics of the game, it gets the genre staples right - mining, farming, tech, building up a town, etc. The world generation is pretty cool, I enjoyed the landscapes and flora and fauna.
There are some minor issues that work fine, it would be cool if they were more fleshed out but they're not game breaking. Mining only goes straight down (as far as I could tell), building stuff just instantly happens with a mouse click, goods storage/retrieval is instantaneous magic, animals you've herded into pens tend to clump up in one spot instead of wandering the space you've given them.
The first major issue is performance. On big maps it tanks hard, but even smaller maps hit major processing lag. I'd say the #1 culprit is pathing, especially if you're trying to do stuff across rivers. The #2 culprit appears to be when you have a build/crafting menu open, especially if a spinning object preview is being displayed.
The second major issue is that once you've got food production set up, there isn't anything to do. You can build to your heart's content, but there is zero pressure to survive. Not a problem for people who just want to build, but I prefer to have some kind of challenge.
The third issue is resource generation. Lots of food and crafted good require specific materials, and if you don't spawn with the right seeds and your world doesn't generate the materials you need, I don't really know what you're supposed to do. For example stone is an important component for several key crafting buildings, and I scoured my small map for hours looking for stone until I'd built everything I could without it and I had to just give up. Increasing the spawn rate for key goods might help, or making the recipes more flexible by allowing alternate materials might help.
I really like games like this and I think this game has a lot of potential. After 13 hours of mostly enjoyable gameplay, I won't say I'm disappointed with the game, but I think it could be better. People who enjoy just building stuff should be able to even more playtime than that, but until some of the above issues are addressed I won't be playing any further.

This really breaks my heart but I simply cannot recommend this game, if you want a 2d exploration world please, just play terraria, if you own terraria then replay terraria, if you wish terraria had space exploration then I still cannot reccoment this game and that is due to this fundamental point:
Space exploration in a 2d exploration/survival game simply does not work.
Let me explain: in terraria you set up a base of operations which starts small and grows and grows as you grind, explore and mine. You get a real bearing with the world and form this really weird relationship with it subconsciously "oh yeah this place is past that hill on the left, theres that snowy place on the right" etc etc as you slowly expand in either direction (including under and above ground) you really learn your world and by the end you know every nook and cranny. It sounds boring and rubbish and the idea of having multiple/infinite worlds would surely be better for exploration? Well no, not at all because now theres no journey or "homliness" to each world, you don't learn that land as you trek around the planet because in the back of your mind this is simply a pit stop before the next one. You simply wandered from planet to planet taking the barebones best parts from it every time and then beaming back up and onto the next one. The slog and journey in terraria is what allowed you to form this sense of adventure and eventual overcoming of this new world to explore, adding infinite simply takes the charm away from it.
The second key point as to why the game feels soulless links to my previous. The ship. If reworked I genuinely believe it would save the game and allow it to feel like a true deep survival and exploration experience filled with wonder and interaction, however I can't ever see this happening. To link back to Terraria, the base of operations (which tended to be your spawn) started as a mud hut then shack and then grew and grew in facilities, housemates and decorations (if so desired) In starbound the ship simply grows and grows and adds NPCs, this is fine and works well and for a little while you do feel like a commander of a ship. However, the ship completely destroys any sense of exploration or feeling of being part of the universe due to the fact you beamed everywhere. Your ship never interacts with any worlds and sits in this isolated bubble causing this horrible disconnect between the worlds and the ship itself. Seeing as your ship stays with you between worlds this will be your base of operations (where you put crafting bench anvil etc) so this is where you are when you sleep, eat and make things. If you could physically fly and land and sort of see your base of operations be tangible and part of the world then it would be so interesting each planet although would be a pitstop would feel like a journey and you would feel as if you really travelled there as opposed to beaming up watching an animation of a background change behind your ship and then beaming to a planet that instead of being a forest is now a desert. You don't feel like you are travelling across a galaxy you are simply beaming to different biomes which would work better condensed into one world which you actually inhabited instead of living in this soulless safety bubbble, if only there were another 2d exploration game which did so .....

THE KINDRED (Alpha 8/Early Access)
PUBLISHER – Nkidu Games, Inc
DEVELOPER – Persistent Studios
GENRE – Indie, Life sim, building, survival, sandbox
THE BASICS: Take RimWorld and/or Dwarf Fortress and mash it up with Minecraft, and you have a pretty good idea of what this game will eventually be. Reviewed version: Early Access/Alpha 8.
This is a survival/building stuff sandbox game. Your crew of lovable misfits shows up in a world of your choosing, and each has their own strengths and weaknesses when it comes to various skills such as mining, cooking, growing crops, crafting, etc. Specialize your characters based on their strengths, and they'll get more work done and do it more efficiently – and speed is the name of the game. You'll need a solid house to protect them from the elements, beds for them to sleep in, food for their bellies, and clothes on their backs, if they're to survive for very long in this world. That's where you come in: Point them in the right direction, tell them what to build/farm/gather and where, so that they'll work together as a team to overcome the obstacles Mother Nature has in store for them.
Current features include basic farming & crafting, hunting & gathering, and breeding local critters. Down the line, their plans include: Climate and weather, additional biomes, power, health and medicine, the need for hydration, dealing with predators, families and children, and more!
THE FLOW AND THE STORY:
You control a pack of settlers on a Minecrafty, voxel-based world, just from 3rd person perspective. Assign people jobs based on their strengths, cut down trees and mine stone to get components to build shelter. Hunt or raise animals for food, milk, wool, etc, to keep you all going.
CONTROLS:
WASD for basic camera control, plus keys or mouse to fiddle with the view. Click or draw a box to select settlers or define an area to work on; right click a target to harvest it or chop it town, per context.
GRAPHICS:
Looks like Minecraft without any textures at all. At least the cubes are nice and crisp :) This seems like something they'll polish down the line, once the game gets closer to a formal release.
SOUND:
Charming, apropos music accompanies the pastoral feel of the game.
OVERALL:
You could do worse – but, unless you're very very patient, you should probably wait until it's closer to full release before putting your money down on this.

The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth is sort of an odd game.  It holds a unique slot in my gaming where, at the moment, I play at least one playthrough of it each day.  It is kind of like Solitair, Peggle, or Bejeweled in a sense, in that it is a go to game for me when I have a few minutes to spare.
So what is this game?  It is the dungeons of Zelda mixed with rogue-like randomization.  The goal is to kill one of the final bosses by picking up items and growing in power.  What makes this fun is that the items are randomized, but every playthrough is beatable.  You can manipulate the randomness to do some crazy things and just break the power curve.  But you can also get a bad room and loose a run in a second.  The entire game doesn't take long to beat, maybe an hour?  But the fun is not in that this game takes a long time, it is that the complexity unfolds as stuff is unlocked.
So what is there to unlock? There are items, charecters, and whole levels that will be added to the item pool the more you complete the game with each charecter.  And even without that, there are challenge runs and greed mode.  There is the daily challenge (which is a unique gametype with a unique goal sometimes).  The updates add to the game without diminishing the core that is there, and there are modding tools and more updates coming.  This game is the best.
The only negative, for me, is the aesthetic.  The story and art style can be very disturbing and it kind of undermines the fun of the game...that said, I have got to a point in this game where I don't even notice the story or disturbing elements of the art.

Concept: Tower Defense Extravaganza
Kingdom Rush is basically a direct port of the flash game the would be ported onto the IOS and Android platform. Not every game should be ported from tablet form to a full PC game. However Kingdom Rush has already established itself as a major player in the tower defense genre. Before you point out that I paid real money for a game that is literally available for free on websites like Kongregate, there is a reason to buy it. In the app version there is loads of premium content that one has to pay for separately. In the PC version you get the full game, no exceptions. So, if you have it on your tablet or phone is it really any different? No. Not at all. It's the exact same fun game.
Kingdom Rush takes the existing TD genre and gives it character. For such a simple little game there is so much content to it. And if you are looking for that next challenge look no further. Kingdom Rush is a deceptive game that fools you into believing you can do it then crushes your dreams two minutes later. However there is a bigger picture. You can upgrade your overall tower abilities and skills as you beat more of the game by earning stars. And it gets better, you can respec your skills freely whenever you wish. So if a level calls for just arrow towers as a strategy then max out your arrow tower strength. But if another level needs every tower then respec your skills to balance out your strength.
The game is also full of fun easter eggs and achievements that are meaningless but just add more character to this already full game. There is also a hero system that will come in handy. As your hero makes kills on the field he/she/it will level up and gain strength and abilities. You'll have several of these heroes to chose from as well and the best part is that most of them are like 2.99 in the app. Its insane. The game is visually appealing with a fantastic color palette. This may be easier on a touch screen though as I lose some time with my mouse and keyboard.
Second Opinion: I'm not paying for a free game...

Very nicely put together isometric shooter with a vibrant colour theme and addictive gameplay. It's one of the (very) few games I consistently return to play and can also regain my skill with quickly. I wouldn't be a fan of the music outside of the game but it fits near perfectly here. I can't remember how much I payed but the off-sale price of £3.49 is absolutely worth it, and I'm a cheap♥♥♥♥♥when it comes to buying games. Most of my time was spent offline.
+ Gameplay is addictive, easy to learn but takes a little time to master
+ Encountered no bugs/glitches at all
+ Vibrant colours, attractive graphics and music which suits the theme of destroying enemy robots
+ Level up to unlock new guns, melee weapons armour, headgear and other items (you can also prestige)
+ All of the unlockables are upgradable - items have 3 standard levels and weapons have 11 potential upgrade points
+ Play if offline or online - story levels, wave mode and deathmatch (dm may be online only but others are both)
+ Very cheap for the quality and quantity
+ Upgrade default weapons fully to unlock a more powerful variant (e.g.shotgun -> spreadgun)
+ Approach waist high objects to take cover
+ Interesting variety of enemies and levels have a small range of goal variation
+ Load times are short and the game has low requirements
- Small playerbase (but I find there is usually 1 or 2 people online for co-op story/wave mode)
- Some players may not like grinding for loot and gear
- Levels can/do look the same
- If you hate electronic music with an insidious resolve of hatred you will not feel comfortable here
tl;dr - simple, addictive, level-based isometric shooter with a great upgrade system, virbrant graphics and well-made gameplay mechanics. Play it for quick, easy, accessible and often challenging gameplay, not gripping plot lines or thought provoking drama and you'll do all right.

Even though Street Fighter is known as the progenitor of fighting games, SFV is probably one of the worst fighting games on the market for someone to pick up, especially if you're like me and only play games for single player. I'll address why this is by discussing: the gameplay, the state of the game, and the business model.
First off, street fighter is more slow, methodical game. Fighting games have different tiers of movement and, as an example, ArcSys games have air dashing, so you have greater overall options for mobility and as a result, the battles can be a bit more hectic. There is no air dashing in SFV, and that's okay! However, this means your gameplan has to be a lot more intenional. Approaching can be dangerous and you want to do so safely. As someone with no interest in playing this game online as a result of the bad netcode (well, if I'm being honest, I play almost everything alone), I've found that the best way to get in on an opponent is to simply block an unsafe attack and punish it to the best of your ability. It's possible you've heard people call SFV a "turn-based strategy" game, that's because often times you'll find yourself waiting for your opponent to make a mistake so you can properly punish. Outside of that, you have to pay attention to "footsies" which just means punishing people who aren't paying attention to the distance between characters. There's one last element of the gameplay that bothers me, which is the fact that attacks don't link from L -> M -> H. Let's use Melty Blood and Skullgirls as examples to explain why this is frustrating. If you pick up a new character in Skullgirls  you know you can do light punch into medium punch into heavy punch into a special. It's not necessarily a great combo, but it looks good and you feel competent for doing so. This also means that it's easier to swap between characters, because they share a foundation but don't feel like copy characters. Marvel vs Capcom Infinite, which has its own host of issues, has a combo system that is easy to pick up, yet allows for some wild stuff if you can figure it out. I've only ever done things I've learned myself in MvC:I and I've had some wild 50-75 hit combos that looked amazing. In SFV, certain moves can be cancelled and others cant. Outside of target combos (short strings of normal attacks that are guarunteed to combo, like medium kick -> medium punch) there's no intuitive way to figure out a combo. Even though I have thousands of hours in fighting games across the past 12 years of my life, I can't intuitively discover any combos in street fighter, let alone anything good or flashy. I feel like I'm stuck waiting for better players to figure stuff out so I can copy them, because I don't want to go through every character's normals to find out which are special cancelable.
Outside of gameplay, there's just barely anything to do if you don't want to play against other people. Tekken has treasure battle mode, Guilty Gear has that RPG combat system, and Hyper Dragonball Z (the free, fan-made mugen fighter) has simultaneous battle (1v2, 2v1, 2v2). So many other fighting games have little systems to help fight the tedium of going against the AI and, at the very least, they'll have a survival/endless mode so you don't have to worry about menuing in-between matches. SFV's survival mode has a point/shop component to it, so you can buy health-regen to it, but I don't want that survival mode! I just want the game to load up enemy after enemy as I win and I want to see how far I can go. There's not even an arcade mode!!! I mean, sure, they're adding it in an update, but it's been TWO seasons before they got to this point. It's just all the more reason to believe that Capcom's business model for this game is intentionally malicious.
Finally, the way the game is split apart and sold back to you is insulting. I'm not against season passes or anything like that, but there's a $30(!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!) costume pack for characters just for one season! As of right now, there's $51 worth of costumes available to buy. That's nearly as much as the cost of the game. Consider, for a second, that you can customize your characters for free in Tekken 7. I understand that the costumes require work to make, but they feel so overpriced for getting so very little. Also, how come you can't buy a stage pack combo dlc thing? They've released an absurd amount of stages and each one sells for $4 individually. As of right now, there's 7 stages locked behind $28 dollars total. I bought the game full price, for $60 and I bought the two character passes at half off for $25. 7 stages are valued the same as about 1 character pass, but you can't buy them in bulk, which means there aren't discounts on them during holidays, which is when I buy most DLC. It's infuriating, because it would probably take me a month or two of grinding in game currency to get those 7 stages. If SFV was an incredibly fun game with a lot of features I wouldn't mind, for example, I bought Geese in Tekken 7 for $8 and he came with a stage from KoF, the game he's from! For $8 in SFV you can get one character.
It's not that SFV is entirely bad. At this point, there are so many characters that there's a good chance you'll find one person you like and you'll get good with them and enjoy the their combos. However, between bad online, minimal single player content, and price gouging for lackluster content you could just buy a better game. If you want something similar to SFV, then check out the King of Fighters series. Tekken 7 is a blast. Guilty Gear and BlazBlue games are great,  Melty Blood and Under Night are super fun. Skullgirls is great. Injustice 2 and MKX are a ton of fun! Street Fighter 3rd Strike and Ultra Street FIghter 4 are fun as well. SFV isn't terrible, but there are so many other great fighting games to pick up, even some indie ones like Punch Club, Fight of Gods, or even Overgrowth! Plus, Dragonball FighterZ and Soulcalibur 6 are on the way. These are all contemporary fighting games too! There's a history of great fighting games that you can look into and pick up. Just save some money and don't buy this.
As an afterthought: Capcom was more concerned about shutting down people cheesing survival mode to unlock colors and fight money, than addressing the complaints about survival, which is the worst survival game mode I and others have ever played. Whenever a game introduces a new currency to facilitate the unlocking of content (like Shadow of War) it just means the developers want to simultaneously sell content to you for real money so you can go past the grind. Imagine if you had to do specific challenges with characters to unlock their stage? That'd be way better than grinding a laggy online mode until you can purchase it. Plus, it feels like content is overpriced in real life money and they get away with it, because you can grind in-game currency at the rate of like 10 cents an hour. It's pretty insulting. If the game is so expensive, then they should cutback the budget and not screw over their customers to make as much money as they're aiming for. We should be playing fighting games made by people who enjoy fighting games, not fighting games made to generate profit.

In Mortal Kombat 9 we go through 16 chapters playing as the fighters but the overall story is that Nether Realm and the Earth Realm are going to merge and by trying to stop it Raiden get's killed by Shao Khan. The net.code is less than impressive. When i did get into  a match i was either throw out or i lagged so much i couldn't land a hit on my opponent. Overall a very impressive PC port and also an impressive sequel. Without a doubt give this game a shot if you like fighting games. I give Mortal Kombat 9 a 9,5/10

While no commendable effort has been made to adapt the original mobile version's UI for the PC port, making for a crude interface and inconsistent navigation, the gameplay itself feels awesome with a gamepad. The game also runs flawlessly (except perhaps on Ultra settings).
There is no story, just a guy going through some space station of sorts blasting enemy bots, with lots of cool guns and upgrade options. You can tell exactly what the game plays and feels like by the screenshots alone and that is good enough.
The game looks great, though with a single industrial sci-fi environment modulated with about three variations, linear levels soon start to feel repetitive. Similar surprise spawn tactics are used throughout, and you get to pass by the same sections many times despite some basic randomization.
The few boss fights add a welcome variety to the combat setups, as do the inclusion of locked areas where you must defeat waves of enemies before proceeding. Incomprehensibly, loot crates often appear at the very end of the level when all enemies have already been defeated, making the tons of acquired health and ammo entirely useless (except for upgrade chips).
The sound design is nearly perfect, with licensed upbeat electro music and satisfying sound effects blasting their way throughout.
Unfortunately there is almost no one online, which is a shame because the game shines in coop when it does happen.

A dull, predictable platformer, 140 has gameplay that rarely extends beyond jumping on moving platforms or avoiding slow-blinking deathtraps. None of the challenges were at all satisfying to complete.
Super Meat Boy-style finesse is rarely required--just basic timing and a LOT of waiting. Many of the levels are designed to make gracefully darting through them impossible: for every second you actually spend moving or jumping, you'll spend a second waiting for a platform to materialize or move or deactivate, because it wasn't set correctly when you reached it. With such bite-size levels and challenges, these constant five-second mandatory pauses become grating, and clash with the music, which has a tempo and rhythm that encourage a sense of constant motion.
As for the art style? Eh, it's inoffensive, not great. It's going for a sort of pseudo-De Stijl look: each level contains lots of blocks of two arbitrary colors, with slightly different values for different level assets. The music might be tense with warm colors, or softer with cool colors, but that's the extent of the game's tonal consistency: the level mood jumps around from somber to exciting to chill with no real rhyme or reason. What is this trying to make me feel?
Well, I certainly felt bored.

Mortal Kombat is, by all accounts, a very lighthearted and fun game that the whole family can enjoy. With very friendly and inviting characters as well as a bright atmosphere, Mortal Kombat is sure to delight children of all ages and engage them in a very positive, educational experience. It plays like a fast-paced game of tag, with puzzles to challenge the mind, different mini games to enhance response time, and a difficulty that is very forgiving to new players. Don't let the pictures above fool you; Mortal Kombat is all about peace and non-violence.
Mortal Kombat follows the stories of several characters as they each compete in a fabled contest called, "Mortal Kombat." The Mortal Kombat Tournament is basically a tag & hugging contest, with the best tag players from around the world competing to be crowned the winner and earn a years supply of cupcakes and a Starbucks gift card.
However, there is a secret bet between a group of overseers known as the "The Elder Gods," and the previous tag master, Shao Kahn. Shao Kahn wants to throw a big party with music and cake in Earth Realm, but Raiden one of the protectors of Earth Realm, doesn't want to have a party, since nobody likes Shao Kahn since he's a bully. So the Elder Gods tell Raiden that Shao Kahn can have his party unless someone from Earth Realm wins the Mortal Kombat Tournament.
Knowing this Raiden begins training his pupil, a happy-go-lucky man by the name of Liu-Kang, so that he may win the contest. But he is not the only one participating. There are numerous other characters that the game follows, such Scorpion and Sub-Zero, two best friends who dress as ninjas that love hanging out and visiting each other's families. There's also Johnny Cage, a famous actor that respects women and goes out of his way to be kind and caring. Mileena, who is known for having the most beautiful smile in all the realms, and of course Goro, a jolly giant who loves to give hugs and is a very active environmentalist.
Tensions arise though when Raiden discovers that Shao Kahn plans to cheat his way through the tournament and make people come to his party. There's also a minor subplot about a man named Kano, who's being pursued by a lady named Sonya Blade in an effort to find him the perfect Christmas present, the ever-gentlemanly Johnny Cage assists in this, and it teaches a valuable life lesson about sharing and giving and respecting the law.
At some point you'll play as most of the characters, and you'll discover that all of them have unique methods of tagging. Each character even has special moves ironically named "Fatalities," because they're completely non-violent and send messages of peace and good sportsmanship to the players.
Other than the story, there are numerous game modes, such as challenge tower, that are increasingly fun and not at all too difficult for the average player. In addition you have the fun mini-games I mentioned before; Test Your Might, Test Your Skill, Test Your Luck, each adding a little something extra to the formula.
This edition also comes with a few new characters , such as Skarlet, a girl with good intentions that has difficulty spelling words with a C in them. Rain, a funny weather man from Miami Florida, and let's not forget Freddy Krueger, who is not at all the same person from those terribly violent horror movies, but rather a kind doctor who helps people suffering from terrible injuries and is also incredibly good with children.
All in all, when it's finished, you'll feel incredibly fulfilled and your children will have learned a lot of things about themselves and about how to treat other people. Definitely recommended.

It's the little things that can make or break a game.
Starbound gets so many of them wrong.
-No pause in single player.  Not even hitting escape works.
-Container menus open in front of everything.  You can move them, but the game forgets where after a while.
-Pressing 'E' to close a container sometimes works but not always.
-Text speed in dialogs is fixed.  Can't press a button to skip it, or pause to read it.  Most of the time it is annoyingly slow, but sometimes it is too fast.
-Navigating stairs is horrible.  Having to press down and jump would work if you only fell one level, but hold down a fraction of a second too long and you often fall to your death.
-Hunger generates too fast, and most food isn't stackable.
This game has been in early access for years, and the little things still make this game a chore to play.

Attention: This game has potential and please...buy this game in order to support the development.
However, do NOT expect a finished and stable game (at least I don't think it is stable and I am sure I am not the only one thinking it is not yet finished).
The Kindred appears to be a game in the genre of survival, (town/city) building and (ressource) management.
You start with a couple of people and need to survive with them on your map...give them orders (or manage their jobs in order to get things done) to survive, gather food, wood, stone, iron (and more). You can develop the things you can build and produce.
It appears that this game is a mixture of Rimworld (management of jobs) and Stonehearth (look and feel) with some minecraft (modded) thrown in.
Your 3D view in block/minecraft you give orders to mine, chop, craft, etc. You yourself can plant/put blocks in there to even out the area or make houses and such.
It even has electricity (which very much reminds me personally of minecraft modded with all the industrial mods - I like it).
Why am I not recommending this game (yet)?
It is unstable. While I understand that there might be more or less content in an early access game and that there are certainly bugs, I am not quite sure it is there yet. In my (a little less than) one hour game play it froze several times and I had to revert back (reload) from earlier starts...lucky for me I was saving quite a lot after a while. Also there are performance fixes needed (in my opinion), but those usually come at some point in development.
If this is fixed I am more than happy to change my recommendation.

Left 4 Dead is the classic cooperative horror shooter from Value software. The game holds up remarkably well despite its age, and the maps are well tried and tested classics: well-balanced, replayable, and atmospheric. The game is darker (literally) and more serious than the sequel, and the campaign is clever enough to allow for some truly emergent gameplay. I would personally have preferred more of a story to link the 4 base campaigns, rather than the disconnected episodes we have here, but that's a petty gripe really. I've played dozens of hours on this on Xbox and, while 4 campaigns would be short for any other game, the fact that they are so replayable is a testament to their design. Versus mode is fun (playing as infected in actually my preferred option) but the few flaws in the game are evident in this mode. Survivors have the definite advantage and are able to camp quite effectively, particularly in the finale of the Blood Harvest campaign. The characters' minimal dialogue is well written and their voice actors (including Jen Taylor) do their jobs very well. A classic with superb replay value and a strong community online.

*EARLY ACCESS REVIEW*
This game was a pleasant surprise for me and I feel it needs some more reviews since not many have reviewed it since it came out last February on Early Access.
This game manages to do a lot of things Stonehearth does but better. More efficient crafting and building makes for a much more relaxing and interesting creative building experience. The frustration of waiting for my "hearthlings" to construct scaffolding and ladders and carry blocks one by one to a new building is gone with Kindred because I design and build the houses myself instead after the "Kin" do the work of mining and crafting the materials. To me this is a far better teamwork effort and requires a lot less micro-management of the Kin.
The biggest plus for me with this game is how smooth it runs. There are some camera angle issues and occasionally a hiccup or two after an auto-save but for the most part, even with 50 Kin all running around doing their various jobs, the game runs nicely and doesn't bog down. Again, games like Stonehearth haven't managed to get their AI and pathing to work nearly as well as this little game has done!
The modern look may turn some people off but I found it to be a refreshing change of pace from games like Timber and Stone, Stonehearth and others where 'fantasy/medieval' is the main theme. That's fun but it's nice to have a change of pace. Clean lines for the textures and wind generators and electricity are great and work well for the art-style.
All that being said, this game is VERY early on in it's development and there are some issues that may make you want to wait a bit for more development such as:
- Simplistic unfinished interface does not always work well yet
- Missing or bugged out tooltips not appearing makes it difficult to see what materials you need or are looking for.
- Work assignment menu is a little cumbersome and needs work.
- Notifications for Kin growing up, growing old, being born or falling in love are either missing or easy to miss if build menu is open.
Most of these issues I have are interface (UI) related and are definitely going to be fixed and polished by the developers before it's ever close to being finished. If you're good at figuring things out without a perfect interface telling you everything then you'll probably still enjoy this game. I got used to the quirks of it and have now put in 30+ hours of enjoyable building. My Kin Town has nearly 50 Kin and 3 generations of 'natural born' Kin. I love the way the Kin will naturally pair off (gender does not matter) and you can build them a house with beds and a cot and the stork will eventually bring them a baby! The tiny "Pixel Baby" will grow into a child in about 3 game days (approx 3 years) and join the work-force as a kid (child labor!). This reminds me a lot of Dwarf Fortress except the babies stay in their cots instead of the Mother Dwarves carrying them everywhere. A lot of these colony-builder games avoid children and aging but I never understood why. It seems like such a great addition to the gameplay as your community grows. People are born, they grow up, they fall in love and they have kids, that's the circle of life and really helps give purpose to your village, town, city as it grows.
Lastly, the game is fairly easy right now because resources are abundant and they have not yet implemented 'enemies' of any kind. I think there are plans for predators which will try to hunt your livestock but I'm not sure what other types of threats there will be to your Kin other than weather/temperature concerns and whatnot. Having played a lot of Stonehearth where the monster attacks are frequent and often annoying, I don't mind the peaceful mode right now for Kindred!
I'll update my Review as they develop and add more features. I definitely recommend this game if you enjoyed builder games like Gnomoria, Timber & Stone, Stonehearth and other similar colony-builder simulators with voxel building.

Now, I know what you’re thinking:
“You have over 400 hours in this game and have the season pass. How can you not recommend this?” To play that much means that you have to at least like this game.”
Well, to answer those questions I’d have to say that Fallout 4 is like Heroin, it’s addicting and dulls the pain but it’s not really that good in particular and you’d have to be a real♥♥♥♥♥to recommend heroin to someone. This game is very addicting and there is a lot of content, but it’s all disconnected and not very rich. There’s a lot of stuff to do but not much reason to do any of it.
First, let’s start with the content of the game, it’s not all that special. I tried to get through the story and DLCs but I couldn’t bring myself to it, I was so uninterested in the game that I couldn’t even complete the game, let alone play the DLC. The only content I did “play” was the workshop DLC which was honestly terrible, overpriced, and should’ve been in the base game. If I had to do it all over again, I wouldn’t have bought the season pass. But when it comes to the game, the parts that will tear those precious hours of life away from you are the repetitive combat and, for some, the settlement building. Despite liking the settlement building, it’s very clunky and even with the DLC it’s fairly barebones, the only thing that keeps you doing it is the insane amount of settlement building locations. The combat is good, it’s definitely the best in the series but isn’t very challenging. If you were to play the game, I’d recommend playing on survival mode because despite being incredibly unbalanced and often infuriating, it’s the only challenge you’ll ever have playing this game. So far the game’s presentation is mediocre but at least engaging even if it’s more on the addictive quantity side rather than the quality side.
But how good is it as a Fallout game? In my opinion it’s not very good at all. The perks system can go kill itself. It’s just awful, the perks are uninteresting and limited to 70 because the terrible design of the system, and no, ranks aren’t new perks they just make old perks better. Whoever thought that the perk system was good enough to replace the original perk system and skill system should be fired. Even those who like it have to admit that it’s very limiting with only 70 perks and the loss of interesting DLC perks. The skill system wasn’t perfect in Fallout: New Vegas because there were too little skills, and in Fallout 1&2 the perks system wasn’t all that good either because it was a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥plus they were pretty boring too. I can’t speak about Fallout 3 because it doesn’t run on my computer which is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. The original skill system could’ve been solved by making the skills more interesting, like how you could use them for special dialogue options in New Vegas but expanding beyond that, like having higher stats unlocking milestones abilities along with unlocking new perks. The new speech system is awful, you never know what you’re going to say which makes dialogue unimmersive and frustrating at times. The limit to 4 options is a dumb change because it limits the many ways your character can act. The random dice roll for speech is a bit annoying for me but not terrible, personally I prefer the New Vegas system because I have♥♥♥♥♥♥luck with dice rolls and it’s dumb that having higher Charisma doesn’t cause you to have more options but instead make it more likely that you have more options. In fact, all of the Special stats are pretty much useless, the only ones that are useful are Strength and Endurance as Perception only makes it more likely that you hit in VATS which is obselete because of the improved combat, Charisma being useless for the reasons stated above, Intelligence only affecting XP, Agility only affecting the number of action points which on paper sounds good because of the new action point uses, but is made obsolete by Endurance which reduces action point usage, and Luck which only affects how quickly your critical meter in the obselete VATS fills because there are no criticals outside combat. And like I said before, the story is uninteresting and the world is bland, it looks nice and is big but I barely remember anything about it because it’s not very rich. The big thing that makes Fallout so good is the expansive world that draws you in with it’s conflict and choices, this game was railroady until you get to the institute which is the point when I lost interest. But what about the quests? We’ll they’re not good either, they’re either radiant quests or forgettable with a few exceptions, which are the Fort Strong quest, which I remember for being infuriating without Power Armor on survival mode; The Frosted Flakes memory quest, which was long ugly and uninteresting, and finally The U.S.S. Constitution quest which was so good that it made me angry. It had everything you would want in a good side quest, a fun interesting story that’s weaved in naturally with good humor and a moral choice that isn’t black and white. The inclusion of skill checks was a nice touch too (even if it was just intelligence) and rewarded having a high stat by letting you skip the boring parts. The reason this quest makes me angry is because it’s a beacon of what this game could have been, even with the dumb design choices, if the entire game was as good as this quest I could complete forgive it, although it wouldn’t be free of criticism. Whoever designed this quest deserves a medal and should’ve been the person directing this game’s entire development.
Now, onto the weapons and armor, the weapons, in my opinion, are disappointing. Don’t get me wrong, the combat is fine but it’s the number of weapons and their design that I have a problem with. In my opinion the design of most of the weapons is just ugly. The designs that I’m okay with are, the .44 revolver, deliverer, flare gun, western revolver, handmade rifle, hunting rifle, lever action rifle, the syringer, Fat Man, Harpoon Gun, and the Gatling Laser (sort of). I excluded Melee weapons because all of them are fine (excluding the deathclaw gauntlet which looks ugly). Also, the amount of weapons (excluding unique ones that look exactly the same as the base weapons) is pathetic. There are 6 pistols, 10 rifles, 2 shotguns, 3 pipe guns, 7 big guns, 5 energy weapons, 5 “other” weapons, 1 gamma weapon, 19 grenades, 6 mines, 4 traps, 12 blades, 14 blunt, and 5 unarmed weapons. That comes out to a weak total of 99 different weapons. I know that it doesn’t include the modifications for pipe and energy weapons but it pretty much comes down to stock choice because of the advanced receiver although the plasma gun does have a plasma thrower which is nice. 99 may sound like a lot but there isn’t much variety among them is the problem making them very similar and boring. The armor variety is absolutely terrible though with only 13 armor types which is just pathetic. Tfw when the character limit doesn’t let you talk about power armor :(
I almost forgot to talk about the enemies which are the best in the series despite super mutants, feral ghouls, and deathclaw looking really dumb. Plus unless you’re playing on survival mode, the enemies are way too easy to kill and if you are playing on survival mode, the enemy scaling makes you want to kill yourself because of how bad it is. It’s nice that the enemies are unique, it’s not nice that they scale so there’s no sense of enemy progression. That’s all I’m willing to write and can write about this game I just learned today that there’s a character limit, and because of it I didn’t touch on many topics I wanted to touch on. In conclusion, this game had a lot of potential but didn’t live up to any of it which makes me sad
Also, for those of you who are going to call me a Bethesda hater and a Obsidian fanboy, 1: ♥♥♥♥ you, 2: I played this game well before I played New Vegas and it disappointed me then as much as it does now.

Are you sick of people playing a game for 300-700 hours and then trying to convince you it isn't worth 60 bucks (or even 30 on sale)? I know I am.
Overall this game is fantastic. Like any other Bethesda game it has it's drawbacks and it's upsides. It does it's best to balance player choice and having anything interesting to do in the first place. Overall I believe it strikes a great balance.
The biggest downsides in the game are that the initial faction you are introduced to is extremely lackluster and uninteresting, the factions ultimately demand that you kill the others off, even when they aren't in direct opposition to them, and settlement crafting/management is both too time consuming for anything but the most avid builders (for more than one settlement) and extremely clunky without mods.
The biggest upsides to the game are transparency at the very beginning for making builds work (no more wiki build planning required), an interesting story that you can at least moderately be invested in while still preserving wide options to play the game how you prefer, a far, FAR more interesting power armor mechanic than any past fallout game (even if energy management can largely be ignored from midgame onwards - and lack of ability to use it well (without mods) if you don't intend to use it all the time) and a large amount of very interesting areas to visit (as opposed to things like an endless amount of generic subways from fallout 3).

I don't even know how to articulate how good this game is to me. It's so polished. So fun. There are like 20-30 stages that have three different difficulties that force you to use unique strategies. The gameplay consists of paths with preset locations upon which you can build towers. There are four tower types and each has three upgrades and two specializations each. Each specialization has its own set of upgrades. The depth of tower upgrades reminds me of some AAA RTS games. The enemies consist of orcs and wizards and other generic baddies with varying resilience and counterstrategies.
A lot of tower defense games rely on tower placement as gameplay. Towers in Kingdom Rush have such a diverse set of utility and manual management that placement may not even be in the top 3 strategic priorities. You have a fireball spell that you cast yourself, and you also have a hero of your choice for some levels that you manually move around the map and engage enemies. You can also call two reinforcement warriors into battle at the location of your choice on a 20 or 30 second cooldown. So much to micromanage. The onslaught of enemy hordes is relentless, so you are constantly fighting an uphill battle that requires split second analysis and action, sometimes even sacrificing towers to fortify another path.
I highly recommend this game to everyone who enjoys tower defense and also to everyone who doesn't enjoy tower defense. You may be surprised how fun this game is for you.

I have many fond memories of this game's progenitor when I played it on my beloved Amiga A500. The graphics were simple, but functional for the experience of tactical and strategic gameplay. The entire premise of the game was almost like a naval chess battle. When I heard there was a remake in the works I did have expectations that the core of the game would still be there, but in a very modern wrapping. The carrier itself has visually transformed and like all the visuals, is very impressive. The audio is good too, but the execution of this games core is poor. Blending first person shooter elements into the game helps take the stale out of being locked into vehicles, but there's no multiplayer to really validate it. The need to be moving in and out of vehicles and structures feels like a bolt on to a RTS game.
Actual vehicle combat is good enough, The AI is thin, pathing for friendly vehicles is often poor, and I've had to manually retrieve a fair few Walrus that got themselves trapped. The enemy doesn't show a great deal more sense, and the challenge they present isn't in their tactics, but their numbers and loadout as you progress through the campaign. I was aching to get my carrier toe-to-toe with the enemy's. I loved brining down the ACC Omega on the original version, but the naval combat is almost pointless, it's mostly defending your own ship from island defences and when you do finally meet your nautical nemesis, you feel like a bug on a windshield. (The originals enemy carrier had weaknesses, the modern version only becomes vunerable after a certain point, beware of this)
The two modes of play differ mainly in that one has specific story based missions and goals in a near linear campaign format. The other is more likened to the original, though it's best to point out here that it is a LOT slower leaving an imprssion that playing through it will be an immense chore.
This game would have flourished as a multiplayer experience with players piloting or on foot, either in direct engagement or attacking/sabotaging supply lines. I had fun, but couldn't help feeling that they just didn't really go the distance with Carrier Command they could have.
Good - Solid visuals, good management and vehicle combat can be a lotta fun.
Bad - Cardboard thin depth of play and no multiplayer (and no real excuse for its absence)

A tower defence game, and a great one at that! :D
Kingdom Rush is a game I found out about from a friend years ago. He told me to check it out in an email and gave a link to the free version. I loved it, and I think I finished it. Tower defence games are one of only two genres that I actually like as a whole (the other being platformers), so I might give this game credit where credit isn't necessarily due, but the point is that it's good.
You get four types of towers to defend your... defendable... things with. I'll describe each one briefly:
-Barracks: Barracks train soldiers called footmen who block enemies paths. The main draw is that they slow the enemy down to allow more hits from your ranged towers. Footmen are the only units that can die. They deal melee damage, which is affected by armor.
-Archers: The barracks can't do everything, though. That's where ranged towers like archers come in. Ranged towers do most of the damage usually. Archers do melee damage for some reason (think of it more like physical I guess?), which means their damage is affected by armor. The thing is that they're faster than footmen and have more range. They stay in their tower and shoot things from high up, so they can't be killed/destroyed by enemies like the footmen can.
-Mages: Magic has a unique type of damage--it's not affected by armor. This makes mage towers VERY useful. They do more damage than archers, too, but they're slightly slower. Even so, I prefer mages to archers, usually. There are enemies that are resistant to magic, though. Just like archers, mages are ranged.
-Artillery... cannons: Artillery is ranged bombs, basically, that are shot into the air and rain down on groups of enemies. The explosions do damage by area instead of by enemy, which makes them good for taking out groups of weak enemies. They're slow and expensive, though. I think they do melee/physical damage.
I should mention that there are flying enemies that will go right over your footmen. You'll need a good ranged defence to fight them. You also get meteors and reinforcements. Meteors are for emergencies and do a lot of area damage. Reiforcements are like free extra footmen. Finally, there are heroes, which are characters you always start with. You can only have one hero at a time, but you pick which one. As you can see, there's some depth in this game. I'd recommend this, especially if you like tower defence.

It also looks like the developer releases new content and campaigns here every few months, which in addition to the multiple challenge modes on each map gives a huge amount of gameplay. Also, finding the easter eggs is a lot of fun, and it's clear from those and the achievements that someone's got a sense of humor.

140 is a rhythm-based platformer that challenges you with increasingly difficult stunts as your geometric character progresses through the game. Each time you complete a segment you save at a checkmark, which makes it less painful when you fail over and over again. Some people may struggle with the timing or precise controls required to complete some of the challenges, but I wouldn't call any of them impossible.
Most objects on the screen, besides your character, are simple squares. It doesn't get much simpler than that, but somehow it works. The graphics are vibrant and trippy at times, moving and changing colors to match the electronic music. The music by the way is fantastic! As you complete chapters and other key parts of the game the music will shift to reward the player with some awesome sounds.
My only complaint is that the game took me less than 90 minutes to complete. When you complete the 3 main acts (which takes 1-2 hours),you unlock the same 3 acts, but in reverse and without checkpoints. This should provide me some extra play time, but I'm certain that I will get frustrated and give up without the checkpoint handicap. So for that reason, the game doesn't have much replay value and the campaign is short, so I would only recommend this game if you find it on sale for $1-2.

In my opinion, this is the best fighting game on the market at the moment (until MKX is out). This game offers so much content at its price, it is worth buying it even if it is not on sale. This reboot of the franchise went back to the roots , it goes back to 2D, it has a good story mode ( in my opinion it could be better, sometimes you might get caught up in a fight for a stupid reason) , ladder mode which you can play alone or with another friend as a team. The energy bar is a great addition along with the X-ray moves which are already a signature to this franchise just like fatalities. This game even allows you to play with 3 more friends which is so awesome because you can kick their asses and this makes you feel so good because sometimes they deserve it. Additional modes like Test Your Luck are pretty good, but nothing compares with a good old fashion MK 1 on 1 fight where only your skill matters. After I finished the story mode and learned 3-4 characters pretty well , I wanted to try my luck on multiplayer and I was really dissapointed, the only way I could play on multiplayer was by joining a King Of The Hill match, because on 1vs1 the lag was incredible and I couldn't do anything. This is a big problem with the game, because nowadays only 30-40 people are still playing multiplayer and I don't know how they do it considering the bad netcode.
The Krypt is back with many additional things to unlock if you have enough money which you can collect by playing the story or ladder. If you ask me, some of the unlockables are pretty useless, for example you can unlock some fatalities which you can already use in the game even if you didn't find it in the crypt, this makes it pointless to unlock.
The rooster is big enough with plenty of fighters to pick from, every one of them is different and offer so much fun.
I spent hours in practice mode trying to make my own advanced combos and it's worth it.
I advice you to buy this game only if you want to play the story or you want to play with friends, because on multiplayer you will play a game without lag 1/15 or not at all. Overall it is a great game and it deserves a place in your library.

Hello, everyone.
On the surface, this game may seem like a clone to the popular game Terraria, which I own. But this game goes much further than Terraria and I personally place this as one of my favorite games of all time. There was so much new content that has been added since the previous updates, when this new content, such as the plot, crafting devices, GUIs, and much more, was only available via Starbound- Unstable Nightly mode on steam, and now this content has been made official.
This game feels and looks fun to play, with races to play, a giant community to back up the game, and so much potential. You just want to start building from day 1 in the game.
Since the beta versions, there was never any protectorates, no relics, no reason for the sudden dissapearance. This was just a simple sandbox game that you would use just to build stuff or beat the crap out of everything. Now there is actual plot, interesting missions, and much more content packed into this tight little package of a game. Honestly, there's so much to explore and even after playing this game for so long I was still wowed by most of the newer stuff in this game.
Multiplayer is still so much fun, maybe even more so than before. I've played with my dad on the Nightly 0.9 package the before the game was released and I had so much fun. Me and my dad died more times than I can count, we ended up taking shelter inside a rotten tower in my starter planet just to survive!
In conclusion, there is so much content than the Beta edition of the game and this game is so worth your money. I would recommend this to anyone who like building, sci-fi, or thought Terraria was a good game.

Meltdown is a good game. It's an addicting twin stick shooter with drop in, drop out multiplayer. I played little more than 3 hours, so this is my first impressions of the game.
It's an okay mobile port. It's not the best, nor the worst. There are not enough settings. Just graphics quality, resolution, music and fx sliders and Vsync. Keys are not rebindable. Also there is option for Aim-assist and I think it might be a good idea to be on. I'll explain later way.
There isn't a story here. Well, it's not entirly true, but I wouldn't call it this a plot. You are traped in a space station as result of system malfunction. That's it. In this case I don't mind the lack of any story, because the game is all about shooting. Tense, fun and addicting.
Graphics are alright. All charaters have this black outline to feel cel shaded, but actually they are not. At close inspection the main character is not that good looking, but you see him only when you buy stuff. Overall levels, enemies and your character are nice to look at, but not great.
You've seen this kind of gameplay a milion times before. Here it doesn't offer something new. It's simple and generic, but at the same time fun. You just run, gun, collect coins, chips, mystery boxes and gain XP. Basic stuff. You buy new firearms, armor, melee weapons. Guns have six different stats that can be upgraded. They are all standard – more damage, increase fire rate etc. But beside money for them you need chips. The catch is you can't upgrade the six of them, only three, so choose wisely or if you want to make correction, reset them, but i'm not sure if you will get back your money and chips. The two of them are gathered from dead enemies. And armors can be upgraded too. You can also pick up two power ups – double damage and nuke.
The coolest feature here is drop in, drop out multiplayer. You start alone, but at any time others can join you, up to three more people. It's defenently more fun and little bit more easy to have someone by your side to watch your back literally. You can do the same thing, join someone else to play together.
At the end of each level you will open mystery boxes. From them you can get xp, chips, coins, lives or nothing. Yes, here you have lives. If you loose all of them you have start at the beginning of the level.
Beside all those things, you can buy additional cosmetics like eye patch, hats, shoulder pads and so on. They don't just change the appearance, they also have additional buffs like more health, more damage etc.
After you level up, you have points to distrubute in three directions – specialist, medic and soldier. They also can be reset. In the beginning they are standard buffs, like more damage, but later they become more interesting – health regeneration, fire rate increase with weapon overheat and so on. Weapons can overheat and when this happen you have to wait them to cooldown.
Enemies are all robots with different attacks. They are diverse and require different tacktics to kill them. The two bosses I encounter are fun and tough to fight, especially when you are alone.
Level design is okay. In the beginning the levels are small, but later they are getting bigger. All have similar design – bridges, sandbags, boxes, cars, froklifts, small walls to take cover and so on. Here there is a cover system, but I rarely use it. First 10 levels have different design, than later ones are different, so you have a little bit diversity. Sometimes you'll get locked in a area and to get out you have to kill everything  to progress. There is one “But”. As I said all are similar to each other. You will see the same boxes, the same sandbags and after 3 h with the game the layouts and design are still the same
Sound is great. All weapons sound appropriate and feel meaty and explosions are good. The soundtrack is really great. You will hear techno and dubstep, fitting excelent in this sci-fi setting. I won't listen it every day, but throughout my time with the game I never wanted to stop the music.
I have one big issue with the game and few small ones. You can clearly see in the video that the crosshair have to be near a target, not on him to hit him, but this depends where the enemy come from. This is so bizzare and annoying. That's why I said in the beginning maybe the aim-assist is not a bad idea. Through my time with the game I encounter two bugs, one was game breaking. The first was I was frozen when I respawn and I lost a life. And the other was, I fall through the floor in to the abyss. Both bugs are just one time experience. Also the game is build around grinding and there is no doubt about it. I reach a point where I have to repeat few levels to get a better gun. And lastly, almost all menus have to be draged with the mouse to move them and it's annoying. Obvious mobile port.
The game doesn't do anything bad, nor anything great and that's fine. It's a really simple, yet addicting. Easy to pick up and play. But to be fair after 3 h I start to get a little bit bored. I've seen what the game have to offer. You are doing the same thing over and over again. It's a perfect time killer, a game where you can go in play 1or 2 levels before you go somewhere for example. There two additional modes – Wave Attack and Deathmatch, but I didn't try them. As much as I have problems with the game, i'm kinda addicted to it, maybe because of the simplicity and almost great gameplay. It have good gameplay, great sound design and it still have few players online, but it have this annoyance with the crosshair, suffers from repetition both in gameplay and level design. I recommend it, but on sale.

It was a fun game back in mid 2015-early 2016, after that period of time it became fairly dead. I would put a lot of time into the game, and even a little bit of money to see what all there was. But after nearly 500 hours of gameplay I can tell you that, yes, the game is very fun at first, however, will become quickly boring given you play it a lot. By all means, give it a try, it might be just the grind-heavy, looter type game you've always dreamed of, but it gets repetitive, quickly. All of the worlds are very much the same, with very little variation. After awhile you'll realize that you've seen the same dungeon quite a bit. You go through the same biomes, clearing the same dungeons, getting the same loot, just to dismantle it, level your stuff up, and repeat the process. It's a never-ending grind. I'm recommending this game for the pure fact that it is very fun for awhile, it's just difficult for it to stay that way. I wouldn't recommend spending money on this game, especially if it's going to become boring after so long, but I'd say give it a go, see if you like it, and go from there.

This is a really cute game, and a quick look at the discussions easily shows that there's a LOT of communication from the devs, which is a major factor for me concerning early access games. Feedback is definitely being taken into consideration, and bugs are being addressed appropriately. I haven't logged a lot of hours as of yet, but I can already tell that this is gonna be a great time-spender for me.
The building aspect (while a little buggy, as most early access games are) has a good amount of depth, and plenty of room for creativity, with a wide selction of building materials and fairly intuitive tools. In addition to building voxel homes, there are power sources required for things like lighting, which adds realism.
The survival simulation is pretty straightforward - grow crops, raise animals for meat, milk, wool, etc. and generally just keep your peoples happy and healthy. An exciting planned feature is the population being increased through childbirth, which is something most sim games like this lack.
The only drawback is the somewhat confusing UI, but after poking around a bit, it's not too hard to get the hang of, more or less, and while it's something I can live with, I'd love to see it improved at some point.
If you are into survival games, sim games, voxel games, or just looking for something peaceful to play and be creative with, this is definitely worth consideration.

Alien Vs Predator is a long running comic book series turned video games series about the titular Aliens fighting the titular Predators. Set in the distant future where xenomorphs and Predators (Or Yautja if you're a huge nerd) fight one another while humans try to survive in the center of their little frenemy bromance.
The Weyland-Yutani corporation, a stinky idiot corporation, is led by Karl Bishop Weyland, the stinkiest idiot. For a few games now, these stinky idiots thought that it was a not stupid idea to capture xenomorphs and try to turn them into bioweapons. This goes as well as you think and the xenomorphs escape to create new poop caves on a new planet.
The predators, smelling the poop caves, and in return, spicey Alien butts to tongue, travel to the planet of BG-386 so that they can hunt both xenomorph and the most dangerous game...MAN, the spiciest of butts.
Now with the humans at the mercy of both the alien poop caves and the Predator butt groping, a distress signal is sent out that is answered by the United States Colonial Marine corp, who's sole job is to clean up Stinky Idiot Corporation's messes and getting dragged into alien poop tunnels.
You get three campaigns, which is a nice but the Marine campaign is clearly the most fleshed out. In the Alien campaign, you play as Specimen 6, an alien who is apparently the best and creating slimy poop caves and dragging poor humans to make more aliens in said poop caves. This campaign is more focused on stealth as you sneak around and beat up humans who are just doing their job and happened to be in the wrong place at the wrong time. You awful, awful monster.
Predator campaign is a mix of both stealth and action, while you sneak around and beat up humans once again, every now and then the xenomorphs show up for a good butt tounging and you have to oblige them. The stealth in this one is also pretty cool, but the beat-em-up alien sequences kind of lose their luster really quick. It's not bad, but it's not that good either, it almost feels like an after thought, like they remembered that the Predator was there to tongue aliens butts last minute instead of just bullying humans.
The Marine campaign, I will admit I enjoyed immensely. There's this foreboding sense of dread in every thing you do, especially during the first hour or so of the campaign. It almost feels like one of the original AVP games or even Aliens while you skulk around an apparently abandoned colony. You don't even see any enemies for quite some time until an alien decides to bully you, unlucky for them you are unbullyable and shoot the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ right in his little mouth.
This being said, the campaigns are still rather short, especially the Alien campaign which can be completed in 2 or 3 hours or so.
But enough about that, what about the multiplayer?
AVP is known for it's online mode, with AVP 2 standing out from the rest of them in my opinion. Once again, you pick between Predator, Alien, and Marines in a fight for supremacy between yourself and the 20 or so Brazilian guys who still play this game. I ended up playing with a few fellow hobos. Out of all the game modes we ended up playing Deathmatch the most while one of us usually played as the marines, the others would pick alien or predator. The sense of dread stays with you as you play marines in multiplayer, only this it's your friends trying to eat you with their little mouths or bully your butt. But that sense of dread is quickly passed on to the alien and predator once the marine finds grenades or the smart gun.
The melee...Works, I guess,  the alien and predator both have a strong attack, a normal attack, and a block, while the marine only has a block and a rifle butt to stop the alien from using his little mouth on you. You can block and counter normal attacks which knocks your enemy on their backs, but the block can be broken by a strong attack which in turn can be countered by a normal attack. This sounds alright in theory, but in practice, it's kind of janky, the first person view doesn't do much to help in this matter. The predator and alien can also lunge at you from a distance which can knock you down at the right angle.
Alien players need to rely on speed and stealth, skulking in the shadows or camouflaging into one of their many poop caves that litter the maps. While predators can take a more patient approach with the use of stealth camouflage as well as their many gadgets like the spear, the plasma caster, or the stupid ♥♥♥♥ing boomerang blade that NEVER WORKS EVEN IF I'M LOOKING RIGHT AT YOU ISNT THAT RIGHT DIBBIN
Even with it's faults, the multiplayer is still fun and takes me back to my younger years when I would play the AVP2 multiplayer demo for hours, always picking marines because it doesn't feel right if my white undies aren't a strange mix of yellow and brown. It's fun to taunt and tease your friends as you hunt them, little mouth and all.
But should you play Gayliens vs Redditors.
Eh... Sure. It's basically the epitome of mediocrity. It's not amazing, but it's not offensive either. The online community is practically dead, you can find some games every now and then, but there really isn't a point to staying with it in the long run.  Get it on the cheap, no more than 5 bucks I would say. Mess with the single player a bit, play with a few friends, get your money's worth and then call it a day.

Take two enjoyable games (Minecraft, Banished) borrow positive aspects of each and mold one new game. It might just be that simple for The Kindred. The Steam version however may contain some GFX colour errors when you play in-game like the vehicles with a distinctive yellow glow; plus your saves from the PC Retail Version - that if you choose to transfer into the Steam Version may corrupt it.

And when you get a Mission from Shoreside Vale, except the PayPhone from Southside Hoods, DON'T buy anymore weapons. Trust me you need the cash for the final showdown.
Now I believe this game appears to be the only game in the GTA 3D series onwards that don't reduce your Criminal Rating stats, so you can cause some cheating mayhem as you want. But don't use them for the newer versions of GTA as those Stats will be ruined.

Well, I have only 10 hours into this game. I enjoy it so far. The radio could use a little overhaul as some of the same tracks are in there from the New Vegas and the Fallout 3 soundtrack. It could really use a buff because you have to walk long distances and the radio makes it less of a struggle. The game function itself is overhauled and things work differently than the previous versions. It's better. The graphics are stunning. Some parts look and feel so real. I just can't believe my eyes. You can also build and scrap items around the world so it's super customizable and that is fun in and of itself. I would reccomend this to anyone who enjoyed the previous ones. I played them for a while, and I really had some fun with it. This new one is just as good if not better. Dungeons are pretty scary. The enemies are a bit more responsive and the tactics they use when attacking you are more refined. At times, it feels like they are alive and not just drones following a set path. That's one thing that makes this game. The monsters come at you out of nowhere and just when you think it's safe, something new will try to kill you. That's the wasteland for ya. The story so far is interesting and easy to follow. Sometimes, however, characters will end up getting killed and you will need to either reload a save, or just continue on. I've learned from the first one that sometimes it's just best to keep going and not to micromanage every aspect or else you will spend countless hours on something. The level design is great, the new features are pretty neat, and the game itself is worth playing. I think there are some places it needs to be improved, for instance cars, maybe some type of vehicle to drive or use, even if it's for a short distance. The radio needs some work. So far I've been listening to some of the same music forever it seems. There are a lot of the same charecters, but I guess that keeps with the theme so really there is no problem there. All in all it is a great fun game so far. I reccomend it if you enjoyed Fallout 3 and New Vegas. If you didn't enjoy those, then this one might not be any different as it's got the same things going for it. I'm happy I purchased this game. It's fun and I can't wait to explore more. I've already made it to diamond city, and I'm just learning about synths. I haven't seen one yet (that I know about) but I expect there to be many plot twists and fun things ahead.
