Lets be honest: This game is hard. And seriously, its inconcievable that you are going to be level 20 (max level) first life. And it is a game where raging is perfectly fine. This game takes time to get even moderatly good at, hell, I still can't maintain a character for more than a week (Though I got back into the game a month ago.) Its what makes this game fun for so long, you always are trying to get better.
Here are a few of my other opinions on the game:
1) Really the only con, tops being sold in the Nexus. Tops are the highest tiered, non-soulbound items in the game. They are HARD to get. You have to earn it to get it. But then, you can pull out your wallet and pay up for them. True, they do need money to run this game, but then backpacks, vault chests, keys and cloth are fine. Cloth is really only aesthetic and with keys, you still have to go through the dungeon and fight your way through before getting your reward, its only lowering the time it takes to get to the dungeon (as it is easier to get the dungeon than complete it [most of the time]), backpacks add an extra 8 slots to your character so you can store more (an lose more, at that) vault chests allow you to store items in your vault so that you don't lose them when you die, and you start with 1 when you first play. The only thing about vault chests thats needs to change is to lower their price and/or make them easier to obtain for free.
2) A constant (and growing?) community. This means a constant economy. Those who do get a bit farther into the game do get to trade items they earned but don't need for items they need, which, for those of us who are cursed by the r ng can still get the items they need to go further as well as the person they traded with.

3) Lots of gameplay and variety. There are 4 tiers of mainland (non dungeon & nexus area) lowland, midland, highland, and godlands/mountains. On top of this, there are multiple dungeons for each of them. Each of these areas have different enemies, and all of them are different, in firing patterns, stats, drops, etc. This makes it so that there is always more to discover in this game.

I was hoping to scratch that ARPG itch with this game and it simply came up short.  A Bastion clone it is not.
While there are a variety of enemies and guns, I felt the core gameplay to be fickle and problematic:
1) The aiming does not feel precise.  Often times you will end up shooting next to a foe when you are clicking right on them - use of a controller makes this actually even worse.  The game is meant to be played with auto-aim and this often takes the satisfaction out of a game like this.
2) The biggest problem in the game is that it feels like you are fighting the controls.  You are locked into an animation once you start it which is significantly more cumbersome than it is challenging.  For example, you cannot go from melee to shooting or rolling to anything in a reasonable time frame -- you will have to wait for your character to finish said action, delay and then start your new action.
3) The game relies on grind rather than content.  Making an area too difficult to complete so you have to re-do previous areas is not a good stand in for content -- it just shows you purposely undertune the starting options.  What necessarily comes with this is an inverse difficulty curve - easy at the end and hard at the outset.
The core issue comes down to gameplay.  At its heart the game feels unresponsive and slow -- you will not die because you couldn't react in time, but because the game locks you into animation lag. And this is coming from a Monster Hunter veteran, I am no stranger to animation lag and meaningful gameplay.

It doesn't offer a great deal that can't be found in other open-world games, but the flipside is that it's also almost entirely free of the guff that drags many of its competitors down. Sleeping Dogs is a lean, refined GTA clone with an emphasis on putting as much of the game at your fingertips as early and often as possible.
Gameplay boils down to melee, gunplay and driving sections. Melee fights are the most prevalent part of the game and anyone who's played the Arkham games will feel right at home with the counter-driven one-button fighting here. Melee weapons and environmental kills are offered for some variety but don't add much complexity or depth. Shootouts can be conducted as either an exercise in cover-based pop-and-shoot mechanics (if you're boring), or a more arcadey system where stylish kills can be chained together to rack up continuous bullet time. It's very reminiscent of John Woo's Stranglehold and handily my favourite part of the game, although it errs on the side of being a bit too easy. Driving is fairly standard; cars handle well with the right amount of weight and chases are enlivened somewhat by the presence of that same chained bullet-time mechanic as well as the ability to freely hop from one car to another a la Just Cause.
The game's simulated Hong Kong is wonderfully detailed and always lovely to look at, but you'll find that it's not hiding a great deal of interesting content to be discovered. Aside from stores dotted around the place, you'll only ever really find yourself heading from map marker to map marker for story missions or sidequests. The obvious debt the game owes to classic Hong Kong action/martial arts cinema aesthetically will probably make it more interesting to genre fans (like myself).

For the game itself, it's bland. I could see why someone would buy it because they like the street fighter franchise, but I mostly just buy fighting games for the system and fun behind it. This game doesn't do me that service. It's the same rock-paper-scissors, inhuman reflex based fighting formula that I could have played my old dead or alive or even my old street fighter copies for. Contrary to the naruto ultimate ninja storm series for example(with 4 also being my personal recommendation to anyone who likes fighting games), there is little to no innovation. Anything that street fighter adds, mostly in terms of special moves and v-strike, is quite tedious to execute as the buttons are overloaded with quite a lot of commands. Not to mention that they're not even that creative nor good compared to what you can do with the regular abilities. Special moves are supposed to be a finisher, or simply something difficult yet rewarding to pull off. Naurto ultimate ninja storm generation 4 does this well, the special moves are hard to execute, easily interruptable by anything and sometimes hard to even hit, but they do a lot of damage and have a long, well-done and incredibly epic animation that really makes you feel like you've accomplished something. Or ♥♥♥♥ed up if you're on the receiving end. Street fighter doesn't really give you this feeling. Some moves do have an animation and can be quite satisfying to land, but I don't feel like they're any harder or more rewarding than regular abilities.
As a final verdict, street fighter has surprised me graphically, but let me down in most other aspects. dead or alive 5 which is significantly older still has more features. There are other things that redeem this game, the charm of the characters, the design, silly and entertaining, but as a game, it's not for me.

This game took me completely by surprise. I recently picked it up in the Humble Eye Candy Weekly Bundle, in which it was included for its aesthetic. I hadn't read anything about it yet, so I decided to just fire it up and go in cold. What I ended up playing was one of the best games I've ever played that uses music to engage the player with the gameplay mechanics.
The game's pretty good about ramping up the difficulty moderately, introducing new stage mechanics at a decent pace. The only time I really felt it was at all unfair about it was the boss fight at the end of Level 2, which seems to just involve guesswork if you don't know the pattern already. The rest of the time, my deaths were due to my own mistakes, either getting off rhythm or trying to rush too soon. Getting a feel for the rhythm of the music is crucial to successfully navigating a level and completing the boss fights.
The visuals are minimalist, but colorful, with the backgrounds pulsing in time to the music as the stage elements change. The bright palette is in stark contrast to Limbo, which was directed by the developer of 140, and it fits well with the electronic soundtrack (which I'll likely be purchasing).
The game was fairly short, as I finished the main levels within a little over an hour. There are additional levels which are mirrored versions of the main ones, but they're without checkpoints. I'm not sure I'll ever be able to finish those, but they're an option for those looking for an even greater challenge.
I'd advise using a gamepad if you're more comfortable playing platformers with one, even though the controls are very simple (just directionals and jumping). As you can imagine, it's unfortunately not a game I'd recommend for anyone who has difficulty with hand/eye coordination.
I thoroughly enjoyed this game, especially at the price I bought it at, but even at its (low) full price, I'd still recommend it at its short length, just for the simplistic brilliance of the way it melded gameplay and music. Even though I probably won't be able to finish the challenge levels, I'll probably go back to play through the old ones just to re-experience them.
If it's playable for you and you're a fan of platformers or music games, definitely check it out.

I definitely enjoy playing this game; it lets me unleash my inner engineer. I have had a lot of fun building unnecessarily complicated rovers. Despite having only a handful of parts (or maybe because of it), Rover Builder is a deceptively challenging game.
However, there are a few bugs/issues that I have found rather detracting. Fixing these will greatly improve the game.
- Bearings don't always load correctly when the simulation starts. Sometimes they disappear and sometimes steel beams coming off of the bearings are in the wrong orientation. In order to fix this, I have to go back to the builder, delete the bearings, and reinsert them. Sometimes even that doesn't work.
- Steering boxes can also disappear when the simulation starts. When this happens, they can't be replaced in the exact same spot in the builder.
- The simulation is noticably slower when you have larger rovers or multiple rovers at once.
I also have a few suggestions that I think would make this game a bit better.
- Increase the stiffness on steel beams and joints. It would make it easier to build steering and suspension systems.
- Make the stiffness of springs and pistons adjustable.
- Increase the stiffness of the steering box.
Overall, a very fun game. It has some bugs and quirks, but I am optimistic they will be fixed soon.

Oh I am so damn conflicted about this review! I really don't know which way to go with it.
Look, this is a flash game. It has gorgeous visuals and sounds but it is still a flash game. This is okay though. I am absolutely a million times behind small time indie developers getting a more minimalist yet heavily polished experience onto steam so they can make some money and start off, even if the whole experience feels like a flash game. An example of this done right is Antichamber. It has the most blindingly shiny polish ever and it has length to boot. 140 has....well it has the polish at least.
140 is a moderately challenging platform game. Sadly though it only has 3 very short levels and it can be completed within a lunch break. Now you may be thinking that this might be a Nintendo hard game that makes up for its short life span with complicated levels, and really the levels aren't that hard at all, in fact the game doesn't really start to show its teeth until the third and final boss fight, and that's only because I'm completely thick and it took me a while to get used to the switch of gravity. I expect with practice you could probably speed run this without glitching in 25 or so minutes.
That is not to say that this is bad, by no means at all is it bad. Were it a free flash game it would be up there in most peoples top 10s. My only real complaints is the hit box seems to be a little bit out.
You see this is a platformer with static areas that will kill you and push you back to the last check point. There are no enemies to speak of which makes the experience feel a little lonely, rather the environment reacts with the music in the background which means that you have to get into rhythm with the sound track in order to progress which makes a very nice experience. The graphics are very simple and programmer arty which is fine with me. I see this as a very clever way of doing your first steps if you know a little about code but don't have the resources to hire a team. However everything is incredibly blocky but its stylistic, I am kind of on the fence for graphics. The hit detection seems a little unfairly sided to the static too, resting against a wall that suddenly changes will kill you, its only a pixel but you should really give the player the benefit of the doubt in most cases.
When you finish the game you can play a hard mode version of it, sadly though all the stages just go from right to left instead and they removed the check points. Not really worth much but at least its there, might add another hour or 2 to the game if you want to get your moneys worth. I would also like to point out that this game runs fine on low graphics for me but was a bit slow on high with my native res. I personally could not tell the difference and as its just 2d squares coloured I don't really see how you could up or lower the graphics, my rigs a little old now but it might be something for you to look out for.
At time of writing the game is £4 on steam and when I give my rating and recommendation I have to take that into account. Now remember I like the fact that these smaller flash type games are getting on steam, they are good fun little games, but they need a little bit more than what this offers and in this case its length. As I say, were this a freebie on newgrounds it would probably be getting an 8 or a 9 but as it stands I can only really give it a 4.
Don't take that as it being crap though! This score is just relative to its price. Make sure that you do play it if its in a bundle and you own it. But unless you really really really love the music/minimalistic genre you might want to wait until its a steam sale for at least half price or you might feel disappointed.
Remember 4/10 just means its below average, it doesn't mean you can't have fun with it. You may feel differently and I would love to hear your reasonings. Feel free to comment :)

GTA III is a really fun game, but I think there's a common misconception with the GTA series that I'd like to write about. This misconception is: In GTA you can do whatever you want. Any fan of the GTA series will tell you that there really isn't that much to do in GTA, because it's meant to be an arcade styled open world driving game. And this is pretty obvious in GTA III, the main character doesn't speak, which honestly... I've come to really prefer over some of the other characters in this series. Title: The Kindred
Genre: Indie, Simulation, Strategy, Early Access
Developer: Persistent Studios
Publisher: Nkidu Games Inc.
Release Date: 24 Feb, 2016
Review copy was supplied by the publisher.
Please note that The Kindred is in early access at the time of writing this review. The game is subject to major change, so please check out their update page on the Steam community.
--------------------------------------------------------------
Steam is a popular breeding ground for a variety of games that are currently in development known as Early Access. Some of these are extremely popular and are great fun to play. Most, however, are terrible – there are games that should not be being sold on a storefront, and there are games that just never get finished with development as the developer runs with the cash. Where does The Kindred stand? I’m pleased to say that I have been have been getting immense enjoyment out of playing this, and I hope that the game can only improve as it gets further into development. Persistent Studios have been working on The Kindred for 3 years before bringing it to Early Access, I feel like this game is a good example of what Early Access should really be about.
You must have either played or heard of Minecraft at some point? When you look at The Kindred you will be quick to see the similarities between the two games. I like to think of The Kindred as a cross between Minecraft and Banished. Your job in the game is to manage a group of voxel people called the Kin, they live in a voxel world surrounded by pretty flowers and large lakes. However, the Kin cannot function without you managing them and giving them tasks to do. You, as their God, must make sure that they have a place to live with enough food to suffice (none of this is actual ‘lore’ in the game, you are not their God – I just like to play the game thinking that I am)
Currently you start off with 6 Kin that you need to care for. As the game is in Early Access, there is no reproduction – so do not bother trying to set them up with each other, it won’t work – I’ve tried. Your first step would be to make sure that they have a place to sleep and food to eat. This means that you need to go and chop down some trees or mine some stone, and set up some farms. The map will randomly generate as you initially start the game (You can also enter in a ‘Seed’ code, so feel free to share yours around the internet, or take someone else’s if you think their starting map looks good). Dotted around the map you will find ores and plants/vegetables. There should be one of each vegetable that you can harvest, from there you can cultivate them and grow more and more, thus getting food for your Kin.
Using a small selection of tools and objects, you can build your dream world. Although, with the current amount of objects your dream world will be very limited. You can create a crafting bench, a dairy machine and even a kiln. Being an Early Access game, there is an extremely limited amount you can do on The Kindred. I have played the game for 17 hours at the time of writing this review, and I can safely say that I have built every item that the game has to offer. For me, 17 hours is a large amount of time to spend on a game and have a blast constantly. It is very rare that a video game will keep me entertained for 100% of the time, but that is mainly due to how relaxing The Kindred is to play. You know what makes this even better? Knowing that there is always more content on the horizon.
The 17 hours that I spent have been on multiple maps, as I have had to restart my map a few times to try to get the patches working (Again, it is Early Access), have just been building up a farm and getting all the items I will need. I have yet to start working on some amazing architectural wonders, but that is mainly down to how awkward and time-consuming building structures is. Building a square building that is 6 X 6 with a roof, door, window and a nice window plant for each of my Kin took a very long time. I had to cut down a bunch of trees, and then I wanted to use the crafting bench to turn these into planks so that they looked a bit prettier than just using the standard logs. My Kin are a lazy bunch of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s and just seem to take forever to complete the build queue, this makes building a large building out of the same material a task that I just cannot be bothered to currently do. What doesn’t help is that when I want to do some farming with one of the Kin that is just standing around doing nothing, all the others that were building will come and ‘help’ with the farming (Work allocation is something that is being added into an unstable beta version of the game).
I’ve played many Early Access games, and they are going to have lots of bugs, that even goes for AAA games. The Kindred is quite low on major bugs that I have seen reported in the forums, and I have encountered only a few. The staff at Persistent Studios are easy to approach in the forums of by email with any big requests and are extremely friendly and helpful, they have fixed a number of bugs that I and other people have found and reported. There is still some things that definitely need to be fixed, such as Kin just idling around and doing nothing when there is a large queue of things to actually get on with – this bug has been worked on and has been made better, although a better fix is on the way. I’ve also had some problems with Kin just falling down large holes and then dying of Starvation (which I didn’t notice about until it was too late, much too late. You will be remembered, whatever your name was). The FPS seems to dip down quite frequently to the 45 range when rotating the camera or panning around the screen – but this does not have as much of a bad impact as it is a slow-paced strategy game.
The Kindred is one of a small amount of Early Access games that I would recommend to anyone that enjoys relaxing to small town management game. With the craze of everyone making terrible voxel games, it is always wonderful to find a game that is a joy to play and an honour to the genre.  If you are the type of person that needs lots of content in a game, probably best to hold off until the game is out of Early Access. I strongly believe that the game has enough content to justify the current price tag, and although I have done everything that the game currently has to offer, there is still plenty of hours I can sink into the game by making my town look the best. By looking at the development roadmap, you can see that Persistent Studios has a vision of how they want the game to be later on down the line, and I cannot wait to see all these features come into the game. The Kindred is the perfect game sit down and help you relax. Put on some music, your favourite podcast, or even a movie and cut down some trees and build a fort.

This is not a "no" because the game is bad, it's a "no" because it just isn't quite there yet.
I can't recommend this game in its current state to the average person.  It's always tricky evaluating these early access titles because there's always a promised feature set, but I strive to give an impression of the game as it is and not what it promises to be.  As I'm sure many of you reading this know, this type of game (the god game/city building game) has had a very harrowed early access experience with the terrible situations we have in Towns, Stonehearth, Castle Story and more.  It's an awesome genre plagued by failure, and because of that (not the devs' fault here) I am very cynical about this genre.
There currently isn't a whole hell of a lot to do because it's still very early in early access and the included features are very limited.  HOWEVER, I will say that the features that are in are working pretty damn well and the developers are VERY hard at work to improve the game day after day after day.  The in-game change log is damned impressive and shows some passion for the work their doing.  I believe that one day this game will be amazing, but right now it's just a pretty game with cool concepts and a lot of potential.
If you want to support this game and dive in, by all means do so!  Like I mentioned, the developers are clearly passionate about what they're doing and are very communicative, which is an enormous selling point that inspires confidence.  However, if you're more wary about your purchases, I advise you to just add this to your wishlist or watch list or follow list or however you follow early access/indev titles.
Now about the actual game, since I've rambled about early access enough:
The game features a beautiful voxel aesthetic and includes some neat ideas like shepherding wild animals into fences to create a ranch, cook complex meals with food, and buildings that you have to power with electricity-generating machines.  The electricity part is very bare-bones at the moment and hard to do (because of reasons I'll mention in a bit), but that's a mechanic that, at it's core, is enough to really differentiate itself from many other titles in this genre.  Not many care about electricity *at all*.
Another reason it sets itself apart: THE AI ISN'T HOPELESSLY BROKEN.  They're a little confused at times (it's early access still, after all), but you don't have the AI pull a Stonehearth and just refuse to work ever again.  The one time I saw it, it was identified by the devs and fixed very promptly!  Nothing's more frustrating then lazy AI people.
Main reasons I can't recommend this game at the moment (aside from relatively small feature set) is because the game can become really tedious pretty quickly.  The UI is clunky and the game is currently missing a lot of small quality of life things like farm auto-harvesting (must right click each individual crop and click harvest) or easy crafting of a ton of building materials (gotta click one at a time).  Placement of building materials is a bit spotty, and the interface sometimes doesn't quite respond the way you want it to leading to a bit of confusion.  Plus you're stuck with a measly 6 kin, so if you wanna go crazy and build a lot it will take about 50 years (hyperbole) to build anything big.
If you're like me and this is a genre where you desperately want a game to succeed and deliver, at _least_ watch this game to see how it grows over time.  Follow videos and development.  Or if you're excited, go ahead and buy it and speak with the developers!  As far as I can see they're very communicative and open to feedback. It may seem fun at first, but this just lacks the amount of polish needed to be more than mediocre.
The good:
- The cover system works pretty well and is very intuitive to control
The bad:
- Too shallow to be a 'tactical' action game. Enemies just randomly spawn in front of you, so you have no time to plan an approach. Only two weapons and basically nothing else to do. No grenades, no powers, no flanking, no combos, no strategy, no nothing. Most shots don't really hit multiple enemies, exploding enemies don't damage each other, etc... so positioning is of very little importance. Just avoid their damage zones and shoot. Cover is not 'tactical' enough, it's mostly a gimmick. Ironically enough, you will find more 'tactical' gameplay in the hardcore action twinstick competitors this tries to differentiate itself from.
- Too slow paced to be an action twin stick shooter. 2-3 enemies on screen at a time is just boring for an action game.
- EXTREMELY repetitive levels. Basically all the maps are linear and predesigned with the same 10 or so areas (that are made with some generic assets to begin with). No PCG maps and no variety in level design.
- Bad design in general, like inconsistent pacing (most of the game is boring while bosses are extremely hard), game breaking (life regen) or useless upgrades, you simply run out of ammo during boss battles because see point below. Enemies can stunlock you at full health and you die without any chance of retaliation
- Bosses are just regular enemies with more HP.
The ugly:
- The unlock system is designed as a F2P game for mobile and is a chore as expected. While there are no paid microtransactions here, the difficulty ramps up horribly, forcing you to grind earlier levels so you can get good enough gear for later levels. But hey, levels are all the same anyway, so you probably can't even tell the difference between level 5 and level 10. Oh, and after you unlock stuff in single player/online, have fun doing basically the same thing AGAIN for local coop. Having fun yet?
So maybe after a 10 hour grind you could have enough variety in this game for it to actually be entertaining for once, but by then you'd have uninstalled it.

Combat feels a bit heavier than it does in other Street Fighter games but I personally prefer it, as it gives the moves a bit more punch. Inputs are a bit easy, and combos aren't that difficult as a result, but it does make preforming combos very enjoyable. This does obviously sacrifice a bit of depth as a result, which is unfortunate. Each character feels distinct and fun, allowing for a fair bit a variety. However, this variety is very dependent on how much you spend on the DLC characters, which I am very willing to admit is far too much. The game cannot justify the cost for the DLC characters when the base roster is so small. It's such a shame too, because the DLC characters are some of the most unique and fun characters in the game. The price is bearable during a sale, but it is still unreasonable. Learning the ropes of the game will soak up a nice chunk of time, but the lack of content does eventually become visible (which is something that the Arcade version should fix). I would say to wait for the arcade version of the game however, as it will eclipse the base game in content.

The art is amazing and the protagonist has a pretty cool design. However its biggest flaw is sadly the meta elements the creators wanted to draw the players in. Cons:

If you can get this game under $10 grab this game, however its replayability is low sadly.

ICEY is an action beat-em-up platformer sort of deal, with the added element of narrator shenanigans, a la The Stanley Parable, but the game lacks a certain level of polish that, at least to me, made the game pretty unrecommendable. The art and artstyle is pretty great actually, but isn't animated very well, so the enemies, as well as ICEY herself, all look very fake. The fighting is pretty samey, and aside from boss fights, don't seem to add very much to the experience at all. I think I counted four or five total enemies aside from bosses. Even the boss fights aren't particularly memorable. The game doesn't do a good job explaining your moves, combos, or really anything, and I only know that combos even exist because I looked at an upgrade list that the game never once directly tells you to check. Thinking back, the game really doesn't even explain the combat hardly at all aside from a few quick text lines when you first start. The narrator's voice isn't all that amazing. It almost sounds like it might just be some guy, or perhaps even just the game developer. He didn't make me laugh once. The game glitched out at least two times: once for a repeated voice line, and once (in the part where you jump around in a different game, once again bringing The Stanley Parable to mind) where the camera shifted perminantly too high to see anything. This was made particularly irriatating when the narrator continuously insulted me for missing jumps that I couldn't see.
All in all, can't say I recommend it, although I might just need to try it some more. While the story might be interesting, I can't really bring myself to finish it because the narrator isn't funny, the combat isn't fun or interesting, and the game as a whole seems like it needed a few more testers before it was released. Try The Stanley Parable instead.

A very good game.
The star of the game is obviously Hong-Kong itself. I have no idea if it bears any ressemblance to the real city, but Hong-Kong in Sleeping Dogs is a town bustling with life, with shops everywhere and citizens going about their business. It feels like an actual place where people live, rather than a succession of hotspots for a player to experience like you find in other sandbox games. For someone not native to an Asian culture, it's also a very attractive jump into a different culture.
As for the gameplay, it's solid. The car handling is great, and it's a real pleasure to drive around the city, just for fun. The melee fight, though somewhat limited, is still satisfying, especially after you get a few upgrades that allow you to fight like you want. As for the gunfight, it's extremely fun, especially the action scenes when you're gunning down enemies while in a car. It feels like an HK-action film.
However, the game is not perfect. The story is servicable, but not much more. It's somewhat disjointed here and there, and not believable at all. There are also a few things that lack polish, like the Car Valet system which fail you regularly for unknown reasons, or the taxi system, which use the same button as the car thief, making for some awkward mistakes. Theses are small things, but they do add up, and that's something you wouldn't find in Saint Rows III or GTA IV (even though i dislike that game). Finally, the game is too easy, with no way to customize the difficulty, which is somewhat sad for people looking for a challenge.
On the whole, the game provides a very nice experience, especially if you enjoy the Asian setting. But in the heavy weight category of open-city sandboxes, its few misteps make it falls down a notch compared to games like Arkham City (which has a much better melee combat), or Saint Rows III (which has more variety and polish). Still if you like the open-world genre, you will not regret buying Sleeping Dogs.

I thought nothing of this game when I got it in a bundle. That's probably a great way to enter it, because it turns out it's actually a well crafted little platformer.
Like many other great platformers that strike a balance between challenging, inventive, and not too long (VVVVVV, Thomas Was Alone, Limbo all accomplish this in different ways), 140 is a very nice little game.
There is a sort of rhythm component, in that the music will assist you in timing a jump or move just right with the soundtrack. But aside from that, it's just simple, clean, and nicely honed gameplay that makes this game definitely enjoyable. The jumps feel weighty and good. The responsiveness of a stop is very comfortable.
The charmingly inventive character is a great touch. A square when you're still, a circle when you're moving, and a triangle when you jump, with nicely flowing animation between shapes. The simplicity really works in favor of 140, rather than against it.
The only part of the game configuration I'm not a huge fan of, is where save-points exist. Only after you complete each grouping does the game save. I'd love to take a break and come back to the final stage for example, but I have to play the several levels beforehand each time I want to get to that level for example. Not a dealbreaker in a game of this size and scope, but annoying if you can't devote enough time to completion of a group of levels in one sitting.
The game isn't much more than a few hours (you can play it through the first three stages, then in reverse direction back through those same stages). But those are well made hours, and only the final stage is really punshing (for me it's equivalent to a mental tongue twister, which I find too frustrating to see through). I didn't finish it entirely, got to the final level, and maybe I'll try again one day, but I don't know... The remaining 90% of the game though is worth the time.

The original Carrier Command, while primitive by modern standards, was a really good game for it's time. A good combination of strategy and action. BIS has rebooted this game and fixed many shortcomings of the original's design...well, almost.
First thing I will say is that the graphics are very nice. There is a "film grain" effect you cannot turn off, but that aside, I have no complaints whatsoever. The models of the carrier look awesome and the animations are pretty solid. Good job BIS!
The interface has also had a huge overhaul since the original. Commanding units is very easy to do (once you get the hang of it). I get a feeling this was designed with consoles in mind, however it works fine on PC, so again no complaints from me.
I'd also like to praise the unit customisation added to gameplay. You can now outfit your Mantas and Walruses with different armour and weaponry to engage threats more effectively...but sadly, this is where the praise ends.
The story mode is just a glorified tutorial with bad voice acting. Some parts of it are good for learning the game - the sole reason I played all the way through it was to prepare me for the REAL game; Strategy Mode.
The lack of multiplayer is also quite disappointing. Why this was not implemented is not clear - some forum posts suggest it was axed due to development costs, other say it was to be added in a later patch. I personally suspect the former was more likely the case. Either way, it's a pity as multiplayer could have probably boosted the sales of the game.
The Walrus pathfinding is so bad it's not even funny. Mantas are OK, but Walruses have trouble driving in a straight line. I've tried every patch released since day one and some third party mods, but nothing works. I'm not exaggerating here, feel free to look it up on YouTube.
The pathfinding is the deal-breaker for me. The lack of multiplayer and the lame story mode I can forgive, but not this. The amount of sheer frustration I've had just trying to get units to get from point A to point B is too much. It's highly unlikely that BIS will ever fix this - they've released seven patches already and still can't get it right.
Don't bother.

Each carrier can hold 4 amphibious assault vehicles and 4 aircraft,  As the game progresses, you'll unlock more tech.
The idea is to either destroy the enemy Carrier, capture all islands, or both, depending on your setup. What makes the game sweet is that, while a strategy game, you can also control any of your units, including the carrier itself, while still being able to issue orders to other units. It's a hybrid, really, and fairly well done.
All in all, take it for what it's worth, there's a demo, try it out.

Personal Background with Tanki Online:
------------------------------------------------------------
I have two accounts, both of which have multiple pieces of best stock-equipment and one piece on each account that is fully micro-upgraded to their highest potential stats. I have been playing for over 4.5 years now.
Pros:
------------------------------------------------------------
-Fast paced PvP action
-Intermational, play with people from across the globe
-Wide range of maps, from 1v1 to 20v20 and everything in between.
-Deathmatch, Team Deathmatch, Capture the Flag, and Control Points gamemodes
-Various short, medium, and long range turret options and light, medium, and heavy hull options
-Decorative paints are seperate from protective modules, so you can look awesome while adapting to your situation since you can change your equipment in the middle of the battle.
-Supports mouse controls for those who prefer to use a mouse to look
-Auto-aim along the vertical axis
-A chance every time the battle fund increases for a Gold Box to drop, containin a larg sum of in-game currency.
-Regular special events for holidays with special themes, extra rewards, contests, and sometimes a special gamemode, Assault.
-There is a clan system, and as a clan member you can set up battle that only you, your clanmates, and another clan can battle in (reducing the presence of mults ruining your battle)
-Each week the developers release a V-LOG on YouTube, talking about the developments from the last week and plans for the near future.
-A thorough database of everything you need to know about Tanki Online can be found on the official site at
Cons:
------------------------------------------------------------------------
-Old graphics (the game was first made in Adobe Flash)
-People that sink a lot of money into the game can ruin battles, especially in the early ranks. However, once you unlock PRO battles and get get the pass for them (small sum of in-game currency) you can participate in battles without supplies
-Critical errors can occur at seemiingly random times (entering the game quickly after restarting can sometimes save your place in the battle so you don't lose your hard earned fund!)
Major Future Developments that have been announced (as of Mar 3, 2017):
------------------------------------------------------------
-Supplies will most likely be altered from their current cooldown time and stat alterations while active
-An artillery turret is almost finished
Related
------------------------------------------------------------
If you enjoy Tanki Online but can't get past the Flash graphics, try out Tanki X instead. Made in Unity, it has much more modern graphics. The main issue with Tanki X is, as of this post being written it is still in Open Beta, and the physics interactions can be...difficult at times. As of Mar 3, 2017 Tanki X is still only a downloadable client and not listed on Steam, so you have to go to
to download it.
Final Thoughts:
-----------------------------------------------------------
Overall, I thoroughly enjoy Tanki Online. It is probably the one game I have sunk the most time into. It can get deprtessing at times when your team is mode out of complete noobs, but then you have that game where your opponent can't even turn their turret and you know you are going to have a good time. Take the time to practice with your weapon of choice, because aim is everything and the effort will pay off. Don't get discouraged, and good luck hunting the elusive Gold Box!

Northgard is one of the tightest experiences I've ever played.
Everything works the same way - but differently.
Everyone is just your villagers, given different tasks - even your military units. So provided you have the cash, you can refit your warband to the task at hand.
The economy is all about flows, generated by said villagers. If you have a positive food flow, your stockpile will go up, and if it's negative, it'll go down. Same for gold, and wood. Villagers can learn to gather pretty much anything, and as soon as they're tasked, they start generating resources. Once again, all these systems work the same way, but with different tweaks.
Combat is small, and not overly focused on a clickfest to retask units and so on. I think the low population caps help with this. There are few enough unit types that you feel you can master them all, but enough to still provide a bit of variety. Like, if you're going up against towers, you know you need shieldbearers, that kind of thing.
There's enough going on that you always feel like you're about to lose track, but not so much that it's inevitable. It's real seat-of-your-pants stuff, and for me at least, it pulls me into a flow state right from the start. The game, and its systems, just fit in to the human working memory, and the set-and-forget nature of a lot of the subsystems (the fact that villagers won't just stand around idle, for example) make it easy to grow your camp without having it grow beyond your ability to manage it.
I'd like some slightly more complex rally point mechanics, and some slightly smarter behaviour from villagers (why not have them start working in a building as soon as they finish it?) but overall this game is just beautifully crafted and seriously hits my sweet spot for RTS.

If you're looking for a review you're at the wrong place, but heres a receipe for spaghetti!
Step 1: Get Your Supplies
Before you can start making your spaghetti you will need to first get the proper supplies and materials. To make this spaghetti you will need:
a box of spaghetti
a jar of marinara sauce
1-2 pounds of ground beef or Italian sausage
two large pots, one for boiling the pasta and the other for making the sauce
serving untensils
salt
water
You can use as much meat as you want, really - but anywhere from 1-2 pounds per large jar of sauce should work out best. I tend to use 1 pound of meat nearly every time.
Step 2: Cooking the Meat + Get the Water Boiling
Before you start, fill up a large pot with water and add a handful of salt. Put it on the stove and turn it to high so it'll start boiling!
Next you will need to cook the of meat. Take all of the meat out of its container and set it all in a large pan, then put the pan on the stove and set the stove to medium.
After that you will need to break the meat into smaller pieces. When the meat is in small pieces you will then need to start flipping the meat and make sure it gets brown all-around and cooked thoroughly. The cooking should take approximately 10-15 minutes. When all of the meat is brown and cooked you can add in the sauce.
Step 3: Mixing in the Sauce
Next you will need to mix your marinara sauce with your cooked meat. Take your jar of marinara sauce and pour all of it on the cooked meat and then stir it all around until it is all blended together. Then turn the heat down to low and let it simmer while you cook the pasta.
Step 4: Cooking the Spaghetti
Once the water has come up to a boil, you can throw the spaghetti in. Typically it should cook within 7-11 minutes - just follow the time on the box!
Make sure to stir every couple minutes to keep it from sticking.
Depending on your timing, you can either strain the spaghetti and set it aside, or you can put it right into the sauce.
Step 5: Serving Your Spaghetti
You can do this in a lot of ways but I prefer mixing the noodles in the pan with the sauce. I use tongs to drain the noodles and place them in the sauce, and then put in a couple spoons of pasta water. Stir it all together really well - the pasta water coats all the noodles and lets the sauce stick more.
You can also put plain spaghetti on individual plates and spoon the sauce over top. Whatever works for you.
Top with cheese and enjoy!

Meltdown is a really solid indie RPG twin stick shooter in a futuristic setting devoid of any story.
Some of the main features are VR support (the reason behind my purchase), 4 player co-op, and semi-randomly generated levels.
There are 3 resource types: XP which unlocks skills in a 3-branch tree,  money and upgrade chips (weapon/equipment purchases/upgrades).
You can only carry 2 firearms and 1 melee weapon.
The gameplay is solid, and the controls are tight using an x360 controller.
I quite enjoyed the energetic music as well - fits the game well.
There is generally really nothing wrong with this game, but there is absolutely nothing new under the sun either. And there is too little visual variation in the maps. Some more enemy types, attack/movement options might prevent the 30 "campaign" levels from feeling as repetetive as they did.
The VR support for Oculus rift (DK2) is really solid, with large easily readable menu texts, and while it doesn't really immerse you (or attempts to), it definately heightens the sense of involvement and intensity. Only complaint is the zoom effect when someone levels up - it's too much in VR.
If you're just looking for a non-VR twinstick shooter, try the Halo Spartan Assault/Strike games instead which are similarly priced. But if RPG or VR ticks your boxes, then this is a no-brainer at the price.

Tanki online(browser version available), a simple third person arcade type shooter featuring various tank constructions (turret and hull). Advertised as free to play.
The game itself plays as simply as it presents itself in the tutorial with wasd and spacebar(controls may differ to person to person). Move, shoot and survive(respawns available). Reaction speed plays a crucial role in the combat wise, the slightest miss-time could be detrimental. Ranks are many and require much experience while turrets/hulls unlock unleashing new elements of gameplay with new mechanics. Attatched to these parts are modifications(M0-M4) where mini upgrades can be brought.These of course bring about upgrades. Crystals(in-game currency) which are earned are what drives the players tank progression,allowing the player to buy numerous in game content. Which if one buys into the game allows the player to pay to progress.Some may question even pay to play.
It is now a convenient time to discuss the concept of free to play in the game which is true. But pay to win seems evident. Within the game crystals can be purchased for real money leading to skipping the grinding process as already suggested. Granting early access to turrets and hulls which may be a modification above the average ranks. Also what is known as supplies(consummables) or "drugs" provide advantages temporarily for a tank which may lead to some unfair battles.Yet finding a game which players decide not to use supplies may yield some balanced gameplay.Some extra slight pitfalls to add apply to sometimes lack of communication within teams and potentially intentional griefing by players.
If looking for something quick, give such a game a shot if fantasy tanks excites.

If you play this game as it was meant to be played - as a mission-based game, with the possibility of diversion - it's the best GTA by far, and one of the best games ever made.
The cars are unstable and break apart quickly, and walking is not a viable option for more than a block, meaning that you will have to keep commiting crimes and attracting police attention. This ensures that the pacing will never bog down. The high difficulty of the latter missions is completely necessary to the game, as it brings out the greatest strengths of the open world genre - the player will often HAVE to get creative and find an alternative way to solve a mission, because the "standard" way is either too hard or outright impossible. Couple this with a ton of potential for utter chaos to occur, due to rather chaotic, "loose" mechanics, and you have possibly the greatest use of the free-roaming model ever.

This is a lot like Trouble in Terrorist Town in Garry's Mod. That's the best comparison I can give for this game.
You are randomly assigned a role, from a Lookout, to a Godfather, to a Serial Killer, to a Mayor. 15 People are randomly assigned roles, some with multiple chances of appearing.
Your goal is to eliminate the opposing teams, without killing your teammates. But that's where it gets tricky; You see nobody elses role. Each person in the game is trying to figure out everyone elses, without giving away too much information themselves, at the risk of being lynched by an angry mob.
There is a day phase and a night phase. Day phase is where you talk to the other players, sharing information, discussing theories, and lynching those found guilty by the 'jury'.
The Night Phase is all about the night time talking, the murders, and writing your will to help others deduce the culprits, should you be killed by a lunatic or a member of the Mafia.
Deception is your friend, and your worst enemy at the same time.
The only thing you have to worry about is other players choosing to play against their own team, but that isn't a fault with the game; it's a fault with the player.
It is true that this game is free, as a website. Give it a try there, if you would like. But I recommend you do buy it. If not for supporting the developers, to get the awesome Robot player skin.

Influenced heavily by the Hong Kong crime movie genre, Sleeping Dogs tells the story of Wei Shen, an undercover police officer infiltrating the Sun On Yee, one of Hong Kong’s triads. Because of this unique premise, United Front Games provides us with what is not only an excellent open-world action game but also an emotional journey by the end of which we can no longer by sure on which side of the law should we stand. As matter of fact, on numerous occasions throughout the main story I found myself unwilling to perform my duties as an officer because of the strong sense of allegiance and attachment to some of my fellow triads. While the linear structure of the campaign did not allow me to make any choices, United Front Games deserves credit for effectively channelling Wei Shen’s emotional struggle onto me by populating the criminal world of Hong Kong with such memorable and likeable characters. Overall, while Sleeping Dogs is particularly appealing to those familiar with movies such as
and
, it is a masterclass in storytelling that anyone will enjoy... possibly over more than a single play-through.
As for the gameplay, while the driving controls can feel a bit odd at times, the fighting system is where Sleeping Dogs shines. On one hand, it is simple enough for anyone to master. On the other, because of the variety of enemies’ ‘special powers’, beating all opponents into a pulp takes a bit more than mindlessly pressing both mouse buttons. What makes the numerous scuffles particularly fun is the interactive nature of the surrounding environments, which allow you to finish an enemy off in a variety of ways, including smashing their head into a phone booth or beating them up with a frozen fish. The only downside is that in some close quarters, the camera may not necessarily be your best friend, but this is relatively rare.
When it comes to the visual aspects of the game, United Front Games' Hong Kong looks great. The deep colours make it particularly appealing at night time, but even during daylight the streets of the city have nothing to be ashamed of. Most of the characters we meet in course of the main and side missions have been designed in great detail, which appropriately compliments their unique personalities. On the other hand, all ‘generic’ enemies of the same type wear virtually the same clothes and share the same face.
Turning to the aural experience, while the Cantonese accent of some actors does sound slightly off, it is only those familiar with it that might notice it. Nonetheless, the overall performance of the voice cast is good, with Will Yun Lee stealing the show as Wei Shen by delivering an emotional performance that helps understand our protagonist’s inner struggle. As far as music is concerned, the inclusion of a Cantonese hip hop station playing songs from the group 24 Herbs adds to the authenticity of the overall experience.
In summary, while Sleeping Dogs is an outstanding game on all accounts, it is worth recommending particularly because of its unique and intense plot.

If your looking for something mildly mindless but enjoyable and like games 'where the numbers go up' this is sure to deliver.

Sleeping Dogs is an open world-action game developed by United Front Games and Square Enix London. It is a single player game that focuses on Wei Shen, an undercover American-Hong Kong police officer placed on an assignment to infiltrate the Sun On Yee Triad. The game was originally announced to be part of the True Crime series, but was cancelled by Activision and the rights of the game were bought by Square Enix.
Opinion:
I was very much pumped and looking forward to playing this game, as the True Crime games were part of my childhood. I very much enjoyed playing True Crime: Streets of LA when I was younger and was looking forward to this game of similar quality. I must say, Sleeping Dogs is nothing like True Crime, although it incorporates SOME elements from True Crime, there's a sense of a more openly free and better gameplay than True Crime. You start off with missions guiding you through the game mechanics and the abilties of the player. Thus, finishing this, Wei is allowed to freely openly explore the world by taking side missions or completing the main ones. The gameplay is nicely excuted in this game. It has a certain feel playing as an law enforcer and playing also as a triad member at the same time. Elements like XP, parkouring ability, hacking abilities, fighting mechanics, side missions, melee unlocks still make the game interesting when you finish the game. The graphics aren't too great and I had my fair shares of bugs and glitches that occured when I was in gameplay, but neverless, they're are easily solvable (the ones I've encountered).
Pros:
+Detailed gameplay
+Side missions, face/xp, melee and various locks adds more gameplay in when you've finished the game
+Alot of gameplay, should be around 15-18hours of gameplay if you're dedicated
+Voice acting is great
+Soundtrack nicely accompanies the gameplay
+Easy gameplay, not hard
+Great DLC's from what I saw (haven't played it myself, but will get to it)
Cons:
-Bugs/glitches (there's one missions very close to end of the game called "The Election", and you have trouble with mashing the buttons to parkour, just lower graphic settings or change the parkour key to something else. Not the only glitch/bug)
-Boss fights are too easy (falls into the pros catergory)
-Not a wide range of weapons :L
Overall, I recommend this game, there's alot more to it when you finish, and of course with the DLC's, there's more gameplay. You should take advantage of the sale right now and purchase this game, 'cause it's amazingly fun and worth it's value.

Promised to be released all the way back in 2013, Starbound was a prime example of "how you DON'T do early access" for a long time. Did it change with the release?
Now, don't get me wrong. It isn't a bad game - would you expect someone to play bad game for >400 hours? But it's... shallow. It doesn't have a decent amount of content that it had, but that was cut just for the sake of cutting.
Example: tech system. Bubble field that negates fall damage and lets you bounce off the surfaces; badass rocket boots; on-demand teleportation to another point of the screen; health and energy regenerators; friggin power mech suits! Sounds sweet, right? Well, if you liked this assortment of power-ups then sucks to be you: all of that was in the game, it IS in the game's files even now - but it was cut right before the 1.0. Current available tech system consists of "lower-your-size" skill with some variations, "jump-higher" skill with some variations, and "run faster" skill with some variations. That's all. Before i could fly from the ground all the way to the board of Avian Airship with rocket boots alone, but now? None of these new techs will give you anything similar.
That applies not only to techs - there are various codex entries, weapons and entire biomes traces of which still exist in the files, but you'll never find them - unless they're reimplemented with the later update, but then you'll wonder - what's the point of "1.0 version" anyway?
(By the way, if anyone can confirm that Uzis, Tesla Spears and Lightning Coils still can be found legitimately, i would greatly appreciate that - those were my weapons of choice for the most part of my Starbound playtime)
Next point is, they promise you "7 playable races", That's a lie. Game has 6 playable races and 1 playable character. If you play as any of the 6 vanilla species, you'll meet a lot of towns, camps and just stray folks of your kind while exploring stars, as well as some written pieces of history. That is not the case if you are to choose Novakid. I just want to point out that saying "they are nomad race so they don't have any settlements and/or recorded history" ISN'T the same as making them
and it ISN'T a valid reasoning to the fact that player's character is literally one and only Novakid in the entire universe.
And at the same time, developers really don't like to give players a choice in small things. Not always, yes, but when it happens, it is on the edge of stupidity. Community didn't like the hotbar change to less intuitive version? Well, we will implement new one anyway, although it could be easily selectable in settings. People liked need to warm them up through fire and clothes to survive on cold planets? Aw shucks, let's have this "craft once and forget" system. Don't like the onboard pet that just sits here, doing absolutely nothing? Too bad, beause you HAVE to hold this useless pile of pixels on your ship instead of acquiring one if you want to. And god forbid you to build a colony without taking into account the fact that NPCs can't close the doors after walking through them - one stray monster, and entire settlement could be wiped out. It could be easily changed with a few adjustments to the script. But it isn't. Why? Beause reasons.
Honestly, after looking at main features of release version (storyline, fossils, backers' items) i can't help but think that the main vector of work for 1.0 was "Finally put in all stretch goals and be done with it already". I may be wrong, I WANT to be wrong, but simply can't shake the feeling.
Also, some of those cut codex entries implied that
. This and Novakids' "implementation" busts immersion in the game's world for me REALLY hard.
But if you have some friends to fool around with, or want to roleplay as your character with complete disregard to intended atmosphere of the game, then grab Starbound. Despite all negative parts, it is still a real deal for its price/content ratio. As to me, i'll wait until there's enough mods to restore and fix what was cut and broken.

Sanctum 2 is not about tower defense, it's about monotonously shooting waves and waves of enemies with sub-par guns and grinding your way to decent towers so that some day, you might be able to play a game that starts to look like it could be called a tower-defense game. Instead of unlocking towers per map (Like Defense Grid 2 did), you only unlock towers and weapons by leveling. This means, in theory, that you could grind level 1 over and over and have all the towers. It also means that if you don't like grinding and just want to play through the game, you'll be stuck with some very basic towers, upgrades and weapons that may not suit your play style.
The updated graphics and larger array of weapons, playable classes, passive abilities and towers does not make the game feel any less inherently broken.
"Boss" creatures can break through your walls and towers and seeing as they can do so rather randomly, they might end up targetting vital blocks forcing you to pretty much restart your game because all of a sudden your initial investments become a complete waste of money. Some maps are well-designed and fun to play but a lot of maps are either an exercise in boredom or an exercise in futility as you struggle to find the tower set-up that the developers had in mind when they created the map.
Your main weapon can never be exchanged, only your sidearm can. Unfortunately, there's no way to upgrade your main weapon and although powerful, it will never evolve to deal with situations on the battlefield. Instead, memorisation of enemies is key.
If you enjoy running around and holding down the left mouse button constantly listening to lasers go "pew pew" constantly and putting very little though into creating and optimizing your tower maze then Sanctum 2 is for you.
Everyone else should just avoid it unless it's for sale with a 80% discount or higher, go play Defense Grid 2 instead.

Carrier Command: Gaea Mission is ultimately a good (not great) game that blends strategy, tactics and action, but it suffers from the most god-awful annoying campaign I think I have ever played.
You'll hear a lot about the bad bad BAD script and voice acting, but the campaign is terribly paced too, being, as it seems it was intended, a very, very long tutorial for the Strategy Game option. Having said that, I persevered with the Campaign, and after you take Fulcrum and push into the enemy's territory, which is around the same time you unlock missiles for your Mantas—and around the time the AI starts pushing back!—the game finally lives up to its promise and gets awesome.
Taking the islands become a real tactical challenge each time, and your strategy of which islands should be Production, Mining and (oh so important) Defense becomes critical to success. When you get to that point, the Campaign is actually pretty good and the game finally lives up to its potential.
Whether or not you can stick it out that long is another story...I have a LOT of love and nostalgia for Carrier Command, having played it ad nauseum on my Amiga when I was a kid, but without that good will, I'm not sure I would have had the gumption to push through the bad bad BAD start of the Campaign game. If you can, though, I think you'll find you are rewarded.
Subjective Assessment: 7/10

Grand Theft Auto 3 is the first game in the series to be in 3D. It's a fantastic jump too. Being the first open world 3D GTA it has it's fantastic but not a perfect game. The City is large for being the first 3D GTA game and not as alive as Vice City (Vice City only came out not even a year after GTA 3). The Radio is decent having Push it to the Limit otherwise there is only a few recognizeable songs. The Story isn't too great. Your character doesn't talk all he does is go to a person and get a job and then execute it. Not much more than that just rinse and repeat. You are told to hold all sorts of fantasy scum from reaching a certain point. The bad guys are coming in waves and groping along predefined paths. You provide them with classic towers in four variants like infantry, archers, mages and artillery. The building sites are also predefined, sometimes they are distributed quite sparse on the level. For destroying enemies the cash register is ringing, the money will naturally be put back into new buildings or upgrades.
That sounds not very exciting at first. And truely it is not, especially for TD-veterans. The gameplay is well known, but by the initially very low difficulty the excitement kept within narrow limits. But before you can turn away bored, Kingdom Rush puts on continuously. The developers have a whole bunch of little details that incorporate fresh ideas and additional game elements. It just exudes tons of charm, impresses with lots of funny ideas and loving details. In the second half it becomes  quite a hard nut to crack, so it will become interesting for TD-veterans, too.

This whole game is incredibly awkward.
It's a hack and slash/beat em up type game where you kill some enemies and continue to the next screen. But it also tries to be a fourth wall breaking experience like the Stanley Parable; it even has a narrator that talks to you and gets upset when you don't follow his directions. The narrator is probably my biggest problem with this game; his voice is incredibly obnoxious and hollow. It sounds like they found some random guy at Subway and payed him $10 to read the script. He verbally pronounces "ugh" and "sigh" sometimes which is pretty painful to listen to. He makes the whole experience of playing this game so much harder to put up with. And everytime you respawn or load up the game he'll say the same lines over and over again. If you buy this just turn your volume off, theres subtitles for him anyways. You don't even get a way to respond so he just talks down to you for half the game and you have to listen to his crap.
The second worst thing about this game is the combat because it is inconsist and just frustrating. You can't guard which is annoying and there are no invincibility states. You're dash isn't very useful and most of the time eneimes can grab or hit you out of it. The game gives you a bunch of combos to buy and upgrade to use, but they all take too long to finish and you'll get hit and knocked out of your attack constantly. There are also these small dot enemies that come in swarms that shoot lasers and warp around just making it even harder to not get hit. There have been countless times where I just get smashed into a corner with 3 enemies just gangbanging me until I die. Enemies and bosses just spam moves and there isn't a real good way to telegraph their attacks. There's a red exclaimation mark that pops over their heads sometimes but it's a split second before they attack. Also when you attack you have this annoyingly giant afterimage from your sword and covers the enemies you're attacking, so you can't even see what they're about to do.
The game also has these bits where it just resets you to the last checkpoint after doing certain actions. These are scenes that happen when you stray from the main path. When you reach the end of it you go back to the last chekpoint but it just feels really disorienting because they happen so abruptly sometimes. Also when this happens all the enemies in the area respawn, including bosses. It makes you feel like you aren't really accomplishing anything other than getting checkpoints to teleport to. You can only teleport to certain ones not all of them. The background can also make it look like you can keep going in one direction until you hit an invisible wall. I don't know how to describe it other than awkward. You're dash also has a meter to "limit" you but from my experience it feels like you can just dash forever. it makes the upgrades to your meter even more meaningless.
If you want a game that is all meta and breaks the fourth wall a bunch go play The Stanley Parable, One Shot, Undertale, Doki Doki Literature Club or Pony Island.
If you want to play a fun hack and slash go buy Odin Sphere Leifhaser, Nier: Automata, or Bayonetta.
I also don't like the music, overall its like a 5.5/10.

Ahhhhh, Starbound. You're finally out. 2 and a half years in Early Access. But I'll try not to dwell on that time period for this and focus on what the 1.0 update has brought so far.
The good:
They've focused on the story a little more since the last EA release. There's more pre-determined guaranteed stuff in your starting world, and a little intro quest that helps out newbies. It was alright.
The bad:
Unskippable cutscenes are my favorite! And they added a hunger system that was originally removed VERY early on in the development of the game because it was downright frustrating (and still is). The default difficulty also will have you drop all of your food, blocks, and other important items. You keep only your weapons and armor and a few other basic things, from what I've seen. It's not fun and there's no easy way to get back to your corpse at all. There's an extra arbitrary layer to crafting anything now because you need a special crafting bench to craft other kinds of crafting benches and everything requires slightly more resources. Making armor seems to have been bumped up a decent amount in resource requirement, and to get those resources, you deal with tedius mining, or enemies that deal far too much damage to start out with. Otherwise, customizing and building things is... kind of fun, but feels pointless on planets because you know you'll be leaving and you could just make room for farming on your ship, so the only thing you'd need is trees (which you can find on any planet). All in all, the 1.0 update is actually among the bad ones the game has gotten, and it was more fun the last time I played it. Even then, it was easy to burn out on.
And just a small reminder, but if the devs say something'll be in a future patch even now after release, don't bother hoping they'll deliver.

A perfect sorbet to cleanse the palate between mind-wrenchers, McPixel is the ultimate in un-puzzle games. Straddling the fine line between Zen and Beavis-and-Butthead-grade toilet humor, McPixel throws you into a high-speed gauntlet of idiotic scenarios, almost all of which involve some manner of high explosive about to go off. Using every resource available (examples of which include dynamite, cows, balloons, vodka, firearms, more dynamite, and an endless supply of kicks to the groin), you must disarm the danger within 20 seconds and save the day. Or, failing that, die in a hilarious and moronic way.
Separating it from the usual Wario Ware clone, there's little logic to any of the game's many stages; more often than not you'll muddle your way through by clicking random things and getting lucky. When an actual sense of challenge DOES arise, it's usually due to the necessary key object being barely visible. What saves McPixel from being a completely unjustified waste of time is the fact that it's one of the funniest casual titles you're going to find anywhere. Admittedly, it's extremely low-brow, but my first time playing it basically amounted to 3 hours of near-brainless clicking broken up by a constant stream of disgusted, wonderful laughter. Somehow, the combination of Gary Larson-style cows and humans rendered in 8-bit graphics with 4th grade toilet humor works amazingly well, and after clearing each level correctly I had no problem going back and trying to find every idiotic failure cutscene in order to achieve a 100% completion. It's not the sort of game you'll want to discuss with coworkers around the (likely to explode) water cooler, but sometimes you just need to shut your brain off and laugh as some jerk kicks Batman in the nards a few dozen times, y'know?

140...as others have stated; is a platformer with obstacles that are in sync with rhythm.
Let me start off by saying that the soundtrack was amazing...at first. I was pleasantly surprised to find that there wasn't much variety to the soundtrack so it quickly fell off and became boring. Though, it did slightly change...you can still feel it being recycled.
The graphical choice was probably more so due to lazyness, lack of imagination, time restraints, or even budget. Either way, this kind of style has been done before. Despite the fact that graphics obviously don't make the game...the devs could at least tried to do something new with it. (I do like the equalizer, though. That was somewhat nifty.)
Gameplay is straight forward. However, it becomes almost tedious. Your timing has to be absolutely perfect otherwise, you're going to have to hear the annoying static sound along with a checkpoint set back. At least there's checkpoints...
Though, I do not mind pinpoint precision. Games like Super Meat Boy and Electronic Super Boy require such. But...they have more of a satisfaction to it once completing levels and a better soundtrack.
I do understand that soundtrack and graphical choice are matter of opinion. Nevertheless, I believe that only goes to an extent.
If you're interested in this game; I suggest waiting for a pricedrop. It is definitely not worth $5 with the amount of OTHER indie games you can get for that price. Or, you know...get Super Meat Boy or Electronic Super Joy. (Or...Super Hexagon if you're fond of seizures.)

Great graphics and original gameplay come to add-up to the already top quality AvP series. The multiplayer also adds many new game modes (survival co-op being a great plus) that could keep you going for hours without notice.
Changes to the combat system and controls make battles more diverse and bring up the game's pace, in such way it feels not only as a mere update of the late AvP 2, but gives the sensation of a whole new game (as every good sequel should).
The only negative point would come not such from the game itself as from the community. Few weeks after launch, hacks were already common in multiplayer, spoiling much of the fun of online playing with strangers, and little changed as far as the last time I played.
Anyway, if you have a group of friends of any size, the diversity of multiplayer modes makes up for the short commings of cheating players, giving you planty options to serve different numbers of players.
If you like the prequels, or enjoy alternative shooters with original gameplay, fret not, it's worth the money.

The Short: Buy this game, it's fun, beautiful, and has a fun story.
The Long: My god, the art! Everything in this game was lovingly crafted, all of the sounds from the weapons and menus are extremely satisfying, the colors of the enviroment, enemies, and main character all blend together beautifully and compliment the soundtrack. Speaking of music, this game has a lot of it. The music is beautiful and ethereal and really just gets the player in the mood to explore and immerse themselves in this crumbling world. The world and story that is presented to us is a world just awakening after a mysterious apocalypse, the world that you knew is gone but its ok, you're not alone, new enemies stand in your path but new friends stand by your side, civilization may have crumbled but the lost will not be forgotten and it's up to you to rebuild. Literally, the world reforms around you as you explore. Yes, the night was dark but the dawn is breaking. (I didn't really want to spoil the whole story, this is something you have to experience for yourself) Now for the gameplay, its enjoyable and compelling, you unlock new weapons as you progress through the game and upgrade them with collectables and currency. You can carry two weapons at a time along with one limited "super". Each weapon has 2 skill "trees" which can be swapped between at any time, and you are also given over a dozen perks which you can mix and match to suit your needs. To unlock each tier of upgrades you need to use a collectible resource, these resources are finite meaning you can only find enough to unlock every tier, many of these have to be won from challenges or discovered in levels. The same rule applies to the perks and "supers" they have to be either won, discovered, or bought and most of them can't be bought. The number of perks you can have active is determined by your character's level (yes there is XP in this game) and where there are levels there is grinding. There are a handful of training grounds of varying difficulty where you can grind currency and levels and train with different loadouts until you become a GOD, lol not really. Everything in this game can kill you like that* (I just snapped my fingers). And if you are just to pro for this game there are a series of unlockable anti-perks which buff your enemies to near god-like levels themselves and give you a cash/experience boost. So yeah there's a ton of awesome stuff to do in this game.
If I were to have any complaints regarding the game, it's that some of the challenges can be total B.S.
