This is going to be more of a comparison than a review. I HIGHLY recommend this game to all FPS Lovers! especially to those that have only played L4D2.
If you can tell the difference between a game that *deserves* (subjective) an 8 out of 10, vs a 9, or 10 out of 10, you might understand where I'm coming from (once again, subjective).
What makes a game good? that could be a number of things. I believe that more features does NOT make a game better. Neither do flashy visuals. What do we remember a game for?
~A bit of my background: I play old school games more often than newer games, and prefer them much more becuase they were, more often than not, a 'complete' package when purchased, and more often than games today, had 'polish'. I'd underline polish if I could (maybe I can and I don't know how hahaha)...
This game is WAAAAAY better than L4D2 in my opinion (if only it had steamworks! p.q).
The difference between Left 4 Dead and Left 4 Dead 2 is that the former is of the Surival/Horror genre, built around a Co-op FPS. L4D2 is of the Survival(/Action? *kinda vague*) genre (lacking the Horror), built around a Co-op FPS. -The difference between the two games is night and day to me (literally and figuratively). L4D2 feels more like an action arcade game than a Survival/Horror game to me.
-The First L4D has a better atmosphere, the lighting throughout the game and the time of day immerses me much more than L4D2 does, often times I'll peek sides of a door, enter the dark room, and check my corners. Depending on how thorough I am, I might literally jump in shock because I backed into the one Common infected in the room and she got 10 free damage on me with one smack! The First L4D has suspense to me, it leaves me wondering what's going to happen, how the Developer is going to do things, this feeling of unknown whilst still being somewhat 'familiar' (learning spawns/map changes with repetitive play) as I can think on my feet and know how best to handle a situation.
L4D2 has a similar familiarity, but it's more of an "imminent wall of death is coming at this part..." familiarity with the tedious events involving turning off an alarm or loud noise. I get that it takes a degree of preperation and I dig that, it obviously takes teamwork... it just feels as though it occurs too often.
L4D2 feels like a chore with just about everything that I do in it. I had to 'patch' the game up (with custom content) to make it a more 'complete' game, but even with Steamworks and the vast amount of devs *thanks to you all for your content making it more like the first L4D!*, some things just can't be changed.
Do I have a bias? I sure do. I'll admit it (don't we all?), but that's because my idea of an 8/10, & a 9/10 or 10/10 is glaringly obvious. An 8/10 isn't a bad game by any means.
9's & 10's have polish. I would say Halo CE had more polish than the other Halo's (Halo 2 had little time for polish, being rushed, but was VASTLY more polished than the sloppy Halo 4, H4 had collisions with invisible walls, and other laziness).
I believe a big bullet point is that the first game in a series makes or breaks the (potential) continuation of the series.
-After that, a company doesn't have to try as hard to 'make a name' for the franchise if they can just ride off of the first game's successful momentum. It's the same case with L4D2. Sure it has the original Campaign and survivors, sure I can download Steamworks mods and copy L4D1's sounds over and make it more like the first, but I would rather play the First. Because I don't have to fix it to my liking. Everything's already there.. **it could just use more content** (time to turn to custom campaigns :).

-L4D1 has better infected/weapon balance than L4D2 (naturally, due to the game having fewer variables for game devs to consider regarding balance). *Fewer Variables=Better Balance* "way she goes bud".
-L4D1 has better sounds (music included that draws me and my friends in), etc.
The Jockey, Spitter and Charger bacterias sound jarring (when paired with contagion sounds) and negatively impacts the Survival/Horror atmosphere I seek in the Original campaigns in L4D2, some sounds/music just don't mix well, it feels forced, like it wasn't thought out.
The most important part would be that the First L4D has polish (9/9.5 out of 10). A lot of little issues that can easily be overlooked by most people that are present in L4D2 (8/8.5 out of 10), are not in the First L4D.
^I'm referring to 'little glitches', etc., a particular example that comes to mind, is when the Common Infected do that 360/720 degree spin while doing the 'looking around' type animation, sometimes they throw up in a circle, it just... screws up the atmosphere/immersion and results in me looking down, shaking my head, and wondering where the hell video games' quality standards have gone. Could this simple thing not be patched?? It shouldn't even need to be, but I bet it woudn't be too hard to fix... considering it wasn't in the First game :p
+Some would say I'm nitpicking, but I don't compromise on my gameplay experiences. I started with SNES games. and LOVE many N64 games because SO many of them had polish. I enjoy 9/10 * games and 10/10 * games, an 8/10 * is unacceptable to me when I could play a game that I'll enjoy more. -So go play somehing else!' you might say, to which I reply, what the hell is wrong with you? you just take what devs give you?? you don't voice your opinion? we speak with our money and our voice, but unfortunately more-so with our money when buying a product. I digress
-The two games are equally challenging, but the First L4D feels like a more meticulous, 'play it slow, play it smart' game (which I enjoy thoroughly :) rather than the constant running in L4D2, and the punishment for exploring areas (being thorough) which partially ruins the Survivor aspect of the genre.
These two games, while very similar, are vastly different in playstyle, execution and presentation.
~I only play L4D on Expert, ONLY Expert because I enjoy a challange, I Love being punished for my mistakes and learning from them, not the watered down "hold my hand" gameplay experience that's quite prevalent in today's games.
~I play this game in Single Player and Co-op on both Xbox 360 and PC, but more-so on Xbox 360 about *every other weekend*. To be fair, I've played a lot more L4D1 in Co-op than I have L4D2, but that's due to my preference for the First game.
~I'm 24 years old

This game has two things that make it better than most 4x games imo.
1) You have a limited number of turns to win. So you have to be strategic, make decisions and sacrifices to get to the end game on time. Most 4x games go on for-freakin-ever. Including the rest of the franchise, as far as I can tell.
2) You get a worthy enemy for the end game. Most 4x games, if you get to the end game, you are so op the last battles are a boring grind (I find this lately with Galactic Civilizations). With Colonization, after you've killed off the other colonizers and declared Independence, you get a fresh new enemy - the mother country. Here your decisions all along will really matter: building up a strong infrastructure, training the right colonists, choosing good founding fathers for perks, etc. You have to fight tooth and nail up until the last enemy.
Side-note: I think this game should be called Revolution (which is the object of the game) - not Colonization
Recommended if you like games with strategy, resource management, trading, decision making, turn-based combat.

Not recommended at this stage-
The game borrows many concepts from Civ. and Rise of Nations, neither set being implemented well.
[Territory]
-You get 1 capitol/population center and losing it is an instant loss.
-The map is divided into sectors of territory with a maximum number of supported buildings per sector. This limitation/capacity is not well display in the UI, and really only visible when you find out you can't build something.
-Discovering territory requires scouts to explore the "unknown", then military force to clear out any defending entities- crossing territory with soldiers is perceived as a hostile act by the AI.
-Failure to capture cleared out territories can result in the AI seizing the land, putting oneself at a serious disadvantage in both diplomacy and power. There is non-faction mob spawning that one may choose to clear out- failing to claim the cleared land is generically a mistake.
[Game play Mechanics]
-The resource collection system borrows its influence from Rise of Nations and other similar games. A collection facility must be placed near a resource; that facility, in-turn, has a limited number of supported harvesters. Over-mining is not an option.
-The healing mechanic operates the same indirect way as healing: a fixed number of healers sets the healing rate of the health facility, then one individual is selected (in an obfuscated and uncontrollable manor) and healed. The selection algorithm is not specifiable and seems to favor high-health individuals over low-health ones-this greatly disadvantages the longevity of military forces.
-The base military structure offers a "Warchief," but fails to communicate the strength of this hero-type unit. Without making a concerted effort to acquire one, principle combat strength is substantially disadvantaged.
-The game introduces a season system where winters offer reduced productivity and military disadvantage much like one might encounter in the TotalWar series with occasional events posing potential hazards such as earthquakes, blizzards, and rats. These events appear to be global in nature, but never are directly positive for the player.
[Interface/Optimization]
-The interface is best avoided, rather than used. A construct for selecting units by type is over-layed in the bottom right. It appears to make no consideration of the player's camera when directed to select a unit of a given type-one will be selected at random from anywhere in the player's collection.
-When a villager is assigned a role, he or she is sent to the respective resource facility then converted to a practitioner of that role. They only may be restored to villagers when sent to the capitol/population center. It is both easier and faster to assign a villager to a role and restore a worker to villager status, then have a worker change types directly. This is an implementation/design problem that ought be rectified.
-Building structures and tasking villagers to construction are two separate actions. One may not directly instruct a villager to construct a building of a chosen type. Instead, the building site must be designated, then a villager must be assigned to construct it.
-Over- building, mining, healing, etc. are not supported. There are very limited means of speeding up processes by means of tasking excessive numbers of workers.
-A market type structure exist to be build, allowing the player to purchase needed resources from competing clans, however there exists no sell feature. Quantities both produced and consumed are integers in the sub-ten range/unit and this makes over-production a huge issue. When a base productivity of 3 resource/time is achieved, but only 2 resource/time consumed an excess of 1 seems small, but in-fact is 50% above consumption or well beyond most malices offered by status effects.

The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth is sort of an odd game.  It holds a unique slot in my gaming where, at the moment, I play at least one playthrough of it each day.  It is kind of like Solitair, Peggle, or Bejeweled in a sense, in that it is a go to game for me when I have a few minutes to spare.
So what is this game?  It is the dungeons of Zelda mixed with rogue-like randomization.  The goal is to kill one of the final bosses by picking up items and growing in power.  What makes this fun is that the items are randomized, but every playthrough is beatable.  You can manipulate the randomness to do some crazy things and just break the power curve.  But you can also get a bad room and loose a run in a second.  The entire game doesn't take long to beat, maybe an hour?  But the fun is not in that this game takes a long time, it is that the complexity unfolds as stuff is unlocked.
So what is there to unlock? There are items, charecters, and whole levels that will be added to the item pool the more you complete the game with each charecter.  And even without that, there are challenge runs and greed mode.  There is the daily challenge (which is a unique gametype with a unique goal sometimes).  The updates add to the game without diminishing the core that is there, and there are modding tools and more updates coming.  This game is the best.
The only negative, for me, is the aesthetic.  The story and art style can be very disturbing and it kind of undermines the fun of the game...that said, I have got to a point in this game where I don't even notice the story or disturbing elements of the art.

I am not a fan of fighting games, I am not very good at them and kinda bored easily after playing a few hours. So why do I love MK you ask? Let me answer..
First It has a cool story. You are not a fighter that show up just to fight on streets or sth (Did you see what I did there? :) ). Also story mode is a good way to know your way around all characters.
Second this game has lot of side activities if you finished the game and don't like playing online. There are some mini games, challange tower with lots of activities and also there is a krypt that you have to earn kombat points to collect stuff like character pics, concept arts, alternate fatalities and costumes (I don't think they are useful in this version because they were all open from begining). So after you finish story mode, you still have lots to collect and while you are doing it, you won't get bored.
Last but not least, game is really easy to adapt (but hard to master I think) so any newcomer can learn the basics easily. Graphics and gameplay are also a plus. Even with the worst graphics you can see the beauty in it.
In conclusion, if you haven't played MK yet, this one is a perfect way to start (cause it is a kinda reboot). If you are a longtime fan, I know you already got it. It is great to be able play a MK game on PC (They didn't release the last few games on PC). So have fun as you have it.

This is a really amussing game. The narrator tells you to do nothing more than "Follow the arrow." However, if you don't you are rewarded with money, secret endings (which crash the game), and a lot of fun. The combat is quite fun and easy once you get the hang of it and get the timing down. The game does not over stay its welcome as it is rather short. Hands down the narrator was my favorite part of the game. The game gives you some choice in that you can find the above said secret ends by NOT FOLLOWING THE ARROWS and refusing to do what the narrator tells you to. Your choices will even let you skip a boss fight close the to end.
Now lets get to the stuff I didn't like. Our protag (ICEY) has no personality or character (at all). She doesn't even speak or groun in pain through the entirety of the gameIs she a robot? A human? A Cyborg? I don't know because it's never revealed. We get almost no background on her and the plot is almost (if not) entirely Kill Judus. The only explamition given is he will destory the world. We don't get to see his side, why he's doing this, or even why we want to kill him. It's simply because the narrator said so. The combat his a MASSIVE flaw that almost made me quit the game in that the enemies can juggle you if you don't touch the ground after being hit (and shield being broken). The game punishes you for using high air attacks (which are almost always better) in that you can go from full HP to 10% in one juggle combo from the start of battle, and NO. You cannot control where you land or which direction you fall. Once you are hit, it's up to the RNG Gods how much damge you take (or if you even live). Needless to say this is beyond frustrating when some of the bosses (including the final one) can only be hit with air attacks (ground attacks almost never hit) and you have to rewatch the intros EVERY TIME YOU DIE. The money for upgrading is so limited if you try to spread it out like I did among your most used skills you'll get them to lv 2 and that's about it.
If it was not for the narrator, all the estereggs and secrets in the game I would have not recommended it, but I've devopled a love hate relasionship with this game. The combat is fun if you can get past the unforgivable juggling, the plot is increadably weak but the eastereggs make up for it. ICEY is kind of souless but the narrator has more than enough for both of them. The game's flaws are very visable but so are it's profections. Over all I enjoyed the game. All the times I died was not enough to make me hate it. I recommend you buy and play. Remember, true gamers always hope they go the wrong way first. Just ignore the arrows and narrator's directions till you think you found everything and you're good.
To my fellow gamers I wish you luck in finding the eastereggs and have a fun time.

A very poorly made version of the old Colonization game.
All the interesting mechanics that made the old game fun are gone and replaced with much simpler or easier versions. The native Americans no longer own their land -- you just take it where in the old game you had to buy it piecemeal for huge sums. After a while, the natives will just surrender and destroy their own cities.
The Natives never attack you first -- you have to deliberately push them a lot to get them to ever react, and their troops are a joke where in the original, the natives were a real threat, that could break you.
The AI is more stupid than a sack of bent nails, and is almost entirely unable to play the game. Seems like the only way it can ever be a threat is on the highest difficulties, where the AI cheats massively and simply relies on having gigantic stacks of doom.
The building system is likewise broken, with all balancing gone (many upgrades simply give you free stuff with no real explanation as to why it is possible to generate free items).
The "colonial congress" system is also strangely implemented, though it is the one bit, that is only half-broken. The bonuses you get are still really weird and unbalanced.
All-in-all a poor excuse for a game, and not worth playing. Get a copy of the original Colonization, if you want a fun and challenging experience.

I can't recommend the vanilla game, because it's very tedious, there's a lot of micromanagement, the UI is impractical (and it's easy to accidentally click something wrong) and, as in any other

These issues are partially solved with
mod.
However, even with the mod, the game becomes very tedious later on, when you have established your trade routes and achieved high resource yield. Later in the game, it feels that all you're doing is just exporting/importing goods and monitoring storage capacities. It's very tedious, even after automating the trade routes. There's not enough options to automate resource gathering, import and export. That's why I never declared independence and never won the revolution, and, thus, never finished the game. I just ran out of patience; and growing my army and building defences and susteinance got boring.
mod adds two more victory types: Industralization (the first one to reach a certain manufacturing capacity) and Domination (the first one to control half of the New World). So, it provides some alternative ways to win the game, but, imo, they are not so interesting. After all, the ultimate battle for independence against the king is what makes
different from other
games.
Nevertheless, the faults mentioned above are not so bad. I got this game cheap on sales and still feel that it was a good deal. There are many good ideas in this game and something to enjoy for all fans of the
games. It just should be noted that patient players will enjoy this game more.

Sanctum 2 is a FPS tower defense game that not only lets you build towers to protect the core, but join in the slaughter on the incoming invasion.
This version of the game is very simple yet complex like its predecessor, Sanctum, however the game was glitchy and there was a dense learning curve. This game removes that learning curve and drags you right to the point. Build towers and aid them before the core is destroyed. I'll rate this game by its playability/replayability/Gameplay, graphics/settings, customization, and audio. At the end of this review ill give it a overall view and is it worth a buy.
Playability/Replayability/Gameplay:
Pros:
-This game makes you think of where to build towers and blockades to see if it is benefiting your play style so theres no doubt you can try different tactics.
- Its way different from any flash oriented tower defense game because you are heavy factor whether you succeed or fail.
- It actually draws you in and engage with the game, which is why it makes it just so fun.
- You can die and respawn in the game which makes it realistic and intense.
- You can increase the difficult in each mission.
- During the mission you are given limited resources to construct your maze allowing for quick thinking.
- There are many missions and DLC's you can play making it extremely delightful to have endless fun.
- Game has a ton or recoil so make your shots count.
- Towers/bases fall from the sky like a Terran supply depot.
- YOU CAN PLAY SINGLE PLAYER OR MULTIPLAYER.
Cons:
- It can be played over and over again, but it may get repetitive because some creeps are just way stronger than others.
- Creeps and towers are usually the same early missions.
- Some creeps can walk though tower fire and you always have to finish them off.
- Reloading takes along time forcing you to switch weapons constantly.
- You have very limited ammo capacity.
Graphics/Settings:
Pros:
- It has a borderlands-like graphics, which makes it great.
- You can adjust your settings in-depth allowing to run smoothly on♥♥♥♥♥♥computers.
- Beautiful environments.
- Towers look amazing even in low quality.
Cons:
- You cant run it high quality with a♥♥♥♥♥♥computer.
Customization:
Pros:
- You can choose from 4 character classes, automatic rifle, sniper, rocket launcher, shotgun.
- Each character has its own unique primary weapon and ability.
- Before a mission starts you can choose your secondary weapon, towers, and perks.
- All secondary weapons, towers, and perks have a secondary effect allowing you to make thought provoking decisions.
- As you play along you level up (leveling system) and unlocks new, secondary weapons, towers, and perks.
- You can level up certain towers after everywave and create blockades for your maze.
- The towers and the character are like ying and yang, you cant just have towers or no towers.
Cons:
- You cant customize the skins of your character unless you buy the skin, it isnt bad but it could have more.
- You can only have a few tower and perk selections and open slots in the early stages.
- Only 4 characters and 4 primary weapons.
- Can't make your own character.
Audio:
Pros:
- Has nice music  soundtrack and ambient background
- Voices are really well done and match the character
- You can choose to turn the voices off
- Creeps, weapons sound unique
Cons:
- Im not sure yet, but you cant use different soundtracks from other games
- Voices do get repetitve and annoying
Overall:

Ahhhhh, Starbound. You're finally out. 2 and a half years in Early Access. But I'll try not to dwell on that time period for this and focus on what the 1.0 update has brought so far.
The good:
They've focused on the story a little more since the last EA release. There's more pre-determined guaranteed stuff in your starting world, and a little intro quest that helps out newbies. It was alright.
The bad:
Unskippable cutscenes are my favorite! And they added a hunger system that was originally removed VERY early on in the development of the game because it was downright frustrating (and still is). The default difficulty also will have you drop all of your food, blocks, and other important items. You keep only your weapons and armor and a few other basic things, from what I've seen. It's not fun and there's no easy way to get back to your corpse at all. There's an extra arbitrary layer to crafting anything now because you need a special crafting bench to craft other kinds of crafting benches and everything requires slightly more resources. Making armor seems to have been bumped up a decent amount in resource requirement, and to get those resources, you deal with tedius mining, or enemies that deal far too much damage to start out with. Otherwise, customizing and building things is... kind of fun, but feels pointless on planets because you know you'll be leaving and you could just make room for farming on your ship, so the only thing you'd need is trees (which you can find on any planet). All in all, the 1.0 update is actually among the bad ones the game has gotten, and it was more fun the last time I played it. Even then, it was easy to burn out on.
And just a small reminder, but if the devs say something'll be in a future patch even now after release, don't bother hoping they'll deliver.

I've played the game on and off for a year or two, but decided to have a serious sit-down once 1.0 dropped.
I'm liking the game because that is what it is, a good game. Lots of items and strange places to find, lots of choices for building, and the game's randomly generated worlds always have something to look at or discover.
Despite these pros that the game has had for a very long time, the 1.0 update also brought a lot of hate from the community including myself.
For one, characters have been wiped again with this update. Pretty obvious why that♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥people off.
Two, the inventory system is now much harder to manage because it has so few spaces and certain items can only go in certain tabs of the inventory. (Ex. Iron in crafting materials tab.) This limits the main theme of the game: Exploration.
Three, progression in crafting stations and gear have improved in terms of convenience, but is limited by the story.
Overall I can't say I hate the game because of a few steps back even though the developers had a looong time to get it figured. Besides, the ame took a few steps forward with crew members and bringing back survival mechanics. In fact, I'll probably play the game for another week or more.
EDIT: The game gives a lot of options for building and there is a colony creation system. Different experiences with playing different races and I think the game is better than I originally got in to. (Mods can fix the inventory stuff.)
8/10 Worth the price if you aren't the type to get annoyed by cluttered storage and inventory.

I feel so sorry for whatever motivated people to write a bad review for this game. After just one playthrough lasting 6 hours, it has easily made itself room into my top three favorite games of all time list. How about we get to the pros and cons eh?
Pros:
Story is gripping, unique, and narrated by the manliest voice on Earth (It sounds like two expensive cigars wrapped in Belgian chocolate replaced his lungs and throat). Almost everywhere you go and nearly anything you do is narrated in some manner.
Gameplay synchronizes with the story flawlessly. The gameplay is mostly hack-and-slash with a few RPG elements, however with a plethora of weapons and skills the combinations are endless.
The visuals of the levels and the few cutscenes are just gorgeous, completely unexpected from a small indie company. Each area feels unique and has its own secrets.
Cons: (Not many cons here, but a few to note)
There is a section of the game where it feels like you are fighting the SAME EXACT SET OF ENEMIES FOR UPWARDS OF 2 HOURS OF THE STORY. This changes shortly afterwards however. (Edit: While running through the New-Game + mode, this problem lessened due to having all the gear up front)
I used practically the same exact set of weapons the whole game through, because even though the player has a ton of options, there seemed to be only ONE and I mean ONE group of weapons/skills that felt fun playing with. I don't consider this a con but rather I felt like sharing this in case someone else had the same issue.
Overall: Play this game. Do it. Just do it. Don't let your dreams be dreams. The few cons listed are absolutely no reason why you shouldn't play this game.

This is a F2P game hidden in a AAA game.  I'm not talking about the Seasons for characters.  At the time of this writing, there are 12 unlocked stages upon purchase (one of which is a very plain "Grid" fighting arena, so let's call it 11) and 11 locked stages.  The 11 locked stages range in price from $4.40CDN to $11CDN. You can unlock them with in-game currency, but the best way to get in-game currency is by doing each character's story, which you only get rewards for doing the first time.
Doing the base characters only (takes about 20 minutes, the story for each is extremely short, easy-mode button-mash content) will net you ~100,000 currency.  This is enough for one or two stages depending on what you select, but keep in mind this currency is also used for unlocking characters, color schemes for costumes, alternate UI schemes, BGM (though the Street Fighter 2 BGM pack is only available through real $, of course). Outside of that, it's a huge grind to get enough in-game currency to unlock anything, as the payouts for your time in other modes are extremely minimal.  The obvious encouragement here is for the consumer to buy all the characters with $, blow through the entirety of the story mode, use whatever Fight Money you get from that to buy as many stages as possible, and buy the remaining ones with real $.
There is an optional Full Story mode that comes as Free DLC, you have to check the box in your Library page in order to activate it.  I don't play these sorts of games for the story, so if you're like me you'll be glad you can skip all the cutscenes (and there are a lot of them).  The Full Story mode takes about 30 minutes to finish when skipping all the cutscenes, and gives you 30,000 currency upon completing the first time.
There is also a Survival Mode, which is this game's Arcade mode (sans bonus stages).  You do get currency rewards for completing this mode, but *only* for completing this mode, and the difficulty has a massive spike during the last encounter.  When you die, you need to start from the beginning.  The reason for this spike also seems clear - if the final battle didn't have a spike compared to the rest of the game mode, you could easily (though tediously and mind-numbingly) farm this mode for the in-game currency.  Capcom clearly didn't want that to be a consistent method of currency acquisition.
It's worth noting that if you buy any characters with the in-game currency and then obtain one of those characters through purchasing a character pack that includes them with real $, you don't get any sort of discount or virtual currency refund for already owning that character.
Of course, because it's Capcom, there are also a *ton* of costumes to buy, but you can only buy these with $, not in-game currency.
It's also worth noting that this plays a lot simpler than SFIV, but the community is larger here, so if you want online... thankfully there is crossplay with PS4, which is nice.  If you get 5 bar games it runs beautifully, however if you set it to that exclusively you will rarely get games.  Even 4 bar games will have frame skip/stutter, but if you want to play online, you should at least set it to browse 4 - 5 bar range.  3 provides abysmal connection quality for a fighting game (while 4 is already pushing it), anything below that is unplayable and shouldn't even be considered as an option.
Graphics are good but are a pretty modest improvement over SFIV.  The music is nice and inputs are responsive, but this is all dirtied by having the F2P model in the back of your head when you're doing anything in the game.  If they were going to F2P anything, it should have been making ingame currency that allows you to buy the costumes for free and that's it, stages and characters should unlock through other methods, even if it's only having them unlock through purchasing character packs that then come with those stages (as it is you only get additional characters in Season packs).  This however is still bypassing the fact that we never should have ended up with cosmetic DLC to begin with.  Costumes should be unlockable through doing challenging content or achieveing certain play milestones (ie. win 100 online battles or reach a certain rank), adding F2P models inside of AAA games that have costume DLC that is real $ only was the next step in customer screwjobs I suppose.
From a technical perspective, this game is well optimized and runs perfectly smooth (aside from when there are latency issues in online versus, but that's seperate from this) at max settings on my machine, which at time of this writing is an i7-7700k, 16gb DDR4 RAM, and a GTX 1070 8gb.  I also have it installed to an SSD - load times are incredibly brief.
Get it really, really cheap, and you may enjoy it.  That's the only reason I'm not regretful about my purchase, but I'm still bitter about what Capcom's done here.  I do enjoy it, and I will be dipping in for online play here and there, but realistically, this is an improved SFIV Engine with a AAA entry point and F2P all over its insides.

140 is more like a piece of abstract artwork than a game intended to be played and enjoyed. It's simple elegance pervades every corner of the experience, to the extent it almost manages to push gameplay entirely out of the picture. The basic shapes and purposeful use of contrasting colors invokes comparisons to Mondrian, with a calculated simplicity and conspicuousness that elevates the presentation from rudimentary to a captivating example of minimalism. Moved by the beat of a reserved yet distinctive audio track, the experience feels alive as you move through levels, perfectly in sync with each other as if performing an elaborate dance.
In this way, you are something of an outlier; awkwardly progressing through areas you ought not to be in. This creates an odd sort of disconnect between the gameplay and the atmosphere, as while both work wonderfully together to create a brilliant rhythm based platformer, their is just something
about all of it that left me somewhat unsatisfied over the whole affair. I enjoyed every second of the one hour experience, but I also feel no need to spend anymore time within the game.
140 is undeniably a very cool game, one which demands a closer dissection of its elements than you would assume at first glance, the core of which is incredibly tight and polished. It made me think and left me feeling smarter for overcoming its challenges, but as the small side project of a single developer it is, it shouldn't be expected to have the amount of content or range of mechanics to feel like a fully fleshed out concept. It's an experiment, one that succeeds at what it attempts while prompting you to dig deeper into its refined define, but that is all it is and expectations should be set accordingly before entering its psychedelic world.

140 is a captivating platformer indie game. You play as a shape which changes forms based on what action you're doing. If
you're running, you'll be a circle, if you're jumping you'll be a triangle, and if you're idle you'll be a triangle. This game's visuals
and sounds are a major part of the game's mechanics, which is interesting and relatively original.
The game begins quiet and very simple, but as the game progresses it throws more and more mechanics at you, until you reach a point where the game is extremely tense and a bundle of fun at the same time.
Throughout the short campaign you will experinece 3 chapters, each with a unique boss at the end. At this point the game becomes less of a platformer and more of a bullethell game, as you crazily dive from side to side trying to dodge the mass of  bullets flaling across the screen.
The major fault with this game is that the campaign is far too short, barely lasting an hour. Which leaves you just getting started with the game by the time you're asked to pack up and leave. Which is a shame as the game has alot going for it.
and considering the ramp up time of this game you barely get any time to enjoy the game at all.
In conculsion this game is enjoyable, ignoring the somewhat cumbersome beginning the game is fast pased and envigorating. But the major downfall of this game is that the campaign is far too short to justify spending much more than 1-2 GBP.

Ahhhhh, Starbound. You're finally out. 2 and a half years in Early Access. But I'll try not to dwell on that time period for this and focus on what the 1.0 update has brought so far.
The good:
They've focused on the story a little more since the last EA release. There's more pre-determined guaranteed stuff in your starting world, and a little intro quest that helps out newbies. It was alright.
The bad:
Unskippable cutscenes are my favorite! And they added a hunger system that was originally removed VERY early on in the development of the game because it was downright frustrating (and still is). The default difficulty also will have you drop all of your food, blocks, and other important items. You keep only your weapons and armor and a few other basic things, from what I've seen. It's not fun and there's no easy way to get back to your corpse at all. There's an extra arbitrary layer to crafting anything now because you need a special crafting bench to craft other kinds of crafting benches and everything requires slightly more resources. Making armor seems to have been bumped up a decent amount in resource requirement, and to get those resources, you deal with tedius mining, or enemies that deal far too much damage to start out with. Otherwise, customizing and building things is... kind of fun, but feels pointless on planets because you know you'll be leaving and you could just make room for farming on your ship, so the only thing you'd need is trees (which you can find on any planet). All in all, the 1.0 update is actually among the bad ones the game has gotten, and it was more fun the last time I played it. Even then, it was easy to burn out on.
And just a small reminder, but if the devs say something'll be in a future patch even now after release, don't bother hoping they'll deliver.

Sleeping Dogs is a game that can perhaps best be summarized as a GTA clone set in the context of a Hong Kong martial arts film, with a dash of Assassin’s Creed added in for extra flavor. Still, stating that Sleeping Dogs is merely a GTA clone is doing it a disservice, since it is a surprisingly fun, and, in some regards, even an original game.
Sleeping Dogs places the player in the shoes of Wei Shen, an undercover cop infiltrating the world of Triads. As Wei Shen, the player will go through a pretty simple and run-of-the-mill undercover cop story, whose main driving theme is Wei Shen’s struggle to figure out where his loyalties lie – with the police or with his brothers-in-crime. In practice, the player will be able to freely roam the streets of various districts of Hong Kong Still, while driving a multitude of vehicles, freerunning, and engaging in various side activities, such as karaoke singing,♥♥♥♥♥♥fighting and martial arts arenas.
Let’s get the bad out of the way first. Overall, the game could have used some more development time to properly refine it. As it is, the core gameplay is fine, but some of the side activities are very undercooked. A prime example of this is the dating mini game, where Wei Shen has the opportunity to take a number of women out on dates. In reality, this does not amount to much (think GTA IV’s dating/social relationships minigames), but hey – at least they got Emma Stone to voice one of the dateable women! Surely that counts for something, right? Another aspect of the game that could have been developed further is Wei Shen’s moral dilemmas about operating on both sides of the law – he is shown having nightmares about the things he does during the story, which works quite nicely in increasingly building tension for the oncoming resolution. Unfortunately, this tension is never utilized in any meaningful way, which is definitely a missed opportunity. Relating to issues with the game’s story, I found there to be somewhat of a conflict between the story and the gameplay: the problem is that the gameplay is rather ‘arcadey’ and fast paced, but the story is entirely serious and even turns quite dark towards the end. Finally, there are some weird visual issues with the game. First, the entire game has about three different character models for non-plot related characters, which means that you will see identical characters ALL THE TIME when roaming around in the city. Secondly, the firearms in the game simply look odd; they look like plastic toy guns rather than real weapons. While the visual oddities are not enough to truly make a difference to one’s enjoyment of the game, they are still impossible not to take a note of.
Fortunately, the good outweigh the bad. The core strengths of Sleeping Dogs are its original setting in Hong Kong, Wei Shen’s conflicting afflictions between the police and the Triads (even though it could have been refined further, as mentioned above), and its brilliant hand-to-hand combat system. First, Hong Kong, as portrayed in the game, looks really good. Everything you see is vibrant and colorful, and all of the different districts look distinct from one another. Furthermore, it is an original and entirely fresh setting, which makes it much more interesting to explore than, say, a fictional city in the US. The setting is also brilliantly utilized in the game’s audio: the characters fluidly switch between English and Cantonese in their dialogue, and the game’s radio stations play a mix of Western and Eastern music. Secondly, while the story is nothing groundbreaking, I found it to work quite well in the context of the game. It was simple and straightforward enough to not overpower and distract from the freeform nature of the game, and yet compelling enough to provide the player with a constant drive to progress in the game and see what happens next. Finally, there is the hand-to-hand combat system, which was marketed as one of the game’s main selling points. It is basically the combat system from Batman: Arkham Asylum, but expanded to also include some light grappling elements and, of course, the glorious environmental takedowns. The environmental takedowns are performed by grapping an enemy and dragging him to a pre-determined background object, such as a telephone booth or an electric eel tank, and then pressing a button to execute an instant kill move with a visceral death animation. Overall, the combat system is reasonably simple, but has enough depth in it to make melee combat fun and satisfying throughout the length of the story.
TL;DR: Sleeping Dogs is an open world sandbox game set in Hong Kong that focuses mainly on hand-to-hand combat as opposed to firearms. It feels unrefined in some aspects, but is definitely worth playing for fans of the genre.

I've played the game on and off for a year or two, but decided to have a serious sit-down once 1.0 dropped.
I'm liking the game because that is what it is, a good game. Lots of items and strange places to find, lots of choices for building, and the game's randomly generated worlds always have something to look at or discover.
Despite these pros that the game has had for a very long time, the 1.0 update also brought a lot of hate from the community including myself.
For one, characters have been wiped again with this update. Pretty obvious why that♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥people off.
Two, the inventory system is now much harder to manage because it has so few spaces and certain items can only go in certain tabs of the inventory. (Ex. Iron in crafting materials tab.) This limits the main theme of the game: Exploration.
Three, progression in crafting stations and gear have improved in terms of convenience, but is limited by the story.
Overall I can't say I hate the game because of a few steps back even though the developers had a looong time to get it figured. Besides, the ame took a few steps forward with crew members and bringing back survival mechanics. In fact, I'll probably play the game for another week or more.
EDIT: The game gives a lot of options for building and there is a colony creation system. Different experiences with playing different races and I think the game is better than I originally got in to. (Mods can fix the inventory stuff.)
8/10 Worth the price if you aren't the type to get annoyed by cluttered storage and inventory.

I feel so sorry for whatever motivated people to write a bad review for this game. After just one playthrough lasting 6 hours, it has easily made itself room into my top three favorite games of all time list. How about we get to the pros and cons eh?
Pros:
Story is gripping, unique, and narrated by the manliest voice on Earth (It sounds like two expensive cigars wrapped in Belgian chocolate replaced his lungs and throat). Almost everywhere you go and nearly anything you do is narrated in some manner.
Gameplay synchronizes with the story flawlessly. The gameplay is mostly hack-and-slash with a few RPG elements, however with a plethora of weapons and skills the combinations are endless.
The visuals of the levels and the few cutscenes are just gorgeous, completely unexpected from a small indie company. Each area feels unique and has its own secrets.
Cons: (Not many cons here, but a few to note)
There is a section of the game where it feels like you are fighting the SAME EXACT SET OF ENEMIES FOR UPWARDS OF 2 HOURS OF THE STORY. This changes shortly afterwards however. (Edit: While running through the New-Game + mode, this problem lessened due to having all the gear up front)
I used practically the same exact set of weapons the whole game through, because even though the player has a ton of options, there seemed to be only ONE and I mean ONE group of weapons/skills that felt fun playing with. I don't consider this a con but rather I felt like sharing this in case someone else had the same issue.
Overall: Play this game. Do it. Just do it. Don't let your dreams be dreams. The few cons listed are absolutely no reason why you shouldn't play this game.

As a side note, there's a Metroidvania tag. Quite dissapointed. I was expecting massive exploration, and finding upgrades, because that's what Metroidvania does. The game that started the phenomenon. There's a lot of fun to be had tearing through the city on  your own personal crime wave. Offensive, yes, but the game doesn't take itself seriously. It's fun precisely because you do stuff you would never do in real life. Arcade action.
While fun, the game doesn't hold up well against modern open-world games. Some missions can be difficult, so be prepared to try and fail multiple times. Difficulty isn't a problem, though. I like a challenge. Poor controls on the PC, limited camera control, lack of in-game map, and overall fragility of your character/vehicles cause a lot of frustration. Half the time I feel like I'm fighting the game itself, rather than overcoming a challenge. The costs of failure is high, and you are more likely to just reload a previous save, meaning you'll need to visit your safe house to save between every mission. I may eventually finish this game, but I have to take it in doses. I'm hoping Vice City and San Andreas are less frustrating.
About controls... I like to use keyboard/mouse on foot and an XBox 360 controller while driving. The game does support controllers, but it doesn't recognize all of the buttons. If you want to use a controller, save yourself some grief and spend an extra $10 on XPadder. It's still not great, but at least you'll be able to use all buttons. You'll need them.

Things I Didn't Like

Broken.. and it's such a shame.
The 1994 original was a classic. This re-release isn't. The graphics may be a little bit fanicer but so much of the game is broken that it's virtually unplayable.
Firstly, the automated and essential wagon train trade route system is now useless. You no longer tell each individual wagon train what to pick up, where to go and what to drop off. Instead you set imports and exports for each colony. This soon results in a huge list of possibile locations for possible products and the list soon gets confusing. Then, if a wagon train's ususal route gets interrupted by an enemy unit or rival nation's new colony, it forgets what it was doing and it's down to you to work it out - which can be impossible. The only solution is often to cancel all automated trade routes and start again. Also, be careful what you automate, as they zoom around the map so fast it can be hard to find them, let alone remember what orders you gave them.
Secondly, everything is much more expensive yet the opportunities to make money don't balance it out. In the classic game a veteran soldier cost 2000 to train and the price stayed at that. Now it's about 3800 and goes up each time you train one. This drains your bank account in no time. To train them yourself rquires significant infrastructure to be in place, all of which costs time and money. And by the time you have such infrastruture in place, the game's AI has made your home nation's king so greedy with taxes that even a boat full of cigars will make you peanuts. Even on this easiest difficulty level this makes the game extremely difficult as you struggle to both develop AND defend your colonies.
Thirdly, the game is full of bugs; ships that set sail from the west side of the map reappear on the east side of the map after visiting Europe, forcing you to send them on a huge detour if you want them on the West side of the map again. Some commodities simply don't show up in the wagon train trade route options list. Want to automate the transport of cotton from colony B to A? Tough. You can't. Forcing you to manually keep an eye on one particular wagon train to do this - which becomes next to impossible once you've got loads arriving in a certain colony at the same time.
Additionally, the colony screen just looks a complicated mess and not only do the commodities barely look like what they're supposed to (cigars are tiny purple sticks in huge boxes - why not just a picture of.. erm... a cigar?) but the colony buildings are terribly sketched outlines so difficult to make sense of you find yourself hovering the mouse over each, nearly every time (and that's if the game decides to tell you!) (bugs, remember!).
It's not all bad. The unit upgrades system is nice and works well, giving you the choice of what upgrade to pick and where to allocate it. You can now get treasure from just visiting native settlements where as before you had to raze a native settlement to the ground to do that. And the Europe screen is neat and clearly shows what's inbound, what's outbound, what's waiting and even lets you load different people and cargo onto different ships. Sounds simple but in the classic game you could not do this with people and had to adjust the order of people on the docks to get the desired effect.
I've played the 1994 original for well over 1,000 hours but after not even 50 hours on this version I can't take it anymore and have to abandon it. I had just set up over 20 different wagon train trade routes to feed my capital colony with all that it needed. Then a rival nation founded a colony on the route these wagon trains used, forcing them to stop in their tracks and forget what they were doing - forcing me to set it ALL up again. This took hours and is just ridiculous when the old system worked so well, so efficently and was so easy to do.
The game is just broken - there is no better way to describe it. Just like No Man's Sky, there are some beautiful elements here and some genuinely great gaming aspects. But so much of it is fundamentally broken that it fails to work as a cohesive whole and as such is just unplayable and not fun.
Unless a re-re-release comes out soon, take my advice and stick to the original - it might be getting on a bit now, but at least it works, beautifully.
Not recommended - just a crap :/

A quaint little game.  I definitely enjoyed a few games of it and played it enough to understand it.  If I could give it a mixed review, I would
However, I see only a thumb up or a thumb down box, and in the end, this game is just too humble.
Your ability to thrive is enormously throttled by diminishing returns and a reverse economy-of-scale, where as your population grows, each person consumes more resources.  Building improvements give small bonuses and have high costs.  Basically, expect to pay 9% of your power for every 10% gained.  You really have to scrabble and claw for any tiny advantage.
Compare a game played with extreme care, pausing often and choosing the best possible thing that every person can be doing at all times, gathering food during growing season and performing tasks that are equally effective in winter like scouting heavily during the winter -
To a game where you just carelessly build whatever your shortsighted lack of planning has put you in need of:
The optimal game will produce only about 20% better economy than a careless game.  It's an environment it's really not possible to excel in.
On top of that, it wants to be a RTS.  There is no tactical pause, but without the crisp controls of a real RTS like say Starcraft, you will have a lot of guys die unneccessarily to raids where either good controls or a tactical pause would allow you to save them.

I usually don't write reviews, but this game frustrates me and here is why.
The game has much potential and I will list 5 pro's below.
- Many customization options
- Lots of references to sci-fi material
- Extensive crafting system
- Decent story serviceable to the game
- Decent gameplay
Now I will go into the negatives why the game doesn't work for me. The game feels bloated, it has a lot of ideas and content but it doesn't feel coherent. There is too much cluttered together and though I feel an RPG or a similar game should be extensive. The core components of the game should be streamlined, yet it feels like a mess.
This game has taken forever to come out, and I felt it would only be honest to review it once the game is officially released. I have seen builds come and go of this game and the final product is dissapointing even compared to the earlier versions of the game. It plays unbalanced, frustrating and just a chore to get through.
Now I am sure there are a lot of proponents for this game, all the more power to you if you enjoyed it, I didn't and this is the first game I have reviewed ever, yet I felt just to write a review for this game just to inform you. Buy it if you really like Terraria and you look for something similar, otherwise don't waste your money and time on it. Because how often i have tried i can't enjoy this game.
After all this time, still a favorite.

Meltdown is a sort of dual stick shoot 'em up in space. Actually it's set on a space station that seems to have gone mad and is intent on ending your life by sending all of it's robots after you. Using an isometric perspective the game seems to give a nod to gaming of yesteryear.
You will have to fight wave after wave of them, but you can bring some friends along with you as the game has a neat multiplayer mode. You can play online of locally if you prefer, but the more players you have the tougher the enemies become. There are plenty of objects to hide behind making the game a sort of cover based shooter. Every few levels feature a boss which makes for some great multiplayer action, but can seem a little daunting when you're on your own.
If there's one small complaint it is that most of it looks the same, but this doesn't really matter when you're busy blasting the hell out of those metal nut cases.

Great isometric action indie-shooter!!!
+ Well-designed gameplay with simple and accurate controls.
+ Very challlenging if you're playing on your own. A lot easier (still challenging though) if you play with other players.
+ Great variety of weapons, gear and enemies.
+ A lot of weapon, gear and character upgrades.
+ 3 different bosses, that are very difficult to beat if you are playing on your own.
+ The multiplayer mode is lots of fun and quite necessary if you want to beat the last levels.
+ A lot of levels that are randomely generated.
+ Very nice graphics and pretty fitting soundtrack.
+ The wave-attack mode is very challenging and I spent a lot of time in it!
+/- The game has a lot of grinding that might tire some players, however that's what kept me playing it again and again.
- Some random disconnects when playing online.
- The game doesn't have a big community, although almost every time you will find someone else to play with.
- Sometimes you get the feeling that you play the same level again and again, however, after all the hours I've played, I don't think I've found two exactly identical levels.
-
*The skill was fixed with the latest update and is now working perfectly!
Strongly recommended to fans of action shooters, even at the original price, since it can offer you quite a lot of hours if you like grinding!

About 2 and a half years ago, I was a few months into my freshman year of college. I'd lost my 3 closest friends from high school (the only friends I've ever really had), was tanking my classes, and was going through a period of alcoholism and depression. I spent my nights alone. Even my roommate told me I was too depressing to be around, and would avoid any attempts I tried to make at becoming friends.
Then I discovered Starbound.
Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ did this game blow me away. The sheer amount of exploration, the utterly free and non-restrictive nature of the construction system... It was like I was immersed in my own universe. I finally had a place to do anything I wanted. I made myself a vast system of cities, complete with merchants and civilians. I'd go into this more, but it's impossible to describe with words how much fun I was having. The best part? I actually stopped drinking, because the game was more fun when I was sober. Hell, my grades even started improving as a result.
After the first major update when outposts were added and systems were wiped, I was really bummed. But it wasn't a huge problem- the update added plenty of stuff to do, and polished combat and construction, so I didn't really mind all that much. It was just another start for another adventure. This time I made a system of planets with societies- on one of the lava covered planets, I successfully constructed a HUGE housing system under the lava. And on one of the ocean planets, I made what I thought was a pretty good recreation of the first level of Bioshock 1.

A game that's about island-hop-conquering an ocean full of enemy bases from an advanced carrier that acts as a mobile base, allows you complete control over your units, research, construction, and even allows you to run around in first person?  Sounds awesome right?  Well... it's not.

Sure, the game looks great and the world you're in is huge, but there's just too much wrong to enjoy any of it.

UPDATE 6-20-14: This game is still broken as hell.  Yeah, they've patched pathfinding, terrain clipping and some of the dumber AI behavior, but the rest of the game is still abysmal.  The core problem is that the game requires you to heavily rely upon the AI's scripting and for your vehicles to be at least half-way competent at navigation and combat, but they are incapable of handling themselves and will require you to personally assume control in almost every situation.  So in reality, it's not an RTS or even team-based game in any way; it's just you jumping from vehicle to vehicle to avoid getting them killed and fighting every battle for them, or driving them around the more complicated terrain cause they all got stuck.
Avoid this, at all costs, even if it's going for a dollar.  It's just not worth your time.

140 is a very short (~45 minutes or so, maybe less) platformer with ultra-minimal geometric graphics, a little reminiscent of Thomas Was Alone with even more of a commitment to visual minimalism and trashy, angry-psychadelic graphics. What sets it apart is that the platforming is built around rhythm elements, much like something like Beatbuddy or Sony/PSN's "Sound Shapes". Basically, as you go through the levels there are timed obstacles, platforms, and other mechanics that play along with the dirty, dub-step / glitch electronica that comprises the music. Periodically you will collect an orb which you bring to a set point, which causes the colour palette, sound, and mechanics to shift. At the end of each of the three levels is a boss which functions kind of like a shoot-em-up-ish genre. If you die, the screen dissolves into analog TV fuzz as the music glitches out even further and you respawn at the nearest checkpoint.
Cheat code: If you want to make the game easier, go slowly and count out a beat. Mostly the rhythm patterns seem to be 4/4 or 8/8 so if you can count the beat in your head you'll be able to crack the code no problem.
Whether you feel like you'll get $5 out of such a short game is up to you, but I found it to be a great experience. Often times when I died, I chuckled in spite of myself because I found the rhythm mechanics very clever. I especially liked the bosses.
Because of the emphasis on music, I recommend headphones--certainly you would find it very difficult to play without audio.
Hopefully this review has given you the information you need to try to decide whether or not this is for you.

Game is great, very few bugs for an early access game too. I would recommend anyone who loves RTS games to give this a try. The only thing is, besides some parts of the gameplay and the gorgeous Nordic atmosphere, this is almost just like any other RTS game. If you're happy playing The Battle For Middle Earth, Age of Empires or Warcraft, you wouldn't really be missing out on much.
I'd like to make a few points to the devs that I, a casual RTS player, think could really improve the game, make it stand out from the rest of the genre and open up to a wider audience.
1. I love how there are random events every now and then, rat infestations, earthquakes, blizzards, Helheim invasions and wolf/draugr attacks, but there should be an option to turn each event on/off individually. If you think you can handle rat infestations but blizzards are a bit too tough for you, allow us to choose which we want to include in our game, and with what frequency/magnitude. This is crucial if you want a wider audience to be able to enjoy your game. Casual players like me won't be turned away and you can give the pros an option to give themselves a bigger challenge.
2. Every clan has their own special unit which is nice and all, but what would be really awesome is if you could make your own custom Hero. Make it so that we can level it up so it becomes stronger over time, let us choose what perks it has (for example, increases tower defenses, increases production in this territory, increases overall army power), allow us to personalize it. This is the kind of thing I have never seen in any RTS game but I believe that could make Northgard stand out. Besides, you can make big bucks by selling outfits to expand a player's customizable options.
3. Map editor would be cool.
4. When you make the campaign don't forget to include a tutorial level. New players are thrown in the deep end.
5. Improve the combat. The game is currently focused heavily on economy and capturing enemy territory is painfully slow. It's intense for all the wrong reasons. It's intense because it's hard to control, frustrating because your units have to stand vulnerably and do nothing for a long time before being able to move on. If you want to keep the combat similar to what it is now, at least add battle healers. They are just like regular healers except you can recruit them in a barracks, instead of healing everything on your territory, they heal everything within 1 area, be it yours, neutral or enemy, as long as your units are not currently fighting.
Those are some points I'd like to see in the future of this game. It is already a great game, but it has a lot of room for improvement.

I am only writing this and recommending Colonization because the original one from 1995 was so much better. For starters the Navy in the original actually meant something. Having privateers was actually useful. your opponents were much more aggresive and had way more ships. The new COL barely utilizes it's navy.
The MOST important thing about the navy were the battles. In the originaol you capture loot which made the navy battles so much fun and having a privateer was actually useful! Not to mention your opponents would have privateers attacking your ships as well so having a few frigates for defense was actually needed!
Next come the Indians.
Indians would constantly attack you, and that was a lot of fun. When the attacked settlements they actually stole cargo from you and could steal horses or even guns. This would mean that they could get an easy upgrade if they got lucky. Again, this brought a lot of unpredictability to the game. Indians were able to steel your settlement goods when they raided. Nothing like that in the new COL.
The scoring system is very bland and boring in the new COL. All you see is a replay and a score card that doesn't mean anything. The original COL from  1995 showed your score based on how many Indians you killed, the amount of gold you had at the end of the game, colonists etc..(founding fathers)
The founding fathers system is a bit boring. The random founding father from the original was more interesting, but it's not that big of a deal.
However, whatever happened to the 'Fountain of Youth'? That was a big part of the original and COL.
Overall, the new COL is 6/10.
I recommend this game only because I recommend the original from 1995. It has a lot of replay value even in 2017. I haven't played it in a long time because I managed to get the highest rating possible on Viceroy. GG, good times.
Also, one more thing... the original also had a lot of charm. The new one lacks a lot of the colonial role play.
And..... one more thing.... in the original you could have the kind of another nation come in and grant you an elite expiditonary force for a very hefty price when you declare indepence. Mine was from the King of France when I was playing the Netherlands. The package contained Man-O-Wars and lots of cavelry, soldiers, and cannons.

Not particularly hard or unfair, all that 140 asks of you is a consistent performance at a pace of 140 beats per minute.
'140' is a minimalist platformer (up until the bosses) in which all of the challenges are set to music. It doesn't sound like anything special but its execution is excellent. Controlling the game is easy. Your low speed and high acceleration make every move easily predictable. Every challenge is layed out before you in a way that allows you to almost instantly know what to do to overcome it. There was never death that I felt was unfairly due except perhaps for the bosses. However, even those really were my fault. The feeling of unfairness just came from how overwhelmed I was by them on the first try.
Every motion in the game apart from yours is set to a steady rhythm. Obstacles move in time with the music and platforms appear on-beat. You are a geometric shape that changes as your state does. A circle while moving on the ground, a triangle while airborne and a square while standing still. Every level consists of simple, timed platforming during which you must, at regular intervals, collect a little pick-up (whose movement represents a mechanic you're about enable) and take it back to a specific point to progress. Each level culminates with a boss. All of which are slightly different but are all basically about avoiding obstacles thrown at you as opposed to the ones you jump at in the platforming sections.
The music is sort of recycled for use throughout the entire game. Specific elements of it are only heard when particular mechanics come in to play so it's not always entirely the same but it's definitely not a different song. Again, the exception to this is the bosses. They come whith their own musical flavours. Consistent with the rest of the game but separating them from the platforming sections and each other. This all works in the game's favour. The music feels a part of the game's design and it helps you play. It's also awesome music.
'140' is very short, consisting of only three levels each taking around 20 minutes on the first try. The game does offer replayability to you through a mirror mode in which there are no checkpoints. I can easily see only a minority (although not necessarily a small one) being drawn in by this since, once you've beaten the game, you've seen and conqured every challenge. What more is there to do? Well, this "hard mode" poses its own challenge by asking you to remain consistent in your abilities for an entire level. Fail and you must start from the beginning. Even if you reach the boss.
Personally, I liked this. I seems a solid enough goal to aim for seeing as you know what's coming is simple timing and fairly easy platforming. Even the bosses aren't as fraustrating a second time. If the game hadn't set this challenge for me, I might not have decided to try it but since it did, I gladly took it on.
'140' is an enjoyable distraction. If you liked things like 'Thomas Was Alone', 'Element4l', or 'Limbo', you could probably get into this.

It's just... not good, man. Not in the least. The combat is pretty much the most basic system of combos and button prompts you can get, like if you're trying to make a spectacle fighter. But in Icey, there is no spectacle. The moves look cool for a little while, but it wears thin pretty quickly. Like, look at my game time. PRETTY quickly.
Usually for games like this I'd say something like "You might enjoy this if you like blah blah blah", the blahs being replaced by something like "2D Side Scrolling Fighters" or "Narrated Meta Games". But... honestly, if you're a fan of stuff like that then you'll probably end up like me after playing an hour of the game. Bored and somewhat annoyed.
I don't want to harp on the narrator as a person or anything, but so help me God if his voice just is so freaking annoying, like jeez. Unlike a game like The Stanley Parable where the narrator at least has a voice you can listen to for the time you play it, the narrator in ICEY just... doesn't have the voice for it. To be honest, it sounds like the narrator in a one/two person Fallout mod.
Touching back on the combat for a moment, specifically the part about lacking spectacle... see, the reason why these combo-button-press-button-prompt games work so well in spectacle fighters like Bayonetta or Devil May Cry is BECAUSE of the spectacle of it all! It LOOKS nice! The combo attacks are cool! ICEY has a... it's not a BAD art style, per se, but it's not one that really... pops. It's not quite simplistic but it is lacking in complexity. Which is OK! Every game doesn't have to look AMAZING. But games like this, games that tote themselves on enemy design and whatnot, they should at least have a unique art style. I don't think ICEY has that. Okay, okay, I've been talking about art in the combat section, but let's be clear here. There is a reason why art and combat go hand in hand. Games like this should not only be fun to play (I really enjoy mashing buttons somewhat randomly and somehow coming up with a combo, I REALLY do, hand to God), but they have to be fun to LOOK at as well. ICEY just... isn't.
Though, the bosses DO have pretty good designs and are a LITTLE nicer looking than the rest of the game. So that's a plus, especially since bosses are such a big part of ICEY. And ICEY herself is pretty nice looking too (10/10 would date).
But yeah, all in all, after this long-winded, meandering review, I have to say... I do not recommend this game. Maybe if there's a sale and you REALLY want to experience whatever meta-narrative this game pushes onto you (again, I have not played all that much of this game), and you don't mind dealing with somewhat bland (mostly combat) visuals, then maybe, just maybe, you should buy this game.
And hey, maybe this company will make another game that actually IS as good as the reviews say it is.

A light hearted wonderful game with a great sense of humour.
McPixel is a fast paced indie game that stars “McPixel” a strange character that goes around saving the day from all things explosive!
You are thrown into various different situations in various different settings and given 20 seconds to save the day, how that turns out is down to you and your fast thinking. It is not at all a serious game and it’s very likely that 95% of the time you will blow something up on your first try. But it’s still fun none the less and the level comes back around faster than you can even think about it. It has a somewhat crude but hilarious sense of humour, with very bizarre gags in each stage.
There was quite a few times during my time playing that I just thought, “Who the hell would do that?” and had a little chuckle to myself.  But there you go, that is the magic and charm of McPixel.
The music is extremely repetitive, but strangely enough it isn’t annoying. It’s more catchy then annoying.
The main game is pretty short and there is a load of free DLC for you to play afterwards if you want to. (So there are a lot of days to save!)
If you were to play this nonstop the whole thing would probably take you a few hours, and it’s probably a good idea to take breaks due to its fast paced nature.
Generally I really enjoyed it; I thought it was pretty fun; there are a lot of references and things to have a laugh at in this game. So it’s something fun to throw on when you are bored.

Isometric 3D Sci-Fi shooter, a bit bland in solo due to lack of story, but fun in co-op.
Overall, I had some fun with the game, and it was well worth the low sale price, but the game feels somewhat unfinished and there doesn't seem to be any development planned. It looks like a Sci-Fi version of Bastion but actually lack all the details that make Bastion a great game.
+ pretty good graphics for a mobile port.
+ OK controls
+ many perks and equipment
+  your character have 1 melee and 2 two ranged weapons, combined with dodge roll and crouching behind obstacles, gives decent variation in tactical gameplay.
+ up to 4 players co-op
+ 30 levels, including 3 bosses levels
+ Solo, co-op, Deathmatch and Survival modes gives some variations.
- levels design is too generic, most levels feels the same
- limited interaction with surrounding background (only crouching behind obstacles)
- no plot or story, it is just plain arena fighting.
- despite many perks, you end up getting them all anyway!
- A few occasional glitches in MP
-- there are 4 level of difficulty but once you promote to a new level you loose all perks AND equipment, re-gaining perks is not too hard, but having to purchase equipment again is just terrible and nonsensical and leads to unnecessary grinding.
TIP Play in survival to gain xp quickly and wait until level 4 to purchase most equipment.

Sleeping Dogs is an awesome game all around. Obviously this game draws from titles like GTA, but there's something about Sleeping Dog's style that makes it stand out from other open-world games.
Sleeping Dog's story is that of an ultraviolent thriller: You're an undercover cop from the US returning to his hometown of Hong Kong to take the triads down from inside, but things get out of hand quickly. There are also a few subplots in the story which could have added a lot more if they had been carried out fully, especially the revenge story, but I won't go into further detail on that one. The ending is also confusing and disappointing, but game endings aren't really something to cry over. Voice acting is either great or hilariously over-the top. Apparently they only paid Emma Stone twenty dollars, because her role takes the length of one side mission. Visuals are also worth a mention; the game is full of it's own colorful, gorgeous graphical style. Although the game doesn't run extremely well on my Radeon HD 4850, I appreciate the effort that was put into optomizing the game, and this won't be a problem for most people with newer hardware.
Sleeping Dog's gameplay is also notable. The driving handles easily and is some of the best I have ever experienced in an open world game. Races, especially motorcycle races, are very fast and fun. The melee combat is a main selling point of the game. The system is similar to the batman games with regular and heavy strikes, blocks, and grappling. Combat animations are very smooth, which is a relief. Melee items and awesome combos also make the combat unique and dynamic. Shooting is probably the worst gameplay mechanic, but even then it isn't really that bad. It serves it's purpose, but it's generic cover based shooting. Something in the style of Max Payne or Double Action Boogaloo would be a better fit for Sleeping Dogs.
The DLCs I'd recommend are the Zodiac Tournament and Year of the snake. They're pretty cheesy but really fun. If you want to beef up the gameplay content and cosmetics, there isn't anything wrong with any of the others (except for the Halloween DLC, which is dissapointingly mundane). Keep in mind that some DLC gives you XP and money boosts, which will make the game easier if you buy it before you start playing.
So that's it. If you're a sucker for over-the-top action, open world games, or great melee combat, Sleeping Dogs is for you.
