I am a huge fan of both the Aliens and Predator franchises, and as such I love the amazing games both series have to offer. This, is a game that combines both series, and does it quite well. The gameplay is rich, the story is cheesy but enjoyable (and really warrants a sequel if you ask me.) and the atmosphere is spot on. There are 3 campaigns to choose from, each broken into little missions. The terror-inducing Alien, the fearsome and formiddable Predator....and the puny marine. After beating a mission as one of these races, you have the option to play a mission from a different species, or continue the one you are on.
Alien: The gameplay as alien is pretty fun, but challenging. You have to outsmart enemies, as you have no ranged attacks.  Stick to the shadows to stay hidden, climb on walls, ceilings, and through air vents (how original.) to get the jump on the poor marines below. You are the only species that has the ability to regen ALL lost health, and you can also heal by eating the heads of dead enemies. (Metal level: Over 9000)
Predator: FUN. AWESOME. GORY. Nothing stands in your way. Slice through enemies as if they were paper mache arts-and-crafts projects made by 2-year olds. Use your heat vision to spot enemies, and use the xeno vision to spot Aliens. You can leap onto rooftops, sprint at a speed that makes Usain Bolt fall to his knees, and most of all, TURN INVISIBLE! My favorite species by far.
Puny earthling: To be honest, kinda generic. Its basically CoD without ADS. Although, there are some genuinly scary moments, such as going through areas with eggs. (FACEHUGGERS.) You do get a motion tracker that is always on screen (Not lore friendly! Uh-oh!), but it is more useful that the versions, in say, halo. In this game, your motion tracker makes noise when spotting movement, so you can focus what is ahead of you, rather than dart back and forth between your tracker and the reticule. The only real mechanic that breaks away from generic FPS formula is the smart gun. It automatically tracks and homes in on targets. Sweet. Just wish it saw more use. But, all-in-all, this is MUCH better than Colonial Marines, and this isnt even the real focus of this game. Says alot about gearbox, doesnt it?
Conclusion: Buy this game. Please. Do youself a favor.

There are quite a few unnecessarily negative reviews for this game. From what I've read of these, they're either from followers of the series who don't feel that this game adds much to previous games, other than new tracks, or people who feel that it's too short or arcade-feeling.
I feel that these negative comments are a bit unreasonable.
First of all, given the cost of the game at full cost, there's a lot of playability and enjoyment to be had from the game. If it doesn't add too much to previous games, then that's just because there's no reason to change something if it's not broken. If you bought a previous game and enjoyed it, you'll probably enjoy this. I personally haven't played a previous Riptide game, but I love how this plays and would definitely buy a future version with new tracks, racers, jetskis etc.
Secondly, the complaints about this being too arcade-like are highly confusing. Why would it possibly be a negative if it plays like an arcade game? If you don't like arcade-style racers, then don't get this game. I love that it was so easy to get into but yet has a decent learning curve for improvement, particularly as you learn the tracks and the tricks.
Overall, this game is highly enjoyable at full price, but if you can get it reduced (i.e., during a sale or as part of a bundle), then it's an underappreciated gem of a game. It's not a game that will steal your life away or keep you going long into the lonely nights, but if you're expecting it to do that, you really need to learn about how to form realistic live goals.
Best advice: play this locally or online with family/friends.

I sadly can't bring myself to leave a thumbs down review on this game as I've played it so much and will continue to do so, but truly the cons outweigh the pros here.  I wish I could leave a neutral review.  This game can be outrageously fun and entertaining, it can also be insanely irritating and annoying.
Pros:
Hours of online fun.  Can find a competitive match fairly quickly.
An ever growing roster.
Fight money allows you to unlock all characters without purchasing with real money.  While it is extremely difficult to accumulate enough FM to do this, you could pick and choose a new character you wanted to learn, since realistically most people don't play every character.
Both simple and complex combos to learn.  Each character has their own unique combos that you can mix up in some seriously fun ways.
Cons:
This game is essentially an elaborate game of coin toss.
Too many characters have specials that allow them to put their opponent in a 50/50 situation where a guess is as good as it gets.  This really lowers the skill factor in the game and promotes poor thoughtless play.
Some of this may be lag but it just feels like there's not enough recovery time on invincible specials and the like.  If you block an unsafe move or bait someone then you shouldn't have to have lightning fast reflexes and perfect timing to punish them, and their moves certainly shouldn't put them out of immediate range of punishment.  If someone does something unsafe there should be more risk involved.
Some of the new characters seem like they didn't put any thought into them.  Like Abigail, really?  A gigantic mountain of muscle that jabs from half screen and has loads of invincible armored moves that both deal insane damage and can put him out of punish range after lunging across the map.
Most of the roster can just jab anti-air??? Makes no sense.  It used to be that a character was given an anti-air or they weren't and you had to work with it.
There is just too much comeback potential.  Everyone likes a comeback, but it becomes ridiculous when you can be crushing a round 90% Health to 10% health, make one wrong move and lose to a coin flip situation.
Capcom decided to not make us buy endless revisions of the game (sounds great).  So instead they release constant DLC costumes that are outrageously priced.  $4 for a single costume?  There is probably over a hundred alternate costumes available, you shouldn't need to spend more than the game cost to just get a few alternate looks for your favorite characters.
Lately there's been a lot of lag online.  Games just completely freezing to the point someone just gives up to end the round and get out of it.
Having said all of that, this game can still be fun if you don't take it too seriously.  For any fighting game fan, it isn't  a bad purchase if you can get past all of the obvious flaws.  Hopefully they fix some stuff in Arcade Edition.
So would I recommend this game?  Yes, and then at the same time a huge resounding no.

There could be a good game in here. The combat is fun if a little wonky with the counter prompts and a little too generous with the knockback, but it's enjoyable enough action. The character design is fun and the world is interesting, with a decent amount of enemy variety at least in the bit i've played.
But I can't recommend this game to anyone. Absolutely nobody. Unless maybe that person is a game developer with a deep-seated loathing for player agency and non-linear games.
So it's a game with a narrator, but there are options to ignore what the narrator says and go different directions to explore. Kind of like the Stanley Parable. Also like the Stanley Parable, the narrator gets confused about what you're doing and tries to make you follow his directions.
Unlike the Stanley Parable, however, the narration in this game wears out its welcome almost immediately. Go off the path here and he rants for 10 minutes about achievements. Go off the path there and he makes you watch a five minute cutscene. Go off the path over here and he rants at you about how you must hate this game so much if you're ignoring him, then takes you to a locked room with a goldfish simulator, then a meat boy-ish platformer before berating you about how much you suck and how good it will feel to follow his directions next time.
They make a point, have a funny joke about it, and then continue on for about 15 more minutes grinding that point and any humor there might have been into the dust. It is completely overbearing and I don't want to interact with it anymore.
Well you might say, why not just follow his directions then?
Because those alternate paths are in the game. They programmed them to be there. It is content they intended for you to see, because if they didn't then they wouldn't have created it. They are offering this choice and then punishing you for choosing. It's actively malicious against its player.
Good effort guys, but maybe try again once you get the chip off of your shoulder.

You wont have huge armies fighting it out with walls to protect you. Northgard is about having an efficient and healthy economy to keep your clan happy, fed and feeling protected. There's 3 types of basic infantry, and some unique soldiers that come in the form of the Warchief which depending on which clan you pick can also be the Beserker or the Hand Maiden.
You'll spend most your game gaining a footing, establishing trade and expanding into nearby territory which could be infested with enemy gaia such as wolfs or mythological creatures. Each territory has advantages or disadvantages that help you or work against your progress. Depending on which clan you pick, you also have things available to you that determine how you should play to achieve victory.

Oh my, this is a masterpiece! If you like electronic music and music/rhythm games, this is for you! In short, 140 managed to provide me one of the most immersive and memorable experiences I ever had in gaming. Let me settle down and tell you about it.

140 is a minimalistic and abstract platformer rhythm game. There are no lives, menus, tutorials or hand-holding: it's just left, right and jump. The levels are composed of platforms and blocks/obstacles with different properties that respond to the "periodic nature" of the music/rhythm, comprising of minimal dubstep with a subtle hint of chiptunes. (At places, it reminded me of Krafwerk). Listening to the music/rhythm is essential to figure out how the obstacles work, enabling you progress. This discovery involves some trial and error, also because the game is a bit challenging, but there are frequent seamless checkpoints that almost immediately respawn you when you fail. As you progress along each level the music and rhythm patterns become more complex, making for more complex obstacle sequences, which creates a sense of momentum and exhilaration as you successfuly understand and manage to execute how to get past an obstacle. At the end of each of the 3 groups of levels, there is a "boss", which is more challenging but also spectacular and rewarding.
The overall design of this game is nothing short of brilliant: the music and visuals/blocks are synergistically woven together; the platforming elements and obstacles nail the sweet spot between recognizability and making you pause a moment to observe and think; the flow and pacing are perfect and the aesthetic, both in visuals and music is the definition of minimal beauty. Because everything revolves around the rhythm of the music, the game subtly demands that you get into it and "feel" the rhythm, which in turn gradually makes the experience more and more immersive as you "attune" yourself to it. Looking back on this, I think it's truly a remarkable feat of game design. Managing to beat the final "boss" was immensely rewarding: it made me feel like it was an epic end to a most amazing adventure. Digital bliss.
Because "dying" hurts the flow of the music, I felt the game instilling me a desire to play without errors on further playthroughs, and mastering this game and being able to finish it in one go withouth dying would be a truly special achievement. You could try just that: after finishing the game you unlock a special mode where you can start from the beginning with the levels mirrored horizontally and, if you die, you start from the beginning...
There are only two minor concerns worthy of note. Firstly, the game is somewhat short (it took me about 1h to complete? in one sitting) and left me wanting more. Secondly, the final "boss" is quite difficult and I suspect will frustrate some people because it involves not only realising the pattern but also using very fast eye-hand reactions.
However, there is something very special about this game, so minimal and yet so complete.

The Binding of Isaac is a rogue-like, perma-death, hard-as-frick, top down shooter. And a dark one.
The plot goes as follows:
Isaac is a small boy whom lives with his mother atop a hill. Isaac draws pictures and his mother watches religious television programming. They're both happy with their lives, at least until Isaac's mom hears a "voice from above", presumably God, telling her that Isaac has become corrupt, and must be saved. Following the word of "the Lord," she takes away Isaac's toys, drawings, clothing, and even locks him in his room away from the world's evil. The voice praises Isaac's mom, but questions her faith. To prove her love and devotion, the voice commands to make a sacrifice of Isaac. Being faithful, she grabs a knife and gets ready to sacrifice Isaac. Fortunately, he finds a trap door to the basement, and throws himself down before she can kill him.
Yep. It's gonna be one of those games.
The main game is a twin-stick shooter. Isaac can move at any angle, but only shoots (and by "shoot," I mean cry projectile tears) in the four cardinal directions, ninety-degree angles. You can find items that have different effects; some raise your health, give you more damage, a faster fire rate, increased range, speed, all kinds of things. And there are literally HUNDREDS of items, all of which can be combined with other items to make synergies that look and feel amazing.
Rebirth is technically an expansion. The original Isaac couldn't have Rebirth because it was made in Flash, with strict limitations. Rebirth became a full game instead, and my God, it was not a bad thing. The graphics are beautiful, the new items are awesome, the new content is great, and you don't even need a powerful computer to play it! Not to mention, the music is pretty dang good.
One of the best parts is that every run is different, thanks to procedural, random generation of the items, floors, enemies, rooms, etc. There are over four BILLION combinations to choose from, enough for over half of the world to play a completely different run simultaneously.
There are only a few problems. For example, sometimes it can feel just a little repetitive. Plus, the FPS lock can slow the game down on some weaker computers. The main problem is the price: the original Binding of Isaac was only $5; Rebirth is $15. A bit much, even though the game is technically infinite.
In the end, Rebirth lives up to its name. Like a phoenix, it died (dang Flash limits), but came right back, completely new and fresh, like an inkling in a fragrance store. You, too, will feel reborn, after experiencing this game you just can't stop playing.

TL:DR – Meltdown is a fun short term game with ‘drop-in’ multi-player co-op and there are still people playing online so you can join in. It’s a grind fest though, so if you’re looking for a quick “play-and-forget” game, this might not be for you. You’ll grow “satisfied” with the game within 5-6 hours
There’s no real story to the game, just a short cinematic intro video that shows the hero Zed landing on a platform ready to kick some♥♥♥♥♥ There are a couple of bosses, but they don’t talk to you and there’s no significant narration. You’re basically killing a bunch of nameless robots like a contestant in a game show.
Meltdown is an isometric or “top down” shooter with gameplay similar to Bastion, but with guns. Like Bastion, you can roll to dodge enemy attacks or get close enough to melee them. It’s similar to the game Alien Swarm in the way that you unlock weapons as you level up and choose your loadout at the beginning of each mission. A key difference though, is that in Meltdown you can upgrade your gear by spending money and chips that you find from fallen enemies.  Bear in mind that while upgrading gear does make a difference, the damage of weapons never really gets that much higher. So it’s not like Diablo where you start with 1-10 damage and end the game with 9,000 – 20,000 damage. Because of this, when a high level player joins the game of a lower level character, the damage difference between the two characters isn’t outrageous.
The level of your character is separate from your gear, and the two only interact when you unlock new gear at certain levels. A high level character might still be too poor to buy the good stuff. Each time you level up, you get a skill point to put into your 3 skill trees. Don’t be fooled when the game says there are 3 character classes. You will end up maxing all 3 trees, and frankly it doesn’t make too big of a difference which skill path you take first. All the skills are passive such as regenerating ammo or +5% damage.
When you reach the maximum level of 55 (all skill trees are maxed), you have the option to “prestige.” This means you reset your level, skills, mission progress, and gear. It’s basically like starting from scratch except you keep whatever money you’re currently holding. The game is broken down into 30 “randomly generated levels” and each time you finish a level, you unlock the next. For example to play mission 20 you need to have beaten mission 19. Honestly, even though the levels are randomly generated, they are all pretty much the same. You just keep moving to the upper -right direction to get to the end. The levels are very linear, you’re not going to get lost.
Pros:
+The game is beautiful in its simplicity. There’s no real inventory system to deal with and only a few things drop from fallen enemies, such as ammo, health, money, and chips. You want all of these. Grinding for loot is easy and the game itself is almost casual at times.
+The multi-player component is fun, though it seems incomplete. I didn’t see any way to actually “talk” even typing messages to people in your game doesn’t seem to be an option. Oh well, each level is like 10 minutes long and you’ll never see the other guy again.
Cons:
-Hard to find info for the game online since it’s so small. Because of this, it may be a little intimidating to get into. It’s not like you can ask a high level guy a question since you can’t talk in game. I didn’t understand what the prestige option did until I did some online research.
-The multiplayer experience gain doesn’t seem scaled correctly. If a level 1 character joins a high level game he will level up very very fast.
Overall, if you have the game and are considering whether or not to try it, definitely do. The download size is small and it’s pretty fun. You can also get about 20 Steam achievements in about 6 hours.

This isn't a terrible racing game, but considering Hydro Thunder Hurricane is the same price, and is a lot more fun, I would give this one a pass. The only reason I'm giving it a positive rating is because it scooches in at just being fun enough at some points, but it is straight up boring and/or annoying at others.
The main flaw that makes it suffer is the amount of tricks you need to pull off to win. These tricks feel kind of wooden, more like what you would find in a Dreamcast game or earlier, and they also hurt the game's sense of racing speed. It starts to feel less like a race and more like a precisely timed sequence of QTE's you have to memorize, as opposed to Hydro Thunder, where jumping still retains the game's sense of speed.
Additionally, other frustrations come up, like for example, police targeting only the player, and the leveling system of the game preventing you from winning new tracks unless you do a decent amount of grinding of the previous tracks. Compare this to Hydro Thunder where you are not gimped and you can have the full power of all boats from the get-go. The RPG like system does not fit a game like this because the tracks quickly start to get samey.
Unlike Hydro Thunder the game has an actual story mode. However, it's about as generic as you can get. While I like story in my racing games, I'm pretty much ambivalent about this one because it's extremely by the numbers. Go to place, win race, get new racer... yeah, that's about as deep as it ever gets. Besides some humorous character traits there's nothing to elicit much emotion whatsoever.
Overall the game just fails in comparison to Hydro Thunder in every way and unless you really feel the need to do a ton of tricks instead of racing then I would grab the former.

I'd had this on my Wishlist for a while after looking for something to scratch that Waverace 64 itch, finally picked it up and ultimately I'm quite dissapointed. I'm a big racing game fan, and I'm pretty forgiving in the genre, but this fell totally flat for me.
The environments and visuals are stunning, and there are a good number of them. This aspect of the game deserves praise.
However the racing I found incredibly dull - right from the get-go. Immediately bored. I think it's a combination of factors to be honest, but I didn't find it challenging or exciting, it really lacks something - the stunts were more like quick time actions, and the general experience was more like being on a theme park. I tried out all the tracks available to me and they all felt more like dioramas than tracks - beautiful but I'm just kind of going round like I'm on a wobbly log flume. Ultimately I can't recommend a racing game I don't enjoy racing in, and this is one of the few I've experienced.
And we need to talk about the water - because great water physics combined with clever track design could have redeemed things. Falling from a height is a very odd sensation, the water is clearly some kind of non-newtonian fluid - that all-important satisfying dip into the water simply isn't there. I'd have avoided drops altogether with the physics as they are, personally. The fact that there are 'slopes' of water, but no water movement is also bothersome, you're never contending with a current. Worse still there are corners with *banked* water - creatve license taken a little too far there I think - it's starting to look like you didn't really want to make a jetski game...
Dissapointing! But it seems a lot of the other reviewers enjoyed it, so it might depend on what you're after.

I don't quite know how to summarise this game as a whole, however this review should make it clear about what I think of it. It is an interesting reboot for sure and I was quite excited about if after first hearing the news. As time passed I calmed down and a few years later I finally played it and completed the campaigns for the three races. And to be completely honest the game felt a tad.... bland. It felt like a generic shooter combined with some neat, however crude visuals by today's standards, however I do not form my opinions just based on the appearance of a product. I would like to begin talking about the Marine's campaign. I found it to be more exciting as that of the Xenomorph's (alien), but not as captivating as the Predator's. The movement resembled that of a modern, generic shooter such as all the newer CoD games and I don't know why they bothered adding a jump mechanic to the Marine as it felt very useless compared to the Predator's and Alien's for say. The jump height is ridiculously low, like he jumps only about 5 inches in the air and the climbing mechanics felt jerky, inconsistent and very unrefined. I did appreciate the variety of weapons, I really could make my loadout my own by picking out different types of weapons, however I did not appreciate how the game reset the loadout at the start of a new mission, however I assume the developers wanted them to match to the bland cinematic videos. The story itself wasn't too bad as there were some characters more momorable than others, however the drama of the chestburster being inside the latino girl's chest still wasn't enough to bring it all together, still a better love story than Twilight. Right, onto the Alien, because I want to save the Predator for last. I found Alien's campaign to be the most lame, partly because it felt so short and partly because I felt so insignificant, despite the rather cool beginning of the campaign. The movement mechanics for the Xeno weren't as fun as they were in the old AVP games. The jerkyness and the constant transitioning with jump key (space bar for me) were quite immersion breaking as I didn't feel very graceful as the character furiously jumps through a vent. I find that the lack of the old "tried and true" mechanics takes away from the fun as these newer ones feel much more complicated, especially for Alien, but I simply dealt with it, however if they were to make a new  AVP game, I'd like for them to revert back to the simpler and more enjoyable mechanics because they shouldn't fix what's not broken. Okay, now for the hunter. Now this is where the game starts to look much more interesting to me... I like the Predator's equipment a lot, just like in the previous games there is a fair variety of it, although some are more useful than others... Nevertheless I probbaly enjoyed playing as him more than the other races. His helmet and vision took me back to my childhood and reminded me of the badass that hunted the poor ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ in the jungle. The stealth kills did feel satisfying, however I think the animations felt a bit TOO long as I often got killed while shoving my wristblades into fresh warm meat... Some faster animations would have been nice, something like those found in the new DooM, which is something that the developers should keep in mind if they decide to produce a new AVP title. The stoey of the young hunter made me feel more significant than the other two. I felt powerful, silent yet deadly, which is what the pred is all about. *SPOILER ALERT* His story involved cleaning up the mess created by humans and being a badass while doing it. That's not to say it was excellent, because it was far from it. Of course the events tie together when you play all the campaigns of the races, but it still feels lacking. The cinematic sequences were a tad cheesy sometimes, whereas the landing animations in the first level where the character uncloaks are totally badass. The boss fights also felt weak, especially the final boss for the Predator. I must say I expected more from it, however it will not stop me from recommending this game, because it is something different. It manages to mix in various gameplay styles in a way that is not out of place, instead they are shown through the medium of the three races. Now I cannot comment on the multiplayer as I do not see myself playing it, because I do not have much interest to it, although that might change in the future. Overall, I think this game is a tad under-rated and diserves more attention, I do recommend it and I think is something people should try.

I used to love Trove. And occasionally it sucks me back in. But even with closing on 700 hours of gameplay, I would not recommend this game to anybody
.
Fact: Trove is a grind-centric game, and always has been. Progression comes from two primary sources:
This would not be so bad if not for the fact that experience is throttled to incentivize buying a "subscription" in the form of "patron status", which effectively doubles progression rate. Then, in terms of mastery, you regularly receive premium lootboxes called "chaos chests" as dropped loot, however recent changes have account bound them and their contents, when their contents amount to more than a common crafting material.
When I started playing, monetization was relatively minimal. Patron always existed, but there were many players buying tradeable passes, driving the player economy. Most of the rewards and currencies could be traded, and the dev lead stated that monetization would not be a focus in the game. This has changed, rather rapidly, over the past year or so as more and more items are being locked to accounts, while cash shop equivalents in the form of loot boxes have popped up. Formerly fair sales have been replaced with a "loyalty currency" that pales in comparison. Tradeable premium currency and Patron Pass options have dwindled to incentivize personal purchase, killing the game economy. Double Experience Potions were added to "weekly sales", and experience gain silently decreased. And yet in spite of all of these revenue sources the servers function as bad (if not worse) today as they did before the monetization upscale, and content improvements are so infrequent that it's easy to believe the game has been abandoned only to suddenly see a news article about a major update some six months to a year later, with enough content to keep you busy for about two days.
To put it bluntly, the developers became greedy. I don't know if this is due to pressure from Trion Worlds (who do not have the best monetization track record) or the development team just fell to the dark side. Either way, I strongly recommend looking to other F2P games to waste your time. Warframe, Path of Exile, and Guild Wars 2 (not on Steam) are all highly recommended and survive and grow on completely non-abusive F2P models and are far more deserving of your time and attention than what Trove has become.
Should things change and the development of this game shifts to stop trying to milk every cent out of its users, I'll happily change this review. I fully understand that they the game has to remain profitable to remain alive, but there's a fine line between being profit-viable and consumer-abusive, and Trove sadly crossed that line a long time ago.

I'm nearing the end of the main campaign and can easily say that Kingdom Rush nails the formula for the perfect tower defense game. Each level is balanced with the right amount of difficulty with tons of replay value. I occasionally found myself stumped in the boss battles and special challenges.
The difference between Kingdom Rush and your typical TD is that the player can build rallied barracks to slow down enemy creeps from their fixed path. In addition to that, Kingdom Rush introduces three types of offense towers that branch out in two paths which can then be further customized with unique abilties; giving the player full control of the field.
I would definitely recommend Kingdom Rush to anyone interested in a tower defense that requires a good amount of thought and strategy.

I'm a huge RTS fan but have never bought a game in Early Access before, so Northgard had been on my watch list for ages, just waiting for the full release. But then yesterday I was bored and it was in the sale so curiosity overcame me and, honestly, I was blown away.
Just to make this clear, aside from the lack of a single player campaign, pretty limited tutorial instructions, and some reported issues with multiplayer, Northgard is more of a finished game than many others are months after release. There's still that campaign, some more tribes, and no doubt some other extras to come, and my only (tiny) gripe is that I think some more work is needed on balancing everything, but at £15 it's an absolute steal.
What you get is the spiritual successor to The Settlers that many of us have longed for for years. Older gamers and those using emulators will see elements of The Settlers 1 and 2, and I detected a bit of Genesia and some other long-forgotten classics. Younger gamers may pick up on The Settlers 7 (my favourite of the later games) and some of the better near-misses vying for the abandoned crown. And that's important when it comes to justifying an early access purchase, because The Settlers was always a game where the real fun was in the huge skirmish maps, not the more restricted campaigns. This is one of those games you'll go back to just for the fun of it.
In true Settlers style, it's pretty and it's pretty slow for an RTS, with the pace changing through the seasons and in response to (pretty frequent) incursions into your territory from the wildlife and your opponents. The expansion mechanic, which requires scouting territories and buying them out, is similar to the Settlers 7 mechanic and it does the job. It's nothing groundbreaking, but then it doesn't need to be.
Likewise, all the usual RTS / city builder mechanics are there, focused around generating food, money, resources, and 'fame', and building a warband to go raiding; and the Viking setting ties all this together very nicely. This means that even though the instructions are a little sparse it's still easy to pick up, and anyway part of the fun of a good RTS is working out how everything works. If this sounds a little less than enthusiastic, it's not meant to be. RTS is a hard genre to perfect because in the heat of a fight small niggles can quickly become deal breakers, but even in its unfinished state I haven't found any.
As other reviewers have said, Northgard has all the signs of becoming an absolute classic. It may already be one.

Sid Meier’s Civilization IV Colonization is essentially a cross between Colonization and Sid Meier’s Civilization IV. You collect Funding Fathers instead of researching, have a 3×3 grid around your colony for exploitation, but a 2×2 field once you get enough liberty bells (used to get FF). You have 300 instead of 100 storage per slot, but production values remain virtually the same, at 3 for non-specialist villagers. Trade with Indians is less lucrative than the original and prices in Europe is 3x for ships and artillery. Furthermore, you need a rancher and stables to breed horses and you get no free liberty bells. Units can enter tiles occupied by Indians or villages. This means that trade is simplified and downplayed in this remake.
Combat is improved to the point you don’t need to load/save all the time. Converts reduce the number of units in villages and might be demolished with no combat necessary. Units gain experience and have hitpoints similar to Civilization and ships are all different than Col in such a way that they’re all useful. The game is a lot easier and faster to play than the original. The map isn’t even big so you’ll end up with fewer and easier to manage colonies. I like placing colonies where the city function as a canal. This is much easier since you can use a village to move through that is located next to your city. You could potentially make it 3 or more in length if you don’t care about making crippled/small colonies.
Verdict:
The game is easy and not frustrating. You don’t need to cheat with save/load like you do in the original. It’s fun, but doesn’t capture the spirit of the original. I actually prefer Freecol (free) since it’s closer to the original. But I like this game as a casual game since it doesn’t force you to cheat all the time and has way better graphics and sound.

ICEY identifies itself as a "meta game" in disguise as an action game, but the action game is shallow, short, and unsatisfying, and the "meta game" is not composed of meaningfully interactive content. In effect, it is just a lackluster action game with some additional (albeit creative) attempts at commentary.
Production values are high; visual and audio content are detailed and polished, and some creative things are done with the storytelling and the interface. However, the most important aspect of a game is its gameplay, and here the gameplay is only a too-shallow vehicle for the delivery of the rest of the content.
Ultimately, the full completion of this game was not a meaningful or memorable experience.

In this game, you can be doing very well.  Your resource income has peaked, you feel confident.  But you just need to wait for the perfect opportunity to launch your assault on the enemy.  Just one more villager, to maximize your potential.  Patiently waiting for your building to be upgraded.  You carefully watch the progress of your village.  Suddenly, you hear the sound of a horn.
What's this?  A Draugr?? Wolves?  It is the middle of winter, so it must be a dimwitted Draugr, crossing into your border.  Quickly you send your warchief, aided with a handful of well trained warriors to defend your land.
Scrolling north, through your proud village, you see no Draugr, but a small group of skirmishers.  The blood thirsty warriors begin ravaging several of your fishermen in that area.  Help is on the way, but by the looks of it, they'll arrive too late to defend your peaceful gatherers.  Hastily, you must ensure your undefended men and women vacate until reinforcements arrive.  It's too late for one of your men, who was the first to rebuke the enemy, and the first to fall to their hands.  The other 2 were safely moved into a neighboring territory, just in time.   The Chief is here to battle now.
You hear the sound of a second horn, and look to the west.   A second enemy clan now marches on your lands.  You must separate your forces, and attempt to thwart the invaders.  Meanwhile, you've neglected to focus on the battle in which your Stoic Warchief fights.   He was faster than your Shield Bearers, too fast.. He's been wounded badly, and the enemy knows it.
It cannot be.... A third War Horn sounds.  This time, it is the Draugr...  3 deadly Draugr begin slashing a pivitol area, your most productive land.  A land where both Woodcutters and Hunters share grounds to hunt and gather firewood.  The Draugr hack and slash your men to bits.. by the time you gain control of the area and move your villagers to safety 3 are dead.
Drastic time call for drastic measures.. You initiate a draft.. any and all healthy must take up arms to fight!  Those once peaceful merchants, now carry swords and axes.  You send your new recruits to reclaim the land the Draugr are slowly claiming as their own.
You look to the north again; Your Chief has fallen.. Only a few battered and beaten warriors stand. You look to the west, the second battalion was victorious.  You look south east.. The draugr have killed 2 honorable men, but your land has been secured.  You hear an unfamiliar sound.  It resembles a coin purse falling to the ground.  Then again, a second coin purse..
Shortly thereafter, you hear a War Horn.. Followed by a second war horn!! 2 of your shores have been attacked by mercenaries!  One of the two is where you landed on Northgard Isle.  Your Town Hall.  You must defend this land at all costs.  Everyone must re-deploy to defend your base!!
Your people are now unhappy.. In the midst of the fighting one must not focus on his stomach... But now your villagers are starving!!!
HOW CAN THIS HAPPEN!?  Moments ago, your lands were flourishing.  Now you can't seem to feed even the remnants of your war party.  Realizing your mistake, you scroll north again to move your fishermen back into their homes..
That is when you notice the unmistakeable sight of a horrifying, formidable, army... And they're going to take your land.  There is nothing you can do about it.
OK, enough story time.. What I just described is a common scene from this game.  Be prepared, be vigilant, and be adaptable.  Otherwise the enemy will march an army right up your rear end.

Very fun game! Civ 4 Col is a remake of the original Colonization. In this game, you play as the English/Dutch/Spain/French. Immedietly, it's alarming to me. No portugese, despite the fact they colonized all of SA? These limitations will become more and more obvious as it goes on.
As you build your colonies, micromanaging the cities as they grow, you need to get Food (for growth outside of immigration), and several resources. Some are useful to build with (ore, lumber), others can be compared to Civ luxuries to sell and barter with. The economy is very detailed, with resources going up and down in price back in Europe. As you countinue building, you have to fight or buy space from natives, contend with your european colonization rivals, and the Royalty overseas. They will raise taxes, demand large sums of money, and they also serve to help you out when you make bad settlement choices. (It does get annoying once you know what you're doing and the king pops up to tell you you're not settling on the coast, or in a food poor location.)
Remember what I said about limitations? Well, there is only one victory condition, which can be jarring to those who come from Civ. You need to win a war of independence. By building bells (i.e culture, which does help borders pop but cities can only use the first 6 tiles around them anyways), you get rebel sentiment. When it gets high enough, and you have enough foudning fathers, you delcare independence and fight off your respective king's forces.
All in all, a fun game, however a few things damper it. It's a short game, although with a lot of replayablily. The AI is horrible, unless you install mods. Mods act just like they do in Civ IV, and mods save the game. I reccomend TAC or AODII, which can be found at Civfanatics.

OVERVIEW (For those with no time to spare)
Realm of the Mad Got (RotMG) is a roguelike that i would describe as both punishing and rewarding. It is most definately addictive and fun when you get the hang of it and getting a white bag (extremely rare, unique loot drop from bosses) only furthers this. The game is very grindy but progression is definately noticeable the more you work on your character.
PROS
+ Gameplay is easy to pick up and learn
+ Objectives marked clearly on a scalable minimap and by a small directional marker on your screen
+ Good sence of progression from level-ups, stat increases and better loot drops
+ 14 classes each with a unique ability and stats
+ Fairly in-depth tutorial
+ Pixelised graphics look retro and in many cases quite nice
+ Vault system for saving or storing loot for later
+ Trading with other people
+ Guilds
CONS
- Occasional massive lag spikes and disconnections
- Very punishing death
- Optional purchases can strongly affect gameplay
- Graphics, whilst nostalgic, are lacking
- Loot system can be very unrewarding in many cases as it is based on RNG
CORE GAMEPLAY ELEMENTS
Permadeath: Once you character dies they are gone forever along with anything you were carrying, as is typical for some roguelikes.
Vault system: This allows you to store loot  so that you do not lose it when you character dies and you can use it on future characters. This is great because it allows you to feel like you are progressing even if you die. Can beexpanded to fit more loot with real money.
Pets: These will keep you alive and support you in combat as they can provide valuable effects, apart from looking snazzy when following you. Most importantly they can heal you constantly for free allowing you to stay in a fight for much longer or get back into one faster. Each pet has 3 abilities and you start with one of those. Abilities can bet upgraded and unlocked by "feeding" your pet unwanted loot and pet food and "fusing" it with another pet of the same type and rarity to get a rarer more powerful pet.
Dungeons: A great source of good loot and stat potions (permanently increase a stat by a bit). Some are harder and made to be done in larger groups. Gateways to dugeons are randomly dropped by some enemies in the main realm, and some rarer dungeons, consequently more rewarding and harder, are dropped by very difficult bosses and enemies which spawn randomly.
Abilities: Powerful useable items which consume you mana points that replenish over time. Each class has its own unique ability which only that class can use. E.g. Priest has a tome which heals the user and any allies in a learge area. Abilities often define the role a class will play with some unique untiered ones heavily changing their effect.
Stats: Each character has 8 stats; life, mana, defence, attack, vitality, wisdom, dexterity and speed. Here is what they do:
- Life: You basic hitpoint. If they reach zero then you die. Regenerates constantly at a slow rate.
- Mana: Points which are used to cast your ability. Regenerates constantly at a slow rate.
- Defence: Reduces the amount of damage taken from an attack by an amount defined by its value. Boosted by armour, rings, and some wapons + abilities.
- Attack: Increases the amount of damage you do. Most weapons have unspecified multiplers which increase the effect of this stat.
- Vitality: Increases the rate at which you health regenerates.
- Wisdom: Increases the rate at which your mana regenerates. Some abilities have effects which increase based on this stat
- Dexterity: Increases the rate at which your weapon fires. Some weapons have separate fire-rate modifiers.
- Speed: Increases the speed at which your character moves (duh).
Each stat can be increased up to their maximum value for that character via stat potions. Further increases beyond that point are done by equiping idems with stat bonuses, using temproary stat increase items or by being buffed by some classes' abilities.
Grinding: This is nessaecary in this game as it allows you to aquire stat potions and better gear, and seeing that most loot dropped is based of RNG particularly when in a group, repetition is needed for the greatest effect. This sounds boring but if you learn to be efficient or do it with a friend it is very fun. Maxing out your stats with potions or getting tot tier loot is incredibly satisfying and make a noticable differance when compared to your state befor grinding.
CONCLUSION
This review was fairly lengthy but I hope that I have provided all of the most important information needed. If you like a relaxing game then this probably isn't for you. The bullethell-like enemies and threat of death will always keep you on your toes, not to mention that time and effort is needed to truly make great progress. That said the gameplay is simple but very fun and can often require quick thinking and surprising enough good reflexes. If you like roguelikes whick allow alot of freedon on thepart of the player and you like games which allow multiplayer interaction then this will be a fun for you. Pick it up and try it if you like. Its free and most likely will always be free, so its great to try with friends.

In my 17 years of gaming, never have I come across a game that is so bad. It is basically a point and click game. The aim of the game is to locate and destroy/get rid of a bomb by clicking on objects on the screen. There are several stages which each has several levels.
The good points are that you get lots of levels (100) which you can happily sink alot of time in.
Now for the bad points. First off, although the game tries to be humorous by having you embarass or do terrible things to the characters in the game, some of the actions that the main character does may be offend/disturb people (e.g. peeing on an alien). Second is that when you start the game there is literally no tutorial which was somewhat frustrating trying to figure out what to do. Third issue is that when you fail to locate the bomb, you will proceed to the next level. The game then goes through all five levels of the stage untill you have disarmed the bomb in each stage. This forces you to remember exactly which items not to click on, but the main problem is that it is somewhat difficult to find which items can be interacted with. Fourth issue is that the game is extremely repetitive. Once you finished the first level, all the other levels are exactly the same except with new scenery. Fifth issue is that the music is really annoying as it plays 1 track for the ENTIRE game.
If you like point and click games, avoid this game. If you like a fun and enjoyable games, avoid this game. It isn't even worth $1 let alone $5.

I'm a twenty-two year old man that plays this game on occasion, and I'm not ashamed of it. It's a pretty fun way to pass the time if you don't feel like playing anything else at the moment. It's basically a minecraft meets mmo sort of deal, and though I don't really play minecraft, I still like playing this sometimes, more for the loot-based rpg aspect than anything else. Yes, there is a "building system", but to say it's a bit restrictive compared to other crafting/building games is a bit of an understatement, to be completely honest, though, personally, that doesn't really bug me. What does bug me at times is the almost occasional delay in the monster's health drop when attacking them, so say you attack a monster four times, sometimes it's health will only drop twice at first, then twice more after a few moments, instead of dropping all four times when it should. Other than that, I don't have any complaints about the game. Though I have to admit, it's hard for me to complain about a game as simple as this can really be, regardless of how many things may be "wrong" with the game. It's just that kind of game, a game that, in my own opinion, shouldn't be taken seriously in terms of player preformance or anything like that, but that's just how I see it. If you just want a nice little hack 'n slash to play to pass the time on something entertaining, then by all means, play this. Kids will like the hell out of this game, and even some adults, myself included, though as I mentioned before, only on occasion. One quick side note about two of the games I just mentioned, if you've been wanting to try diablo 3, try path of exile before spending money on d3. [DISCLAIMER: This review is done based on playing the single player game on Hard difficulty only and comparing it alot to AVP 1999]
Had high expectations for this game. I played the first AVP (1999) gold edition and it's one of my all time favourite. Went through it and did all achievements and completed every normal and bonus level with Director's cut -difficulty. So I thought: "Same people do an even better AVP game with better graphics in the same spirit as the original"
Oh how wrong I was. I started the game with nightmare difficulty, but soon realized there is no saving in levels. Even when I pressed "save game" and even made a save file, it loaded right from the start of level. Frustrated, I started playing the hard difficulty.
I played first the marine campaign. It felt the aliens were too tanky, they took many bursts to head with a pulse rifle from a short distance before dying. And no use to bother shooting them in the body or limbs, because you'll be dead before you grind the alien to death. The story was very straightforward. No different ways to get to places and no use to run from the aliens, because in most cases the next event wouldnt trigger before you've killed every alien... I found that frustrating that - for example - it says "survive until the dropship arrives" and you can run around for as long as you want and the dropship won't arrive before you've killed every single hostile. And that same thing went on in every campaign.
Also fighting the androids was very annoying as you can't crouch for cover. In fact any playable character cannot crouch in the game. The enemy marines and androids on the contrary could crouch and otherwise take cover. Also, the hit stun of the androids was kind of inconsistent as some times a shot in the body or head would activate stunned sequence and sometimes they wouldn't react anyway to continous spray of fire.
The alien campaign was next on the line. I found the controls clunkier than the first AVP game, you couldn't climb every surface properly and had to press space to get into vents.
Stealth killing enemies would have been fun, if not for the long fatality animations... During the fatality, your character is helpless and enemies can still damage you. Also the prompt to make a stealth kill doesn't always appear when it apparently should. Especially when you are attached on a wall, you can stick your alien-face to a marine's hair and still not get the prompt for a stealth kill. If you just attack in that situation, the marine won't die from the first hit, not even the heavy attack... And will alert the others nearby. This gets very frustrating after a while.
In short, as in AVP 1999 the alien felt like an agile killing machine, in this game it feels somewhat clumsy and bugged.
Last campaign to go was the Predator. He has the power meter which wears out as you use energy weapons. In fact, you can get two fully charged shots and you're out. After that, it's close combat for you before you find the next power cell. Of course you can use the non charged shots, but they'll only stun the alien/human. The close combat is a nice idea, blocking, light attack and heavy attack... but as you get disoriented when attacking and there is a very inconvenient delay in the heavy attack (meaning, you can't hold to charge at all, the attack just comes couple of seconds after pressing the button and there is no way to hold nor cancel it). Add the fatality camera lock to the mix and you get very clunky close combat. Why would you ever use the fatality when it's slower to do and locks you still to be an easy target? Also the stealth feels a bit inefficient, but it might be just the hard mode.
I never finished the Predator campaign, as the hand to hand combat irritated the hell out of me. Maybe it gets better later as you get more weapons... If I bring myself to play it to the end, I'll update this review accordingly.
That was all the negative about this game and the reason why I wouldn't recommend it. There was also lot of good stuff and I even if the levels were a grind in some places, it didn't matter as I like hard games. This game just was hard for many wrong reasons... And worst of all, it did worse job in many places than it's predecessor.
I can list some positive stuff in the end:
- Cutscenes introduce quite interesting story, being a fan of the franchise I liked it!
- Predator and alien jump mechanics were quite good when you got used to them
- Game looks overall good for it's age
- The levels look good
- Music is atmospheric (although sometimes the reactive music comes a bit out of place)
- Marine campaign was scary at times
- Mostly good pacing, quiet parts and action parts in reasonable intervals
- Multiple hand to hand combat moves (even if the implementation was poor)
- Fatalities and stealth kills look good, at least the first twenty times
- I feel got my 5€ worth of playing already and there's still the predator campaign to finish and a couple of multiplayer modes to try with friends

I'm a Riptide GP 2 veteran here, so here are my two cents about this sequel
I decided to change my opinion of this game as I put a little bit more hours into it. However, I still mantaining my initial observations about it. The difference is that I would recommend it now instead.
The game has all the annoyances of previous titles in the series, without having any of the fun things that made those previous games enjoyable. It's still a game about grinding so that you can buy a bike and upgrade it, but now the bike gets nerfed down when entering races bellow the stage in which you acquired that bike. What the actual f$%k were these people thinking! However, there are plenty of events to keep you ocupied, that will tend to put you on the same tracks over and over again.
The color palette on some races is super crappy, so you will find yourself racing in cities where the water is grey, the buildings are grey, the sky is grey, and the obstacles that knock you down from your bike are ALSO grey. There are three difficulties in the game, easy, medium, and hard. Hard is unbeatable, and the other two make you feel unaccomplished, effectively making the game pointless.
I don't think I have ever been so angry with a game, and to further exacerbate this, I was (still am) totally hooked with GP2. Riptide GP2, this game's predecessor is a much more simple game, but orders of magnitude more fun to play.  I still believe that most of the flaws in this game can be corrected with a simple patch though. So there is hope for this game still.

Ah, GTA III.
It took me a while to "discover" this game. Sure I had seen it at the store and had even picked up the game to look at the artwork and screenshots but for some reason I never bought it. That is until a co-worker of mine, at the time, did a story on violence in video games. I worked at a TV News station at the time and the story was definately NOT pro game or pro GTA. After watching someone bring in their PS2 and played a bit so they could record some footage I was hooked and went and bought the game.
GTA III is a sandbox game and very non-linear. Actually if you want to visit the rest of the areas in the game you do have to complete the threshold of missions to unlock those parts of the game but you can take your time and do other things in the mean time.
Today the graphics look a bit dated but back in it's day the game was pretty cutting edge.  The controls were pretty easy to pick up though aiming the weapons needed some help. Driving the cars (which is the gist of the game) is straight forward too and all the cars have different capabilities. A sports car drives like a sports car while a truck drives like a truck.
The game has plenty of controversies to be sure. One of them is the ability to pick up ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s to "heal" you.  After you are done with your tryst you can, though are not required to, kill the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ to get your money back. Critics lambast the game for the ability to do this but realistically the game presents you with a moral choice and it's up to you to do, or not do, bad things in the game.
I do enjoy this game though it's harder for me to play it now then it was over 10 years ago. I tend to be the player who only wants to unlock stuff to explore and when I do I get bored with the missions.  I guess in reality, I never did finish the game. I unlocked the last island and did a number of quests but I spent most of my time driving around in cool sports cars and exploring the game world.
This was a defining game and because of that it should be checked out. I have fond memories of my time spent in Liberty City.

ICEY is a 2D side-scrolling action game and a META game in disguise. As you follow the narrator's omnipresent voice, you will see through ICEY's eyes and learn the truth about her world. The narrator will constantly urge you in one direction, but you must ask, "Why? Why am I following his directions?“
Remember The Stanley Parable? The self conscious walking sim? ICEY is like that, but with platforming and hack and slash combat. It nails the narrative and the looks, and the music is great, but the combat is debatable. The mechanics are solid, as per every hack and slash game you have combos, special moves, dodges, etc. The problem with it is the sheer amount of enemies in one encounter and the fact that you can be easily stunlocked. When you're leveled up and/or in easy mode it's ok, but on harder mode after the nth repetition of the same encounter you just start mashing buttons and keep your fingers crossed for the outcome. And one encounter might be 15 enemies in three waves of five (f*** you elevator section). Ugh...
Other than the infuriating combat tho the game is quite solid. There are some branching paths, the narrative is interesting and quite funny and as I already mentioned the game looks and sounds really nice. It's a short one though, at roughly 4-5 hours, plus some time for hunting missed achievements. All in all easy recommendation if you like games breaking the 4th wall and play it on easy (if not on easy it's still recommended, but you'll need lots of patience and/or skill).
I liked:
* the story
* nice gfx
* awesome music
* overall feel of the game
I disliked:
* combat where enemies can easily stunlock you
Get this if:
* you liked The Stanley Parable's and can stomach the combat sections
Don't get this if:
* you don't have the patience or skill to get through the fighting sections

To clarify, that is not to say that the game is a stern critique, it is also very humorous in the way it presents its 4th wall breaking at times, which are accentuated by the narrators quality voice acting (the English-speaking one, haven't heard the Chinese one).
Highly recommended.

About 2 and a half years ago, I was a few months into my freshman year of college. I'd lost my 3 closest friends from high school (the only friends I've ever really had), was tanking my classes, and was going through a period of alcoholism and depression. I spent my nights alone. Even my roommate told me I was too depressing to be around, and would avoid any attempts I tried to make at becoming friends.
Then I discovered Starbound.
Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ did this game blow me away. The sheer amount of exploration, the utterly free and non-restrictive nature of the construction system... It was like I was immersed in my own universe. I finally had a place to do anything I wanted. I made myself a vast system of cities, complete with merchants and civilians. I'd go into this more, but it's impossible to describe with words how much fun I was having. The best part? I actually stopped drinking, because the game was more fun when I was sober. Hell, my grades even started improving as a result.
After the first major update when outposts were added and systems were wiped, I was really bummed. But it wasn't a huge problem- the update added plenty of stuff to do, and polished combat and construction, so I didn't really mind all that much. It was just another start for another adventure. This time I made a system of planets with societies- on one of the lava covered planets, I successfully constructed a HUGE housing system under the lava. And on one of the ocean planets, I made what I thought was a pretty good recreation of the first level of Bioshock 1.
That was about 6 months ago.
This update took what was probably my favorite game of all time and crushed it. The interface is horrible. The systems were wiped AGAIN, and this time it feels like it was for no reason. Nothing new or groundbreaking was added. It's all just gone.
I guess the game would be fun for me if I just picked it up today. But knowing what it once was, and knowing I'll never experience any of that joy or wonder while I play this ever again, it's pretty terrible.

This is a nice compromise for me with most of the features I would want in a game like this. It has genuinely fun gameplay, nice graphics, and even basic multiplayer.
Where it wins:
The short missions make it perfect when I'm just killing some time. I can pick a mission based on anticipated time to complete if I have something I need to do soon. It's also nice to see that the Steam version is a complete game, unlike the mobile version. The gamepad setup is nice, and the aim assist makes it easy to work with. Multiplayer is fun to play as well. Well worth the $1.74 I paid when it was on sale.
Where it fails:
It is made for mobile and there are some nonfunctional remnants left over from that, namely the leaderboard buttons. The multiplayer doesn't let a set or group of players to follow eachother through missions. It also said that if you are having trouble on a level, play multiplayer to make it easier, but when additional players are in a mission, there are more bots that can take much more damage, making it more than twice as difficult, so it more than negates the concept of getting help. The aim assist, while being handy, can also hinder your play. It automatically targets things for you. When there are power nodes, it's difficult to get back on target with bots, or the bots you actually want to target.
Overall, it's worth playing, if you catch it while it's on sale, but I sure hope the devs are planning on making some improvements, especially with the aim assist, multiplayer, and benifits of being Prestige 3 Level 55. I'd also kind of like to see a good way to reset the data to restart from scratch.

Alrighty'o. Now that this game is release and officially in the 1.0 there's a lot more room to give a more in depth review.
As an oldie starbound player, who played since release, the starbound that I see now is nowhere near the starbound I used to know. The oldie starbound had a silly energy system with no regen cooldown and augments that must be found in lone tech chests in some obscure world, along with the stupidest strat of getting enough coal to fuel the ship and jump to the next threat-level desert-planet to instantly mine any of the resources it has since sand worked like snow now with ores inside it, impervium I have no idea still exists (I doubt it does) but it shall forever have a special place in my heart.
, goodness me, they have reworked it in a way where the new energy system and weapons go hand in hand together making the combat experience fun and refreshing once more. From simple single-swings from any weapon now have their own special doodads on it with their own unique playstyle that fits that one special edgy guy in your party. The guns feel like a new set of weapons and definitely made the die-hard me of the old energy system to concede and actually had a great time using the new guns. That was definitely a quirk for me when it came to the unstable stages of old starbound. Each enemy had their own type of skill sets and makes thinking on the fly a pretty important thing for first time players. Definitely for the better since I really didn't like how mobs just walked at you.
The one thing that I quite recently loved is that the
. I know, I know I haven't talked about the new things; I'll get to that later: the important things are first. Anyways I digress. In the ye olden days there was no types of stars, there were threat levels. Started from 1 to X (X being 10) and the speedrun strat for old starbound was to go to said threat level that contained the next ore for better armor. There were just more powerful enemies and the easiest way to deal with that was to tunnel your way through the map and avoid confrontation altogether. That was the flaw for letting fresh characters get access to better armor from the get go with only one thing that's preventing them to just go straight to impervium (end game ores). There were chip cards to upgrade your character to create the next tier armor. You just needed ore from the previous tier to access the next one which was the only thing that was stopping your form getting end-game armor right off the bat.
. What they did I think is genius, bringing better usage for the EPP system since there was little to no reason to go to the moon, and made the system a REQUIREMENT for you to even set foot on the dangerous planets. Once there was no reason to go to extremely cold or extremely hot planets since other tame planets had exactly the same ores in terms of threat levels, to now needing the upgrade your survival system in order to go to those planets which are the only ones who have said special ores.
But everything was tied together with the wonderful
. I was tempted to skip the tutorial since I thought "Oh! Now they made it possible to skip the stupid 're-activate the ship and enable the teleporter and Manipulator' but, I decided against that and boy was I glad that I didn't skip it. It had a very compelling backstory as to why you fled space compared to the old verson's "You're on a ship. Do stuff," without much guidance for the newbies. The quests help give players a sense of direction as they progress through the game and some others like one of my party members who opted to make a little settlement on a planet. The choice is yours. I, for one, wanted to reach end-game armor like I always had. But I realized that could be bad since my fun would be over then and there. Double buts, I could simply look through planets and find side quests, complete the main storyline, expand my ship (through totally legal means) and redo some of the old quests that I have completed and blast my way through with pretty broken weapons. So I decided that I had more than just getting end-game armor to be doing.
Do it. This game has changed and you can take my word since I had played this game since it's early beta release with my brother. So if you saw old starbound, forget her. She's a new game now and you're going to love her now.
tl;dr (I am dissapointed if you are just reading this) New combat system, reworked energy, better story and quest guidance, game progression rework. Game is good now. Get it.

Riptide GP continues its Journey to become a little bit more Hydro Thunder with each Sequel.
Now we have a mix of lap races and A-B point races (which more racing games need cause LONG A-B races are a best), with far more Hydro Thunder style set pieces happening, Such as a track turning into a battle zone with what look to be Pirate ships attacking. Great. Tracks also now have mutiple routes that can open up during a race, and hidden shortcuts to find.
Hot laps are gone, replaced now with Slalom races, which anyone who has played Wave Race 64 would be familiar with, its also kind of akin to the Ring challenges in Hydro Thunder Hurricane (though I prefered those personally)
Controls and general feel of the game is improved over the previous game, Feeling less like a game designed for Mobile and more like a proper racing game for proper games devices. The previous games very much felt like all the corners were just design for full speed and full turning to accomodate less control fidelity. Now they seem a little more varied.
That said, the game still retains some of its Mobile origins, with 3 star ratings per event (whats wrong with just 1st, 2nd, 3rd/Gold, Silver, Brozne, whys it gotta be stars?) and a difficulty curve that seems to be based on the usual mobile approach of come back later when you have better stuff.
Ai is competent, whilst it doesnt take shortcuts and apparently lacks rubberbanding its aggresive enough to keep up via stunts and boosting.
Options wise the game lacks any real configurability, opting to just have a few pre-sets to pick from and then an option to change the rendering resolution. This could really do to be expanded so we can actually confgure individual aspects of the visuals, as it is theres currently no way to turn off the motion blur when boosting and that sucks (cause I'm playing on a toaster and it doesnt like it, no sir.)
In closing, Riptide GP: Renegade is a great improvement over the past iterations and well worth picking up for anyone who is a fan of Arcade racing games in the vein of Hydro Thunder or Wave Race.

At first launch, it seems a bit like a buggy port from a console or phone/tablet. The tutorial starts by saying that you need to chase another racer, and that it will auto accelerate. Cue me sitting there waiting for it to start moving. Turns out, auto accelerate is disabled by default. Cue me trying to press W to get the jetski to move. No effect. Space. No effect. Up arrow. *Starts moving*. Groan - bad default keyboard map. Changing the keys is a harrowing experience too - reminds me of some dodgy old games circa 1995. And you can't use the mouse to move the viewport or boost either - strictly a keyboard affair and the automatic camera mode. Plus, until you restart the race, it gives the wrong hints for what keys to press... It even suggested that I "tilt my device" to turn at one point - er, pretty sure there is no accelerometer in any part of my computer...
I've played the previous Riptide games, so I figure I can try boosting and doing tricks in the tutorial - no go. Turns out they don't become active until you start playing for real, at which point you kinda get infotips showing you how to use them anyway... So, my advice is just skip the tutorial completely. Whether or not you have played the previous games, you are not missing anything except a bit of story...
Apart from that, graphics are pretty gorgeous, race tracks have hints about turns and stunt areas, at least to start with (I haven't seen an option to turn them off for a more authentic experience - I do know how to look at the mini-map, you know!). Will play some more and see how it goes...

Civilization 4: Colonization with the amazing Revolution and Religion mod is among the very best strategy games I ever have played (and I have played pretty much all of the best strategy games from the 1980'ies until now). The 1994 Colonization was a classic and one of my all-time favourites, and this version with the RaR mod installed is a vastly improvement over that. This game offers you gameplay that feel quite unique and fresh even when compared to Civilization 4 and 5. The resource gathering and crafting elements of the game are very important, entertaining and at a moderate level of trickiness that keep you engaged and interested, while not overwhelming you. Exploration is fun with the tribes you meet, and backtracking to keep the treasures you discover safe on the return trip to the colonies with docks. The immigration mechanics are very cool, and the trade system is deep and rewarding. Combat is maybe the most civlizationesque part of the game, while the above mentioned elements are very different from the traditional Civ gameplay, but that is not a problem since it is solid and engaging as it is. Diplomacy is also quite ordinary Civ.
Conclusion: Definitely recommend this game (with the RaR mod installed), it is absolutely brilliant. Man, I love this game. The score is 10 out of 10.

I really am enjoying 140. Minimalist abstract art and design at its best. Every puzzle is unique and rewarding. As I played I became more and more aware of the music until I was relying on it to progress.
140 is a game with no filler. You must use everything you're given to solve the puzzles. But at the same time, this game is not your enemy trying to make you fail while you battle against it to win (like in most games e.g. your typical shooter or racing game), it is there to guide you through by teaching you as you go. When a new element is introduced in a puzzle game, so often I am just left to figure out myself what to do with it. In 140, you are subtly shown the mechanics of new elements before you must interact with them. This allows the player to always feel confident and in control. As the complexity and difficulty increased at just the right pace, I began to find some puzzles had a bit more too them than they seemed. I would have to watch as the elements reacted to the music and learn their patterns. Some of the puzzles may take you a minute or two to complete, but you are never confused for more than a few seconds. It’s the perfect mix of mental and physical skill.
If you’ve enjoyed games like Thomas Was Alone or The Impossible Game you will probably enjoy this.

独特的游戏模式和舒服的环境渲染，很享受那种代入感。
缺点
游戏的战斗机制不是很平衡，前期的游戏模式单一。画面令一部分玩家不适（这虽然算不上）。

One of the best games Ive ever played. Im biased Ill admite, I love this genre. Terraria is one of my all-time favorites and Starbound is just more of what I love, only in SPACE! Which makes it even better! If you love the action RPG-lite, adventure, mine, craft, explore genre - you simply cannot go wrong here.
What are you waiting for? Go Go GO!
Update for 1.0 - While many out there feel like theyve been cheated somehow - I still adore the game. Yes some things we had during the development stages have been removed - and while I do wish those things hadnt been removed - it hasnt diminished my enjoyment in the slightest. Im also firmly of the mind that many, if not all, of these things will be re-implemented as we move away from 1.0. I guess what Im saying is Starbound was worth it, and still is worth it. Too many negative reviews for things that changed from the development stages to live - and thats really not fair to the guys and gals who built the game - as we all know things change as something is being worked on.
I also think alot of folks just dont 'get' the idea of a true sandbox - which Starbound is. Terraria was a metroidvania game stuck in a single, small-ish sandbox map. It worked for what it is was and I adored every second of it. Starbound isnt a metroidvania in the same sense - its more of a giant sandbox with very light metroidvania elements.
Terraria gave you gear (rather quickly if you knew what you were doing) that made you near godlike at 'endgame'. Starbound gives you powerful gear but still relies on your skill in combat more than just numbers. Ive yet to feel like I could destroy everything in the games verse - Im very strong, but still vulnerable. I like that, keep you on your toes.
Folks mention the planets being boring. Well, as sandboxes and procedural generation go - after a while yes, you are going to see alot of similiar and/or identical things. Its the nature of the beast. We ALL know this. So to give negative marks based on the very nature of the system is pointless. Did any of you really think we were going to get millions of completely unique worlds? Im 100+ hours into 1.0 and Im *still* finding new stuff I havent seen, sure its uncommon at this point, but its out there...
Overall I think Starbound is pretty damn great for what it is trying to do. And I feel certain its only going to get better with time =)
Quick 2017 update: Starbound still maintains the bar - no matter what negativity people like to throw around - there is nothing else out there like it.
