Though my steam won't show you this, I have sunk many, many hours into this game; mainly due to the fact I played off of the original launcher and not off of steam itself. Also, this is from a guy who says, "Free-to-play, all the way!" So take it with a grain of salt, Pay-to-players.
The game itself is a fun one featuring unique classes like the Fae Trickster (a cute lil' fairy) or the Candy Barbarian (a big fellow with two swords and a sugar craze) or even the Tomb Raiser (a literal necromancer with an army of yes-men-skellies behind him). The variety of classes is nothing in comparison to the gigaton of mounts you can find in this game, which the game seems to constantly remind you of. Trove even offers a rare feature most mmo's seem to shake their heads to: flying fast. Later in the game, you acquire flight (gliding really) that allows you to cover insane amounts of distance and that completely blew my mind! (Move over Aion!)
But let's not sugarcoat it, the game's story is a lie. In my time of playing this game, I have been the hero that slayed many a foul beasties. But no matter how many foul beasties my experience bar consumed, I never felt satisfied. This story is of a hero (that's you) fighting insane amounts of the same enemies (too many reskins) to force your level bar to go up just one more time. All the while, you will be leveling your Master Bar up and getting cool rewards for your effort. But after you realize that being God is boring and all the mounts in the game won't make you fight again, you start to loath this game more and more.
I won't lie: this game was fun and I enjoyed it thoroughly, but having to ride (often fly, which was fun) from one dungeon to another to kill a boring boss, break a box with (often poor) loot inside, then rinse and repeat was a tad dull. There are events to "spice things up," but they grow dull quickly. Everything in the game CAN be obtained completely free (as I have), but it's no secret that the Dev's like the people who pay more and make the game (SUPREMELY) easy for them. Every class, item, mount, weapon skin, character skin, pet, really anything can be bought from the pleyer-driven market (at least the items for crafting them), but the effort a free-to-play player has to struggle through to get the in-game currency (flux. It's "flux") is almost as ridiculous as the amount of items you have to collect to craft such items in the first place.
I LOVE the concept of this game; the freedom, the abilities, the classes, the seasonal events, the endless stream of mounts... but when the day comes to an end and I watch as the wealthy ride their "exclusive" mounts over my head and wear their radiant armor (REALLY end game armor), I look up from my low branch and think,
"I've worked so hard to get here and get all the things I did," I would laugh, "Pay-to-winners will never understand what treasures I hold."
Free to play, pay to win faster, but winnable all the same. (There's no actual "end," but you know how mmo's work by now, right? It's all about the experience, I think. That's where it counts, I say.)

Where to begin...?
Never an easy task. As the cryptic narrator with a badass voice that slightly resembles
James Coburn's gruff bass performance cooked with Tommy Lee Jones' dry wit and with a pinch of Eastwoodness likes to say, "Proper story's supposed to start at the beginning. Ain't so simple with this one."
Sounds cryptic enough?
So anyway, the name of the game is Bastion, and it is one of the
best indie action RPG games to date.
The script, the vocal performance(s), the action, the graphics and artistic direction, the beautiful acoustic soundtrack...
I could go on and on and on.
The story is surprisingly good; it is mysterious, very well told, gripping and emotional.
You are a young man, lovingly nicknamed only "The Kid" by the narrator - a tough, laconic and capable
white haired builder in service of Caelondia, the flying city in a fantastic world.
The Calamity (in other words, catastrophe of epic proportions) has struck, leaving only shreds of the entire civilization
that was once your home.
Your friends, neighbours - all gone. Turned to ash statues.
You go in search for survivors. Sooner or later, you find some. Some are friendly. Some are not.
And then, figure out what happened to the world that was your home, and even more importantly, as a
builder, how do you rebuild it?
Your actions are narrated to you; The Kid remains silent throghout the game. There are
not many examples of silent protagonists being a positive thing in video games; let's face it,
main reasons for it are usually budget savings on $$$ voice actors and easier scriptwriting. Or lack of creativity.
Or all together.
Not in this case. You get to be immersed in the role of the Kid, and your actions (even your blunders)
are narrated to you by the mentioned narrator. It makes sense through time that the Kid is silent.
His Cael hammer does the talking for him.
Western trope? You betcha.
Gaming is based mostly around hack 'n' slash, your relfexes will be tested. There are numerous weapons
available to you, remnants of the old world. Your arsenal includes firerams, too.
However, there are numerous special abilites, upgrades for weapons (numerous, you are free to choose), and a huge number
of magical potions that are truly important. You will need a maximum balance to get through some challenges,
especially near the end.
Soundtrack is mostly acoustic, although intense beyond belief in some parts. My favorite instrumental track
is probably "Spike in a Rail". Pure eargasm. There is some banjo, some acoustic guitar, and a little bit of synth tracks.
Some tracks resemble FInal Fantasy, while most of them are Western influenced.
Graphics are truly gorgeous. Not so many details (again, budget of an indie game $$$), although this
reinstates what I always like to say - one fine day, completely photorealistic Unreal #456tnt engine will be here. And no, it STILL won't be able to replace the softness and attractiveness of hand-painted backgrounds in games. It really serves it's purpose, conisdering you play from isometric (basically top-down 2D) perspective. Every similarty with Final Fantasy Japanese style games is purely coincidential. NOT.
The nitpickers would say that because of that, the main character models are not that detailed (with suspiciously large eyes, I might add),
but the beautiful background of the world dominates anyway.
Some minor snags that I would like to point out are, for example,  difficulty - it gets difficult near the end, and there are some real challanges that await you - although for the first 50% of the game, it is really easy.
The lack of difficulty levels to choose from (save for the super easy kids oriented difficulty) is a minus.
There are difficulty upgrades available later in the game, in the form of "gods" of the world of Caelondia,
but they do not change the overall impression significantly.
Also, some levels really do get repetitive after a while - there's only so much you can do with isometric 2D after all.
Still, there is a great replay value, because there are several endings to this fine game, and you will
definitely be intrigued with "what if I had done that at the end...?"
Artistically, the game has sooo many influences - ranging from Western movies, up to Japanese visual arts and Greek
mythology. Story is in no way simple - not only is it the story about choices, you get acquainted with the whole world
of Caleondia that was once here. And it might not have been such a wonderful place all the time...
Did I mention the badass narrator?
An example of great storytelling and rock solid gaming on an indie budget.
Go get it!

I have a hard time finding people that I have a lot in common with.  I have an even harder time finding people who'd like to know me in the Biblical sense.  I fill that void with my love\hate relationship with Capcom.
When I originally bought this game on PS4, I was♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥  There was a severe lack of content and the servers were always going down.  But when I won my first ranked match by converting a crush counter into a v trigger install and cancelled into a super, I couldn't help but smile.
Still, waiting for content was a slog.  Capcom would announce things every month.  I came to expect these things to show up at the very end of the month.  Then I came to expect some of the things would be delayed.  And when characters I loved in SF4 showed back up, they felt funny in my hands.  I cycled back to anger and cynicism.  I guess it didn't help that there was a death in my family and a lot of stress at my job and in my living situation at the time.  But then, Juri and Urien showed up in the story mode, and they were actually really fun to play, so I calmed down.
Season 2 has been a trip.  I haven't really felt the hype for any of the characters since Akuma.  The newcomers have done a lot to flesh out the roster with unique fighting styles.  Still, I would have rather had Rose than Menat, and pretty much anybody from Mad Gear other than Abigail.  Even with all these weird new characters, ninety percent of what you'll run into online is shotos. (Unless you're godlike and you only run into Laura, Boxer, and Guile.) It gets boring.
I think this game is really going to come into its own when Arcade Edition comes out.  The new V-Triggers look sick, and the inclusion of more legacy characters should shake things up.  Also, there'll be single player content other than the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ survival mode and the laughable free story update.
TL;DR: If you're on the fence about this game, wait until Arcade Edition.

Riptide GP: Renegade is phenomenal.
As a massive fan of arcade racers, this series has been a shining light of the genre. It's mobile roots were evident in the first two games, but Renegade builds on what made the last two so great, and goes all out.
Controls are perfect now. Not a single flaw. The Hydrojets are more nuanced, and the trick system is more forgiving, in the best way possible. You still need to know what kind of tricks to pull out and when, but landing them is a lot easier now - making them even more essential to racing.
Graphics are great. Very pretty and colourful. It may lack some of the fancier effects of other modern racers, but for this kind of flawless performance, I'm more than willing to give up some mod-cons.
Sound is as you'd expect from a Riptide game. Great music, satisfying effects, it all just screams pure 'arcade'.
The fleshed out single player is great, a big improvement over GP 2. The storyline is ok for what it is, nothing special. But you don't play games like Riptide for the story.
The only problem I have is that the game at certain points gimps you on purpose, to make the game harder. I've spent a fair amount of time grinding races for money - I don't really appreciate you giving me races where my hard earned upgrades don't count, with the time I'm putting in to make sure I CAN give myself an advantage over the competition. It smacks of unfair. I'm more than willing to grind racers to afford the upgrades I want, so don't punish me, the player, for playing, basically. It's not a dealbreaker (yet), so I'll let it slide for now.
Everything else though is golden. I'm having so much fun just playing. The variety is there, the audio/visual presentation is excellent, and the controls are SUBLIME.
Absolutely recommended.

This is ridiculous game. I had to figure out the controls after 30 minutes of playing because otherwise I would be lost. After I have learned to control my units, I have beaten up my 2 enemies which were 2 difficulty. There are maybe 10 difficulties. I tried the easy first to see what it does.
You will get a leader and a town who can lead some units. In the beginning you have one farm or resource which gives you +1 gold. Accumulated gold is used for units. There are some special units offers during some months. Each turn is one month. The world changes depending on the seasons.
During gameplay I got one special leader who was useful mage.
Battles are simulations on screen, each unit takes its turn, you can speed it up or skip the battle.
There are running creatures in the world which are neutral and can attack you as well as enemies.
You can see by right-clicking on them what stats they have. If you remember old M&M right-clicking on opponents, it also stops the game during combat, but you can see all their abilities, buffs and damage.
There are some hidden units and you uncover the world from fog of war.
By losing your leader or killing the enemy leader, you eliminate the faction. Units, if not leaders, can not move on their own. They must be transfered to leaders. Otherwise they only defend current tile.
Leaders can move from 1 to 3 tiles, maybe more...
So far I like the game, it is a little challenging, you must accumulate enough units to defeat some enemies, but hard to say if it is challenging on higher difficulties as I only played the easy.

Seeing as I nominated this game for the "Defies Description" Steam award, (You may want to nominate it as well if you have played this.) telling you what this game is going to take a bit of wording.
Picture a comic book esq. movie like the matrix, add in a narrator, and then scrap the movie idea and make a nonlinear game instead, and throw in a dash of self-awareness and 4th wall cracking, and you would have Icey. Now if all that scared you, just think the combo system of a fighting game, (Super Smash bros. style games aside that is, no offense if you like those.) and the exploration and discovery of a platformer or Metroidvania style game, and forget about the meta game style and just enjoy the fun, and deep gameplay, the meta stuff can come later.
Though I have not completed the game yet, I can say that what I have seen is amazing, mind bending, and one or two times it made me laugh when I messed up the narrator’s plans. And if also can make you think, not in the same way as the Stanly parable or the creators guide, but more in the line of a psychological thriller film. Not so much a satire or consider the mind of a creative type, (If it has that I have yet to get to this point.) and more making you think like Holmes would if he were stuck in one of Lovecraft’s works.
TLDR,
If you enjoy meta works, artistic creativity, or psychological thrillers, buy this game. It's also coming to PS4 and Nintendo Switch, so if you prefer to support consoles, you can buy it there.

I assume that Kingdom Rush is basically the Steam/PC port of a popular mobile game that was really first popular on Amor Games' popular flash site made by Ironhide games.  Sorry if that is a little confusing, but really the game is a flash tower defense game and why would you pay money for something you could probably play in browser for free?
The short answer to that question is that you should pay for it becasue the game is really good, challenging, and supported.  The game itself isn't really innovative because the whole tower defense game genre is pretty stacked full, but this is a well executed TD with a great theme.  I really liked the art becuase it brought me back to the days where I did sit around and play flash games online. I have always liked action games made by Platinum, so this game already got my attention of looking like something I already like but 2D. Dropping in notion that it's mixed with another type of games I have liked recently, which is playing with meta, felt like something I would definitely enjoy. Got into sale, bought it.
First thing I heard when talking about the game with others was that almost everyone seemed to hate the english voice actor to death. I played whole game trough with english voice acting myself, because I did not feel like focusing on subtitles when playing fast based action game with near frame precise dodging. I think I understand it from both sides, because of the premise of the game, narrator is supposed to be your stereotypical game coder guy who is in no way voice actor but on the other hand they don't seem to get the reactions they are suppose to be having trough properly and even the parts which aren't supposed to sound like being read from paper sounds exactly like they are read from paper. However original chinese is option, so english does seem like good option to have over none.
Another small issue coming from that aspect is that the game and narrator are pushing the meta aspect maybe bit too heavily. It's far too obvious when game is trying to play you, breaking the illusion of it. It was pretty easy for me to switch my brain to just ignore it, but I could imagine this being game breaker for those who wanted something much smarter or what they haven't already seen. There are already several games doing this as well or even better now.
That all said, meta aspect for me personally was really enjoyable, but I actually ignored all of that in my first playtrough and was still really amazed with the experience. Outside of couple last bosses, I was having really fun going around really fast and just destroying monsters. It's clearly indie level so animations are bit puppet tool looking etc. but overall once I got the hang of the system I was feeling really powerful and awesome. I would've maybe wanted to play with ignoring every instructions initially instead of obeying, seems like the game was designed to be played this way as it'll conviniently reset you back before you disobeyed and you get bonus money on the way.
So if either action or meta aspect interests you even slightly, both are really fun. Most definitely worth even the full price.

Olen melkein aina tykännyt Platinumin tekemistä toimintapeleistä, joten tämä peli on julkaisusta lähtien ollut kiikarissa koska se näyttää joltain mistä jo tykkään mutta kaksiulotteisena. Kirsikkana päällä että peliin on miksattuna mukaan metapeli josta olen viimeaikoina tykännyt, joten kaikenkaikkiaan peli näytti joltain mistä varmana tykkäisin. Tuli alennukseen ja ostoonhan se meni.
Kun keskustelin pelistä niin ensimmäisena kuulin melkein jokaiselta siitä että pelin englanninkielinen ääninäyttely on aivan järkyttävän kauhea. Pelasin itse pelin alusta loppuun englannin dubeilla, koska en todellakaan ala katsomaan mitään tekstityksia kun pelaan nopeatempoista toimintapeliä jossa on ruuduntarkka väistäminen. Vähän kaksipiippuinen asia on että kertojan on tarkoituskin olla stereotyyppinen koodari joka ei todellakaan ole mikään ääninäyttelijä, mutta toisaalta joistakin reaktioista puuttuu se reaktio, kohdat joissa kertojan ei pitäisi kuulostaa siltä kuin he lukisivat lauseensa paperilta se edelleen kuulostaa kuin he lukisivat lauseensa paperilta. Alkuperäinen kiinalainen dubbi on saatavilla ja vaihdettavissa asetuksista, joten englannin dubbi tuntuu enemmänkin vaihtoehdolta joka on hyvä olla sen sijaan ettei olisi mitään.
Toinen pieni ongelma tulee siitä kuinka pelit ja kertoja tuntuvat tarkoituksella puskevan meta-aspektia ehkä liiankin paljon. Välillä on aivan liian selvää kun peli alkaa pelaamaan pelaajaa, joka rikkoo illuusion. Sain jotenkin sen pois mielestä, mutta voin kuvitella sen olevan aikamoinen pettymys monelle, varsinkin niille jotka pelin tämän takia ostivat ja kaipasivat jotain fiksumpaa tai jotain jota eivät ole jo kokeneet. Vaihtoehtoja kun on ja jotka osaavat tämän yhtä hyvin tai paremmin.
Meta-aspekti oli silti itselle hyvin miellyttävä kokemus, mutta ensimmäisen kerran pelasin jättämällä sen kokonaan sivuun ja pelikokemus oli silti mahtava. Muutamaa viimeista pomoa lukuunottamatta, minulla oli todella hauskaa mennessä joka paikkaan nopeasti ja tepellen hirviöitä. Peli on selkeästi indietasoista tavaraa, animaatiot näyttävät hyvin simppeleiltä nukketyökalulla tehdyiltä, jne. mutta kaiken kaikkiaan kun pääsin jyvälle mekaniikoista, tuntui kuin olisi hyvin voimakas ja mahtava. Olisin ehkä jälkikäteen miettien haluta pelata peliä sivuuttaen kaikki kertojan ohjeet, koska tuntuu siltä kuin peli on suunniteltu niin, koska se palauttaa pelaajan kätevästi juuri ennen tieltä kiertämistä ja joka kulmassa on rahaa.
Kaiken kaikkiaan, oli se sitten toiminta tai meta mikä pelissä näyttää kiinnostavan, kumpikin tuo mukavasti iloa. Täyden hinnan arvoinen peli.

Meltdown is a HIGHLY addictive top-down style shooter for free on Steam. You play as a customizable character with a full range of available guns, melee weapons, shoulder pads, torso armor, hats, masks, and more, each giving various buffs to the player character.
You begin every game the same; riding down an elevator to a facility infested with various robot enemies. Every enemy is extremely different, and adds new challenges as you progress. Some of them fire missiles, some of them melee-rush, some of them are static, some stationary, and most levels end with boss fights. It controls like a dual-stick shooter, but handles very well (if not better) with mouse and keyboard. I haven't tried it with a gamepad yet, and I don't intend to, but I believe the option is available.
Every piece of gear you add to your character is upgradeable, and fits to various playstyles. Some armor increases shotgun damage and range, other armor increases shield amount, health amount, etc. There are at least a dozen different weapons to choose from, both melee and ranged, and two gun slots allow for quick playstyle switching during the game. All weapons (save for the knife that you start out with) are able to be upgraded, allowing you to choose a "class" character. There is also a skill tree, but you aren't limited to a single branch, and never run out of points with which to upgrade.
There is both an arcade mode and an online mode, which allow for up to four friends on a single machine, or joining various multiplayer lobbies (up to four people). Both arcade and online feature three different game modes; a dungeon crawl level mode, a wave-based mode, and a four-player deathmatch mode. The most profitable tends to be the Wave mode, but the other game modes bring about one of the only problems I've had with the whole game.
The grinding. The grinding is real. The most expensive items are 3,000 to 4,000 gold, with the average gold per game rounding out to about 50 or so pieces. While this encourages playability, every game gets old after a while. There are items that increase gold drop rate (by 30% max), and there are mystery boxes (with a very rare drop rate) that could contain up to 200 gold, but these are pretty rare, and often it takes ten or so different games before you're able to afford that new armor you've been eyeing.
All in all, this game is excellent, and for a complete FTP version, it's pointless NOT to get it. High replayability, good team lobbies, and a lot of fun.

Fun timewaster. My first impression of this game was that it was a dual-stick shooter full of microtransaction incentivising you to buy better gear to be less pathetic. I later came to realise there isn't any kind of paid transaction and that this game was simply a grind-fest.
Meltdown is a fun shooter where you go down a randomly generated level and fill robots of different shapes and sizes into smoldering piles of medal. You do this with a selection of weapons that don't win points for originality but are adequate while protecting yourself with different armor pieces and upgrades. It also incorparates quick and easy multiplayer making company welcome and later in the game, kind of nessacary (coming from a guy who deliberitly avoids online interactions). The music is like a mild wubfest, not my cup of tea, but it 's as easy as turning of music and playing some 2SFH in it's place.
After about an hour and a half I was able to "prestige" reseting all my stuff while letting me unlock more armor (you still have to pay for) and upgrading weapons one more level than they could previously. "Cool," I thought but you reset EVERYTHING, including your weapon upgrades and expensive armor pieces. You keep you're money but nothing else, it was then I realised I wasn't the badass in thugged out armor and weapons assisting weak characters, I was the sucker wasting his time and money until he prestiged for the first time, unknowlingy shooting himself in the foot. Unless you don't want the locked armors, you have to grind, and grind, and grind. Then you still have to grind for the money to afford the items and having to have enough chips to upgrade selected items. You also can't get the good weapons until you FULLY upgrade the subpar ones and if you are going to prestige you're going to be stuck as an armorless, smg-toting weakling for a few hours, adding to the difficulty. I IMPLORE YOU, IF YOU GET MELTDOWN, IF YOU READ THIS, SAVE YOUR GOLD SHOULD YOU WANT THE GEWD STUFF, DON'T ADD ANYMORE TO THE GRIND THAN THERE ALREADY IS. IF YOU DO AT LEAST GET TO LVL 3 PRESTIGE THE JUMP OUT THE NEAREST WINDOW.

Man if this isn't one of the most unique games in a while I don't know what is.
TL;DR BUILD TOWERS, SHOOT ENEMIES, FORGET TO EAT

So, the game itself is almost arcade-style in that each level is a different, relatively small map.  Your basic objective is to defend the "core" from waves of aliens, and you do this by building walls and towers that automatically shoot them.  The game itself is divided into two stages.  To start, you build towers by setting bases to direct the enemies to where you want them to go (like any tower-defense, you try to make the path as long as possible).  However, what makes this game so brilliant is that, rather than just watching your towers go to town on the enemies, you suddenly take out your oversized gun of choice and get to blast them away yourself.  Enemies come in stages, usually around 11 for each level, and they have special attributes that make them different which often requires you to change your offensive approach.  I won't list all of them but to give you an idea: some enemies are heavily armored from the front which requires you to follow them and shoot their exposed areas, but this can be difficult because if you get two close they will stop and begin to attack you, some are very weak but small and fast and will almost certainly slip by you, a few enemies can fly and can ignore your walls.  You will also see stronger variants of many of them, as well as bosses that are even more powerful.
You can choose from four playable characters to do your business (or five if you get one of the expansions), which all have varying attributes and primary weapons.  You can also outfit yourself with varying "perks" which give you additional stats and abilities, and choose what type of towers you want to be able to deploy.  What this means to you is that you have the freedom to create a character that matches you and your gameplay style.  Experimenting with these options is one of the most fun features of this game.
This game is very well suited to multiplayer, however it is fine when played alone.  If you do decide to play like this I would advise against using the more specialized classes like the sniper or rogue.  By default your games will be public and people will join your games to help you out while you play.  A nice feature that I found was that when your text chats are spoken by a speech-generator, so you don't have to look away to read what your teammate said.
Though this game is all about gameplay, I really like the graphics and art style.  The story is told through brief comics at the beginning of each level; none of it will particularly move you, but it's enough to get you into the action.  None of this is should really be a selling point, but it definitely shows that the studio put a lot of heart into it.

Best described as a mix between Hydro Thunder and Wave Race 64 (as far as stunts are concerned, anyhow), Riptide GP: Renegade has a fairly long single player mode that includes a mix of race events, stunt contests, time trials, and elimination events, in addition to 8 player online events and 4 player splitscreen modes.
There's also an excuse plot that serves as a way to explain how you end up unlocking new characters and vehicles (there's 9 characters and 9 vehicles total), and why you'll have to deal with police hydrojets (their term for the boat/bike things, not mine) chasing you every now and then.
The only drawbacks I can think of at the moment is that the AI can be a tad ruthless at times, the music is fairly bland, and that playing with a gamepad is essential (although this goes for just about every racing game). Overall, if you enjoyed any of the previous games in the series, or any other arcade racing game involving boats, Riptide GP: Renegade is well worth its low asking price.

One of the best games Ive ever played. Im biased Ill admite, I love this genre. Terraria is one of my all-time favorites and Starbound is just more of what I love, only in SPACE! Which makes it even better! If you love the action RPG-lite, adventure, mine, craft, explore genre - you simply cannot go wrong here.
What are you waiting for? Go Go GO!
Update for 1.0 - While many out there feel like theyve been cheated somehow - I still adore the game. Yes some things we had during the development stages have been removed - and while I do wish those things hadnt been removed - it hasnt diminished my enjoyment in the slightest. Im also firmly of the mind that many, if not all, of these things will be re-implemented as we move away from 1.0. I guess what Im saying is Starbound was worth it, and still is worth it. Too many negative reviews for things that changed from the development stages to live - and thats really not fair to the guys and gals who built the game - as we all know things change as something is being worked on.
I also think alot of folks just dont 'get' the idea of a true sandbox - which Starbound is. Terraria was a metroidvania game stuck in a single, small-ish sandbox map. It worked for what it is was and I adored every second of it. Starbound isnt a metroidvania in the same sense - its more of a giant sandbox with very light metroidvania elements.
Terraria gave you gear (rather quickly if you knew what you were doing) that made you near godlike at 'endgame'. Starbound gives you powerful gear but still relies on your skill in combat more than just numbers. Ive yet to feel like I could destroy everything in the games verse - Im very strong, but still vulnerable. I like that, keep you on your toes.
Folks mention the planets being boring. Well, as sandboxes and procedural generation go - after a while yes, you are going to see alot of similiar and/or identical things. Its the nature of the beast. We ALL know this. So to give negative marks based on the very nature of the system is pointless. Did any of you really think we were going to get millions of completely unique worlds? Im 100+ hours into 1.0 and Im *still* finding new stuff I havent seen, sure its uncommon at this point, but its out there...
Overall I think Starbound is pretty damn great for what it is trying to do. And I feel certain its only going to get better with time =)
Quick 2017 update: Starbound still maintains the bar - no matter what negativity people like to throw around - there is nothing else out there like it.

TL;DR, the fighting stuff is bad and the game would've been better with another playstyle.

Kingdom Rush is one of the best tower defense strategy games out there that is only let down by the lack of truly strategic tower commands.
+ Excellent graphics
+ Linear game-play with RPG-esque progression
+ Hours of game-play
+ Difficult (could be considered a con, see below)
+ (new!) Difficulty level can be adjusted
- Very short campaign, I'd personally prefer a longer campaign and fewer side missions
- No real tactical control over towers compared to Defender's Quest
- Cannot view enemy/tower documentation while playing
Kingdom Rush is a tablet ported tower defense game set in a medieval high fantasy world. Like most tower defense games you are given a puzzle-like map stage and have to build towers along the enemy's predefined path in an attempt to obstruct said enemy as they pass through.
Overall it's a good looking game with a fair sense of progression; as you play stages you are awarded stars which allow you to unlock new perks which upgrade the performance of just about every aspect of your defenses. Kingdoms Rush also allows you to pick from a pool of heroes, each with different statics and abilities to utilize in each stage. Some stages will necessitate a ranged hero, in others a melee hero is optimal. Who you choose for what stage can impact the overall difficulty of the level.
In my opinion all these variables add to the overall strategy of the game but I feel that additional depth is needed. The game lacks a certain finesse that I've seen in other tower defense games; notably the ability to tell each tower which type of enemy units to target. Maybe I want my mage to target only the strongest enemies and leave the weak units for my archers. Maybe I want my soldiers to spread out so as to block as much of the path as possible instead of all ganging up on one enemy while all the other enemies walk on by just as happy as you please. Maybe I'd like my artillery to target the enemy units nearest their spawn point for better collateral damage instead of always targeting that one loner way up front. Well in Kingdom Rush you can't, you are left at the mercy of the AI which has caused me to restart stages more often than I'd like to admit.
The campaign story is no Shakespeare but it gets the job done.... until it ends when you are 33% done with the game. Heck, I figured I must have at least another half dozen or more stages to go yet when the credits started rolling. Apparently the remainder 66% of the game tasks you with individual stages which are hard (in contrast to the campaign stages).
For some perspective: it took me one try on all but the final stage of the campaign to get through those stages with at least one star. Stages following the campaign require repeated playthroughs just to get that one star and often stages are large enough to last a good half hour. It's a very time consuming trial and error process during which your interest in the game continually ebbs due to a lack of passive progression even through failure.
Another facet I bemoaned is the lack of accessible documentation while in-game. When on the campaign map you can access a bevy of useful information about different enemies/towers in the game and what their stats are but it's only accessible from the campaign map, nowhere else, especially not during a stage when such information can really come in handy.
Overall I enjoyed this game - polished graphics and linear story are just long enough for you to grab your Steam trading cards and scram. Some players may appreciate the brutal challenge later levels present but there are those of us who play causally and I, for one, am delighted the devs added a difficulty setting post release.

This game has a very "The Settlers" type feel to it, which is what my friend and I were hoping for.  It does a lot of things right and is easy to pick up.  There are some major faults though, which makes me wish there was some sort of middle-ground between a Thumbs Up and Thumbs Down rating.
If you have any previous experience with city-building type RTS games, this will be extremely easy to jump into.  Which is good, because the game does a very poor job of giving explanations on what you must do to succeed.  There are no helpful "advisors" to tell you why your happiness has plummeted, or why your food production suddenly went from +10 to -25.  You need to know how to trouble shoot the problems yourself.  Seeing that the game is very simplistic in nature, with only about two dozen buildings or structures, it's usually not too difficult to figure out what you need to balance... but some times you don't have the time to sit their troubleshooting when your entire population suddenly starts starving to death.
Resource gathering is fairly simple and balanced, with the exception of stone... stone is used in the majority of building upgrades, which are very important in such limited confines as this game gives you.  The problem is that stone is a very rare resource, which seems kind of silly.  You can only mine small amounts from rare stone nodes you find in about 1 out of ever 4 land tiles.  And they worst part is, they aren't renewable... they give you about enough stone to upgrade 2-3 buildings before running out.  This alone forces you to do 1 of 2 things.... quickly expand your borders in a panic'd attempt to acquire more tiles with stone... or start mass producing as much "Krown" currency as possible, so you can pay the absurdly overpriced Trading Post prices for stone. There needs to be a much better way to manage this resource.
The biggest and most dissapointing flaw with this game is THERE IS NO SAVE OPTION.  My friends and I like to play large drawn out games with heavy development that can span multiple nights of gameplay.  But thats not a possibility here, you can't save the game and rejoin it later.   And with the average game easily lasting a MINIMUM of 2-3 hours, this is a big problem.  On the other hand, the game is overly simplified... with little to no "end game".  You're army is small, consisting of 6-12 bland units that you drag into other borders to auto-fight the opponents.  You get one "special" unit, that represents your tribe... but they have no redeeming qualities... just a bit more health and attack than a regular unit.
Your buildings only upgrade once, and there is no evolution to the types of buildings you can create as the game goes on.  You will be using the same Farms and Houses at the end of the game that you used at the beginning of the game.  There is no progression.
So is this game worth picking up?  Sure... but don't expect an in depth city management style RTS.  The bulk of the challenge in this game comes from the restrictions of how many buildings it will let you place in one land tile, and playing whack a mole with different world NPCs pelting your borders with attacks.

I remember when I first started playing this game. I was scared of everything. I moved very slowly, cautiously, and ran from place to place, looking for the safest and shortest path to the next saferoom. When I finally finished a campaign and got to watch the ending cutscene roll, it felt like a real achievement.
Then I tried joining my first multi-player campaign and discovered a whole new world. Having someone running along with me, giving me helpful advice, and us all generally looking after each other as a team was a great experience. This is a game where good team-based gameplay is rewarded, and where people who go rushing off alone commonly end up getting themselves killed. Left 4 Dead feels like it was built for cooperative gameplay, from the ground up. There's safety in numbers, and when you're the last one standing and trying to survive on your own, you'll really feel just how alone you are in a hostile world where pretty much everything is out to kill you.
The game can be played in both single and multi-player. Up to four players control one each of four survivors as they all attempt to move from one safe area to the next. Any survivors not being controlled by a human player will be automatically taken over by the survivor bot AI. As they move through the levels in the campaigns, the survivors will encounter various enemies, including hordes of common zombies and some rarer 'special' infected. These special infected come with unique abilities that make good teamplay essential, as their attacks can disorient and even render lone survivors helpless.
Levels are premade and static, meaning they never change from game to game. After playing the same campaign enough times, you'll end up memorizing the most efficient routes through the levels. Item spawns are also preplaced, so if you find a bottle of pills behind a dumpster in a certain alleyway, then that's what you can expect to find in that location in all future games you play. There is some variation in the fact that items won't always spawn where they're available to be spawned, but that's it.
At certain points throughout the game, you'll encounter various events that trigger attacks from hordes of zombies, or even spawn 'boss' infected, which helps break the monotony of simply going from point A to point B. Otherwise, the meat of the campaign mode consists of moving from one location to the next while shooting zombies and finding items. There are six campaigns; most of them have a total of five maps. In each campaign, there is constant visible evidence of the decay of society and the collapse of civilization through wrecked buildings, vehicles, piles of dead bodies, and more.
Besides campaign, 'versus' and 'survival' game modes are also available. In versus mode, up to eight players can join a single game session. Versus mode is basically a campaign where there are two teams of human players - one team controls the survivors, and the other spawns as special infected. The survivor team must attempt to make it as far as they can before being killed, while the infected team attempts to stop them as quickly as possible. Once the survivors have been killed or make it to safety, the teams switch roles, and the map is played again. This rotation continues until the entire campaign has been completed, at which stage, points are tallied up to determine the winner.
In survival mode, the survivors are trapped in certain areas found throughout the campaigns, and must hold out as long as possible against relentless waves of enemies that get more difficult as the game progresses. Gold, silver, and bronze 'medals' are awarded for lasting ten, seven, and four minutes respectively.
Music in Left 4 Dead adds not only atmosphere, but is also dynamic in that it changes depending on the situation. Impending horde attacks are met with the sound of intense drumming, the presence of an attacking 'Tank' (boss infected) comes with its own 'epic' theme, unique 'terror' music plays while being strangled by a 'Smoker' special infected, and so on. Leaving the music in this game on can actually help the player maintain situational awareness.
Survivors also call out and comment on things they see throughout the game, and the voice acting is generally good. Players can make the character they're controlling say certain things with the press of a button for quick communication in case they can't or don't want to type messages or use a microphone.
The survivor bot AI does an adequate job of keeping together and shooting enemies, but has a habit of running directly into the player's line of fire. I also noticed frequent pathfinding issues, causing bots to get stuck before 'warping' to the player's location. Sometimes, fellow survivor bots also take an inordinate amount of time to rescue other survivors from the clutches of special infected if there is even a minimal amount of zombies occupying their attention. Incapacitated survivor bots also have the uncanny ability to close doors, which is not something the player can do.
The infected AI is very accurate and effective, and often 'cheats'. Hunters are able to claw survivors while in mid leap and even after getting shoved away, and Boomers instantly hit survivors once they get within range, before even completing their swiping animation, There is also some kind of oddity with hitboxes involving rocks thrown by Tanks, which allows Tanks to hit survivors round the corners of buildings.
Game sessions can be hosted on dedicated servers or locally via a player's computer. The game runs very well on a slow connection - on a connection that had a maximum transfer rate of 8.5kb/s, I've managed to maintain a ping between 50-70 on a dedicated server within the same country. Depending on how quickly players rush through a campaign, game sessions can last anywhere from 11 minutes on the shortest campaign, to up to roughly an hour for a standard one.
+ Great multiplayer functionality (netcode, built-in voice comms)
+ Quick drop-in, drop-out ability
+ Maps have decent atmosphere and varied settings
+ Great mod and add-on support
- 'Cheating' infected AI
- Linear maps
- Weapon variety is somewhat lacking
- AI has slight pathfinding issues
- Survivor bot AI can be annoyingly incompetent
Left 4 Dead is a game best played with good, human teammates. Survivor bots will suffice in the beginning, but as your skill increases, you'll quickly see just how deficient bots are. Linear maps limit replayability, but this may be offset by the fact that so much community-made content has been released and is readily available for download -
What's the point of getting this game when Left 4 Dead 2 has everything the original has, and more? The gameplay in the original Left 4 Dead feels different compared to the sequel. In Left 4 Dead 2, there is more of a focus on rushing through hordes while under continuous attack. In Left 4 Dead, the focus is more on waiting the horde out while staying in a defensible location. The maps that were ported over to Left 4 Dead 2 from the original game have also been modified to reflect this.
If you've got no one to play with and are just looking for a server to join, at this stage, you may have difficulty finding games online, depending on where you live. The game's lifespan can be significantly extended if custom add-ons come into play, and the game can also be tweaked using various command-line startup options. I found a lot of entertainment and cheap humour in watching the bots play campaign and survival by themselves while I spectated.

Very different from Civ IV, just a fair warning that even though it is done in the same engine, it is a very different game. The mechanics for movement and combat are the same, but barring that, things change quite a bit; more micro, less macro. Your units are taken straight from the population of cities, and while in cities they work either tiles or production buildings -- taking raw materials and refining them into finished products. All of your citizens also have a profession attached to them, this affects their yields or combat modifiers; of course in addition to the promotions that they can earn through combat. Money management and trade routes to deliver the raw materials and finished products are a huge part of the game, and constructing buildings are based off of having a supply of wood, with citizens working the lumber mills.
I really enjoyed the way that the micro managing was handled, and I wish that a Civ V variant -- mainly for the hex and single unit tile occupation mechanics -- would be made.

Gameplay of Binding of Isaac: Rebirth is quite simple. You descent randomly generated dungeon killing mosters, collecting items that grant you different abilities and synergies when two or more items are combined. At the end of every floor you have to fight a boss monster. There are eleven playable characters (thirteen with Afterbirth DLC), hundreds of different room layouts and crazy amount of secrets, items and item combinations to discover.
Game may seem quite difficult at first, even though it felt somewhat easier to me than the original Binding of Isaac. Difficulty of the game is mostly based on your skills, but even your worst run can become your best (and vice versa) depending on which items you get during the run. However, game will get easier once you've played enough and you start to remember different room layouts, monster attack patterns, item effects and item combinations.
It took me around 300 hours to unlock every secret and achievement in the game (with Afterbirth), so I would say that it has pretty good replay value. The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth with the Afterbirth DLC is easily one of my favorite games that I've ever played across any platform.

Buy? Maybe. (My experience is based on the Android version) McPixel is a very stupid minigame-fest, where you must save the day by preventing a bomb from exploding in a variety of 20 scenarios. The idea is a sort of comedy based, retro-style take on MacGuyver, where you improvise a way to stop a bomb from exploding. This includes stuffing bombs into people, causing somebody to accidentally kick the bomb out, or straight up urniating on the bomb. The comedy overtly crude and immature, and probably the reason for it's popularity of "Let's Play" videos with the younger audience. There are a few moments of laughs for me, especially the "Insert Virigin" mission.
It's point and click adventure gameplay will unfairly throw people off - unlike most adventure games where you may find yourself stuck without a guide, this is the only adventure point and click I know of where there is a constant failure state built in either the 20 second time limit of each level or in your inability to find the right answer. Plus, the extreme simplicity of the controls where you can either click to interact or swipe/right click to skip removes unnecessary complexity from the genre. Yes, it's a tad annoying to fail, but it's over quickly and since you can only click on so few things, you will eventually find the answer. This alone makes this game worth playing or at least checking out to people with huge backlogs - the game is very short (3-5hrs) and it means you can play the game, even mindlessly and be able to finish without scratching your head very often (there are a couple head scratchers though).
There are no sound effects in the entire game beyond the title screen. It's strange how a game about explosions only uses it in the title screen versus the rest of the game. It could have been a conscious decision to let the zany, silly chiptune style music make the situation seem crazy, lazy game design, or possibly both. The biggest legimate annoyance is the humor of the game♥♥♥♥♥♥jokes, dry humping, crotch kicks - it all sounds like something written by a pre-teen and it will definitely annoy some people. Another very annoying aspect is having to replay level to "find all the gags" in every level before you can reach the ending. This may offer some entertainment to players that enjoy this comedy, but for everybody else, it's an unnecessary grind, which is accentuated in the irritatingly boring, and unnecessary "click everything and hope for the best" last level. Still, I'd say the $5 price tag matches the value of the game, though I'm glad I got this in a bundle which made it really cheap - I could say I wasted my time with this game, but I played it on my phone while there was down time at work - wasting time was the whole point.
By the way, I'd argue this game is better in short bursts on a mobile device than sitting down and playng on PC. The only reason why I have 10 hours logged was to farm trading cards - I wouldn't have installed it otherwise.

After 16.116 reviews, there's nothing else to say about this game right? Wrong.
Everybody feels this game differently, that's one of its assets, but some things just never change. There are some mechanics that are not explained in the game at all and I for one would have liked to know 'em before I started playing. Hence this little reviewlike walkthrough of mine came to be:
First, I'd like to say you won't regret buying this game. But you already knew that, didn't you?
After all, Bastion is a really fun game, Aciton RPG oriented, with a somewhat limited combat system that wil♥♥♥♥♥♥you off from time to time but don't worry. You'll get it eventually!
Where was I? Oh, right...
Instead of talking about the strong suits of the game, I'd like to talk about its flaws. 'Cause yes. It's got them.
Above all, I'd say there are two ways to play Bastion. Casual or Completionist.
If you're heading for casual, congratulations! This game's made for you. Most levels don't last more than ten minutes and there's a specific game mode meant for you called "painless mode".
However, if you intend to get everything in this game I must warn you. It won't be easy...
Know this. You're gonna have to beat the game at least twice.
Enjoy your fisrt playthrough, learn the paths, try out different weapons, smash Scumbags, feel the music and try to understad what the hell's going on. Don't worry yourself about challenges and leave the Idols for later. Just enjoy!
Eventually, you'll reach the grand finale and will need to face a story changing decission. To get all the achievements you need to play both scenarios, so just pick whatever you feel like and enjoy the show. Both decissions will allow you to keep playing so don't worry yourself unnecesarily. Alas, the game feels like the best options are:
1st) Left - Left.
2nd) Right - Right.
One down, one to go. Once you complete the stoy for the first time, you'll unlock "New Game +" mode and "Score Attack" mode. You should know that the latter counts as a New Game + for the "Calamity Kid" achievement, so there's no real need to play the NG+ mode, at all.
The second playthrough's where you'll have to give your best. Start off with no less than five Idols to get the higuest amount of money and experience possible, finish the remaining challenges and enjoy your new traits. Another special move will be unlocked in the Armory (you don't need to own "Portal" to get it) and the History books in the Bastion will now lead you to a brand new "Who Knows Where" battle arena.
Don't push it. Battle arenas can be "easily" beaten with your mortar and pike fully upgraded. But it will take some time to complete the arenas. Strategy is key, choose the right tonics to aid you and take full advantage of your surroundings.
In addition, since you should already be playing in "Score Attack" mode, you can get the "Hard bargain" achievement as well. It is not an easy achevement to get, but a valid method to obtain it has already been discovered. Advance in the story until you unlock the Pipe, then equip "Black Rye" and "Whale Ale" choose a long and short range weapon in the armory, equip the "Gel Cannister" as your special move and renounce "Acobi", "Roathus" and "Olak" at the Temple leaving the remaining Idols active. All you have to do now is enter the Kid's Dream and try to keep the chain with your turrets. Have fun!!
After a while, you should get all the remaining achievements. Thus concluding the completionist path. Congratulations, you did it!!!
Now, regardless of the path you've chosen to enjoy this game, the experience is definitely worth it, but for he completionist gamers it feels like it is a bit harder than it should be unlike what happens in Transistor for example, the next game you should be cheking on! (^_^)

Tower defense games are my preferred game style for the last few years.  Many developers have tried to come into the space and capture the experience but Ironhide Game Studios has set the bar to epic with Kingdom Rush.
I have purchased this game for iPhone, iPad and for the PC and have done a full play through almost 4 times (once for each platform, twice on the iPad).  The PC version sports a few differences that are worth mentioning if you already have played through on the iOS.
PC differences of note:
1) There is no more collecting crystals during in-game play for purchasing "extras" for use during levels.  On the PC you have what you are able to do during the level and that is it.
2) There is no difficultly settings to play with.  On IOS there is Normal and Hard mode; PC allows no selection.
3) On PC you have open access to all of the heroes; no need to purchase them as you did on the IOS versions.
If you are a fan of any Tower Defense games and would like to explore the genre a bit more, Kingdom Rush is a very easy recommendation and carries with it quite a bit of replayability.  Go forth and defend the kingdom!

Bastion is a really beautiful game and definetly not your average game.
The art is really beautiful and the story gets told in a special way that I didn't encounter like that in any game I've played until now. Paired with the good voice acting, the really beautiful soundtrack and the already mentioned art it makes Bastion a beautiful, heart-wrenching story.
But of course a good story is nothing without some good gameplay. And Bastion really nails it. There are many weapons, skills and spirits to try and combine so you can play in your own favored playstyle. Even the weapons themself can get upgraded they way the player likes. There are also secret spots filled with fragments, Health Tonics and/or Black Tonics that are fun to find. Same goes for the pets that are kept in the Bastion once they are found.
The levels themselves are well designed and beautiful drawn, they don't look like each other and don't play like each other and contain different enemies supposed to fit the current level, or rather island. Playing through those islands was really fun and the balance is not too hard but also not too easy. There are also the training grounds which add, combined with the memorial, several challenges for the kid/player. Well there are also the steam achievements which are also a challenge itself.
The only thing I'm sad about is that I wish there was a sequel to Bastion because I really fell in love with this game.
So I strongly recommend this game to anyone who didn't buy and play it yet. It's definetly worth it.

This game is a piec--- not good. The devs should be ashamed and Steam should take it down. Why am I so harsh with this game? Let's see.
Graphics:
They're kinda ok, but the sprites seem a little big to me. Like when you're playing one of the older Commander Keen games but zoomed in WAAAY too much. Somehow, even with its simple graphics, this game results in the most horrible screen tearing which I rarely encounter (the background image distorts badly). So maybe VSYNC is a must. But why bother?
Dying ISIS troops fall down and stand up right again before vanishing in an instant. No bloodsplats or any other graphical change.
The muzzle flash on Donald's gun only appears while he's jumping and shooting, not while he's walking.
When Donald shoots, he shoots from his wrist, not from the tip of his (shot)gun. The bullets are yellowish orbs. No buckshot or anything. Kinda weird. Once he dies, only then his animation changes - for the remainder of the game he always looks the same - at least as far as I can tell because I can't beat the first 30 seconds of the first level (more on that later).
Sounds:
Music and sound are meh. Kinda okayish, nothing special as far as I can tell. It is not too bad but nothing really stands out for me. Ok, one thing does: the dying Donald sounds like a wimpy ghoul getting lobotomized.
Edit: Also holding down the shoot key lets you spray out many bullets, but there's only the audio for one shot. Hooooorrrrriiibbbllleee.
Edit 2: You can trigger a nice sound bug if you shoot with space bar AND simultaneously clicking the shoot button on screen. Let's you fire a huge barrage of bullets too.
Controls:
Jumping feels weird. Donald stays in the air for a kinda long time. However, this feels "in tune" with the horribly big zoomed graphics. Walking left and right and shooting is responsive. There don't seem to be any more relevant controls.
You can also shoot by clicking the shoot button on screen, but why would you do that? Maybe this was born as a mobile game, which could explain lacking quality.
Design:
Horrible. Just horrible. Enemies can walk through barrels, while you can't. They can shoot through barrels - which you can not do (correctional edit: You can, but you can't shoot past barbed wire). One hit and you're done by the way; I wouldn't have a problem with that if the game wasn't that bad. Standing on top of the oil barrels (first level) does not allow you to dodge your enemies, since they walk right through the barrels and are so big you're done for, since your feet will always be touching them.
Then, a few screens into the first level is a part where there's a barrel, a good length of barbed wire behind it and of course an enemy which comes shooting at you and passes through the barbed wire unhurt. I'm almost sure this jump needed here can't be done, although there are people claiming they've reached Level 2. I've tried the aforementioned jump several times and always I've landed at a tiny edge of the barbed wire or got hit by the enemy spawning there.
Edit: Yay, I get that jump once in a while, so it is possible. But there are more just like this one in the level.
Another edit:
You just have to not care for the graphics, you can walk further on top of most barrels than it seems. I've uploaded a screenshot to my gallery if you want to see "my Donald" after a tough jump. In comes the crazy overpowered camel! It can be defeated of course, just as usual, just spam your gun everywhere you go. That's great!
My final verdict?
Stay away, don't even get this at a discount like me, you'd need to be a hardcore masochist to even get a tiny bit of enjoyment from this "game". THIS SHOULD NOT BE SOLD AND ANYBODY WHO VOTED FOR THIS ON GREENLIGHT (I'm assuming that's how this piece of code got here) should lose the ability to rate a game on Steam forever. GRRR. No, I'm not that angry, I'm just overdramatizing. Because anger.
It's probably e-Solutions first game, so we can cut them some slack. But... it just could've been better. A lot.
TL;DR:
Fu--- ignore this game, not worth too many cents in its current state. Horrible execution, lame, bugged. My verdict might be different if at least some of the issues would be fixed. Maybe the Devs could fix the barrel graphics or change the jumping distances. That would be a start.

It's not Terraria. It's supposed to be a more ambitious approach to the genre but it's still a few steps behind after it's official release. With this game out, my understanding is that people still want more from this genre. While games like Minecraft, Terraria, and now Starbound definitely scratch certain itches, none of these feel big enough to be THE game with it all. I like the competition that Starbound has created, though. Some of the ideas implemented in here will become standards in the genre. With that being said, once other games borrow what works with Starbound to make their game more complete, we will be a step closer to having a very satifying experience within the sandbox/creative genre. I still need to discover all the game has to offer after it's official release. These games are amazing even if it lacks what the other has.
TL; DR - While it may not be Terraria, it's exciting to see what it adds to the genre. Recommend!

There seems to be a trend for experience based games cropping up over time, like Dyad or in this case 140.  In all cases, the price is a little high - not because the game is not worth that much, but because experience-based games tend to be overshadowed by sweeping soundtracks and beautifully rendered RPG games, or FPSes which have been with us as a gaming community since the early days alongside RTSes.
I might not have bought this for five dollars - heck, I didn't even know this game existed.  However, the Weekly Humble Bundle this week was an excellent time to learn it existed and to plop it into my library.  I might be biased - I produce music of all sorts for fun, and I've always had my eye on music-based games.  I also know when to say no to a game, and this was not that time.
140 is not a normal music-based game.  At least, when Normal for music-based games is Audiosurf or Beat Hazard or DDR.  140 turns everything upside down to create a very simplified gaming experience that lends itself to actually experiencing the game.  In the end, a short set of gameplay sessions is what this game is meant to provide, as are most game-like experiences, though I do wish there were more levels.
So after all that, is it worth five bucks?  Ask yourself this - are you looking for a normal game, or a game-like experience?

First of all, these trailers just dont do the game justice! Also, since the game very recently updated to 1.0, some of the negative reviews may have had issues fixed.
As of now, Starbound has a large storyline with lots of unique and interesting quests, but that's not all! It has an amazing soundtrack, an asthetically pleasing art style, many types of planets; from worlds filled with alien life to ocean planets with underwater cities, and so much more! Starbound is a very fun game, and it's one of my favorites! I have been playing Starbound for quite a while, and I'm VERY excited for 1.0! One of the best features of 1.0 is that you can instantly create a multiplayer world by just inviting your friends, and now has a great built in workshop feature. Also, Starbound has 7 playable races! They are as follows:
Novakid: A race of wild west themed beings made of pure energy, forged from the core of a star long ago.
Hylotl: A race of fish-people, which are a lot cooler than they sound may I add, that have a culture of ancient and modern Japanese culture combined. They're my personal favorite. They have underwater Tokyo-like cities!
Glitch: A medieval robotic race. They have a cool speech pattern that states their feeling before the statement.
(Afraid. Why are you here? -- Inquisitive. What is your homeworld? etc.)
Avian: A race of bird-like humanoids that worship the god of the aether; Kluex. They are themed mostly behind the Aztec and the Myan cultures, with a little bit of Egyptian thrown in.
Human: What's a human? I'm not sure.
Apex: Another humanoid race that, as the name may suggest, looks like a gorilla. Their story is that they used a serum to make themselves much smarter, but a side effect made them look like they do now. They used to look almost human. Their culture is ultramodern, and themed a little around George orwell's 1984.
Floran: Floranssssss talk like thisssssss. They are a plant civilization themed around hunting their prey. They have a tribal theme, and they took over the Hylotl homeworld. They always talk in third person.
Starbound has many types of biomes, as well as civilizations! You may come across an avian village, or maybe an underwater Hylotl city, or even a Glitch castle! There are also microdungeons and other smaller generated builds underground. You can go to some planets normally, but some require radiation shields, cooling or heat systems, or even just an oxygen tank. The game has a huge exploration and roleplay based system. NPC's in villages give out quests that you can go do for a reward. Starbound also has musical instruments you can find and play, paintings and furniture you can collect, and even fossils! I cant even begin to tell you how much I reccomend this game. I hope you are interested in purchasing it, because it can provide you with hours of fun!

As I'm not american, prior to this game I didn't know much about american history. But from playing the game I learned so much. The civilopedia has a bunch of historical information about the building, the units and the great historical persons involved in the gameplay. You get to "hire" historical persons like Ben Franklin, Pocahontas, Lewis and Clark, John Harvard, Alexander Hamilton, Peter Minuit (who purchased Manhattan for 24$), William Penn (founder of PENNsylvania) just to mention a few.
And lastly, a great quote by John Adams mentioned in the opening cinematic:
"If we do not lay ourselves in the service of mankind, whom should we serve"

Sanctum 2 took the best parts of the Original and brought it to the next level, adding something of a story to the mix, expanding on the First person shooter aspect by allowing the player to traverse through the game world from one level to the next and involves the player more in the defense as opposed to just focusing on towers. Visually speaking, Sanctum 2 is crisper, cleaner and more up to date with graphics of newer games even though it was released in 2013. There were some changes to the tower building component as well as the use of personal weapons. In the original you built towers by spending resources, now you are given a number of towers to start with and can place them anywhere, with more towers given to you upon completion of each wave. This makes the challenge a little different as it may take a few waves to redirect the flow of enemies. The changes to personal weapons are that you now need to reload, as opposed to the auto-reload of the original. This makes it more realistic and presents challenge by forcing you to manage your ammunition.
I thought Sanctum 2 took everything to the next level and was a great sequel from a pretty fun game. It has similar options to the first regarding single player or multiplayer, so if you enjoyed playing the original Sanctum you should really enjoy Sanctum 2.

- The LARGEST concern is how slow the game is compared to something like Ultimate Mortal Kombat 3. Let's take a sweep move for example. We are pretty nerdy over here, and timed the sweep move in both games. This latest MK game was 200-300ms SLOWER in sweeping and almost all other moves, than the mk3 moves. This might seem silly, but it all adds up to what feels like a "babied" experience. It's also a bit frustrating as you WANT to go faster, but can't. :\
- You can't, or it's very hard, to start a move while you are falling down, or are down. This is a major flaw as it slows down the fighting experience even more. Say you are Scorp, you've just been knocked down, so you should start that harpoon so that when you are up, you've pressed the last button to execute the move and... nothing. It doesn't count the buttons pressed while you are down, which they did in the old games, which adds a lot to the action. Lame.
- They let you practice fatalities. That seems kind of lame. The thrill was learning them during the actual fights and see if you could pull them off in time.
- The voice acting is simply terrible. Every time you start a new match, the characters say some cheesing, cringe-inducing line. Ugh. Additionally the "FIGHT!" voice sound weak... lame.

After 16.116 reviews, there's nothing else to say about this game right? Wrong.
Everybody feels this game differently, that's one of its assets, but some things just never change. There are some mechanics that are not explained in the game at all and I for one would have liked to know 'em before I started playing. Hence this little reviewlike walkthrough of mine came to be:
First, I'd like to say you won't regret buying this game. But you already knew that, didn't you?
After all, Bastion is a really fun game, Aciton RPG oriented, with a somewhat limited combat system that wil♥♥♥♥♥♥you off from time to time but don't worry. You'll get it eventually!
Where was I? Oh, right...
Instead of talking about the strong suits of the game, I'd like to talk about its flaws. 'Cause yes. It's got them.
Above all, I'd say there are two ways to play Bastion. Casual or Completionist.
If you're heading for casual, congratulations! This game's made for you. Most levels don't last more than ten minutes and there's a specific game mode meant for you called "painless mode".
However, if you intend to get everything in this game I must warn you. It won't be easy...
Know this. You're gonna have to beat the game at least twice.
Enjoy your fisrt playthrough, learn the paths, try out different weapons, smash Scumbags, feel the music and try to understad what the hell's going on. Don't worry yourself about challenges and leave the Idols for later. Just enjoy!
Eventually, you'll reach the grand finale and will need to face a story changing decission. To get all the achievements you need to play both scenarios, so just pick whatever you feel like and enjoy the show. Both decissions will allow you to keep playing so don't worry yourself unnecesarily. Alas, the game feels like the best options are:
1st) Left - Left.
2nd) Right - Right.
One down, one to go. Once you complete the stoy for the first time, you'll unlock "New Game +" mode and "Score Attack" mode. You should know that the latter counts as a New Game + for the "Calamity Kid" achievement, so there's no real need to play the NG+ mode, at all.
The second playthrough's where you'll have to give your best. Start off with no less than five Idols to get the higuest amount of money and experience possible, finish the remaining challenges and enjoy your new traits. Another special move will be unlocked in the Armory (you don't need to own "Portal" to get it) and the History books in the Bastion will now lead you to a brand new "Who Knows Where" battle arena.
Don't push it. Battle arenas can be "easily" beaten with your mortar and pike fully upgraded. But it will take some time to complete the arenas. Strategy is key, choose the right tonics to aid you and take full advantage of your surroundings.
In addition, since you should already be playing in "Score Attack" mode, you can get the "Hard bargain" achievement as well. It is not an easy achevement to get, but a valid method to obtain it has already been discovered. Advance in the story until you unlock the Pipe, then equip "Black Rye" and "Whale Ale" choose a long and short range weapon in the armory, equip the "Gel Cannister" as your special move and renounce "Acobi", "Roathus" and "Olak" at the Temple leaving the remaining Idols active. All you have to do now is enter the Kid's Dream and try to keep the chain with your turrets. Have fun!!
After a while, you should get all the remaining achievements. Thus concluding the completionist path. Congratulations, you did it!!!
Now, regardless of the path you've chosen to enjoy this game, the experience is definitely worth it, but for he completionist gamers it feels like it is a bit harder than it should be unlike what happens in Transistor for example, the next game you should be cheking on! (^_^)

Town of Salem is one of those games where you either love it or you hate it and, for me, I'm with the former. The core game is as solid as it gets, requiring a lot of strategy to perfom well at. Being able to read your opponents AND your teammates is the key to success, meaning that cooperation is a must. Since role selection is randomised, it means you can't get away with only learning the strategies of a handful of roles, but it also means it rarely ever gets stale. Another thing is all of the roles are very varied in terms of playstyle, and no 2 roles feel too much like each other, though certain skills can transfer over between roles (Investigator <-> Sheriff, Doctor <-> Bodyguard)
While I do love the game, I can't give it more credit than it deserves, and even though it's not the game's fault, how well your matches go depends entirely on the people you are matched up with. Bad teammates can ruin any hope of a fun game and this is especially obvious when playing a mafia role. I've encountered multiple people that will deliberately 'throw' games and out their fellow mafia. There are also those people that leave at the start or midway through a game as an important role (e.g. jailor, doctor, sheriff etc.) and running into someone like this is inevitable, but that still doesn't make it any less frustrating. On another note, despite how simple the game may look on the surface, learning the proper playstyles of each role takes a fair amount of time, but there are plenty of guides to follow within the community.
Even though a few negative points were brought up about how players may ruin games, don't let that put you off buying this. There is a free browser version of this game, but the steam version comes with some bonuses. If you're into strategy/murder-mystery based games and love playing with people's heads, I can't recommend any other game.

At first, it kind of reminded me of the old game, "Questron".  It was a C-64 game that was pretty good.  The old-school graphics reminded me of something that I found enticing about those old exploration/combat games a la Ultima I - VI.
The more I played, however, the more I began to understand that there's a difference between something that looks old school and is remniscent of my days past and something that is old school.
Old school is just that -- old.  I don't mind the retro style of programming and gaming, but the content should be contemporary, the mechanics should be modern.  I found the controls in this game to be unnecessarily clunky and burdensome.  I couldn't easily figure out how to check the statuses of various units and really couldn't understand.  The animations didn't just look old school  -- they WERE OLD.  Again, it seems as though I'm splitting hairs by saying this, but  there are plenthy of retro games out there that truly are innovative and cutting edge in the content they provide.
One way I could express my experience with this game -- I always felt as though I was on the cusp of an enjoyable experience.  At times, I almost began enjoying what I was playing.  Almost.  But then the clunky interface would strike or the ancient game mechanics or the old (not old-school but OLD) graphics would take away the enjoyment.
I couldn't figure it out and I didn't feel like putting the time in to do so.  Sorry.

Bastion is a really beautiful game and definetly not your average game.
The art is really beautiful and the story gets told in a special way that I didn't encounter like that in any game I've played until now. Paired with the good voice acting, the really beautiful soundtrack and the already mentioned art it makes Bastion a beautiful, heart-wrenching story.
But of course a good story is nothing without some good gameplay. And Bastion really nails it. There are many weapons, skills and spirits to try and combine so you can play in your own favored playstyle. Even the weapons themself can get upgraded they way the player likes. There are also secret spots filled with fragments, Health Tonics and/or Black Tonics that are fun to find. Same goes for the pets that are kept in the Bastion once they are found.
The levels themselves are well designed and beautiful drawn, they don't look like each other and don't play like each other and contain different enemies supposed to fit the current level, or rather island. Playing through those islands was really fun and the balance is not too hard but also not too easy. There are also the training grounds which add, combined with the memorial, several challenges for the kid/player. Well there are also the steam achievements which are also a challenge itself.
The only thing I'm sad about is that I wish there was a sequel to Bastion because I really fell in love with this game.
So I strongly recommend this game to anyone who didn't buy and play it yet. It's definetly worth it.
