Starbound holds  a special place in my heart. I've had the game since 0.1, and on multiple steam accounts. The game has always had the best oppurtunities to become one of the greatest games around, but it never QUITE made it.
All of that changed with the recent 1.0 update, marking the full release of the game.
You know have a fully pledged story, with interesting and deep characters, insane ammounts of lore and backstory and over 8+ bosses.
Talking about bosses, they range from everything between a spider made of flesh, to a penguin in a futuristic war machine. Every boss is very unique, and their attacks never cease to suprise me.
There are 6 classes to choose from; A robot, A fish, A plant, A collection of gas, An ape and of course human. This sounds very bazare, but as soon as you create your character, you can already read a simple recap of the races backstory.
Starbound is a sandbox gme, and it is a prime example of what a sandbox game should be. You can choose to never mine a single peice of ore, never craft a single peice of armor and wether you want to live on your ship, or on one of the unique procedurally generated worlds. There is thousands and thousands of different blocks and furniture, which comes in great use with the colony system.
The colony system consists of you creating a house, and putting a colony deed inside. The colony deeds cost 750 pixels (the ingame currency). You can choose who will live in the house by either decorating it with old chandeliers and bookshelves, or weapons and armor. You can get everything from a merchant to a guard, and they all come together with the procedural quest system.
Quests (That arent outpost or story related) are always procedually generated, yet they're still all very unique and fun to do. The people who will give them to you are either random NPC's or inhabitants of your colony.
If you so happen to complete a lot of quests for a specific NPC, will he request to join you on your adventure, as a companion. It is only possible to have to companions with you at all times, but it can range verything from a penguin to one of the many races of starbound. The sandbox aspect comes in very real here aswell, as you can either get companions by making colonies, ore buying your way to illegal penguin mecenaries.
If you get enough companions on your ship (You can have as many as you want, just only two with you) your ship will get bigger, leaving you with more room.
There is an infinite universe to explore with many weird and funny biomes, and deep and interesting dungeons.
The weapons of Starbound; The weapons come in many shapes and forms, some silly and some deadly. They, like so much else in this game, have prodcedurally generated stats and looks, which means you will find something cool about almost every weapon you find.
Verdict:
If you want a game with litterally endless things to do and create, and many unique enemies and weapons, you're at the right place. Starbound is huge, and for the gamer that likes to read, there is huge amounts of lore to dive in to. There are plenty of easter eggs and references scattered around the massive diverse planets, just waiting for you to find them.

Alright, I know I'm gonna get flak but I have to be upfront and honest.
First of all.
I first got into Bethesda with oblivion, then skyrim (then I discovered the fallout games) and I fell in love with these games. Sure, they aren't perfect, no game is- but they are an experience. You can always pick those games up and immerse yourself in the worlds. And beyond that you have tens of thousands of mods to choose from, some of which add entire new freaking regions extending your time in the game by hundreds of hours at least.
Fallout 3 was a rough-ish game, we all can agree. It's controls (PC that is) are a little janky, especially when in tense situations. Some people say the NPCs were dull, and to a point I can agree. The voice acting sometimes is a bit iffy, for me personally I just find Megaton's Moira Brown to not contextually, but vocally lack enthusiasm. (and, yes I realize that there is a lot of reusing involved with bethesda's NPC voices, but I let it slide because I can respect the sheer magnitude of the worlds and the number of characters you can meet)
My favorite by far is New Vegas. Developed in partner with Obsidian, while sure the physical game may not be much different from Fallout 3, it's lore, characters, factions, and locations were fascinating. (Many gameplay elements improved too!) If you haven't played FNV I won't spoil anything and all I can say is if you haven't played it, give it a try.
Now we have Fallout 4.
And hell, I was excited for this game.
A brand new fallout game!
Initially, I was greatly impressed.
I won't dare to argue, Fallout 4 is beautiful, and Bethesda truly worked to masterfully create a combination of the lessons learned from the visuals of Skyrim, New Vegas, as well as brand new directions as well. (For example, the Mirelurks, which are familiar big mutant crab/lobster/crayfish abomination from the prior fallout titles, return in a brand new coat of paint, and that's just one of many examples.) Lighting is very well done, and sound design is pretty well executed, as well. One thing that really catches my attention is the parallax mapping of bullet impacts on concrete. (this was a feature in the prior fallout games as well) I could sit and look at that for hours.
This is where I came across my first bump in the ride. There are few reused items from the prior games, and certain objects repeat OFTEN. I get sick of seeing that damn broken wood bedframe in every house! Some of the little objects, from food and chems, as well as junk is definitely a revamped version of things in the previous games. Before any arguments start, I will say, this is a tiny issue, but I have to be honest with what I see. (this doesn't change my opinion of the game.)
The -cough- "new" crafting system, (scrapping as well) is interesting at first, but then I realized- wait, wasn't this a mod (or similar to one) from previous titles? Scrapping gets dull and downright painfully boring as you progress through the game- feeling more like a chore than a feature. Weapon mods? Those were in Fallout New Vegas, nothing new. The armor enhancement, however, that is something I personally found to be really neat. Sure it may not be much different from just modifying a gun, but it unlocks so many new options and abilities according to your playstyle- from heavier but tougher to weaker but lighter.
One thing I will say right off the bat is adding a player voice for Nate/Nora was a mistake. It breaks immersion- and don't even get me started with the trouble of choosing the right dialogue option. (and yes, I know there are mods, but that's the problem. Why does the community have to fix the game's problems!) It doesn't make it feel like you are playing your own unique character sometimes, it feels like you're playing as Nate, or Nora, respectively. That's what made the previous games special! You wanna be the ultimate hero? Go right ahead! Or do you want to shoot everyone you see in the face? We've got you covered! I just feel that it's a step in the wrong direction- and if Bethesda want a more guided experience, that's fine, but make it in a different game, please.

The animations are for me a mixed bag. They can be really good at times, and others, just awful. It's always been a problem with Bethesda's titles: sometimes when fighting it can seem a little playful, for lack of a better word, as enemies (especially melee) can seem like they are pretending to be a kitten pawing at it's owner. But again, this particular issue is minor. The facial animations are also hit or miss. Nate's/Nora's expressions when speaking sometimes are stunning, and do effectively portray deep emotions. (this can first be experienced when speaking to Codsworth at the beginning of the game.) Other times it's as if characters get really wide-eyed or jittery when absolutely nothing is happening, or oppositely stand like a brick wall during times of strife.
Combat, however, is a good point. Maybe too good. I can tell that a large amount of time and effort was put into improving gunplay, and it shows. As many say, Fallout 4 plays as a good FPS but not a good RPG, and there is truth in that. It goes back to the problem of the guided experience and linearity in Fallout 4- it doesn't make it a bad video game, but it does have an effect on how it stands up as a roleplaying experience. The sounds of guns in Fallout 4 are very well done, not so loud to burst your eardrumps like waterballoons but not so quiet that it sounds like you're firing a weaponized typewriter.
Whew. Now that all is said, here's what I can tell you with certainty. If you have never played Fallout, or hell, anything like it, you'll probably love this game.
However.

If you're a longtime regular of Bethesda's titles, and you're looking for a next-generation line in the Fallout Franchise, you may be disappointed. I am in this category, and yes, it hurts to admit it but, I was very disappointed by Fallout 4.
On a number scale, it depends.
If you like FPS style gameplay, it's a solid 7 or 8 out of 10, and I would definitely recommend it.
But if you were in the group who really were looking forward to a new story driven fallout, it's only a 6 of ten at best- and I just can't recommend it.
I don't want to get into any sludge about the whole controversy but, because of the whole Creation Club, and as a modder myself, I give it a thumbs down ONLY to show my position to Bethesda, as many others have. For the game itself I would rather just rate it as slap dab in the middle- just because there is a sharp division over the new style of gameplay introduced in Fallout 4.
Play it for yourself, is the best advice I can give.

Having been asked whether to purchase L4D or L4D2, I've always said wait for a sale and purchase both. It may sound like a cop-out but there are good reasons to play each game on their own.
L4D plays like a zombie apocalypse experience. Everything is darker and more gritty - there is an actual feeling that you may not survive. The dialogue is slightly different and so are the levels. You also learn the fundementals of weapon management and teamwork as weapon drops seem further apart and you will be going through your ammo much faster when you're given a choice between your secondary weapon and a pair of pistols. Pipe bombs and molotovs are fairly common but you'll learn to always keep one in reserve.
On the downside, there are no melee weapons in L4D and the selection of secondary weapons is limited. Likewise, there are fewer special infected. Mechanically, the AI is not nearly as good and there have been many times I've died while my computer teammates are camped out at the exit or room beside me. They're also not intelligent enough to follow you in the event you're laying a trap with a fuel can. I've also had hordes spawn directly on my head, as opposed to around the corner or from another room in L4D2. The graphics have also been updated in the second game but this is to be expected.
The negatives are greatly overwhelmed by the positives, however. The AI can be frustrating but L4D plays as a complete experience. You won't regret buying it if you purchase it as a stand-alone but you'll notice the difference if you've play L4D2 for any amount of time. Highly recommended if you're looking to kill some time...and zombies.

A Fun little 'Twin-Stick' title with a thumping electronic soundtrack, bright cartoony visuals and an interesting upgrade system to keep you hooked.  Although Meltdown shows its roots as an IOS title (primarily in the simplistic Menu), Theres a lot of fun to be had here for the relatively small price-tag.
Content wise theres a great variety of Robotic bad-guys to blast, and an extensive armoury of unlockable guns, knifes and chainsaws with witch to blast them! It must be said however that the visual style (tileset) of each level seems to be  identical throughout the game, which can get a little stale.
I'm generally not a fan of IOS games being Ported over to the PC, but I'm glad to say once you jump into the gameplay, Meltdown does not necessarily feel like game that was designed with a touch screen in mind.
With some emphasis on taking cover over running and gunning, you might find the pace of Meldown a little slow by comparison to other arcade twin-sticks  (think Ultratron or Bullet Candy), but I would say theres enough going on here mechanically to keep most engaged for a few hours at least.
Would I reccomend? - Yes!

This is definitely not a game meant for marathon play sessions, just short bursts of action every now and then.

I see a lot of people, who are comparing this to Terraria, i'v come to make my point on this topic.
Like i did with terraria and minecraft i will point out what i find to be the features and parts that create the game's personality and how its different.
I'll start with a brief description of Terraria since most people know what that is if they are here.
Terraria is a 2-D Sandbox survival game by Re-Logic in where as you simply have to beat every boss in the game and upgrade your gear to its optimal state in accordance to your prefered weapon type and playstyle. the main game has constantly expanded from its conception with a total of ♥♥♥♥ tons (I may be a fanboy for the game but i dont know the exact number) weapons, items, trinkets, armor and all that♥♥♥♥♥♥ also building, which is a massively important feature of the game as it has a system in which when you make a suitable house (Light source, table, chair and being an actual building with walls) you can move one of your npcs into said building where they will stay during night to avoid the monsters at night. the brunt of your time will be spent early on when you have to spend time traveling to certain places and looking for certain things.  so the game is a bit grindy when it comes to prep work since bosses are also part of that prep since some bosses will only spawn with a item or just randomly when you least expect it and if your not prepared the boss you will have a run for your money.
TLDR : make the best gear, kill the hardest bosses, do the events and then the rest is up to you and mounts make speed all of that up.
Now onto starbound. first i want to say that i have not played starbound as much as terraria so i may be a bit inaccurate with some things.
Starbound from what i can tell is about space exploration, base building, a story and dungeons with a boss at the end. At the beggining of Starbound you had very little assistance since you were helped right upto the first boss (Which was a push over) and after that you get no help and no direction to what you should pursue next, now there is a mission system that will guide you along your way allowing you to get a sense of progression that Terraria had very little off since from that start your only assistance was a guide who gave you vague hints at best. While in Terraria you may be just one world and four directions (up, down left and right) in Starbound you also have the same on a possiblity infinate scale due to SPAAAAAAAAAAAAAAACE. in terms of combat it has improve a lot since the start, in the start you just had regular swing, regular stab, regular slice, regular blugeon and shoot, now theres a attack progression system that for example for two handed sword you have a three hit combat that starts with a swing into a stab and then slice, and to top it off two handed weapons have a skill attatched to them like attacking your left and right or by spinning your weapon behind you and then following up with a ranged energy slice. then you can apply 1 handed weapons with either another weapon or another item which opens up a ton of possibilities, plus there have been plenty of new weapon types added over the course of the development effectively one upping terraria's combat system click to swing, aim a spell or ranged weapon. another thing i want to touch on though quickly is despite what i just said Terraria's combat isn't that bad, its just simple. Onto exploration, Since starbound planetside exploration is mostly the same as Terraria i'll just talk about space exploration. Exploration in space is done inside your ship and requires fuel to power the FTL drive, said fuel can be aquired in the outpost for the ingame currency or mined planet side, it costs no fuel to travel between planets in a star but it costs fuel to travel between stars with the farther away the star is to the one your currently in the more fuel it costs. to help get between your bases, settlements and the hub which is outpost you can set waypoints which you can warp to via a teleporter that your ship has build in and a teleporter you can buy for ingame currency. in terms of variety from last i played with a character who could travel between stars there a several different types of stars each with unique properties and each planet has unique properties and unique monsters. this last is based off research on the wiki but it also appears that they are taking a page from Terraria and altering it a little with armour for specific types of weapons each crafted in a different station which i'll say is really awesome since that is one of my favourite things in games. my last point is the armor itself, each race has different looking armour meaning that each race has a unique look as well as they all have their own unique names that tie in with their race while also not making players split up because they need a different meterial for their armor.
TLDR : Starbound is simular to Terraria in terms of art direction, planetside exploration, combat system and npc housing while being its own game.
Would i suggest buying this?
Yes
Would i say buy it instead of Terraria?
What i would say is support both Re-logic and Chucklefish since the games they made are each unique in their own rights.
TLDR : Space and planet side exporation with a mission system.
Also the only game i can say where you can mine out a astroid and make a pool in space.
Terraria in space. Buy this game.

Intro:
Conquest of Elysium 3 is the latest in the CoE series made by Illwinter, who are also the designers of the Dominions series. In simple terms the game is about raising armies to defeat your opponenets. At the start of each game you select a class to play which determines how you go about raising your armies or what your fighting style is. An example is the enchanter class, at the start most of your army is composed of generic soldiers until you get resources to summon powerful constructs and golems in the mid to late game.
Pros:
-There are 18 different classes to pick from each having cool special abilities and playstyles unique to them.
-There are many cool units and magic spells to mess with.
-Games play quickly and end faster than most strategy games.
-Random generated maps allow for endless play.
Cons:
-The graphics are rather lacking.
-The unit animations are also rather lacking.
-Lots of unit stats to sift through.
-Some matches are doomed from the start due to bad spawn areas.
Bottom Line:
If you enjoy a strategy game where everytime you play you learn something new this game is for you. If you are short on time a lot but you love to play complex strategy games this is for you as well. If you are a person who cares about graphics do not pick this up, likewise if you are not willing to (possibly) read a manual sometimes then do not pick this up either. Illwinter has made many improvements from Conquest of Elysium 2 and at the cheap price of ten dollars it could be argued that this game beats many modern strategy games in terms of features and replayability.

As a single player FPS, this game is about 15 hours of non-stop fun. I'm sure it's even more fun if you're familiar with the three movie series: Alien, Predator and Alien vs. Predator, and their sequels. The game shows a lot of respect for the lore established in those movies and expands a little on it.
The aliens and predators look great. The music and sound effects are spot on. I found it impressive how the storylines of the three campaigns (marine, alien, predator) are nicely interwoven.
As you can imagine, the way to play each campaign is completely different depending on the species you play and their weapons and skills, but each campaign even has a different HUD that really fits the species, which adds to an already immersive experience.
You can adjust the difficulty to fit your play style and your (in)experience with FPS games. You can play the game with a gamepad, but I'm not used to the 'twin stick' thing where one stick moves your character and another stick moves the camera. So I quickly switched to mouse and keyboard, which was a lot smoother for me. You can bind keyboard keys for each species seperately in the options menu.
I haven't tried multiplayer but I gather from other reviews that multiplayer for this game is dead, so if you're looking for a good multiplayer FPS, I suppose you need to look elsewhere. This also means that steam achievement completionists will have a hard time because 12 of the 50 achievements require multiplayer action.
All in all, I'd recommend this game to anyone who reads this because that means you're at least remotely interested in FPS games or in the movies this game is based upon. But since three single player campaigns of about 5 hours each is all you'll get out of it, I would advise against paying full price for the game and instead waiting for it to be on sale.

Gameplay of Binding of Isaac: Rebirth is quite simple. You descent randomly generated dungeon killing mosters, collecting items that grant you different abilities and synergies when two or more items are combined. At the end of every floor you have to fight a boss monster. There are eleven playable characters (thirteen with Afterbirth DLC), hundreds of different room layouts and crazy amount of secrets, items and item combinations to discover.
Game may seem quite difficult at first, even though it felt somewhat easier to me than the original Binding of Isaac. Difficulty of the game is mostly based on your skills, but even your worst run can become your best (and vice versa) depending on which items you get during the run. However, game will get easier once you've played enough and you start to remember different room layouts, monster attack patterns, item effects and item combinations.
It took me around 300 hours to unlock every secret and achievement in the game (with Afterbirth), so I would say that it has pretty good replay value. The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth with the Afterbirth DLC is easily one of my favorite games that I've ever played across any platform.

24 hours and 67 achievements later...
Kingdom Rush has been around for a while, and this is how it started, but ported from Flash and to Steam with some additional content for a relatively good price. quite frankly, this is the best version to own, better than Android/iOS and definitely better than the freemium version on Armor Games website, where the game can be made easier via purchases.
so, let's get down to business (+/- for pros/cons respectively.)
+ GRAPHICS (or, rather, looks)
game looks good. that about wraps it up.
+ GAMEPLAY
it starts off very simple but gets progressively harder/deeper from there. it's very simple, really, 4 basic towers available, you build them in predefined spots, and you also get to use two spells, rain of fire that deals AoE damage and reinforcements, which are simply reinforcements.
+ CONTENT
there's quite a few levels, and there should still be at least few more coming. if you include going for 100% achievements/3 stars on every level/Heroic & Iron challenges that's easily 20+ hours of gameplay. i'm done with the achievements but not the game yet. there's quite a few heroes to choose from too.
there's also a meta-game of using stars you get from clearing levels to upgrade tower skill trees, however these are very straightforward most of the time and choice does not matter much.
- AIMING MECHANICS
i'm just gonna say it - they're clunky sometimes. they tend to target the furthest targetable enemy in the lane they can still reach, that's where trouble comes in. slow firing towers will waste their damage shooting into an enemy that's already dead, artillery tower will shoot a projectile that misses the first time for 90% of the time and enemies will not be blocked by soldiers even though they are in their reach sometimes.
- TAPPING MECHANICS
soooooo unsuitable for PC. you have to tap like you would tap a smartphone/tablet to not get your towers frozen in two boss levels, second one being the main boss level which is simply unnacceptable.
- MOST POTENT STRATEGIES
it boils down to Tesla+Barracks around mid-game, since that is the most powerful strategy given you have upgraded the damage fall-off removal on Artillery skill trees.
- BALANCE
there are few enemy types that are just plain overpowered, rendering some tower combos simply obsolete. mainly the enemy that duplicates itself indefinitely uninterupted and enemy that jumps over your reinforcements despite having already gotten involved in combat.
- LACK OF OPTIONS
it would make life easier for me if i could turn off character callouts since they get a little repetitive with each tower/character/hero having 2-4 phrases they repeat constantly.
all in all, it's a great game. small tweaks could be made to make it more enjoyable, but yes, it would become easier then, and difficulty is one thing this game got going for it. it's no rival for Defense Grid, but it's an enjoyable title nonetheless.

ICEY is an  2D - sidescrolling action game that focusses on animations, combos and the narrative.
IF you do like a slight humour stretching throughout the game, combined with decent fighting mechanics and style, this game is probably for you. If you easily get annoyed by jokes being cracked again and again (arrow- jokes, looking at you ), you should probably stay away.
Although the gameplay is up close to the current standard, which I would consider decent, it fails to really do something very new. You can upgreade your moves damagewise, and purchase some new ones by collecting money, which you can also just farm by repeating missions.  ICEY also features quite some boss fights, which are a core aspect of the game.
Instead, I consider the game's forte to be the narrative style and visualization. It isn't a AAA title with supreme graphics, but the animations are very well done  and it fits into a great theme. The narrative focusses a lot on things that aren*t necessarily the main storyline. You can, AND SHOULD, explore the world more, to find out what this game has to offer. There are some very humorous passages in the "monologue" which made me enjoy my playthrough a lot.
The difficulty is alright, some bosses aren`t that easy, but not that much of a hazard as well, balancing out the game rather well. If you really struggle with a passage, just farm some money on earlier missions and you will be fine !
The Achievements are well placed and hint at the extra content that the game has to offer.
If i were to rate this game, it would be a solid 8/10.
-1 because it is rather short
-1 because there is nothing really innovative and the enemy variety could use some help
Apart from that, this is a clear recommendation, get this game if you want to go on a small little, well-crafted journey.

I can totally understand if you don't want to support Bethesda because of the Creation Club fiasco!  I can also understand if you'd rather your Fallout games actually be in-depth RPGs that put more emphasis on character interaction than combat.  If Fallout 4 had been marketed as a spinoff like Tactics or Shelter instead of as a main-series entry--even "Fallout: Brotherhood of Steel 2" would have fit well--it would probably have had a much better reception.  My initial thoughts on the game, after putting 100 hours into it and some of its expansions, went something like, "What I played of Far Harbor was incredible, and Automatron is really useful, but the base game's world is kind of boring, and I'm ready to move on."  Then I decided to go back and start experimenting with character and combat builds instead of worrying about story or writing, and I began having much more fun.
-------------------------
You'll probably be happiest if you approach Fallout 4 as a shooter with RPG features rather than the other way around, as while you do have conversations and dueling factions, they mostly feel like a pretense for lots of action sequences rather than serious moral discussion.  The game world isn't written with a lot of relevant detail, but the art style becomes lovelier as you venture farther into the game's southern and downtown areas, which are gorgeous to look at despite the game's low poly count.
The story is nothing special--if you tried Binary Domain (which I also recommend, and there's a Steam demo), you have a fair idea of what to expect--and it feels like it exists to give you lots of morally unambiguous enemies to shoot at, but there are a number of genuinely, if briefly, compelling twists and appeals for emotion, even if that's most of what the story feels like it has going for it.  However, a few moments in the narrative were genuinely moving in ways I'd like to see better games do more often, such as one instance where the game humanizes one of its villains after he's already dead, then offers you a chance to feel remorse after the fact (I'd like to see more games examine not just your choices, but your motives and feelings afterward, especially after unintended consequences).  There's a returning face from Fallout 3 who's being tugged between two factions and is justifiably cynical toward both, and while the story could have used more of this, mini-plots like this are enjoyable while they last.
The side quests tend toward hit-or-miss extremes, with a lot of these quests being repetitive "go here and complete a basic task" affairs (usually killing things but not always--one hidden but major faction's quests often involve setting up monitoring systems in locations that are difficult to reach and usually high up), but the upside of this is that you tend to gain character levels very quickly, especially if you abuse the save/reload system and a certain perk to earn psychotic amounts of experience easily.  However, some side missions are absolute gold, such as a seemingly generic SOS mission that turns into rescuing a Shakespearean ambassador from the Super Mutants he's trying to culturally uplift, or a series of crime-fighting quests where you're a costumed vigilante receiving orders in the style of an old-fashioned radio drama, or a very out-of-the-way quest that invites you to empathize with or betray a monster that has basically the same plot driver you do.
A lot of criticism of the game seems to lend the impression that you don't get any moral choices, but you do--sometimes.  There are several problems here--you have to search far and wide to find these choices, most open-ended quests are only a few minutes long (with some notable exceptions), there's no end-of-game denouement slideshow, and the game's opening does a poor job of showing the player what to expect since it ushers you into repetitive content very quickly despite hardly any of that being mandatory.  Several factions have repeatable "go to randomly selected area XYZ and do thing" quests, and some of the game's best quests lend the false impression that they're just as generic, because that's what the game's conditioned you to expect.  I held off on completing one quest until after I'd beaten the game (you CAN play afterward), since the mission sounded like a generic delivery, but it mutated into a non-violent cult rescue, a shootout in an occupied asylum, and a very bizarre moral choice where the stakes in the long run are probably death-or-death.  The game's quality of content, in my opinion, improves the farther away you get from the northwest corner of the map where you start, with some of the most interesting places being near the opposite coasts, such as a creepy and dangerous witchcraft museum, or a boat occupied by Raiders who speak Norwegian.
I do miss the number/percentage-based skill system, but I do like the newly emphasized real-time combat and the odd skill/perk hybrid system.  Perks are now offered in a grid, with your S.P.E.C.I.A.L. statistics (Strength, Perception, Endurance, etc.) on one axis and with stat ranks 1 through 10 on another.  You have to have a certain rank of a certain stat, not counting clothing/food bonuses, in order to take that perk, and you can generally take perk ranks out of order.  "Cannibal" becomes available at Endurance 8, for example.  This frankly feels more balanced than I expected, since the various high-level perks don't feel like they break the game or make more basic investments in combat skills irrelevant.  Being able to pounce your targets in melee is handy, but it's no substitute for improving your sneak ability or weapon damage.  Caveats on certain abilities like disarming land mines (simply mash the Interact key regardless of stats or perks) feel like they would have fit well even here, and there's a lot of this inattention to detail given the neat things you can do.  Perks often have multiple ranks, with high level requirements, which feels grindy but keeps you from quickly becoming overpowered.
The new emphasis on real-time combat and the smoother aiming mechanics make this more fun to play as an action game than as one where pausing the game to pick targets is the safest way to proceed.  VATS now only partially slows time, so you might actually die while using it, and unless you've put a lot of ranks into certain Perception skills, it might seem unreliable anyway, especially since to-hit percentages can change instantly if an enemy walks behind a wall.  Environmental hitboxes can be annoying. Likewise, since the Alt key by default is overloaded with functions--weapon bashing, grenade throwing, or holding one's breath while sniping (very useful, especially since Skyrim's stealth-damage increases are here), it would have been nice for more of these functions or New Vegas' alternative melee options to be available in VATS.
However, the modification system for weapons and armor is one of the game's highlights and is one of my favorite changes from Fallout 3 and New Vegas.  Instead of making weapons from scratch like in Skyrim, you use "Bethesda-clutter" items from the environment to add lots of customization options to guns you already have, like different barrels, receivers (including some that alter ammunition type and damage output), magazines, scopes, suppressors, and so on.  Many weapons can be made automatic or sniper-friendly with the addition of a few parts, but the odd consequence of this is that I felt more of an emotional connection to my guns than to the actual characters.
-------------------------
Fallout 4's "RPG features" are mostly ones that lots of other genres have now anyway, but you'll probably enjoy the game more if you're fine with it being a crafting shooter first and only occasionally involving role-playing--and by the time that rolls around, you've probably already leveled up again.

This game originated on iOS, and it shows with the grind-centric gameplay. It starts off promisingly enough, a decent twin-stick shooter with satisfying feedback, rolling and cover mechanics, and an upgrade system. Trouble is, that's it. Each new mission is essentially the exact same thing, through the same basic scenario (some generic future industrial rooms), with the same type of gameplay: strafe and shoot. As you level up your weapons, so the enemies level up in strength, which means it actually doesn't feel like you're getting anywhere at all. Really, level 10 feels exactly the same as level 1. The only variety is a gradual reveal of different enemy types, although nothing here will surprise you, and a slow unlocking of weapons and armour that you have to upgrade with coins and upgrade tokens. It's here that the iOS origins really show, this quest for coins that you gradually amass, the need to repeatedly play the same levels to find the right tokens to upgrade your weapons, so you can keep up with the enemies. Around level 10 is when the game introduces stun-lock enemies that are a massive pain in the butt, and very hard to avoid as they travel quite a bit faster than you can, and take some putting down. That was about as much as I could take. I'm sure you could get a couple of hours out of this, but that's not enough to recommend it.

I've played realm since the beginning of 2013 and most people will probably tell you not to play this game because its not good anymore. They are wrong, its still good just a different game than it used to be.
See the problem lies with the game changing companys 3 times. It is currently now in the hands of Deca Games who are producing more content than the previous 2 years under Kabam's reign (previous owner)
Now the gameplay loop of realm is somewhat like this....
You make a new character on a new account, which is a Wizard. The first of the 14 unlockable classes ( you have the ability to pay for them, but that would be dumb because you can easily unlock them all for free.)
Now with this new character you spawn in the nexus, the safe haven of the game. You have one vault chest that has 8 slots for you to store items for your next character and thats it.
You go in to the realm and you kill enemies in the lowlands and midlands ( highlands is hard until level 20 ish) and try to get to level 20.
Now it starts to get complicated. In the mountains there are gods that drop potions and dungeons. The dungeons have garunteed potion drops to 1-2 people. You need potions to make your character better beyond level 20.
The most common of these potions is Dexeterity, which makes you shoot faster. On wizard at level 20 you will be at around 40-50 dex and you need to get to 75 which is the max. So you do the sprite world which drops dex 30-40 times to max the stat then rinse and repeat for all the other stats. They have their own dungeons and mostly everything is harder to get than dex. But this is what you are going to be doing over and over until you get good enough to max a character completely.
Realm takes quite a bit of time to get decent at, and once you are good its still just as frustrating as before. But that doesn't mean its not a good game. Its just very different from anything you've probably played before.

I have been playing Starbound here and there for years. Seeing it grow has been a very enjoyable experience, but seeing what it has become has been both amazing and awful.
While there are some systems in place that I am very pleased with how they've evolved, there are others that still feel shallow or lackluster. Take the Combat for example, no matter what you do in the early game you will inevitably get damaged after almost every encounter with the indigenous alien life which forces you to pop salve after salve in between every encounter. Combine this with the hunger system and you are sure to die the first time you go underground for an extended expedition for Core Fragments.
Another big mistep in my opinion is the way they handled death post-alpha. It used to be you lost pixels(the in-game currency) at a flat pecent rate upon death, you would keep all of your inventory but be forced to respawn on the ship. Now when you die, you lose building materials, health items and ores AS WELL AS the pixel penalty from before.
Chuckle Fish, this isn't the Souls series. I'm here to explore, build and collect, not fight with the boring and broken combat system just to die time and time again to something ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t like being conered by four monster that fell ontop of me after a sandvalanche caused them to pile up proximity hitting me every half second. If you wanted the combat to feel "tactical" or "stategic" as you've plainly put it before - only do the damage when they attack, not when they are touching you. That mechanic has always been dumb and I'm surprised it passed so many updates without a change.
All in all, this game is worth the buy. It is massive and overall an enjoyable experience. Although with how many years we've been beta testing this for them, you'd think it would be a masterpeice. . . oh well.
Now that the game is out, I suppose I should give it a shot.

So what's new? Actually alot, way more than I thought there would be and way more than the developers led on. Chucklefish well played, you brought back tons of features since the beta and really streamlined the game to be more like a fun campaign. Some of the features I personally liked:
- No more taking chairs and light fixtures to the ship computer to gain the ability to build it, you just point and click as part of your character.

- Backpacks actually work and have different features now such as breathing in areas you could not normally, before this was just a tech ability but now its a real thing!

Feature(s) I still want to see(really its only one big thing):
- Block modification, I really want to have the ability/item to slant blocks so I can slide down mario style / make waterfalls with.
- Maybe a map editor? Since this game is more like a campaign now it would be fun to see the maps that fans might make.
All in all a 9/10 (I'm about to put some real hours on this game!)

Icey was an enjoyable experience I can easily recommend as long as a certain default language setting is changed. Which took me just shy of five hours to 100% its achievements and find all its hidden secrets. The game on hard, for the most part, wasn't all that difficult for me personally except for one optional boss taking a bunch of deaths to learn his patterns. The combat was a solid 2D combo-based beat'em up fair much like Dust: An Elysian Tail.
The meta aspect was enjoyable and funny most of the time. As long as you changed the voiced dialog to the Chinese voice actor with English subtitles. Some of the time the narration did get a little unnecessary wordy when you did something that went against the narrator's directions. Kind of the point of the game, so you'll have to sit through some most-of-the-time funny rants that lasted up to five minutes or so. Also, the English translation of the script was a tad rough at times and could of use a bit more editing.
If I was to pick a con with the meta aspect itself: It would be that at times you have to sit through the narrator going off on his rants over and over again while being unable to progress in a stage until he finishes. Even if you had already viewed and heard it. Particularly, can be aggravating after repeated death(s).
Now for the real bad: I almost raged quit the game and requested a refund within mere minutes of the English voiced narrator first opening his mouth following the tutorial segment. Frankly, whoever did the English narrator voice work, in my opinion, is flat out horrible and adds no value to the game what-so-ever. It sounded like an extremely forced attempt at a dramatic reading by an amateur that the developer probably got on the extremely cheap to fill an English dub checkbox. Plus, for some reason, he sounded like he was patronizing the player even when they were doing what he as the narrator wanted. So it kind of felt like the actor(?) really was not enjoying himself and maybe had no interest in the role what-so-ever. Short version: he'll grate on your nerves real fast as other reviews have also have pointed out. I truly commend anyone who could actually finish the game with the English voice narrator setting active and the volume not turned down.
Thankfully, I decided to give the Chinese actor a chance. Although, I would of rather not had to read subtitles while playing this fast-based combat game. The acting quilty difference was night and day. Which changed my view of the game from outright loathing to enjoyed. It was a solid performance that was funny and enjoyable for me that felt natural and never overly forced. Nor did the Chinese actor's performance ever grated on my nerves like the English narrator. With this being said, I'm a person who watches tons of English dubbed anime and foreign shows. Who normally would defend most English dubbing that been done in recent years. So to me, it was truly a failure in the choice of the English actor(?) and not so much the choice to have an English dubbing. If we had gotten someone else I imagine it could have been a lot better.

While I'm generally more of a cat person myself, when it comes to the games industry, dogs are seriously the way to go. From Dog's Life to Watch Dogs, canines fail to disappoint. Sleeping Dogs is definitely no exception.
You are thrown into Hong Kong, as an undercover cop infiltrating the notorious Hong Kong triads that are very much real. Similar to Mafia 2, the game describes the criminal underworld realistically and does not sugarcoat it as much as some other games might. This is definitely a plus. In Sleeping Dogs, you make friends, you make enemies, you lose friends and you take down your enemies. The characters in Sleeping Dogs are awesome. They have personality, and you really want to know more about them.
From your best friend Jackie Ma to a Red Pole on the Sun On Yee (The in-game version of Sun Yee On, the biggest triad in HK & China), this game really has an awesome cast. My favorites are definitely the Red Poles on the Sun On Yee. It's clear all of them wield a lot of power in the city, and they all have something unique about them.
I really like the game's setting. Too many modern blockbuster games "play it safe" and pick some generic setting (generally from the U.S.) which you've probably seen before. How many blockbuster games with top level graphical fidelity are set in Asian countries? (I don't even want to talk about how badly represented African, South American and Asian settings are in the games industry, historical or modern)
Hong Kong is a lively place with plenty of activities and much to do. The game has plenty of side activities which are actually interesting. It's not an Ubisoft game so you don't have to fear the repetitive and boring side activities which just reward you with map vision. You can take part in illegal street races, cockfighting (yes, cockfighting), gambling, karaoke, street fights and more. There are even some romance options with their own missions (They're not radiant activities, though, just a few missions) and some nice collectibles as well.
And absolutely, one of the jewels of this game is the combat system. There are guns, but guns aren't your main weapon. Your main weapon is martial arts (or just fighting in general) The game is realistic and accurate in the sense that gun control in Hong Kong really is tight (You also drive on the left). The fighting system is fun and functional. While it's hard to compare it to the Arkham combat or the AC combat even though in essence it's influenced a lot by them, I would compare it to the combat in Remember Me the most. It's very fast and sometimes very challenging. You have various different combos (which you get to learn and upgrade as the game goes on) and a very fun grab & smash system where you can use the environment to kick people's faces in, so to say.
So, the pros of this game are absolutely:
+ An awesome combat system, with a working combination of weapons / guns and martial arts. Very fun and has depth and difficulty to it for those who want it. The gunfights are fun as well with some bullet time action which makes it feel like an action movie sometimes.
+ An awesome setting, a vibrant city with plenty of things to do.
+ Great graphics, definitely consider picking up the Definitive Edition for even more. Just seeing the Hong Kong night market in the game makes me want to pick up my passport.
+ A great story with awesome characters. The story will not disappoint you. The characters will not bore you.
But what about the cons, then? Well. The combat is fun, but it's also a bit long. Some opponents and thugs are really, really tough. And of course, it's mostly fistfighting so you can't expect to be rid of a guy with a few punches (with guns it is of course easier). But still, sometimes it feels like a fight with 3 people is taking way too long. Might get repetitive.
Also, I really dislike the fact you have no inventory or scroll option for guns or melee weapons. You can only have 1 gun at a time (realistic, true) but equipping and holstering your gun is very hard. I end up dropping my gun on the ground most of the time. It'd be nice if I had a weapon wheel of some sort.
The driving mechanics are very arcadey. Some will love it, some will not. If you expect realistic and GTA or driving game-esque mechanics, you might be disappointed. The driving mechanics are definitely functional, but if it's not a long journey, I'd rather just walk the streets than drive. The "arcadiness" extends to some other areas as well, such as the fighting and the character animations. It's not a problem for me but some people might not like it.
So, cons:
- Driving is average
- Martial arts combat might draw out a bit. At certain points it might get overly difficult or repetitive.
- The arcadey feel might not be for everybody.
All in all I still love this game and I really hope we get more games like this that are willing to explore the criminal underworld without sugarcoating or satirical vibes (Like GTA). Games that bring you a very good story with awesome characters with epic voice acting. Games that aren't solely set in either the U.S. or a fictional world (this game was made by western devs so it's not like all western games must have western settings). Assassin's Creed does that a lot but it still hasn't hit African, Asian (Apart from the M. East) or South American soil, and it's all historical and not really realistic. Sleeping Dogs really is a great game and I hope they continue the franchise and other devs take notes on how to have a good setting, good character design, a good and relatable protagonist and awesome story and side missions.
Unique, challenging and fun to play. You won't regret buying it.

The Good: Action-oriented combat is addictive, locations feel lively, story is very well written and delivered, brutal enviromental takedowns provide a nice variety of satisfaction, fun leaderboard challenges set by friends, a good amount of combos to learn over the course of the game to flesh combat out further
The Bad: Combat can occasionally feel unresponsive, police experience can sometimes be hopeless, shooting mechanics could be a little better, the fact that its a port from consoles is very apparent in controls, story loses a little traction towards the half of the game before gaining it back, dialouge can occasionall feel forced to include Chinese words in it
Premise: Sleeping Dogs is compelling and most definately worth the money and time to play through, at the very least the triad missions.
Story: Meet Wei Shen, a very successful undercover cop. He has a pretty good reputation in the police force for his ability to close cases, even though he's known to grow a bit excessive. This leads to him being sought out by Detective Pendrew to go undercover into the Triad. This brings Wei Shen home to Hong Kong where he's back to running the streets as a gangster. Over time, his motives become clear while his allegiances become more and more blurred. The story becomes more and more compelling to around the middle of the game, but picks back up quickly following that. The dialouge is well-written for the most part, with occasional Chinese words being thrown in seemingly at random as if the developers wanted to say "Hey, we understand Chinese!" Regardless, from start to conclusion, you're bound to get just the right amounts of satisfaction. However, there is virtually no risk involved, as the checkpoint system is very lenient, sometimes skipping you ahead.
Mechanics: The controls occasionally (though very rarely) handle poorly on keyboard, and it becomes apparent that PC gamers were an afterthought to the developers. However, it can be overlooked more often than not. The combat is mainly focused on melee, with gunfights being frequent, but not taking the spotlight. And for a good reason. The combat is based on attack-and-counter, similar to entries of the Batman: Arkham series. Where the combat deviates is that it introduces combos, which can be unlocked by leveling up your cop or triad levels or gathering jade figurines for your sifu, to the scene. As you play through the game you gain the ability to learn new combos which change up the combat based on your ability to execute them, some even having completely different functions than just to damage the enemies. But though the combat feels really refined and fleshed out, the gunplay is merely decent. In order to aim, you have to hold the shift key, which begins to feel really awkward very quickly, and right mouse button could be much more comfortable to use. Pair that with the slightly annoying cover mechanic, and sometimes gunplay segments can find themselves frustrating. Thankfully, these moments of frustration seemed to be far from frequent throughout the entire story. The driving can have its moments, as I found it far too easy to accidentally press the right mouse button while changing the camera with the mouse and launch myself out of a high speed vehicle to do a hefty amount of damage or outright kill myself. Other than that, American players will be disoriented at first, as the driving is done on the left-hand side of the rode, rather than the right. This adds a great deal to the overall atmosphere of the game, making you feel like you're on vacation to Hong Kong. The customization of clothing is quite nice, some clothes requiring you to level up your "face" level to a cetain point (achieved by doing small missions for random people across Hong Kong, though easily ignorable).
Multiplayer: While there is no competitive/cooperative multiplayer aspects persay, there are leaderboards for challenges like driving a high speed without taking damage for x amount of time that automatically track you and your friend's times or score, which can lead to some satisfying moments when you climb over friend's scores, but the victory will be short lived as you realize that there's no real reward, and most people won't really care for the place they land.
Graphics: The game looks very nice. From riding a boat into the ocean, to walking down the street and looking at the people you pass. To the way the rain affects the roads and smoke rises from mufflers, and espeically the gore from enviromental takedowns, you will not find yourself requesting better graphics.
Final Verdict: Sleeping Dogs is a great game for those who love great stories. Its an absolute must-buy for anyone who loves sandbox crime-based worlds, as well. The current asking price is fair, and getting it on sale is a steal. Very highly recommended.

This is probably going to be one of the hardest reviews I've ever written because the game itself is fun, and while are a couple of really big parts of the game that almost seem to go against each other, yet the more I think about it the more I appreciate about the game and its complexity.
So before I start explaining the features of the game, the best way to describe this, as I'm sure many other reviews have also said, is it is basically a Stanley Parable mixed with any 2D sidescrolling kind of game. If you are into games that break the fourth wall and meta game, you might get a laugh out of a few parts of this.
Gameplay
Let me start by saying that the gameplay in this is purely going screen to screen fighting various enemies along to a story. With that being said, it seems pretty dull, but for some reason the combat is extremely satisfying and something that is simple, yet complex and elegant. Sure you could button mash your way through majority of the battles, but the number of different combos you can conduct and experiment with through your adventures makes it almost impossible to stick to a same two move routine.
Everytime you kill an enemy you get money, which you can spend on upgrading new moves and getting new combos. I had to play through the game twice to get all the achievements, and I didn't even unlock everything, showing how much room there is to mess around with unlocking different things. For someone who can barely remember combos in fighting games like mortal combat and soul calibur, being able to start small and learn more combos, while upgrading your favorites through your adventures is definitely something I won't forget
The Narrator and Meta-Gaming
While I think meta gaming (narrator talking to you directly instead of your character) can be something really well done and funny, I think in a 2D combat platformer there isn't enough potential openness for it to be such a big part of the game. Constantly throughout the game there are arrows telling you where to go, and if you follow the arrows, the game is extremely short and straightforward.
If you don't listen however, you find new secret areas and hear the narrator yell at you for not listening to him. That may be funny for the first few times, but after hearing it time and time again, along with the narrators not so great voice acting when trying to sound emotional about it, it starts to get somewhat annoying. Especially when sometimes you are standing in a room for up to ten minutes, yes ACTUALLY 10 minutes just hearing him rant about something. Honestly the narrator kind of ruins the game, sometimes you'll love the meta-gaming, sometimes you'll hate it, either way it is just an option so whether you actually want to go through it with is up to you.
The Deeper Story
For this last category, I'm not exactly sure where I stand on it, but it is extremely interesting. By going off and disobeying the narrator, every once in awhile, without spoiling anything, you are greeted with another story that you'll hear constantly brought up, but odds are if you are like me you won't understand any of it at first. After awhile however, you will start to piece the story together, something that ties both the game and the story into one, and actually left me thinking the more time went on about how everything ties together.
And to think that there could be so much hidden under the game that you wouldn't know about if you simply just follow the narrator is pretty cool.
Score: [7-8/10], for 11$ it isn't a top pick, but it's worth it if you want a shorter but good game.

Fundamentally a good fighting game, but riddled with flaws that are unforgivable by a company that should know MUCH better by now.
First off, just have to state that Street Fighter is one of my favorite games of all-time. I've played since SF2 first came out in arcades, I've played SF1 in arcades, and every version of SF2 and SF3 that came after. I've placed in tournaments before, bought many of the home versions (SNES version was incredible back in the day, and Saturn/Dreamcast/PS1 had excellent versions of SF3/Alpha2/3 as well), and enjoyed 4 for a while there too, but not as much as the older titles.  Street Fighter 5 is what happens when a company caters to only a very particular sect of their audience and ignores the majority of players. This was evidenced by the game's poor release state, which was functionally an alpha version, lacking many of the staple modes and options that have been a hallmark of the series since inception. They have done things to remedy this over time, but they have also done some terrible things that should not be forgotten.
First on the list: Having to download the *ENTIRE* game every time a patch is released.
This has happened since the game released, and is very amateur of Capcom to apparently not know how to patch their game properly. Literally every time an update comes out, expect to download all 8+gb of the game each and every time.
Second: Releasing a patch that installed a rootkit on people's computers.
They did this last year, in an attempt to stop people from cheating the system to get fight money through various methods. They released another patch to remedy this, but it did not remove the virus-like rootkit that was installed on many people's computer even after that. I'd imagine some folks still have capcom.sys floating around their operating system installation. What were they thinking trying to pull garbage like this? The funny thing is that people were going to such lengths in the first place to get around their fight money system because it was so poorly thought out and implemented to begin with. (see third point below) Because of their $h!t system, they got this result. To punish the abusers, whether they were cheating the system or not, they installed rootkits on ALL players' PC's. Let that sink in for a minute: This is a system level modification that could be exploited by others and lead to your entire computer being compromised by theives/trolls/hackers. That was their solution.
Third: The fight money/unlock system is a joke.
Expect to get half the characters for the full price of this game, and pay double that to unlock the other characters. The average cost per character is $5 each. Not to mention new stages will cost you as well.  If you want to unlock them by playing the game, it will take weeks of playing to get a single character unless you grind non-stop and by the time you get a couple of them you will probably be tired of playing in the first place. The best way to get fight money should be online ranked matches, as those are the only way to really get better at the game unless you have a local SF5 group/friend to train with. Problem is, online matches are so slow to find anymore, and when you do the connection is a crapshoot and your enemy is warping around the screen half the time. This isn't an unlock system. It's intentionally made to torture players who are trying to unlock characters and stages to the point where they crack and spend money on this additional content. They want you to grind out the same worthless survival modes and content over and over again and follow guides to maximize your fight money payout for this monotonous process. None of this non-online grind actually makes you any better at the game, it really just makes you dislike it more by suffering through the same poorly made single player content over and over again. It is a terrible system apparently made by amateurs who have no idea how to engage with their players/fans sensibly.
I get that they are trying to adapt to a new model with their games, instead of releasing updates as full products over again as they have in the past. You can trace this method back to their arcade roots, when they would re-sell the same game with new characters and such to arcade operators and charge for an entire new board and graphics to update an existing cabinet. They had been used to this business model for a long time, and prospered with it, as Street Fighter is one of the most successful arcade games ever, if not the most successful one. They are having a hard time adapting to the current home console industry and it shows. It's like your grandfather trying to learn how to use computers. He may have learned AOL back in the day, and knows how to do certain things, but it's hard to adapt to learn other stuff when you are stuck in a routine like that. Capcom is the stubborn grandfather of games developers, learning to cope with modern life, essentially.
This game was rushed out the door for the tournament players across the world, without any forethought on building a solid foundation besides the base mechanics of the game. These players are always reliable to buy all the DLC and characters to stay relevant in the professional scene. Capcom knows this. That's what this game was catered towards, with all other classes of players a complete afterthought. It took them years after the initial release to finally implement a legitimate system to punish uncouth players who were abandoning (rage-quitting, LowTierGod-ing, griefing) matches when they were losing. Wait 10 minutes for a fight, do good in fight, opponent leaves because there is no penalty for him doing so, and you get NOTHING for the time you spent or for doing well in the match. They finally just implemented a system for this recently, as well as the ability to blacklist players if you notice them doing this, or having a $h!tty connection, etc..
Capcom is stuck in the past, and have seriously lost their way.  Without some serious reorganization within their ranks, I don't think they will stay relevant in gaming much longer. I would love for them to prove me wrong on this, but as I see it, this is the current state of affairs.
Unless you're willing to pay 2-3x the cost of the game itself in DLC, steer VERY clear of this game. Even if you do spend all that it takes to unlock the things that should be unlockable in the game itself, or available for a reasonable price ($1.99 per character, for example), you will be met with poorly made netcode for online battles, and long waits to even get into a match, only to pray it isnt a lag-fest, which it will be 50%+ of the time.

This mix of retro inspired indie games is an easy recommend for me. Collects seven shorter 8-/16-bit era retro games that manages to feel a bit fresh and avoiding to outstay their welcome, with only the one exception. Will expand the review with more titles as I get through all of them.
Super Clew Land - Slow but tough side scrolling platformer that reminds me of a mix between VVVVVV and Kirby. With a little bit of a Metroidvania-vibe the player must traverse through the open world collect food to evolve, gaining new abilities and therefore opening up new areas. Super Clew Land is quite simple but charming and offers a nice challenge. Only downside is the last Boss that ended up being truly frustrating due to a slightly too high reliance on random elements. - 4/5
End of Line - Cute and quite unique puzzle game where the goal is to die. Pushing buttons and switches and changing through different abilities the goal is to prevent the resurrection bots from bringing you back to life. Charming, pretty and puzzly but with a few too many frustrating pixel perfect box moving puzzles. - 3/5
GAIAttack! - Arcade style score attack in this sort of Bubble Bobble brawler. Not really my cup of tea due to the heavier focus on score chasing rather than progress, but a well controlled and smooth looking game non the less. - 2/5
Paradox Lost - This Metroid style time traveler seems like a given home run on paper fails in it's execution. Why I can't recommend the game YET:
I hoped for some sort of "The Settlers"-atmosphere and gameplay, but I didn't really get a lot. The look ist cute, visually appealing. Implemented Stuff works. But: It's not "The Settlers" at all - no complexity in resource production. Only complexitiy in resourcemanagement ("on which resource do I focus?"), there are absolutely no production chains. The RTS-part ist okay, but the gameplay feels hectic and the actions in fights not very plannable. No complexity in fights (e.g. no cover system etc.) but complexity in where to station units (actually you tend to use a mob....). Some game mechanics have to be worked on, like buildings catching fire and burning down unless manually and for resources being repaired - a scratch is enough...to start the fire...so no strategic comfort by bulding defense towers...
Lacking a campaign to this date, it feels like I've seen most of the game in single player mode in less than 10 hours. Despite a positive attitude towards the game from the beginning, 15-20€ is in my opinion simply too much money at this stage of development. I mean, compare the content with Rimworld, for example...!
ATM I recommend waiting for more content and gameplay improvements OR at least for a sale price <5€.

If there's such a thing as a video game dictionary, you'd find a picture of Meltdown listed under "repetitive design".  The mechanics are solid, the graphics decent, and the music almost catchy, but it never changes even a slight bit from the very first level in the game. It's almost as if the developers created a single level and felt that was enough to sustain the entire game, repeating it to incessant amounts to pad the experience which might as well begin and end in the few minutes it takes you to complete the tutorial.
Meltdown is an isometric shooter that favors simplicity for complex mechanics or enemies. Enemy AI is mostly nonexistent, weapons are self explanatory, and the leveling system generous enough that you'll never need to choose between upgrades as you have more than enough points to level them all with more to spare. And if I'm being completely honest, the basic design is actually enjoyable to an extent (at least in coop), but its design is so stagnant, so painfully repetitive that it was literally on the verge of putting me to sleep as I struggled to retain interest while playing through what felt like the exact same level I'd played a dozen times before. Enemies, encounter designs, environments and level layouts; they're all exactly the same from each level to level, leaving on to wonder what exactly the point of continuing is.
Rending progression even more useless, is how you are restricted from so much until you prestige your character (which first requires you level up every skill tree), which then completely erases all progress you've made (including unlocked missions) and expects you to play it all again with nothing more to show for it but a new color on your username. It's incredibly poor design decisions like this that make Meltdown feel as if the developers didn't bother to think how the player would take this forced repetition past that which you experience by default going through the game, as if they expected them not only to endure the grind but actually enjoy it.
To be entirely fair, there are actually a few interesting ideas presented with Meltdown (such as the automatic cover system), but they are so entirely useless that there really is no need for them to be in the game at all. So many elements seem out of place or pointless, making an even bigger case for the game being less than finished or thought out.
Meltdown at its core is a solid, if largely unremarkable, coop focused isometric shooter, but the amount of content it contains wouldn't fill the average demo. It's one of the worst offenders at artificially padding a game's length by reusing the same content I've ever seen, and isn't worth bothering with for anymore than a mindless time waster. Even as that it fails to entertain, with the most enjoyment to be found in the numerous moments the game decides to break and glitch you and enemies onto objects.

The few exhausted orc warriors continue down the dirt path. Many of them are wounded, some even fatally. Looking back they see the remains of their loyal trained wolves, burnt and pierced by arrows. But now is not the time for sorrow. They must continue.
The strongest, not counting the chained ogre, of the orc warriors feels fear creeping in his heart as another one of his bretheren passes on by the lingering poison of elven arrows. The orc does not even have a name. He doesn't need one. He is replacable.
"We're just puppets." he thinks to himself. Is conquering a small patch of land really worth hundreds of casualties? The answer was obvious and he knew it. No.
But do the highest of orc warlords care if an orc falls on his best friends' arms in the battlefield? Do they even bother to inform his family? No.
"We are replacable." he silently says out loud. The few orcs that hear him lower their head, knowing what feelings were going through him. The ones that heard only a few silent whispers were too tired to ask what he had said.
The group regain some of their strength and march over an old wooden bridge. They can already see what waits ahead.
A patch of 6 knights, armored so heavily detecting their species was impossible.
"Hah!" An orc yells, "We have three times more heads in our group!"
The strongest orc, or just Strongest, says "No."
"Do you see those wooden towers around the roads? Thought they were just guardhouses? Think again."
The orc sprints about 15 meters forward to get a good sight of the buildings. As soon as he stops, he spots small movement on top of the tower.
"There's someone up the-" The orc was silenced by a man-sized wooden barrel falling on top of him, crushing both of his legs.
Two more orcs run to him to pull him to safety, but the moment they reach him the barrel explodes, creating a wall of flame around the scene.
"We must push on!" Strongest exclaims. "We have no choice."
The orcs release a warcry stronger than any warrior has ever created, and charge towards the guards.
Strongest hunches himself forward on the road. He has placed his sword between his arm and the ground, supporting his left leg wich had a small piece of cloth tied over it. Fresh blood was dripping from it. "Why did I run." He thinks as he keeps going. He still remembers most of what happened, even after getting a major blow in the head. He remembers them striking down a guard using the element of suprise, and then going sword-to-sword with the other five, while bombs were being hurled at them. He remembers how he saw his bretheren go down one by one. He remembers realizing there is no chance of victory. He remembers sprinting past the distracted guards. He remembers the physical and emotional pain.
Strongest pulls an arrow off his left arm. The arrow had hit the muscle. This hand will not be helping him anymore.
He keeps going, leaving a clear line of blood behind him.
Strongest looks forward for the first time in fifteen minutes. His jaw hits the floor.
The exit.
The way to leave this place stands less than a hundred meters from him.
"I survived." he whispers with tears falling from his cheeks.
Having to leave his family did not do it. Watching his pets die did not do it. Betraying his friends for his own survival did not do it. But seeing the exit, the portal to get away from all of this, to live. That is what finally broke his emotional wall.
Fifty meters. He repeatedly raises his speed.
Twenty-five meters. He is running, his mind overcoming the physical pain.
Fifteen meters. He will survive
Ten meters. He can see his family again.
Five meters. "Here I g-"
Strongest was cut off by a huge clank.
Again.
Once more.
A gigantic colossus of a being emerges from the forest, walking in front of him, blocking the road.
The giant is covered with black armour, wielding a shield bigger than Strongest himself in his, or it's, left hand.
The colossus unsheats his black sword. It's hilt is decorated with the largest ruby Strongest has even seen.
This weapon could decapitate an ogre with almost no effort.
"I am coming, brothers." Strongest whispers, as the colossus swings down it's massive blade.

I have been playing Starbound here and there for years. Seeing it grow has been a very enjoyable experience, but seeing what it has become has been both amazing and awful.
While there are some systems in place that I am very pleased with how they've evolved, there are others that still feel shallow or lackluster. Take the Combat for example, no matter what you do in the early game you will inevitably get damaged after almost every encounter with the indigenous alien life which forces you to pop salve after salve in between every encounter. Combine this with the hunger system and you are sure to die the first time you go underground for an extended expedition for Core Fragments.
Another big mistep in my opinion is the way they handled death post-alpha. It used to be you lost pixels(the in-game currency) at a flat pecent rate upon death, you would keep all of your inventory but be forced to respawn on the ship. Now when you die, you lose building materials, health items and ores AS WELL AS the pixel penalty from before.
Chuckle Fish, this isn't the Souls series. I'm here to explore, build and collect, not fight with the boring and broken combat system just to die time and time again to something ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t like being conered by four monster that fell ontop of me after a sandvalanche caused them to pile up proximity hitting me every half second. If you wanted the combat to feel "tactical" or "stategic" as you've plainly put it before - only do the damage when they attack, not when they are touching you. That mechanic has always been dumb and I'm surprised it passed so many updates without a change.
All in all, this game is worth the buy. It is massive and overall an enjoyable experience. Although with how many years we've been beta testing this for them, you'd think it would be a masterpeice. . . oh well.

A remake of a classic, Civ IV: Colonization could be considered Civ 'Light´. It´s also really worth giving a shot.
The game has you colonizing the New World by founding settlements. These settlements are more than just dots to cover the maps with. Rather, each individual settlement is important and needs careful resource and population management. As you expand, you will have to deal with the natives and, more importantly, the royals back home. Although it´s one route you can take, you can do much more with the natives than just smash their heads in - in fact, choosing for cooperation probably provides you with a more worthwhile experience, as these are anything but Civ´s standard barbarians. As for your royals, their demands increasingly test your economy and your colonists' patience over time. This mechanic has been done so well that you really feel you have a good reason to fight when the war for independence finally rolls around -- and winning this war feels all the more rewarding for it. It also means that the pacing of the game is done really well: each stage feels meaningful, not too easy or hard and never a grind.
The game tends to be shorter than your average Civ game and can often be finished within a few hours. That makes it an ideal game for a quiet evening or a rainy afternoon. The game has also been around for quite a few years, but still looks just fine.
Highly recommended.

After playing a lot of the main Civilization IV, I started sampling the different variations that I had received in the same bundle. While my initial impression of the others was "this seems just like Civ IV," Colonization is definitely a different experience. In a sense, your primary enemy is your own motherland rather than competing empires and your mission is to develop your colony quickly and strongly enough to achieve your independence.
What makes it interesting is that the focus on trade and infrastructure, rather than conquest, creates a more nuanced relationship between the different factions (which include the motherland, other colonies, and native tribes). It takes a little while to get used to since approaching the game in a Civ IV mindset doesn't lead you down the right path. Once you're used to the concepts, though, the inherent limitations of a new colony and competing resource priorities makes for a lot of challenging, compelling decisions that keep the game interestin
