At first glance the game seems great. With a character that wouldn't seem too far out of place in TRON and a fractured world that begs to be explained. Our main heroine, ICEY, is silent, though, so the only person capable of fleshing out this unknown world to us is Mr. Narrator. I'm not spoiled when it comes to voice actors, but Mr. Narrator delivers his view on our actions and the world around ICEY with woeful amounts of skill. Quite frankly, it detracts a large amount of pleasure from exploration and ruins any seriousness or excitement that the story has.
The story allows for multiple branches to be explored, but most, if not all of them, feel hollow and unfulfilling. Other game worlds allow you to defy the critical path with much more satisfaction and a feeling of accomplishment. Veering off the critical path is supposed to flesh out different parts of the world, but fails to do so in my eyes. The information gained from these side-routes raise more questions than providing tangible explanations to the events that cause them.
Getting on to the combat of the game we see a RPG-like upgradable skill system which uses currency obtained by defeating enemies or finding money containers. Although there seems to be plenty of skills at your disposal, few of these skills feel impactful in their execution and left me wanting. ICEY also has a dodging ability which allows for devastating punishment on an enemy when executed right before a hit, but this comes at a high cost if done incorrectly. A lot of the enemies can juggle ICEY when she is hit and more than a few times I have lost my healthbar to frustrating juggling by the enemies. Although punishment is part of making mistakes in any game, the juggling feels cheap and becomes extremely aggravating after a while.
Overall I cannot recommend this game. From the other mostly positive reviews I've seen I can assure you that I am in the minority. If you've read my entire review and you're still unsure whether you should get it or not, I would recommend watching an online video of someone playing some of the game to see if it's for you.

140 is an excellent music/rhythm platformer where, as you progress through each level new layers are added to the music and to the mechanics present in the level. You play as an object which transforms between circle, square, and triangle (when moving, stationary, and jumping, respectively), seeking to make it to the end of the level.
The game is a lot of fun, but quite short - it can be beaten (the first time) in a single sitting, as there are only three levels. The music is excellent and I wish that there was a soundtrack available to purchase.
The stylistic minimal graphics are a delight with how they interact/match with the music, and once you've beaten the game there is a mirrored version of each of the three levels available where you can attempt to beat the levels without any continue points (which is EXTREMELY difficult for the latter levels).
Basically, it's a lot of fun and wholly worth the price of admission.

I hate that Capcom released this game in an alpha state, but as of now it is a pretty good game, expecially if you play online
Good:
-Easy combo system, there are no 1 link frames. That's a very good think for me, because playing mostly online the lag can screw off my timing if the combos have a strict execution
-A lot of players, it's very easy to find online matches (at least in Europe), also thanks to the PS4 cross-play
-Most characters are very well done
-Large variety of characters
-Large selection of stages
-Tutorials for Beginners
-A lot of options in training mode
-You can buy almost anything in the game with fight money. If you finish the story modes and do some survivals/trials it's not that hard to earn over 1 million fight money. DLC characters cost 100.000 fight money, so that's not bad at all
-The netcode has some flaws, but has been improved. It's surely better than SF4, at least there's some sort of rollback
-The lobbies finally work quite well. When the game was released they were a mess
-The ranking system works quite well now, rage quit is punished and in ranked matches you usually find opponents of your level
-The music and sounds are quite good
Bad:
-There's not an huge variety of combos
-The gameplay is too much aggressive, the rushdown game is much more rewarding than zoning and defence. That can be annoying if you prefer some variety or simply prefer defence over offence. I'm a rushdown player myself, but I'd like to play versus more defensive characters/opponents
-A lot of guessing game, you can win or lose a game for single good or bad guess. That can be frustrating, because you can feel that you lost or won by luck and not skill
-I find harder to punish unsafe moves here compared to SF4, the frame data, spacing and animations of a lot of moves are made in a way that makes harder to punish them
-Some characters have an ugly expression in the select screen (mostly Ken and Ibuki)
-The netcode is not bad but could be surely improved. Sometimes only one player has lag, while for the other one it runs smoothly
-Not all stages have corner animations
-The taunts are too slow and it's pretty much impossible to use them in a real match, I'd like to see shorter ones
-No arcade mode (but they will put it in the SFV:AE update in january 2018)
I think that as of now SFV is a pretty good product that is worth trying if you like the genre

There are a great many special snowflakes out there that say this game is awful for <insert reason here> and I feel like this game was a victim of the hypetrain more than anything. Sure, the protagonist is voiced; never bothered me any. If you don't like it, theres a mod for that. Complain that this isn't as good as New Vegas? News flash for ya: Obsidian made FNV, not Bethesda. Don't compare the two. Start a petition for another one instead. Don't like Preston? I didn't either (I don't like him because his voice actor is just so... bad). There's a reason the guy is a meme. Send him to live in some far off settlement that you never go to. Problem solved. Don't like the main quest? Don't do it. Explore, play DLC instead, download some quest mods. "But, Zinda! I dont like X, Y, or Z!" There are seriously like 21,000+ mods on the Nexus. Go find one to fix your problem.
Now, for what is good about the game? I find the graphics are very nice and some of the views throughout the game are gorgeous. Character customization is fun and you can make some truly epic faces. Building up your settlements could be better, its kinda wonky as it is - but again, there are mods that help to make it less frustrating should you choose to do it at all. Crafting weapons is a little underwhelming but I guess you have to stop being able to improve it at some point. I would just like a little more customization overall.
The companions were fun to have around, and I enjoyed playing with almost all of them. Most of them have a little story surrounding them, some better than others. I always love the music in game, and they included FO3's score along with new tracks. I had an issue with the DJ at first. He is definatley no Three Dog, but he eventually grew on me and I don't mind him so much anymore. My favorite thing about the game, however, is exploring. The scenery and detail is far different from FO3 or FNV and there is loot and monsters to be had around every corner. I love ducking into old buildings, shooting a bandit in the face, and picking up everything I find and hearing my companion complain about it.
A popular Twitch streamer that I watch often says that if you get 1 hour of gameplay for every dollar you spent, you got your money's worth. I believe this wholeheartedly. I have over 300 hours in the game and I still haven't seen and done everything there is to do. I still plan to be playing for many years to come. I pack a sniper rifle and a shotgun in my travels. I have Dogmeat at my side. I run screaming from Deathclaws - sometimes even in power armor. I make my companion carry my loot. What's not to love about this game? Solid 8.5/10 from me.

So after years in beta, and almost 200 hours total play time, the game has finally gotten a 1.0 release, and it is glorious.
After creating a character, and playing through a tutorial that seems strangely similar to the opening of Mass Effect 3 (but not in a bad way) you find yourself stranded in orbit around a strange planet, with nothing but your trusty Matter Manipulator, a busted old sword, a flashlight, and a few cans of Spam to keep you alive. From there you fight, build and explore to your heart's content, until you finally fix your ship and head out into the cosmos, doing quests, fighting *huge* bosses, and grabbing all the loot you can get your hands on.
There's just so many great features in this game that I can't even list them all off the top of my head. Seriously.
Like Pokémon? Wanna catch all the creatures? They have a feature for that.
Wanna dual-wield machine pistols while dressed like Neo from The Matrix? You can do that.
Want to ride a hover bike though the desert, go sailing, explore abandoned labs, go scuba diving, build and ride skyrails (ala BioShock Infinite), and so much more? You can do that too.
Honestly, I just can't recommend this enough. I've even told my friends on Xbox that I'll buy this for them when it comes out there. This game is just such a great product, and a great value for the price. Just go ahead and buy it, you'll be glad you did. :)

Starbound, Starbound, Starbound... What to do with you? I was first introduced to you when you were just a baby. My friend had suggested I try you out but due to Early Access I never gave you a chance. I guess I was unsure, scared even, about where you were headed. You looked like a bubbly version of Terraria with a charming art style and proper survival mechanics to boot. Still, I could not bring myself to get involved with you early on and I'm glad I didn't. If the reviews, posts, and odd video of people's disapproval are anything to go by then you've done a lot of growing up for better or worse.
So, why is it that I got involved with you last year during, what appeared to be, the final stretch of your long awaited release? I guess I was just looking for something different. Starbound, you evoke strong hints of Terraria with your every move and yet you're different. Where Terraria, for the most part, lacks story and context you demonstrate (after several updates I should add!) that such considerations are still important. However, to compare you with Terraria would be unfair on both games as you both fill a particular niche. In short, you stand out among an onslaught of similar releases. If there is one thing I can say with certainty it is that I am happy with the path you ultimately travelled. As fun as it is to be thrown into a world without any explanation as to what's going on, or why I should care, I think that the little nuggets of story go a long way to making the experience special.
As for your shortcomings... I have no REAL issues. I do think that the building system could be a little better, and there are definitely improvements to the user-interface that could be made. That being said I don't think you're an experience worth missing out on!

This game is not winning any graphical awards; it looks a bit 8 bit retro, except that isn't intentional, I think. The tactical battles are not interactive. The interface is workable, although it's easy to notice details that could be smoother. The soundscape is middling to fair, mostly due to the soundtrack and not the effects.
But the gameplay is great. The variety in factions and how they play is great. You have 17 factions. None of them are all that good. The 'holy church of El' wants to break the seals and release the apocalypse. The deep ones... yeah. Necromancers, Demonologist, and a Troll King. Holy Priestess? Nope, worshipping a demon god. There are a few that are not intrinsically evil, I think that's about as far as you can stretch it in the alignment scale. Still, to illustrate the factional differences.. the Troll King is awesome in battle. He can lay waste to armies on his own. (And at start, that's what you have to do). But after a while, an overly critical mum sends a cauldron of gold because you're not doign so well. That helps a lot, you can finally buy a few units... and then suddenly the dread message: Mum is coming over to take over because her bumbling son is an idiot. New unit spawns in the HQ: Mom. Which is a troll witch of considerable skill, and a definite gamechanger.
You don't get high price games that try to pull all the wacky, wonderful, or scary stuff going around here. It is described as a 'strategy rogue-like', a surprisingly apt description. Your grand armies can be destroyed in moments and your empire reduced to crumbling ruins by a bad choice, it is fast-paced and light-hearted. I can highly recommend this to anyone who want a novel take on the fantasy wargame genre... and at the price*? It's a no-brainer.
* Steam sale, at time of writing.

you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

I'm about to describe a solution to a level, but I feel it is the only way to really appreciate the humor, weirdness and wonderful options you have in this game.
You are standing on the edge of a volcano. Etched into the side is "INSERT VIRGIN" You are faced with a bone, a cow, and a woman. You have 20 seconds to save the day.
Option 1: I click the bone, then the cow: McPixel inserts the bone into the cow. The cow emits hearts. The volcano blows up.
Option 2: I click the bone, then the woman: McPixel shakes the bone at the woman like she is a dog, then turns and throws the bone into the volcano. The woman leaps after the bone into the lava. The volcano blows up.
Option 3: I click on the volcano. McPixel throws himself into the lava. The day is saved.
If that didn't make you want to buy this game, then nothing will.

I strongly recommend limiting yourself to the stock weapons and towers while clearing the initial 16 levels. (with feats of strength) They were designed to be played that way. The extra difficulty will also go a long way towards extending the length of the game, before you run out of content.

Though I'm saying I don't recommend it, I will say that this title has interesting ideas and it executes some of them well. However, it has glaring issues that prevent it from being truly enjoyable. As of this writing, I've beaten three of the offered games, with one of the others being a card game which has no end and one being a hack and slash gauntlet-type deal that's based more on high-score than completion. The other two I have no intention of finishing.
There are seven games featured here, but each will last you only about an hour to an hour and a half from start to finish. Which is pretty cool, I'd pay 50 dollars for seven hours worth of quality content. However, this leads to the issue of none of the games really 'sticking' with you, with one solid exception. I'll give a brief overview of each of the games without spoiling any content, as best I can:
-An open-world platformer where you grow into a stronger creature to get more powers to access new areas. This is a cute title, where progression is easy and a puzzle element is mixed in. However, in order to grow, you need to eat smaller enemies. These don't respawn until you have eaten every single enemy in the area, which is annoying. The open world is solid, but the game moves at a rather casual pace. Imagine a combination of Super Meat Boy and VVVVVV, only walking a bit slower and with flutter-jump mechanics as opposed to gravity or speed wall-hopping. Good intentions are here but they don't all come together, and the slower pace of the title really shoots it in the foot.
-An action-puzzle game ala Adventures of Lolo, wherein you have to eliminate all enemies and then kill yourself. This is a nicely built game, kind of a Mega Man vibe to the graphics and soundtrack. The issue I find is that, simply, you can easily put yourself in an unwinnable scenario later on. The joy of puzzles is figuring out the next step, not repeating previous steps, which would require a minute or so to recreate. It's a good concept and if you like the Eggerland series, this one won't do you wrong, just not my cup of tea compared to good ol' Lolo.
-An arcade action game where you beat things up. It feels good and responsive, hitboxes are fairly solid if strict. Not a lot of depth to it, I felt, but it's a fun distraction.
-An open-world platformer that's pretty much 'hey we wanted to make a Metroid thing. Here's some Metroid for you'. Honestly it has a very clever concept, wherein there are three overworld maps and you warp between them as different 'time periods', making for a very well thought-out map system. The issue is that, unfortunately, the game is dull. There is no sense of danger, very few enemy types, only two boss battles (which are both very easy), and no real environmental hazards outside of a few rooms. This leaves for a very barren-feeling map, as opposed to a Metroid title, where lava, various terrain obstacles, and a variety of enemies kept the player engaged. It's... rather dull work, honestly. Which is a shame, as the core controls are very good.
-An arcade platformer similar in vein to Donkey Kong and Donkey Kong Jr, wherein you're a helpless creature who has to use the environment to get past obstacles. There's some clever concepts, but like the afformentioned DK games, the main character moves at a snail's pace and can't survive long jumps. This makes repeating segments unbearably slow. Unlike DK and Son, additionally, enemies follow set patterns, so there's no element of action or randomness to react to; it's just figuring out the puzzle and hoping you're fast enough to do it. It was fun through the start, and the graphics and style and undeniably charming, but it grates and I doubt many will finish this segment.
-A card game. Frankly, it's just a unique concept that doesn't pan out due to being a single-player card game that you likely won't be asking a friend to play with you.
-A vertical shooter set in feudal Japan. If there's a game that's worth your money, it's this one. Different enemies giving different types of shots, being able to reflect enemy fire with quick enough reflexes, an upgrade system, managing your special weapon types, and reasonable enemy placement. It's a bit on the easy side, but mechanics are well thought out and constantly engaging. Easily the best of the bunch.
The issue with Retro Game Crunch is that it's a game that doesn't quite live up to its potential. It's very solid, but for a fifteen dollar asking price and competition as stiff as VVVVVV, Meat Boy, and Eversion for 'simple concepts harkining to a retro time period', it really does not hold up. If this game goes to $5 on a sale, I'd say it's worth your time. Odds are one will appeal to you, and that one might even be really good. But I'd wait until then, and not jump on a 50% off - wait for the lower. I love retro games, the entire retro vibe, and I want to see more from this developer, they're smart people. This outing just leaves a poor taste in my mouth at the end, unfortunately.

Sleeping Dogs is an interesting take on an open world game. Interesting not because it does something incredibely different, but interesting because of its setting, story and combat elements. While none of them are anything special, they haven't really been presented in this way in an open world game.
Set in Hong Kong, you play a Chinese born American who comes back to his home town and goes undercover to take down the triad. The game is seperated into two parts, the triad and the police. This separation is important to the story, however it does have some effect on the gameplay as well. But it is undeniable that the triad way is the more fun ways to go.
The most visible and important gameplay element is the combat. Most of the time you will be in melee combat, although from time to time you will get access to weapons and the game turns into a cover based shooter. Neither of those two parts are particularly excellent, however the melee combat keeps things enjoyable at least even if it soon becomes clear that it is quite simple and that you can win most fights simply by mashing the attack key.
The driving mechanics are ok, again nothing special here. It's fun enough to drive, however I did not feel particularly excited to do most of the optional race missions. And even to get to the mission starters I preferred to get a taxi which basically instantly teleports you to your destination, however a lot of the time it is frustrating enough just trying to find a taxi,
The story is probably the most interesting part of the game. In big budget games there is nothing quite like this one, the game does a fine job at exposing you to the culture in Hong Kong and it doesn't let you forget that they haven't created just some generic town for you to roam around.
A definite recommendation for Sleeping Dogs from me, just make sure to not get the complete edition. Getting all of the DLC means that you also get the DLC which gets you a bunch of extra stuff like money and experience, and you can't avoid that. You basically skip the progression part of the game with this, which ruined the first few hours for me.

This isn't a game, this is art. Bastion is an experience, and it's beautiful in way this game made me feel. It says I only played 30 minutes, but in reality I beat it twice starting the game by the base application and not Steam; it didn't register game time.
The starkness of confusion in the beginning of the game adds a wonder and thirst for exploring and discovering the fate of this new experience that you have begun. The Narrator's voice in par with the flawless soundtrack add a palpable love and warmth when learning the story and finding new places. This game, like Dark Souls for instance, is best served on a plate of confusion. Hopefully, when you start the game you will have no clue or knowledge about the story and will have to pay attention the know anything yourself; this feels self accomplishing in itself. The only thing that is knowledgable, is that most of the ground is missing, and that most people are gone, dead, or perhaps even changed into the monsters you fight themselves. You are eventually lead to the Hub; this is like a main menu for the story's progression. From here you can change your difficulty by turning on god idols, change your personal preference of weapons, and change the buffs you get from the elixirs you unlock.The remainder of the game is an amazing self discovery of the truth behind why everything is the way it is.
The ending of the game was created gorgeously well. Each time I finished the game I had to first make a moral decision that really made it feel like it was an actual life experience. I felt so morally obligated I chose the one path I thought was the best BOTH times; regardless of wanting to know what the other ending was like on behalf of moral confliction. The endings, whichever you chose, both seemed rewarding and sad in each way. None of the decisions you make really seemed to chastise you for your views on the matter either. In all, the game began, and ended, perfectly.
Keep this game on your wishlist (to keep track of sale offers) if you are smart and only wait for sales, or even buy it rightout and play it this moment; neither decison matters. But you absolutely have to play the game at least once in your life. As I have mentioned, this is an experience.

In the story, the world has been destroyed by "the Calamity" and you play as the Kid a young man who survives the explosion and begins a journey to find other survivors and piece the world back together. The characters are all mute, aside from the narrator, whose dialogue is very expressive and adds another dimension to the game as he vividly describes every action the Kid takes. It is very interesting to piece together the story of how the world was destroyed through the narration and backstory.
The gameplay is a simple isometic hack and slash, and while not very deep, it is fun to play and satisfying to experiement with different weapons and loadouts and perks. While not a long game and with a focus on the campaign and story, there are also weapon challenges and side modes to complete.
The visuals are on another level compared to most games, the hand drawn graphics makes the world feel rich and alive, somewhat ironic considering the world is destroyed, which adds to the beauty of it.

This review is meant to be helpful. First thing I do when I find an interesting game is to check the reviews, looking for positive and negative comments to understand why people like or dislike the game and I was surprised how unclear the comments are. It seems that many unhelpful reviews are marked as helpful.
The only really useful review I found is this one:
+++ Pros:
+ Great soundtracks:
Electronic music, perfectly suited for the many fights you're going to encounter. Some tracks are stuck in my memory so I believe they are very catchy.
+ Great graphics:
The character animation seems to have no flaw, she has style during combat (she feels in control). But also the level design seems draw by hand and unique. The overall looks artistic and beautiful. The screen effets are also amazingly timed to make you feel yourself in the story. The light ambiance is amazing, even the character is glowing and feels like she is powerful. This game is really a master piece in term of 2D graphics, effect, design...
+ Fun story:
Infuriating the narrator is just so funny, I couldn't help laughing. Unfortunately you can't skip the dialogs if you "don't follow the arrows" so don't take the alternate path twice: it will only waste your time and make you salty because of the waiting time (that's what I believed happened to many players in the negative reviews).
+ Tight controls:
You really feel in control of your character, it's responsive, if feels like you can travel anywhere on the screen, even the enemies have sometime difficulties to reach you.
+ Entertaining gameplay:
The game is not overly challenging nor easy, I got fun discovering and going through the game.
+ Replayability:
If you follow the arrows and take only a few shortcuts, I believe you have very little time to wait for the narrator. This is clearly not a Metroidvania.
+++ For all of that, I give the game a positive review +++
--- Cons:
- Gameplay mechanics:
This game has "Bayonetta" game mechanics in my opinion: a simpler version of fighting games in an adventure game. Fortunately for me, ICEY has less sophisticated combos to remember. Unfortunately, this is also a flaw in the gameplay since you can finish the entire game by using only 2 combos: pressing I-don't-know-how-many-times the light attack button or pressing I-don't-know-how-many-times the heavy attack button.
It seems to me that this kind of game mechanic has nothing challenging. You just smash 2 buttons and looks very cool on the screen and win most of the time. There are also a few patterns to learn like: what enemy to prioritize and keep checking the life bar because when you run out you need to kill a minion and this will regenerate your life. Just like Bayonetta you need to dash/evade at the right time.
The weapon upgrades seems kind of useless just like the variety of weapons in Bayonetta. It will just look cooler on screen, more smooth, maybe you will kill enemies and bosses more easily. But then this becomes a flaw for the replayability: why would you play the level all over again if it's so damn easy and fast? And I mean, not because of your skill, because of your upgrades. In other words, you need the game to be easy in the beginning and harder later, these "upgrades" turn the game in the exact opposite direction.
- Enemy variety:
There aren't many different enemies:
* some are very well designed: like Thor, his brother-like, the guy on the horses, all the bosses
* some are too damn easy to be any interesting to fight: like the screamers (like in the movie Screamers 1995) or the walking guns
* some are just ridiculous and feel poorly designed: seriously, one looks like an eye ball with two big hands to punch you, is that even a robot? And this is one of the most frequent enemy...
Last words:
I don't regret buying it. Overall it was a very cool experience and I believe a game doesn't need an amazing and flawless gameplay to be good.
To the developers:
I believe this game would get a great additional value if you add a "hardcore" mode which: minimize the story, disable alternate paths that end the game, disable all upgrades (only activate all the combos at level 1) and one life only.

The game design and combat for ICEY is AMAZING! Truth be told those were what mainly piqued my interest for getting the game. The artworks are very aesthetically pleasing and I loved every moment I spent being immersed in it! A friend of mine who also owns the game recommended I play on a controller to make combat a bit easier but I stuck with a keyboard. Default keyboard controls are a bit odd and take a bit to getting used to, however, it doesn't really negatively impact the game (except for combat in harder difficulties I imagine). My only issue with in-game combat is the lack of invincibility frames, especially the further in you are in the game or the higher difficulty you play. When I first started, I chose normal mode and at one point in the game I got so frustrated I wanted to stop playing because I kept getting caught in a chain of knockdowns that would lead to countless inevitable deaths. I eventually restarted to set it to easy mode just so I could enjoy the story rather than rage at my deaths (no regrets).
If you play through ICEY following the narrator's instructions with full obedience, I doubt you'd feel like you got much out of the game so here's a friendly reminder: you have choices. Once you realize that these choices are available to you, you'll be a step closer to the truth. I mean full obedience isn't necessarily bad but it wasn't until I started playing ICEY with a rebellious attitude that I came to fully appreciate the storyline and the game itself. Getting all the achievements is probably the best way to get the most out of the game as these achievements will bring you the true ending so I highly recommend doing that.
Please give ICEY a chance! The game is worth its price. It may not be very long, but in the time it took for me to complete the game (including getting all the achievements) I enjoyed every single second of it and I hope that you do as well.

Sid Meier said that good games are a series of interesting choices. This game fits that bill, in spades.
The genius of this game is that the interesting choices start on Turn 1 of this turn based strategy game, and they never let up. There is no down time. Do you go for that coal mine, even though that will leave you far from your home base? Do you even have an army that can win, if you do decide to attack? Should you wait a couple turns to summon more creatures, even though you really, really, really need that gold? Did you leave enough defenders at your home base? Shold I save up my Druid herbs to upgrade my apprentice, or should I spend them now to better go on the offensive? The interesting choices never stop, all through the game.
However...
If you just fire it up and click Start New Game, you won't know how to do anything, you'll think the game is stupid, the graphics are ugly, the UI is unintuitive (actually, this part is kinda true) and never play it again. This happened to me, in fact. This is an old fashioned game. You gotta use the manual, I won't say read the manual, but use it. Leave it open while you play and Alt-Tab. If the game clicks for you, after a game or two you will be dying to read the manual all the way through. But it's gonna take a bit of work at the beginning because of the wonky UI. I think your effort will be richly rewarded.
This game is easily worth full price, and if you can catch it on sale, it's the steal of the century.

A bit of an Empire Management Roguelike. I lost within 10 minutes of my first game, which is exactly how I like my games to start. Conquest of Elysium 3 is a simple game. Move, attack, trade. recruit, etc. But while the mechanics themselves are simple, they're executed perfectly, and set the framework for what's really a complex strategy game.
The game offers 17 starting characters, all of which have their own unique playstyle and mechanics. The Baron can enlist locals to defend their towns and villages free of charge; the Necromancer can reanimate the dead to aid in battle, etc. etc. During combat your commanders might find magic items to aid in their conquest. I've only encountered one so far, which was the Bottle of Living Water. This item let my commander summon a powerful Water Elemental during battle. Awesome.
The amount of factions to try, and the amount of combinations to make while recruiting soldiers for your armies is insane. This game is definitely worth the price.

Starbound is one of those games I find extremely hard to talk about. Not because its a bad game, or because I don't know why I enjoy it but rather because the aspects of it I love are extremely broad and hard to explain, but damn it, I will try anyway! I bought this game for my birthday, a couple of weeks after it hit early access and I have been playing the game every now and again, checking out the new features added with the rather infrequent updates. It was only recently when I decided to donwload and play on nightly builds due to my excitement of 1.0 and it were those updates that really got me to love this game. Gone is the linear and fetchquest riddles progression, replaced with a much more natural and fun feeling questline. No longer does the game feel like a mess of features cobbled together with no thought.
As it stands, the game provides a pretty entertaining storyline, fun boss battles and dungeons and a huge universe to explore. The universe it self was made vastly more interesting with new world generation the increases planet variety, new structures to find and for once, some reason to look for them. Whether you are looking to collect new blocks to build with, find new furniture to spawn a new type of NPC or find new weapons to use in combat, the world will provide interesting structures to suit your needs. This combined with the new quest line and the game's progression feels more natural than ever before. Mainline quests will have you venture out and collect "clues" by scanning objects which generally fits perfectly with the normal gameplay. As a reward, you will gain access to new missions that will allows you to move forward in the story.
While the game got much better at rewarding your curiosity and exploring its vast universe, it also created some reason for you to have a planet you can call home. With the Colony system, you can place Colony Deeds inside your houses and depending on what furniture is found in the house, an NPC will spawn. Those will vary from your usual glitch knights, to people in Llama costumes (if they are costumes). These residents will joyously live around your world, talking to one another, interacting with their environment and generally making your home planet a much more lively place. Over time, they will also pay rent, give you quests and eventually even join your crew to accompany you on your adventures. While these procedural quests are not anything note worthy, they can be quite fun side activities which will aid in gradually evolving your village and its inhabitants.
That being said, while I adore most of the content added in this update, there are some parts of it that will take some getting used to. A great example is the new hotbar. If you haven't played the game before, the chances are you will not notice much wrong with it. I find that the change is a good one, this new hotbar fits the game's weapon and building system a lot better than the old one, it allows for the creation of loadouts players can switch between in combat. That being said, with the game putting quite a focus on building, some might see it as a detriment and while I cannot say this is an incorrect statement, I also cannot relate as I generally build from my inventory anyway.
Additionally, the crafting timers are a very horrible addition and there is no way it benefits the game in any way what so ever. They take up time and stop you from playing for pretty long periods. There is no animation to look at, nor is there way to contribute in order to make the wait less tiresome. I would recomend modding this one out before playing, unless you enjoy some down time for cheking your mail while playing.
Overall, this game is pretty great. Its a sandbox but its not a sandbox just in the sense of altering the environemnt like other games of similar type, its a sandbox which allows you to play the game in multiple ways, taking branching paths, rarely forcing you down a specific turn. While there is still room for improvement, in my opinion its better than it ever was  and not is the perfect time to give this game a go.

I've been searching for a new RTS similar to Settlers for years and Northgard achieves that while feeling very original and enjoyable. I love the aesthetic, its very clean and smooth. There's a few issues both big and small but it is an early access game so I'm sure these will be ironed out in time and if its a thoroughly enjoyable game now, I'm hyped for its completion. I'm really excited for all my future games, discovering all the game has to offer. The map generation is superb, all my games so far have felt very balanced and have a very natural appearance. Every start feels playable so big well done to the programmers with that one.
For the developers: Here are the areas I'd personally like to see improvement:
Small things:
1) Please allow healers to choose primary focus (e.g. military, citizens, healers). I'd rather my healer heal up the missing 20% of 5 citizens than heal 30% of the health of my armoured bear at some points for example.
2) AI scouts sometimes (rarely) seem to get stuck on trees when pathfinding.
Bigger things:
1) A lot of the game can feel like trying to fix deficits rather than maximising surpluses. It feels like a constant juggling act where you're constantly and desperately waiting for a new citizen to spawn for them to occupy a building to prevent happiness, food, wood or krown deficits. I guess some of the time, rather than it feeling like a race to win, its a constant struggle to survive, which is definitely a different feel to a game.
2) Map specials such as the Wyvern or giants feel impossible, partly because of the game duration. Throughout the game, I find myself constantly lacking citizens. I often can't spare someone to be military because I need them to fix a deficit (as discussed above). I struggle to have a military big enough to protect myself let alone defeat a Wyvern! Since the game feels like you're desperately waiting for the next citizen, existing citizens feel precious and to lose multiple military units feels like you're throwing the game away because then you're a few citizens behind your opponents. It feels like games don't last long enough to send enough food to the giants to convert them (and due to deficit problems, its often difficult to spare food to send to them).
3) My attacks to cripple the opponent feel like they cripple them a lot less than their attacks cripple me. Not sure if this is really the case but it feels like it. In one game, I asked myself "How many times do I have to liberate this territory before the AI runs out of food to buy it back?" (I was leaving it open to liberate to cripple their food and wood but they bought it back 4 or 5 times lol, every time being able to afford to buy a building)

Northgard is a lovely little Early Access RTS that is growing into a strong, well crafted juggernaut. I have had minimal experience with strategy games, having dabbled in the "Civilization" and "Age of..." series', but Northgard has captured me completely. Coming from a non-Strategy background, I've faced a minimal learning curve that I believe is highly attainable for anyone to pick up and really get things rolling.
There is a minimal "hints and tips" style tutorial that is anything but overbearing and can easily be ignored or turned off while playing, which I found to be a fantastic approach to nudging new players in the right direction while not forcing them into a gridlocked tutorial sequence. This is effective and comfortable as you learn from each randomly generated world you jump into and find a strategy that works best for you and the clan you choose to play. It's a slowburn process, but it's satisfying to watch your territory grow larger and more successful with each sequential match.
The win conditions are diverse and keep multiplayer and singleplayer experiences interesting. Perhaps a rival clan will rush for a domination victory? Build your defenses! Maybe you'll want to focus on stockpiling and trading resources to multiple clans to become the best merchant? Better yet, study and explore this fantastic world and increase your lore and wisdom to become the wisest clan! How will you stop the others from usurping your lead? You are kept on your toes and even a loss is enjoyable in the end.
When I first bought Northgard there were only three clans, now there is a total of five and growing! (August 2017) The devs are a fantastic group that seems to always be working towards developing the best version of Northgard that it can be. Balance, content, and variety have been notable focuses thus far and I expect the final version to be extremely well polished and attended to. I am excited to see how multiplayer develops further and how the campaign will turn out.
The community online is friendly and growing. While a server may not always be readily hosted, I've noticed that hosting your own will more often than not draw in another group of players, who were probably waiting for a new server to pop up just as you were. I have shared and gifted this game with many of my friends and don't doubt that many other folks are doing the same. The online population will continue to flourish as new updates roll in and as content is developed. I have met some of the most wonderful individuals while playing FFA, 2v2v2, and 3v3 modes online. It's been a good while since I've been able to say that I "made friends" with someone in a game, and I'm pleased that Northgard was the platform to do so.
I highly recommend Northgard to anyone interested in something new, norse mythology, history, time/resource management, RTS, and adventure. Northgard has quickly become one of my favourite games on steam and I'm more than happy to return to it time and time again. I hope that you'll find it the same; I look forward to seeing you all on the shores of Northgard!

Wow. This is my favourite game on Steam - and among other platforms, including console.
I would never had originally thought you could experience so much out of a click-and-point game. I'm glad I decided to play this myself, to get the full experience, instead of only watching videos of it on YouTube. However, I do believe it's best to play (or at least watch) the game twice to better understand it.
'An intense story of pain, loss and acceptance'  is how the official site described the game, and falls under the genre(s) of an indie psychological horror adventure.
The storyline is incredible and mysterious, the main characters are lovable (in their own little ways) with distinctive personalities, and the puzzles are both challenging and fun. It also has a good quality length of play time. The ending is quite interesting; it's ambiguous - although I could say the entire game is cleverly unclear - but don't let this turn you off from buying it. I love how it makes you wonder and taps into your conspiracy theories.
On that note, I've never played a game that made me think about life so much as what Fran Bow did. I'm certain it's because I can relate with the underlying theme of mental illness that's clearly visible, yet wonderfully portrayed in this game. You really can't help but feel sorry for Fran, and if you become emotionally attached to her (among other characters) like I did, you might want tissues on stand-by. It's worthy to say the game provides a deep exposure.
I should warn that if you're sensitive to mental sickness and gore-violence, play with caution in mind.
Another aspect to mention is the original soundtrack; it's hauntingly pleasing - quite fitting.
(It's a little difficult to write a detailed review without giving away spoilers!)
Over all, this is a great game, and I struggled to find any notable flaws.
I'm now obsessed and I'll definitely play it again, many times. 10/10
~ Just to add, I bought a handmade Palontras plush toy quite some time ago, and I kept him close by whilst playing. ♥ :)

If you think this is sold on NEStalgia alone, think again.
Super Clew Land and Paradox Lost both rethink the Metroid formula well, first allowing you to acquire your abilities rather rapidly, and then re-exploring the world once you have them. Shuten's system allows you a choice of weaponry through the gameplay itself, rather than some sub-menu; then throws formations that are tuned to one type and not another - effectively letting the player choose their own 'easy part' and 'hard part' of each stage. The level design in Wub Wub Wescue and End of Line take very few elements and do a large variety of things with them which keep the game fresh and fun. The AI of Brains and Hearts is challenging and competent, and yet totally beatable - it's just a player with the understanding of the rules, after all. And GAIAttack is just a fun, brilliant balance between Smash Bros fighting and Kid Icarus-style vertical platforming (sans the screen-wrapping); it's tough as nails! You will Game Over plenty, and just resetting your score is the perfect punishment/compliment to infinite continues, and it's Souls-like bonfire continue points.
This package is a ridiculously awesome deal, but not because it's retro. It's because it's freaking brilliant. The only thing it leaves me hungry for is a top-down adventure game from them, since End of Line has the adequate framework for that already. But if all is good, this team will stick together, and continue to crank out the brightness.

I was gonna buy this game with the Steam Link but didn't want to spend like $20 total so I decided to get this instead by itself.
In all honesty you should probably just go into this blind as it's easy to ruin the experience, so I'll try to keep this spoiler free. I 100%ed the game (including achievements), but haven't played the free DLC yet.
This is a 2d sidescrolling beat 'em up similar to what you'd see from Vanillaware (Muramasa, Odin Sphere, etc) with a strong focus on metanarrative storytelling. Without going into details, if you've played The Stanley Parable, you know what to expect.
The game isn't very long. It took be about 5 hours to 100% it, but that's because this game has absolutely no filler and no padding. You're given the ability to jump between chapters of the game so that you don't need to retread parts of the game you're done with (similar to how Nier: Automata allowed you to do that once you were close to finishing it) which reduces play time astoundingly but I much prefer it over the alternative. I felt the game's length was just right but that's because I'd rather have a 5 hour game with nonstop fun than a 20 hour game with frequent luls.
The combat is flashy and has a number of combos that you can purchase. ICEY controls well and I didn't feel like I had any problems with her movement. I thought that the counter ability was finnicky and I was not able to do it consistently, which in turn with the enemies' tendency to have tells that were way too short, ended up making some encounters needlessly frustrating (the arm robots come to mind specifically). Also a small number of the abilities you can purchase felt very overpowered and essentially carried me throughout the majority of the fights.
I also felt that it was too easy to end up being juggled when there are too many enemies, but I admit that could be my own problem.
The combat aside from the above comments is very fast and responsive. The higher your combo, the more damage you do so it's encouraged to dash from enemy to enemy in long flashy combos to maximize your damage output. This game also has a healing system like Doom 2016's where when you get an enemy weak enough you can do a finishing move which restores health.
The art is gorgeous and the animation is very well done. Even though the animation isn't frame-by-frame and instead skeleton/tweening, it still looks and animated beautifully. The backgrounds and very well done and manage to be beautiful enough without being distracting to all the mayhem on the screen. In fact the whole game has a very attractive painted aesthetic that isn't unlike Vanillaware's typically aesthetics.
A lot of the story was lost on me but I feel that is mostly because of my lack of familiarity in the themes the game was relying on. Your mileage may very. I however really enjoyed The Narrator's voice acting. I heard complaints about the game's English dub, so I switched the voice language back to the original Chinese. Even though I can't audibly understand it and had to read the subtitles while in fights, I thought the voice actor did a fantastic job.
Music is amazing. It's mostly electronica with a bit of dubstep mixed it at times. I'm not a fan of dubstep typically but I thought that it was done well here. You'll be tapping your foot throughout the game and the best part is the OST is free DLC in .mp3 and .flac which I'm thankful for.
The game isn't cheap and I can imagine it being hard to justify $11 on a 5 hour game, but I honestly recommend it. It's a game that respects your time and cuts the crap to get to the point which is something I really appreciate. After all money can be earned but time can't.

Like many others of its kind, Kingdom Rush is a td to its very core. There are not many tricks or gimmicks presented throughout the game, beyond building your towers, seeing how your solution pans out and readjusting said plan. The games progression comes in several forms. There are passive skills, tower unlocks, hero unlocks, new enemies, new armour types and more lanes. Pretty standard fare overall. At its bare bones, this game is both functional and enjoyable.  Though it comes with flaws. I should preface this by saying that this game is a td, balance and design are key to an enjoyable experience for the player.
As you progress through the game, you'll get a new tower type or hero that will assist you on the current map, and will carry over to the next. With a level that is designed to be tackled with a specific tower or hero, this can conflict with the out of level passive trees. Each tree has a power curve that can potentially ruin or improve your experience. If you don't know what the level is you're facing, you can enter with entirely the wrong tree for the task at hand. If the game presented on the level selection screen information as to what the player both unlocks and will face, there would be no arbitrary difficulty added.
The passive tree's are not made equal. Some tree's add exhorbitantly more damage than others in all situations. The militia tree is particularly strong compared to its counterparts and comes with no real flaws or weaknesses. Without this tree being at max level the game can feel a little harder than it needs to be, increasing to downright impossible on some levels.
Towers as well have balancing and design problems. Some towers are just functionally better than others for all situations once unlocked. One comparison in particular is the difference between barbarians and paladins. Barbarians are meant to deal large amounts of damage in return for being very easy to kill. Instead their paladin counterparts take twice as much damage, deal more damage as a result and have a reliable AoE. The ranger tower for example does more damage per second in an area of effect than its counterpart the musket tower which albeit has a different design path. Intended to assassinate larger targets, instead it will frequently shoot fodder instead.
Being unable to control towers, to make them do what you intended them to do can be frustrating as well. Far too often the ranger tower will apply its poison on the same unit multiple times before switching, or paladins will completely ignore enemies a few feet away. This leads to an unnecessary frustrating experience as the game requires more precision and planning in later stages.
Heros as well are not cut from the same cloth. Some heros skills are just not helpful. Why would you wish to lock one enemy down for an extended period when you can cc several at a time or outright assassinate one or more enemies. The majority of heros are just plain weaker compared to the exceptional few who excel at the roles provided for them.
While these problems exist the game is still fun once you find what works. The game really kicks off when you beat the main campaign that presents a challenge and requires creative thinking.
Bosses are always a very tough and tense experience. There is a real threat of losing the level, as they all have mechanics that you will have to account for on the fly. Bosses never seem unfair as well. Tough but enjoyable all around. Enemies are in the same vein as well. They interact with each other and your mazes in enjoyable and challenging ways.
While there are flaws to the game that detract to your ability to control, or experiment within it I would still recommend this game. There are not only few td's, but even fewer are done as well. I enjoyed myself throughout, I suggest taking a relaxed or mellow stance while playing this game.

Starbound.
The game that took 2..maybe 3 years to get to 1.0 launch!
Still inferior to Terraria. Note: Terraria will be the direct comparison, since it's basically the other, superior product for the game to be compared to.
STARTING OUT:
Terraria? Talk to the guide! Game has been made very convenient to get rolling off the ground. Play! GRADUAL DIFFICULTY INCREASE MAKES FOR FAIR PLAY!
Starbound? Follow a quest and basic story..and once you get onto the planet, enjoy your death. Game also still has a BUGGED QUEST UI. "Find the core fragments" doesn't explain what that means, minus one little tiny popup window of dialog that is not only easily missed, but easily skipped.
Apparently Starbound gets better, but the start of the game is just such terrible trash..the fun parts are separated far far away. In multiple attempts, it's either been "camped by boss at planetary beacon" (early) or "can't survive caves to find Fragments or whatever, die repeatedly, lose all pixels, and can't make resources due to TORCHES being locked behind pixels!"
Personally not too entertained by Starbound, 1.0 or otherwise. Terraria's STILL better! Probably cheaper at this point too. Might be shorter because the game isn't padded out by♥♥♥♥♥♥quests though. It's the one thing that Starbound has over Terraria.
Framerate: Goes to Terraria. Starbound's a clunker.
Graphical Style: Goes to Terraria. Starbound's dark for the purpose of being dark and blotchy.
Music: Who cares? Play without it to hear your crawling, slithering doom approach
Combat System: LOPSIDED due to how difficult it is to get to the actual depths of content in Starbound due to slogging grind and difficulties numerous. I'll give it to Terraria unless proven otherwise in a proper explanation.
Crafting system: Simplicity of crafting being materials only? Terraria gets it. However - Starbound has a "decent" crafting interface. Pixels being needed to craft is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ however. Unless I didn't get far enough yet, you can't bank pixels like you can currencies in Terraria.
"FUN STUFF" Weapons/Mobility/Etc. - Terraria once again gets it. Quicker gratification. Starbound starts you slow and helpless, and with digging being a chore early, there's no damn way you'll do anything unless you take the 50 hours to dig yourself a nice slope. I hear Starbound has vehicles and more weapons, but..when it takes 2 years just to get the game playable? Nope.
Nope nope nope nope nope. I'll gladly wait 2 years for Terraria 2 or Otherworld. It'll -still- be better than this game.
Meanwhile, ~98 hours in Monster Hunter Generations. If I could afford EDF, I'd be all over THAT instead of wasting time on Starbound only to hate it all over again!

The first game was pretty nice, but sadly the Shotgun-gatling was a lie : / Then again it was a lot of fun, placing down millions of towers, fighting alongside with your maze/towers, it was the first FPS + TD combo l ever played.
True, you had only a few weapons, no unlockables and one main char. In multiplayer except from the host everyone else was wearing a helmet, you could level your towers and your weapons. Using huge cubes to kill dozens of lumes, which just kicked you away and being magnetized by the core....
Then Sanctum 2 came!
We got the classic main char and 3 (later on with DLC 4) brand new charecters!
Each of them having unique abilities.... like... setting lumes on fire, having greater accuracy, dealing more damag close range and so on.
Tons of new unlockables, perks, weapons, maps. Starting with base 25 levels (50 is you have all 4 DLCs).
Compared to Sanctum 1, where you could places "millions" of towers, here you started with 10 in early game, then later on with some updates it became 15, making it more tactical where to place down those few towers, which increased the challange.
Perks could give you extra dmg, core stun, core regeneration, exploding lumes and many more~!
You could unlock new weapons and towers too. My favorite is the "Drone Launcher" launching off around hand size drones that attack the enemy. Using them with Sweet will make the lumes catch on fire too.
For her a nice perk combo was -for me- (Hip Fire - Tactical.... something... "it made your slow weapon fire faster" - Corpse explosion). Since the tactical something reduced your dmg by 40%, using the hip fire perk gave that 40% back.
Also, this game finally got a story mission too, each map hard than the other.
All bosses! Those darn bosses! Patriach, smashing all your towers, Super Heavy that moves slowly like a tank and one shots you if you get near, Queen Howerer having bullet proof front armor.
And the lumes weren't magnetized by the core anymore, true, they were running towards it, but if you crossed path with them, they headed after you instead. Also, instead of just disappearing in the core like in the first game, they started to hit it.
Chat is silly, since if you hit enter "Microsoft Sam" with an alter voice starts to read up your msg, can sound really funny though.... or bein really annyong.
Graphics changed a lot too, true, l didn't play on full graphics, but it was still an eye candy for me. They did a great work with how they did the maps and everything.
In my opinion, Sanctum is a one-of-a-kind Tower Defense... sure.... there are tons of one-of-a-kind TD games, which are ofc great too. With sanctum you wont get bored, the drag to get on higher level, to unlock more perks-weapons-towers, to be able to solo a map with all 5 feats turned on, thats pure awesomeness!
So if you want a TD game that includes taking the action and not just watching your towers do the job, then I recommend you this game!

This is my first steam review... yay!  CoE3 is a nicely put together Turn-Based Stradegy game.  It reminds me a lot of Master of Magic.  There is no control in combat, and the game does not focus on research or city building, but instead, the acquisition of units and capture of cities/towns/villages/mines/outposts/towers/etc.  With each capture, you increase your income, build your army, and set out to explore the map and find and conquer your enemies.
There are numberous races in this game, and most of them play differently.  It's enough to keep me interested to keep playing and learning how they each work.  There are a massive number of unique units, there are magic items you can find and equip, and random world events which can be good or bad... losing a town due to a meteor is never fun, but it sure keeps it interesting!
The game has multiplayer as well.  My friend and I play all the time, and I can say after numerous games, that this is a stable, polished, and enjoyable game to play, either single-player or multiplayer.  If you are into the turn-based world domination, my army is bigger than yours but not necessarily better type games, which offer randomly generated maps, exploration, and a whole bunch of other cool stuff, I'd highly recommend this one.
The learning curve for CoE3 is a bit steep, but most of the information you can find in the games manual.  The graphics are not top-notch, but if you grew up on 90's gaming, the nostalgia is great!

Love it! I was concerned when I first launched and realized there was no campaign, that I'd have to learn an RTS just in a free-for-all against the computers. I was pleasantly surprised when I saw that the game guides you through the first several steps with tips. It's not much, but it's just enough to give you a sense of how the game works, and then you're left to explore the rest on your own. It made the first game especially challenging, but I won on the Normal difficulty.
That first experience made me think, wow, what an incredibly well-designed game. The learning curve was minimal but I could tell that the game would be difficult to master, which is a great thing for an RTS to aim for.
The game mechanics themselves are a breath of fresh air in the genre. The most noticeable is the pace of the game. Compare Age of Empires and Starcraft. AoE is pretty slow-paced compared to Starcraft, but it's still an RTS. Northgard is even slower paced than AoE, and is also still definitely an RTS. I've never played a game quite like it, and I really enjoy the fact that it's an RTS but isn't quite so chaotic (read: stressful) like they usually are.
Back to the mechanics. What I found most different right off the bat was resource gathering. It's similar to other RTSs, but in Northgard, much more emphasis is placed on the *rate* at which you're gathering, rather than how much you have at any one time. Your units also don't need so much micromanagement (which is part of why this game feels slower); villagers will at least gather food while idling, even if they could be gathering food at a more optimal location.
Combat is pretty simple but not without strategy. There are three basic unit types and you're only ever going to control a handful of military units (I don't think I've gone above 7). I haven't played on Hard yet or against any humans, but I imagine if your opponents were more aggressive, you'd have a hard time defending yourself, whereas against Normal AI, it's pretty easy.
My only complaint at the moment is I've played 6 games (9.5 hours) and feel like I've run out of stuff to do (I've tried all of the clans at least once). I could play against Hard AI or against human players, but I'm not compelled to. That's why right now I can't recommend a $20 purchase (I purchased during the Steam sale for $16 I believe) but it's easily worth $10. Once this is out of Early Access and has a campaign, I think it'll definitely be worth full price. If nothing else, I feel justified in my purchase just for having experienced unique gameplay that's fun.

Using a pad is great for the games themselves but the game never tells you what button does what. Tip- If a game ever tells you to press tab, it means left shoulder button.
There isn't an easy way to switch games, you have to take the game out of fullscreen and quit to bring up the selection menu and I feel there should be an easier way, such as pressing B.
The games themselves are fun, some are deeper than others. Gaia-ttack, the side scrolling brawler has local co-op, but the button config looks like a nightmare to play. I don't understand the card game properly but it will probably see the least play even if I did. Each game is crafted with care, but you may not like them all.
At the full price of $14, it makes each game $2, but it still feels pricey. Without wanting to devalue the hard work of the devs, the experience feels like something in the $10 range. Maybe steam spoils me and I'm a bad judge, but for the full steam price, I think more care should go into game pad support, switching games and giving the selection menu a splash screen title that fades into the menu wouldreally help tighten the experience and push the game firmly into the $10+ price point.

As I completed Retro Game Crunch before it came to Steam, I'll write my review here with "10 minutes" played on Steam.
In-depth video critique for all games included in Retro Game Crunch:
Super Clew Land - Metroid inspired platformer with demanding platforming and satisfying exploration - very good game!
End Of Line - Puzzle game with a unique way in progressing by dying - worthwhile experience
GAIA-ttack - Simple brawler with platforming elements, rather shallow combat and very weak level design though - one of the weakest games in the bundle
Paradox Lost - Highly metroid inspired with puzzle elements, rewarding exploration due to significant rewards - very good game!
Wub-Wub Wescue - Retro platformer (rather slow moving) with very slight puzzle elements, rather frustrating - weakest link of the bundle for me
Brains & Hearts - Two player card game with rather unique mechanics (with plain tutorial) that features a strong AI (that takes rather long to take its turn) - fresh ideas and fun for a short while
Shuten - Classical shoot 'em up with the ability to "steal" the enemies weapons, however with weak enemy design - Mediocre SHMUP, worth checking out however
TL;DR - DEFINITELY WORTH THE MONEY!

I really enjoy SF5 despite it having several shortcomings.
The main selling point for me is SF5's smooth gameplay. I think this might be more personal taste but having really fluid movement at all times sets this game apart from many more mechanically stiff fighters. I feel this allows for a better more gradual learning curve for new players and doesn't immediatly force you into a stringent play style.
I also really like the overall look and feel of SF5. It has amazing animation quality, a great soundtrack, and a fun cartoony aesthetic that have always been strengths of the franchise.
The character roster is diverse and caters to many different play styles. Many characters that I initially didn't think I'd like ended up being some of my favorites. Some still need some rebalancing but all in all I'm pretty pleased with the current lineup.
The game features things like Story mode, Survival mode, Training, and Challenges but those are also pretty much staples in fighters so I feel  they fall more into that middle ground of "these need to be included" rather than being a straight positive or negative. I would call them adequate in SF5.
As far as negatives go, of which there are a few, I will try to go over some that bothered me the most.
Arcade Mode: Where is it? Maybe not the worst of the games negatives but I liked Arcade mode and I miss not having it. Also with the way the game feels somwhat unfinished it's even more noticeablely absent. Rumor is they will be adding one soon though, hopefully. Also if they do release one I hope they don't use just the base characters and stages  but also allow any DLC ones you've aquired to be used in it as well.
Fight Money: An in game currency earned by leveling up fighters, by beating certain challenges, and playing online matches might be the best/worst idea in a modern video game. At first it's great that you can earn Fight Money to unlock DLC characters,  skins, and various other things without having to pay real money. However, in tying a large amount of content to a virtual currency they've also created bottlenecks (like 100 round Survival mode) to slow and ultimately frustrate players into spending real money instead. Almost everything extra in the game has some kind of price tag attached and at times playing becomes more about gaming the system then enjoying the game. I feel like this also allows them to charge more than normal for certain things or even omit things that might have been included in a game without the feature.
Online play: Online consists of Casual (non ranked), Ranked, and a Battle Lounge which allows you meet up with 8 people and gives you more customization options. These are pretty good varitions but a couple things hurt online play.
Lag. It's not uncommon to run into lag in online games but usually they do a better job of matchmaking. Using the default settings of 3-5, meaning trying to connect to another player with a "3" above average connection to a" 5 " good connection, will still dump you into matches with horrendous lag and the only solution is to block everyone who lags bad. Why have a filter that supposedly does that but doesn't work half the time?
The other problem with online matches ties into character leveling and Fight Money. Because a small amount of experience is earned during online matches whether you win or lose and because leveling earns Fight Money people are constantly afk queuing using everything from scripted bots to holding down a kick button on a turbo controller to earn exp.
The combination of those two things can make playing online a real hassle sometimes.
I probably could have given SF5 a negative rating based on either of the last two things but ultimately I think despite it's problems it's still one of the best fighting games I've ever played and continues to be improved upon.

Sorry folks, I can't recommend this game. I've played it a lot but I've struggled with it horribly.
Cons:
-Capcom's business model, they'll go as low as it's needed to squeeze every dollar out of you.
-Too many 50-50 situations, especially when a character was knocked down and he's about to get up. The game needs a refreshing 3rd option at least in wake ups, to make the game less basic. Characters like Laura and Mika are especially annoying to play against because of the 50-50 system.
-The netcode for lobbies works horribly for some countries/ISPs, and this is mainly why I stopped playing this game. The game either works perfectly (with people that are somewhat nearby), or is completely unplayable with the very same people, depending on if the lobby set was randomly assigned to work from P2P or not.
-Matchmaking and going from one ranked/casual match to the next is slow. Even having fiber optic I've had to wait more than 10 minutes to find a match some times (looking for connections of 4 and 5 bars only).
-They intentionally made some characters look ugly to force you to buy (with real money) their classic costumes (check Akuma and Ibuki).
-You cannot play keyboard vs controller. You can play 1-player modes with keyboard if you want, but if you want to play 2-players local, you're forced to have 2 controllers.
-You can't assign the keys to whatever key you want in your keyboard without an external program, however, you can change what each button does from within the keys you're forced to use.
-When the game updates, you have to download around 10 gb.
-When you go to the stage/character select screen, instead of feeling happy for finally being able to play the game you bought, you'll feel punished because there are so many stages/characters that are locked.
-Fight money (in-game currency) was planned to benefit Capcom, not the players. I'll explain myself: it's impossible for you to buy all the characters, all the costumes, all the colors and all the stages even if you play 24/7. In fact, you wouldn't even be able to just buy all the characters if you played 24/7.
-Capcom's support, even though it's fast to answer, is not very helpful, and they can be disrespectful at times.
-Some of the character's faces don't really look like how the characters were in the past games. It's sad because some other characters like Chun and Ryu look so beautifully done.
-Story mode is: movie, fight, fight, movie, movie, movie, fight, fight, fight... you get it.
-Objectification of some of the female characters. There was some objectification in SF4, but it's gone to the next level here.
Pros:
-The fighting system is very accessible in comparison to the previous SF games, especially at the time of doing combos.
-Crush counters are very pleasant to land. Some people take crush counters as a negative, but in my opinion they're a welcome addition.
-VTrigger system replaces Ultras from SF4.
-Crossplay between PC and PS4.
-You can play as many of your favorite old SF characters (many with ugly new designs though, if you want the classic versions you have to pay extra).
I suggest you go buy some others of the fighters in the market, you have Killer Instinct, Tekken 7, King of Fighters 14, Mortal Kombat X, etc.
