Starbound is one of those games I find extremely hard to talk about. Not because its a bad game, or because I don't know why I enjoy it but rather because the aspects of it I love are extremely broad and hard to explain, but damn it, I will try anyway! I bought this game for my birthday, a couple of weeks after it hit early access and I have been playing the game every now and again, checking out the new features added with the rather infrequent updates. It was only recently when I decided to donwload and play on nightly builds due to my excitement of 1.0 and it were those updates that really got me to love this game. Gone is the linear and fetchquest riddles progression, replaced with a much more natural and fun feeling questline. No longer does the game feel like a mess of features cobbled together with no thought.
As it stands, the game provides a pretty entertaining storyline, fun boss battles and dungeons and a huge universe to explore. The universe it self was made vastly more interesting with new world generation the increases planet variety, new structures to find and for once, some reason to look for them. Whether you are looking to collect new blocks to build with, find new furniture to spawn a new type of NPC or find new weapons to use in combat, the world will provide interesting structures to suit your needs. This combined with the new quest line and the game's progression feels more natural than ever before. Mainline quests will have you venture out and collect "clues" by scanning objects which generally fits perfectly with the normal gameplay. As a reward, you will gain access to new missions that will allows you to move forward in the story.
While the game got much better at rewarding your curiosity and exploring its vast universe, it also created some reason for you to have a planet you can call home. With the Colony system, you can place Colony Deeds inside your houses and depending on what furniture is found in the house, an NPC will spawn. Those will vary from your usual glitch knights, to people in Llama costumes (if they are costumes). These residents will joyously live around your world, talking to one another, interacting with their environment and generally making your home planet a much more lively place. Over time, they will also pay rent, give you quests and eventually even join your crew to accompany you on your adventures. While these procedural quests are not anything note worthy, they can be quite fun side activities which will aid in gradually evolving your village and its inhabitants.
That being said, while I adore most of the content added in this update, there are some parts of it that will take some getting used to. A great example is the new hotbar. If you haven't played the game before, the chances are you will not notice much wrong with it. I find that the change is a good one, this new hotbar fits the game's weapon and building system a lot better than the old one, it allows for the creation of loadouts players can switch between in combat. That being said, with the game putting quite a focus on building, some might see it as a detriment and while I cannot say this is an incorrect statement, I also cannot relate as I generally build from my inventory anyway.
Additionally, the crafting timers are a very horrible addition and there is no way it benefits the game in any way what so ever. They take up time and stop you from playing for pretty long periods. There is no animation to look at, nor is there way to contribute in order to make the wait less tiresome. I would recomend modding this one out before playing, unless you enjoy some down time for cheking your mail while playing.
Overall, this game is pretty great. Its a sandbox but its not a sandbox just in the sense of altering the environemnt like other games of similar type, its a sandbox which allows you to play the game in multiple ways, taking branching paths, rarely forcing you down a specific turn. While there is still room for improvement, in my opinion its better than it ever was  and not is the perfect time to give this game a go.

Sleeping Dogs was a great surprise! Yes, it is a GTA clone indeed, but it only takes the best aspects from Rockstar's games and then tries to add something new to it, like a good hand to hand combat system, a big selling point for this title.
You play as an undercover cop with a dark past who infiltrates the dangerous Honk Kong triads, trying in the meantime to solve some intricate cases for the local police department.
This dualism between the good and the bad sides of the main character is well used by the developers, missions are always interesting and fun to play, you want to go ahead and discover what happens next.
Secondary missions are not bad either, even buying vechicles and clothes in order to obtain different bonuses is well implemented and not a mere filler.
Sleeping Dogs is also very easy to play, a bit arcadey if you want, and with some small control glitches, but immediate to master. Technically I really liked the graphics (download the highres textures!) and the voices of the characters, very well interpreted. Honk Kong is a big city with its different districts, not so diversified as any other GTA, but interesting to explore nonetheless. The story is well narrated, nothing breathtaking but good enough to keep you playing for at least 20-30 hours.
In the end I think I can suggest this game to any other GTA fan who wants something a bit different and fresh, while maintaining a well know gameplay infrastructure. If you don't already have Sleeping Dogs maybe this is the right moment to buy it, the Definitive Edition just went live with better graphics and all DLCs included!

Tower defense is a passion of mine.  Some try to be visually fun, some think they need to add something to the genre and some feel like a simple flash games.  Replace "some" with "this game" and you've got a grammatically difficult sentence that is accurate none the less.
The flash game references is a little unfair, as this game really does have solid visuals and quality execution, but at the same time it seems that there's nothing it gained from being a standalone game apart from the ability to charge people for it.
Kingdom Rush is fixed position tower defense with the addition of a "hero" that can roam around the battle field (at your direction) and activated abilities to throw down some temporary defenses or a fireball from the heavens.  Progressing is had during the rounds by upgrading your towers and your hero leveling up (levels that only persist for each game) 'causing him/her to do more damage and have a greater amount of hitpoints.  Progression out of game is served by spending stars (1, 2, or 3 stars are given for successful completion of a level, based on how well you did) to increase the strength of towers or powers.
In total, there are about twenty levels with your typical late-game unlocks for harder mobs or sudden death (single life) runs in that level.  Level design has your typical duel entry, duel exit, splits, joins, bypasses that you've seen in other fixed map tower defense games.
Kingdom Rush is unexcitingly typical tower defense.  It may sate that occasional tower defense game, and while it may be a fun play on a tablet, that'd only if you compare it to the poor quality of the tower defense in the Android and iOS ecosystems.  I'd call this a buy at $3.  It's well drawn, but simple.  Level designs lack inspiration.  Progression lacks anything new or intriguing.

If you like grand strategy or were a fan of the old Lords of Magic, give this a try.

Northgard is a very casual RTS game with a lovely viking themed asthetic and a focus on survival and resource managment more so than aggresive expansion and military conflict. Though there is plenty of fighting to be had if that is your thing, it is not the paramount way to achieve victory in this game, nor the major focus of game play like other RTSs.
Northgard is one of those games that causes you to frequently adapt your stratgey mid stream, from the build orders of your structures, to frequently the adjusting your populations roles, to dealing with the lastes world event (im looking at you blizzard).  It takes a little time getting use to the unique mechanics which it incorporates, making the experince different from other RTS games ive played.
While simple in nature and quick to pick up after a few play throughs, I am still finding it engaging. Once the general game mechanics are mastered it remains a fun and casual experince. Emphasis on casual. At this time it lacks the depth and grand strategy of other games...but its simple charm and ease of play make for an enjoyable experince none the less.
This being an early access exeprience, that is subject to change some...but even if it doesnt i think there is a market for casual RTS games like this. Easpecially if they manage to balance multiplayer welk and make that a fun way to kill time, and dire wolves, and frost giants, and each other; with your friends.
If you enjoyed games like Age of Empire, Majesty, or the original Warcraft...it's probably worth a look.

Getting rekt by a 2 weeks old Charmer class (lvl22) without any decent gear coz it was just created and still levelling up ( 28 is max atm) .

Same thing with the support class druid and warlock.

Bastion is the perfect combination of audio, graphics, gameplay, and story; all of this rounds out to a game that is more than just a game -- it's an experience. The character development is interesting and by the end of the game they feel a little more "real" than expected -- which is great. The world is also very deep and interesting; usually games where you can fall off every edge♥♥♥♥♥♥me off, but this one took that concept and really made it work. Plus, it was tons of fun going around bashing things to try and earn some dough.
This game is quite short (the initial story only took me about 5 or so hours to complete), but that just means that it keeps moving and can keep you on your toes. There are many things other than the main story that you can do in this game, though: practice with various weapons to earn items, try to survive a chain of battles (and learn a little about the characters) in reflections, unlock achievements (both in-game and Steam achievements), and try to set high scores in the after-stories.
This games brings everything that I look for in a game together. When you finish the initial run, it will leave you wanting more. Hell, if you're anything like me you'll probably head out and drop $10 on the soundtrack because
. And then you'll spend the next couple of days listening to the soundtrack or playing the game instead of studying (procrastinating is what students do best, right?).
So, yeah. Buy the game. Support the game. Play the game. Enjoy.

The journey was good, but the ending was bad.
This game was very fun to play. It satisfies a morbid-fairy-tale itch if you can't afford $60 for a horror shoot-em-up.
However: the drive of this game is its mystery, yet once it ends it has answered none of the questions that have been pressing you forward.
Sure, people say that there are "different interpretations." What they really mean is that there are so many contradictions and open ends that you pretty much imagine what you want to believe. I was quite disapointed.
Yet as I said, the journey was good. Each chapter was a spooky, moody, beautiful world I could really sink my teeth into.

Beautiful game with very simple mechanics but very competent at what it does. Carried by it's narrator, the story and the art style!
The game itself is an isometric 2D action game with some very simple RPG elements. You can equip 2 weapons at anytime (each weapon can be upgraded 5 times and each time you can choose between two impromvements) from a growing arsenal of very different weapons. 2 melee weapons? 2 ranged weapons? A shotgun and a hammer? A bow and a machete? That's all up to you! Each weapon plays completely different and adds a lot of variety. Additionally you can equip a special skill for one of your 2 weapons or a weapon independent skill. You got also a shield to block and counter (with good timing) enemy attacks, a dodge roll and a button to drink heal tonics. So the basic mechanics are very simple but always spot on.
So while inexperienced gamers will probably enjoy this game (there is even an easy mode if you basically just want to enjoy the story), there are also a lot of challenges for hardcore gamers. For each weapon there is a location with a certain challenge and depending on how you perform you can unlock upgrade materials and skills for this weapon. While acing each challenge can be quite difficult (and rewarding) all this is completely optional. So if you don't like a weapon, there is no need in doing these. You can also invoke so called idols, basically deities, that each will add a certain challenge to the game. Enemies may just get tougher, drop bombs at death, deflect your attacks, and so on. But each invoked idol also increases the gained ingame currency and experience gained. So you can nicely tailor the difficulty to your likes.
But the main reason, why you should play this game: The narrator. He will narrate and comment almost everything you do with such an awesome voice, it will get stuck in your head. For each weapon combination you equip, for each level you have to redo, because you failed the first time, he got a comment for you and the way he narrates the story is just beautiful. The story itself is also quite touching but is really supported by the way (and voice) of narration. The art style is also amazing and fits perfectly into the game and the story told.
The first playthrough took me about 7 hours (with almost everything done) but I just started with NewGame+ that unlocks additional idols and let's you keep you all your upgrades. It's also nice how NewGame+ fits in with one of the 2 possible endings (you can choose between them in the end).
The only thing I can actually critizise about this game is that restarting the weapon challenges takes a bit too much time if you already know that you can get the high score anymore. But that's also just a few seconds. And that you cannot replay levels that you've finished (you may have missed certain items) but that makes sense within the story.  Yeah...this game is awesome! Buy it!

(Wrote more than I expected to, see TL;DR.)
Some people seem to have a problem with how heavy-handed the "meta" aspect is - my only issue is that there's no real need to ignore the narrator, outside of a natural curiosity to explore. He indignantly overreacts to your disobedience... and there's only one point later in the game I can recall right now where I actually really questioned an order from him. ICEY is tagged as a Metroidvania, I wouldn't go that far, I don't think it necessarily has all the Metroidvania elements but it does have that sort of feel to it. (This game reminds me of others like Guacamelee and Valdis Story, but much more casual, especially in terms of plot.) The combat is a lot of fun, I'm such a sucker for getting a character who can be quick and have lots of maneuverability. ICEY has a bunch of different attacks to choose from so you can fight just about however you want, and the combos are satisfying. I did play on the normal difficulty, not sure how the higher difficulty level compares.
I noticed in some reviews people were complaining about the narrator, I gave the English one a chance but definitely ended up preferring the Chinese VAs. It can be tricky at times to be reading the subtitles and playing/fighting, but once you spend enough time exploring you'll become more than familiar with the dialogue. I was fine with it but I know some people are pickier than others when it comes to subtitles.
One last thing I'll mention, once you reach checkpoints you can travel back to them at any time. This will sort of do like a soft reset on that checkpoint's area, meaning you can benefit from secret areas again, and also bosses come back - so you can go duke it out with your favorite bosses whenever you want.
TL;DR
Overall if you like platformers with a hack-and-slash, Metroidvania feel, give ICEY a go, especially if you can catch it on sale. Comes with free OST and a small DLC addition, not a bad deal at all.

The Binding of Isaac is a slot machine. There is no better explanation I can give of this game. Everything is random and all of your actions have consequences you cannot prepare for. You constantly have to gamble your items/health away with the hope that by doing so you will be rewarded. Frustration is realizing you used one of your precious few keys to open a locked door only to find it was an item store. Is it worth sacrificing one of your 3 hearts of health to gain a potentially powerful weapon or item locked behind one of those doors that hurt you when you walk through them?
There is no depth to this game. The only goal is to get as far as you can before you die in a procedurally generated experience. I would recommend that everyone play this game without collecting or using a single item as your playthrough can come to an abrupt end by simply using the wrong item. Trade off your maximum health capacity for a few gold coins? Eventually you'll get to a point where you'll know which items are helpful and which to avoid, but when all is said an done, there is no item or weapon that is crucial to you furthering your adventure.
This sandbox of randomness is one of many in a sea of procedurally generated worlds that developers rely on. It's a crutch that publishers rely on to keep development costs down and exploits the gaming community. How many Binding of Isaacs need to be published before people tire of this lazy game design format? I'd rather play a slot machine all day, at least then I could win my money back. I won't be getting my money back from The Binding of Isaac no matter how many times I roll the RNG.
UPDATE: It says a great deal about a person's congnitive capacity when they tell you that you can't form an accurate opinion of a game within the first few hours and that you have to dedicate hundreds of hours to truly understand it. I've put in 65 hours, beaten it multiple times and the game is still as random and pointless as the first time I played it. I guess that 40+ additional hours is necessary to get the full experience.

Kingdom Rush, and Kingdom Rush: Frontiers are free-to-play apps available on Android and Apple devices. So, what do you get extra for the paid version? For a start, the free apps aren't quite 'just free'. You have to pay to unlock extra heroes, etc., within the game, whereas the Steam version allows you to just unlock them as you go along by playing the game.
Kingdom Rush is very cartoony, bright, with quite a fun and 'cute' style to its design. Don't let the cute visuals fool you however, because this game can be quite brutal.
The gameplay world unfolds as you complete each level, eventually leaving you with a map full of levels that you can play over and over for more unlocks, challenges, and awards.
The types of towers available in this game will be very familiar to those people that already like tower defense - arrows, magic, barracks, and artillery. These towers can, of course, be upgraded as you progress through the game, and get significantly more powerful because of it. It can be very expensive to fully upgrade one type of tower, however, so you will need to balance upgrading with the need to put more 'basic' towers down also.
You don't just play with towers alone in this game, once a level begins you also have the ability to use two additional resources 'for free' to help you kill oncoming waves of enemies, though these are on a timed cooldown. These resources are the Meteor, and Reinforcements. The Meteor has a long cooldown, but placed in the right area with a big group of enemies it causes devastation. The Reinforcements have a much shorter cooldown, and can be placed wherever necessary at the time to try and bring down the enemy as quickly and effectively as possible, and these reinforcements are also very good for separating large groups of enemies.
As you move through each level in Campaign mode you unlock stars with a maximum of 3 per level, with 1 star awarded for completing Heroic mode, and 1 star awarded for completing Iron mode. Ultimately 5 stars are available per level. These stars are used to upgrade your towers prior to starting a level. These upgrades can be reset for free before and after every level you play, enabling you to customise your play style to suit the type of level, and the enemies that you'll face.
Throughout the game, you unlock a number of different Heroes to play with. These Heroes can be moved around to locations of your choice on the map to attack oncoming enemies. These Heroes can level up to a maximum level of 10, and while leveling up they become stronger and stronger with more ways in which they can damage enemy troops. A different Hero can be selected for each level depending on requirements.
If you find that you are struggling with a particular level, there is a useful Encyclopedia that comes with the game that details what some enemies are immune to, what will damage them the most, and you can then cater for that prior to starting the level by upgrading the relevant towers, and choosing the most suitable Hero.
The levels can be played with one of 3 different challenge modes: Campaign mode, Heroic mode, and Iron mode.
Campaign mode awards you up to 3 stars for completing the level, depending on how well you do. You have 20 'lives' in this mode, meaning that you could potentially let some enemies through the finish line and still complete the level, though you would not get your maximum amount of stars for letting enemies in.
Heroic mode and Iron mode only allow you 1 life meaning that to complete the level you need to kill off all attacking enemies. Heroic mode still contains waves of enemies (usually 6 waves), whereas Iron mode only contains one long wave of enemies. Both of these modes disallow the use of Heroes, and Iron mode disallows specific types of towers.
For the money, this gives excellent value. I have 9 hours of play time racked up on this already (at the time of review), and still have some of the last few Red unlocked levels to do (they're too hard!!). I've also made a start on completing the Heroic and Iron modes just to see if I can actually do them!
If you like tower defense, I see no reason why you wouldn't like this. It's fast, frantic, and fun. The little extras in place to allow flexibility with levels, allowing you to use towers you prefer, or heroes you prefer, is always a bonus. Some tower defense games can feel like they only want you to play things a certain way, whereas this (once you master it) can be customised to suit your style and strengths.

Fallout 4 is one of those games you don't even have to play the others to really enjoy. This game, much like TES5 Skyrim, is a game that sucks you into it's world and has you investing a ludicrous amount of your life playing and doesnt let you go without a fight. I found myself playing this game for a good 12hrs straight more times then i can count and I don't regret a single minute of it. Obviously Fan made Mods are what make these games so timeless but the fact that Bathesda is so liberal with modding is what sets them apart from otehr developers.
When you complete any other RPG out there, you can maybe replay it once and after that, the replay value is gone. Skyrim and Fallout really let players expand on the world infinitely so it's truely impossible to have done it all. With DLC sized Mods adding new maps, Even if you complete every nook and cranny of FO4, The right Mods will give you another reason to start all over again. Before playing this game as my first Fallout game, I was a huge skeptic. Now, I can't imagine a day I was against playing this game.
While this game doesn't quite live up to it's predecessors, this game is more then fantastic enough for me of all people to fully endorse to anyone. There's tons of lore and an immense amount of history and effort put into these games. It's so easy to over look them so before you decide this game has no content, Look up the Fallout Lore videos of Oxhorn on Youtube. ONly then will you be able to really appreciate the blood sweat and tears Bathesda as put into this game.
The Vanilla game is a 7/10. Some parts feel tacked on at the last minute, imcomplete, missing or just flat out broken but the game works where it counts and it's performance is pretty damn solid. With the right mods to complete the game (Depending on how you want to play, anyone not doing a Minuteman Playthrough probably won't need many mods at all) This game easily makes a straight 10/10. Those 3 points lost by the developers are regained in full and beyond by the modding community.

If Nukaworld is the first DLC you get, and you like being a massive A-Hole, and the idea of being a savage overlord excites you, then Nuka World is YOUR DLC and is worth it's price tag.)

Even if you don't wanna raid and pillage villages, Nuka World offers more then anough to be of use and entertainment for everyone. Beautiful game with very simple mechanics but very competent at what it does. Carried by it's narrator, the story and the art style!
The game itself is an isometric 2D action game with some very simple RPG elements. You can equip 2 weapons at anytime (each weapon can be upgraded 5 times and each time you can choose between two impromvements) from a growing arsenal of very different weapons. 2 melee weapons? 2 ranged weapons? A shotgun and a hammer? A bow and a machete? That's all up to you! Each weapon plays completely different and adds a lot of variety. Additionally you can equip a special skill for one of your 2 weapons or a weapon independent skill. You got also a shield to block and counter (with good timing) enemy attacks, a dodge roll and a button to drink heal tonics. So the basic mechanics are very simple but always spot on.
So while inexperienced gamers will probably enjoy this game (there is even an easy mode if you basically just want to enjoy the story), there are also a lot of challenges for hardcore gamers. For each weapon there is a location with a certain challenge and depending on how you perform you can unlock upgrade materials and skills for this weapon. While acing each challenge can be quite difficult (and rewarding) all this is completely optional. So if you don't like a weapon, there is no need in doing these. You can also invoke so called idols, basically deities, that each will add a certain challenge to the game. Enemies may just get tougher, drop bombs at death, deflect your attacks, and so on. But each invoked idol also increases the gained ingame currency and experience gained. So you can nicely tailor the difficulty to your likes.
But the main reason, why you should play this game: The narrator. He will narrate and comment almost everything you do with such an awesome voice, it will get stuck in your head. For each weapon combination you equip, for each level you have to redo, because you failed the first time, he got a comment for you and the way he narrates the story is just beautiful. The story itself is also quite touching but is really supported by the way (and voice) of narration. The art style is also amazing and fits perfectly into the game and the story told.
The first playthrough took me about 7 hours (with almost everything done) but I just started with NewGame+ that unlocks additional idols and let's you keep you all your upgrades. It's also nice how NewGame+ fits in with one of the 2 possible endings (you can choose between them in the end).
The only thing I can actually critizise about this game is that restarting the weapon challenges takes a bit too much time if you already know that you can get the high score anymore. But that's also just a few seconds. And that you cannot replay levels that you've finished (you may have missed certain items) but that makes sense within the story.  Yeah...this game is awesome! Buy it!

Before starting this review, I'd just like to mention that I've played on both the main website and Kongregate, but barely touched this version. TL;DR at the bottom
When I heard everyone talking about how DECA 'saved the game' and how RotMG was alive again, I knew I had to give the game a shot again. However, to my disappointment, I found that, while they were indeed better devs than Kabam,they didn't really resurrect the game as much as I hoped. First of all, the main complaint about Kabam was the addition of PTW mechanics in the game. The lack of updates came later, and was just a nail in the coffin of a pretty much dead game. Fortunately, DECA kinda fixed this, by rolling new updates (some of which were good, but others redundant and cosmetic), but didn't really help fix the PTW mechanics of the game. You can still buy items, pets and whatnot in Nexus which TOTALLY gives you an advantage over others of your level who can't. I remember a joke I used to hear about how we actually had to PLAY THE GAME to get all these stuff, and unfortunately, this joke still works. Sure, DECA started giving away free character slots and vault chests, but does this make you even with all those players having 30 vault chests and 20 char slots? I doubt it. They also started giving away pet eggs, but I'm sure no non-payer will get a legendary/ divine pet any time soon. Dropping free dungeons during events, doesn't really improve the game in any way. And don't even get me started on the infamous multiple Oryx 2 spawn on the desert/beach by ADMINS.
The next thing I'd like to mention is about the community, and not really about DECA. I've noticed that the community has gotten more selfish over time, with people boosting themselves in corners and running in to grab all the loot for themselves. I remember in the days of Kabam, things like this didn't exist, with most of us actually helping each other, but this isn't the case any more. this is bad enough in normal boss fights, but is the worst with that Test Chest thing that DECA added. I can see why they added it, to help everyone get a chance at loot, but nowadays I see majority of the people leeching at dungeon entrances or at the corner of the boss room, waiting for the rest to kill the boss. Once the Test Chest appears, they just swoop in and grab the loot without even helping at all. They claim to help by 'anchoring', but honestly they couldn't care less about any of that.
And then there are the other issues. I'd like to find the guy who decided it was a good idea to put skins and vanity items in a white bag and smack him on the face. When I last logged in, there were still, beggars, bots and hackers (yes, there were). Honestly, if they made more updates on improving the actual gameplay instead of, I don't now, adding an NPC in your guild hall you can talk to, or 'pet skins', the game would be much better off.

This game is certainly an improvement upon SFIV, which is saying a lot for me, as my favorite character is not included in this game. (Abel... ;_;)
I thoroughly enjoy the critical arts and fighting mechanics of this installment. While many hardcore players (which I would not define myself as, so take my opinion for what you will) would write off this game due to the increased skill gap, I think this is a very good thing for casual players. The entire reason why fighting games haven't had the largest market (compared to that of FPS) is because of the sheer difficulty & complexity involved in executing a good combo. With SFV, it's rather obvious that Capcom is trying to make Street Fighter more accessible, and it really shows. At the same time, I think there is plenty of skill still involved in Street Fighter.
Moving on from the technical point of this game, the roster in this game is comparatively small compared to that of SFIV right now. They are progressively adding more DLC characters, and at the time of writing this, there are 27 playable characters with Menat being the newest. But if you are to buy this game now after playing SFIV, this will be an immediate issue you notice. With the characters that ARE currently in the game, they play great! The range and diversity of moves is large. Many returning characters have stayed true to their original abilities (with the exception of Juri...), and many new characters bring plenty of new styles to the table, specifically Laura.
From a graphical & design standpoint, it should pretty much go without saying that SFV is the best installment. The level design is crisp, and the characters each have a great design. Abigail, a new character, would probably be an exception to this statement for many players, and I can definitely see why. He is by far the biggest character in the game, towering at 8'0 according to the wiki! He is a behemoth the likes of which we've never seen. I don't think he's completely irredeemable as far as design, but that's completely subjective. Visually, this game is just beautiful.
As far as the story mode goes, this game is definitely lacking. Of course, I doubt anyone really came to a Street Fighter game hoping for a riveting story mode, but it is just so cheesey and even cringeworthy at some points. The dialogue is just so corny for many characters, and the setting jumps from country to country for no other reason than so they can change up the background for every one of 3-5 fights in a specific character's story mode. If you're looking for the arcade mode many people loved in the other Street Fighter games, at the time of this review, it just isn't in this game yet. Survival mode is in the game, and it is largely very entertaining, as it progressively gets more and more difficult as the stages go on. But it will likely be a few months before arcade mode is implemented.
In short, if you are looking for a very technical, complex, and skill-oriented Street Fighter, SFV may not be for you. If you're a new player, and you're looking for something more accessible and easy to pick up, SFV is definitely what you'd want.

Fran Bow is a delightfully disturbing point-and-click. The indepth story alone is enough to keep you playing, let alone the anticipation and shock of what is unseen... I wouldn't recommend the game for children younger than 14 or 15 but I most definately give this a 10/10 for everyone else. Fran Bow is a ten year old girl, traumatized, orphaned, and institutionalized after witnessing the horrific murder of her parents. After being put on a supposed experimental medication, she beings to hallucinate a demonic presense that is slowly trying to kill her, bloody writings on the wall, dead, mutilated corpses, and other wonderfully awful things. But as the story unfolds, you find that perhaps Fran is not hallucinating but is perhaps awakened to other dimensions she must travel through to find her way back home. With the help of unforgettable characters like her adorble cat Mr. Midnight, and a quirky talking skeleton Itard, Fran takes you on an interesting adventure. The only thing I can think of that bothered me was the slow progression of dialog especially when I went back to hunt for achievements. You can't skip what you already know. An otherwise awesome game that I really enjoyed.

Not too sure what to write here so heres a recipe for Pancakes instead
Ingredients:
1 1/2 cups all-purpose flour
3 tablespoons sugar
1 tablespoon baking powder
1/4 teaspoon salt
1/8 teaspoon freshly ground nutmeg
2 large eggs, at room temperature
1 1/4 cups milk, at room temperature
1/2 teaspoon pure vanilla extract
3 tablespoons unsalted butter, plus more as needed
Now to make it
1. In a large bowl, whisk together the flour, sugar, baking powder, salt, and nutmeg.
2. In another bowl, beat the eggs and then whisk in the milk and vanilla.
3. Melt the butter in a large cast iron skillet or griddle over medium heat.
4. Whisk the butter into the milk mixture. Add the wet ingredients to the flour mixture, and whisk until a thick batter is just formed
5. Keeping the skillet at medium heat, ladle about 1/4 cup of the batter onto the skillet, to make a pancake. Make 1 or 2 more pancakes, taking care to keep them evenly spaced apart. Cook, until bubbles break the surface of the pancakes, and the undersides are golden brown, about 2 minutes. Flip with a spatula and cook about 1 minute more on the second side. Serve immediately or transfer to a platter and cover loosely with foil to keep warm. Repeat with the remaining batter, adding more butter to the skillet as needed.
6. Procedure for adding fruit to pancakes: Once the bubbles break the surface of the pancakes, scatter the surface with sliced or diced fruit, or chocolate chips, nuts, etc. Flip with a spatula and cook for 1 minute more, being careful not to burn toppings.

I kinda want to like this game, but I cannot quite like it in it's current form.  I have several problems with the game, starting with the feel, then the difficulty options, shortly followed by the controls and user interface, and last but certainly not least the combat mechanics.
To start the feel is one of a open beta that someone accidentlly put out as a release.  Knowing what I am like I do not play beta's because I like to form my opinions on complete games.  After saying that I do not know if I can say this game is complete, but it has been released so the developer thinks it is.  It has a "stable" and an "unstable" build still for all users.  I put them in quotations because stable is relative.  It still has alot of bugs, but that is to be expected of a recent release.  It has a major bug where whenever you start it up it transports you to a new system, too.
Changing gears, there are three difficulty options.  easy which is where there is no penalty for death, normal where you lose thirty percent of your money and drop items from your inventory, and hardcore where you die permanently.  I have only tried normal difficulty, and in order to change it I have to start all over again.  It is not immediatly clear what you drop, because you do not drop weapons, seeds, or crafting stations, but you do drop food, permanent upgrade items, and building blocks.  I had the great privelege of finding out about the upgrades in a pool of lava.
On to controls and UI.  I did not seperate these two since they overlap so much.  The control scheme is irritating after switching from terraria's.  I think it might get better after alot of work, but that work remains to be done, and the game has been released.  I do not like that I cannot change the interact button to click, but I need to highlight whatever I am looking at with my mouse then press 'e' to interact.  add to this that when I interact it immediatly blocks my screen with the menu, and doesn't pause the game since it isn't designed for single player.
I like the idea of this game, but the implementation is lackluster.  for the reason's I have just outlined I cannot recommend this game.

After playing the first game I was a bit hesitant to get in to Sanctum 2.  While interesting and fun for a bit, Sanctum lacked a lot of depth and felt really rough around the edges.  The gameplay wasn't too smooth and sound/animations/models were pretty lackluster, and then after you found the best strategy there wasn't too much more to do.
Sanctum 2 has fixed every major problem that Sanctum had, and it has turned the series in to one of the more rewarding FPS experiences I've had in recent years.
My favorite character uses the Rex; it's a Doom-style missile launcher that does pretty decent AoE damage and allows you to rocket jump.  Take this and combine it with the Battle Rifle and you've got a croud control unit that can hop around everywhere applying DoT damage to all of her enemies.  I typically play with a friend or two, so there will be an assassin (there are 3 you can choose from, each with their own unique special abilities) and/or another DPS (the soldier is good at this).  Coupled with the greatly improved shooting mechanics you're in for one hell of a ride when you pick up one of these characters and enter an arena.
The game is much more polished.  It's beautiful; models are great, animations are great, and sound is fantastic.  It runs well (though some maps seem to have some issues) and the wide variety of maps you can play ensures you'll always have another challenge around the corner.  Enemies attack you now so the FPS fighting is much more intense, and the towers this time around are much more interesting with.
Frankly, I don't think I can recommend this enough.  For the price you pay you're getting a great deal.

Did you ever watch the "McGrubber" sketch at Saturday Night Live? It's a parody of the '80s TV series "McGyver", which features a man who can basically disable any single bomb using the simpler things, like a rubber band or a paper clip.
This game carries the parody even further, mixing scenarios of many pop culture TV series, books, movies and games, with the most absurd solutions.
The game only needs you to click on something - up to three or four things, but mostly just one - to solve the scenario and save the day. If you clicked the correct thing then the bomb will be disabled; if not, then it will blow up and you'll lose the scenario.
However, most of the scenarios have their own logic, and you have to think out of the hat to choose the correct answer.
It's a fun game, but really short. Anyway it will make you laugh in more than one way.
It's totally worth the $0.99 price tag that it has right now in the summer sale, so if you can spare a dollar you should consider this among your options.

I think it's about time I write a review for what is probably my favourite game of all time.
Bastion is something that I view as the pinnacle of games as an art form. Not only does it have great art in many forms (music, aesthetic, the writing of the plot and the narration), but the main instrument of that art is still the gameplay. By this point, you probably already know the main "quirk" of the game: its narrator that comments your actions, sometimes important, sometimes trivial. However, Bastion goes beyond that. It's packed full of music that wouldn't shy away as a standalone album, visuals that would probably sell as paintings, and a story that warrants a book. And on top of that you have the action packed and surprisingly complex gameplay that serves both as a challenge and a tool to explore and reveal more of the game. The beatiful environment literally builds under your feet as  you walk. The story unravels through the narration of your actions. And the wondeful music supports it all.
If you love indie games and somehow never picked up Bastion do it. You will not regret it.

Bastion is a fun hidden gem within indie games. It's price is pretty low for games with an amazing art style, fun weapons to toy with and one hell of a new story that I have never experienced. Now I'm going to go over some fearures that make Bastion the game that it is.
Gameplay-7/10
It really is a Beat E'm Up with some RPG elements mixed within it and the chemistry was good. The main gripe I have with the gameplay is that it will get repetitive once you've tried out and upgraded every single weapon, but tearing through maggots and monster plants with a sniper musket was very satisfying to do. :)
Story-9/10
This game has something which modern games seem to forget from time to time: Originality. This game takes a No-Name Kid and puts him in a series of epic and sad events that were caused by "The Calamity" which caused the Earth to break into peices. The goal is to try and survive the calamity, find sanctuary and find away to fix this mess and I've got to say, this game makes me want a rusty-voiced narrator say the things I do.
Music-9-10/10
The music in this game is outstanding. However, I found it pretty overrated compared to games like Brave Frontier and Edge of Space. (To bad those two games are pretty bland :P) The music just fits in perfectly in a story where a boy is faced with unimaginable disasters.
Art Style-10/10
This game looks stunningly beautiful. The graphics are amazing, the colors fit so well and the look and beauty of this game can sometimes distract you from the situations you are in. However, the enemies and weapons look pretty bland and uninspired. This really sucks because this game is the kind where a colossal beast would suit it. I'm still in love with the look of this game.
In-game features-8/10
The weapons in this game are really standard in my opinion. You've got the fast weapon with weak damage, slow weapon with alot of damage and the moderate speed weapon with moderate damage, but upgrades do exist and make the weapons more flavorful and fun to use. (Musket Sniper FTW) Other features include a Forge, a Potion Station, etc.
This game has alot of creativity with potions and power-ups to use o gain an advantage in battle, but some are to OP like the Bastion Potion which restores ALL your health, but nevertheless, it's still fun.
Final Rating-8.7/10 (If any one of you wonder how I got this score, I just get the average of all of the categorizes scores)
If you're an indie gamer, RPG adorer or a guy who likes games with generally good stories, then this game is a MUST HAVE. With stunning visuals, awesome music and an epic story, Bastion is a game that is worth every penny and is DEFINITELY goin on mt Top 5 best indie games list. (In My Opinion) If I were you, get this game NOW!

Did you ever watch the "McGrubber" sketch at Saturday Night Live? It's a parody of the '80s TV series "McGyver", which features a man who can basically disable any single bomb using the simpler things, like a rubber band or a paper clip.
This game carries the parody even further, mixing scenarios of many pop culture TV series, books, movies and games, with the most absurd solutions.
The game only needs you to click on something - up to three or four things, but mostly just one - to solve the scenario and save the day. If you clicked the correct thing then the bomb will be disabled; if not, then it will blow up and you'll lose the scenario.
However, most of the scenarios have their own logic, and you have to think out of the hat to choose the correct answer.
It's a fun game, but really short. Anyway it will make you laugh in more than one way.
It's totally worth the $0.99 price tag that it has right now in the summer sale, so if you can spare a dollar you should consider this among your options.

Ah, the multi-player game developers' dilemma:
Making great games that should survive into classics but are played by awful people and fall into oblivion. And not the good kind of Oblivion either.

I just want to have a little fun in my waning years as I barrel at a slow crawl towards the long dirt nap; so you can read this review with a peck of salt is what I'm getting at here.
Something I have noticed in the past few years that is becoming all too common concerning multi-player genre:
The game content and mechanics are great and on-target - but the players who show up to play are simply horrible humen beings who would be stabbed to death in real life for behaving and speaking similarly as they do virtually.

Town of Salem is truly a fun game and I have to confess to some talent in winning games as a Godfather. The developers have done an excellent job in responding to glitches as well as adding variety and advice on strategy.

This is a very sick game, with some disturbing scenes and creepy atmosphere. Story follows an eleven years old girl whose parents get killed one night. During the night her parents get killed, you see some goat-like monster who tells you that he feeds on your pain and that he will drive you insane. After this you try to find your kitty, your bestfriend, but you pass away in woods, and you wake up in the insane asylum. In this asylum you find some red pills which are the core of the gameplay of this game. When you take these pills, your perspective of reality changes, and you see the dark world, filled with monsters. However, real monsters you will meet in real world, people who work in this asylum. So your goal in this game is to find your kitty, and to go back to your aunt. Ending of the game is kinda weird, and at first I didn't get it completely. I felt a bit disappointed, but after reading theories, it all made sense, and I realized how great is ending of this very intriguing game.
As for gameplay, there are many puzzles, and a lot of them are not that easy to solve, When you pick items, sometimes you can combine them to make new items, in order to solve puzzles. Those puzzles are pretty good imo. When you take pills, perspective of reality changes, like I said, so to solve puzzles sometimes you have to go to that another reality to get some items, or to do some actions there.
Game is locked at 30 fps, but it's Point&Click game, it's enough, and only thing technical-wise that is bad about this game, is that you can't use steam overlay's screenshot ability. You can post screenshots, and there is explanation on forum, but too much bother for me.

This game is lovely. The air of narration with a nudge to go against the grain of your instructions does really make me think back to the Stanley Parable. While I loved the Stanley Parable, I wouldn't really call it a game, it's more of a narrative experience, however ICEY shines in being an enjoyable and beautiful game too.
The visuals are great, the combat feels fluid and provides a surprising amount of unique attacks given the purposefully limited control scheme. I would generally consider myself averse to action games, platformers, and 2D games of that sort in general, and I have to say ICEY won me over.
Sound was good, music was nice, if a bit unremarkable to my ears.
What must be said however, is about the narration, don't play with the English narration. Don't do it. I'm surprised so few reviews mention it, but the original Chinese voicing is so much better. I started playing with the English narration and was like... Something feels really off. While this might have been intentional to make the players question the narrator, it lacks any real emotional impact and the game became a lot better when using subtitled dialogue.
Yes subtitles can distract, however I found the dialogue to mostly be delivered during pauses where I could way for it to play out, most of it's part of the "meta" component anway, rather than being tied to combat.

This may just be the best point-and-click adventure game I've ever played. The artwork is beautiful, the atmosphere is really creepy, the story is intriguing, and the characters are full of life. What more could you want from a game? Our titular protagonist, Fran Bow, is a disturbed young girl trying to escape a mental institution and find her way home. In order to do so, you have to navigate between the "real" world and her own terrifying psychological landscapes. However, despite all the horrors she experiences, Fran never once loses her childlike sense of wonder and curiosity about the world(s) she inhabits. In this way, the story can be compared to a darker Alice in Wonderland, and indeed, there are actually explicit references if you catch them (if you look around, you'll find there's a picture of Alice and Fran as childhood friends, which was a nice touch I thought.)
I know many will take issue with the game's ambiguous ending and much of the ambiguity of the game as a whole. What is real? What isn't? What actually happened to Fran? What did she actually do? The creators took lots of risks with these narrative decisions and I applaud them for it. For me, it just made the overall experience all the more haunting.
Despite all the darkness in the story and Fran's grim circumstances, you still manage to find a sense of hope. As someone who has experienced severe depression and mental illness, this story really resonated with me. I'm amazed all of this was accomplished just by a two-person team! This indie dev team has my heart, and I'm sure they'll win yours too.

8.6/10 - A good platformer that is just right for younger kids.
Ok so it's no Rayman Ledgends, but it has got appeal to kids looking for a bright and fun platform game. Level progression is clear an concise, and boss fights are challenging and entertaining. You gain additional 'powers' as you progress, which gives oppertunity to adapt to the way you tackle puzzles.
The only gripe I have is with the levels are the bonus stages, in that it is a one-time deal. If you mess up, you do not get to try again (like Rayman) but instad you have to play the entire level until you find the hidden door again, at a later point. This can be especially infuriating for a 6 year old.
The music is lovely and fits well with the game. The sound effects as-a-whole are good, and not aggravating. There is a 'power' that utilises JUJU playing a set of bongos, which is quite fun, as it makes the enemies dance and the little one's seem to like this.
There is a small point to be made for the presence of 'a death'. Its not GTA style with WASTED written accross your screen, but when JUJU 'dies', it gestures toward that as fact. Typically for this type of game, the character would re-spawn to an earlier point immediately, but in JUJU, you fall off the screen, screaming with flailing arms, then the scary bat character appears on the screen, fade-to-black, then restart from a checkpoint. In local two-player mode, you turn into a bubble, and get to pop yourself out and carry on, which is alot nicer.
Overall, this is a good game. Challenging and rewarding in equal measures. I reccomend local co-op with your kids, especially if they are young, as there are a few points that encourage teamwork. I would say that this sits between ages 6-10, just purely on the content and ease of use.

I'm very impressed with Juju. The graphics are absolutely beautiful, full of vibrant colors. The scenery and gameplay mechanics remind me of elements of Candyland, Mousetrap, Giana Sisters, Toki Tori, and even older NES games. It's absolutely perfect for kids, but I was surprised to find that I enjoyed it as well.
Degree of difficulty builds gradually throughout the game, and controls are very basic. There's no need for a tutorial here, but players will find brief "hint bubbles" when new elements are introduced. Character abilities are obtained through normal gameplay, adding new dynamics to the game.
There are multiple worlds and areas with a lot of secret areas and hidden gems. Checkpoints are frequent, and death is in no way permanent, allowing for the player to restart from the last checkpoint. After multiple deaths, the player will also be given the option to play in easy mode if desired. There's absolutely no reason for rage fits with this game, yet there is enough of a challenge to entertain nearly any gamer with a fondness for platformers or casual games.
The controls are very responsive, and full controller support is provided with the game. While not noted in the game tags, there is also a co-op feature, allowing for a second player to join the game as a different character. Juju also sports challenging yet attainable achievements, which will appeal to gamers looking for their next 100% game.
There is definite replaybility here, as well. The hidden portals within each area work very much like a timed minigame, and finishing an area with a perfect score for all 3 portals, as well as finding all gems within the level, is a challenge for even seasoned adult gamers.
All in all, I've enjoyed it very much. While not complex, it's extremely well done and thoroughly enjoyable. It's very difficult to find a good platformer, because somewhere along the line, jumping, ducking, "easter egg" hunting, coin/gem collecting casual platformers went by the wayside to make room for the more convoluted "puzzle-platformers." If you're looking for a casual platformer, or if you long for the days of a straightforward platformer, you're going to want to give Juju a look.

Help Juju and his fellowship Peyo in their quest to save Juju's father Jambee and fight the evil bat. You'll need to restore the power of a magical key through 4 worlds of 24 levels, 9 boss levels and also 4 bonus levels. Each world features a different environment (
) and also a boss in two waves : the first give a power-up and the second the key part. You'll then unlock a total of 4 powers (
)
The game has 3 difficulties : Easy (yellow hearts) and medium (crystals) as well as the hard mode (golden mask) which is unlocked for each world after beating the bonus level. Juju is really close to Rayman and have also a few parts from Donkey Kong, Mario and Crash Bandicoot. In each level you'll get up to 3 coins (like the 3-star rating) for the amount of crystals you get at the end. At the beginning you'll need to find almost every crystal to get a 3-coin rating. Almost because at the end of every level is a wheel of fortune which will let rain some crystal from the sky.
During your first journey you'll be able to beat some foes by jumping on then or by passing through them with the rush ability. Depending on the difficulty you'll have more or less heart at the beginning of each level (2 hearts for medium and 1 for hard) but you can always get an additional heart when gathering a heart or hundred crystals. Also don't worry if you die, you'll always come back to the latest checkpoint undo-ing what you did after that point except if you succeed a portal event. In this game you have no lives, you can play as long as you wish restarting at the same checkpoint. If you die too much the game will ask if you wish to lower the difficulty.
Another great point of this game is the portal event, after reaching a level in world 1 you'll have 3 portals in every level. Portals are hidden, like Rayman you mostly need to approach some wall that hides a portal or sometimes you need to gather some crystal in a specific area to spawn the portal. During the event you'll need to gather every crystal in a limited amount of time (about 30 seconds or fewer) and not fall of the screen. If you succeed a golden coin will appears and you need to get it without falling of the screen too. If you fail, you can always retry the portal without restarting the whole level. All you need to do is to die before reaching the next checkpoint and try it again. Also when you finish or fail the portal event you'll know the rank of it. Meaning if it was the first portal of the level or the second one or the last one. This greatly help you to know if you missed one or if you're doing well. Finally you'll get up to 6 coins for every level which has portals.
As I said, at the end of each world you can get a bonus level which is harder than the normal levels but you only need to reach the exit and you don't unlock any coin for beating it. If you dare you can try to get all crystal but it can be really tedious.
To conclude about this game : that's a lovely and relaxing game very colorful. There are 4 different worlds and in each level you get new enemies, new traps, new platforming concepts and gameplay concepts. there are also 2 or 3 level in the dark where the crystals and some other stuff show you the way. And bosses and bonus stage as well as finding some portals are well challenging. The only bad point is that the portal event are the same ones after the first world but that's also good so you are less likely able to fail it.

Incredibely limiting and casual, don't expect a hardcore RTS like Starcraft/AoE/Warcraft, this game is more like Setlers.
The game makes villagers for you, you are only allowed to build a couple of builings and just one watchtower per portion of land, you can make very few soldiers, you can't speed up your production by making more town centers, etc. All of this decreases the skill gap and makes the gameplay casual. You have little freedom as a player because you are constantly curtailed by restrictions that slow down your progress. For example: Why the hell can't I build more than 2 houses per region when I have tonnes of resources? Why can I only put a handfull of villagers on woodcutting? These restrictions have been implemented to balance the game and make it more casual, but it will annoy the hardcore RTS player. Most gamers are casual gamers and that's why the majority of the reviews are positive (and also because of the cute music and nice art style).
There are also weird design flaws:
- if you have used your wood and have no woodcutting shed (because it was destroyed or you didn't make one) you can't simply send your villagers to cut wood. You actually have to tear down multiple of your buildings to get the required materials.
- if you want a villagers that has just mined stone to build a new structure in a new region YOU HAVE TO SEND HIM ALL THE WAY BACK TO THE TOWN CENTRE JUST SO CAN DROP HIS PICKAXE SO THAT HE CAN BUILD! This is also a problem if you, for example, want to villagers with axes to, for example, gather berries.
So, if you like a casual, non-competitive game that protects the noobs from good players by restricting the good players in their progression then you should buy this game. This is not a hardcore RTS.

This game is a great entry level game into fightin games. I never played much fighting games (just some mashing buttons in Tekken 2, SF2 and vanilla SF4) when I was younger, but when I heard this game was easier than the previous titles, I decided to try to get into the genre.
Single player content is somewhat lacking, so if you're into arcade modes and such, this game is not for you.
From a technical perspective, the game is hit and miss. The visuals and audio side of the game are excellent. Both English and Japanese voice acting are available and are of a high quality. The netcode has gained a lot of criticism, and for good reason. When playing against players with inferior internet connections, the laggy rollback matches are unbearable and terrible to go through.
A lot of content is behind a paywall, but you can earn a lot of in game currency by playing the game. The character roster is already quite extensive and is still slowly growing.
The style of the game favours aggression and rushdown. The game also puts a lot of emphasis on come back mechanics, so a lot of times you may feel robbed by the opponent. For me personally, only problem is the wildly different usefulness of these mechanics. Some characters' v-skill and v-trigger are universally useful whereas some are only situational or matchup specific. Some are even close to useless.
The game can be played with a controller, keyboard or fightstick. I personally started with an xbox360 pad and recently moved to a fightstick. Both seem perfectly good enough.
All in all, a great gateway title to get involved with a genre that typically is daunting to get into. The title has gained a lot of negativity, but I encourage anyone interested to give it a go.

This progression and unification of elements is consistently satisfying and results in a truly gestalt video game experience. It’s a short game, but carries no fluff or fat and accomplishes exactly what it sets out to. I picked this up while looking for something similar to the Rusty Lake games. I wanted an adventure game with puzzles and horrific elements, but no timed puzzles, no running from monsters, etc. I sort of got that - some of the mini games required that you escape from monsters, but they were all skippable (although if you want the achievements...). I was able to complete some of them and skipped the ones I couldn't.
The puzzles were pretty good and usually made sense. I liked how the pills and their effect on Fran were worked into the puzzle-solving. I occasionally consulted a walkthrough, mostly to figure out if I was even vaguely on the right track and looking in the right room/scene, but it never felt like any of the puzzles were unfairly difficult.
If you're sensitive to depictions of violence and gore (people, animals, and other things), this probably wouldn't be a good game to play. The screenshots on the store page barely scratch the surface - some of what's in the game is incredibly disturbing stuff, especially when Fran is under the influence of the pills. Although the game wasn't exactly scary (a few jump scares and gory images and that's it), I did occasionally find myself having to take a break because some of the things the game revealed had happened to the characters were so awful.
The story was compelling, but I'm still not sure how I feel about the ending. It
I kind of wish that the ending had been a little more clear-cut and unambiguous.
Pros:
+ Good and well-integrated puzzles.
+ Interesting story and characters. I liked Fran, even though she simultaneously creeped me out a little.
+ Creepy art style.
+ The mini games added a bit of variety to the game. And if you have terrible timing/reflexes like me, you can skip them if you'd like.
Cons:
- It was sometimes hard to figure out what you were supposed to do next and where you were supposed to be. A hint system of some sort might have been nice.
- Horrible things happened to Fran, and
- Not exactly a con, since it added to the game's disturbing feel, but it took me aback that solving puzzles occasionally involved doing horrible things, like killing a creature that was just minding its own business.

Man, if you need a game to prove that first impressions might be wrong this is the one to look for. I was quite frankly prejudiced about this game as I was expecting one of those casual-oriented, way too easy, "experiences" with cute visuals and the usual tear-jerking story.
Well... it's not.
Balthazar's Dream is a pretty tough and hardcore platform game composed by many rather short stages, each of which sees the introduction of a new kind of mechanic that gets usually added to the mix with those you already learned. The gameplay is fast and action-packed and you'll need to react quickly and use the environment to your advance, thankfully there are a lot of checkpoints to help you through your journey but they're not mandatory and can be avoided if you're looking for a tougher challenge.
The plot kicks off as these games usually do but you soon come to realize that, even if the story itself tries to be moving, it's just a tool to justify some pretty weird imaginary you find in the game.
The pixel art is wonderfully drawn in some stages and much less impressive in others but I think it's pretty good overall.

Balthazar's Dream is a good 2D platformer where you play as a Doggo trying to rescue your hooman from a dark creature. It's a quite fun and cute little platformer that can be challenging in some spots. It's an "avoid everything" type of platformer as touching anything bad will kill you, but there is quite a few checkpoints littered through out the game and you have infinite lives, so there is no penalty to dying... Unless you want that "No Deaths" achievement, in which I say GOOD LUCK!
The main BIG feature/mechanic in this game is the "Fear/Stamina" bar on the top of the screen. Certain enemies will emit a pulse that, when close to them, will drain this bar, and once fully drained, your doggo will quickly try to get away from it. (Think of a dog being scared of a vacuum.) You have to use this feature to give that extra speed boost to jump over certain sections of the game. It's a very interesting idea, though in some parts you have to time it almost perfectly to get it. There were some parts I got stuck on for awhile because I just could not time it and would have to try over and over... Though it's probably just me being very bad at the game.
You also get a few items at your disposal such as a ball, a stick, and a Frisbee. You would use these items to solve some puzzles, but mostly to progress in the game. The ball for example you would use to throw at cats to "defeat" them, or throw it in a hoop to active a switch. The stick is used by throwing it at a wall where it will stick to it and can be used as a platform. And the Frisbee... Well I actually didn't make it that far to get it.
My only REAL complaint is the lack of an options menu. You can't change any settings and because of this, the game is VERY loud! Otherwise I didn't really experiance and glitches or bugs or crashes.
PROS:
- You play as a Doggo.
- Platforming feels solid most times.
- Great Pixel art!
- Levels are quite good.
- Soundtrack is great.
- "No Deaths" run a real challenge!
- Achievements.
- Steam Trading Cards.
CONS:
- Lack of an Options menu.
- Sounds/Music is VERY loud because of no Options menu.
- Some deaths feel to be cheap.
- Will have to make "Blind" jumps in some parts.
- Not a lot in terms of "secrets."
- No collectibles.
- You can kind of "cheat" in the forest level by jumping to areas you are not supposed to. (I broke my checkpoints doing that.)
- No replay value, play through once and you're done.
Even though I never finished it (not the games fault, more less my fault for having a terrible attention span and get bored/distracted easily,) it's a great game and would recommend any time!

Usually, I split my reviews on Steam in two parts: In the first part I explain what I do like on the particular game and in the second one what I don't like. But this game isn't finished yet so the second part will be proposals and suggestions for
and how the game could be improved.
So, first, I really like
, it is a very unique real time strategy game. I think it could be described as a mixture of "The Settlers", "Anno", "Banished" and "Age of Empires". The game is unique, because it takes many ideas of existing games, but the feeling it creats is absolutly special. I don't know a single game that "feels" like
.
In the game, you play as the chief of a Viking clan, who have just landed on the 'Island of Northgard'. The setting of this island is quite particular: Nordic mythological island, crowded with monsters but also with the opportunity for a new settlement area and hidden treasures. The island is sectioned in many territories, the very most territories have some sort of speciality, like a forest for logging, a lake for fishing, fertile land for farms, hunting grounds, ancient ruins for trasures and knowledge and also dens and caves with brutal animals and monsters. The key is to conquer and settle these territories to use them for your clan, but this is not easy. You have to support your people with food, housing and don't forget to keep them happy! Enemies of your conquest are not only the monsters, but first of all the harsh climate and, last but not least, the other clans on the island. The game is about managing your ressources, defend your territories and try to expand as fast as possible - which is very often quite stressful but fun.
is much faster than "The Settlers" and much more violent but they have much in common, for example the ressource management. The game also reminds me of "Anno" because of the many territories you occupy for the materials you can find there - but in the case of
, these game is not playing on islands, it is a single island. And the different seasons and their impact on you food production and consumption is a little bit like in "Banished". But you can play the game quite aggressive if you like, that is why i see some connections to classical RTS games, like "Age of Empires".
This is what
is like for me, if you're interested in the game, please enjoy some gameplay videos on Youtube, they have confirmed my purchase decision.
At this point, I want to talk about the suggestions and proposals I would like to communicate to the developers.
All in all,
is a great game and I have absolutly enjoyed the time playing it. It is great the the developers are continuously improving and expanding the game. It is really not like in other early access games.
Thank you Shiro Games for this great RTS game!

Overall a decent, game that can casually entertain you for a few hours every so often. While it does have its problems, I think I'd still recommend this to others at the current price. I don't think I'd recommend this game if it were any more expensive. (It's currently $20)
The Good:
-Quick gameplay allows you to complete Civilization-type games in a single sitting
-Decent graphics
-Entertaining cross between Civilization and Age of Empires
-Enjoyable gameplay mechanics
-Variety of jobs for your villagers
-Difficult to build too large of an army due to increasing recruitment costs
The Bad:
-Almost no difference between each clan (there are 5 of them as of now)... the only difference between clans is that each clan has an extra starting tech/resources/abilities... other than that, there is absolutely no variety
-No unit variety... you've got a ranged unit, melee unit, and a defensive "soak up damage" unit
-Any damage to defensive towers sets them on fire, and they continue to burn until you find a villager to repair the damage and put out the fire
-Forgettable tech tree. They obviously do make a difference in your empire, but I wish there was a larger tech tree with more techs so you could obtain techs that fit your empire's future and immediate needs
The Ugly:
-Frustratingly difficult to find buildings in your empire after you've expanded
-Frustratingly difficult to find your troops in your empire. I wish the game allowed you to assign a hotkey to a group of soldiers so that you could respond to threats in a more timely manner. Pressing "E" will allow you to select EVERY troop in your empire which is okay for emergencies, but it's generally not a good idea to have your entire army in one area of your empire
-The game needs a military drag only option... when you DO find your troops, sometimes a villager is performing a task right next to them. If you highlight the villager too, then the villager will also go out and fight enemies
Recommend!

140 is a music-based platforming game. Heard something called that before? You may be ready to write this off already, but please read on:
In 140, every single object in the game relates to the soundtrack. Every single voice in the soundtrack has a corresponding physical manifestation in the game world. This tightly woven relationship is the core of 140, and what makes it so brilliant and euphoric to play.
Levels are split into layers or sections, and their progression reminds me a bit of Rez. The anticipation while one layer of the world peels away and another, more complex layer, is put on top. I love that transition!
The graphics are simple by design. They are often called "ugly", but I find the palettes were chosen with care and nothing grates. Your primary focus is on listening to the world and figuring out how to traverse it using the auditory hints.
If you love brutal/precision platforming, this is for you. If you love music and games that are based around music, this is for you. If you can't get past the graphics, this still is for you.

Imagine a world of only two dimensions: length and height. Color that world with neon shades, sharp geometric landscapes and bind it together with minimalistic tech-house music. A world of stark beauty and remarkable simplicity; the player exists as a transforming piece of geometry - a square, triangle and circle altogether.
The geography of this flatland is not inert though. Environments comes to life in synergy with the music - music that is dependent on the player's progress in each of the three vistas. Can't make that jump? Well, the backing-track is probably missing an instrument; escorting a mysterious, floating orb to a docking station will add it to the soundtrack. Obstacles that were previously laying stubbornly static will come to life, rhythmically shifting all the way.
Glide, jump, roll, and shoot - 140 is an auditory and visual delicacy.

If your idea of horror revolves around various animal parts stitched together wrong and eyes crying blood all the time, this is your game. Expect no tense psychological states, deep character development or plausibly meaningful interactions.
Given Fran Bow's overwhelmingly positive reviews, I am not quite sure what it is I actually expected. Sometimes I could glimpse some of its elusive genius but mostly it left a dull impression on me.
It started with a black screen that required manually patching the game. The developers are fully aware of this simple common issue but will not fix the game's default installation cleanly.
My main gripe with Fran Bow's narrative and gameplay is that it is built around strings of borrowed ideas that seemed forced together, rarely truly unique or gripping, such as outdated interpretations of mental illness and overdone gore, or the awkward combination of charming child-like discovery and complete darkness.
With dialogue options that rarely feel useful (basically carry on or prematurely end a conversation), multiple unintuitive puzzles (such as stuffing a toad with sodium bicarbonate as a means to cross a river), persistently clunky UI (some of the worst inventory management of the genre) and inconsistent navigation (particularly when moving to the next screen), most interactions are remarkably disappointing.
Its plot twists surprised me more than once, sometimes positively, leading to one of the most unusual stories in any adventure game.
Severely uneven, some of its chapters feel deliriously different. The vibe becomes so completely dissimilar by the 3rd chapter it almost fees like a whole other game. More charming, filled with life, with a better mechanic to alter the world by changing seasons. Yet the darkness never goes away.

It's... well... like... remember MacGyver? What if he was mildly ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥? And in a Warioware game? But it's also a point-and-click adventure game? It's silly, but not much fun, actually. 3/5 for the silliness alone.

Numerous "spells" to equip give you the chance to experiment and find what you like. Loads of 80's pop culture references are supported by catchy synth music and great pixel animation. Only 5 chapters is a bit of a bummer and the game may be slightly overpriced for its' length but arena mode, endless mode, and that tantalizing %100 completion give you a decent bang for your buck. I hope to see a sequel. A sequel with no stickers.
